Throw Away Your Mask
by MollyPollyKinz
Summary

Instead of dying, Akechi finds himself eight years in the past. With his persona abilities still
intact, he has to find a way to stop the end of the world.
And work with a bunch of teenagers who thinks he's a child.
Akechi would've preferred to stay dead.

“Ice cream, really?” Akechi asked as Kurusu thrust a cone in his hand.
“It’s the day before we steal Sae’s heart,” Kurusu said. “We’ve got to celebrate our near
victory.”
“Wouldn’t it make more sense to celebrate after we succeed?”
Kurusu shrugged and began to lick his ice cream. “Usually we do something more
extravagant.”
“I see.” Akechi stared at his ice cream, but he found he wasn’t very hungry.
“And besides, you’re leaving the team after this.” Kurusu lowered his cone and stared at the
sky. “Do you think… we’ll be able to do something like this again?”
Akechi almost didn’t respond. Any positive answer would be a lie.
Instead, he smiled and said, “Of course.”
Kurusu’s smile didn’t reach his eyes. “Of course,” he echoed softly.

Part 1: My Ghostly Shadow

Akechi never gave the afterlife much thought.
When his mother died, the few people that bothered to attend the funeral gave him halfhearted platitudes. Phrases such as “she’s in a better place now” or “she’s watching over you”
did little to comfort a child already bitter toward the world. It didn’t matter if she was happier
where she was. She was the one who abandoned him, who decided that he wasn’t worth
fighting the harsh battle of life.
Akechi didn’t have much time to dwell on it as he was moved from foster home to foster
home. He was more concerned with himself, with fighting tooth and nail to escape his
dooming situation.
When Akechi killed for the first time, he allowed himself to wonder about death. He
wondered if he had sentenced someone to heaven, hell, or nonexistence. He wondered what
words were exchanged between those who grieved for the person he killed.

After that brief moment of weakness, he pushed all such thoughts aside. The endless debate
of immortal souls didn’t matter. He had a plan, and he could not be distracted by such
thoughts. All that mattered was the people he killed were out of Shido’s way, furthering
Shido’s trust in Akechi, bringing Akechi ever closer to enacting his revenge.
In all truth, as Shido’s cognition of himself leveled his gun toward Akechi’s head, Akechi
expected that to be the end. One bullet and his existence would cease entirely. If not that, he
expected to end up in some form of hell as punishment for his very long list of sins.
Then, when he woke up in Maruki’s dystopian utopia of a reality, Akechi refused to think
about what would happen to him after Akira put things to rights. He’d vastly preferred
nonexistence over another one of manipulation and lies, but he was lying to himself when he
thought he was not afraid of what came after.
Akechi’s face pressed against the windows of the Morgana Helicopter Monstrosity. He could
barely see Akira leap back into the wreckage of Maruki’s palace to have a fist fight of all
things. He wondered what the hell was wrong with his rival as the walls of the palace
crumbled around them and Morgana’s helicopter choppers beat against the air–
Silence enveloped Akechi like a suffocating blanket.
Akechi lay completely still. His face was still uncomfortably pressed against a hard surface,
but it wasn’t a window. The surface was much smaller, and the sharp edges of it were surely
creating red marks on his cheek. Akechi could barely breath the hot, suffocating air, and
Akechi realized that the silence wasn’t a blanket at all. There was actually a blanket draped
over his head, soft and heavy and covering his entire body.
In the silence, a clocked ticked in the steady rhythm of counting the seconds.
Tic, tic, tic, tic…
Impatience suddenly seized Akechi. He would not allow death to be silent, still, or
suffocating, not if he had any say in it.
Akechi’s arms felt light and ungainly as he grabbed for the edge of the blanket. When he
finally brought his fingers around the fabric, his grasp felt much weaker, not to mention
smaller, than he expected. He yanked the blanket off of himself and sat up.
He blinked as his eyes adjusted to the darkness in his surroundings. A familiar painting of a
beach sat on the wall across from him. His chest tightened
It seemed Hell decided to take the shape of one of his old foster bedrooms.
Akechi tried his hardest to breathe.
Assess the situation. It would do no good to panic, especially if his old guardians were
sleeping in the room adjacent to his. Waking them up would only cause more difficulties than
what was worth.

Akechi inhaled sharply. The hard surface his face had previously been planted against was a
textbook. Akechi picked it up. It was heavier than he expected, but he focused on its contents.
Some of the printed text was in Latin letters, and Akechi could make out simple English
words and phrases.
Akechi recalled spending sleepless nights studying underneath the covers of his bed, not
wanting to be found out by his guardians. They didn’t take kindly to their sleep being
disturbed by Akechi’s mumbling or the bright light of his flashlight coming from the other
side of the door. And while Akechi made sure to complete all of his homework immediately
after classes were done, he took the time to study extra whenever he had the chance.
I have to prove those bastards wrong. He would think to himself, even at the young age of
eleven. I’ll show them all what I can become.
Akechi was always obsessive when it came to his goals. He was determined to reach the top
of his class, even if he sacrificed the notion of making friends or having any other hobbies.
Friends and hobbies were useless if he ended up in the gutter.
His studies, of course, had paid off, but he could already imagine Kurusu’s incessant prattling
about the importance of bonds and other similar crap.
“What’s the point of achievements if you don’t have anyone to share them with?” Kurusu
asked once on one of those lonely nights at the jazz club. He wore a confused expression, as
though he truly had no idea what hid behind Akechi’s motives.
Akechi was deeply preoccupied, seeing as he was going to disappear from existence in a few
days, but he didn’t think mentioning that would do Kurusu or himself any good. He also
didn’t mention that once Akechi knew he could get revenge on Shido, his own life was of
little consequence to him.
Akechi returned his attention to the textbook, closing it as silently as possible. While doing
so, Akechi realized why his entire body felt smaller and entirely too weak.
He was smaller. His hands were free of any scars and blemishes, and they were admittedly
thinner as well. His fingers were notably smaller, and as Akechi stretched his arms out, he
couldn’t reach nearly as far as he was used to.
It made sense. Hell took the form of his old foster home. Hell apparently made him take the
form of his ten-year-old self, who had lived in it.
Typical. Hell took him back to one of the worst times of his life, barely a year after his
mother had died. In hindsight, of course, Shido was far worse than some neglectful and
verbally abusive swine; his foster parents had never encouraged him to murder innocents. But
back then, when Akechi was ten and motherless, this was yet another taste of how vile and
disappointing the world could be.
Breathe, damnit.

A flashlight rested against Akechi’s legs, and Akechi recognized it as the one he used to
study with. Akechi picked it up and pressed the button awkwardly with his smaller hands. No
light emerged from the bulb. It must have run out of batteries. That, at least, explained why
Akechi had been asleep when he woke up. Akechi wasn’t prepared to steal batteries in the
middle of the night, not at the risk of being discovered. His younger self probably thought it
best to attempt to read the words on the page in the darkness and ended up falling asleep
instead.
Not that he thought he had actually time traveled. Although anything was possible after
everything Akechi had seen and experienced, it was far more likely that something else was
at play. Perhaps Akechi really was in the afterlife. Or, perhaps, he was in some version of the
metaverse, which took advantage of his deepest fears and insecurities.
If that were the case, Akechi best look for some sort of weapon to use against the shadows.
Although Akechi could still feel his personas’ power, tucked beneath the far recesses of his
mind, he wasn’t sure how much stamina this younger body had.
Akechi slid out of bed, and he struggled to gain his balance as his feet landed on the floor.
His legs were certainly much weaker than he was accustomed, which was to be expected.
Fortunately, this wasn’t technically his first time being in an altogether new body. He’d been
turned into a mouse plenty of times while running around in palaces.
Admittedly, this wasn’t remotely the same thing, but it was enough for Akechi to grit his
teeth and take a few experimental steps. He careened forward, and he grabbed the bed before
he fell flat on his face.
He glanced at the clock sitting on his nightstand. It was still ticking away as the minute hand
got closer and closer to reaching midnight. That gave Akechi plenty of time to rehearse and
prepare for the next morning, as long as he was quiet about it. With any luck, nobody would
notice anything was off at all about him.
Akechi still glanced around the room for any weapons, just in case this was a trick of the
metaverse. Unfortunately, at this point in his life, Akechi hadn’t quite reached the point of
carrying a knife illegally on his person, and he certainly didn’t have any toys that could
function as weapons in the cognitive world. The best he could hope to do was throw his
textbook at any shadows that tried to attack him, which, while an amusing thought, wouldn’t
be all that effective.
Akechi grabbed the dysfunctional flashlight. It felt good to have something in his hands, even
if that something was used for neither stabbing or shooting things.
For now, Akechi would just practice walking and–
The sudden silence was deafening.
Obviously, it hadn’t been loud before. As a matter of fact, the only sounds in the room had
been Akechi’s scrambling and the ticking of the clock. It hadn’t been overly difficult to tune
out said ticking, but it was easily the loudest noise in the room.

Now, it was gone.
It was probably paranoia that caused Akechi to react so strongly to the absence of a ticking
sound, but he spun around toward the clock anyway. It didn’t explode, although Akechi
wasn’t sure he expected it to in the first place. The seconds hand merely stayed perfectly on
top of the hour hand, which was centered on top of the twelve. The minute hand indicated
that it was a few minutes past twelve.
The clock broke suddenly. That was it.
Akechi cursed himself for his own skittishness, and he turned away from the thing. He was
ready to continue his own plans of walking practice, but a flash of green emerging from the
window caught his eye.
Akechi looked out the window, and he nearly let out an exclamation of surprise.
The sky was green.
That at least confirmed his theory about being in the metaverse. Or hell. Certainly not the real
world. Akechi walked up to his window, stumbling a few times, and he took a better look at
what was happening in the city outside.
In addition to the green sky, the city seemed to be filled to the brink with coffins. Either hell
liked to hammer home the fact that Akechi was dead, or the ruler of whoever’s palace he was
in considered everyone else in the world dead to them.
Akechi felt an uncomfortable nagging sensation. Was he in his own palace?
No. He still had his personas. Persona users couldn’t have palaces. Maruki was an exception,
not the rule. Besides, Akechi frequently checked his metanav to see if he had a palace that
could be exploited by either Shido or the Phantom Thieves. No such palace had ever existed.
So, he was in some other deprived soul’s heart. Probably one with some sort of childhood
trauma, if Akechi being his childhood self had any indication. This warranted far more
investigation, and Akechi couldn’t exactly proceed if he stayed huddled away in his bedroom.
It was a palace. His foster parents were likely not even in the apartment complex.
In spite of that possibility, Akechi crept out of his bedroom as quietly as he could manage. He
wasn’t as stealthy as he would like, but his past experience infiltrating palaces did not fail
him. He hated himself for being afraid of two adults who ultimately held no true power over
him–Akechi had the power to kill them at any time–but habits that used to protect him were
hard to kill even eight years later.
But, if all of the people out on the street were coffins…
Curiosity overwhelmed Akechi’s anxiety, and Akechi crept up to his foster parent’s bedroom
door. He wrapped his fingers carefully around the cold doorknob and slowly twisted it.
Cracking the door open slightly with a terrifyingly loud creak, Akechi peered inside the
room.

Two coffins sat on top of the queen-sized bed, and Akechi’s hand dropped to his side
immediately. That was one thing Akechi needn’t worry about.
Without another thought to stealth, Akechi ran to the kitchen and grabbed a large knife. It
would have to do as a weapon against shadows. After looking back outside the living room
window, Akechi hadn’t spotted any shadowy figures, but it was better to be safe than sorry.
Carefully handling his new weapon–Akechi did not need to accidentally cut himself due to
his newfound clumsiness–Akechi hurried down the stairs of his apartment. Although in the
past he might have just gone ahead and leapt out the window, Akechi did not trust this body
to obey the metaverse’s incorrect conception of how physics worked. If it turned out he
wasn’t already in the afterlife, he was not going to die by misjudging his own abilities. That
would be pathetic.
Akechi exited the apartment building and hid behind a nearby trashcan. He looked to his right
and left for any enemies. None came. The streets were emptier than Akechi had ever seen
them, and the deathly quiet was unsettling.
Even though there wasn’t a shadow in sight, Akechi still used stealth as he progressed
through the city. It was better to be safe than sorry. Akechi was in no state to be engaging in
combat on his own, even with Hereward.
Besides, if this was a palace-- and it almost certainly was-- there logically had to be a center
in which the ruler’s treasure resided. It was only a question of where. During most of his
conquests through palaces, it was unnecessary to make it all the way to the treasure. He’d get
deep enough through the palace security that the ruler’s shadow would come to investigate,
and Akechi would kill the shadow without a second thought.
Sometimes, however, Akechi was pressed to draw out the ruler in more creative ways. In
those cases, the easiest solution was always to head in the direction of the ruler’s treasure.
The ruler would almost always rush to defend it.
In palaces such as Niijima-san's, it was easy to ascertain that the treasure would be at the top
of the building. In other palaces, Akechi would speculate the location of the treasure based on
both the whispers of the shadows and the ruler’s own goals. In Okumura’s palace, it took no
time at all to discover that Okumura would be fighting the Phantom Thieves where his new
ship was being launched.
In this new palace, Akechi was at a distinct disadvantage. He did not know the ruler of this
palace. By extension, Akechi did not know the ruler’s distorted desires. To make matters
even more difficult, there was seemingly no center building that would serve as a stronghold
for the treasure. Even Kaneshiro’s palace, which was technically the entirety of Shibuya, had
its own floating bank.
Akechi glanced at the skies, but only the murky green crescent moon floated above him.
Very well. Akechi would just have to engage old-fashioned reasoning. He was a detective,
and while many of his “deductions” had been mere deception, he wasn’t incapable of logic.

Based on the scope of the palace, it was safe to assume that the ruler’s desires were extremely
distorted. Akechi had already explored multiple city blocks, and the shadows and coffins
were all the same. As Akechi wandered around more, it seemed that the distortion had no
intention of fading away, as it would with most palaces.
Akechi hated to think it, but this sizable distortion was almost at the same scale as Shido’s
sunken Japan.
Focus. The distortion seemed to center around some sort of death motif. Where citizens
should be, coffins stood instead. The sky was green, and a few puddles near the curb were a
blood red color.
Perhaps they think themself a vampire, Akechi thought derisively.
To organize his thoughts, Akechi tried to bring the possible keywords that the metanav would
designate to this palace. The entire city was likely the location… Iwatodai, if Akechi recalled
correctly. As for the distortion… tomb? Graveyard might be more fitting, or perhaps even
hell?
Akechi wished he could be absolutely certain that he wasn’t in his own palace. His desires
were certainly warped enough to require one. And from his appearance to his current
location, he was in his own personal form of hell.
Akechi once again dismissed the thought.
After perhaps another twenty minutes of sneaking around and trying to find more clues,
Akechi finally found what he was looking for.
It was distant and somewhat difficult to make out, but there was definitely a towering
structure on the horizon. The building seemed alarmingly massive, but Akechi didn’t allow
himself to be too perturbed. At any rate, that was the place to go to get more answers. The
shadows had likely all congregated there. It was certainly far away, but Akechi had been
conserving his strength. While his weak legs were getting sore, he was sure he could manage
at least as long as it took to find a safe room–
The city burst alive with a fit of noise. Cars honked and engines roared, and Akechi flinched
at the sudden appearance of people where coffins once stood. The sky returned to its original
black, the moon once again pearly white.
Akechi froze in place, trying to understand what had just happened. Had he accidentally
exited the palace? But he hadn’t even moved. Was it possible he hadn’t been in a palace at
all? But everything that just occurred reeked of the metaverse.
Akechi stood to his full height, refusing to be caught crouching behind a garbage can. His full
height was still at least a full head shorter than the rest of the adults that wandered past him,
which was proof that Akechi still was in the body of his ten-year-old self. His age hadn’t
been an effect of the metaverse.

This certainly left Akechi with fewer possibilities. This was the most bizarre afterlife Akechi
had ever heard of, or he had time traveled. If Akechi had time traveled, he reserved the right
to be royally pissed at whatever deity had decided to continue making Akechi’s life an utter
shit show.
Regardless, Akechi should operate assuming the worst case scenario. That is, Akechi really
had time traveled to when he was ten years old, and he no longer had the emancipation he
had so deeply valued in past years. It was one of the only things Shido had done that Akechi
had genuinely appreciated, even if his freedom had come with chains.
Akechi reached into his pocket to pull out his phone before he realized he had no such
device. No watch sat around his wrist either, which meant Akechi had no way of knowing
what time it was. The sky was still significantly dark. Akechi could assume it was deep into
the night, which gave him time to relocate his apartment building and return to his bedroom
hopefully undetected.
Akechi would have better luck sneaking around shadows.
Although it was years since Akechi had even lived in this city, he still remembered enough
from his past, as well as from his walk just now, to get back to the apartment building. After
climbing the stairs, he found the front door wide open from when he left earlier.
Clearly, the metaverse affected the real world in this case. It was deeply unsettling, but it
didn’t seem that any burglars had taken advantage of the opening.
Akechi carefully crept inside, closing the door behind him as carefully as possible. He would
have to return the knife to the kitchen as well, lest his guardians notice that it was missing.
Akechi was already an illegitimate child. He didn’t need ‘dangerous delinquent’ added to that
description.
Akechi’s footsteps were much louder than he would prefer, but these floorboards always had
an over tendency to creak. Grimacing at the noise, Akechi entered the kitchen and placed the
knife back into the knife block.
Muffled swearing and heavy footsteps echoed from down the hall. Akechi stiffened, but his
chances of making it back to his bedroom before he was discovered were impossible now.
Instead of wasting precious time, Akechi immediately began wracking his mind for a decent
excuse as to why he was wandering the apartment in the middle of the night.
Akechi began walking toward his bedroom as calmly as possible. He had barely taken two
steps out of the kitchen before his foster father, Fukui Katsuro, intercepted him.
His short black hair was matted around his pale face, which was pulled into a tight scowl. For
what he lacked in bulkiness, he made up for in height, and he easily towered over the still
rather short Akechi.
“What the hell do you think you’re doing?” he demanded. His eyes darted over to the kitchen
behind Akechi. “You brat, you were stealing, weren’t you?”

Years of working with Shido and his associates allowed Akechi to stay calm. He forced an
innocent expression on his face as he said, “I was doing nothing of the sort, Fukui-san. I was
merely using the restroom.”
Fukui narrowed his eyes. “You really expect me to believe such a crappy lie? I know how
brats like you are, acting all innocent and sad when you really want to strip us of everything
we own…”
Akechi tuned out the rest of his speech, trying to look appropriately ashamed for his
“misbehavior.” Eventually, Fukui would begin telling Akechi that he had made so much
racket that his wife, Yui, had woken up. Then, he’d tell Akechi that if he had found time to
sneak food from the kitchen in the middle of the night; he wouldn’t need breakfast the
following morning.
In the past, Akechi would zone out thinking of all the ways he would one day make vile
adults suffer for mistreating him. They mostly involved gaining a position of power and
creating laws that would prevent evil people from taking care of children ever again.
Akechi had been more idealistic back then. This time, he tried to remember where the
grocery store on the way to school was. He could grab some free samples for breakfast,
assuming he left early enough in the morning.
God, he was beginning to sound like Kitagawa.
Speaking of school, did Akechi remember where it was? He recalled having to take the metro
to get there, but he wasn’t sure if he remembered the way. He couldn’t exactly pull up the gps
on his phone either, seeing as he didn’t have one.
Why did he have to get sent back here of all places? Akechi had escaped the horrors of the
foster system, and now he would have to go through it all over again? At this rate, Akechi
would end up going back to Shido just to get out–
Akechi jolted back to reality at the sound of Fukui’s hand smacking against the wall. “Are
you even listening to me, you little–”
“I think,” Akechi interrupted, his frustration causing him to forget himself, “that if you’re so
concerned about Yui-san’s insomnia, you shouldn’t shout at me so loudly.”
The slap wasn’t unexpected. Akechi stumbled backwards at the force of it, narrowly avoiding
collapsing backwards onto the floor. He grabbed the nearby chair as an anchor point, catching
his breath as he tried to stay calm.
Fukui was just a man. A pathetic, disgusting whelp of a man who hurt children because that
was where he found the most power. Akechi could kill him in an instant. He wouldn’t even
need the metaverse.
“Don’t talk back to me!” Fukui shouted. “You’re lucky we’re kind enough to even take you
in! Brats like you should learn to be grateful for what you’re given, but if you think you’re
too good for us, I suppose you won’t need dinner tomorrow either…”

Akechi would be collecting some free samples on his way back from school as well, it
seemed.
Akechi was chewed out for approximately fifteen more minutes before Fukui sentenced him
back to his room.
“If I hear another peep out of you, there will be hell to pay.”
Akechi didn’t bother studying. He trusted himself to know basic elementary school material,
and, fortunately, at this time, he was already at the top of his class. There would be no risk of
Akechi arousing suspicion at suddenly knowing everything.
Instead, he crawled into bed and stared at the clock sitting on his night stand. His cheek still
stung slightly–for such a skinny man, Fukui was certainly strong–but Akechi managed to
ignore the pain well enough. It was the emotional trauma that was trying to crawl its way
back out of Akechi’s chest.
He couldn’t go through this again. He refused to go through this again.
But if this really was reality, if he really was trapped in the past, Akechi had few options. He
still had many years until he could emancipate, and Akechi wasn’t willing to wait that long.
Death was always an option, but it clearly didn’t stick as well as it was supposed to.
Besides, Akechi wasn’t sure he liked it all that much the first time. Akechi would save that as
a last resort.
What was his life coming to? Akechi sighed as he watched the second hand on his clock tick
mechanically onward. He should just try to get as much sleep as possible. Hopefully, it would
be as nightmare free as possible.
Wait a moment… hadn’t his clock broken? Hadn’t it been stuck on a minute past midnight?
Admittedly, that was in the metaverse, but Akechi would have assumed that the clock, like
the front door, had carried over into the real world as well.
Apparently not. The clock happily displayed that it was fifteen ‘til two, as though it didn’t
realize how much confusion it was giving Akechi.
Akechi rolled over and closed his eyes. He would worry about clocks and palaces and time
travel later. For now, he wanted to fall asleep and pretend that his life hadn’t gotten
insurmountably worse.

A piano melody floated around the corners of Akechi’s consciousness. It was followed by
someone singing, and Akechi’s entire soul swelled up with the music.
He opened his eyes.

He wasn’t lying in bed. Instead, he was sitting straight up in a chair. Another chair sat next to
his, but it was empty. A round table covered with a violet tablecloth stood in front of him.
Behind that table sat the strangest looking man Akechi had ever seen. His was clearly
ancient, but his nose was shaped like a crow’s beak. His round eyes stared at Akechi
piercingly, and Akechi returned the gaze.
“Welcome to the Velvet Room, my child,” the man said in a strange, high-pitched voice.
The Velvet Room seemed to be a giant elevator, but it was the fanciest elevator Akechi had
ever seen. For one, a large mechanical clock sat on the back wall, golden gears clicking
against each other as they turned. Violet-blue velvet curtains seemed to hang from every wall,
and the floor of the elevator itself was a rich blue color.
Akechi had no idea what the Velvet Room was, apart from the place he was currently sitting,
but anyone could tell that it had connections to the metaverse. It could even have the answers
as to what the hell he was going on with Akechi’s life.
It was also clear that whoever these people were, they were very powerful.
“Thank you for welcoming me,” Akechi said as pleasantly as possible. “I’m honored. But, if
I may ask some questions. Who are you? What is this place?”
“I am Igor. These are my attendants, Theodore and Elizabeth.” Igor gestured to the two
figures standing on both sides of him. Their blonde hair matched their yellow eyes, and their
blue attire mimicked those of old elevator operators. Their skin was the same light beige tone
as Igor’s, and the only true difference Akechi could discern between them was their
difference in gender. “However, Theodore will personally be attending to you.”
“It will be a pleasure working with you,” Theodore said. In spite of his overly polite tone, he
actually sounded genuine. There was no fakeness in the way he smiled, although Akechi did
not miss a certain sharpness in Theodore’s golden eyes. “I look forward to assisting my
master in your growth.”
“Are you shadows?” Akechi asked unthinkingly. “Pardon me for asking.”
“We are neither shadow nor human,” Igor said. “This place resides between dream and
reality, mind over matter. The sea of humanity’s subconscious surrounds us here. Please, do
not feel the need to hide your true face. I can see through any mask you may put on.”
That was certainly cryptic, but there was no way in hell Akechi was going to show his true
colors to Igor, no matter what he said. Regardless, this place was definitely connected to the
metaverse.
“What exactly is it that you do here?” Akechi asked, glancing around at his curtained
surroundings. He couldn’t imagine that these beings just sat around all day, but there were no
tools or furniture that indicated they did anything at all.
“This is a place where I assist guests in creating new personas,” Igor explained. “I fuse
personas to create more powerful assets to aid a guest on their journey.”

“Fuse personas?” Akechi’s polite tone lost some of its softer edges in his shock. “What is that
supposed to mean?”
“Personas are merely manifestations of humanity’s subconscious.” Igor gestured around
himself. “Each person has their own persona, unique to themselves. Consider it a mask used
to face life’s hardships. The sea of souls houses many broader such beings, less unique than
an individual persona. These creatures are what you know as shadows. However, those with
the power of the wildcard are able to take these shadows and turn them into personas of your
own.”
“That was Joker’s power,” Akechi said. Names had power, and in a place like the Velvet
Room, Akechi didn’t want to risk using Akira’s proper name. Besides, Akechi didn’t yet
know if Igor’s intentions were as benevolent as he made them sound. “Did you create, or
fuse, personas for him?”
Igor shook his head. “You speak of a time that has not yet come to pass. But your friend did,
or should I say will, possess the power of the wildcard.”
“You know what’s happened to me, then,” Akechi said, seizing onto this thread and refusing
to let go.
“I’m afraid I do not know for certain what has brought you here. My attendants and I merely
exist to help those along their separate journeys. That is what I have summoned you here
for.”
As if Akechi was going to trust that for a moment.
Akira hadn’t given all the details of what happened after Akechi’s death, but in his vague
summary of the world nearly ending, he did briefly mention that someone he trusted to help
him turned out to be the god of control. Could Igor be this entity? Or was it someone else
entirely?
“If you’re their master–” Akechi gestured to Theodore and Elizabeth “--does that mean you
have a master as well?”
Igor nodded, his smile not waning. “I am the servant of Philemon, the manifestation of all
that is good in humanity.”
Well, that gave Akechi a good measure on how much he could trust this Philemon, then.
Humanity was about as good as coffee was sweet, and Akechi could trust this Philemon, as
well as Igor, as far as he could throw them.
On the other hand, if Akechi wanted to figure out what brought him back to this time, it
might behoove him to try to get closer to Igor and his attendants. Stronger personas certainly
couldn’t hurt, especially if Akechi was to be expected to clear out such a large palace on his
own.
“What would be the terms of me becoming a guest here?” Akechi asked.

“This is a room that only those bound by a contract may enter,” Igor said. “You have already
signed the contract, although you don’t know it.”
Akechi frowned. He signed many contracts in his lifetime.
“What were the contract’s contents?” Akechi asked.
“You agreed to accept the full consequences of your actions, however those consequences
might unfold.”
Akechi would have remembered signing such a ridiculous contract. He definitely had done
nothing of the sort.
“I’m afraid you’re mistaken,” Akechi said. “I haven’t signed any such contract.”
“Not all contracts are made with pen and paper,” Igor said. “Those are just symbols,
humanity’s proof that such a contract has been made. True contracts are signed within
humanity’s hearts.”
Akechi nearly scoffed. “You mean to say that I signed a contract on my heart saying I would
accept full responsibility for my actions?”
“You have resolved to let your life be your own, and that you will face the hardships that
come with it.” Igor tilted his head. “Is that not the resolution you made to your friend?”
Akechi grit his teeth. Obviously, he hadn’t wanted to accept Maruki’s reality. That life was
built on lies and manipulation. Akechi would have control over his own choices, even if that
meant his own death.
Which was exactly what Igor just said. Maybe Akechi had mentally signed an unwritten
contract.
The concept was still ridiculous, but according to Igor, the deed was already done.
“Were there any other terms of this contract?” Akechi asked, hating to think what he had
inadvertently gotten himself into.
Igor raised his hand, and a clipboard appeared out of thin air. Igor placed it on the table in
front of Akechi. Akechi stared incredulously at its one paragraph. Underneath it, Akechi’s
signature sat on a dotted line.
“You worry about fine print, but I assure you, we hold you under no obligation than what is
written on this page.”
There was no way this was real. There had to be some kind of trick. “You grant me the power
of wielding an arsenal of personas, as long as I ‘accept the consequences of my actions’?”
“Our services are ultimately for your own benefit,” Igor said. “You may choose to use or
deny them as you wish, but we will never require you to take action against your will. Your
choices are yours and yours alone.”

“So it seems,” Akechi muttered, staring at the word consequences. If Igor could be believed,
they took free will quite seriously. Seriously enough that they weren’t going to intervene if
someone chose to do something stupid or dangerous. If all of their guests were like Akechi,
then there was a good reason for that.
“I’m sure you have many more questions,” Igor said. “And I understand your mistrust.
However, I hope, in time, we can come to have an excellent partnership.”
“I’d hardly call it a partnership if you're helping me and I’m doing nothing in return,” Akechi
said.
“On the contrary.” Igor clasped his hands together. “It’s always a joy to work with each and
every one of my guests. They always find new ways to surprise me.”

Akechi woke up to the sound of voices, which immediately put him on alarm. He lived alone.
There shouldn’t be anyone in his apartment, unless one of Shido’s goons had decided to pay
him a surprise visit. Even then, they usually had the wherewithal to ring the doorbell.
Akechi sat up, intending to investigate, but he once again found that his arms were much
smaller than they should’ve been.
That’s when he remembered.
It hadn’t been a dream, but Akechi wasn’t typically idealistic enough to hope for that anyway.
On top of that, Akechi had that strange Velvet Room dream. It was so bizarre that Akechi
couldn’t count it as anything but a very vivid dream, and yet…
It had seemed so real. But what sort of powerful beings would have a contract with virtually
no conditions at all? It was too ridiculous to even fathom.
Regardless, Akechi had bigger things to worry about than strange beings that fused personas
and lived in an elevator.
Akechi’s bedroom was much less sinister with the morning light filtering through the
windows, but it was still enough to make Akechi feel nauseous. The walls were painted a
light blue color, matching nicely with the painting of the sea shore that still sat on the wall
across his bed.

It looked like it came straight out of a magazine. Unlike Akechi’s life.
Akechi forced himself out of his reminiscing and reminded himself where he was. Unless he
was unlucky enough to find that today was a Sunday, it was fairly safe to assume that Akechi
had school. The morning was bright enough that Akechi assumed it was no longer winter, but
it hadn’t been particularly hot outside last night either. Akechi would play it safe and wear the
winter uniform. Worst case scenario, he would take off the outer coat if he looked too
strange.
Akechi found his uniform in his dresser drawers. He put it on with some difficulty–he still
wasn’t adjusted to his new body–and he found it was bigger than was strictly necessary.
Come to think of it, Akechi remembered that his school uniforms never quite fit. It would be
strategically sound, considering that Akechi would be growing anyhow, but the shirt fell
loose around his malnourished body.
Akechi gathered his books in the bag sitting in the corner and took it with him as he exited
the room. Naturally, the voices that had woken Akechi up were of his foster parents, who
were arguing about some mundane topic that Akechi could not care less about.
Fukui gave Akechi a glare as Akechi entered the kitchen. Akechi resisted the urge to roll his
eyes. Instead, he turned to Yui, who was sitting at the kitchen table. He bowed, forcing his
expression to remain unresentful.
“I apologize for keeping you awake last night, Fukui-san,” Akechi said. “It was not my
intention to make unnecessary noise.”
Fukui scoffed, and Yui merely nodded. Akechi rose back to his full height.
“Don’t expect that apology to get you any food,” Fukui said, his voice as bitter as always.
“Of course not,” Akechi said.
With that interaction out of the way, Akechi extracted himself from the apartment. Almost as
soon as he left the building, Akechi felt his entire body relax a bit. It was alarming to think
that Akechi was still instinctively afraid of two people who were ultimately insignificant in
the grand scheme of things. Was he really that much of a coward?
Well, it was hardly cowardly to be cautious. If Akechi wasn’t careful, he could ruin his life all
over again.
As per his plan, Akechi located a nearby Junes and grabbed a few free samples for his
breakfast. It wasn’t nearly enough food for a growing child, but it kept the biting hunger at
bay. As he exited the building, Akechi could spot a few other children in uniforms matching
his own heading in the same direction. Akechi followed them from a distance, relieved to
know he would be able to locate his school building.
Akechi could vaguely remember what his teacher looked like during this time, and he
miraculously found his classroom amidst the confusion of his memories. He recognized a girl
with dark pigtails as the girl who had always sat to his right. Sitting down at the desk next to

her, Akechi tried to reorient himself in this new learning environment. Although it had been
years, a small part of Akechi felt as though he had never left.
Nothing particularly of note happened during the school day. Everyone behaved as he
remembered them behaving, and Akechi was able to answer any question thrown his way
with ease. He spent most of his class time looking out the window nearest to his desk. It
wasn’t as though he needed to pay attention to the “new” material. Once, while his teacher
explained the concept of prime numbers, Akechi spotted a black butterfly land on the
windowsill. It only sat there for a few minutes, but it was enough time for the girl sitting
beside him to look at it too.
“Wow,” she whispered. “Pretty.”
“Yamamoto-kun,” his math teacher, Sato said. Akechi’s spine prickled slightly at the
sharpness in his voice. “Would you mind telling the class if 31 is a prime number?”
The girl, Yamamoto, sat straight up in her seat. Her medium brown skin paled, and Akechi
had half a mind to let her suffer the consequences of not paying attention.
Yamamoto glanced at Akechi pleadingly. Akechi bit back a sigh. He could sympathize with
the utter dread of not having an answer, especially under the gaze of harsh authority figures.
And it was partially his fault for looking at the butterfly to begin with. Keeping his
expression perfectly neutral, Akechi gave Yamamoto a barely noticeable nod.
“Um, yes?”
“And can you tell me why?”
“B-because it’s only multipliable by one and thirty-one?” At least, Yamamoto had been
paying attention to some of the lesson.
“Very good.” Sato continued on with the lesson, and Yamamoto shot a grateful smile in
Akechi’s direction. Akechi pretended he didn’t see it.
When lunchtime rolled around, Akechi was able to eat a proper meal. Even the school system
would be forced to take notice if his foster parents didn’t allow him to eat lunch with the rest
of the class. As he sat down at his desk with his newly acquired bowl of soup with a side of
rice, Yamamoto sat down next to him eagerly.
“Thanks for saving me earlier,” she said. She bounced slightly as she spoke. “I didn’t think
you would help me.”
“Don’t mention it,” Akechi said, forcing a smile. It was best that he kept up appearances in
the classroom too. He really hoped that Yamamoto would stop mentioning it and return to her
own friends, though. Akechi wasn’t particularly up to conversation.
No such luck. “I really thought you thought you were better than the rest of us,” Yamamoto
continued, “but then you helped me, so maybe I misjudged you? Sorry.”

Akechi really wanted her to shut up, but he couldn’t deny that there was a ringing of truth in
her words. Rumors spread quickly, and children had a habit of being just as nasty as the
adults that surrounded them. Since people took pleasure in talking about how Akechi was a
bastard child behind his back, Akechi decided to close himself off from his other classmates.
Once Akechi started getting good grades, he supposed that from a certain perspective, that
closed-offness could be perceived as arrogance.
“I understand the confusion,” Akechi said cheerfully. “I tend to keep to myself. No need for
you to apologize.”
Yamamoto gave Akechi a suspicious look. “You kind of sound like my sister when she wants
me to leave her alone but has to act nice in front of our dad,” she said. “Am I annoying you?”
Yes.
“Not at all!” Akechi tried to school his voice into something more genuine sounding. “I’m
just not good at talking to other people my age.”
“Oh, me neither!” Yamamoto fell silent as she began eating her lunch. Akechi breathed an
internal sigh of relief.
After school ended, Akechi slowly walked back to the Fukuis’ apartment. He returned to the
Junes to collect more free samples for his dinner, and he almost considered buying himself
something before realizing he had no money to speak of. He couldn’t get a job either, not
officially at least. And, at his young age, he’d doubt any adult was going to hire him as a
tutor or babysitter either.
Akechi grimaced inwardly. Without money, his situation only got more and more precarious.
And although, yes, technically Akechi had lived through all of this before, he only got out of
the situation with Shido’s assistance.
Akechi wasn’t going to be so foolish again. He’d find another way to escape. He just needed
more time to figure out how.
After eating as many free samples he could find without looking absolutely ridiculous,
Akechi stepped outside and began heading back to the apartment. He could lock himself in
his room to do his homework, and he wouldn’t leave for the rest of the day. The less contact
he had with Fukui the better, and it wasn’t as though they were going to feed him either.
Akechi hesitated. Maybe there was a nearby park where Akechi could do his homework…
but no, then Fukui would demand to know why Akechi arrived back home so late. He’d
accuse Akechi of trying to run away, and that was the last thing anyone needed.
Akechi was stepping back onto the sidewalk after crossing an intersection when something
large and heavy slammed into him. Akechi stumbled backwards and lost his balance. He
barely had time to throw his arm out underneath him to catch his fall. A burst of pain filled
Akechi’s arm, but not enough for it to be broken.

“Oh my god, I’m so sorry!” a deep voice of a man exclaimed as Akechi looked around to find
his attacker. “Are you alright?”
Akechi took a deep breath. He wasn’t being attacked. It was just some asshole not paying
attention. Akechi bit back a sharp remark as his eyes finally landed on the person who
bumped into him.
Kurusu Akira stared back at him, and Akechi’s heart nearly stopped. Kurusu’s glasses
covered his eyes, but Akechi would recognize his face anywhere. His chest burned and all of
the air felt as though they were being squeezed out of his lungs as he stared at Kurusu.
What was he doing there? Why did Kurusu look old when Akechi was stuck looking like a
toddler? What was going on?
Akechi’s thoughts raced a mile a minute as Kurusu’s eyebrows furrowed with concern. “I
must’ve hit you pretty hard, huh? Here, let me help you up.”
Kurusu held out a hand. Akechi grabbed it on instinct, and the man pulled him up to his feet.
“K-Kurusu?” Akechi said, feeling as though he had lost control of all of his wits. He tried to
pull himself back together, but Akira was there, looking as he always had been.
For a moment, for a brief, shining moment, Akechi wondered if he was in some nightmare of
a palace, and Kurusu had come to get him out.
That moment ended suddenly as Kurusu’s mouth twisted into a confused frown. “You know
me?”
An instant was all it took for Akechi to pull himself back together. He smoothed out his
expression and bowed. “My apologies. I must have mistaken you for someone else–”
“No, no, I am Kurusu.” Not-Akira shook his head. He pulled off his glasses, and–
He wasn’t Akira. His face was older than Akechi had realized in his initial shock. There were
lines beneath his eyes that Akira hadn’t quite begun to develop, and, most importantly of all,
Akira’s eyes weren’t yellow.
Akechi instantly went on guard. The only people Akechi had ever known to have yellow eyes
were shadows and the strange attendants in the Velvet Room. Admittedly, Akechi was aware
that a miniscule portion of the population was born with yellow irises, and this wasn’t a
bright yellow hue. Goro wouldn’t have seen it if it wasn’t for the sun hitting them. But
Akechi wasn’t in the habit of relying on the chance that this person wasn’t supernatural.
“My name is Kurusu Tsuyoshi,” Kurusu said, seemingly oblivious of Akechi’s shock. “It’s a
pleasure to make your acquaintance.”
He bowed, and Akechi bowed in turn. If Kurusu truly was a man, there was nothing to worry
about. Sure, it was a strange coincidence that he of all people would bump into Akechi, but
weirder things had happened.

Akechi never operated by the best-case scenario. Besides, there was something in Kurusu’s
expression, something sharp in the way he smiled.
His face reminded Akechi of Shido’s. The expression of a fox trying to ensnare its prey.
“What do you want, Kurusu-san?” Akechi asked calmly, just in case he was reading too much
into things.
Kurusu raised his eyebrows. “Me? Oh, nothing. I just thought I’d apologize for bumping into
you. I know wildcards such as yourself have enough to worry about as it is.”
Wildcards? Wasn’t that the ability Igor had mentioned?
“You don’t know anything about me,” Akechi snarled, dropping all pretense of politeness.
This man clearly knew more than he let on, and Akechi was beyond sick of being toyed with.
“Who are you?”
Kurusu’s grin widened. “Didn’t I just tell you? I’m Kurusu Tsuyoshi. Damn, kid. There’s no
hope for you if you can’t remember even that.”
Akechi grit his teeth. “I’m not a child–”
“You sure about that? You look like one to me.”
“And you look like a shadow–”
Kurusu tutted. “Close, but no dice.”
“If you interrupt me one more time, I will rip your heart out of your chest myself.”
Kurusu laughed. He sounded like a cartoon villain, and Akechi had half a mind to punch him
in the gut. The threat of going to prison was the only thing that stopped him. “You’re just as
fun as I hoped you’d be. I’m going to have a good time watching you.”
Akechi’s ears started ringing.
“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Fool Arcana…”
What. The. Hell.

Time seemed to stop as the words were spoken by a mysterious voice inside Akechi’s own
head. However, the moment was fleeting. As soon as the speech was done, the world returned
to its usual flurry of motion.
What the hell had just happened?
Akechi didn’t want to have a bond with this bastard. Akechi wanted to figure out what type
of monster this bastard was. Then, he wanted to kill him. Wherever that freaky voice had just
come from, it had poor taste.
“See you around,” Kurusu said, turning around and walking away.
Akechi was too furious to say anything else as Kurusu disappeared with the mass of other
people. He’d love nothing more than to scream every expletive he knew at the man, but he
still had some sort of public image he wanted to uphold.
Hopefully, Akechi would never see him again.
Somehow, Akechi didn’t think he’d be that lucky.
What had he meant by “just as fun as I hoped you’d be”? Was he responsible for Akechi's
time traveling? If he was, then he was far more powerful than any mere shadow. Or, was he
merely connected to the cause of his time traveling, and that’s why he knew enough about
Akechi to form expectations?
Why did he have to look so much like Joker? If he was a mere human with connections to the
metaverse, that would be a coincidence so extraordinary that it was hardly worth considering.
If Akechi was dealing with a creature that could shapeshift outside of the metaverse, how
powerful was this Kurusu Tsuyoshi? Could Akechi stand a chance against such a being in a
fight?
Regardless, there wasn’t much use contemplating in the middle of the sidewalk. Akechi
would try to gather more information tonight, if he could figure out a way to get back into the
metaverse. It surely couldn’t be that difficult, if he was able to do it accidentally the night
before.
As Akechi resumed walking to his apartment, he turned his thoughts to the strange poem that
he had heard. Was he developing auditory hallucinations? At this rate, it wasn’t impossible,
but Akechi found it unlikely. In a world of personas and metaverses, it was just as likely that
some supernatural element was at play.
Apart from the cause of the poem, there was also the contents of the poem that Akechi found
extremely bizarre. The first couple of lines about establishing a bond were self-explanatory
enough. Akechi had just made a brand new enemy, and a voice in his head thought it would
seal the deal.
It was the final three lines that were strange. A bond that would lead him closer to
redemption? His own redemption, or was it a more abstract concept than that? Could it be
humanity’s redemption?

And then there was the gibberish of being blessed when creating personas of the Fool arcana,
whatever that meant. One didn’t create personas. Personas were the manifestation of the inner
self. Sure, Joker would be able to turn shadows into personas of his own, but that had nothing
to do with making personas.
Well, there were times that Joker had personas seemingly out of nowhere. Akechi had always
assumed that Joker went into the metaverse without the Phantom Thieves, or maybe just
without Akechi, to get more powerful personas. Could it be that he was creating them
instead?
Could the Velvet Room really be real? Akechi had thought that entire encounter with Igor
and his two assistants had merely been a dream, but what if it wasn’t? Hadn’t Igor mentioned
that one of the services he offered was the fusion of personas? Was that the same thing as
creating personas? Not to mention, Kurusu mentioned the power of the wildcard, which Igor
had brought up as well.
No. This was ridiculous. Akechi speculating far too much for the sake of a random voice in
his own head. It could be nothing. It was probably nothing. A fluke. A hallucination. Not
some abstract concept of creating personas to further redemption. Akechi had bigger things to
worry about.
If he time traveled, which was growing more and more likely, something must have caused
Akechi to do so. He’d just have to find whatever deity had considered screwing with Akechi
was funny, kill them, and then go back to his own time. Hopefully without ruining the
timeline altogether.
And Akechi had a feeling that this Kurusu figure had answers.
The rest of the day proceeded without any notable incident. As Akechi planned, he locked
himself in his room and completed all of his homework without interruption. Seeing as he
was not invited to dinner, Akechi couldn’t think of any good reason to grace the Fukuis with
his presence during meal time. His foster parents didn’t ask it of him either, so both parties
were perfectly satisfied with the arrangement.
Well, the Fukuis were satisfied. Akechi had almost forgotten what it felt like to be truly
hungry again. Yet another sickening reminder of how much Shido had allowed him to escape.
The thought made Akechi want to shriek. He slammed one of his books shut instead. It
wasn’t nearly as satisfying.
In one day alone, Akechi had thought about all that Shido had done for him at least three
times. Akechi had the audacity to be grateful to the monster who put Akechi in this situation
to begin with. What the hell was wrong with him? At this rate, he was going to fall into the
exact same traps he had fallen in the first time around.
When Akechi had first made a deal with Shido at the ripe age of fifteen, he had been so
pleased with himself, so smug. He had managed to fool Shido into trusting him. His
deception was causing Shido to provide for the person who would be his doom.

It all felt so petty, so naive now. Back then, Akechi had been so confident in his ability to lie,
in his skill of hiding his true face.
Now, Akechi wasn’t even sure what his true face really was.
The homework was easily enough completed, and Akechi was left lying in bed. He
considered going to sleep, but he still needed to figure out how to get back into the
metaverse. Last time he had entered, it had been late at night. Once it got close to midnight,
Akechi would retrace his steps exactly and see if things played out similarly.
He simply had to wait.
Tic, tic, tic, tic…
After hours of waiting, the clock finally hit five till midnight. Akechi was pretty sure that it
was around this time he began walking around the room. He slid out of bed and tried
retracing his steps. He quietly paced next to his bed, staring at the clock.
Sure enough, at one minute after midnight, the clock stopped. The sky turned green and the
city became littered with coffins. Akechi vaguely recalled his clock being a minute off, so it
was more likely that this phenomenon was caused at midnight exactly.
Was it really a palace, then? Time had never mattered when it came to entering palaces.
Maybe this was a different type of palace. Maybe it was something else entirely.
Akechi tried to remember if anything similar to mental shutdowns had occurred while he
lived in Iwatodai, but nothing came to mind. It was quite possible that Akechi had been too
focused on his own life to worry about others. Still, one would think Akechi would have
taken notice if entire trains had been derailed as when Akechi was the one wreaking havoc.
Regardless, there was no time to waste. If time was a deciding factor in entering the palace,
time was almost certainly a deciding factor in exiting it as well. Last night, Akechi
remembered having only an hour before the world returned to normal. Akechi would only
have about thirty minutes to continue investigating. He didn’t want a repeat of last night, so
he would have to waste time returning to his room before his time ran out.
Akechi grabbed the knife from the kitchen and hurried back out onto the streets. He was
fairly confident that he wasn’t going to get attacked by shadows, but Akechi was never one
for being unprepared. This time, he didn’t bother to sneak around as he headed in the
direction of the giant tower in the middle of the coffin-filled city.
As Akechi got closer, though, he realized it would be impossible to make it on foot within the
hour, much less with enough time to get back to the apartment. After at least fifteen minutes
of careful running, the tower had barely gotten bigger on the horizon.
It was quite possible that the only possible way to get to the tower in time was to go to the
location of the distortion before entering the palace. Of course, this fact was obvious. It was
what Akechi and Joker’s little group had done every time they entered a palace as well.
Unfortunately, Akechi didn’t see how that was going to be an option.

He could always sneak out, but Akechi didn’t like his odds with that strategy. If he didn’t
return home at all for the night, the Fukuis would probably lock him in his room for the
entirety of the next day. And that plan would only be worth it if Akechi could figure out the
tower’s exact location–
“Hey, are you alright?!”
Akechi spun around mid-run, slightly losing balance as his shoes skidded against the
sidewalk. He adjusted his grip on his knife. He could jump whoever, or whatever, was
attacking him.
A teenager about Akechi’s age ran toward him, wearing a heavy red coat that looked more
suited for the winter than the spring. His expression seemed concerned as he quickened his
pace to close the distance between them.
Akechi didn’t trust him for a moment. He was in a palace. This was likely just a cognition, or
worse, a powerful shadow.
“Who the hell are you?!” Akechi snarled. His opponent was slowing to a jog. “I’d stop right
now if you know what’s good for you.”
The teen stopped, raising his arms in surrender. Akechi raised his knife slightly higher.
“Look, kid, I know this is scary–”
“Don’t you dare talk down to me.” Akechi had nearly forgotten for a moment that he wasn’t
eighteen years old anymore. To this enemy, Akechi wasn’t the same age as him. “I’ll rip you
to pieces if you say another word.”
His opponent fell silent, staring solemnly at Akechi. Akechi set his jaw and braced himself
for the inevitable attack.
None happened.
After a few more moments of awkward silent, Akechi decided that he might as well try to get
some answers. “Are you a shadow?”
“Do I look like a–”
“Yes or no.”
“No.”
“A cognition, then?” Akechi grinned bitterly. “A little far from home base, don’t you think?”
“What are you talking about?” The teen frowned, his brows furrowing. There didn’t seem to
be any deception in his tone, but Akechi knew he could be fooled. “I’m a human, like you.”
“Prove it.”
“I haven’t attacked you yet.”

“Not good enough.” Akechi tightened his grip on his knife.
The teen made a frustrated noise from the back of his throat. “Fine. I’m Aragaki Shinjiro. I’m
seventeen years old, and I have a penchant for getting into trouble.”
Most shadows didn’t have full names, and most cognitions didn’t have a habit of having such
a dynamic personality. Aragaki’s eyes weren’t yellow, so Akechi doubted he was the ruler of
the palace.
“Tell me something only you would know,” Akechi snapped. Cognitions didn’t have any
memories past the memories of the palace ruler. “Something you’ve never told anyone.”
“What’s that meant to accomplish?”
“I will not hesitate to obliterate you if I think you’re a threat.” Akechi’s threatening tone was
more effective when his voice wasn’t so small and squeaky, but it still got the point across.
“Fine, fine. I really like cooking.”
That was the most absurd thing Akechi had ever heard. That wasn’t a specific memory at all.
“Are you playing with me?”
“No.” Aragaki rolled his eyes. “I don’t tell anyone that. It’s embarrassing.”
“Cooking is embarrassing?” Akechi was so flabbergasted that he nearly lowered his knife.
He raised it slightly higher. How could anyone think that baking was embarrassing?
“I don’t know, man, okay? Look, what else do you want from me? My life story?”
Akechi bit back a sigh. Aragaki hadn’t attacked him yet, and he was wasting precious time
talking to him. Akechi would just have to believe that Aragaki wasn’t a shadow.
Akechi lowered his knife slightly. “Leave.”
Aragaki raised his eyebrows. “Are you kidding? I can’t leave a kid like you running around
the Dark Hour on their own.”
Dark Hour?
“No.” Akechi started walking back in the direction of his apartment. He’d find out more
about this dark hour on his own. “I don’t trust you. Leave.”
Aragaki followed him. Akechi snarled.
“What part of leave do you not understand?”
“The part where leaving you involves your untimely death. The Dark Hour is dangerous,” the
stranger said. “I’m following at a distance and have no ranged weapons–”

Clearly, the Dark Hour was what Aragaki called the metaverse. Clearly, this palace had some
connection to time. That would make sense, seeing as Akechi could only enter it at midnight.
“Why do you even care?” Akechi looked over his shoulder at Aragaki, who looked more
irritated than concerned. “You look like you have better things to do.”
“Maybe.”
“Then, why are you still following me?”
“Call it a moral duty.”
“That’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever heard.”
Aragaki shrugged, his hands shoved inside his pockets. Akechi rolled his eyes at his apparent
apathy. For someone who looked like he didn’t give a damn about what happened to the
world, he certainly was persistent.
“If you’re going to follow me, walk alongside me,” Akechi snapped. “I’d rather be able to see
you try to kill me.”
“Alright.”
The footsteps quickened in pace, and Aragaki began walking alongside him. Akechi took a
few steps to the side to keep a safe amount of distance between them.
Aragaki glanced at him with an awkward scowl. “You never gave me your name.”
“I know.”
Aragaki snorted, and his lips quirked up in something that might be called a smile. At least
Akechi wasn’t dealing with one of those condescending, overly concerned types. “Fair
enough.”

“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Moon Arcana…”

Again?
Aragaki was giving no indication he heard the voice, or the dramatic music that came with it.
Akechi did his best not to show his surprise. Whatever was going on, Akechi wasn’t about to
broadcast that he was hearing voices to anyone, and certainly not to strangers.
Once Akechi reached his apartment, blessedly before he exited the palace, or Dark Hour,
Aragaki stopped following him. Clearly, he was satisfied that Akechi wasn’t going to get hurt
in the place he lived.
How naive of him.

Akechi mostly kept to himself the following day, staying up to enter the metaverse at
midnight. He didn’t encounter Aragaki again, which meant that the teen hadn’t been
concerned enough to wait for Akechi to emerge from his apartment.
Akechi was grateful for the lack of interference, but a part of him wished he could become
more acquainted with Aragaki to get information out of him. While Akechi didn’t know
Aragaki well enough to trust any answers he’d provide if Akechi asked flat out, anyone was
capable of letting information slip in a casual conversation.
The next day was Showa day, which meant school was out. It also meant that the office Fukui
worked at was closed for the day. Yui had decided that a day off from school was the perfect
time to make Akechi clean the entire apartment complex. Fukui and his wife watched
ridiculous sitcoms while Akechi scrubbed the kitchen floor, cleaned the bathroom, dusted
every surface, and took all of the laundry to the dry cleaners. It was rigorous work to do all at
once. Paired with Akechi’s utter lack of sleep the past few days, Akechi nearly passed out
multiple times.
By the time Akechi collapsed onto his bed, his eyes were closing without any of his consent.
He was beyond fatigued. Maybe it would be best to take the night off and continue
investigating tomorrow.
And what would he accomplish? Akechi knew that the only way he could make any more
progress was to get to the center of the distortion by arriving at the location before midnight.
Such a task was impossible with Akechi’s current situation, even if Akechi knew the realworld equivalent of that strange tower.
Akechi’s best option was to try to find Aragaki again. But the city was big enough that there
was no guarantee that Akechi could find him within the hour.
Akechi did know he would hate himself if he took a day off, only to find out that Aragaki had
been nearby that night.
Akechi reluctantly stayed awake, completing what little of his homework he hadn’t done
during his chore-filled day.

Once Akechi entered the Dark Hour, he crept out of the house as he always did. He
immediately retraced his steps to where he ran into Aragaki the first time. As Akechi
expected, Aragaki was nowhere in sight. It would have been too much to hope that Aragaki
retraced his steps every single night. For all Akechi knew, Aragaki was sleeping in the safety
of his own home.
From that point, there was nothing left for Akechi to do but wander around aimlessly. Any
shadows had yet to reveal themselves in the city streets, so Akechi walked with relative
confidence.
He had the good luck to spot Aragaki sitting on the steps of Iwatodai Station. His expression
was sullen, but the short amount of time Akechi had spent with Aragaki indicated that
Aragaki was always in an irritated mood.
As Akechi approached him, Aragaki tensed, and his eyes hardened. His expression morphed
into one of surprise when he recognized Akechi; his body relaxed.
“Oh. It’s you.”
“You’re just going to keep sitting there?” Akechi demanded.
Aragaki raised his eyebrows. “I don’t feel like standing up.”
“You’re vulnerable. I could slit your throat.”
“I have something better than your knife,” Aragaki said. “You can’t intimidate me, even if
you're hell bent on it.”
Something better than a knife? Akechi couldn’t see any weapons on Aragaki, but that coat of
his could easily conceal a firearm.
“You have a gun?” Akechi demanded.
“Woah, relax. I don’t have a gun. What are you even still doing out here? Don’t you know it’s
dangerous?”
“There’s not a shadow in sight,” Akechi said shortly. “And besides, I have my own means of
defending myself.”
Aragaki snorted. “A knife?” he asked, eyeing the blade in Akechi’s hand.
“No,” Akechi said. Although Akechi didn’t intend to tell Aragaki about Hereward, Aragaki
would be less likely to doubt his abilities if he thought Akechi had more than a mere knife in
his arsenal.
“A gun?”
Akechi supposed he deserved that. “Where would someone my age get a gun?”
Aragaki hesitated a moment before saying, “A persona?”

Akechi wasn’t sure why he was surprised by that statement. Aragaki wandered the metaverse.
It made sense that he would know about personas.
“Is that what you have?” Akechi asked, instead of answering. Perhaps he should have played
dumb, but Akechi didn’t take Aragaki as one who would buy his crap.
“So, you do have one,” Aragaki said, looking bored.
“Look, I’m not here to waste time,” Akechi said. “Tell me what I want to know.”
“Are you with SEES?”
Aragaki did not perceive Akechi as a threat at all. Frustration overwhelmed him, but Akechi
grit his teeth and did not slit Aragaki’s throat. Aragaki hadn’t done anything to warrant such a
reaction. It was better to be underestimated than overestimated anyway.
“I don’t know what the hell you’re talking about,” Akechi said. “Are you going to answer my
questions, or are you going to be asking me questions?”
“I’ll answer your questions once you ask them.” Aragaki raised his eyebrows. “If you’re not
with SEES, how do you have an evoker?”
Akechi supposed that this was one way of gathering information, even if it was an
infuriatingly roundabout method of doing so.
“What’s an evoker?”
Now, Aragaki looked genuinely surprised. “You don’t have an evoker? How do you control
your persona?”
“Is it possible to not have control over your persona?” Akechi asked, trying not to feel
unnerved at the thought. Sure, sometimes personas didn’t come out when you wanted them
to, but Akechi couldn’t imagine them acting outside of his orders.
Aragaki’s expression shifted to something that could only be called self-loathing. “Yes. It is.”
Akechi was not in the mood to unpack whatever the hell that was. “I don’t use an evoker,
whatever that is.”
“So, you do have a persona.”
“Yes, I guess I do.”
“How do you summon it?”
Akechi glared. Aragaki wasn’t going to learn everything about him that easily. “I don’t see
how that’s relevant.” Akechi pointed his knife at Aragaki’s neck. If he wasted any more time,
he wouldn’t be able to get back to the apartment before the dark hour ended. “My turn to ask
questions. What the hell is the Dark Hour?”

Aragaki glanced between the knife and Akechi’s face, but his expression wasn’t particularly
afraid. “This is the Dark Hour.”
Akechi rolled his eyes. “Really? I had no idea.”
“That’s not what I meant. I mean that we’re currently in it. It’s a hidden hour of the day, or
something. It starts at midnight and ends an hour later. The sky turns green, everyone turns
into coffins, water turns red, etcetera.”
“And people don’t notice that they’ve blacked out from midnight to one?” Akechi asked. “Do
you take me for a fool?”
Aragaki shook his head. “When I say hidden, I mean hidden. It’s an extra hour of the day.
Time basically stops. Electronics don’t work, either, so that’s why clocks don’t keep going.”
So this was the real world? Not the metaverse? Or, in a sense, was the dark hour its own form
of the metaverse? None of this made any sense.
“So, we’re not in a palace?” Akechi asked.
“I mean, I know Tartarus kind of looks like a castle, but I wouldn’t call it a palace,” Aragaki
said. He clearly had no clue what Akechi was talking about.
“What about items outside of electronics?” Akechi asked. “Do they stop working as well?
Does time stop entirely?”
Aragaki shrugged. “I guess you’ll have to do your own experiments. Hell if I know.”
Akechi’s brows furrowed as he thought. Obviously, they could move around, and they could
move other things. Additionally, gravity worked on them. Maybe time didn’t come to a
complete stop, but that only gave Akechi a whole host of additional questions.
Aragaki was right. Akechi would be experimenting with this later.
“Is Tartarus the tower in the distance?” Akechi asked. “Are there shadows there?”
“How do you know about shadows if you don’t know where they congregate?” Aragaki
demanded, narrowing his eyes. “How do you have a persona without an evoker?”
“I don’t owe you answers.”
Aragaki rested his head against the brick wall, staring up at the green moon. “No. Guess you
don’t. But unless you plan on actually killing me, you might as well lower that knife. Give
your arm a break.”
Akechi hesitated before lowering his knife. Aragaki wasn’t likely to kill him, especially since
Akechi couldn’t see any evokers around anywhere.
Not that Akechi knew what those were.

“What are evokers?” Akechi asked.
“They’re guns.”
“They’re what?”
Aragaki shrugged. Akechi pointed his knife back toward Aragaki’s throat. “Where is it?”
“Where is what?” Aragaki asked.
“Your goddamn gun.”
“Oh, I don’t have one,” Aragaki said. His expression shifted into something unreadable. “Not
anymore. Besides, it didn’t shoot bullets. You can calm down.”
“You clearly have no conception of the metaverse if you think even model guns don’t shoot
bullets,” Akechi hissed.
“The metaverse?”
Akechi wasn’t in the mood to explain things to someone who thought guns were harmless.
“Forget it,” Akechi snapped.
“How many times do I have to say it? I don’t have one. I’m not going to shoot you or
anything.”
Akechi could trust Aragaki as far as he could throw him, but even if he had a gun, Aragaki
could have reached for it at any time.
Akechi slowly lowered his knife. Aragaki didn’t reach into his coat.
Akechi’s heart rate slowed.
They stared at each other for a moment, and Akechi realized how eerily quiet the Dark Hour
was. No cars. No wind. Just Akechi’s heavy breathing and Aragaki’s bored stare.
“How do you summon a persona with a gun?” Akechi asked once he was satisfied Aragaki
wasn’t going to shoot him.
“You don’t want to know.”
“You don’t know me.”
“No, but I do know you won’t like my answer. I do prefer my throat unslit, you know.”
Akechi glowered. “Is that meant to be a joke?”
Aragaki sighed heavily. “Look, if you want to know more about Tartarus, I’m not the one you
should go to. You’d be better off with a guy I know, Akihiko.”

“I threaten your life and now you want to help me?” Akechi asked incredulously. “What
happened to me being too young to walk around during the Dark Hour?”
“I can’t stop you. Might as well make sure you get some allies to have your back.”
“I don’t do allies.”
“Figured.” Aragaki sat up and rolled his shoulders. “Well, if you change your mind, you can
find him at Tatsumi Memorial Hospital on Sunday. His name is Sanada Akihiko.”
“The hospital?”
“He had a rough fight with a shadow recently. Broke some ribs, the idiot. He’s getting a
checkup.”
“He really seems like the sort of person I want to trust with my life,” Akechi said
sarcastically.
Aragaki’s expression hardened. “Trust me. You do.”
Akechi didn’t have a good response for that. Because, for a terrifying moment, that
expression reminded Akechi starkly of Akira.
Moon Arcana: Rank 2
