Yamamoto found him at the library after school.
For the next few days after that second encounter with Aragaki, Akechi took it upon himself
to learn what the hell arcana even were. A few trips to the school library allowed him to
quickly discover that they correlated with tarot cards and the twenty-two major arcana.
Akechi was reading yet another chapter on what the Fool Arcana meant–his encounter with
the entity otherwise known as Kurusu still deeply unsettled him–when Yamamoto sat down
across from him.
“Are you working on homework?” she asked. It was a fair assumption, since it was directly
after school.
“Of a sort,” Akechi said lightly. Yamamoto took it upon herself to speak more and more often
to Akechi. Occasionally, it was to ask questions about the homework. Other times, she asked
questions about Akechi.
Akechi was always vague with his answers.
Yamamoto didn’t say anything, and Akechi was able to focus on the paragraph he was
reading.
The Fool can represent the beginning or the end of a journey, particularly of an individual's
life.
Well, that was spectacularly vague. Most other sources agreed on what the Fool Arcana
represented, but it never got Akechi any closer to figuring out who the hell Kurusu was. And

nothing spoke of voices that declared bonds were being formed or ranked either.
Maybe Akechi really was losing it.
“I was thinking,” Yamamoto said. Akechi had almost forgotten she was there. “We’ve been
talking for a while, right?”
Akechi didn’t recall ever speaking to Yamamoto before he found himself in this time
approximately five days ago. He would hardly call five days a while.
“We’ve spoken for a bit,” Akechi said, trying to be polite about it.
“Yeah!” Yamamoto’s voice was cheerful, as though that was exactly what she had met.
Strangely enough, she reminded Akechi distinctly of Takamaki. “So, in a way, we’re friends,
right?”
Akechi blinked down at the page he was still staring at. Never, in his entire schooling career,
had anyone so eagerly asked for his friendship. Even Akira had looked annoyed when Akechi
offered that they continue their conversations on that first day in the TV station. Although, in
hindsight, that annoyance may have come from Akechi insulting his precious sense of justice
Akechi would prefer to get through his time travel situation without “friends” to hinder him.
But, if he said no, Yamamoto would probably turn around and gossip about him being stuck
up. While that wasn’t the worst fate, Akechi didn’t need to make his life harder than it
already was.
Besides, it wasn’t as though she was complimenting Akechi’s stellar personality. Even if she
liked his overly polite facade, she was likely just hoping that Akechi would help her with her
studies more.
“Of course, Yamamoto-kun,” Akechi said. “I’d consider us friends.”
Yamamoto beamed, as though she had never heard those words before. “Really? Wow, thank
you!”
Akechi wasn’t exactly sure where he was meant to take the conversation from there, but her
gratitude confirmed that she was only hoping to get better grades out of this acquaintance.

“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Strength Arcana…”

Yamamoto launched into a description of all the things they could do together now that they
were friends, including but not limited to walking to school together, going to the park,
playing games, and hanging out at each other’s houses. Yamamoto clearly had no proper
conception of Akechi’s current situation if she thought that she would ever be allowed to
come over to Akechi’s home, or vice versa.
While Yamamoto chattered, Akechi began flipping the pages of the book he was reading until
he found the section on the Strength Arcana.
The Strength Arcana represents taking control of one’s inner emotions in order to face life’s
trials–
“Are you even listening to me?”
Akechi smiled pleasantly and looked up from his book. “Of course. Something about your
cat?”
“Yeah! His name is Momo. You should come over to see him.”
At least it wasn’t a dog. Akechi couldn’t stand dogs. They were overenergetic and had a habit
of jumping up and down all over Akechi’s nice clothing. Cats were more than capable of
taking care of themselves, and didn’t give a shit about the humans that fed them.
“He sounds like a very nice companion,” Akechi said, although he knew virtually nothing
about the creature. “Maybe I’ll meet him one day.”
“So, you’re not going to my house today?”
Akechi stood up and gave Yamamoto an apologetic bow. “I’m very sorry, Yamamoto-kun,
but I’m afraid my guardians will not allow me to stay away after school for long. Maybe
another time.”
Akechi waited for Yamamoto’s face to morph into one of understanding when she realized
who she was dealing with. When she remembered that she was speaking to a bastard child, an
orphan, who had been abandoned by anyone who could have possibly cared about him.
Sure enough, Yamamoto frowned. “Oh, that’s too bad,” she said. “I guess we’ll just have to
hang out at school, then.”
Yamamoto was annoying. She was too talkative, oblivious, not thinking before butting into
Akechi’s personal space. She decided that Akechi was her friend because Akechi had done
one charitable thing for her, a decision that was beyond ridiculous.

Therefore, Akechi had no damn idea as to why his entire body relaxed at her lack of
rejection.
Craving attention to the end, Akechi thought to himself bitterly as he bid Yamamoto farewell.

“Where the hell do you think you’re going?” Fukui asked as Akechi made to leave the house
that Sunday. “We didn’t give you permission to go out on your own whenever the hell you
want.”
Akechi bristled inwardly, but his expression was calm when he turned toward Fukui. His
foster father was standing over Akechi with his arms crossed, as though he enjoyed lording
over those weaker than him. He probably did.
“I’m sorry, Fukui-san. I was just going out to get the groceries. I noticed that we were
especially low on eggs.”
Fukui narrowed his eyes, but he grunted. “Fine then. Next time, remember to ask. Do you
even have the money to pay for groceries?”
Akechi widened his eyes innocently. “Oh, I forgot. I’m sorry. I guess I won’t be going out
today–”
“No, you are.” Fukui went to his room before returning with a wad of yen. “I expect you to
return all the change to me, got that? I want to see the receipt too. I don’t trust you not to be
spending all of my money on useless shit.”
“Of course, Fukui-san. Thank you very much.”
Akechi bowed before stepping out of the house as quickly as possible. He shoved the yen
into his pocket, cursing Fukui’s paranoia. Although he had checked the fridge just in case he
needed an alibi, he hadn’t actually planned on going to the grocery store. He would have to
extend his trip.
It didn’t take long to get to Tatsumi Memorial hospital. Hopefully Sanada was still there for
his checkup. It would be embarrassing to get the time wrong.
After managing to convince the receptionist that he was indeed a friend of Sanada Akihiko,
Akechi located his room with relative ease. He opened the door to find a fair-skinned boy
with silver hair sitting on a hospital bed, punching the air.
“I thought you had broken ribs?”
Sanada froze, staring at Akechi warily. “Who are you?”
“I’m an acquaintance of your friend, Aragaki-san.”
Sanada’s hands fell to his sides. His eyes went wide. “You know Shinji?”

Shinji? They must be quite close to use such informal nicknames.
“We met a few nights ago,” Akechi said. “Aragaki said that if I had questions about the tower
that appears during the dark hour, you were the one to ask.”
Sanada glanced down at his lap. “He really said that, huh?”
“He also said you were quite reliable,” Akechi added, choosing to butter him up. “He clearly
trusts you quite a bit.”
Sanada gave Akechi a strange look. “You sure sound mature for your age.”
“I get that a lot.” Akechi closed the door behind him. He doubted Sanada would be much of a
threat with a rib injury.
“So, you want me to tell you more about Tartarus?”
“That would be preferable, yes.” Akechi gave Sanada a winning smile. Sanada was still
frowning.
“Have a seat then, I guess.” Sanada nodded toward the chair next to his hospital bed, and
Akechi sat down. “Where do I begin? So, you know what the dark hour is, right?”
“It’s the hidden hour in the day,” Akechi said promptly. “It begins at midnight. Only persona
users are aware of it. Everyone else turns into coffins.”
“Close,” Sanada said. “Actually, you don’t necessarily have to have a persona to be aware of
the Dark Hour. People who are aware of the dark hour have the potential, but there are a few
cases where those with potential don’t have personas.”
Akechi frowned. That explained why Aragaki had been so concerned for him at first. It
couldn’t be safe to just wander around the metaverse without any access to a persona.
“I see,” Akechi said. “What does Tartarus have to do with all this?”
“During the day, Tartarus is our high school, or well, I guess my high school. You’re still in
elementary school, right?”
“That would be correct.”
“Thought so.” Sanada looked way too self-satisfied for having such an obvious assumption.
“Anyway, during the Dark Hour, Gekkoukan High turns into Tartarus. It’s filled with
shadows–those are monsters. We don’t really know much about it, but we think that the
secret of the Dark Hour might be at the top.”
“We? Could this be the SEES Aragaki mentioned before?”
Sanada nodded. “Specialized Extracurricular Execution Squad. We fight shadows in the
hopes of putting an end to the Dark Hour.”

That was quite the name for what was likely to be just a ragtag group of students taking up
saving the world in their free time. Akechi had once thought that The Phantom Thieves was a
slightly dramatic name for Akira’s group, but now he thought it was quite modest.
“Who is in charge of your group?”
Sanada did not have any reservations about spilling all of his group’s secrets to Akechi. He
either had a great deal of trust for Aragaki, or he was deeply foolish. Perhaps he was just
underestimating Akechi for his age, but what if Akechi was a spy for an enemy faction?
Surely Aragaki’s group weren’t the only persona users in the entire city.
“It depends on your perspective,” Sanada said. “A fellow student leads the battle operations,
but the chairman is the one who brought us all together.”
“The chairman?” Were these children funded for their antics? Or did an adult in power just
think it fortuitous to have a group of very powerful teens underneath their thumb?
“Do you want to meet him?” Sanada grabbed a notebook that sat on his bedside table. He
scrawled an address on one of the pages before ripping it out and handing it to Akechi. “Here.
This is the dorm we all live at. He’s not there every day, but if you catch him, he can tell you
more. Mitsuru will be there too.”
That name sounded familiar. “Mitsuru?”
“She’s another member of SEES. She typically knows more about what’s going on than I do.
I’m sure she could explain things better.”
Akechi glanced at the address. “Does your entire group live in the dorm?”
“We have the whole building to ourselves,” Sanada said. “It’s somewhat ridiculous, but at
least we don’t have to be quiet about our operations.”
Akechi frowned. “I hope you don’t think I’m going to join your squad.”
Sanada laughed. “That’s a relief. I’m not sure how I would feel about an elementary schooler
joining the team.”
Akechi’s grip on the paper tightened. “When did you join?” Akechi asked, his smile full of
teeth.
Sanada shrugged. “Middle School.”
Ah yes. Sanada had been much older than Akechi was now when he first started fighting
shadows. This chairman clearly had little care for the wellbeing of children if he was letting
middle schoolers fight shadows on their own.
“What is the chairman’s name, if you don’t mind me asking?”
“Ikutsuki Shuji.” Sanada sighed. “He insisted that I visit in the hospital for a few more
checkups while I recover. Talk about annoying. I already promised I wouldn’t train, why

can’t that be enough?”
Akechi raised a single eyebrow. “I saw you punching the air in your hospital bed.”
“That barely counts. I need to get my energy out somehow.”
Akechi had all the information he needed. He hadn’t come to pat Sanada on the head while

“Thank you for your time, Sanada-san,” Akechi said. “I won’t impede on it any longer.”
Sanada made a face. “Um. No problem.”
As Akechi headed toward the nearest Junes, he mulled over the details of his conversation in

Akechi wasn’t particularly thrilled at the thought of joining yet another group fighting the
injustices of the world.
Well, Sanada never said that they were fighting any real people. Just the Dark Hour. But the
Dark Hour had to come from somewhere. Hidden hours of the day didn’t just appear and
vanish at the drop of a hat, and there certainly wasn’t any such hour when Akechi first
awakened to his power.
Akechi would do more investigating. He could try to find this chairman during the next Dark
Hour; the dorm didn’t seem too far away from Akechi’s current residence. Ikutski was
certainly eager to recruit if he was willing to have middle schoolers on his student execution
squad. Akechi doubted his age would be a problem if he said he was considering joining.
Akechi reached the Junes and pulled his shopping list out of his pocket. The Fukuis were

sat on the top shelf of the aisle.
For not the first time, Akechi cursed his incredibly short body. There were other yogurts, but
none of them were as cheap as the one that he wanted to grab. Akechi needed to conserve as
much yen as possible if he were going to be able to return home with everything he indirectly
said he was going to buy.
Oh well, there was nothing to be done. Akechi would just swallow his pride, smile prettily at
a tall person, and ask if they could grab the yogurt. It wouldn’t be the first time. How many
times had he gone shopping for his mother? Adults were usually more than happy to help the

at least.
Akechi turned around to find the nearest tall person, and he found himself staring directly up
at Kurusu Tsuyoshi.

His yellow eyes glinted as he smiled, and rage churned up inside Akechi’s gut. “Need some

“I’m doing fine on my own,” Akechi said, because he refused to be indebted to the likes of
Tsuyoshi, even if it was as inconsequential as yogurt.
“Is that so?” Tsuyoshi picked up the yogurt from the shelf, glanced at it, and dropped it into
Akechi’s shopping basket. Akechi fantasized about throwing the yogurt back into Tsuyoshi’s

“What do you want?” Akechi demanded. “Are you having fun watching me?”
Tsuyoshi tutted. “Are you accusing me of stalking? That’s just rude.”
“I’m not accusing you of anything,” Akechi said through gritted teeth. “The last time we met,
you said you would enjoy watching me.”
Tsuyoshi glanced up at the ceiling contemplatively. “Come to think of it, I did say that, huh?”
“Who are you?” Akechi demanded.
“I think we’ve already introduced, but if you want more clarification, I'll have you know that
Akira's my nephew–"
Bullshit.
“No, who are you?” Akechi took a step forward, although he knew he wasn’t all that
intimidating in his current state. “What are you? I know you’re not really related to Kurusu. I
think he would’ve mentioned having an uncle who’s a shadow.”
Tsuyoshi shrugged with a wry smile. “I’ll tell you later. When I’m bored.”
Akechi took a deep breath. It was clear that Tsuyoshi was toying with him, enjoying Akechi’s
frustration. The best thing Akechi could do right now was ignore him.
Akechi began to turn around.
“You know, for someone who claims to hate friendship and teammates, you sure are
interested in those kids,” Tsuyoshi said. Akechi bristled. “Having second thoughts on playing

Akechi bit back a sharp remark about ignorance being poison, but he kept his mouth shut.
Tsuyoshi wasn’t going to give him any of the answers he wanted. Akechi refused to keep
entertaining him.
Fortunately, Tsuyoshi didn’t follow him. Akechi wasn’t sure how long he would have lasted
without punching him.

“I met your friend the other day,” Akihiko told Shinji, who was leaning against the window
of the hospital room. “Talk about a weird kid.”
“Oh, yeah.” Shinji’s expression turned into one of even deeper annoyance, if that were
possible. “He didn’t happen to give you his name, by any chance?”
Akihiko frowned, slightly dumbfounded. “No, I don’t think he did. Maybe it slipped his
mind. I know I forgot to ask. I was surprised that you would send anyone our way.”
“He’s a kid wandering around during the Dark Hour like he owns the place,” Shinji said,
rolling his eyes. “That would make anyone nervous. He needs people to watch his back.”
“I guess so.” Akihiko shook his head. “Man, but with the way he called me Sanada-san… he
was so polite it was almost creepy.”
Shinji gave Akihiko a confused glance. “Are you sure we’re talking about the same kid?”
“Um, did you send more than one kid in my direction?”
Shinji made a derisive noise from the back of his throat. “No.”
“Then, I’m pretty sure we’re talking about the same kid. He came to me saying he was ‘an

“Yeah, that sounds like him. I’m hung up on the part where you thought he was polite.”
“He was polite. Overly polite. Does he know how fake he sounds?”
“That doesn’t sound like the kid I know. He was threatening to shank me both times I met

Akihiko snorted at the nickname, but it was fitting if the kid really did wave a knife in
Shinji’s face. “No way we’re talking about the same kid.”
“Short? Brown hair? Looks malnourished?”
Akihiko frowned. That did match his unexpected visitor’s appearance. “He has a twin?”
“Don’t be stupid. He must be a good actor.”
“Why would he do that?”
Shinji rolled his eyes. “You really think you get anything out of life if you’re rude all the

“Huh.” Akihiko did remember seeing a calculating look in the kid’s eyes. “Talk about a
strange kid.”
“You said that already.”

“Shut up.” Akihiko sighed and leaned his head against his pillow. “Man. I hope he doesn’t
stab the chairman.”
“Oh, he definitely will.”

Akechi was going to stab the chairman.
Akechi had found the dorm building easily enough. It took only about fifteen minutes of
jogging to get there, although Akechi found himself decently winded afterward. He would
have to start a running regimen so that he could get back in shape.
Akechi had already considered his options. He could try to spy on the group, although that
would be absurdly difficult if they only talked about their operations within the dormitories.
If they had experience fighting shadows, they would surely notice someone opening and
closing their front door. There was also the question of being able to get into the dorm in the
first place. It wasn’t as though he had the keys.
Therefore, Akechi had decided that the strategic decision was to try to gain SEES trust. He
already had Sanada’s, but Akechi hoped that the rest of his team wouldn’t be so easily
manipulated. It would be truly disheartening to know that yet another group of “justice” were
also a pack of fools.
Akechi knocked on the front doors of the dormitory and waited. There was no response.
Akechi knocked again. Had they gone out to Tartarus during the Dark Hour? That would be
inconvenient, but Akechi could always–
The door swung open. A light-skinned man with long brown hair smiled down at him. His
glasses made him look the perfect cliché of the kindly mentor.
It sickened him.
“Hey there,” Ikutsuki said. His voice wasn’t as condescending as Akechi expected it to be,
which made Akechi’s mistrust only heighten all the more. Ikutsuki’s expression was mildly
surprised, but it didn’t show exaggeratedly. “I didn’t realize someone so young could wander
about during the Dark Hour.”
Akechi inhaled sharply through his nose and bowed deeply. “Ikutsuki-san. Sanada-san told
me about your little organization. I thought maybe I could join as well.”
“He did, did he?” Ikutsuki sounded perfectly cheerful and not at all horrified that an
elementary schooler wanted to risk his life fighting shadows. “Well, since you came all this
way, it’d be rude of me not to invite you inside. Why don’t you come in?”
“Thank you, Ikutsuki-san.” Akechi followed Ikutsuki inside the building.
The first floor seemed to simply be the lounge area, with a couple of couches and a kitchen in
the back of the room. Ikutsuki sat down at the only armchair, which sat at the head of the
coffee table. It was a clear show of authority.

“You can have a seat,” Ikutsuki said. He gestured toward the sofa to his right, and Akechi sat
down. He kept his expression perfectly mild, even though he was certain that Ikutsuki was
just as fake as he was.
“So, you want to join SEES?” Ikutsuki leaned forward slightly, clasping his hands together.
“How much did Akihiko tell you?”
“Everything of note,” Akechi said. “Your group goes into Tartarus during the Dark Hour. You
use personas to fight shadows in the hopes of finding a way to get rid of the Dark Hour,

“Mostly.” Ikustuki sighed, pushing his glasses closer toward his face. “Unfortunately, I do not

That explained why Ikutsuki was the only one in the dorm. It also lessened Akechi’s respect
for the man immensely, and there had hardly been any there to begin with. Of course he
would send children out to fight monsters without actually joining them.
“A shame,” Akechi said. “It must be difficult for you.”
Ikutsuki laughed. “It is a bit hard to watch them go off while I sit here like a bum, but I’ve
come to terms with it. Besides, I don’t need a persona when I have my amazing persona-ality.
Get it?”
Ikutsuki snorted at his truly abhorrent pun. Akechi reminded himself of the knife he had
foolishly decided to leave behind in the hopes of seeming more trustworthy.
Akechi decided he hadn’t heard him instead.
“Are the others currently at Tartarus?”
“Oh, yes–” Ikutsuki recovered himself, straightening his back “--we’ve recently gotten some
new members, so Mitsuru took them out to train their abilities.”
Clearly, Mitsuru was the most experienced out of everyone in the group.
“Sanada mentioned joining SEES in middle school,” Akechi said. “Has it truly taken so long

Ikutsuki sighed, his expression heavy. “Unfortunately, there are other issues we contend with

“You only have two members?” Akechi asked, some of his incredulity shining through in his
voice. “And you have an entire dorm to yourself?”

Ikutsuki laughed. “Oh, I see why you might be surprised. We actually have four members

“Excuse my rudeness, but that didn’t answer my second question.”
“Man, you sure do ask a lot of questions,” Ikutsuki said long-sufferingly. “But that’s good.
It’s always important to be informed before you get into things. If you must know, the Kirijo

The Kirijo group funded SEES? Such an influential organization actually put their trust in a
bunch of high schoolers to save the world? The idea was ludicrous. Sure, Shido trusted
Akechi, but that was because Akechi was the only one who could do what Shido wanted. He
was valuable.
Then again, that was likely true for SEES as well. Ikutsuki himself said that persona users
were so rare that they resorted to recruiting middle schoolers.
“What do they have to gain from the dark hour disappearing?” Akechi asked. An
organization like that was more likely to try to weaponize the metaverse than to try and get

“That’s a story for another day,” Ikutsuki said. “And it’s not mine to tell. However, seeing as
one of our members is of the Kirijo family, it’s not that far-fetched that they would help.”
Akechi knew he had recognized the name Mitsuru somewhere.
“You mean that Mitsuru is Kirijo Mitsuru?” Akechi demanded. “Heir to the Kirijo Group?”
“That’s correct,” Ikutsuki said, his eyes betraying some surprise. “You’re quite well
informed.”
The Kirijo group had never given Shido too much trouble, but they were largely unaware of
the rising threat that Shido posed against Japan. They certainly held enough influence that
Shido regarded them as a potential threat. During Akechi’s time, Kirijo Mitsuru was the
leader of the Kirijo group. He had never given much thought as to what happened to the
previous leader, Kirijo Takeharu, but perhaps it was connected to his daughter’s involvement
with the Dark Hour. Perhaps the entire organization was involved.
Akechi was still surprised that Kirijo Takeharu wasn’t trying to weaponize the metaverse.
Maybe he truly cared for his daughter to respect her wishes. More likely he was lying.
Had the other members of SEES even known what they were getting into? They were now
wrapped up in a potential conspiracy tied with the Kirijo group. There was no way they
weren’t being manipulated to some end.
Akechi didn’t have anything to do with it, though. He could walk out of the dormitory and
never come back. He hadn’t given Ikutsuki his name yet. They’d have at least some difficulty
tracking him down.

But if the Kirijo group was trying to weaponize the Dark Hour… Akechi knew firsthand how
disastrous that would be. And as much as he didn’t give a damn about this rotten world, could
he really stand by and do nothing while more evil people brought it closer to ruin?
God, he was starting to sound like Akira. This wasn’t any of his business.
“Are you alright?” Ikutsuki asked. “You look a little pale.”
Akechi smiled and nodded. “Oh, I’m fine. Just a bit tired. This hidden hour hasn’t done my
sleep schedule any good.”
“Fair enough.” Ikutsuki frowned. “Now, I know you want to join us, but I’m afraid that I
can’t let you join unless you have a persona. You need to be up for the task. I can’t just send
any elementary schooler into the line of fire.”
“I don’t think that will be a problem,” Akechi said. He stood up. “However, I will give it
more thought. Will I have to move into this dorm if I join?”
“That would be ideal, yes.”
Akechi hated that he almost considered joining right then and there. The Kirijo group
certainly had enough influence to make it so that he was allowed to stay in the dorm. He
could kiss the foster system goodbye for at least a little while.
But would it really be worth it if Akechi trapped himself in yet another conspiracy?
Akechi didn’t know.
“I’ll return another time,” Akechi said. He bowed. “I should be getting back home.”
“It’s been a pleasure, um, oh this is embarrassing. I never asked for your name.”
Akechi gritted his teeth. He could flee right now, but it would only make Ikutsuki suspicious
of him if he decided to come back. Lying wouldn’t do him any favors, either. If Akechi was
to be potentially released from the Fukuis’ custody, he’d need to give Ikutsuki his real name.
Damnit.
“It’s Akechi Goro,” Akechi said.
Ikutsuki nodded with another small grin. “It’s been a pleasure, Akechi-kun.”

“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Devil Arcana…”

Of course it was the devil arcana. Akechi sarcastically thanked the voice in his head for
reminding him that adults could never be trusted. He certainly hadn’t known that before.
“We’d be glad to have you on the team if you make that decision. I’m sure I can persuade
your parents to let you live in the dorms.”
Akechi smiled bitterly. “I don’t think that will be a problem.”

Yamamoto had taken to walking home with Akechi. She enjoyed pointing out monotonous
things that really did not matter, or talking about petty problems that Akechi couldn’t give a
damn about. She was currently discussing all the things she had done during golden week,
since this was the first day back to school.
“--and then my dad got me ice cream,” Yamamoto was saying. “He got pistachio, which is

“Coffee,” Akechi said without hesitation. He tried not to sound exhausted as he said it.
“Really?” Yamamoto made a face. “I don’t like the bitter aftertaste. My sister says I'm just
not old enough for it.”
“Your sister sounds condescending,” Akechi said.
“No, I think she’s right.” Yamamoto sighed. “She’s so much cooler than me.”
Yamamoto practically worshiped her older sister. She brought her up at least once in every
conversation. Akechi was distinctly reminded of Niijima, except that Yamamoto wasn’t being
raised by her sister.
Another elementary schooler suddenly brushed past Yamamoto as they crossed the
crosswalk, and Yamamoto waved. “Bye, Amada-kun!”
Amada glanced over his shoulder with a quiet “bye” before turning his back toward them and
walking ahead.
“He lives in the dorms,” Yamamoto explained, even though Akechi hadn’t asked. “When his
mom died–”
“You should know better than to gossip about other people,” Akechi interrupted. He refused

how would you like it if everyone talked about it behind your back?”
“Oh.” Yamamoto’s shoulders sagged, and her expression became suddenly sad. “My mother
died when I was born, but I didn’t think about it like that. I just wanted you to know why he’s

Akechi was not about to tell Yamamoto that it was okay. “Apology accepted,” he said
reluctantly. “Just think before talking about other people’s business next time.”
“You’re right.” Yamamoto nodded, resolve in her face. Then, as if the whole exchange had
never happened, she said, “Did you do anything fun during Golden Week?”
Akechi’s golden week had been about as fun as all of his other weeks, with the added stress
of not spending most of the day at school. While he had not done chores every day, he hadn’t
felt particularly safe holed up in his bedroom either.
“Nothing as exciting as ice cream,” Akechi said. “I mostly stayed at home.”
“Oh, well, that sounds like fun too,” Yamamoto said. “What do you like to do in there?”
All of Akechi’s conversations with Yamamoto ended up sounding like interrogations
somewhere along the line. Akechi knew it was because he never asked any questions of his
own, but he only indulged Yamamoto’s company because Akechi doubted anything he could
say would deter her.
“I do my homework.”
“You did your homework for all of golden week?” Yamamoto asked, sounding astounded.
“Among other things,” Akechi said vaguely. Like sleeping. He didn’t have much in the ways
of entertainment.
They reached the part of their route where they had to part ways.
“See you tomorrow, Akechi-kun!” Yamamoto said cheerfully.
“I look forward to it.”
Yamamoto turned around and walked away. Akechi let out a small breath of relief. He was
coming to hate her constant chatter less over time, but he very nearly lost all of his
composure over her gossiping. What was it her business if Amada’s mother died, even if it
was to explain he was grieving? Akechi highly doubted Amada told her that himself. Even if
he had, it wasn’t any of Akechi’s business.
No wonder Amada had been so dismissive of Yamamoto’s greeting.
That evening, Akechi once again stayed up until the Dark Hour. He was hoping he could
catch SEES in action, but Akechi realized early on that such a feat was impossible. They
clearly reached Gekkoukan before the Dark Hour hit, and they likely didn’t leave until after
the Dark Hour was over. Akechi’s only hope of finding them while they fought was if they

were fighting a shadow that escaped Tartarus. If SEES became a threat, Akechi wanted as
much information on their fighting strategies as possible.
Akechi also needed to find out how he time traveled. He had a feeling the Dark Hour had
something to do with it, or perhaps it had something to do with the Velvet Room?
Akechi walked over to the SEES dorms, glancing through one of the windows. It seemed
they hadn’t gone out for the night. He couldn’t hear anything of what the residents were
saying, but they didn’t seem to be saying much of anything. Kirijo Mitsuru was sitting on the
sofa, reading a book. A girl dressed in pink was standing on the other side of the Lounge, and
the boy with the saddest facial hair Akechi had ever seen was asleep on the other sofa.
Ikutsuki was nowhere to be seen. Maybe he didn’t live in the dorms.
According to Akechi’s research, the Devil arcana represented man’s involvement in the
material world and giving into selfish desires. Akechi thought that fit the bill quite nicely for
someone who was likely spending all of his time manipulating children into doing what he
wanted.
The thought infuriated Akechi. He had half a mind to march into that dorm and demand that
they grow some minds of their own. What could they possibly have to gain from fighting
shadows without knowing why? Surely, they didn’t think that the people running their group
had the best of intentions.
No, they probably did. Ignorance was fatal, especially when it came to seeing what you
wanted to see. They wanted to end the Dark Hour. Ikutsuki provided a means to do so.
Akechi wanted to kill Shido. Shido took that opportunity and squeezed.
Akechi turned around. He wasn’t going to get any information out of this, and he could spot
some security cameras on the outside of the building. He probably wouldn’t raise too much
suspicion, since he already spoke with Ikutsuki, but there was little point in taking
unnecessary risks. He wouldn’t throw away everything by barging in and yelling at everyone.
It wasn’t as though they would listen to a word he said anyway.
Perhaps Akechi should join the group. If he could gain everyone’s trust, he could figure out
what Ikutsuki and the Kirijo group really wanted. He could reveal such information to the
other members, and they could at least make their own educated choices on the matter.
Akechi scoffed at himself. What was he even thinking? Who cared about those dumbasses?
Akechi should be more worried about himself. Something had caused him to time travel, and
whatever it was, it was probably still around. Wasting time worrying about the wellbeing of
others was Akira’s thing.
But if his time traveling was connected to the Dark hour…
No. Akechi was not getting himself wrapped up in anything. He was not going to make his
life more difficult than it already was.

Out of the corner of his eyes, Akechi spotted a few shadowy figures sitting on top of the
building across the dorm. Akechi immediately snapped his attention to them. Were they
shadows? People?
As Akechi got a closer look, however, they vanished.
“What are you looking at?”
Akechi spun around and pointed his knife at the voice. He lowered it when he only saw
Aragaki standing about six feet away from him.
“Shouldn’t you know better than to sneak up on people?” Akechi demanded.
“Maybe I should know better than to sneak up on you, Knife Kid,” Aragaki said. “I heard you
talked to Akihiko.”
Akechi sputtered. “Did you just call me Knife Kid?”
“That’s what happens when you don’t give out your name.” Aragaki rolled his eyes.
“I prefer to keep my personal information private,” Akechi said, irritated.
“Didn’t know a name was so personal.”
“It is when the Kirijo group is behind this Specialized Extracurricular Execution Squad of
yours.”
“Hey, I’m not with them.” Aragaki actually sounded a bit offended. “Not anymore.”
“But you were?”
They both knew the answer.
“That’s not the point,” Aragaki said. He followed Akechi as Akechi walked further away
from the dorms. “It’s not as though they’re going to arrest you if you don’t join. I would
know. I quit almost two years ago.”
“It’s too late now,” Akechi said. “I told Ikutsuki my name. I’m sure he’s already found out
where I live.”
“Probably. Has he made any house calls?”
“Not yet.”
“Good.”
Aragaki broke out into some painful sounding coughs, and Akechi paused midstride. He
glanced back at his companion.
“Are you sick?”

Aragaki shook his head. “No, I just have something stuck in the back of my throat. I’m fine.”
His voice was so defensive that there was no way that he was telling the truth. There was no
real reason to lie over having a cold, either, unless he didn’t want Akechi to worry. All those
factors considered, Aragaki’s health might well be in a serious condition.
Akechi frowned but didn’t belabor the point. “If you say so.”

Yamamoto did not see him the next day. As a matter of fact, she was not in class at all.
Akechi assumed she simply got sick, but he was surprised to realize that he almost missed
her constant chatter. Lunchtime was very quiet as he sat in his private corner of the
classroom, ignored by the rest of his fellow students.
Exhaustion weighed down at Akechi throughout the rest of the day. His state was bad enough
that even Fukui mentioned how large the bags underneath Akechi's eyes were. It might be
prudent to take the night off from pointless wandering.
As Akechi walked alone back from school, he found himself incidentally walking alongside
Amada. Amada didn’t pay him much mind, and Akechi was very inclined to do the same.
They traveled in total silence. As Akechi slowed to a stop in front of his apartment, he gave
Amada a short bow, out of politeness more than anything else.
“Have a good afternoon, Amada-kun.”
Amada’s eyes widened, but he was frowning. “You too… sorry, I don’t know your name.”
After so many years of being internationally famous, it was refreshing to hear those words
from someone who likely wished him no ill will. At least Akechi knew Ken didn’t pay much
attention to the rumor mill.
“Don’t worry, I only know your last name from Yamamoto yesterday. I’m Akechi Goro.”
Amada nodded. “It’s Amada Ken. See you around.”

“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Justice Arcana…”

As Amada walked away, Akechi watched him carefully. Where would Amada’s apparent
justice take him?

The following night, Akechi went to sleep at a reasonable hour. Fukui had demanded to know
if Akechi was somehow sneaking out at night to deal drugs, and Akechi had barely managed
to persuade him that he was just having trouble sleeping.
Even with a few nightmares, the sleep did him some good. He felt less inclined to rest his
head on his desk during class, at least. Yamamoto wasn’t at school that day either, so he
walked back to the apartment in the same general vicinity of Amada again. For the first five
minutes, they walked in silence, each daring the other to speak.
Amada surrendered first.
“What happened to Yamamoto?” he asked, glancing over at Akechi awkwardly. “Don’t you
normally walk home with her?”
“She hasn’t been at school the past two days,” Akechi said. He didn’t think Amada would
appreciate excessive cheerfulness shoved in his direction, so Akechi only remained mildly
polite. “I think she may have fallen ill.”
“Oh, that’s a bummer.” Amada’s eyes were wide, but Akechi had a feeling it had nothing to
do with Yamamoto’s apparent illness. Amada’s expression quickly became complacent. “I
hate falling ill, personally.”
“As do I.”
They continued walking in silence, their footfalls barely audible over the sounds of city
traffic. Amada briefly opened his mouth, before saying nothing for the rest of their walk.

“Yamamoto must be really sick,” Amada said almost immediately on Saturday afternoon. He
didn’t even bother pretending not to see Akechi.
“It’s only been three days,” Akechi said mildly.
“I guess.” Amada’s mouth was turned down into a frown, and he stared at Akechi for
multiple uncomfortable seconds. Akechi opened his mouth to politely ask what the hell he

Akechi had gone out during the Dark Hour again the night before. While he hadn’t fully

find clues as to the cause of his time travel. His gut told him he’d only find answers in
Tartarus, which, of course, he could only get to if he actually joined the Specialized
Extracurricular Execution Squad. He planned on spending tonight to find a way to get to
Tartarus that didn’t involve taking the train before midnight struck.
Tartarus likely held the key to getting back to his own time, if such a feat were even possible.
Akechi didn’t know he had died in his original timeline. If he could find what caused him to
time travel in the first place, he could go back. He could go back to a time where Shido had
faced the consequences for his actions. A time with Akir–
Akechi stopped such sentimental thoughts before they escalated out of control.
Of course, wandering around during Dark Hour meant that all of the rest he got two nights

“I just didn’t get much sleep last night,” Akechi said. “I’m not sick.”
“Oh, I get that,” Amada said. “The other kids complain about being forced to go to bed
earlier than they want, but I envy them.”
Akechi remembered hating children who complained about their parents caring about them.
He still did.
“Do you have your own sleeping troubles?” Akechi asked.
Amada shrugged. “Sometimes.”
Sometimes. Such a beautifully vague word. Akechi only ever “sometimes” had nightmares
either.
“Well, I hope they get better over time,” Akechi said, even though they probably wouldn’t.
Things never got better over time. They only ever got even more damn worse.
“Thanks.” Amada shook his head. “You don’t need to worry about me, though. I just stay up
all night reading manga…” His eyes widened as he hastened to explain, “Not because I think
it’s super good or anything, but because I’m bored.”
Akechi decided to humor him. “Of course.”

The moon was full that night.
Its glowing green face stared down at Iwatodai oppressively. It was certainly larger than the

That, of course, was ridiculous. Nothing quite that ludicrous had occurred in the metaverse.
But, it was probably technically possible.
Akechi forced himself to look away from the sky. He was being ridiculous, being distracted

Akechi stepped out of his apartment building to hear the sound of an engine revving. A bright

Leader? They had elected this apathetic asshole to be their leader?
This group was more doomed than Akechi had initially realized. Junpei had more leadership

This group was an absolute disaster. Junpei didn’t respect authority, which was a feat even

Questions for another time. Akechi stumbled in his tracks as the train suddenly began

“Persona!”

Not to mention, if they didn’t kill this shadow soon, the monorail would collide with another

Junpei was the only thing that stopped the kid’s skull from hitting the floor.

evoker, are you talking about those guns you used to summon personas?”
“Oh, that’s right,” Yukari said, looking startled out of her pity for the tragic orphan in her

couldn’t cast it once without fainting.
Kirijo was right. He would become a liability if he couldn’t get his own stamina in check.

He turned to sink back on and properly washed the plate with soap. He then picked up the

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Death Arcana…”

The next day, Akechi returned home from school to see Ikutsuki sitting in his usual armchair.
He smiled and stood up as Akechi approached.

Akechi frowned and glanced up at Ikutsuki. The last time anyone had gifted him a cellphone, it was one of Shido’s drones. Akechi was certain the thing had been closely
monitored, and so Akechi only ever used it for calls that he knew Shido would approve of.
When Shido asked why Akechi was wasting so much time taking the leader of the phantom

Akechi wondered what would happen if he proved himself a useless member of the team.

The phone began ringing again. It was the same number.

“I would like to keep that private, if that’s possible.”

Akechi didn’t need to be taken care of. He hadn’t needed anyone for a long time.
Empress Arcana: Rank 2

Akechi hadn’t the slightest clue as to where he might locate Aragaki, but he figured he would

As much as Akechi would like to learn more about this rogue group running around the Dark

There was no exit. The back alley was quickly interrupted by more wall.

Akechi realized that the three of them had left just before he summoned Loki. He stopped

Mitsuru was never going to let him go outside again.

Of course. The protein bars Sanada had given him earlier that afternoon still sat inside his

Without hesitation, Akechi unwrapped one of the protein bars with trembling fingers slick

as a part of the healing process, and Akechi trusted that it would be no different here if the
bullet was still lodged in his side. He shoved the bar into his mouth, chewing and swallowing
so hastily that it threatened to come right up.

Immediately, the pain in his side lessened, but not a great deal. Akechi yanked another
protein bar out of his pocket, unwrapped it, and shoved it into his mouth.
By the time Akechi made it through all five protein bars, only a lumpy scar remained of his
injury. Unfortunately, it seemed Akechi’s shirt was not quite as lucky. Blood stains covered
the thing, and no amount of bleach was going to change that.
How the hell was he going to hide this incident from Mitsuru?
Akechi sighed, his breathing far more shaky than he would prefer. The Dark Hour was surely
almost over. He should return to the dorm before he got arrested for carrying around a sword
in public.
When Akechi returned, Mitsuru wasn’t in the lounge. Akechi had no idea if she was in the
bathroom or asleep, but he wasn’t about to complain. He quickly crept upstairs to his room.
He’d find a way to deal with his blood-stained shirt in the morning.

“Oh, they just appear after we have a really good fight,” Iori said. “Pretty neat, huh?”
“Minato’s the only one who can choose, though, unless…” Takeba glanced at Akechi

“Maybe,” Akechi said elusively.
“You can try to take a card during the next shuffle time,” Arisato said. “Then, we’ll see.”
It took two more battles for another shuffle time to occur. The cards appeared in between

familiar from Joker’s arsenal.
After a few seconds, the cards flipped over and began shuffling themselves. After they
stopped, Akechi picked up the card that had the persona symbol on it.
Akechi successfully took the card. A strange voice that didn’t sound unlike the social link

The power of Eligor is yours. Lend him the strength of your heart.
The card shattered in Akechi’s hand, and Akechi’s chest constricted as he felt the presence of
another persona within his core. Eligor, was it? That was certainly one of the personas that

It was strange to have more than Robin, Loki, and Hereward’s power at his command. Near
the end, Joker had twelve personas in his control at once. How did he stand it? Even now,
Akechi felt as though his soul was too crowded.

Iori whistled. “Wow, I guess he is like our leader. Watch out, or this kid will take your spot!”
“Don’t call him ‘this kid’, Junpei,” Takeba sighed. “That’s just impolite.”
Arisato shrugged, and Akechi pretended he wasn’t ticked off by Iori’s statement. “You can

“We’ll take turns,” Arisato said simply. And so they did.
Apparently, the card with the sword represented weapons. Akechi got a new saber out of one

The coin cards, unsurprisingly enough, gave the group money. Arisato split it up between the

blood on it. He’d also stop having to operate on so much charity.
The cards with the leaves gave them more clarity after the battle, which made future battles

And then, of course, there were the cards with the personas.
Those cards were rare enough, but Akechi acquired two more personas throughout the

But it didn’t. Everything stayed exactly where it belonged, and Akechi was able to switch

There was no dramatic change in outfit, no pain or exhaustion. It almost felt natural.
Akechi hadn’t tried to summon Hereward yet. Akechi knew he was there, nestled between

It was a bit unsettling to know that Akechi had the same power that Joker had this entire

explained that the metaverse had been taken over by some evil deity, and that was why
Morgana was born. Was that also why Akechi was left to the dirt?
It wasn’t fair. But, then again, Akechi had already known that.

Since the last time Akechi had visited, Igor had returned to his rightful place behind his table.
Whatever it was that he spoke with his master about, he clearly didn’t consider it anything

worth discussing with Akechi or Arisato.

So this is what Igor meant by his bonds granting him power.

It’s true that sometimes Joker would bribe shadows with yen in negotiations. Akechi had

More or less.
“I suppose I do.”
Arisato fused a few more personas of his own before he let Akechi try it. Akechi was slightly

After Akechi was finished, he and Arisato both exited the Velvet Room at the same time.
Upon returning to the entrance, he found that everyone was giving the two of them worried

looks.

Nobody else could see the Velvet Room? That made sense, of course. Akechi should have

Akechi was never going to enter the Velvet Room in the presence of other people ever again.
He refused to look like an airhead.
“Sorry for worrying you,” Akechi said. “But we’re both perfectly fine.”
“I guess you have to have some strangeness to compensate for awesome powers,” Iori

Mitsuru shook her head. “The hour’s almost over. We should head back.”
Another strange part about Tartarus. They could only ever explore it one hour at a time, so
exploration was much slower than it ideally should have been. And Akechi had learned

Akechi hated this place.

The following night, Akechi went out during Dark Hour again. This time, he was fortunate

“Oh, it’s you,” Aragaki said, when he finally saw Akechi. His eyes landed on the sword and

“Who said I quit?” Aragaki said in a tone that was way too defensive for someone who

The next day was Sunday, marking a full week since Akechi joined SEES. Akechi decided he
would celebrate the occasion by going out all day.
With his newly acquired yen, Akechi purchased a new gym shirt. He also bought a large

“You should come over to my house today,” Yamamoto informed Akechi the following
Wednesday, sounding more serious than usual. “I want to show you my cat.”
This wasn’t the first time Yamamoto had invited him out. Akechi had usually found an
excuse as to why he couldn’t spend his entire time playing with animals, but Yamamoto’s
social link hadn’t ranked up at all since it was first formed. Akechi had a feeling that the
universe was insisting upon Akechi visiting Yamamoto’s home.
“Very well,” Akechi said. “I suppose I don’t have any conflicts.”
“What about you, Amada-kun?” Yamamoto asked.
Amada had started joining them on their walks home. He didn’t say much, but Akechi knew
that Amada appreciated having the company.
“Oh, um, I can’t,” Amada said. “I have… homework.”
The bags underneath Amada’s eyes were far more pronounced than they usually were. Was
something going on? Or did Amada simply not want to invest energy in an outing?
“Oh, too bad.” Yamamoto grabbed the straps of her bag cheerfully. “But at least you can
come, Akechi. Momo needs some new friends. He keeps spending most of his time curled up
underneath the bed.”
“How old is your cat?” Akechi asked.
“Momo is older than me!” Yamamoto puffed up her chest. “My sister raised him from when
she was a kitten.”

Momo was likely reaching the end of his lifespan, but Akechi decided that telling Yamamoto
that would be counterproductive.
Instead of parting ways when Akechi reached the dorm, he continued to follow Yamamoto to
her apartment complex. Her apartment was on the second floor, and upon entering, Akechi
found that Yamamoto had a rather comfortable living situation. The kitchen and living area
was reasonably sized, albeit a bit cluttered. The furniture was in good condition, and Akechi
couldn’t spot any signs of alcohol sitting out in the open.
Momo was an orange tabby cat who was currently sitting on top of the sofa in the back of the
living room. Yamamoto quickly took off her shoes, dropped her book bag onto the ground,
and swooped down upon the cat. Momo hissed as Yamamoto picked her up and ran back
toward Akechi.
“This is Momo!” Yamamoto said happily. “Isn’t he the sweetest?”
Momo had surrendered to his fate of being carried around, but his pupils were wide with
discomfort. Akechi had a feeling that if he tried to even bring his hand close to him, he’d be
none too pleased.
“I don’t think he likes being carried around,” Akechi said diplomatically. He understood how
he felt. “Maybe you should put her down.”
“Oh, right.” Yamamoto placed Momo back down on the ground. Momo instantly sprinted
down the hall to their right, slipping into a room that had the door cracked open.
“Oh no, come back!”
Yamamoto chased after the poor cat without another thought. Akechi took off his shoes and
followed her into what he assumed was Yamamoto’s bedroom. The place was tidier than
Akechi expected. No stray books or homework were strewn on the desk sitting by the
window, and there wasn’t any laundry on the floor. Yamamoto clearly kept her room tidier
than she kept her desk at school.
Yamamoto was on her knees, looking underneath the purple-quilted bed. “Momo, don’t be
scared,” she said in a gentle voice. “I promise I won’t pick you up this time.”
Momo did not emerge.
Yamamoto’s laptop was sitting on her desk, and the screen displayed a strange looking
webpage. Akechi walked up to it for a closer look, peering at the small white text on an allblack background.
Is there someone in your life you want revenge on? Just put their name and birthday here,
and we’ll do the rest.
A small white textbox sat beneath the words, and a sick feeling sat inside Akechi’s gut. It
reminded Akechi strangely enough of the Phantom Thieves’ ridiculous Phansite, where
people put out requests for change of hearts.

Except this time, it was for hits. And Akechi had a feeling he knew who was behind it.
Akechi looked at the url, and, unsurprisingly enough, the word strega was in the website’s
domain. But what was Yamamoto doing on a site like this? Could she really be just as two
faced as Akechi–
“What are you doing in my room?” a voice demanded.
Akechi spun around, trying to look as though he hadn’t just been snooping. Fortunately, the
teen that was standing in the doorframe was staring at Yamamoto, who was still hunched
underneath the bed. The new arrival looked very much like Yamamoto, except her hair was
tied up into a ponytail, instead of the two pigtails that Yamamoto always wore. Akechi had no
doubt in his mind that she was Yamamoto’s sister.
“I was trying to show my friend Momo,” Yamamoto said, sitting up and looking up at her
sister unapologetically. “He went underneath your bed.”
“I’ve told you not to go into my room without permission,” Yamamoto’s sister said. “Get
out.”
“But Momo–”
“Does it look like I give a damn about that cat? Get out of my room.”
Akechi took multiple steps away from the computer. But, seriously, if Yamamoto’s sister was

“I apologize for the intrusion,” Akechi said, bowing. “It was my fault. I encouraged

“I don’t care who’s fault it was,” Yamamoto’s sister said. She stepped further into the room

Yamamoto followed Akechi out of the bedroom, and Yamamoto’s sister slammed the door

“I’m really sorry, Akechi-kun.” Yamamoto’s voice was softer than Akechi had ever heard it.
“You shouldn’t have tried to protect me when I was the one to get you in trouble like that.”
“There’s no harm done,” Akechi said. It was true. Akechi couldn’t care less what

Unless Yamamoto told her. Which was actually very likely.
Akechi still wasn’t all that worried. Takaya had already attacked Akechi once, and Akechi

Although, a responsible citizen would tell Yamamoto that her sister was using a hit site. But

Somehow, he didn’t imagine Yamamoto would respond cheerfully to that answer.

If Yamamoto’s sister had enemies, Akechi wasn’t going to learn about them through

But perhaps it was better if Akechi was in control over all of the variables anyway.

“I’ve seen things that would give you both nightmares,” was something that Akechi dearly
wanted to say. Unfortunately, that wouldn’t fit with his pleasant persona, so he kept those
words to himself.
“I’m not saying that,” Iori said, grinning in a way that meant he was definitely implying it. “I
just wanted to know if Akechi was into that sort of thing.”
Akechi smiled but didn’t sit down. “I have a ghost story for you, Iori-senpai.”
“Oh yeah?” Iori asked, looking especially pleased. “Do tell.”
“Ugh, I’m going to my room.” Takeba stood up and scooped all of her books into her arms.
“You both are the worst.”
“My apologies, Takeba-senpai,” Akechi said. “I won’t impose upon your time if you don’t
want me to.”
“No, no, I’ve already picked up my books.” Takeba rolled her eyes as she marched toward
the stairs. “Besides, Junpei was going to keep telling me ghost stories regardless, and how am
I meant to get homework done like that?”
“Hey, it’s not my fault!”
“It is totally your fault!”
Takeba stormed up the stairs, leaving Iori and Akechi alone. Iori looked slightly
uncomfortable, and Akechi hoped he was seeing the error of his ways.
“Well, she was a spoilsport anyways,” Iori said, not seeing the error of his ways whatsoever.
He clapped his hands together and leaned forward. “Alright, let’s hear this ghost story of
yours.”
Akechi took a deep breath, still smiling.
“Once upon a time, there was a child who lived alone in his house. His parents were away on
some business trip, and he was left to take care of himself–”
“Those are some pretty terrible parents–”
“No interrupting,” Akechi snapped.
Iori nodded. “Right, right. Sorry.”

“As I was saying–” Akechi inhaled deeply, forcing himself to still smile “--The child was shy,
and didn’t have any friends. But one day, he fell asleep while doing his homework or
something. Instead of waking up in the morning, however, the sound of television static woke
him up instead.”
Iori grinned, leaning closer. “And then?”
“The boy was quite confused, because he had never turned the television on. It was raining

Iori shivered.

“The next morning, as he walked to school in the early hours of the morning, the boy spotted

“Oh, that’s freaky,” Iori said, shivering. “Was her ghost trying to send a message to the kid

“It just goes to show what will happen to people who bother others with no consideration for

And with that, Akechi turned around and entered his room.
Akira told the story more skillfully, of course. He told it in such detail that apparently
Sakamoto had asked if the story was true. Although it wasn’t impossible thanks to the many
forms the metaverse apparently could take, Akira told it in such a way that made Akechi
believe it wasn’t a real event. If it was, Akira wouldn’t have told it with such gusto.
Although, come to think of it, Akechi could remember Shirogane Naoto’s career as the first
detective prince taking off with a serial murder case in Inaba. Akechi couldn’t remember
much of the details, something about some kid being responsible for the murders. Or was it a
delivery truck driver?
Akechi opened up his computer and looked up: serial murder case in Inaba.
Nothing of note came up, and Akechi remembered that those hadn’t started until around
2011. Damnit.
Akechi sighed and deleted his search. He had more important things to look into anyhow.

Junpei came downstairs and sat down next to Akihiko, who was also working on his

“What’s up?” Akihiko asked, not looking up from his book.
“Akechi is kind of scary,” Junpei said.
“So I’ve heard.”

“I don’t know!”

“What’s that supposed to mean?!”

As soon as Akechi ran into Yamamoto on his way to school, Yamamoto launched into
conversation.
“Did you hear?”
Akechi frowned, distracted by his own findings on the explosion ten years ago. Or the lack

“Hear what?” Akechi asked.
“Apparently, a student fainted at my sister’s high school yesterday,” Yamamoto said. “She

“Is she ill?” Akechi asked.
“Nobody knows–” Probably because it wasn’t any of their business. “--but my sister says that
everyone’s talking about it now.”

“...What school does your sister go to?”
“Gekkoukan High.”
That explained why Iori was telling ghost stories to Takeba last night. Though, honestly, how

Then again, this was the entire human race Akechi was thinking about. Why wouldn’t they

Seeing as this was the reason Yamamoto had wanted to become friends with Akechi to begin

Akechi spent the entire walk to school explaining the past week’s worth of math lessons to

“Oops,” Yamamoto whispered under her breath. She gave Akechi an apologetic smile.

Later that day, Arisato accosted him as Akechi tried to go up the stairs to his own bedroom.
“Do you want to go out for coffee?” Arisato asked.
Akechi raised his eyebrows. “Are you asking me out on a date, Arisato?” Akechi asked, just

Arisato’s expression became more animated than Akechi had ever seen it, turning to disgust

coffee is good for that. Therefore, you should go out for coffee with me.”

“Are you reciting a logical statement to me?” Akechi asked, forgetting his manners entirely.
“Akechi is tired. Coffee is good for tired people. Therefore, Akechi should get coffee?”
Arisato nodded.
“I’m ninety-percent sure there’s a fallacy in there somewhere.”
“Do you want coffee or not?”
Akechi hesitated. He had originally planned to continue his research, but if he got coffee with

“Of course, I would like to go out to coffee with you,” Akechi said, reminding himself to stop
being so damn rude. “Thank you for inviting me.”
Arisato shoved his hands into his pockets, looking unsettled. “Cool. Let’s go then.”
Arisato was one of the most socially awkward people Akechi had ever met. That was saying

“Is the coffee at least good?”
“It makes you charming. Not that you need it, I guess.”
What the hell was that supposed to mean?

“This coffee is terrible,” Akechi said, staring down at his cup with disgust. “Did they recycle

“It’s coffee,” Arisato said like the unintelligent person he was.
“It’s a travesty.” Akechi put his cup down, refusing to take another sip. Arisato, meanwhile,

“Coffee is coffee.”
“Intelligently said,” Akechi said sarcastically. “I’m sure they’ll be hiring you for all of their

“It makes me more charming too,” Arisato said, placing his now empty cup onto the table.
“I don’t need charm.” Akechi took a deep breath.
Arisato shrugged. “Suit yourself.” He didn’t look at all perturbed by Akechi’s rude behavior.
“Although, I admit I have not been myself today.” Akechi picked up his mug again and took
another experimental sip. It was somehow simultaneously the bitterest and blandest cup of

coffee Akechi had ever sampled. “I apologize.”
“I don’t really care.”
This reaction wasn’t altogether surprising, considering Arisato’s typical demeanor. Still,
Akechi couldn’t help but to be slightly surprised. Most people found the pricklier side of his
personality to be jarring, or as Yoshizawa so eloquently put it, “ruthless.”
“Regardless, I’m sorry.” Akechi stared down at the murky black liquid that had been dubbed
pheromone coffee. Maybe it was the nonexistent pheromones that were making the drink so

“Sure.”
Akechi put down his drink and pushed it away, deciding there wasn’t much point in
pretending he liked the drink after already revealing his true feelings about it. “But, while

Arisato nodded with not an ounce of shame on his expression. “I was bored,” he added, to

“As long as we are on the same page,” Akechi said.
They stopped exchanging conversation after that point.
Death Arcana: Rank 2

Akechi returned to the dorm the next day to see everyone huddled around each other by the

Well, it wasn’t as though the story could possibly be true anyway.

Iori had not understood the moral of Akechi’s ghost story if he was so interested in measuring

“Of course.”

“Did you celebrate your birthday at all today?” Takaya asked.
Akechi texted Aragaki earlier that evening, asking if they wanted to speak together. Akechi

Had Takaya done this on purpose? Akechi himself hadn’t even bothered to remember it was
his birthday. It wasn’t as though it was an occasion that held any weight in his life. Even
when his mother was still alive, birthdays were just painful reminders of how hard life could
be. Sometimes, she would be too spread thin to remember his birthday. The one year Akechi
reminded her, she burst into tears and apologized. The tears were so horrible that Akechi
stopped reminding her after that. Still, on years she did remember, their celebrations
consisted of a small cake and Akechi’s favorite meal.
After his mother died, Akechi discarded the occasion entirely. Nobody else felt bothered to
bring it up, except for parasocial fans who tried to dig it up.
“It’s not any of your business.” Akechi shifted his grip on his evoker. “Why? Do you have

Akechi might as well take advantage of this rude interruption while he could.
“I’m afraid I don’t know my birthday,” Takaya said. “So I never bothered to celebrate it.

“The world doesn’t revolve around you. Besides, you made it quite clear that you weren’t

A small part of Akechi, the part that was eager to please anyone and everyone, wanted to rise

“I don’t exist to please you,” Akechi said, walking past him. Takaya followed.

That small, stupid part of him won.
“Fine,” Akechi bit out. He stopped and spun around, he hated feeling Takaya’s eyes on his

“They created it, of course,” Takaya said, smirking. “You couldn’t figure that much out for

They created it? With what power? And was it intentional, or an accidental byproduct of
some other project? Not that Akechi would be surprised if it were intentional. A hidden hour
of the day would make a marvelous weapon against opponents. Poison someone’s drink
during the Dark Hour, and they would be none the wiser.
“I had my suspicions,” Akechi said coldly, refusing to let his shock show. “How did they
create it?”
“Children shouldn’t be greedy with what they’re given.” Takaya tutted. “It’s more polite to

“I’m not a polite person,” Akechi said. “If you’re not going to give more answers, I’m not

“Actually, I don’t mean to impose, but I have a question of my own.” Takaya took a few steps

Akechi felt a prickle go down the hairs on his spine. “Again, I don’t see how that’s any of

“Another time, then.” Takaya turned around and began walking away. “I’ll have my answer.”
Akechi didn’t bother to respond. Takaya could believe all he liked that he’d find out
Akechi’s greatest fear, but he never would. Not when Akechi didn’t know himself.
As soon as Takaya was out of sight, Akechi turned around and ran the rest of the way to the

Aragaki hadn’t gotten fed up and left, fortunately. He was sitting on the steps where they

“I almost thought you weren’t going to come,” he said.
“I’m sorry, Aragaki-san.” Akechi bowed. “I got held up.”

“What? No,” Akechi scoffed. He hadn’t even realized he had put on his pleasant face for

“Sure.” Aragaki raised his eyebrows and tossed something in Akechi’s direction. Akechi

“Of course not.” Akechi glanced at the small item Aragaki had thrown at him. It was a small

Aragaki snorted as he sat down. “Could’ve fooled me. I thought I told you to stay away from

Obviously. With no other people or electronics, there was no noise pollution. Akechi wasn’t

Why had Akechi made such a stupid mistake?
“Don’t call me kid,” Akechi said, unwilling to admit he had been a total idiot.

“Alright, Akechi.”
At least Shinjiro didn’t immediately jump to using Akechi’s first name.

“And you decided that all on your own, huh?”

Moon Arcana: Rank 3

“Doing homework” had turned out to be code for “going to a dangerous alley behind Port
Island Station full of dangerous people.” No wonder Iori was trying to get out of it. For once
in his life, Akechi was inclined to agree with him.
Akechi intercepted them before they could actually enter the den of shadows. Arisato didn’t

“He’s not stupid, Yukari,” Iori said. “He would’ve found out on his own. Besides, this means

reason, she looked at Akechi when she asked.
“Don’t worry, Yamagishi-San,” Akechi said. He gave her a weary smile. “You’re perfectly

Iori chuckled. “Yeah, when Akechi-kun awakened his persona, he fainted after using one
ability.”
“I didn’t awaken my persona then,” Akechi snapped.
Iori’s eyes widened. “Oh. My bad.”
Wait. That was more embarrassing. Why did Akechi say anything?
Moriyama stared at Yamagishi’s prone form with a heartbroken expression. “Fuuka, Fuuka
I…”
Sanada turned to Kirijo. “Where did these two shadows come from?”
“Somewhere outside of Tartarus, just like before,” Kirijo said.

“They did a number on the wall,” Arisato observed, looking at the hole where the exit doors
once stood.
“It should fix itself tomorrow night.” Kirijo sighed. “Speaking of which, we should get out of
here. The hour is almost up.”
“What are we going to do about Moriyama?” Takeba asked. “She knows about the Dark

“She’s not like us,” Sanada said. “She won’t remember any of this. Fortunately, she didn’t

“How do the shadows call their victims to begin with?” Akechi asked. “Is there any way to
prevent that from happening?”
“We don’t know nearly enough to even know where to begin…” Kirijo’s voice lowered to a
mutter, and she frowned.
“Does this mean that Moriyama won’t remember what Fuuka did for her?” Takeba asked,

Everyone glanced over at Moriyama, who had finally started crying. “Fuuka, I’m so sorry…
I’m sorry…”
It was remarkable. A bully actually feeling remorse without being brainwashed.
“I don’t think that will be a problem,” Kirijo said, smiling a little bit.
“Huh,” Arisato said.

That bastard.
What the hell was Akechi meant to do with that? He gave that information freely knowing

Akechi didn’t have a good response to that, but he knew saying nothing would be just as

The city noisily came to life, and Takaya disappeared amidst the random pedestrians that

He really hated that man.

“What’s on your mind?”
Akechi glanced between his phone in his hand and Shinjiro. It was still the Dark Hour, so his
phone wasn’t functional. That didn’t stop Akechi from staring at it as though it were an alien
object from a children’s cartoon.
Shinjiro seemed to have caught onto Akechi’s strange behavior. Akechi pocketed his phone.
“A classmate invited me to see a movie on Sunday,” Akechi explained. “I was startled by the
invitation.”
“That’s one word for it,” Shinjiro snorted. “Who’s this classmate? A friend of yours?”
“That’s a bit strong,” Akechi muttered. “He’s just an acquaintance.”
Shinjiro raised his eyebrows. “Am I just your acquaintance?”
“We hardly see each other. What else would we be?”
Shinjiro nodded approvingly before standing up and staring at the sky. The stars weren’t
visible during the Dark Hour, but the murky clouds were still a sight to behold. Just not a
particularly nice one.
“Good,” Shinjiro said. “You don’t want to be friends with me. I’m glad you have different
friends.”
“He is just an acquaintance,” Akechi reiterated. “I don’t know why he’s invited me to this

“Why is it bothering you so much?” Shinjiro asked. “People get bored and hang out with

Akechi had never been invited out before. Not without an ulterior motive, that is, and

Amada hadn’t even asked permission. Akechi had just been lying in bed the night before

Amada Ken: Want 2 see a movie on Sunday w me
Akechi barely had time to blink at the invitation before a new message came through.
Amada Ken: Its superheroes.
Akechi began composing an appropriate response—he dearly missed smart phone keyboards

Amada Ken: Thought u might like it no pressure lol.

Akechi Goro: Id be happy to come. Thank you.
Amada Ken: U text like a old man
They agreed to meet at the shrine at noon. Akechi was still confused.
“Don’t get too worked up over this,” Shinjiro said. “I can guarantee that your acquaintance

“I’m not worked up.” Akechi irritably pocketed his phone. “I’m being cautious.”

“I hope the movie is good.”
Akechi stood up. “Just shut up.”
Shinjiro’s scoff sounded much more like a hacking cough.

A ridiculous plot for a ridiculous show. But if Amada wanted to continue prattling on about

The strangest thing was that Akechi wasn’t even sure he had been lying.

The room was deathly silent as the elevator continued his endless ascent. The never-ending

“He is not my father,” Akechi whispered. “And don’t you dare say this is my fault. I didn’t

“Of course, you’re not to blame for your circumstances, but I do not believe that is a good

He was still smiling with all of his teeth.
“But Elizabeth is right,” Igor continued. “While it is hard to determine what exactly makes a

The contract appeared on top of the table, with those same stupid words.
Whatever happens, I chooseth my fate of my own free will.
Akechi picked up that piece of paper and crumpled it up into a ball. “I do choose my fate of
my own free will,” Akechi hissed. “I will not go along with whatever fate you and your

Akechi hurled the ball at Igor’s face. It bounced off of his nose without any fanfare.
Elizabeth snorted. Theodore made a whimper of dismay.
Akechi left.
Judgement Arcana: Rank 3

That Friday, Akechi was interrupted from his homework by an obnoxious knock on the door.
“Who is it?” Akechi sighed.
“Um, it’s me. Junpei.”

Akechi pressed his hands together and took a deep breath. He did not have the emotional

Although, perhaps that was debatable. Takeba wasn’t pretending to be on good terms with

“Yeah! One minute you’re all nice and friendly and more polite than me, and the next minute

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

The next day, after school, Akechi found Takeba and Yamagishi playing with a dog in front

“You never told me you had a dog, Yamagishi,” Akechi said. The dog didn’t have a collar.
Yamagishi should remedy that. Unless, of course, the two girls were just playing with a stray.

Akechi felt a little ridiculous greeting a dog as though it were a human being, but he had to

Come to think of it, the dog did look a little familiar. Maybe Akechi had seen him around the

“Happy Birthday, Ken-kun!” Yamamoto told Amada cheerfully on their way to school that
Wednesday.
Amada frowned. “How did you know it was my birthday?”
“You briefly mentioned it when I was talking about my own birthday celebration that
happened in January,” Yamamoto said. “I always remember people’s birthdays. Speaking of
which, what day is yours, Akechi-kun?”
Akechi smiled. “I’m afraid it already happened this year.”
Yamamoto pouted. “That’s too bad. If you tell me what day it is, I’ll make sure we have a
proper celebration next year.”
“June 2,” Akechi said reluctantly.
“But that was recently!” Yamamoto looked horrified as they walked up the front steps of their
school building. “Why didn’t you say anything?”
“I didn’t want anyone making a fuss over it.” Akechi hadn’t realized Yamamoto was going to
care so much, either. “Please, don’t worry about it.”
“I’ll sing happy birthday to you right now–”
“Oh no, that’s not necessary.”

“It’s important to sing happy birthday,” Amada said with a sly grin on his face. “It makes
your next year more blessed.”
“Nobody has ever said that–”
“Alright, here we go,” Yamamoto said. “Are you ready, Ken-kun?”
Amada nodded, still wearing a mischievous grin. Akechi wanted to smack them both as they

It was the worst twenty seconds of Akechi’s life.

“Oh, that sounds pretty good actually,” Amada said. “But maybe no happy birthday–”
“We should be getting to class,” Akechi interrupted. “We look forward to celebrating your

Amada sighed, knowing when he was defeated. “I look forward to it too. I guess.”
There was a bounce to her step as Yamamoto walked to her classroom. As they sat down in

“You know exactly what you’re doing, don’t you?” he asked.
Yamamoto raised her eyebrows. “I have no idea what you’re talking about,” she said happily.
“I love singing Happy Birthday. I even sing it when others sing it to me on my birthday.”
“You love embarrassing people on their birthday?” Akechi clarified.
“Yep!” Yamamoto placed her schoolbooks on her desk. “It’s a birthday tradition.”
Akechi couldn’t stop himself from snorting in amusement.

After class, Yamamoto and Akechi met Amada outside of school like they always did.

Yamamoto nodded and pulled a small pouch from her pocket. “I’ve been saving! I’ve never

“What was the math problem?” Akechi asked.
“The square root of 169,” Amada grumbled. “I mean, how am I supposed to know that from

“13,” Yamamoto said suddenly, her eyebrows knit together in concentration.
Akechi had already known the square root of 169, of course, but he hadn’t expected

“It would be my pleasure.”

At this rate, Akechi doubted he’d ever have the opportunity to surpass the age of twenty.
