submerged.

“Relief is what you truly want. You stand before the doorway to bliss.” That was an odd thing
to say. Goro wasn’t standing. “You cannot deny your instincts… Embrace your desire…”
Goro was growing to like that voice. It was soothing… kind of like his mother. The water felt
good too… like a warm embrace. It was all the way up to his nose now.
Goro missed his mother. If he closed his eyes, could he see her again? She had gone away
this way too. The voice had said bliss.
Something inside of Goro screamed. The fire flared up inside of him. This was wrong;
something was wrong.
But what could possibly be wrong? The hot water was so inviting. Goro held his breath as his
entire face became submerged in it. Everything could be fine… just one more nap… one
more release…
“Why do you resist…? Do not avert your eyes from the truth…”
Well, if the voice said so… he kept his eyes open, even though the water stung them. He
couldn’t see much, just the dim red light from the ceiling rippling above him. It was almost
beautiful.
Nobody would miss him anyway.
Who was he again?
Well, if even he couldn’t remember who he was, then nobody else would either.
He couldn’t hold his breath any longer. He inhaled, and burning water filled his lungs. He
tried to cough it up, but more water kept flooding in—
A different voice broke through the fog.
“I chooseth this fate of my own free will.”
No. Akechi refused to die like this. Not with some god whispering lies that crawled into his
brain and suffocated him. He would not die like this.
Akechi burst out of the bathtub, tumbling over the side and onto the tile floor. He coughed
furiously, hacking up the water he had already inhaled. Akechi’s entire body shook as his
unsteady fingers scratched at the tiles. He just needed some stability, but his lungs and
sinuses burned. Tears of pain automatically rose to Akechi’s eyes, and he furiously clawed at
his face to keep them at bay.
Unsurprisingly, it didn’t work.
Someone was knocking on the door. Akechi attempted to stop gagging.
“Akechi, are you in there?” It was Sanada.

“Yes.” Akechi’s voice came out much hoarser than he expected, and he grimaced. “Just a
minute.”
Akechi forced himself to his feet and fought off the wave of dizziness that came with it. He
quickly shoved his jacket, which was the only thing he hadn’t been wearing, over his sopping
wet clothes. Everything about him was so off balance. How dare that disgusting shadow try
to mess with Akechi’s brain?
Mostly, Akechi was disgusted with himself.
“Are you okay in there?” Sanada asked.
“One more moment!” Akechi put his shoes on and opened the door for Sanada. Sanada
lowered his hand, clearly about the knock again.
“You’re… wet,” he said. He looked past Akechi. “So is the bathroom.”
“I don’t want to talk about it,” Akechi snapped, brushing past Sanada.
Sanada stepped further into the bathroom. “Wait. The Dark Hour probably won’t set things
completely to normal–”
“Does it look like I care?” Akechi looked around the hotel room. “Where are my weapons?”
“On the dresser,” Sanada said. “I’m going to drain the bathtub.”
“You do that.” Akechi marched up to the dresser and put his evoker in his holster. He grabbed
hold of his sword too, breathing more easily now that he had something he could stab that
shadow with.
Speaking of that shadow… this was a love hotel… and everyone was being brainwashed.
“Sanada!” Akechi turned toward him, feeling mildly panicked. “Did you wake up in this
room?”
Sanada shook his head. “Nah, I woke up in a different room. Almost fell asleep. It was really
weird.”
Akechi’s grip loosened on his sword. “How did you know I was in that bathroom?”
“I heard you coughing.” Sanada exited the bathroom and closed the door behind him. “What
was going on in there?”
“It was nothing.”
“Are those scratch marks on your face–”
“It was nothing.”
Sanada’s expression hardened. “Fine. We should find the others. Fuuka?”

“The others are heading up the stairs to you,” Yamagishi said through their trancievers. “The
enemy was interfering with you guys’ thoughts, and you all got separated. But the enemy is
still in the same room as before.”
“Got it,” Sanada said. “Thanks, Fuuka.”
“Also, the door leading into that room is sealed. I’ll try to find a way to break the seal, but
focus on finding the others first.”
Finding the others was not as difficult a task as Yamagishi and Sanada made it out to be.
Sanada and Akechi took two steps outside of their room as Yukari and Arisato ran toward
them.
“Oh, thank goodness you guys are alright,” Yukari said.
“Are you alright?” Sanada asked.
“W-we’re fine!” Yukari’s voice rose in octave, confirming a personal theory Akechi had
about this stupid shadow. Her hair was slightly damp as well, but not her clothes. “Nothing
weird happened to us or anything.”
“How about you guys?” Arisato asked. His face was somewhat pink, but his voice didn’t
show any change.
“Nothing happened.” Akechi glared at Sanada threateningly.
“You’re soaking wet,” Yukari said with her abounding observational skills. “And what
happened to your face–”
“You heard him,” Sanada said. “Come on, let’s find a way into that thing’s hiding place. I
have a bone to pick with him.”
Everybody could agree with that sentiment.
“I’ve got it!” Yamagishi cried out victoriously. “It’s the mirrors! They’re connected to the
shadow’s seal. If you break them, you might weaken the seal.”
“I do remember the mirror on the third floor being different,” Yukari said. “I felt strange
when I looked at it.”
“The fact it had no reflection might have something to do with that,” Akechi said, crossing
his arms.
“Oh, yeah, that’s what it was,” Sanada said.
“Break mirrors with no reflection, then,” Arisato said. “Got it.”
“Should we all split up?” Akechi asked. “We would make more progress that way.”

“But then a shadow might catch one of us off guard,” Sanada countered. “There’s safety in
numbers.”
“There’s time wasted–”
“There’s no time for this,” Arisato said. “We’re going together.”
Akechi and Sanada shut up.
It took far longer than Akechi would have liked for them to locate and destroy all of the
mirrors without reflections. Occasionally, Arisato looked as though he were about to break a
mirror that showed his reflection clear as day. On those occasions, Akechi would grab tightly
onto Arisato’s wrist.
“Break that mirror, and you won’t like what happens next,” he whispered dangerously the
first time it happened.
Arisato’s expression became more closed off after that.
In the properly functioning mirrors, Akechi could see the state of his reflection. Apart from
looking like he just walked through a downpour, obvious scratch marks covered his cheek
adjacent to his left eye. Akechi didn’t seem to have drawn much blood, but the scratches
themselves were becoming raised lines on his skin. No wonder everyone was asking about
his face.
It was nothing a dia spell wouldn’t fix.
Finally, Arisato broke the final reflectionless mirror on the third floor. Yamagishi delivered
the news gratefully.
“You’ve broken the seal door!” she said. “You can fight that shadow now!”
“Thank god,” Akechi muttered as they exited that room. If he had to look at another one of
those disgustingly large and overly bedazzled mirrors, he was going to kill someone. Maybe
Takaya. Preferably Takaya.
At least all of the running around dried him out somewhat. Water was no longer dripping
onto the carpeted halls, which was a small mercy, but his entire body was freezing.
Yukari and Sanada still shot him concerned glances. Arisato barely looked at him at all.
That was fine. Akechi didn’t care what Arisato thought of him. As a matter of fact, he was
grateful Arisato wasn’t inclined to pry into his business like the others.
They hurried to the double doors again, and Yukari pushed them open with a vengeance. A
giant shadow in the shape of a human heart with wings floated inside the middle of the room.
“You mind-controlling freak!” Yukari shouted in a fit of rage. “You’re going to pay for what
you did!”

Akechi seconded that.
Now forced out of the open, the shadow itself was not terribly impressive. It attempted to
charm all of them, and it suddenly turned out to be a good thing that Yukari was in the party.
Arisato was the only one successfully charmed, and Yukari merely used charmandi on him,
releasing him from the spell.
“Thanks,” Arisato said, looking embarrassed. “Akechi, how much energy do you have?”
“Do you really have to ask? I will turn this thing to ashes.” Akechi pulled out his evoker.
“Loki!”
Akechi decimated that beast with three attacks.
“W-wow,” Yukari said, her eyes wide. “That was impressive.”
“Great work.” Sanada patted Akechi on the shoulder, and Akechi jerked away from him.
Sanada yanked his hand away. “Sorry.”
“Don’t be,” Akechi grumbled.
They returned outside the hotel, where the others were waiting. Yamagishi had dispelled her
persona and was leaning against the wall with Iori. Mitsuru was standing by the entrance with
her arms crossed. Her expression visibly relaxed when she saw Akechi and the others come
out of the building.
Yamagishi’s expression brightened, and she pushed herself off of the wall. “I’m glad you all
are safe,” she said.
“That’s the last of them, right?” Akechi asked. He would pass out if he had to fight any more
that night.
“Yes.”
“We couldn’t have done it without you,” Sanada said.
Yamagishi blushed and looked away. “Akechi-kun figured out the mirrors before I did,” she
said.
“But you found the shadow to begin with,” Akechi said. Partly because Yamagishi did
extremely good work for them. Partly, Akechi just wanted to try and save face after scaring
the wits out of Yukari during the last fight. “We’re in your debt.”
“O-oh.” Yamagishi smiled. “Thank you.”
“What happened in there?” Iori asked. “Why are both Akechi and Yukari wet?”
Yukari pulled at her still damp hair. “It was… a water attack! Right, Akechi-kun?”
Akechi nodded. “It only hit Takeba and I, though, as you can see.”

Iori narrowed his eyes. “Yeah, sure.”
“All of you did well to withstand the enemy’s mental assault, whatever form it happened to
take,” Mitsuru said. She seemed to possess some common sense, because she did not ask
what exactly occurred. Yukari and Arisato looked too embarrassed to even speak of it, and
Akechi would die before uttering a word of what happened to anyone.
“Let’s call it a night,” Sanada said. He stole yet another concerned glance at Akechi that
Akechi pretended not to see. “It’s been a long one for all of us.”
They started walking away from the hotel, although the girls lagged behind. Akechi tried to
listen in on what they were saying, but Yamagishi only got as far as saying, “About that thing
you both mentioned…” before Iori loudly spoke up.
“So, you’re the hero once again, aren’t you?” he asked Arisato.
Arisato’s expression became genuinely confused, and he stuffed his hands into his pockets. “I
barely did anything. It was a team effort.”
“Don’t go acting all humble on me,” Iori said. His voice was bitter. “You’re our great leader,
aren’t you?”
“What’s this about, Junpei?” Sanada asked.
“It’s nothing,” Iori muttered convincingly.
“If you hate me, you can just tell me to my face,” Arisato said. “I don’t care.”
Sanada’s eyes widened. “Where’d you get that idea–”
“Whatever,” Iori said before storming off. Arisato’s expression became sullener.
A strange feeling stirred up inside of Akechi. “Arisato…”
“Don’t apologize,” Arisato said. “You didn’t do anything.”
Sanada looked hopelessly confused as the girls caught up with the rest of the group. Akechi
lost his entire window to eavesdrop on them.
“What’s going on with him?” Yukari asked, watching Iori walk further ahead.
“He’s throwing a pity party for not being put on the team, I guess,” Sanada said. “Not very
mature of him, if you ask me.”
“We were all worried about you when you guys got separated,” Mitsuru said diplomatically.
“He’s probably just venting some of his frustration from that.”
“That’s a bit generous,” Yukari said. “Don’t let him get to you, Minato. You did great today.
You didn’t break the wrong mirror once!”

“That was with Akechi’s help,” Arisato said.
“Why is everyone praising me all of a sudden?” Akechi asked. A strange feeling of being
watched prickled down his back. “Just take the compliment.”
The conversation died down, and Akechi looked over his shoulder. Three familiar figures
stood on the roof adjacent to the hotel.
Takaya had taken to spying on him, had he? That was wonderful. Just fantastic.
Akechi was going to kill him.
“What’s wrong?” Mitsuru asked.
Akechi looked away. “Nothing.”

“Nothing” came in the form of a text message the following morning. One that made Akechi
want to burn his phone.
Unknown: Meet me by Tartarus.
Did Strega think they were being subtle? Everyone else Akechi knew who knew about
Tartarus had actual contacts on his phone. Akechi blocked the number. He was not about to
indulge in whatever trap Takaya was planning.
On his daily run that afternoon, Akechi received a call from another unknown answer.
Against his better judgment, he answered it.
“Akechi Goro speaking. Who is this?” Akechi asked pleasantly.
“Hello, Akechi Goro.” Takaya’s voice was light and mocking. “I know you blocked my
number.”
“Figured that out all by yourself, did you?” Akechi huffed. He had been running extra
aggressively, already going an extra mile of distance. The exhaustion helped him forget the
mortifying experience of last night. “Using Jin’s phone, then?”
“Are you going to meet me, or are we going to keep playing this game of cat and mouse?”
Takaya asked.
“Only you?” Akechi asked suspiciously. “What about the rest of Strega?”
“Them too,” Takaya conceded. “We have questions for you.”
“If you have questions, there’s nothing stopping you from asking me now,” Akechi said. He
maneuvered around a couple walking their dog.

“Ah, but talking on the phone is just so impersonal,” Takaya said. “I’d much prefer to speak
to you face to face.”
“So you can shoot me?”
“So accusatory. I’m hurt.”
“Deal with it.” Akechi rolled his eyes. “What the hell do you want to ask?”
Takaya tutted. “So impatient. If you must know, we would like to know more about your
friends. You had quite the exciting excursion last night–”
Akechi hung up on him and shoved his phone into his pocket. A few moments later, it began
ringing furiously. Akechi ignored the call and violently blocked the new number.
No other calls came through. Apparently, Chidori didn’t have a phone. Or maybe it was
Takaya or Jin who didn’t have phones all along.
That night, Akechi sat restlessly in his room, trying to sleep and failing horribly. It was a
small mercy that his shower was just a normal stand-up shower with no bathtub attached. He
wouldn’t have been able to wash himself without feeling sick to his stomach.
Akechi’s phone pinged from where it was sitting on his desk. Much to his overwhelming
relief, it was Shinjiro who sent the text. It was unusual for Shinjiro to text, but it wasn’t the
first time.
Aragaki Shinjiro: Heard yesterday was rough. Want to talk?
Akechi frowned. Shinjiro wasn’t one for talking about his feelings.
Akechi Goro: Meet at our usual spot by Tartarus?
It only took a few seconds for “Shinjiro” to reply.
Aragaki Shinjiro: You know it.
Akechi had to give it to whoever had stolen Shinjiro’s phone. They certainly knew how to
copy his mannerisms. Did Strega and Shinjiro talk frequently? Not frequently enough, if they
were dumb enough to think Akechi and Shinjiro talked at Tartarus. They mostly spoke
together on the steps of Iwatodai Station.
“Fantastic,” Akechi muttered. Oh well, it wasn’t as though he had been getting any sleep
anyhow.
He armed himself with his evoker before getting onto the train to Port Island at around thirty
minutes ‘til midnight. When he was with the entire group, Mitsuru put their weapons in
suitcases to make them seem less conspicuous. Akechi didn’t want to lug a suitcase to an
ambush. His evoker would serve him just fine.

He reached Gekkoukan high five minutes before the Dark Hour began, and he scanned the
area for any sign of Strega. They clearly preferred the lay low until the Dark Hour, which
wasn’t a terrible strategy. Akechi kept a tight hold on his evoker as he waited for the world to
suddenly fall asleep.
Sure enough, as soon the Dark Hour began, Akechi heard three sets of footsteps walk behind
him. Akechi immediately pulled out his evoker and turned around to face Strega.
“Are you always this ready for combat around friends?” Jin asked, crossing his arms.
“First of all, Aragaki isn’t my friend,” Akechi said. “Second of all, I’m not stupid. I knew
you stole Shinjiro’s phone.”
“How perceptive,” Chidori said, looking bored.
“Indeed.” Takaya smiled. “And you chose to meet with us regardless? How bold.”
“Don’t feel too flattered. I was bored.” Akechi glared. “What are your questions?”
“We wanted to know what you and your team hope to accomplish by fighting these shadows
on the full moon,” Takaya said. “It seems to only lead to more pain on your end.”
“Don’t be ridiculous,” Akechi said. “We’re just ridding the world of scum. I should kill you
too.”
Jin rolled his eyes. “I knew he wouldn't cooperate. Come on, Takaya.”
“You won’t attack me,” Takaya said. “I still have information for you.”
“And what’s stopping me from killing the other two?” Akechi snarled.
“As if you could,” Jin scoffed. “Let’s get out of here, Chidori. Leave Takaya to his
plaything.”
“What the hell did you just call me?” Akechi pulled the trigger on his persona and summoned
Loki, performing megidolaon on the entire group. Chidori and Takaya managed to dodge, but
Jin stumbled backwards as the blast hit him with full force.
“You’ve got a temper on you,” Jin snapped, turning around and running. Chidori sighed and
ran after him.
“You scared them off,” Takaya observed. “How fascinating.”
“I’m not your toy.” Akechi pointed his evoker back toward is head. “Get the hell out of here,
or next time, I won’t miss.”
“Ignore Jin, he’s just jealous,” Takaya said, which was the most absurd thing Akechi had ever
heard. “Besides, I had a few questions of a more personal nature for you.”

“I’m not answering a damn thing unless you finally tell me something about you. What’s
your relation with the Kirijo Group?”
“Very well.” Takaya leisurely sat down on the sidewalk, inspecting his revolver. “I was once
a homeless orphan like yourself–”
“I’m not homeless.”
“A dormitory is hardly a home, but I digress. The Kirijo Group took me in and helped me to
become something more.”
“That’s vague,” Akechi said disdainfully. “Care to share a little more?”
“I think it’s your turn now, actually.” Takaya aimed the gun at Akechi. Akechi tensed. “What
happened when you were split up from the rest of the group?”
“How did you know about–”
“I have my ways, but it’s my turn to ask questions.” Takaya tilted his head, smiling gleefully.
“So? What happened?”
“It tried to kill me. Satisfied?”
“There’s no need to be coy. I won’t judge.”
“I’m sure you have your theories, but if you get to be vague with your responses, I have the
right to be vague as well. Are you done now?”
“No. I believe that was just your question, so I get to ask another.” Akechi cursed himself
inwardly. “How exactly did it try to kill you?”
“Why the hell do you care?”
“I can’t be concerned about a business partner?” Takaya narrowed his eyes. “Now answer my
question.”
“We are not–”
Takaya clicked the safety off of his gun. Akechi froze.
“A question for a question, an answer for an answer,” Takaya whispered. “That is the game
we are currently playing. You owe me an answer.”
Akechi clenched his fingers around his own evoker. “It tried to drown me in a bathtub.”
“Chidori sensed no specific presence of a shadow in the room with you,” Takaya said. “How
did it drown you if you were the only one in the room?”
So Chidori had an ability similar to Fuuka’s. Good to know.
“It’s my turn for a question.”

“Even if this were my next question, you already wasted your turn on asking why I cared.
However, you’ll recall that my initial question required exact details. Your details were not
exact.”
Akechi set his jaw. “It manipulated my thoughts to make me lethargic enough to drown
myself. Next question.” Akechi was careful not to phrase that last part in question form.
Takaya would undoubtedly use it against him.
“Was it frightening?”
Takaya was a massive creep. Akechi hated himself for even thinking he’d get any useful
information out of him.
Then again, without Takaya, Akechi might have never uncovered the secrets Mitsuru was
hiding about the cause of the Dark Hour.
“No.” Akechi stared at Takaya without wavering. “It wasn’t. What exactly did the Kirijo
group do to you when they took you in?”
Takaya’s grin widened. “Oh, experiments and the like. They wanted to inject artificial
potential into humans, which is how I have a persona of my own. I barely survived the
process.” Takaya stood up. “This has been an enjoyable conversation, but I’m afraid Jin will
be irritable if I linger too long. Farewell.”
“I’m not done–” With the thundering sound of gunfire, a bullet whizzed past Akechi’s ear.
Akechi’s heart stuttered.
“My apologies.” Takaya lazily put his gun away. “My hand slipped.”

Chapter 15: July 9–13, 2009
Chapter Summary

Some Dorm Shennanigans
And maybe a lore dump?

Chapter Notes

tw: ptsd, self-loathing, drowning, nightmare, references to unethical experimentation on
children :(

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Akechi was sinking. Water surrounded him on all sides. His soaked clothes weighed him
down as he tried to swim toward the surface.
A cold hand grabbed Akechi’s ankle. Akechi swam harder.
“Join me,” his mother’s voice echoed as the hold on his ankle tightened. “Goro, dear, come
now.”
Akechi opened his mouth to protest, but more burning water filled his lungs. He continued
swimming.
Another hand grabbed his other ankle. “Join us in hell where you belong,” Isshiki Wakaba’s
voice snarled.
No matter how hard Akechi kicked, the surface didn’t get any nearer. More hands grabbed
hold of him, pulling him further and further down. His vision began fading.
He was going to die. He was going to–
A hand came from above. Akira was swimming toward him, holding out both of his hands.
“Grab on,” he said. “I’ve got you!”
Akechi reached out for a moment.
Then, he retracted his hand. Akira didn’t know what he was offering. Akria didn’t deserve to
hold his bloodstained hands.

“Akechi!” Akira screamed. “Akechi, you stupid–”

Akechi woke up.
Akechi stared dully at his ceiling, feeling completely normal. The dream had been utterly
bizarre, but his heart rate hadn’t elevated like it sometimes did. Akechi rolled over and
glanced at the clock on his bedside table.
It was only two in the morning.
Akechi sighed and closed his eyes again. He might as well try to get some sleep, seeing as he
had only gone to bed an hour ago after his unfortunate encounter with Takaya.
Akechi wasn’t sure how long he lay there, his eyes closed, staying perfectly still. He did
know it was long enough for him to ascertain that he was never going to fall asleep.
Akechi sat up and exited his dorm. He was somewhat hungry, and nobody would care if he
snuck into the lounge for an apple. Maybe the excursion would make him tired enough to
actually get some rest. Although, from past experience, it was unlikely.
When Akechi reached the bottom of the stairs, Sanada was already sitting on top of the
kitchen counter, eating some cereal. His eyes widened when Akechi approached, his spoon
halfway through his mouth.
“Hello there, Sanada-senpai,” Akechi said. “What keeps you up this late?”
“Oh.” Sanada quickly swallowed his mouthful of cereal. “I kind of lost track of time, and
then I got hungry. How about you?”
“The same, I’m afraid,” Akechi lied.
“Uh huh,” Sanada said, looking doubtful, but he shrugged. “Well, help yourself.”
Akechi took a banana from the fruit bowl, peeled it, and took a bite. Sanada continued to eat
his cereal contentedly, but there was a strange look on his face.
“If you have a question, you might as well ask,” Akechi said, trying not to sound too irritable.
“It’s better than letting it fester.”
“I don’t want to pry,” Sanada said in a way that meant it was precisely what he wanted to do.
“You wouldn’t be the first,” Akechi sighed. “As long as you don’t have me at gunpoint, I
don't care.”
Sanada stared at him. “Wha–”
“That was a joke,” Akechi hastened to interrupt.

“You promise?” Sanada asked, pointing his spoon at Akechi threateningly. It wasn’t that
intimidating. “You didn’t sound like you were joking.”
“I promise, I was joking.” Akechi rolled his eyes. Technically, he had only been joking. He
had merely made a sarcastic quip about a real event. Practically the same thing, really.
“Right.” Sanada didn’t sound very convinced. “Anyway, this is kind of awkward to ask, but
are you doing alright?”
“I’m fine, Sanada-senpai.”
“See, I feel like you get overly polite when something isn’t alright,” Sanada said. “Also,
you’ve known me long enough to start calling me Akihiko. Nobody calls me Sanada.”
Akechi was beginning to call a great many people by their first name, recently. “Well,
Akihiko, I assure you that I am fine.”
“I know something happened last night,” Akihiko said.
Akechi took another bite out of his banana to hide his frustration. “Yes. We defeated two
powerful shadows.”
“You know that’s not what I meant.”
Akechi didn’t say anything.
“Look, you don’t have to tell me. But tell me that you have someone to talk to. Because I
know you didn’t just take a bath.”
“Don’t you think you’re jumping to conclusions?”
“Yukari showered, and she didn’t come out of it coughing up water and clawing at her own
face,” Akihiko said. “And before you ask me how I know, I asked her, and she told me.”
“Look, it doesn’t matter,” Akechi said. “It’s over. It’s done. I survived, so who gives a damn
what happened?”
“Surviving is never the hardest part.”
Akihiko’s voice was deathly serious, and Akechi fell silent as Sanada finished off the last of
his cereal.
“I know what it’s like to think you have to deal with everything on your own. Talk to
someone. Please.” He slid off of the countertop and left his bowl on the counter. “I’ll deal
with it in the morning. I need to sleep.”
Akihiko left, and Akechi threw away the rest of his banana. He wasn’t very hungry anymore.
He picked up Akihiko’s bowl and began washing it.

Akihiko didn’t know what he was talking about. When did being vulnerable with anyone ever
end well? Akechi was fine on his own. He had been for years.

A couple days later, the chairman came over and summoned everyone to the command room.
Yamagishi said that she had information to share as well, after the chairman left.
Mitsuru explained to Ikutsuki everything that occurred on the night of the full moon. Ikutsuki
listened patiently. When she was done, he nodded.
“I see. It seems Fuuka was right. They are getting stronger. However, it’s not all bad news. I
actually came today to be the deliverer of some quite excellent news.”
“Oh yeah?” Iori asked. “What is it?”

Ikutsuki cackled as everyone else chased him out of the room with their deadpan stares.

“Well, of course.” Ikutsuki chuckled. “He lives in the dorm you’re moving to.”
Amada’s expression was one of pure betrayal. “You never told me you lived in a high school
dorm.”
“Can you blame me?” Akechi asked in exasperation. “Taken out of context, it’s extremely
inappropriate. I’m stunned you’re moving in too.”
“Of course, he is,” Ikutsuki said. “He has the potential.”
That made Akechi feel so much better.
“Well, I guess that’s fair,” Amada conceded. His lack of protesting about the context meant
he knew more about the Dark Hour than he was letting on. “But I wish you hadn’t lied to
me.”
“I’m sorry.” Akechi was sorry he hurt Amada’s feelings. He wasn’t sorry for not causing a
rumor that Akechi was being taken advantage of by a bunch of high schoolers. “But you
should also keep your involvement at the high school dorm quiet.”
“Akechi-kun’s right,” Ikutsuki said. “We wouldn’t want people getting the wrong idea.”
“Um, right.” Amada nodded. “Should we get going?”
“Couldn’t have said it better myself!”

The walk was long and awkward. Akechi didn’t feel comfortable talking with Amada as he
normally did in the presence of Ikutsuki, and Amada clearly felt much the same. Akechi also
still wanted to kill Ikutsuki, which put a damper on things.
They walked past Gekkoukan High, and Akechi spotted Arisato, Yukari, Iori, and Akihiko all

Yukari saw Ikutsuki first. “Mr. Chairman!”
Ikutsuki looked surprised, but there was no way he had been so inattentive of his

Amada took that as his cue, and Akechi followed him as he approached the group.
“Um, hello,” Amada said, suddenly sounding rather shy.

Akihiko looked as though he’d seen a ghost. He looked at Yukari in surprise. “You know

“Oh, I heard about that,” Yukari said. “Something about his parents…”
“My mom… she died in an accident two years ago,” Amada interrupted loudly, obviously

It seemed that Akechi had more in common with Amada than he had initially realized.
“At the moment, one of his distant relatives is paying for his school expenses,” Ikutsuki said,

“He’s a new candidate?” Akihiko asked, looking like he was being told he was going to a

Iori looked equally confused. “Isn’t he a bit young?”
“So you are roommates with Junpei!” Amada exclaimed, giving Akechi a small glare.
“Are you sure it’s the best idea?” Yukari asked.

Everyone fell silent, but Amada was still looking at Akechi scornfully. “And you’re

Akechi sighed. “Yes.”
Amada turned toward Akihiko with stars in his eyes. “It’s an honor to meet you, Sanadasenpai! I’ve heard you haven’t lost a boxing match yet!”
“Oh, um, it’s nice to meet you too,” Akihiko said, looking lost in thought.
Ikutsuki wasn’t heading directly to the dorms, so Amada and Akechi had to part ways. Before
he left, however, Amada whispered fiercely into Akechi’s ear.
“Tell Sanada a bunch of cool stuff about me, or I’ll never forgive you for lying.”
With that sort of threat hanging over Akechi’s head, how could he say no?

“You’ll like Amada-kun, Akihiko-senpai,” Akechi said that evening. “He’s very…
determined.”
Akihiko nodded. “Yeah. I bet.”

The next day, Akechi tried again. “Amada-kun is also very athletic,” he told Akihiko during
breakfast. “I bet he’ll develop a training regime if he joins SEES.”
Akihiko wore a look of confusion. “That’s… cool?”

As they got ready to depart for Yakushima on a boat, Akechi gave it one last shot. He
approached Akihiko, who was leaning against the railings, looking out at the water.
“Amada-kun is a good friend, as well,” he said. “He’s one of the best friends I’ve ever had.”
Akihiko still looked confused. “Akechi… do you have a crush on Amada?”
“What?” Akechi asked, thoroughly taken aback. “No! Of course not!”
The idea of having a crush on Amada was absolutely absurd. He was still mentally nineteen
years old. Amada was literally eleven.
“Oh, does Akechi-kun have a crush on somebody?” Iori asked, popping out of nowhere and
wearing a sly grin. “Who’s the lucky girl?”
“He’s Amada,” Akihiko said.

Iori’s eyes widened. “Oh. I didn’t realize you liked boys, Akechi-kun.”
“First of all, I am eleven and have no interest in romance at the moment,” Akechi snapped.
“Second of all, even if I were interested in romance, I have no romantic feelings toward
Amada-kun. Third of all, yes, I like boys. Don’t be weird about it, Iori.”
“I didn’t say anything!” Iori protested.
“You were thinking it.”
“Hey, don’t go putting thoughts in my brain,” Iori protested.
“Sorry, Akechi-kun,” Akihiko said. “I didn’t mean to make you uncomfortable. You’ve just
been talking about him a lot recently.”
“No, I understand where the confusion came from.” Akechi pinched the bridge of his nose.
“Don’t tell him I told you this, but Amada wanted me to compliment him in front of you so
you’d think he was cool.”
Iori burst out laughing. Akihiko’s expression became grim.
Akechi pulled out his phone and texted Amada.
Akechi Goro: I’m never doing favors for you again.

Akechi rolled his eyes.

“My life is not a serial drama,” Akechi shut his phone and marched away from Iori. Iori only

In fairness, the entire situation was somewhat amusing, if Akechi could look past how

Mitsuru’s vacation home was enormous.
Giant marble columns lined the side of the front hall, which was decorated with floral
arrangements and expensive furniture. Iori stepped near an expensive-looking vase, and
Yukari immediately grabbed him by the arm and yanked him back.
It looked like it came straight out of Shido’s palace, conveying power, grandeur, and status
with only one room. It was the sort of power that Shido had only dreamed of having, and here
it was, all at Mitsuru’s fingertips.
“It’s like we’re in an episode of the lifestyles of the rich and fabulous,” Iori muttered, looking
up at the chandelier hanging from the ceiling.
Two maids went up to Mitsuru and bowed. “Welcome home, Milady.”
One maid looked over at the gaggle of shocked children standing behind Mitsuru. “You must
be Mitsuru-san’s schoolmates, correct? Welcome to the Kirijo Family Vacation home. Follow
me, I’ll show you to your rooms.”
“Vacation home?” Yukari whispered under her breath, sounding faint. “Are we at the right
place?”
“Dude, real-life maids,” Iori said.
“I knew Mitsuru’s family was powerful, but this is more than even I was expecting,”
Yamagishi said, looking almost intimidated by the prospect.
Everyone began following the maids. If this was only the front hall, Akechi was intrigued to
see what their rooms would look like.
They didn’t get very far before an older man came walking in his direction. He was wearing a
tailored suit, and he held himself in a way that only a man in great authority could. He
stopped in front of Mitsuru, saying nothing.
Mitsuru nodded unsmilingly. “Father.”
Kirijo Takeharu left without another word. That brief but simultaneously revealing exchange
did nothing to boost Akechi’s confidence in the man.
Yukari and Yamagishi expressed their astonishment at Kirijo being Mitsuru’s father. Iori, in
his typical fashion of stupidity, asked, “He’s not going to make us walk the plank, is he?”

Was that a reference to the eyepatch covering Kirijo’s left eye?
Akechi forced an amused smile off of his face. It was the sort of stupid joke Akira might
make, although he wouldn’t have said it so unironically.
“Don’t be stupid,” Akihiko muttered, looking around as though he might jump out at them at
any minute.
Mitsuru still looked perturbed, looking behind her where her father had disappeared to.
“We’re not going to be here long, but make yourself at home.”
“Sweet!” Iori cheered as they resumed following the maids. “Let’s all hit the beach! It’s right
there; we can rush on down.”
“Give us some time to change first,” Yukari said. “But I wouldn’t mind going out for a swim

“Did you see the water?” Yamagishi asked. “I’ve never seen anything so beautiful in my
life.”
“You guys can waste your time to change, but I’m heading straight there!” Iori turned around,
probably ready to run through the house like a buffoon.
“You’re not wearing a bathing suit either!” Yukari exclaimed.
“What do you think my shorts are?” Iori asked.
Without another word, Iori sprinted away, nearly running headfirst into a stone column.
Everybody watched him with dumbfounded expressions.
“If he breaks something, do not give him the funds to pay it back,” Yukari told Arisato. “I
know you could afford it, but don’t.”
“I’d never,” Arisato said.
“Good.”

As Akechi suspected, their bedrooms were at least three times the size of their dorm rooms.
A queen sized bed sat against the back wall, and a fancy sofa and table sat in the middle of
the room. For a moment, Akechi wondered if he had been given the right room, but when he
checked Akihiko’s room, he found that it was an exact replica.
Akechi changed into his bathing suit and joined the others on the beach. The girls hadn’t
arrived quite yet, but Arisato and Akihiko were applying sunscreen to their faces.
Iori was glaring at them with looks of contempt. “Sunscreen is the enemy of all happiness,”
he said. “I refuse to put any on my face.”

“Don’t complain if you get sunburnt, then,” Akechi said, squeezing a large glob onto his own

Iori’s eyes widened. “Skin cancer?”

“But babes hate it when men sunscreen!” Iori protested.
“Then, they aren’t worth your time.” Akechi rubbed the sunscreen around his nose. “They

Akechi gave Iori his signature death glare.

Akihiko was right about one thing. Running on the sand was exceedingly difficult. Even as

In the final stretch of the race, Mitsuru broke into a furious sprint. Akihiko tripped on the

Akechi beat Arisato and Yukari, but he wasn’t sure Arisato was working at his full capacity.
Arisato ran around Tartarus nonstop. He should have more endurance.

“Yes. I’m sorry for bringing in such a big crowd.”

“I heard that they all found out about the incident, but not because you told all of them

Now that Mitsuru thought about it, no. The only time she could think of is when she begged

For some reason, those words were enough for Mitsuru. She was right to trust her father.

Akechi sat on one of the sofas in Kirijo Takeharu’s office, staring at him with an innocent

“I pray that this recording reaches safe hands…”
Yukari sucked in a breath.
“My employer has become obsessed with a loathsome idea. This experiment should have

The footage was clearly old, and the events of the accident made the scientist’s voice sound

Akechi supposed that was Ikutsuki’s “good authority” on why it was important to destroy all

Akechi bit back a sigh. It didn’t matter if the door was open or not. Kirijo was one of the
most powerful men in Japan, and certainly the most powerful person in this house. If he
wanted to do something to Akechi, he could easily do so without any consequences.

Akechi clenched his jaw. If Kirijo wanted to fool Akechi into trusting him, he had another

“I’ll bear that in mind, Kirijo-san.”

“That’s very astute of you, Akechi,” Ikutsuki said. “I’ll try to find out more, especially if it

“One more thing, if you don’t mind,” he said.

“So why didn’t you tell her?”
“I guess you could say I was too afraid to tell her,” Ikutsuki said.
That wasn’t satisfying at all.
“With all due respect, you owe her an apology,” Akechi said coldly. “She deserved to know

The next morning, everybody once again found themselves out on the beach. Aigis joined

“Do we have any missions for today?” Aigis asked Iori of all people.

Akechi begrudgingly followed the rest of the girls into the water. Iori was already swimming

“What activity are we engaging in?” Aigis asked, somehow managing to swim.
“Uh, volleyball, duh,” Iori said. He tossed the ball into the air and hit it with his palm. It

The beach ball soared far over Iori’s head and landed in the water a few meters away.
“Oops,” Mitsuru said.

“Fine, I’ll get it.”
Akechi swam to the beach ball and grabbed hold of it. It was difficult to keep his head above

The human mind was a strange and dangerous thing. For a moment, surrounded by nothing

Water filled his lungs.
Why do you resist? Embrace your desire…
Not again. He didn’t want to be here. He didn’t want to feel this helpless ever again.
Akechi began furiously kicking his legs, trying to find his way back up to the surface of the

in. Was he even swimming in the right direction?
Akechi pulled his head above water just as he saw Iori of all people swim up to him. He
coughed furiously, trying to expel the feeling of death from his lungs.

“I was fine.”

“I’m not a trauma victim,” Akechi snapped.
“You almost drowned,” Akihiko said.
“I was caught by surprise.”
Yamagishi dropped the towel around Akechi’s shoulders. Akechi was too tired to shrug it off.

“Aigis told us you were having a panic attack in the water,” Yukari said. “Is that true?”

“Kirijo-san!” Akechi said, his surprise not completely ingenuine. “What are you doing here?”

“My daughter sent me to check on you,” Kirijo said stiffly. “She apologizes for not giving

“Oh, well, in that case”--Akechi lined up his shot, hoping to bounce a solid ball off of a

“Is that why you are playing a two-player game on your own?” Kirijo asked as Akechi hit the
cue ball. The balls collided as planned, but the striped ball barely missed the pocket. Akechi

Akechi walked to the side of the table where the cue ball was nearest. “Well, you can tell

Well, Akechi couldn’t lie and say that he didn’t want to play against someone else.
“Very well, Kirijo-san,” Akechi said. “I’ll reset the game.”
Kirijo won their game by a small margin. It was the first time anyone had beaten Akechi in
pool in a very long time. It was honestly a little bit refreshing.
It was also infuriating.
“Good game, Kirijo-san,” Akechi said. “Perhaps I’ll beat you next time.”
“You were a strong opponent,” Kirijo said, putting his cue stick away. Somehow, it didn’t
sound like he was lying or humoring Akechi. “But your strength is your weakness. You were

“I’m afraid cautiousness is a weakness of mine,” Akechi said. “But I will bear what you said
in mind.”

Akechi stopped himself from telling Kirijo that he didn’t have any friends.

Why wouldn’t the pain stop? Why wouldn’t it-Takaya lifted his foot, and Akechi reached for his pocket with his other shaking hand. If he
could just grab one of the healing items in his pockets, he could maybe get the upper hand.

power?”

Shinjiro dodged out of the way in the nick of time.

If Akechi didn’t do something, Shinjiro might die.
With a burst of adrenaline, Akechi shoved the soma into his mouth. Instantly, his wounds

This time, the burst of almighty magic that followed was significant enough to weaken

tell the others what happened.”
“I need to kill–”
“You need to tell the others.”

“And should I tell them about your involvement with Strega?!” Akechi shouted, still burning

Shinjiro’s expression darkened. “Is that what you’ve been thinking this whole time? That I

Shinjiro swore under his breath. “Akechi, listen to me,” he said. “I don’t work with Takaya

The words shouldn’t have comforted Akechi.
But they did.
As Akechi caught his breath, Shinjiro gave Akechi a severe look. “Now, back to the subject

Akechi had no intention of revealing his weakness to the others. He could deal with Takaya

“I’m fine,” Akechi said, glaring down at his bloodstained shirt. He’d need to buy a new one.

Shinjiro relaxed. “Good.” his expression hardened. “If I let go of you, you’re not going to
start chasing Takaya, are you?”
Akechi rolled his eyes. “He could be anywhere by now, thanks to you.”
Shinjiro let go of him and returned Akechi’s sword to him. Akechi turned around and
marched into the dorms without another word. He had to clean up the blood all over his
things before anyone else noticed.
Hermit Arcana: Rank 5

Aragaki Shinjiro: Have you told them?

“It’s Shinji’s birthday today,” Akihiko told Akechi two days later before he left for summer
classes.
Akechi frowned. He hadn’t known that, and he hadn’t realized that Akihiko knew enough
about Akechi’s relationship with Shinjiro to mention it to him. “Why are you telling me
this?”
“You owe him for saving your life,” Akihiko said.
“He told you about that?” Akechi asked, feeling sick at the thought of Akihiko knowing just
how weak he was.
“Not the details, just that he saved you from a tough scrape,” Akihiko said, shoving a protein
bar into his mouth. “In Shinji speak, that means you were probably half dead.”
Akihiko wasn’t exactly wrong.
“Just visit him and wish him a happy birthday or something.” Akihiko shouldered his
bookbag. “And thank him if you haven’t already.”
“I hope you take your own advice,” Akechi said.
“He’s my best friend. He would just think I’m a sap.” Akihiko started for the door. “Just
make him feel appreciated. It’ll be good for him.”
Akechi ran his fingers through his hair as Akihiko left. He was right about one thing: Akechi
did owe Shinjiro. Birthday wishes would hardly repay a life debt, but it might be enough to
pay him back for the candy bar from the other day.

Akechi had never found himself buying birthday presents before, and he had a feeling that
Shinjiro wouldn’t appreciate anything too over the top. A card would be too disingenuous,
but Akechi didn’t know where to begin when it came to Shinjiro’s preferences. Should he
give Shinjiro something that might help him on the streets? What was Shinjiro’s living
situation?
After searching the mall and finding nothing satisfactory, Akechi finally stopped by the drug
store and bought some healing items. Then, so he didn’t seem too practical, he purchased a
candy bar from the nearby vending machine.
Akechi shoved his gifts into a small gift bag and stared at it with an overwhelming feeling of
embarrassment. He should have called Emiko and asked how she managed to pull off giving
Ken such a successful birthday celebration without shame, but she was at the beach. He
didn’t want to disturb her vacation.
To avoid Shinjiro getting angry at him for going to the dangerous back alley, Akechi pulled
out his phone and called him. After a few rings, Shinjiro answered, much to Akechi’s relief.
“What’s up?” Shinjiro asked.
“I wanted to speak with you in person, but I didn’t think you’d want me to find you,” Akechi
said. “I’m sitting outside of Paulownia Mall.”
“Sure.” Shinjiro hung up, and fifteen minutes later, Akechi saw his hunched form amidst the
other pedestrians.
As Shinjiro approached Akechi, Akechi hid his gift bag behind his back, feeling ridiculous.
Ridiculous for having gone as far as getting a gift bag to begin with, and ridiculous for hiding
it behind his back like a toddler.
“What’s going on?” Shinjiro asked, looking around. “You’re not doing something stupid
again, are you?”
“Not in the way you’re thinking,” Akechi said.
Shinjiro did not look impressed by that response. Akechi decided to get this embarrassing
affair over with before he did something truly foolish.
“Akihiko-senpai told me it was your birthday, and I owe you quite a bit,” Akechi said, putting
on his prince face. It was the only way he wasn’t going to melt from mortification. “I know
this won’t make us even, but Happy Birthday, Shinjiro-san!”
Akechi thrust the gift bag into Shinjiro’s hands and bowed.
Shinjiro took the gift, wearing a perplexed expression. “Are you possessed?”
“I’m not possessed, idiot,” Akechi snapped, getting rid of his polite facade now that the
present was in Shinjiro’s hands. The August sun was suddenly oppressive. “Just open the
damn gift. Or don’t. This was Akihiko’s idea, you know.”

Shinjiro relaxed and nodded. Akechi was quite sure he heard him mutter, “There he is,” as he
pulled out the healing items from the gift bag.
“I hope you bought some of these for yourself,” Shinjiro said as he put the items into his
pockets. “Seeing how often you’re almost dying.”
“I’m not stupid, I always have something on me,” Akechi said.
“Good.” Shinjiro pulled out the chocolate bar and gave Akechi an unimpressed expression.
“Isn’t this the exact same thing I tried to give you for your birthday?”
“I’m not creative,” Akechi said. “People often give people things they enjoy as well, so it

“Fair enough,” Shinjiro said. “Lucky for you, you’re right.” He tore off the wrapper and took

Akechi didn’t have a good response for that, so he decided to ignore that final comment as he

“You’re stealing my bag?” Shinjiro asked.
“It was my bag, and I’m saving it for later,” Akechi said.

“How old are you now?” Akechi asked, realizing he didn’t know how old Shinjiro was.
Wasn’t that one of the first things you learned about a new friend?

Akechi returned to the Velvet Room after one of his runs. The shadows in Tartarus were only

Akechi began to perform some much-needed fusions. Much to his annoyance, personas of the

Akechi supposed Igor had a small point. He didn’t bond with someone unless he talked to

“I thought I would take you to the park today, Theodore,” Akechi said when he was done

On their way to the train station, the insufferable booming of a campaign speech grated

As Theodore led him further away, Akechi couldn’t let Shido just go about his life as if he

“FUCK YOU!”
Shido’s expression shifted into one of irritation for a fraction of a moment, and Akechi

“It’s the film festival,” Minato said. “They’re playing a bunch of movies with like a specific
theme every day for the next week.”
Akechi thought he remembered Ken bringing that up. “What’s today’s theme?”
“Nature documentaries,” Minato said, squinting at a distant sign. “Do you mind?”
Akechi had watched a fair few of those with Akira, who said he liked to watch the animals
work together. Akechi had expected him to cry when the animals got killed by predators, but
Akira just nodded and said the predators needed to survive too.
Akechi had a feeling this experience would not be the same.
“I don’t mind at all,” Akechi said. Minato only nodded.
The documentaries were interesting enough. Akechi and Minato sat next to each other
without exchanging a word for hours as Akechi learned about the importance of teamwork
when taking down large prey. He was also emotionally manipulated by cute baby animals
that would then die gruesomely.
When they finally left the theater, Minato glanced at him tentatively. “What’d you think?”
“They were fun,” Akechi said. “Thank you for taking me.”
“Oh, you’re welcome.” Minato looked away. Akechi’s phone buzzed. “You should check
that.”
Akechi pulled out his phone to see multiple texts from Iori.
Iori Junpei: Can u describe that Chidori girl for me
Iori Junpei: See someone who might look like her in the station

Iori Junpei: Red hair white dress
Iori Junpei: Oh wait nvm
Iori Junpei: Ignore all these messages
Minato looked over Akechi’s shoulder. “Huh.”
“If he’s let the actual Chidori fool him, I’m going to be deeply annoyed,” Akechi said as an
understatement. He would actually kill him.
“He’s trying his best,” Minato said. “You should give him another chance.”
Maybe Akechi had been a little harsh toward Iori. He had been slightly less insufferable
recently. And Akechi would never rank up Iori’s social link if he didn’t at least pretend to be
nicer.
That was a problem for later. For now, Akechi was going to get answers. He called Iori.
“Oh, hey, Akechi-kun,” Iori said. “Sorry for those texts. I thought that I saw Chidori, but
she’s really some other chick who looks similar. I kind of freaked her out.”
Akechi pinched the bridge of his nose. Only Iori would walk up to a random stranger and
demand to know if she was secretly a member of a mercenary band.
Unless the actual Chidori lied to him, and Junpei believed her.
Minato gave Akechi a nudge. Since when was Minato qualified to give friendship advice?
Akechi bit back the urge to groan.
“I’m glad you’re not hurt,” Akechi said stiffly. “Maybe you would like to go to the movies
with me tomorrow?”
“For the film festival?” Iori sounded surprised. “Sure, man.”
“Sounds good.” Akechi hung up. Minato was right; that conversation would have been ten
times more agonizing in person.
“Good job,” Minato said.
“Oh, shut up.”
Death Arcana: Rank 5

Junpei was just minding his business, grieving the approaching end of summer vacation,
when he saw this girl drawing in the middle of the station. She wore this weird white dress
and frilly headband, and her hair was such a startling shade of red that it would be hard not to
notice her.

Curious, and admittedly hoping to maybe score a date, Junpei began to approach her. As he
made his way over to her, however, a small memory unlocked in his mind. Hadn’t Akechi
described a girl who looked just like this as the third member of Strega? What was her name
again, Chidori?
Junpei whipped out his phone and sent a few frantic texts to Akechi for confirmation.
Oh wait… wasn’t Akechi was watching movies with Minato? There was no way he’d be
hearing any message notifications in the quiet theater.
In that case, it was up to Junpei. Easy enough. Junpei would just walk up to her and ask,
straight out.
“Get out of my way,” the girl said.
Junpei jumped, not prepared to be addressed first. “Huh?”
“You’re in my way,” she said. “Move.”
“Oh, um, sorry.” Junpei began walking away before he got a hold of his senses. What was he
doing, walking away like a coward? He was a man. He needed to face the situation head on!
Junpei spun around and marched right back toward the girl. She looked up at him with an
expression of annoyance, but he wasn’t going to let that deter him.
“I’m not interested in you,” she said.
“W-what?” Was he just… rejected? He hadn’t even asked her out yet! Not that he had been
planning to. There was no way he was going to accidentally ask a member of Strega out.
“You’ve returned to ask me on a date, did you not?” the girl asked.
“Um, no, actually,” Junpei said. He needed to regain control of this situation, and fast. “Are
you a member of Strega?”
The girl made a confused face. “Strega? Is that a game company?”
“No, not Sega,” Junpei said. Maybe he had made a terrible mistake. “Strega. They’re a bunch
of mercenaries that wander around during the Dark Hour.”
“What is the Dark Hour?” the girl asked, looking more and more unimpressed with Junpei.
“Is this some sort of pick-up line?”
“What, no!” Junpei was going about this all wrong. “I, um, what’s your name?”
“It’s Chiho.”
Chiho? That barely even sounded like the name Chidori! Maybe this was just some weird
sister of Chidori’s, and that’s why their descriptions were so similar. Or maybe she was just

completely unrelated. There couldn’t be only one red-haired girl in Japan with a white dress,
right?
“Oh, um, I’m sorry,” Junpei said sheepishly. He chuckled nervously. “This has all been one
massive misunderstanding. My friend described someone who liked kind of like you, and
um… No hard feelings?”
“Sure.” Chiho returned to her drawing. Junpei left, feeling beyond embarrassed. He sent
Akechi a quick text. A few hours later, Junpei sent another text just to make sure that Akechi
didn’t freak out. Akechi was pretty good at freaking out.
Sadly, Junpei received a call from Akechi anyway.
Less sadly, he got invited to the movies?
Akechi was really unpredictable. And weird.
At least Junpei had movies to look forward to tomorrow! What could go wrong?

“That was… that was… that was the saddest movie I’ve ever seen!”
Iori was crying. Tears rolled down Iori’s face, and Iori covered his eyes as they exited the
theater.
Akechi could not believe what he was seeing.
“Don’t look at me, Akechi,” Junpei said. “I’m indecent.”
“Sure,” Akechi said, not looking away.
The movie was about a kid who lived alone with his drunk father. The kid became close
friends with a girl in his class, and the girl encouraged him to emancipate. Just when the kid
had successfully emancipated, the girl died of some disease that she had had the entire time.
It was sad, but it didn’t make Akechi feel inclined to cry his eyes out. The entire ordeal was
borderline cliché.
Junpei sniffed. “Okay, I think I’m good now,” he said, scrubbing at his eyes. “Man, they
weren’t kidding when they said tear jerkers, huh?”
“I guess so,” Akechi said. “I suppose I was unlucky with the day I invited you.”
“Eh, you couldn’t have known,” Junpei said. He grinned. “It was a good movie. Thanks for
inviting me. I gotta admit, I was surprised that you bothered.”

“Yes, well, Minato said I should give you another chance,” Akechi said. “So consider this a
peace offering.”
“I’m all about peace offerings,” Junpei said cheerfully, wiping a few stray tears from his eyes.
“I’ll try not to let you down.”
Akechi nodded in approval. Maybe Junpei had the potential to rise in his estimation. “Also, I
appreciate that you remembered my description of Chidori. It really demonstrates that you
take these things seriously.”
“Of course, I do.” Junpei looked around. “The lookalike was around here, but I guess she
doesn’t live at the station.”
“Of course, she doesn’t,” Akechi said, rolling his eyes. “In the future, you should just ask for
her name instead of accusing her of being in Strega.”
“Yeah, I kind of figured that out too late,” Junpei said. “I’ll bear that in mind for next time.”
Temperance Arcana: Rank 2

It seemed that inviting people to the movies was a surefire way to rank up social links, and it
was the easiest possible way to go about it. All Akechi had to do was sit in a dark theater for
a few hours and then have a vaguely interesting conversation with the person he was with.
Unfortunately, that day, Ikutsuki was literally the only person available. He sat contentedly in
the lounge, reading some stupid book on fashion. Was this seriously the man who blamed
Akechi for his own actions?
Akechi was not going to invite Ikutsuki to a movie. There was no way he would do that to
himself. As a matter of fact, Akechi wasn’t going to pursue ranking up this manipulative
asshole at all. Ikutsuki wasn’t worth his time.
“Oh, Akechi-kun,” Ikutsuki said, finally looking up from his book while Akechi deliberated.
“I didn’t see you there. How can I help you?”
Damnit. Well, if Akechi was going to make conversation with him, Akechi was going to be
as productive as possible about it. The sooner he increased Ikutsuki’s social link rank, the less
he’d have to speak to him later.
Akechi sat down on the sofa. “I had a question for you, actually,” Akechi said, thinking
frantically for a good question to ask. “Have you heard of the trolley problem?”
It was a cliché ethical question, but maybe it would be enough for the forces of the universe
to deem it worth a rank up.
Ikutsuki closed his book and put it down on the nearby table. “Ah yes, I have. A trolley is
approaching five people trapped on the track, but you can flip a switch and have the trolley
change the track and kill one person. That’s the one you’re thinking of?”

“The very same,” Akechi said.
“It’s an interesting dilemma, isn’t it?” Ikutsuki asked. “What would you do, Akechi-kun?”
Akechi had caused several real-world trains to crash and hit onlookers, which made this
entire debate an uncomfortable subject for him. Why did he even bring it up?
Back when killing Shido was all that mattered, it all felt like a necessary cost. Besides, it
wasn’t as though all of those people on the train weren’t also as corrupt as the rest of
humanity.
But Akechi wasn’t living that life anymore. What would he do if he was faced with the actual
trolley problem?
“I’d divert the train,” Akechi said. He knew it was the popular decision, but it was the only
one that made sense, even if it put that one person’s death in your hands. “If you watch the
five people die, you might as well have killed them. The needs of the many outweigh the
needs of the few.”
It was strange that Akechi used to think otherwise. That Shido’s death was more important
than the lives of hundreds, maybe even thousands of people. Had Akechi really been that
selfish?
Of course he had been. Would he do it again, if he were in the same position?
Akechi pushed those thoughts from his mind. If he thought about it any further, he might
actually feel sick.
“Understandable,” Ikutsuki said with a nod. “But consider. If you do nothing, the tragedy will
be even more pronounced. People will call for trolleys to be safer, which will lead to more
lives saved in the future.”
It was brutal. Ikutsuki didn’t care about the one person on the other track. He only cared
about a vague number of people in the future. And yet, Akechi could understand exactly
where he was coming from. Humanity was messed up. They didn’t care about issues unless
the issue was dramatic enough to make them care.
It was still an unsettling prospect.
“That’s an interesting approach,” Akechi said diplomatically. He stood up. If he stayed in this
conversation for much longer, he might continue to think about all of the people he had
actually killed for such petty reasons.
“Are you alright, Akechi-kun?” Ikutsuki said. “You look pale.”
“I’m fine, Ikutsuki-san,” Akechi said. “I think I just need some rest.”
Akechi returned to his room and stared at the goldfish Emiko had gifted him. She didn’t
know who Akechi really was. Taiyaki didn’t know that he was owned by a killer. Nobody
knew.

Somehow, that thought was almost as terrifying as the number of lives he ruined.
Devil Arcana: Rank 6

After his disturbing realization, Akechi almost didn’t do anything the next day. But doing
nothing would only make him more miserable, and the best thing he could do was to just
forget his disturbing thoughts to begin with.
And how better to forget than to waste half of his day watching movies?
Emiko had only just started her summer homework, and her father had forbidden her from
leaving the house until it was completed.
Ken was also still finishing off the last of his summer homework; he wasn’t the fastest
worker and had a bad habit of zoning out while trying to work. Seeing as summer was rapidly
coming to a close, Akechi didn’t want to disturb him.
Lately, Ken was more and more irritable. Akechi didn’t know if it was the homework that
was bothering him or something else entirely, but it was unsettling. Ken wasn’t the happiest
person in the world, but he never looked so stormy either.
“What’s going on?” Akechi asked him.
“Nothing,” Ken said, glowering. “Just this homework.”
“You look like someone told you your dog died,” Akechi said bluntly. “Are you sure it’s just
homework?”
“Yes,” Ken said snippily.
Akechi decided not to pry, lest he accidentally destroy his friendship.
Left with few other alternatives, and not wanting to spend another day trapped in the same
building as Ikutsuki, who was still hanging around for some damn reason–Akechi refused to
admit it likely had to do something with Akechi’s argument with him–Akechi was forced to
pull out his phone and text Shinjiro.
By some miracle, Shinjiro didn’t laugh in Akechi’s face or brush Akechi off. Instead, he
agreed to meet Akechi in front of the cinema within the hour.
As Akechi approached the movie theater, a flash of red and white stood out in his peripheral
vision. He looked in that direction, reminded of Junpei’s false alarm for seeing Chidori in this
very same station.
Akechi blinked. The real Chidori was sitting on the edge of a flower bed and drawing in a
sketchbook. She looked up at Akechi and gave him a deadpan stare.
Had Junpei actually met Chidori? If so, Akechi was going to kill him.

Akechi marched up to Chidori. “What the hell do you think you’re doing here?” he asked.
Chidori sniffed. “I’m drawing,” she said. “Move, you’re in my light.”
Akechi opened and closed his mouth, baffled by her audacity. “That’s what you’re choosing
to focus on right now?”
Chidori glared at Akechi. “What are you going to do, kill me in broad daylight?”
“I could stay here in your precious light until the Dark Hour, and then I could kill you,”
Akechi said. “How does that sound?”
“I would just move,” Chidori said. “And if you followed me, I could tell security you were
stalking me. And if even that didn’t deter you, Jin could always kill you as soon as the Dark
Hour fell.”
Akechi grit his teeth. “As if he could.”
He didn’t want to admit it, but Chidori was right. He had no power in this situation.
“Would you get out of the way now?” Chidori asked, ignoring Akechi’s last statement
entirely.
“Were you the one talking to Junpei the other day?”
“Junpei?” Chidori asked.
“Tall, wears a baseball cap, acts like he has no braincells?”
“It doesn’t ring a bell.”
Akechi inhaled deeply, turned around, and walked away. He was not going to get charged for
assault because Strega liked tormenting him. He’d just warn Junpei that if the girl he met was
using a sketchbook, it was almost definitely Chidori. If Junpei wasn’t a fool, which,
unfortunately, he had a bad habit of being, he would leave Chidori alone after that.
“What took you so long?” Shinjiro asked as Akechi finally met him at their agreed spot.
“I ran into unpleasant company,” Akechi said. “Come on, let’s just go.”
Shinjiro raised his eyebrows challengingly, but he followed Akechi into the theater without
complaint. Akechi was grateful.

“Okay, what the hell is going on with you?”
Ken gave him the most pathetic look imaginable. “What’s that supposed to mean?”
Akechi put his hands on his hips, not caring if he was acting extremely condescending.
“You’ve been doing nothing but sitting at this table for the past few days,” Akechi said.

“You’ve finished your homework, and you still look like your dog died. What’s going on?”
“Nothing’s going on,” Ken said, crossing his arms. “I’m just in a bad mood.”
“I’m always in a bad mood, and you don’t see me sulking all day,” Akechi said.
“Yeah, instead you just fly into rages and break our television,” Ken snapped. “Why can’t
you leave me alone?”
“I have left you alone.” Akechi wasn’t daunted by Ken’s insult. “For two days we’ve barely
exchanged any words at all. But enough is enough, either tell me what’s wrong or get off
your ass and do something with your life.”
“You don’t understand what’s going on,” Ken muttered. It turned out lecturing someone who
was in a bad mood didn’t improve the situation.
“I could try if you would talk to me.”
“You wouldn’t understand.”
“Try me.”
Ken said nothing, glaring at the wall as if it were the one that had caused Akechi to start
nagging him.
“Look, I’m not your boss,” Akechi sighed. “I’m not going to demand to know every little
part of your life. But if you’re not going to talk to me, can’t you at least stop moping? That
doesn’t accomplish anything.”
“I’m not moping,” Ken said sulkily. “I was brooding.”
“Cooler word, same definition,” Akechi said shortly. “I understand the desire to hate
everything and everyone, but sitting for days on end accomplishes nothing.”
“I guess you’re right,” Ken said reluctantly. He didn’t look away from the wall.
Akechi wondered if he had just made a terrible mistake, but he was too tired to care. The film
festival was ending soon, and Akechi would be damned if he didn’t at least attempt to rank
up all of his social links during that time. He had taken Mitsuru to a movie the day before,
and Ken or Emiko were his only options.
Besides, Akechi hadn’t forgotten the first time Ken had invited him to see a movie. Akechi
needed to even the score before he continued to feel like he owed Ken. “Now, I was going to
invite you to the movies, but I guess you don’t want to go.”
Ken looked up at Akechi hopefully. “You’d be paying?”
“Yes.”

Ken stood up, visibly brightening. He still looked like he’d rather be brooding at his table,
but at least he wasn’t glaring at Akechi anymore. “I suppose I could use a distraction.”
“I knew you’d understand,” Akechi said dryly, hiding his relief.
Upon watching the movie, Akechi wished that Ken had been a bit more stubborn and refused
to come. Then, Akechi wouldn’t have had to watch this utter dumpster fire of a movie.
Between bad acting, poor camera work, and horrendous writing, Akechi would have been
better served staring at a blank television screen all day than to watch this travesty.
The worst part of all was the villain, who was some shortsighted fool who was willing to
destroy everything in his path just to kill some other antagonist. The movie depicted the
villain as some tragic hero who had just lost his way, instead of the heartless monster that he
really was. His death wasn’t some noble sacrifice. It was just a cowardly way to avoid the
consequences of his actions.
Needless to say, Akechi came out of that movie so angry that he wanted to punch the wall.
He would have too if it weren’t for Ken’s presence beside him.
“Are you okay?” Ken asked. “You look a little sick.”
Akechi wasn’t sick. He was absolutely furious, which is why it felt like his lungs were
closing in on him.
Akechi needed to pull himself together.
“I think I need to use the restroom,” Akechi said. “Give me a moment.”
Akechi entered the public restrooms, entered a stall, and had a silent panic attack.
Akechi wasn’t sure how long he sat on the toilet lid, trying to get his breathing under control.
He couldn’t let Ken see him like this. He had to get it together. Why was a stupid movie of all
things making him behave like this?
Had the Phantom Thieves seen him like that? Some tragic character to be pitied? Is that why
Akira wanted him to return to life? Because he thought Akechi had changed? Hadn’t he
realized that Akechi was no different than he was before? Just because his goals shifted
slightly, it didn’t mean that he wasn’t the same heartless–
“Goro?” Ken’s voice echoed from outside the stall. It sounded far away from the panic inside
Akechi’s own head. “Are you okay?”
“I’m fine,” Akechi said, his voice sounding grating against his own ears. “I’ll be out in a

“Okay…” Ken sounded doubtful, and Akechi covered his face with his hands. He couldn’t be
like this. He had to calm down.
Eventually, Akechi managed to take enough deep breaths that he felt as though he had
returned to reality. He exited his stall and washed his hands and face. The cold water

grounded him even more, and Akechi took a deep breath. He was fine.
His young, baby-faced reflection stared back at him. Even after months, it still looked wrong.
This wasn’t him. This face belonged to a shadow who had died long before Akechi sold his
soul to Shido.
Akechi’s hands shook, and he splashed more water furiously on his face. He dried it with a
coarse paper towel, scrubbing his face harder and more painfully than was probably
necessary.
He was fine.
Akechi stepped outside of the bathroom, where Ken was anxiously waiting.
“Sorry for taking so long,” Akechi said, putting on one of his winning smiles. “I hope I didn’t
make you too worried.”
“Um, it’s fine,” Ken said, still looking extremely concerned. “Are you alright? You didn’t
sound very good in there.”
“It must’ve been something I ate,” Akechi said with an amused tone. “We should probably
head back.”
“Yeah…”
As they walked back to the dorms, Ken continued to give Akechi concerned glances. Akechi
needed to divert his attention before he started asking more concerned questions.
“Did you like the movie?” Akechi asked.
“Um, it was fine,” Ken said. Akechi couldn’t blame him for his noncommittal response. The
movie had truly been mediocre at best. “I thought the villain character was kind of dumb,
though. I mean, he only wanted to get revenge on one guy. Why’d he bother killing all those
other people? How does that make him any better than the guy he wants revenge on?”
Akechi felt a strange sort of weariness come over him, but he let indignation rise in its stead.
Of course, Ken wouldn’t understand how it felt to feel trapped in a corner, only able to finish
what he started.
Then again, it wasn’t as though Ken was wrong. It was petty selfishness. Akechi had known
that for years. He’d only realized recently how foolish he’d been.
“You’re right, Amada-kun.” Ken made a startled noise. Akechi hastened to correct himself.
“Sorry. Ken-kun.”
“That’s alright,” Ken said. “Anyway, if I were that villain, I’d just have found a way to
privately kill the guy without any unnecessary bloodshed.”
How simple Ken made it all seem. Of course, it was always easier to make assumptions when
a situation was purely hypothetical. If Akechi wanted to avoid suspicion, he should play

along.
“Doing it at night would be a wise decision,” Akechi said. “And somewhere private. You’d
have to do it in such a way that any evidence of the crime wasn’t traced back to you.”
Ken hummed. “Yeah.” He looked subdued for a moment before his expression brightened.
“That reminds me of this episode of Featherman R the other day, the villain…”
Justice Arcana: Rank 5

Junpei knew what Akechi told him. That Chiho chick was probably Chidori, and Junpei had
probably been played like a fiddle. Admittedly, Junpei could admit to a weakness when it
came to beautiful women. But he wasn’t completely stupid! He’d talk to Chiho and find out
the truth for himself, regardless of what stupid Akechi said.
Assuming Junpei ever saw her again.
Fortunately for him, Junpei was having yet another existential crisis at Port Island Station–
was he seriously going to be a third-year in just a few semesters?--when he spotted Chiho
sitting at the same place Junpei saw her last time. She was still drawing in that sketchbook
too, looking completely unbothered by the idea that Junpei might have found out her identity
for real this time.
Junpei approached her cautiously. He’d have to be stealthy and subtle; none of this direct
questioning crap like last time. That was how he fell right into her trap.
“You again?” Chiho asked, giving him an unimpressed look.
She was probably trying to intimidate Junpei. Well, she was in for a surprise. Junpei had seen
many deadpan stares from Yuka-tan. And neither girls’ glares compared to Akechi’s angry
glower.
Seriously, how did an eleven-year-old manage to inspire the fear of death in Junpei?
“Oh, I’m surprised you remember me,” Junpei said, not letting his overconfidence show. That
would be impolite, and it would indicate that Junpei was wise to her scheme.
“I could say the same,” Chiho said, returning to her drawing. It didn’t look like much, just a
violent collection of scribbles, but Junpei wasn’t exactly an art person. Mitsuru would
probably be able to recognize the deep meaning in Chiho’s piece right away.
“Well, you’re pretty recognizable, with that dress, I mean.” Junpei chuckled nervously.
“Funny story, actually. My friend, um, he can remain nameless right now, actually. He insists
that this girl he hates has a sketchbook too. Weird coincidence, huh?”
Chiho’s unimpressed stare grew even more unimpressed. “Are you still accusing me of being
in Sega?”

“It’s Strega, and no! Of course, not. That would be rude.”
“Then, why are you here?”
“Well…” Think, Junpei! “I wanted to see what you were drawing! Yeah.”
“It’s not finished yet,” Chiho said. “I doubt you would understand it anyway.”
“Oh yeah?” Junpei asked. “I think that’s kind of cool, actually. It’s like having some sort of
secret language all to yourself. Except its art. Obviously.”
Chiho tilted her head, giving Junpei a slightly less annoyed expression. It looked more
calculating than anything else.
“I’ve never thought of it that way before,” she said.
“Maybe you could let me in on the secret?” Junpei asked. “After you’re done.”
Chiho didn’t say anything and just continued with her art. Junpei decided that he should leave
before she became suspicious of his sticking around.
She definitely didn’t seem like those other members of Strega. Takaya and Jin had been
scary, waving weapons around like they enjoyed hurting people. Chiho was just minding her
own business drawing.
Maybe Akechi was wrong. Maybe Chiho really was just some ordinary girl who liked to
dress in frilly white dresses. Sure, she was cold, but nothing about her seemed evil.
Junpei would keep investigating. In spite of what Yukari liked to say, he really was an ace
detective.

“Thank you for inviting me to this movie!” Emiko said cheerfully as they met up in front of
the theater.
The film festival was almost over, and Akechi was relieved that he could pause on social
gatherings after this one. While watching movies were (usually) a very relaxing social
activity, Akechi was tired of all of this inviting people to places. It wasn’t exactly his strong
suit.
“Think of it as a reward for finishing all of your summer homework in time,” Akechi said.
“I’m so embarrassed that I procrastinated on it for so long,” Emiko said mournfully as they
entered the building. “I bet you got it all done right away.”
“It doesn’t matter when it gets completed as long as it does get completed,” Akechi said.
“Besides, Ken procrastinated too. And a few high school students I know are still working on
theirs. Procrastination is perfectly normal.”

Ken used a spear with a good amount of proficiency.

The scribble really looked like one of the big shadows they fought at Tartarus, but Chiho

A sudden thought occurred to him. If Chiho really was Chidori, maybe she was trying to get

Focus! This situation could still be salvaged. Junpei would just feed Chidori with false

“We would take turns,” Junpei said. He was actually kind of having fun making this up as he

Junpei jumped again, and the hairs on the back of his neck pricked up when he heard

She disappeared into a nearby crowd without another word, leaving Junpei to deal with one

He wasn’t yelling. This meant that Junpei was heading in the right direction. Junpei nodded.

That was a new name. “Who’s Sakamoto?”
Akechi made a weird expression with his face. It was like anger, surprise, and pain all mixed

“A classmate,” he said. “An annoyingly loud classmate, by the way.”

Oh well. At least Akechi wasn’t screaming at him. He wasn’t even giving Junpei his

On the night of the full moon, Minato was nowhere to be seen.

Minato woke up with his wrists bound tightly together with rope. His face pressed against a

Blood, his brain helpfully supplied.
“Ow,” Minato intoned, because his head did hurt.
A girl who matched Akechi’s description of Chidori stood over him. She wore a scowl that

Minato made a confused noise. He wasn’t going to waste air on asking who she was or what

What happened again? Kazushi invited him to do a movie marathon at his house… Minato

And then...
He couldn’t remember. A kidnapping, presumably.

“I’m sure you have a way to communicate with your teammates,” Chidori said, not wasting

Especially with his kidnapper.

Didn’t Akechi say Chidori had a persona like Fuuka’s? Because Lucia had no attack

“Have you never heard of hostages?”

Mitsuru’s bus looked nothing like the Morgana bus. Where Morgana’s bus was dark and fat,

Mitsuru got into the driver’s seat and, without bothering to put on a seatbelt, she slammed her
foot against the gas. Everybody let out a mixture of gasps and yelps as they sped forward,
weaving in between cars that were stalled on the road during the Dark Hour.
Akechi discovered he was a terrible backseat driver. He was fine when they were on the road,
and Akechi never had any problems when Akira was driving the Morgana bus in Mementos.
But as soon as Mitsuru got the bus onto the train tracks, still driving at full speed, Akechi had

During the Dark Hour, club Escapade radiated the same eerie feeling that the love hotel
generated. Akechi had never been inside this specific club himself, but he had gone into a
couple during his time as Detective Prince. People were far more likely to spill critical details
pertaining to potential palace locations over a drink.

What would normally be a dark atmosphere was now not only dark, but coated in the green

surrounded by empty glasses.
A bartender. People looking for a good time. People drinking their lives away. All of them
reduced to their inevitable fate. A nameless coffin to be buried.
Upon entering the room with the control panel, they were faced with a shadow that was an

Without Minato, he battle was much harder than it could have been. While Akechi’s personas

So. Ow.

Minato was a foe.
