defensively proclaim that he never told Chidori that you were the leader. She must have
overheard.”
“Huh?” Junpei said. He hurried to Akechi’s side and bowed. “Don’t let Akechi take the
blame. It was really all just my fault. I was trying to be cool, but I was really just being
stupid. I’m sorry, Minato-kun.”
“Junpei…” Yukari said.
Minato only nodded. He opened his mouth to say something but closed it again.
Ken entered the living area with a tray of mugs full of hot chocolate. “My mom used to make
me hot chocolate when I was sad,” Ken said, placing the tray on the coffee table. “Shinjiro
helped me.”

There were enough mugs for everyone, but Akechi waited for everyone else to take their own
mugs before taking one of his own. He sat back down next to Yamagishi and sipped at the
hot, rich drink. Chocolate released endorphins, so it was no wonder that Akechi felt slightly
better.
They sat in silence as they drank. Eventually, Akihiko put his phone back into his pocket and
sat down with them, taking the mug that was left behind on the tray. “She’s been successfully
situated,” he said. “No unwelcome Strega visits.”
“They should keep a guard on that door,” Akechi said. “Not that it would do much against
Strega.”
“I’ll bring it up with Mitsuru.”
“Are you… alright?” Yamagishi asked Minato, who was staring into his mug of hot chocolate
with a strange expression on his face.
Minato nodded.
“You looked hurt pretty bad,” Yukari said. “I… I didn’t realize that Strega were that brutal.”
“They wanted me to call off the mission,” Minato said, his voice hoarse. He took another sip
from his mug. “You did good without me.”
“It wasn’t easy.” Junpei chuckled awkwardly. “Mitsuru-senpai really rose to the occasion.”
“It wasn’t the same without you, though,” Akihiko said immediately. “Try not to get
kidnapped again, got that?”
Minato’s lips quirked up, and he nodded.
Half an hour later, Mitsuru returned to the dorms. She surveyed the scene of tired children
bundled under blankets and holding empty mugs.
“You should all be getting to bed,” Mitsuru said. “We still have school tomorrow.”
Nobody moved.
“Would you like hot chocolate, Mitsuru-senpai?” Ken asked. “I think there’s still some water
left in the pot.”
Mitsuru sighed and sat down next to Akihiko. “Very well.”
Minato put his mug back down on the tray. “Thank you,” he said. Akechi wasn’t sure who he
was talking to. “My mom used to make us hot chocolate too.”

Chapter Notes

They ended up falling asleep on top of each other. When morning arrived, Akechi woke up
with his face squashed against Yamagishi’s shoulder, which was so mortifying that he quickly
stood up and hid himself in the kitchen.
Of course, the small amount of noise Akechi made spurred all of the others into action, like a
series of dominoes falling on top of each other. Soon, everybody was eating breakfast and
exchanging small talk. They had an unspoken agreement that they were going to pretend the
events of last night never happened.
Minato picked up the tray of dirty mugs and took them into the kitchen to clean. Junpei came
to his aid, drying the wet mugs and putting them back inside their cabinet. Minato was
somehow quieter than usual, but that was the only sign that anything was remotely amiss
with him.
“I’m sorry,” Akechi told Ken on their way to school. “It seems you chose to join us just when
things began to get worse.”
“I kinda figured things would be like this,” Ken said, shrugging him off. “I can handle it.”
Akechi didn’t believe it for a moment, but pushing never seemed to work with Ken. He
dropped the subject.
When Emiko joined them, she seemed to notice something was amiss, but perhaps on an
intuitive level, she didn’t press. Instead, she cracked more jokes than usual. Strangely
enough, they almost made Akechi feel better.
Later that day, when Akechi arrived home from his run, Shinjiro was making an unholy
racket in the kitchen. Akechi entered the kitchen to the sight of Shinjiro unpacking bags of

groceries.
“What are you doing?” Akechi asked.
“Making dinner,” Shinjiro said bluntly. “I’m still embarrassed by all of your dietary habits.
And last night was rough for you guys.”
Akechi vaguely remembered the promise of celebrations after each successful full moon
operation. In the midst of Strega and all the drama that kept cropping up, everyone had
forgotten. Shinjiro seemed to inadvertently be trying to bring the tradition back.
“Good luck,” Akechi said.
“You seriously think I’m going to be making such a big meal by myself?” Shinjiro
demanded. “Get back here, I need your help slicing the vegetables.”
“I can’t cook,” Akechi said.
“Then, learn.”
“I’m sure Yamagishi would love to help.”
“I already asked her, but she’s too busy trying to crack Jin’s code and take down Strega’s
website. She hasn’t had much luck.”
So Jin was the technical mastermind. Akechi wasn’t all that surprised.
“Fine.” Akechi sighed. It was clear Shinjiro wasn’t going to give up. Besides, it couldn’t hurt
to have some culinary skills. He stepped behind the counter and took a knife and cutting
board. “Lead the way.”
“That’s a meat knife,” Shinjiro said, snatching Akechi’s knife from his hand and replacing it
with one with a smooth edge.
If Shinjiro needed assistance, he chose the wrong person to help. Akechi was a hindrance
more than a help, and Shinjiro was tasked both with cooking the meal and preventing Akechi
from ruining the meal. They had to throw away a failed batch of rice after Akechi made it a
mushy mess that somehow landed on the floors and counters.
There was a reason Akechi never bothered to learn to cook. The one failure of a cooking
class had been bad enough.
When Akihiko finally returned home, Shinjiro enlisted his aid as well. And while Akihiko
was less pathetic than Akechi, it was clear he was lacking in experience too.
“I swear to god,” Shinjiro said. “Who is going to cook for you guys when I’m gone?”
“You’re planning on leaving us?” Akihiko asked, sounding insulted as he mixed their
vegetables and rice together.

Shinjiro snatched the chopsticks from Akihiko’s hands and mixed with much more deftness
and a little more violence. “Forget I said anything.”
Akechi wasn’t particularly good at forgetting. Judging from the look on his face, neither was
Akihiko.
By the time they were done, the admittedly delicious smell of their food had attracted the
entire dorm downstairs. Akechi gave up on “helping” and set the table while Akihiko and
Shinjiro put the food in dishes.
“Oh wow, is this for all of us?” Junpei asked.
“Call it a ‘good job’ for our performance last night,” Akihiko said as he placed a dish on the
table.
Minato nodded and sat down at the table without a word. Everybody else exchanged various
words of gratitude as they began eating.
“We were so missing out before you came along, Shinjiro-senpai!” Junpei said. He looked
about ready to shed tears of joy. “Man, I needed this today.”
“I must admit that I feel the same way,” Mitsuru said, smiling. “Today has been…
exhausting.”
“No luck with Chidori, then?” Akihiko asked.
“She barely said anything,” Yukari said. “Honestly, I felt kind of bad for her…”
“I’m not as sympathetic,” Mitsuru said. “She nearly killed Minato. The least she can do is
give us some answers.”
“Oh come on, don’t be like that,” Junpei said. “What she did was awful, but… she can’t be
that bad.”
“She seems so sad in the hospital room,” Yukari said reluctantly.
“For all we know, it’s a ruse to generate sympathy and make it easier for her to escape,”
Mitsuru said.
Akechi was more inclined to agree with Mitsuru.
“Drop it,” Minato said, his mouth half-full of food. “Let’s enjoy this.”
All discussion of Chidori ceased. By extension, there was no more discussion. They ate in a
silence only interrupted by the clinking of dishes.
“So… was Akechi a fast learner?” Ken asked Shinjiro. “I know he can’t cook, but he learns
his schoolwork so quickly that it’s almost like he already knew the stuff ahead of time.”
Shinjiro snorted. “Hell no. He was a disaster.”

“That’s an exaggeration,” Akechi said, glaring at his food.
“You stirred the rice.”
“Am I expected to be a master of rice?”
“No, but everybody knows not to stir rice.”
Akechi felt his face heat up in embarrassment, but Shinjiro’s words didn’t seem to be filled
with malice. Unlike all the other critical words Akechi had heard from adults in the past,
Shinjiro only seemed to be teasing.
It was a strange feeling. Akechi didn’t know what to do with it.
“I guess Akechi can’t be good at everything,” Junpei said, grinning.
“We still have the remains,” Akechi snapped. “I’ll use it to seal your mouth shut.”
Everybody, including Junpei, laughed, but Yamagishi also looked embarrassed. “I stirred the
rice once,” she said. “It became a sticky mess.”
“I guess we’ll just have to leave all the cooking to Shinjiro-senpai from now on,” Yukari said.
“This is way better than ruined rice.”
Maybe they weren’t insulting him after all.
Moon Arcana: Rank 5

For the next couple of days, apparently no progress had been made with Chidori. Mitsuru and
Akihiko were out for practically the entire evening trying to convince her to talk, with very
little success.
Three days after the full moon, Akechi joined Mitsuru and the others at the hospital. Mitsuru
was still making no progress in getting Chidori to speak, much less answer any questions.
“Your friends aren’t coming for you,” Akechi said, hoping to rile a response out of her. “They
don’t care enough to wreak havoc on your behalf.”
Chidori said nothing. Junpei had recently burst into the room, and he glared at Akechi.
“Come on, man, how is that meant to make her talk?”
“What is with your obsession with her?” Akechi asked, completely baffled.
“I don’t know, okay? But clearly what you all are doing isn’t working. Can’t you try some
gentleness?”
“Mitsuru already tried appealing to her sense of reason.”

Junpei rolled his eyes and glanced at Chidori’s sketchbook. The markings on the page barely
represented anything legible.
“I’m glad they let you keep your sketchbook,” Junpei said. “I guess you liking to draw wasn’t
an act, huh?”
“It doesn’t matter…” Chidori said. “Only I can understand my pictures.”
Of course. Of course only Junpei of all people got her to talk.
Their small moment of victory was interrupted by Junpei spotting a bleeding gash on her
forearm. Akihiko briefly explained that she did such injuries to herself as they wrapped the
injury with a bandage.
As soon as the affair was dealt with, Mitsuru attempted to get more answers out of Chidori.
Unsurprisingly, it didn’t work.

“Hey, Akechi,” Shinjiro asked the next day. “How long have we been holding that Chidori
girl?”
Akechi frowned, unsure why that information was relevant. “About four days. Why?”
Shinjiro went quiet for a moment, reaching for something inside his pocket. “It’s nothing
important,” he said.
Akechi almost believed him.

It was important. It was so important, in fact, that if Akechi hadn’t told Shinjiro how many
days it had been, Chidori might have died.
It turned out that members of Strega couldn’t control their personas, and that if they didn’t
take a certain dosage of suppressant pills every week, their persona would kill them.
Chidori’s own persona nearly choked her to death before Shinjiro burst in and shoved the
pills down her throat.
While Chidori and Junpei had a heartfelt moment about whether death was something to be
afraid of, Akihiko and Akechi chased Shinjiro, who had fled the hospital as soon as the
ordeal was over.
They managed to pin him by Port Island Station.
“Hey, Shinji!” Akihiko shouted, grabbing Shinjiro by the shoulders and forcing him to stop
walking away from them. “What the hell’s going on? Why do you have those pills?”
“Akihiko,” Shinjiro said, his voice emotionless.

“Don’t you Akihiko me!” Akihiko’s voice cracked. “I’ve heard of those suppressants. They
suppress your persona, yes, but the side effects… tell me you haven't been taking them.”
Shinjiro said nothing. It was as good as a confession.
Side effects.
“Is that why you always sound sick?” Akechi asked, the reality of the situation dawning on
him. “Why you never take your coat off even in the heat?”
“I don’t owe you anything,” Shinjiro told the two of them.
“Like hell you don’t!”
“Save it.” Shinjiro glared. “I’ve heard it all before. You think I’m wasting my power, but
you’re just too thick-headed. I’m tired of your damn preaching.”
Akihiko punched Shinjiro in the face. Nearby civilians gave them a wider berth. Akechi was
still trying to wrap his mind around side effects.
“Damn you… you know the reason. My sister. The fire. They held me back while she…”
Akihiko seemed to have forgotten Akechi was even there as he trailed off, clearly lost in the
past.
Shit. No wonder Akihiko lost his head when Strega first showed their face. He was likely
triggered just as badly as Akechi was when Akechi was held at gunpoint.
“Don’t you remember our promise?” Akihiko asked, his voice cracking again. “To be strong
enough to do what we think is right. Why the drugs? Why didn’t you come to me?”
“I'm back in the fight now,” Shinjiro said. “So just drop it.”
Even in the horror of it all, Akechi couldn’t help but feel an odd amount of relief. While
Akechi was fairly sure Shinjiro never used Strega for their services, Shinjiro’s familiarity
with Strega gnawed at the back of his mind for months now. Now Akechi had a definitive
answer. Shinjiro met with Strega for the drugs. Never for murder.
The comfort felt stale.
“And the side effects?” Akechi asked. His chest felt tight. “Are they long lasting?”
Akihiko and Akechi both stared at Shinjiro unblinkingly, waiting for his response. “I’ll be
fine,” Shinjiro said, looking away from them both. As if breaking eye contact would hide
them from the truth. “There’s something I have to do first.”
“And what’s that?” Akihiko asked.
“Don’t worry about it,” Shinjiro said, walking away. “Just worry about these last few
shadows. Things will work out.”

Akechi had believed him the day before. He didn’t dare believe him now.
Akihiko massaged his eyes and turned to Akechi. “I’m sorry you had to see that,” he said. “I
just… damnit.”
“What do you know about the side effects?” Akechi asked.
“Nothing specific,” Akihiko said reluctantly. “Something to do with the lungs, mostly. I’ve
heard rumors of heart problems too. It’s not exactly the most common drug on the streets.”
Akechi felt like a small child when he asked, “Are they long lasting?”
Akihiko stared at the empty space where Shinjiro was standing moments before. “I don’t
know.”

Akechi sat on the dorm roof, trying not to think about the unsettling news from earlier that
day. Instead, he stared at a small dark spot on the concrete. It looked like a blood stain. Was it
from Minato’s head injury?
Why didn’t Strega just swoop down and kill them all if they wanted to stop SEES so badly?
Why wait to make a move only on nights of the full moon?
The door to the roof opened, and Akechi glanced behind him. Junpei awkwardly approached
and sat down next to Akechi.
“You’ve finished talking to your new best friend?” Akechi asked, a hint of bitterness in his
tone. He couldn’t understand how Junpei could even begin to forgive Chidori for what she
did.
“She’s not much of a talker after a certain point,” Junpei said. “You might think I’m
ridiculous, but I don’t think she’s such a bad person at heart. I mean, the Kirijo group hurt
her, and if she’s only had Takaya for guidance, can you blame her for being so…”
“Murderous?” Akechi asked. “Yes, I think I can.”
Although, Akechi could see where Junpei was coming from. Takaya wasn’t someone Akechi
would even begin to call a good influence. Hell, if Akechi had met Takaya at a slightly more
unstable point in his life, he might have been inclined to adopt all of Strega’s ideologie.
The thought was sickening.
“Yeah, well, I guess I can’t blame you,” Junpei sighed.
“She tortured Minato,” Akechi said vitriolically, unable to stop himself.
“Yeah… she did.” Junpei’s face was queasy. “Um, Chidori isn’t why I came up here to talk to
you, though, if you can believe that, at least.”

“Why did you come here?”
“I wanted to apologize to you, personally,” Junpei said. He fidgeted with the hem of his shirt,
staring at Akechi with an intensity that was rare to see on Junpei’s face. “You warned me
about Chidori, and I totally brushed you off. I mean, our lives are at stake here, and I just
wanted to give her another chance because she was pretty.”
“This apology would be much more impactful if you weren’t still giving her another chance
because she’s pretty,” Akechi said.
“That’s not it…” Junpei glared at his lap. “I mean, yeah, she’s beautiful, but that’s got
nothing to do with it! I know she’s done terrible things, but she’s really hurting, and I don’t
know, I guess a part of me connects with her. How you can be surrounded by so many people
and still feel alone. And when she’s not trying to kill us, she’s pretty good company to be
around too! She’s extremely passionate about her art, even though she has a hard time
showing it, and she’s really nothing like those other members of Strega–”
“Junpei,” Akechi interrupted. “I get it. You care about her. Is this an apology, or are you
practicing your proposal?”
“Oh, shut up.” Junpei slumped. “Anyway, what I meant was… I didn’t know any of those
things about Chidori when I first talked to her. So I didn’t really have a good reason to ignore
your advice. And because of that, Minato got really hurt. I was a real idiot.”
“Truer words were never spoken,” Akechi muttered.
“And then you apologized to Minato, even though you didn’t do anything wrong!” Junpei
continued. “It’s been eating up at me for days now.”
“I didn’t apologize to Minato to take the blame off of your shoulders,” Akechi said. “The
ordeal is partially my fault. You hadn’t revealed anything to Chidori in your private
conversations. I should’ve lectured you in a private space.”
“That’s really humble of you, Akechi,” Junpei said, shaking his head. “Anyway. I’m sorry.
You don’t have to accept it, but there it is.”
Akechi frowned. He wasn’t the forgiving type. But Junpei had shown remarkable maturity to
not only take responsibility, but to apologize after the fact as well. That maturity should at
least be somewhat rewarded.
“I accept your apology,” Akechi said.
Junpei let out a massive sigh of relief. “That’s good to hear. Maybe I can actually sleep easy
tonight.”
“Don't count on it,” Akechi said grimly.
“Yeah, I had a hard enough time sleeping well before this Dark Hour stuff started
happening,” Junpei said. “Now, I think my body’s wired to wake up as soon as it's midnight,
and then how am I supposed to fall asleep?”

“You roll over and close your eyes.” Akechi said, even though that rarely worked for him.
Junpei chuckled. “Right. You’re kind of a funny guy, Akechi-kun.”
Funny was the last thing Akechi was.
Temperance Arcana: Rank 3

The following afternoon, Akechi invited Emiko to join him as he walked Koromaru around
the park. Emiko was thrilled to come along, still having yet to meet Koromaru in person.
“Aw, he’s adorable!” Emiko said with admiration. She scratched Koromaru behind the ears,
and Koromaru gave a happy bark in greeting. “I can’t believe you’ve been holding out on me
for this long!”
“It must have slipped my mind,” Akechi said, which was less an excuse and more the plain
truth. The stakes were getting higher, and it was hard to remember that he had promised to
show Koromaru to Emiko ages ago.
Emiko was holding a small ball, and she waved it in front of Koromaru’s face. “Do you want
to play fetch?”
Koromaru barked in affirmation. Emiko nodded before throwing the ball across the park. As
Koromaru ran off, Emiko’s cheerful smile turned into something more somber.
“What’s been going on with you two lately?” she asked.
Akechi frowned. “What do you mean?”
“You’ve been quieter,” she said. “I didn’t want to bring it up, but Ken still seems really sad.
You always seem kind of sad, or irritable as you like to say. But something’s wrong, isn’t it?”
Akechi hadn’t given Emiko enough credit. She was more intuitive than he realized.
“A friend of ours got hurt,” Akechi explained. “It scared Ken.”
“And you?”
Koromaru chose that moment to return with the ball in his mouth. He dropped it at Emiko’s
feet with a happy bark, and Emiko smiled and pet Koromaru’s head.
“Good boy,” she said, picking up the ball and throwing it again. Koromaru ran to fetch it, and
Emiko turned her gaze back onto Akechi.
Akechi swallowed and put on a smile. “You don’t have to worry about me, Yamamoto-kun.”
“You haven’t called me Yamamoto in ages,” Emiko said accusingly. “Is your friend alright?”

“He’s fine,” Akechi said, letting his fake smile fade away. It was getting harder and harder to
keep it on his face. “Things are just tense where we live. It doesn’t help that a different friend
might be seriously sick.”
“Wow, that is serious,” Emiko said as she picked up Koromaru’s freshly retrieved ball. She
offered it to Akechi, and he took it. “I’m sorry. I had no idea.”
“How could you have?” Akechi asked. Akechi threw the ball with all his might, and it soared
farther than Emiko’s throws had. Emiko made an impressed sound. “You’re friends with the
two most emotionally repressed students at our school.”
“I don’t think you’re that emotionally repressed,” Emiko said. She hesitated for a minute.
“Repressed means bottled up, right?”
“Yes.”
Emiko nodded with a smile. “At least I can always count on you to teach me some new
vocabulary!”
Akechi snorted. Sometimes he almost forgot that his friends weren’t also adults pretending to
be children. Rather, they were all children pretending to be adults.
Then again, maybe that was all Akechi had ever been for his entire life as well.
“That’s enough about us, though,” Akechi said. “How are you doing, Emiko-kun?”
“Oh, I’ve been fine,” Emiko said. “Momo is a little sick, though. He’s been even less active
than usual, and he barely touches his food.”
“That’s distressing,” Akechi said, remembering his previous theory of Momo seeing the end
of his lifespan. At the time, in spite of its inevitability, it was something Akechi was able to
push from his mind. Now, Akechi found himself wondering how he was going to console
Emiko when Momo finally did go to sleep for the last time. His stomach clenched.
It was easier to be worried for a definitely dying cat than to think about a potentially dying
friend.
“Yeah, well, it’s probably the transition from summer to fall,” Emiko said. “It has been
getting a bit colder, don’t you think?”
“A bit,” Akechi conceded, although it wasn’t anything worth mentioning. They wouldn’t
change into winter uniforms for at least another two weeks.
“Yeah,” Emiko said. “Momo will be fine.”
“I’m sure that he’s very happy under your care,” Akechi said.
“Very.” Emiko nodded. “He’s the happiest cat in the world.”

Happiness did not save lives. But it did make worthwhile ones. It brought hope in the face of
the inevitable demise that waited for them all.
“You’ll just have to hope for the best,” Akechi said. “I’m sure Momo is a very strong cat.”
“Definitely.” Emiko’s eyes lit up. “He’s the happiest and the strongest cat in the world.”
Akechi wondered what hope felt like. Logically, it seemed like a massive waste of time, but
maybe it was different in practice.
Hope didn’t save lives either.
Strength Arcana: Rank 6

“Akechi-kun, can I talk to you for a moment?” Mitsuru asked one evening. Akechi put down
the book he was reading, yet another one of Mitsuru’s books on psychology and the new
emergence of cognitive pscience.
“What is it?”
Nobody else was in the lounge with them. Junpei had gone to visit Chidori. Apparently, the

and nail to find a way to take down Strega’s website. Yukari and Mitsuru had to all but drag
her out of her room to take much needed breaks. Yukari, Minato, and oddly enough, Aigis,

no clue as to where Akihiko and Shinjiro had gone. Maybe they were practicing punching
each other in the face in the back alley of the nearby station.
“Last week, on the night of the full moon, I noticed that you were…. Very confident,”

Akechi clasped his hands together, forcing his face not to betray anything. “What do you

“I was only doing what anyone would have done,” Akechi said. “It wasn’t as though I was
leading the group.”

“I suppose I just wanted to thank you,” Mitsuru said. “It was partly thanks to your confidence

Well, this was a surprise. Akechi had been careful to say the word ‘many’ at the time, so that

“You’re reading books far past your reading level. It’s clear you’re quite intelligent.”

It turned out that Minato had fallen quite ill during his unfortunate walk in the pouring rain.
The older members of SEES took turns making sure he didn’t fall into a critical condition,
but Minato mostly suffered from a fever that he elected to sleep through.
Akechi sincerely hoped he wouldn’t be sick for long. The team was enough of a wreck

health by the time they needed to visit Tartarus again.
The typhoon went on for the next two days. During that time, Shinjiro dragged Akechi,
Akihiko, and Yamagishi into the kitchen to teach them some basic cooking skills.
Well, it would be more accurate to say that Shinjiro dragged Akihiko and Akechi. Yamagishi
volunteered to come along.
Akechi could only say that he learned how to cut vegetables without also cutting his fingers
in the process. And he learned that while one didn’t stir rice, one must stir boiling noodles.

His determination had nothing to do with petty competition toward Akihiko.

seriously gotten attached? Had he deceived himself into thinking that he could actually make
friends in this timeline? That he could be different?
People didn’t change. Desires changed, but people didn’t. And corrupt desires came from
corrupt people, which happened to be every single person in the human race. But Akechi
managed to set himself apart from the mess that was humanity. He managed to be worse.
He could pretend all he wanted that he was getting a second chance, that things would be
different, but would they really? Akechi was still the same screwed up human being he’d
always been. And if that didn’t change, what hope did his actions have of changing too?
Akechi needed to leave. He needed to get away from these people and their illusions of
justice and saving the world. But where would he go? Back to the foster system? Akechi
would rather die. And he wasn’t going to skip into Shido or Takaya’s laps either. He was
trapped. Trapped with people who might do away with him any minute now.
Akechi didn’t sleep that night.

The next morning, Mitsuru knocked on his door. Akechi waited for her to kick it open, to
demand that they talk. Criminals didn’t have rights to privacy, after all.
“Are you hungry?” Mitsuru asked. “You’ve been in there for quite a while.”
“I’m not hungry,” Akechi snapped. There was already food stashed in his room. Old habits
died hard.
A pause. “Akechi-kun,” Mitsuru said. “We just want to talk–”
“Maybe I don’t want to waste time with self-righteous idiots.” Akechi jumped to his feet and
paced toward the door. “You think you can just fix things with a simple conversation, as if
that will make the bad things go away. It doesn’t change a thing! Shinjiro’s still dying, and
I’m still a murderer!”
“I know what you’re trying to do, but it’s not going to work–”
Akechi needed to make his next words sting, or Mitsuru might never leave him alone.
“Kirijo-san, I know that you like to think yourself in charge of the group, but absolute power
corrupts absolutely. If you’re not careful, you’re going to turn out just like your grandfather,
so leave me the hell alone.”
It was amazing how carefully choosing the correct words can turn everyone away from him.
Just take one insecurity, one fear, and twist into someone’s ego like a knife. That was all it
took to make someone hate him.

Mitsuru left, but someone else came in her place. Akechi wondered if they had a procession
at the ready just to get Akechi out of his bedroom.
“You’re going to miss school,” Minato’s raspy voice came from the other side of the door.
“Aren’t you a perfect student or something?”
“Have Ken tell them I’m sick,” Akechi snapped. “I don’t give a shit anymore. It’s not like
any of it matters.”
For a moment, Akechi thought Minato left.
“It does matter,” Minato said quietly.
“Are you trying to fool me or yourself right now? Because it’s not going to work.”
Minato backed off after that. The apathy that Akechi used to hate was now working to his
advantage.
Akechi half expected Shinjiro to start knocking down his door, but throughout the day, he
didn’t once demand that Akechi get his head out of his ass. It was almost disappointing, but it
was mostly a relief. Akechi was tired of people getting on his case, of people pretending that
they still cared.
Akechi felt suddenly trapped in his body. Everything was too small. It was easier when he
was pretending he was mentally eleven, but now that the secret was out, he wanted to go
back to what he was. Taller. Stronger. Not this weak child incapable of doing anything.
Akechi stared at his hands and imagined them larger and more calloused. He couldn’t quite
remember what they looked like.
What if Akechi forgot what he originally looked like completely?
Why did this have to happen to him?
About midway through the day, Akechi’s phone began ringing. A cursory glance caused
Akechi’s heart to skyrocket, and he stared at the number with no small amount of dread.
Kirijo Takeharu. No doubt Mitsuru had reported Akechi’s past and behavior to her father.
What did he want? Did he plan on lecturing Akechi about what he said to Mitsuru? Maybe he
was willing to do what the others weren’t and put Akechi out of his misery.
Maybe that was the ideal outcome.
Akechi grit his teeth and steeled himself. How many times had he answered phone calls from
Shido without betraying his true emotions? He picked up the phone.
“Akechi Goro speaking,” Akechi said, already holding the phone in an iron tight grip.
“Yesterday’s report was quite illuminating,” Kirijo said, not wasting a moment. “It’s a
miracle it ended without any loss of life.”

“I know that’s not why you called me, sir.”
“Drop the sir,” Kirijo said sharply. “I know what you said to my daughter. I’d much prefer
you to be frank with me than to treat me like every other adult that you don’t trust.”
“I’m sorry, sir, but I don’t trust you at all,” Akechi said, putting on an extra polite voice.
“Pardon me for asking, but what do you really want?”
Kirijo hesitated before continuing. “Amada and Shinjiro’s testimony in regards to your past
has plenty of holes in it,” Kirijo said. “I imagine you gave the abbreviated version—”
“Get to the point.”
“It says you died,” Kirijo said. “And no, I am not about to call you insane. You have shown
maturity and jadedness beyond your years, and neither my daughter nor I find it surprising
that you may be older than you appear. I wanted to know how you reversed time to get back
to this point.”
“Do you think I’m stupid?” Akechi spat. “Don’t give me that bull about believing me;
nobody in their right minds would believe that story for a second–”
“My father was working to find a way to control time,” Kirijo said evenly. “The fruits of his
experiments led to a hidden hour in the day. I do not find it hard to believe that sometime in
the future, real time travel exists.”
“And you want to exploit it?” Akechi asked.
“I want to find the fool trying to make that sort of weapon and stop him before it’s too late,”
Kirijo said.
“So you want to get rid of me, instead.” Akechi punched the wall with his free hand. He
didn’t grimace or hiss at the bruising around his knuckles. “I’m not a fool, Kirijo.”
“What was that sound?”
“Nothing.”
“I’ll have you know that I don’t want to get rid of you at all,” Kirijo said. “But the ability to
shape the future is a dangerous one. One I don’t trust anyone with.”
“Well, I have good news for you, then,” Akechi said bitterly. “I don’t know how I went back.
One minute I was dead, the next I was here. Is that all?”
“No. Do you remember what I warned you about the last time we spoke?”
“Some crap about trusting others?” Akechi asked, rolling his eyes. “The others don’t trust
me; I don’t see why I should trust them.”
“From what I understand, you didn’t give the others a chance to decide that for themselves,”
Kirijo said. “You just hid yourself away and started pushing them out of your life by force.

How is that meant to accomplish anything? Alone, you are as weak as–”
“Alone, I am safe!” Akechi screamed. “You make people trust you, and what does that get
them? Only pain and betrayal! You exploit our desires and goals, make us do your bidding,
and then leave us in the dirt when you’re done with us! People only hurt you! I can only hurt
others!”
“Without relationships, what is the point in being safe?!” Kirijo asked sharply. “Life isn’t just
about survival. Life is about the people you share with it; the relationships you forge along
the way. Trust is a risk, but without it, you have nothing to fight for, not even yourself. And
when you believe nothing matters, that is when you wish the world nothing but ill.”
“Are you comparing me to your father again?” Akechi asked, staring at the blood around his
knuckles. “Because if you left your father to rot, then you should just leave me behind too.
I’m past saving, whatever you or your daughter might think!”
“When I discovered what my father had done to my daughter…” Kirijo spoke falteringly. “I
was enraged. I almost killed my father on the spot.”
“But you didn’t because you’re so noble and righteous, is that it?” Akechi rolled his eyes.
“You’re nothing but a spineless coward.”
“I agree,” Kirijo said. “Maybe if I had been able to act on my feelings, children like yourself
wouldn’t have to fight this war. But pure selfishness stayed my hand.”
“Because you still loved him.” Akechi might hate relationships, but he had some emotional
intelligence. “This is exactly what I’m talking about. Your love for an evil person only
enabled him in the end.”
“It is the love for my daughter that helps me keep going,” Kirijo countered. “But you
misunderstand my point. Last night, you did not behave like a heartless killer. Your actions
saved the lives of your friends.”
“One good deed doesn’t erase the rest,” Akechi said bitterly.
“No, but people do not let go of those they care about as easily as you think,” Kirijo said.
“You need to give them a chance.”
All of this patient wisdom was becoming overwhelming. This wasn’t how adults were meant
to behave. They weren’t meant to be patient, or kind, or wise. They were meant to be corrupt
individuals who wanted to trample on the lives of the weak.
“Do you think you’re my father?” Akechi asked. The hand holding his phone was shaking.
“My father slept with my mother and then left her in the dirt. He only acknowledged me to
make me do his dirty work. That is what fatherhood means to me. So stay out of things that
you will never understand.”
Akechi hung up and slammed the phone against his desk. His entire body shook as he
lowered himself onto the floor, nursing his throbbing hand. He was so tired. And angry. More

and more people were attempting to blow on the flames to put them out, but they were really
just adding more oxygen to the fire.
Akechi needed to get out of his room. He needed to be able to breathe.
Hanged Man Arcana: Rank 4

During the Dark Hour, Akechi snuck out of the dorms through the fire escape outside the
second floor hall window.
Akechi started marching toward Tartarus. He wasn’t going to make it within the hour on foot,
and he hadn’t brought any weapons, but the goal itself made him feel like he could actually
think. He imagined himself bringing down every shadow inside the tower and releasing all of
his frustrations against anything that had ever hurt him.
“This is a pleasant surprise,” Takaya said, walking alongside him.
Akechi had no traditional weapons, but that didn’t stop him. With a guttural scream, he
launched himself on top of Takaya, reaching to wrap his hands around Takaya’s tiny throat,
ready to crack his neck–
Takaya placed the barrel of his gun against Akechi’s forehead, and Akechi froze.
“It truly is remarkable how a single motion can tame even the most feral of beasts,” Takaya
said pleasantly. He grabbed Akechi’s shoulder with a single, bony hand.
“Let go of me,” Akechi snarled.
“Are you truly so afraid of your own demise?” Takaya asked. “I take it that the death you had
the first time–”
“As if you believe that–”
“The world is such a strange place, and you are no liar,” Takaya said.
“I do nothing but lie,” Akechi said.
“Let me correct myself, then,” Takaya said. “When you are angry, you do not lie. You make
your intentions perfectly clear, by the way you talk, and glare, and even move. You lie, but
anyone who truly knows you can see right through them.”
“And I suppose you truly know me,” Akechi asked. “Let go of me.”
Takaya’s grip tightened. “Your first death was to a gun, was it not?” he asked. “You always

believe that this scenario means certain death.”

“Somehow, I’ve managed to survive you pointing a gun at me for this long,” Akechi snapped.
“I’m not afraid of you.”
“Then, prove it.” Takaya sounded almost excited. “Act as though this weapon isn’t even here.
Attack me again, and I’ll shoot you.”
“Where would I benefit in that scenario at all?”
“I thought you weren’t afraid of me.” Takaya’s smile was so mocking. So proud. It made
Akechi want to scream. “By extension, you aren’t afraid of death. Besides, what is one bullet
to the head compared to a life tormented by others who will never accept you?”
“Stop talking,” Akechi said, feeling nausea rise up inside of him. Memories of a different
man with a different face, but somehow the meaning behind his words had been exactly the
same.
“Make me.”
Akechi lunged forward. Takaya pulled the trigger. The sound of thunder roared in Akechi’s
ears. Akechi’s heart pounded. He waited for the white-hot pain.
Nothing happened.
Akechi’s ears were ringing. His vision blurred. He wasn’t dead, but he should be dead. Was
he really still breathing? Maybe he was dying, maybe it was taking its time to settle in.
Takaya was laughing, his head thrown back. His gun hung loosely in his hand.
Unthinkingly, Akechi snatched the gun from Takaya. With a deft motion, he aimed directly at
Takaya’s heart and fired.
More thunder. More heavy breathing. No blood. No death. Both Akechi and Takaya were still
alive, and Takaya was still laughing his head off.
“Shut up!” Akechi screamed, clawing at the pavement. When had he gotten on his knees?
“Just shut up!’
“Don’t you understand, Goro?” Takaya asked. He grabbed Akechi by the wrist and yanked
him to his feet. “Don’t you see what this means?”
“That you don’t have enough bullets in your gun?” Akechi asked, pressing the gun against
Takaya’s chest. “Maybe I’ll get lucky this time.”
“You don’t fear death,” Takaya said triumphantly. “You don’t fear anything at all, except
those who you once called friends. You’re willing to kill like a man who has nothing to lose.”
With all of his might, Akechi slammed the handle of the gun into Takaya’s skull. “Get away
from me!”

Takaya let go of Akechi, wearing a dazed expression. Not letting go of the gun, Akechi
turned around and ran.
Takaya didn’t follow, probably because he was concussed. When Akechi felt that he had
reached a safe enough distance, he stopped to throw up.
He couldn’t do this, he couldn’t do this, he couldn’t do this.
Akechi couldn’t remember how he got home. One minute he was running, and the next, he
was sitting on his bed, staring at Takaya’s revolver in his hands. This was the weapon that
almost ended Shinjiro’s life. The weapon that brought Akechi near to death multiple times.
Akechi should destroy it.
Akechi pressed the cylinder release. Although most of the compartments were empty, there
were two single bullets ready to be fired. If Akechi had tried to shoot Takaya one more time,
he might have been able to kill him.
With a jutting sigh, Akechi clicked the cylinder back into place and placed the revolver in his
evoker’s old briefcase. He kicked the briefcase underneath his bed furiously.
Hermit Arcana: Rank 8

Shinjiro finally tried to break his door down. Akechi had some very short words to say to
him.
“Don’t talk to me,” he said. “You’re dying. Don’t talk to me.”
“I’m not going to spend my last months with you mad at me–”
“MONTHS?!” Akechi screamed. The events of last night mixed with the events of two nights
ago had made him lose all control of any of his emotions. He needed something to be angry
at, and Shinjiro was the perfect target. “You only have months?!”
“Goro–”
“Stop!” Akechi slammed his foot against the floor like a child who wasn’t getting his way.
“You don’t get to talk to me like nothing’s changed! You’re dying, and you couldn’t even tell

“That’s some strong language for someone who’s hiding away in his room like a coward

“It’s better than taking drugs that could kill me!” Akechi barely resisted slamming his fist
into his door. It had suffered enough damage the day before. “Just get the hell away from
me!”

As soon as Shinjiro had finally left, Akechi received a text. Akechi looked at it, expecting it

It was an unknown number.

Yamamoto Emiko: I heard u were sick :(
Yamamoto Emiko: Kens rly worried. Get better soon!

All of the anger might as well have been forcibly drained from his body. No questions. No
fake concern. Just genuine friendship from someone who didn’t know the truth.
Emiko didn’t know better. She didn’t know who Akechi really was. Clearly, Ken hadn’t told

Akechi let his phone slip from his fingers. He didn’t know what to do anymore. It was a

He wished he could just go back to feeling angry.

The next day, Ikutsuki opened his door and entered the room without Akechi’s permission.
Akechi stared at him in awed horror, and the anger that had been so all-encompassing the day

“I don’t need you to be the adult of anything,” Akechi said. “If you’re planning on killing me,

“I’m not planning on killing you at all,” Ikutsuki said. “But you can’t stay here forever. Have

“If you think it’s going so horribly, then get out.” Akechi said bluntly. “I don’t want you to be

“Come on, please give me a chance!” Ikutsuki pleaded. “I’ll only take up five minutes of

Akechi glanced at his clock. It was fifteen minutes past three in the afternoon.
“Fine,” Akechi said. “Go.”
Ikutsuki put his kindly smile back on. Akechi wondered if he thought he was fooling anyone.
“Akechi, I know this must be incredibly difficult for you–” Akechi opened his mouth to

Akechi promised nothing of the sort, but Ikutsuki kept speaking as if Akechi had agreed with

Akechi was not about to be lectured on cowardice by Ikutsuki of all people. He got to his

“Fine,” he snapped. “Fine. I’ll speak to them.”

At the hospital, Akechi allowed the doctors to straighten his nose and apply stitches to his

“It wasn’t strictly necessary,” Mitsuru said. “There are still rooms to spare, and I didn’t want

She probably wasn’t wrong, considering what had just happened.
“Well, I’m fine now.” Akechi got to his feet. He felt relatively refreshed, and it wasn’t as

into question. He just didn’t want me to see the pile-up of weird recordings. Um, I didn’t
realize what they were at first, though. I only watched the most recent one, and–”
“Has Minato seen these recordings?”
“Mitsuru asked, and he admitted to seeing the first few before deciding it was really weird,”
Junpei said. His face grew more serious. “He hadn’t thought about the implications of
cameras in our bedrooms, or maybe he just didn’t care at first and forgot to think about it, but
he was apologetic at least.”
“That’s comforting,” Akechi said sarcastically.
“Look, I came to tell you about the cameras, sure, but I have something more important to
talk to you about.” Junpei chuckled nervously. “Um, you see, when I was watching that

recording–”
“Just spit it out.”
“Why do you have Takaya’s gun?” Junpei blurted out.
Akechi should have been expecting that. Still, he found himself standing completely still
after that announcement.
“What?” Akechi asked.
“I saw it in the recording,” Junpei said. “You pulled some briefcase out from underneath your
bed, and I saw that revolver. Isn’t that Takaya’s?”
Akechi would gain nothing from lying. He’d only make himself look like a traitor and a spy,
especially considering the kidnapping from earlier that week. Junpei could easily assume that
Akechi joined Strega during that time, and Takaya gave him the gun in good faith.
“I stole it,” Akechi said. “A couple of weeks ago.”
“A couple weeks ago?” Junpei asked. “You mean Takaya has been without a gun for weeks,
and you didn’t think it important to bring it up?”
“I’ve been a bit preoccupied recently,” Akechi said. It wasn’t a particularly compelling
excuse.
“Well, I guess you have a point there,” Junpei sighed. His eyes unsubtly jumped to the
stitches across Akechi’s cheek. He started turning toward the door. “Well, the others will be
pleased to hear that–”
“You can’t tell them.” Akechi tightly grabbed Junpei by the wrist.
“What?” Junpei asked. “What do you mean?”
Honesty. Akechi had to be honest, or he wasn’t going to gain back any of Junpei’s trust.
Not that it mattered, of course.
“They think I’ve disposed of it,” Akechi said.
“Who? The others?”
“No, dumbass, Strega!” Akechi’s grip on Junpei’s wrist tightened. “If they know I have it,
they’ll target me again!”
Logically, Akechi knew the real reason Takaya kidnapped him was to brainwash him. But Jin
only agreed to it because of that stupid gun.
“O-oh.” Junpei looked down at his wrist. “Can you let go of me? It kind of hurts.”

Akechi loosened his grip, but he didn’t let go. “Only after you promise me you won’t tell
them,” Akechi said. “If I’m going to trust you, you have to trust me not to use it for harm.”
“You seriously think this has got to do with you?” Junpei asked defensively. “I said that the

“Look me in the eyes and tell me with full honesty that you’re not worried about the gun

“I mean, it’s not in your hands right now…” Junpei said hesitantly. “Ugh, fine! Maybe I’m a

“Live whatever fantasy you’d like, Jin and Takaya are still hurting people. And I’m sure he

tongue alone is likely to slip around the wrong people.”
Junpei’s expression became very hurt. “You really think I’d try to put you in danger?”
“Not intentionally.”
The words felt like another one of Akechi’s myriad of lies.
“Fine,” Junpei sighed. “Fine. You win. I won’t tell the others. But if Akihiko or Mitsuru finds
out and gets mad, I’m not feeling sorry for you!”
“Understood.” Akechi hesitated before letting go of Junpei’s wrist. Junpei immediately
yanked it backwards and grabbed hold of it with his other hand. “Thank you.”
“Sure, sure, whatever.” Junpei rolled his eyes as he rolled his wrist back and forth. “Man, I
hate being burdened with secrets.”
“Then forget you know anything.” Akechi almost shoved Junpei out of his bedroom before
suddenly realizing– “What about the recording? Is it still on the control console?”
“Nah.” Junpei shook his head. “Mitsuru deleted them all without watching. She said that we

Akechi relaxed. “Good.”
“Man,” Junpei sighed as he started to leave the room. “I hope you know what you’re doing,
man.”
“So do I.” But Akechi was still tense. He stared at the broken clock on the floor. “Why were

“Mitsuru called the chairman,” Junpei said. “He said the cameras were originally there as a
security measure, back when nobody lived in the rooms, but he thought they’d been turned

off when we moved into each of them. He thinks maybe Jin found a way to get them online.
Or that the system is broken.”
“And you believe that?” Akechi asked quietly. His skin crawled to think of Jin potentially
spying on them through the cameras in their rooms. But if he had, why did he bother asking
about the location of Takaya’s gun? He would have seen the same video Junpei had.
No. Whoever was responsible, it wasn’t Jin.
“Has Ikutsuki-san really given us any reason to mistrust him?” Junpei asked, looking slightly
uneasy himself. “I mean, he was the one who found you. And he’s been a lot of help to us.”
“He also didn’t think to tell us about cameras in our rooms,” Akechi said.
Junpei grimaced. “He really made it sound like an honest mistake.”
Akechi bit his tongue to stop himself from laughing derisively. As much as he hated to admit
it, Ikutsuki had seemed rather harmless. If one could call being careless with the safety of
children “harmless”. He had supported Akechi in telling the truth to the others, and he had
assisted Akechi when he escaped Strega.
But who else would be responsible for the cameras being on? Unless some researcher hacked
into the system?
Regardless, everyone else trusted Ikutsuki so readily that even suggesting he had ill
intentions would be pointless.
“Maybe it was,” Akechi finally said. He’d keep an eye on the situation.
Temperance Arcana: Rank 4

Ikutsuki came by the following morning to express his deepest apologies about the cameras.
None of them could get a word in edgewise without him bowing and apologizing. He even
presented them with a tray of extremely expensive-looking sushi, which won Junpei over
immediately.
Akechi wasn’t sure what to make of it, but most adults wouldn’t bend over backwards to
apologize to children.
Akechi wasn’t sure if that made Ikutski more or less suspicious.
By the time Ikutsuki left, having promised to discover the source behind the functioning
cameras while delivering ten puns to boot, Akechi decided Ikutsuki was probably too
bumbling to have nefarious intentions. Whether that made him innocent remained to be seen.
Minato also apologized for the third time about watching the videos and not telling anyone.
Fortunately, it seemed the contents of the videos Minato saw were mostly harmless.

“Shinjiro-kun?” Yamagishi asked later that afternoon. Akechi and Shinjiro had been sitting

interested, but he never felt safe alone in his room.
He came downstairs to brainstorm ways he could potentially use the Dark Hour to get back to
2017. For some reason, his heart wasn’t as into the process as it once was. Maybe it was
because he knew the effort was futile. But he hated feeling like he was just letting things
happen to him. He needed to regain some semblance of control. If that meant pretending he

Besides, everyone was still shaken from the camera debacle. Akechi needed to distract
himself.
“What is it?” Shinjiro asked. He took the television remote from the coffee table and turned

Yamagishi clasped her arms behind her back and looked at the television. “I was wondering if
you could bake a cake for Yukari-chan this evening. It’s her birthday, you see.”
“Man, people are having birthdays left and right,” Shinjiro sighed. He leaned further into the
sofa, looking exhausted. “When’s yours?”
“Oh, mine?” Yamagishi asked. “It’s not until late December. I don’t think anyone has a
birthday soon after Yukari’s, if that’s what you’re asking.”
“Good,” Shinjiro said. “We’ll get sick of cake after a while. What flavor does she like?”
“She said she liked lemon, I think,” Fuuka said. “You’ll do it, then?”
Shinjiro nodded. “On one condition,” he said. “You help me.”
Yamagishi shook her head quickly. “Oh, no, you don’t want me to help you,” she said. “I’d

“Well, yes, but only because I have so many notes,” Yamagishi said. “But I’m so busy

power to find a way to stop them.”
“Didn’t you say you were going to take breaks?” Akechi asked.
“Well… yes.” Yamagishi looked down at the floor. “But after everything that happened… I
wanted to see if we could make a program that tracked Strega’s movements, so that we could

“I agree with Goro,” Shinjiro said. “Take a break. Besides, I’ll make sure you don’t do
anything too dramatic. I’ll get Aki and Goro to monitor the situation. Goro should know how
not to destroy a cake, at least.”

“Thanks,” Akechi said dryly.
Yamagishi giggled nervously. “Um, if you say so, Shinjiro-kun. I’ll do my best!”

A few hours later, Akechi, Akihiko, Yamagishi, and Shinjiro all gathered in the kitchen area.
In the small kitchen space, everyone was close to touching shoulders, but Shinjiro organized

“I suppose,” Yamagishi said. “But I don’t think people are likely to accept that as much.”

Shinjiro took their bowl and began mixing the batter. Without anything left to do, Yamagishi

“The others say the same thing,” Yamagishi admitted. “But I’m not as good as I thought, am

“Just take the compliment,” Shinjiro said as he put the cake into the oven.

“Hey, Akechi,” Minato asked out of nowhere one evening. The next full moon was about a
week away, and Minato had already arranged for everyone to leave for Tartarus. Oddly
enough, however, Minato hadn’t bothered to go out and speak to anyone; he just lay sprawled
on the sofa in the silence of the dorm. Everyone else had left the lounge. Akechi himself had
been considering visiting Emiko. “Do you ever wonder why you’re fighting?”
“Where is this coming from?” Akechi asked.
Minato shrugged. “I was thinking, I guess.”
“Clearly.”
“So?” Minato asked, staring at the ceiling dully. “Why do you fight? With us, I mean?”
Akechi frowned. “I’ve stuck around this long, haven’t I?”
“That’s not an answer.”
“Fine.” Akechi inhaled sharply. “Do you want my genuine answer? I have no other option.
It’s either fight or get sent back to the hell I’ve lived in for a decade. I hate Strega; I want to
see them suffer. And if the Dark Hour doesn’t get eradicated, then some powerful individual
will weaponize it more than even Strega has.”
“That’s a lot of reasons,” Minato said.
“And all of them are utterly selfish.”

“Not that last one.” Minato raised his eyebrows thoughftully. “Not really the second one.”
“Revenge is purely selfish,” Akechi snapped. “I’m not like you guys. This isn’t about the
people Strega has killed. This is about the pain they’ve inflicted upon me.”
“Still a good cause.”
“Well, don’t go praising me for what I don’t deserve,” Akechi muttered. “Why did you even
ask?”
“I was thinking.”
“You said that already.” Akechi rolled his eyes. “Why do you fight, then?”
Minato frowned. “I… “
He shut his mouth without ever finishing his sentence.

“I didn’t have an answer then, either.”

Akechi couldn’t argue with that. Still, he couldn’t help but to be slightly astonished by this

“I can’t tell you why you fight,” Akechi said.
“I know that,” Minato snapped. “I just thought, maybe you’d have a reason that I share. Or
something. I don’t know.”
“We’re not the same.”
“I gave up on the world too,” Minato said. “I still don’t even think it’s really worth saving. So
why am I here? Why do I fight?”
Minato’s expression was so lost, so confused. Akechi opened his mouth, but he had no idea
what he could possibly say to reassure him. Minato continued speaking anyway.
“Yukari has her dad. Mitsuru has her grandfather. Ken and Shinjiro are looking to the future.

“Maybe you don’t need a noble reason,” Akechi said. “You’re fighting. And you care.”
“Do I?”
“I can’t answer that for you either, but you vouched for me. You withstood torture for the

Akechi wasn’t sure why that last part mattered to him, but he couldn’t take the words back
after he had said them.
“Huh.” Minato’s woeful expression mellowed out slightly. “Okay.”
“Did you have an epiphany?” Akechi asked, surprised by the sudden shift.
“Not really.” Minato sat up. “Well, maybe.”
“And that was?”
Minato stared at his hands, looking like a man who realized he had been wearing the wrong

Akechi raised his eyebrows. He hadn’t expected to hear that from Minato; he also didn’t
agree at all. “What parts?”
Minato didn’t look up from his hands. “Friends.”

On the night of the full moon, the tension in the command room was so high that nobody was
sitting down. Everyone gathered around Fuuka in a tight circle, holding their breath as they
waited.
“Is everyone here?” Mitsuru asked, looking around the room.
For the first time in months, everyone was accounted for. Akechi had been sure Strega would
put more effort into dividing their team when SEES was so close to destroying the Dark
Hour, and he couldn’t imagine why they had changed their approach. Maybe it was because
SEES still managed to defeat the shadows regardless.
“I sense something…” Fuuka said. “On the moonlight bridge! It has to be the shadow!”
“Is everybody ready?” Minato asked, casting his gaze onto the others. Everyone already had
their weapons and armor. They didn’t want to waste any more time than necessary.
“Let’s do this thing,” Akihiko said.
“Strega is nearby,” Fuuka said, opening her eyes. “Be prepared for a fight.”
Junpei scoffed, but it held less bravado than it used to. “Aren’t we always?”
He shot Akechi a knowing look. Akechi did not return it.

When they arrived at the bridge, Akechi didn’t see the shadow at all. Instead, Takaya and Jin
stood side by side, acting as a sort of barricade to their goal. Takaya still hadn’t replaced his
revolver. Why didn’t he just steal another gun? Was Takaya really that attached to the one
Akechi stole?
“So you’ve come to face the final shadow,” Takaya said. “You claim you wish to end the
destruction caused by the shadows, and yet thousands of human lives are lost without their
intervention. The power you possess is not inherently evil; you cannot deny that. So why
don’t you just admit it–”
“Admit what, you bastard?” Shinjiro interrupted. “That we don’t want the Dark Hour to end?
Newsflash, we do!”
“I wouldn’t expect you to understand,” Takaya said dismissively. “You do not understand true
power when it hits you in the face. The others here are far less ignorant.”
“We stand by our decision!” Mitsuru said. “The Dark Hour has to end.”
“And what about your noble leader?” Jin asked. “He’s awfully quiet. It’s a wonder that he's a
leader at all.”
Yukari’s eyes flashed. “You take that back!”
Minato stared Jin directly in the eyes. “I’m tired of this,” he said. “Get out of our way.”
“As amusing as this is, it’s clear that you are lying to yourselves,” Takaya said. “Foolish
children, don’t you realize that erasing the Dark Hour is the same as erasing yourselves? Is
even that beyond your comprehension?”
“None of us are backing down!” Ken shouted.
“I can see that.” Takaya’s eyes glinted. Revolver or no, he could still summon a persona. Jin
held a grenade in his hand.
Come to think of it, Akechi had never faced Jin in a fight.
“Let’s destroy these maggots,” Jin said.
Takaya sent an unreadable glance in Akechi’s direction before sighing. “Very well. It would
seem our goals are irreconcilable. Now you will be judged!”
“This time, you’ll come out of it with more than just a little scratch,” Jin told Akechi. Akechi
lunged forward, attempting to stab Jin’s chest. Jin stepped out of the way and threw one of
his grenades at the main group.
“Everyone guard!” Minato shouted.
The battle was grueling, but it wasn’t as difficult as Akechi had initially expected it to be.
Akechi didn’t know if it was because Takaya was less threatening without literal bullets to

shoot in their hands, or if they had grown more powerful in their time in Tartarus. But they
took the two of them down within twenty minutes.
Akechi almost wanted to weep with relief as Takaya stumbled backwards. “So this… is the
power of those whose personas awakened naturally…”
Jin picked himself up off of the pavement, gasping for breath. “Is their power really that
different from ours?”
“Different?” Mitsuru asked.
“Like I said before,” Shinjiro said, wiping some blood away from his forehead. “They’re not
like us. Because of their suppression pills, they have to force their personas out.”
“You were seriously taking those pills from these bastards?” Akihiko snapped.
“You guys really don’t know anything, do you?” Jin asked through gritted teeth. “If the Dark
Hour goes away, it might not matter for normal people. Those idiots don’t remember a thing.
But for us…”
Takaya’s face hardened with resolve. “There is only one choice for us. Our bodies are
worthless without their power, after all.”
“What are you saying?” Ken asked.
Takaya backed up toward the railing of the bridge. Jin joined him.
“A fall from that height will likely kill you,” Aigis noted.
“This is how we live!” Jin said disdainfully. “Not some cowardly game of pretend! We’d
rather die than surrender to the likes of you!”
They both tipped backwards.
“Wait!” Junpei screamed, running toward them.
It was too late. They had already fallen into the water, and Akechi heard the sound of a
distant splash. Akechi joined the others at the side of the railing, looking down into the
blood-red sea. But there was no sign of anyone coming up to the surface.
Akechi’s legs felt weak. Whether it was from relief or dread, he had no idea.
They were gone. But it was never that simple. How could they possibly be gone?
“What were they thinking?” Junpei asked.
“They chose their own fate,” Akihiko said coldly. “I’m not shedding any tears on their
behalf.”
“Yeah, but…” Yukari looked a little sick herself.

“Guys!” Fuuka cried out. “The shadow’s approaching!”
Everyone looked up to see a ginormous shadow hanging from a cross-shaped helicopter.
Akechi swallowed back the storm of emotions churning within him. They still had a job to
do. He could worry about the rest later.

One dead shadow later, everybody stood in quiet relief.
“Operation completed,” Aigis said. Even she sounded pleased. “Or, should I say, Mission
Complete.”
“Hell yeah,” Junpei huffed.
“Is it actually over?” Akihiko asked, looking around.
The Dark Hour hadn’t disappeared. The world hadn’t immediately shifted to normal as soon
as they defeated the shadow. The air was still suspended in green silence.
Nobody else seemed to notice, however, and Akihiko’s apprehension apparently wasn’t
enough for him to comment on the strangeness of it all. Maybe this was what was supposed
to happen. Maybe the Dark Hour would end as it normally did tonight, but it wouldn’t return
the next day.
Akechi found this line of thinking extremely optimistic, but for some reason, he didn’t want
to rain on everyone else’s parade. The truth would reveal itself in time. Maybe… maybe
Akechi would let them have this moment.
“I think a victory cheer is in order,” Aigis said. “That is what the other team did in Minato’s
track meet.”
“Way to remind Minato of his failures, Ai-chan,” Junpei sighed.
“Apologies,” Aigis said, not looking remotely apologetic. She put her hand into the center of
their little clump. “What should our cheer be?”
“Can we go home now?” Minato asked. Or maybe he really wanted that to be their cheer.
“One, two, three, can we go home now!” Aigis lifted her hand into the air and did a small
jump.
Everybody laughed. “That was the saddest cheer I’ve ever heard,” Ken said.
“I thought it was genuine enough.” Shinjiro sighed and looked up at the sky. His expression
grew slightly less relaxed. “Come on. Let’s get going.”
As they started walking back, Aigis suggested they have another celebration. It was strange
to hear Aigis so excited over their victory, but nobody objected. Mitsuru said she’d order

some fancy tuna for them to eat in the dorms, and everybody started placing their
preferences.
Akechi decided he’d just eat whatever was left over; he didn’t feel very hungry.
“What’s going on?” Shinjiro asked as Akechi started to lag behind. “You don’t look very
excited.”
Akechi dug his nails into his palms. “Doesn’t something feel… off to you?” Akechi asked,
glancing around. The Dark Hour still hadn’t ended. “I can’t shake this feeling…”
“I kind of feel the same way,” Shinjiro admitted. “But let’s try to have a little optimism. You
can’t live your life always believing the worst is going to happen, right?”
“It keeps you alive.”
“Or it makes you miserable,” Shinjiro said. “All three of us could have died last month, but
we didn’t. The worst doesn’t always happen.”
“You sound like you’re trying to convince yourself more than me,” Akechi said.
“Maybe I am.” Shinjiro stuffed his hands into his pockets. “Let’s just try, alright?”
Akechi rolled his eyes. “Fine.”

The following day was extremely surreal.
Mitsuru looked like she was going to burst into tears at any minute, likely from the sheer
relief of it finally being over. Akihiko and Shinjiro had similar dispositions, although neither
of them looked particularly prone to cry. Everyone else seemed almost upset. The only one
who was externally happy at it being over was Aigis, who frequently congratulated Minato
for a job well done.
Akechi waited for the others to turn on him, to decide that his presence was no longer
needed. But they all seemed distracted by their own lives. The time would inevitably come,
but it didn’t seem that it would happen that day.
Akechi and Ken walked to school rather glumly. Neither of them knew what was going to
happen to them now. There was no good reason for elementary schoolers to live in a high
school dorm. As a matter of fact, if it weren’t for the extenuating circumstances (even with
them, in Akechi’s opinion), it was rather unsafe.
“What do you think is going to happen now?” Ken asked.
“I don’t know,” Akechi admitted. He held back his own doubts about the Dark Hour not
being over. As a matter of fact, he was ashamed to discover he almost wanted it to stay. “I
guess I’ll be sent back to the foster system.”

“Don’t say that!” Ken protested. “They wouldn’t do that, I know it!”
“Then, what is there to be done?” Akechi snapped. “They don’t trust me, and if they do then
they shouldn’t, and I can’t live in those dorms for the rest of my life.”
Ken didn’t say anything. “I don’t want to go back to my old dorms,” he said. “It didn’t have a
dog. Or a robot. Or friends.”
Their conversation petered out into solemn silence.
“I don’t want you to leave,” Ken said.
“When has anyone cared about what we wanted?”

That evening, everybody put on a happy face. Logically, this was a happy occasion. There
was one less threat to humanity. Although this would hardly cause world peace, the Lost
could at least return to their families as their original selves.
Mitsuru had an extremely expensive looking sushi tray delivered to the dormitory. She set it
on the coffee table in the lounge.
“Man, these slices are huge!” Junpei said, a greedy smile spreading across his face. “Can we
eat? I’m starving.”
Shinjiro wore a small smile. “It’s kind of nice to not have to make the meal for once.”
“We all deserve a treat,” Mitsuru said.
“Speaking of all of us,” Ken said, looking around. “Where are Aigis and Ikutsuki-san?”
“He took her to the lab for a tune up,” Fuuka said. “Apparently, she suffered an injury during
battle that’s impeding some of her processing systems.”
“Oh, maybe that’s why she’s been acting so strange,” Junpei said. “With all of that victory

Ryoji too–”
“Well, she’s done with you,” Akechi said. “Respect her boundaries or don’t. I don’t give a
damn, but know it’s probably safer to do the former.”

“I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this,” Akihiko said. His voice was strained, and it

Takaya’s gun?”
Akechi crossed his arms. “I’m not with Strega, if that’s what you’re asking.”
“Nobody was asking that,” Shinjiro said.
Akechi didn’t lower his guard. “I took it.”
“When?” Akihiko asked, massaging his eyes with an exhausted expression.
“October,” Akechi said.
“Was it when you were kidnapped?” Shinjiro asked.
Akechi could lie, but he wasn’t in the mood to have it blown up in his face.
“Did Ikutsuki mention a gun to you?” Akechi snapped. “Takaya’s missing gun was part of the
reason I got kidnapped in the first place.”
“So it was before that?” Akihiko asked.
“It was a few days after the full moon,” Akechi said shortly.
“And how did you manage to one, get out of the dorms, and two, steal Takaya’s precious
revolver?” Akihiko clasped his hands together and leaned forward.
“Fire escape. Dumb luck. What else do you want me to say?”

“Maybe an apology?” Akihiko said. “You aren’t allowed to leave the dorms by yourself
during Dark Hour, and you’re supposed to talk to us if, I don’t know, you steal a gun?”
“I’m not a trustworthy person,” Akechi said. “I’m sorry that you haven’t realized that yet.”
“And I’m sorry that you haven’t realized that you’re a dumbass,” Shinjiro snapped. “Last
night could have been avoided if you had talked to someone. We would have put the gun in a
safer place than underneath your bed.”
“Like in Ikutsuki’s room?” Akechi asked sarcastically.
Akihiko looked aghast. Shinjiro broke into furious coughs, and Akihiko jumped to his feet to
get him a glass of water.
“Look, Akechi,” Akihiko said after Shinjiro’s lungs calmed down. “I want to trust you, but–”
“You don’t, I get it,” Akechi snapped. “For the most part, my stupid decisions have only hurt
me. I’m not brainless enough to damage the entire group.”
But was that true? Chidori had come for Junpei. Not Akechi.
“I don’t think you’re understanding the problem here,” Shinjiro said.
“Then, explain.”
“We care about your wellbeing too, dumbass. You almost got shot last night.”
“And you have literally no way of knowing that one day your secretiveness isn’t going to
hurt all of us,” Akihiko said. “Especially when it comes to Strega.”
Akechi hated to admit it, but Akihiko was right. Akechi had been a fool.
“Fine,” Akechi said. “I will tell you about any future developments between me and Strega.
Happy?”
“Thrilled,” Shinjiro said dryly.

And there were the Lost. Ever since Ikutsuki’s betrayal, the number of Lost seemed to be

Junpei hoped they were eating some way or another. Although, Junpei supposed they must
be. Otherwise, there’d be more death reports.

Junpei hated to admit it, but it was probably true. Still, at least she was willing to let go of her
