“I still think this is a major risk,” Mitsuru said. “What if we’re betrayed? Who knows how
many people we’ll…”
The group grew quiet at the thought of any more death taking place.
“Couldn’t we give her a trial run?” Junpei asked. “Someone can guard her room every night
to make sure she’s not visiting Strega, and we’ll only let her have her evoker when we go to
Tartarus. Maybe after a month, we’ll know she’s trustworthy.”
“Or, she’ll wait for us to let our guard down,” Mitsuru said. “I really don’t think this is a good
idea.”
“I hate to say it, but I see Mitsuru’s point,” Akihiko said. “How can we trust her?”
“You can’t,” Minato said. “But… she wants to try. Are we going to lock her up for the rest of
her life?”
“Please?” Junpei pleaded. “If she does anything suspicious, we can give up on the entire idea,
but she was basically raised by Takaya. A second chance might be exactly what she needs!”

Mitsuru still looked like she had swallowed something unpleasant. Akihiko looked doubtful.
“We should put it up for a vote,” Minato said. “This affects the others too.”

Akechi could not believe this was actually happening.
They all sat in the command room, genuinely discussing Chidori’s potential entrance into the
group. Junpei was glancing at him with an anxious expression, but it wasn’t as though Akechi
could tip the voting in his favor single handedly. If the rest of the group decided to be fools,
there was nothing he could do about it.
“When you vote, state your reason for your decision,” Minato said. “Hopefully, we can come
to a unanimous decision.”
“Alright,” Akihiko said. “All in favor of letting Chidori join the team?”
Minato, Junpei, Shinjiro, and Akihiko raised their hands. Akechi stared at Shinjiro, aghast.
“What the hell are you thinking?” he asked.
“Are you of all people going to deny someone a second chance?” Shinjiro asked. “If Akechi
and I are part of the group, I don’t see why we can’t give Chidori a shot.”
“She tried to shoot me last week!”
“From your story, she had plenty of opportunity to pull the trigger,” Akihiko said quietly.
“She never did. Besides, someone had a gun in the first place and didn’t tell any of us.”
Ken raised his hand tentatively. “But… what if she’s lying?”
“I’ve seen Chidori lying,” Junpei said. “She’s not usually so angry about it. She’s a little
more… bored sounding.”
“That makes her a better liar than Akechi,” Yukari said. She gave Akechi an embarrassed
glance. “Sorry.”
“I guess I deserve that,” Akechi sighed.
Koromaru barked.
“Koro-chan offers to guard Chidori-san’s room,” Aigis said.
“Is that a vote, then?” Junpei asked with a wide grin. Koromaru gave an affirmative-sounding
bark.
“I have a small idea,” Fuuka said, raising her hand. “Could we ask Chidori where Strega’s
base is? Akechi could confirm the spot, and then we could launch an ambush.”

“I don’t know if she would agree to that,” Akihiko said. “She still puts a lot of stock into
Strega’s strength. She wouldn’t want Junpei risking his life. Besides, Strega was a family to
her.”
“Maybe that would be cruel,” Fuuka agreed hesitantly.
“I think we all know why Junpei voted,” Akechi said. “Why did you vote, Akihiko?”
“Call it a gut feeling,” Akihiko said. “And Shinjiro’s right. A second chance is a powerful
thing.”
Ken looked down at his feet. “Yeah,” he said quietly. “I guess you’re right. I’ll put my vote
in.”
“Mine too,” Fuuka said softly. “My bully became my best friend, so I suppose people really
can change.”
Ken, Fuuka, Koromaru, Minato, Akihiko, Junpei, and Shinjiro. That definitely breached the
majority vote. Mitsuru, Yukari, Aigis, and Akechi were the only ones left to object.
“I still think it's risky,” Yukari said.
“She could be dangerous,” Aigis agreed. “She hurt you, Minato-kun.”
“I’ll keep my door locked,” Minato said reassuringly.
“Then she can knock it down,” Akechi said sarcastically.
Mitsuru hadn’t said much throughout the entire conversation, but she looked up with a
contemplative look.
“My father is gone, but… I believe he believed in the power of second chances. I am willing
to try to let Chidori make up for her past actions, if we took the correct precautions.”
Now it was only Yukari, Aigis, and Akechi who stood as objectors.
“Mitsuru-senpai…” Yukari said. “Are you sure about this?”
“No,” Mitsuru admitted. “But I’m hardly sure of anything, these days.” Her expression
hardened. “Majority vote aside, do any of you feel that your safety would be seriously
compromised if Chidori joined the group? This is remembering that for the first month or so,
she would have a guard outside her room, and she would not know where any of the weapons
were stored.”
Well, it was certainly a step up from Akira thrusting brand new weapons and equipment into
Akechi’s arms as soon as he joined the Phantom Thieves. Especially considering that Akira
had known exactly what Akechi planned on doing.
Akechi was not Akira. He could never be that sentimental, that trusting.

But maybe Akira had known the same thing Akechi realized now. Akechi had been one
person. He had never stood a chance in a head-on fight against the entire group, even if they
had less years of experience.
Chidori was one person. If the group of them could defeat Takaya and Jin, it shouldn’t be
difficult at all for them to suppress any potential attack on Chidori’s part. They would just
have to remain vigilant.
Nobody raised their hands. Junpei gave them a grateful smile.

Chidori was not talkative. She reminded Akechi almost of Minato back in May.
“Thank you for this opportunity,” she said stiffly upon entering the dorms.
She looked uncomfortable, wearing a pair of jeans and a frilly white shirt Mitsuru had
provided her. Mitsuru requested that Chidori wear something other than her signature white
dress when she was out and about. While Strega would surely notice that Chidori was no
longer at the hospital, she’d prefer to avoid them seeing Chidori changing locations easily.
“You look nice,” Junpei said immediately. “Um, I can show you to your room.”
Chidori looked relieved to see Junpei there, although it was hard to tell with how impassive
her face was. She gave Junpei a small nod and followed him upstairs. Akechi was still unable
to get over the absurdity of the situation. He stood up.
“Tell the others I’ve gone out,” Akechi told Ken.
“Okay,” Ken said. “Where are you going?”
“I promised to hang out with someone today,” Akechi said, suddenly relieved that Elizabeth
had given him a good excuse to leave the dorms that wasn’t “I wanted to get away from
Chidori.”
Upon arriving at Paulownia mall, Akechi was astonished to find Elizabeth and Theodore
already sitting on one of the benches closest to the Velvet Room. Theodore spotted Akechi
first and waved cheerfully. Elizabeth slapped Theodore’s hand away.
“What are you guys doing here?” Akechi asked.
“You agreed to take us somewhere,” Elizabeth said. “I got impatient, so I stepped outside for
a bit.”
“It is a lovely mall,” Theodore said. “Although, the shadow’s intervention in this world is
growing more obvious.”
Theodore frowned in the direction of one of the Lost standing in the corner of the mall.
Akechi frowned.

“It is growing more and more problematic,” he admitted. “We’re trying to find a solution.”
Although, they were currently preoccupied with Chidori.
Elizabeth stood up. “Where are you taking us today?” she asked. “Perhaps to see one of those
moving pictures Minato told us about?”
Akechi opened his mouth to say that he had something entirely different in mind when he
heard a small pair of feet sprinting toward them. Akechi gaped as a young girl with very
similar features to Elizabeth and Theodore ran up to Elizabeth, holding an empty pouch.
“I gave my offering to the fountain spirit,” she said softly. “Do you think he’ll let me come
now?”
“I’m sure he will,” Theodore said.
The girl, who could be none other than Lavenza, turned toward Akechi with wide eyes. “So
you are Theodore’s guest?” She curtsied. “I am Lavenza. At your service.”
Akechi wondered how much the Velvet Room attendants were even aware of Akechi’s time
traveling. He knew that Elizabeth and Theodore must know that Akechi was from the future.
And Igor and his master potentially even remembered the original timeline. But Lavenza
wore no recognition on her face, no accusations of what he did to her future guest.
Akechi wasn’t going to complain.
“It’s a pleasure to meet you,” Akechi said, partly on reflex to such a polite greeting. “I take it
you’re coming with us?”
“If the fountain spirit grants my wish,” she said. “And you, of course.”
Akechi was tempted to be extremely aggravated with Elizabeth for not warning him about the
child tagging along. But it was clear that Lavenza was more mature than an ordinary human
child. Her presence wasn’t likely to hinder anything.
“Very well,” Akechi sighed. “I was thinking we would go to the aquarium?”
“Aquarium?” Lavenza asked.
“Ah, a water filtering facility,” Theodore said. “It is natural such a place would exist.”
“No,” Akechi said. “It’s where you look at different kinds of fish for educational purposes.”
Theodore flushed. “I knew that.”

Lavenza was extremely taken with the aquarium, but while she stared at everything with
quiet awe, Akechi had to keep a constant eye on the twins. Theodore kept attempting to feed
the fish, and Elizabeth was trying to have a discussion with a shark.

“Surely you do not enjoy being trapped in this glass enclosure,” Elizabeth told the shark.
“I’m sure you could destroy all of these mortals–”
“Elizabeth,” Akechi snapped. “Stop inciting a rebellion. Theodore, you’re not allowed to feed
the fish!”
Theodore grinned guiltily. Elizabeth didn’t look remotely apologetic.
Lavenza giggled as she watched the jellyfish across the room. “Do you think the Velvet
Room could turn into an aquarium?” she asked.
“The Velvet Room matches the guest’s cognition,” Theodore said. “So, I suppose it’s
possible.”
“I hope it has sharks,” Elizabeth said. “That would be more interesting than that cramped
elevator.”
Lavenza’s eyes sparkled. “I hope that my guest makes the Velvet Room an aquarium. With
sharks. I think that would be extremely beautiful.”
Poor Lavenza. Akira never mentioned seeing an aquarium in his dreams.
“Only time will tell,” Akechi said vaguely.
“Do you like fish, Akechi-san?” Lavenza asked.
“I have a fish,” Akechi said.
Theodore’s eyes widened as he stared at Elizabeth’s new shark friend. “How do you fit him
in your room?”
“Not a shark, dumbass,” Akechi snapped. “Just a small goldfish. My friend gave him to me.”
“Can I meet him?” Lavenza asked.
Akechi hesitated. He didn’t particularly want to bring the entire procession of Velvet Room
attendants to the dorms. “I don’t know…”
“I think there’s something you owe me,” Elizabeth said.
“A thank you?” Akechi asked dryly. He had forgotten to say it, in the midst of entertaining
the three children. “I truly owe you my thanks for what you did for me. Your intervention
saved my life.”
Elizabeth smirked. “Actions speak so much louder than words.”

Akechi ended up taking Lavenza to the dorms, but only after Elizabeth and Theodore gave
their solemn oath that they would stay outside.

“I can’t bring all of you in like some sort of procession,” Akechi said. “It would raise way too
many questions. Just stay put.”
“Whatever you want,” Elizabeth said. “Have fun you two.”
Theodore looked seriously disappointed that he wasn’t able to see the fish. Lavenza promised
to describe him in detail.
When Akechi entered the dorms with Lavenza, only Minato and Koromaru were in the
lounge. He raised both of his eyebrows questioningly when Akechi entered.
“You are Elizabeth’s guest, correct?” Lavenza asked. “She speaks very highly of you.”
“Oh, um, yeah,” Minato said. “You are…”
“Lavenza.” Lavenza stared at Koromaru with a fascinated expression on her face. “This
creature does not look like the fish you showed me.”
“No, that is because Koromaru is a dog,” Akechi explained. “He is a mammal.”
“I see,” Lavenza said with a small nod. “Theodore has told me a little bit about dogs. Can I
pet him?”
Koromaru’s bark sounded rather receptive to the idea. He trotted up to Lavenza expectantly.
“Pet away,” Minato said. “He likes it.”
Lavenza smiled as she tentatively petted the top of Koromaru’s head. “Keep protecting our
guests, okay?”
Koromaru barked again with a happy huff. His tail wagged back and forth violently.
“Let’s visit Taiyaki before we draw in a crowd,” Akechi said.
“Very well.”
They reached Akechi’s bedroom without incident, and Lavenza leaned over Akechi’s desk to
get a better look at the goldfish. Taiyaki must have sensed there was company, or maybe he
thought Akechi was about to feed him. He began swimming extra violently around his castle.
“Is your fish the lord of his domain?” Lavenza asked.
“The castle is decorative,” Akechi said. “But since the fish is the only member of his domain,
I suppose it wouldn’t be completely inaccurate to say that he is lord over it.”
“He seems especially agitated right now,” Lavenza said. “Does he not wish me in his
presence?”
“I doubt it.” Akechi picked up the small container of fish food. “He’s hungry. Would you like
to feed him?”

Lavenza eagerly took the container. She carefully read the instructions on the back before
putting an extremely precise amount of food into the tank.
“Fish are easily satisfied,” Lavenza observed as Taiyaki ate. “Humans seem to need much
more in their life than food and a home.”
“Yes, well, we’re greedy creatures.”
“I don’t think so.” Lavenza shook her head. “Aquariums exist to teach other humans, are they
not? I saw many children enjoying themselves there. Where is the greed in that?”
“You pay money to enter,” Akechi said.
“That money supports the livelihoods of the employees, if I understand your economy
correctly.”
“But some if it goes to greedy CEOs who wish to trample upon others.”
“So a small portion of evil makes all of it bad?” Lavenza asked. She didn’t look angry, just
confused.
“It’s complicated,” Akechi sighed. He shouldn’t have tried to explain this to a child, even if
that child was an otherworldly being.
“Or maybe it’s quite simple,” Lavenza said. “There’s good and bad. That doesn’t take away
from the good.”
Akechi didn’t want to engage in moral philosophy at the moment. The good was almost
always tainted with evil, but something told him that Lavenza would never see it that way.
“Your siblings are waiting for you,” Akechi said. “We should get going.”
Judgement Arcana: Rank 5

The morning of the seventeenth, chaos rang out within the dorms. The high schoolers were
departing for Kyoto that day, and a few people had decided not to pack until that very
morning.
A few people only really being Junpei.
“I can’t believe you wasted your entire evening talking to me,” Chidori said from the kitchen
table. Akechi kept a watchful eye on her, as he always did. She hadn’t tried anything yet,
however, and Akechi was slightly more interested in the chaos unfolding.
“I don’t want to talk about it!” Junpei cried out, sprinting down the stairs with a suitcase.
Clothing leaked out of it dramatically. Junpei had failed to zip it up all the way, and the
suitcase left a trail of shirts and underwear on the stairs in its wake. “Damnit!”

Akihiko also left the packing for that morning, but he did so in a far more graceful fashion.
He came downstairs with an exhausted stare and a properly packed suitcase. He placed his
suitcase down with the others’ and walked into the kitchen for some breakfast.
“I’m glad I’m not you right now,” Shinjiro said.
“You should really go to school,” Akihiko said. “Then you get to go on these fantastic school
trips.”
“To Kyoto,” Yukari sighed sadly.
Mitsuru, Minato, Fuuka, Yukari, and Aigis were all standing at the ready by the doors to the
dorms. Junpei sprinted up to them with his properly closed suitcase and a few pieces of
laundry in his arms.
“I hate packing!” Junpei cried out. “I hate Kyoto!”
“Why are you going if you hate it so much?” Chidori asked.
“Because–” Junpei huffed, dropping all his items onto the ground. “Actually, no. I’ve already
explained it to you.”
“I think Kyoto is a nice place,” Ken said. “They have these really delicious snacks. Try to
bring me some.”
Minato nodded solemnly. “On it.”
“It’ll be quiet without you guys,” Shinjiro said. “Try not to get up to too much trouble
without me.”
“Well, you know me,” Akihiko said. His exhausted voice held very little gusto. “I just love
getting into trouble.”
At that moment, someone rhythmically knocked on the doors. Minato’s eyes widened, and he
opened it.
“Hey guys!” Ryoji said, entering the dorms with an easy-going smile on his face. “Ready for
the trip?”
“I thought you were going to meet us at the station,” Minato said.
“I got bored.” Ryoji put on a winning smile.
Aigis glared at Ryoji like he was death itself. “We do not require your assistance.”
Ryoji whistled. “As cold as always, I see,” he said. “I’m sorry for whatever I did to offend
you, Aigis-chan.” He gave Akechi a wave. “Hello, there, Akechi-kun!”
Akechi sighed and waved back. He was too tired for this, but Ryoji was already approaching.

“I didn’t realize you lived in the dorms,” Ryoji said. “It kind of puts Minato’s stories into
perspective, though.”
“What stories?” Akechi asked, glaring at Minato. Minato looked away, wearing an innocent
expression.
“All good things,” Ryoji said quickly. “Why do two elementary school students live in these
dorms anyway?”
“Um, it’s a long story,” Ken said. “You guys should probably hurry to get to the train on
time.”
Ryoji frowned and glanced at his watch. “What? But it’s only five thirty in the morning.”
“Your watch is incorrect,” Chidori said.
Ryoji’s eyes widened when he saw Chidori, and his flirtatious grin returned to his face.
“Maybe after this trip, you and I can–”
“It’s fifteen minutes until seven.”
“It’s what?” Ryoji jumped, his face growing pale. “We’re going to be late!”
The girls had already left when nobody was paying attention. Minato, Akihiko, Junpei, and
Ryoji all sprinted from the dorms, loudly dragging their luggage behind them.

Shinjiro, Ken, Chidori, and Akechi all stared at each other after they had gone. The
scratching of Chidori’s pencil against the page of her sketchbook was extremely loud in the
silence.
“You’re right, Shinjiro-kun,” Ken finally said. “It is quiet without them.”
“I hope you aren’t too short on people for guard duty,” Chidori said.
“I think we’ll manage,” Shinjiro said. “Me and Koromaru are more than enough for the job.”
Chidori sighed and stood up. “In that case, I will be returning to my room now. The quiet is
more comfortable there.”
Koromaru followed her upstairs. Akechi was grateful that at least one pair of eyes would be
on her bedroom door. While Strega almost never made a move in broad daylight, Akechi’s
kidnapping being an exception, it was better safe than sorry.
Ken and Akechi hurried to school. Just because the high schoolers were fortunate enough to
have the next few days off did not mean that school halted for everyone.
“Hi guys,” Emiko said when they met up as they always did. She had brightened up
considerably since the death of Momo. Occasionally, however, Ken and Akechi would say

something to upset her on accident, and they would spend the rest of the day trying to make it
up to her.
On that particular day, however, Emiko already looked upset. She wasn’t smiling, and her
eyes were unusually downcast.
“What’s wrong, Emiko-kun?” Ken asked.
“Oh, it’s nothing,” Emiko sighed. “I just saw this really sad movie about a dog, and it
reminded me of Momo and how sad I was, and…” She sniffed.
“I’m sorry, Emiko-kun,” Akechi said. “How about we go to the Takoyaki stand after school?
My treat.”
Emiko brightened. “Really?”
“Yeah!” Ken said. “We can experiment with flavors too!”
“That sounds like fun! Maybe we can even get Akechi to do the Russian roulette Takoyaki.”
Akechi regretted his life choices, but at least Emiko was happier.
She would not stay that way.

Chapter Notes

tw: sibling drama, attempted murder, violence

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The next morning, Emiko’s expression was somehow more miserable than before. Akechi
tried to recall if anything had happened while they hung out that afternoon, but the only thing
of note was Akechi having to restrain himself from swearing as overly spicy takoyaki burned
his mouth. Emiko was about as cheerful as ever by the time they parted ways.
“Emiko-kun?” Akechi prompted.
“My sister is really mean,” Emiko said. Tears filled her eyes as her expression became more
sullen. “We got into a fight yesterday.”
“A fight?” Ken asked. “What sort of fight?”
Emiko balled her hands into fists. “I–I was telling her about the takoyaki we had,” she said.
“And how Akechi wore that really funny expression when he ate the super spicy stuff.”
Akechi bristled. “It wasn’t that funny.”
“It was pretty funny,” Ken said.
Emiko giggled, but the mirth in her eyes quickly faded. “And, then, out of nowhere, she
started yelling at me! She talked about how all I did was talk or cry, and I was really
ungrateful because I got to spend more time with Momo than she did anyway. And that I
should focus more on studying instead of goofing off, because that was what she had to do all
day long, and it was really unfair!”

Ken scowled. “That is unfair! What does that have to do with anything?”
“I don’t know!” Emiko said. “I told her that it was her own fault she studied all day without
spending any time with me or Momo. And she said that she was doing it so that she could
help people, and that I didn’t understand how hard entrance exams were.”
“I’m sorry she said that to you,” Akechi said.
“And then, then,” Emiko wailed, “she said it was all my fault that Mom is dead. She said she
wished I was never born!”
Emiko started crying in earnest, and Ken gently patted her shoulder. Akechi wasn’t sure what
to do but to be in shocked awe at the pure audacity in Emiko’s sister’s words.
“Don’t listen to her,” Ken said. “She’s just an ass.”
Emiko sniffed. “You shouldn’t say that. You’ll get in trouble.”
“Um, well, she’s just a jerk, then,” Ken said. “You’re amazing, got that?”
“Y-yeah.” Emiko’s breathing hitched as she tried to scrub the tears away from her eyes.
“You’re right.”
A terrible pit formed in Akechi’s stomach as a thought came to him. It was absurd, almost
unthinkable, and yet…
She said she wished I was never born!
Akechi only learned of Strega’s revenge site by seeing it open on her sister’s computer. But
surely, surely, Emiko’s sister wouldn’t do something as stupid and cruel as request a hit on
her own sister.
Then again, people did horrible things when they were angry. Akechi would know.
“This might be a bit forward of me,” Akechi said, his mind moving frantically. “But maybe
we should come to your house to defend your honor against your sister.”
Akechi didn’t remember the address to Emiko’s house. This lack of information could prove
disastrous if Akechi’s theory was correct.
“I don’t think that’s necessary,” Emiko said, scrubbing her eyes with her fists. “I’m sure
she’ll get over it in a few days.”
“A few days?!” Ken exclaimed. “She stays mean for a few days?”
“Well, no, she just stays in her room for longer,” Emiko said. “She might not like it if you
guys came over anyway.”
“We don’t have to confront her, then,” Akechi said. “But, um, my friend has been teaching
me to cook. We could bake cookies together as a peace offering to her.”

Emiko hesitated. “Well, she does like cookies,” she conceded. “I suppose we could give it a
try.”
Well, it was a start.

Akechi wasn’t much of a baker, but he knew how to follow basic recipes. Ken and Emiko
were able to follow along well enough. At the very least, the cookies didn’t turn out to be a
charred mess of nothing.
When they were done, Emiko delivered some of the cookies to her sister’s bedroom. She
knocked on the door quietly, looking tentative.
“Ai?” she asked. “Are you in there?”
“I’m busy,” Emiko’s sister, Ai, said. Her voice was as irritated as ever.
“We made cookies for you,” Emiko said. “As a peace offering.”
Thumping came from the room, and the door cracked open. Ai was scowling as she looked at
the cookies on the plate Emiko held out to her.
“Do you really think cookies are going to fix this?” she asked.
“No…” Emiko looked sadly at the tray. “But I thought it would be nice.”
Ai grabbed the plate and slammed the door shut. Truly a display of sisterly compassion. It
was still more than Akechi expected. Maybe he was jumping to conclusions about this entire
situation.
“That was… something,” Ken said.
“I said some pretty mean things yesterday too,” Emiko admitted as she joined them in the
kitchen to clean up. “Um, I said that she doesn’t have any friends because she was a stuck-up
—um… well, I heard the word on television and thought…”
Emiko sighed as she ran the cookie sheet underneath the faucet. “I’m sorry.”
“Did you apologize to her?” Ken asked.
“I tried to!” Emiko said defensively. “But she said all those terrible things immediately after,
and I–I forgot.”
“Maybe you should try to talk to her later,” Ken said reluctantly. “No pressure or anything.”
“She’s the oldest,” Akechi said bluntly. “She should be mature enough to come to you first.”
Not that it was ever how that worked.
Emiko didn’t look like she felt better about the situation.

When they arrived back at the dorms that evening, Akechi turned to Ken with his deadliest
expression.
“You are to stay in the dorms tonight,” Akechi said.
“What?” Ken asked, looking confused. “Where are you going?”
“I need to talk to Shinjiro.” Akechi began marching up the stairs. Ken hastened to follow.
“You can’t leave me hanging like this! Where are you going?”
“Can’t you trust me?”
“Not if you’re going to keep secrets!”
Akechi bit back a sigh. “Fine. I have reason to believe that Emiko’s sister might have put
Emiko’s name in Strega’s revenge website. I’m going to ask Shinjiro to help me stake out the
apartment.”
Ken’s expression became slack. “You’re kidding, right? The argument wasn’t even that bad!”
Ken hummed. “Okay, it was pretty bad if Emiko called her sister a bitch…and her sister said
she wished Emiko wasn’t born. But it doesn’t warrant death!”
“Teenagers do stupid things when they’re angry,” Akechi said. “And maybe I’m wrong. But I
don’t want to take any risks.”
“O-okay,” Ken said. “But let me come too!”
“No.”
“Why not?!” Ken grabbed Akechi by the shoulder, nearly yanking him backwards down the
stairs. “I can fight!”
“I know you can,” Akechi said. “You’re an excellent fighter under ordinary circumstances.
But over half the team is gone, Ken. They’re at Kyoto!”
“And you think that changes anything?” Ken looked about ready to shove Akechi. “You and
Shinjiro are just going to leave me alone?”
Akechi was panicking. He couldn’t let Ken face off against Strega, even with Shinjiro by his
side. Sure, they won the fight against Jin and Takaya at their full force, but that was with
multiple people providing healing and buffs to the entire party. Ken was smaller, younger. He
naturally had less health and stamina, and there was no working around that. If Jin’s grenades
landed in just the right way–
Maybe Akechi was being paranoid. He didn’t care.
“It’s too dangerous,” Akechi said, trying to stay calm.

“You’ll be there too–”
“Ken, listen to me for a damn second!” Akechi snapped. “Stop acting like an immature child

After hearing Yukari’s shattered testimony and piecing together what they each saw, the
general consensus of what occurred that night was as follows:
Takaya had decided that it would be worth trying to get Chidori back on their team, likely for
her support abilities. He and Jin agreed to infiltrate her room while the guard shift was
changing. Why they chose not to attack during the Dark Hour was largely a mystery, but
Akechi pointed out that they probably felt they stood a better chance in a weapons fight than
a persona fight. Especially considering there were over ten persona users in the building.
Yukari accidentally fell asleep when Akechi was meant to relieve her of her shift. Takaya and
Jin picked the lock of the window by the fire escape, allowing them to get inside quietly.
Yukari was sleeping lightly enough, however, to wake up at the sound of footsteps. She shot
Takaya just before Jin knocked her out with his evoker.

And in Maruki’s reality, Akechi hadn’t felt terror. Frustration, yes. Anger, yes. But he was

“Why is this happening?” Ken whispered.

Year’s Eve, to make your decision. After that, I’ll dissolve into the Dark Hour and become
intangible.”
“What?” Minato asked, his head snapping up toward Ryoji.
“Please don’t let your concern for me impact your decision,” Ryoji said. He smiled brokenly.
“I won’t be around for much longer anyway.”
Without another word, Ryoji fled the room.
To kill or not to kill. He could let the world rot but lose himself in the process. Or, he could
continue this endless charade of hope but at least die fighting in the process.

Neither option was particularly appealing, and yet Akechi was forced to choose anyway.
Confused rage churned inside Akechi, and he got to his feet.
“Akechi-kun?” Fuuka asked.

Akechi sucked in a breath.

“The world isn’t good,” Akechi said. “That doesn’t mean you have to bow down to its every

fight against the impossible.”
Akechi grit his teeth and said nothing. His anger was getting muddied by an emotion that felt
much more akin to grief. He didn’t trust himself to say anything he wouldn’t regret.
“I’m sorry,” Ryoji whispered.

“We haven’t lost yet,” Mitsuru interrupted.
“I… will never give up,” Aigis said.
Both Aigis and Mitsuru collapsed to the ground. Everyone soon followed. Even Akechi, with
his fiercest stubbornness, felt his knees buckle and hit the ground jarringly. He tried to catch
his fall, but the gravity caused him to lie almost completely flat on his stomach.

The stone floor of Tartarus scraped against Akechi’s chin as he forced himself to look up.
Minato and Ryoji were the only ones left standing.
And they both began floating toward Nyx.
“Where the hell are you two going?!” Akihiko shouted.
“Don’t go!” Ken cried.
Their cries did nothing. Minato and Ryoji disappeared into Nyx’s iris.
Akechi glared at Nyx. He wasn’t going to stop them from doing whatever they needed to do.
They’d better rip Nyx apart from the inside.

Ai was pretty sure the world was ending.
The sky had gone this disgusting green color, and the moon was turning into a giant eye. Not
to mention that there was some creepy tower in the distance and doomsayers crying out that
the end had come.
Who knew that the cult actually knew what they were talking about?
Ai left her room and went to Emiko’s bedroom. If the world really was coming to an end, she
should spend her last moments with her sister.
Ai expected Emiko to be crying in the corner of her bedroom. She was big on crying. She
cried when the cat died; she cried when their father snapped; she cried when Ai gave her a
gift, for crying out loud. The end of the world was definitely a reason to cry.
But Emiko wasn’t crying. She was staring out her window with wide, serious eyes. Her
mouth was set in a tight line.
“Emiko?” Ai asked, unsure by her sister’s reaction.
“Girls!” Their father rushed into the room, his face frantic with worry.
Emiko glanced toward their father. “Do you think they’re going to win?”
Ai frowned. “What are you talking about?”
“My friends,” Emiko said. She pointed out the window toward that freaky tower. “They’re
fighting. I know it.”
“Your friends… are fighting?” Their father rested a hand on Emiko’s shoulder. “What are you
talking about?”
Did this have anything to do with that creepy elementary schooler that had lectured Ai on the
importance of family?

Emiko nodded. “They fought to protect me. And now they’re fighting to protect everyone
else. Do you think they’ll win?”
Ai had no idea what was going on anymore. Maybe it wasn’t a stretch to assume that
elementary schoolers were now fighting the end of the world. Even though it sounded
absolutely ridiculous.
Besides, if this is what Emiko was doing to comfort herself, Ai wasn’t going to stop her. It
was better than crying. Ai never knew how to deal with crying.
“Are your friends strong?” Ai asked.
Emiko nodded, her eyes shining with admiration.
“Then, sure. I bet they’ll win. When we wake up, this will all be just like a bad dream.”
Emiko’s eyes welled with tears. Crap. “I hope so,” she whispered.
Ai awkwardly wrapped an arm around Emiko’s shoulders. Emiko leaned into her side. It was
actually pretty comforting, even if Emiko was silently crying next to her. Their father
wrapped his arms around them both, as if that would protect either of them from what was
going on outside.
Maybe handling a crying sister wasn’t that hard. When the world was ending, at least.
Because, oddly enough, Ai felt a little bit like crying too.

From the inside, Nyx looked like a glowing egg connected by millions of neurons. It pulsated
as it released Death upon Ryoji and Minato. Ryoji’s entire body tensed, and he clung all the
tighter to Minato’s hand.
They didn’t die. Ryoji felt the life in his body wane, but they weren’t dead. Not yet.
“Minato,” Ryoji whispered. “What’s happening?”
“We’re ending this,” Minato said, a determination in his eyes that Ryoji had never seen
before.
Ryoji could hear the voices of the others echoing in his soul. Begging Minato to win. Lending
them their strength. Little by little, Ryoji felt less weak.
Nyx attempted to cast death on them again. It missed.
“You’d better win,” Goro’s voice echoed in the room. “Or I’ll kill you.”
Ryoji almost snorted. Goro always had a way with words.
Chidori’s voice suddenly pierced through the others’ encouragements.

“Save him. Save everyone.”
The pain of grief burst inside of Ryoji. Minato gave his hand a squeeze.
“Are you ready?”
Ryoji felt it too. Some strange otherworldly power coming from within Minato, like a million
suns of hope and trust that pulsed in Minato’s soul. Ryoji had no idea where Minato had
come to such an ability, but he was more than happy to assist Minato in his burden.
“Always.”
Minato smiled, and Ryoji tightened his grip on Minato’s hand.
Minato cast Great Seal. Ryoji felt all his power burn within him. A bright light pierced the
room, and—

“Where are we?” Yukari asked.
Stars dotted the void surrounding them. If Akechi didn’t know better, he would say they were
suspended in space.
“Are we dead?” Ken asked.
“Somehow, I don’t think so,” Shinjiro said. He coughed, and Ken grimaced.
“Did Nyx create this place?” Mitsuru asked. “Or did Minato?”
“Where are they?” Akechi snapped, turning to Fuuka. “Where are those two?”
“There was this bright light, but I don’t sense them,” Fuuka said. Her voice shook.
“No,” Junpei said. “Not… but that’s not fair! We only just got Ryoji back!”
“We knew that we were putting our lives on the line,” Mitsuru said, although she didn’t
sound remotely convinced.
“This was exactly what I wanted to prevent,” Aigis whispered.
They had to be alive. There was no way they were dead. Akechi refused to believe it. If he
believed it for even one moment, he would have to kill Takaya and Ikutsuki all over again,
and that wasn’t possible.
“You’re here, aren’t you?!” Yukari shouted. “I refuse to believe that you’re gone! Answer
me!”
“You don’t seriously think we’d give up on you that easily, do you?!” Akechi shouted,
digging his nails into his palms. “Show your damn faces already!”

“Please!” Aigis begged.
“It’s alright,” Minato said. His voice echoed above them. Akechi let out a gasping breath that
sounded almost like a sob.
“Nyx will sleep now,” Ryoji’s voice said. “Normal days will return for you…”
“For us,” Minato corrected.
“What happened?” Akihiko asked. “Where are you?”
“The Dark Hour will vanish from this world,” Ryoji said. “All will be relinquished from its
dominion, and life will continue. You really did it.” Ryoji’s voice cracked. “You won.”
“Of course, we did!” A small grin appeared on Junpei’s face. “We always win!”
Koromaru barked affirmatively.

They stood in front of the school as Tartarus disintegrated. The Dark Hour was gone, and the
deep blue night sky was filled with stars.
Akechi barely felt the cold as he got to his feet. They did it. He wasn’t dead. This chapter of
his life could finally be over.
Minato and Ryoji stood in front of them, smiling and alive. Aigis broke down crying.
Nobody noticed the single tear of sheer relief that rolled down Goro’s face. He preferred to
keep it that way.

Chapter Notes

Yukari was right. The following morning, their memories of the Dark Hour disappeared
along with its destruction.
Fortunately, it hadn’t taken long for Akechi to recover his memories. Waking up in a high
school dormitory still holding the memories of the Phantom Thieves and his time with Shido
did wonders for connecting the dots.
Unfortunately, after the puzzle pieces slotted into place, everything became much more
surreal.
Nobody remembered. They barely even remembered each other, much less what happened
during the Dark Hour. Shinjiro and Akihiko kept to themselves. Yukari, Junpei, and Minato
were their own little posse in the dorms. Mitsuru barely interacted with anyone.
Akechi and Ken were still friends. But their friendship wasn’t the same. It felt fake. It was
like Maruki had picked Akechi up and placed him into his idea of a happy reality. Except
Akechi wasn’t happy.
It was unnerving to see everyone so calm and relaxed. To not have death hanging over their
heads. Maybe it should have been a good thing. Akechi hated it.
“Hey, Goro-kun,” Ken said as they walked to school. “Do you want to go to the arcade with
me this afternoon?”
Akechi smiled pleasantly. “I’m sorry, Ken-kun. I’m afraid I have other plans for this
afternoon.”
“Yeah?” Ken asked. “That’s too bad.”

He didn’t remark on Akechi’s fake smile. Did he even notice?
“Are you alright, Goro-kun?” Emiko asked when she joined the two.
Goro faltered. Emiko remained unchanged by the whole affair, but he hadn’t realized that she
would notice the discrepancies as well.
Akechi forced himself to smile anyway. “I’m fine, Emiko-chan.”
“Emiko-chan, do you want to go to the arcade with me?” Ken asked Emiko.
Emiko narrowed her eyes. “You’re both acting weird…” she said. “Are you sure nothing’s
wrong?”
Ken looked genuinely surprised by the answer. Akechi turned his face away so Emiko
wouldn’t see the lie in his eyes.
“Nothing at all,” he said.
Akechi’s “plans” for the afternoon involved wandering aimlessly around the city and trying
not to feel nauseous. The group promised each other to remember, but graduation was only a
few weeks away. The only ones who showed any sign of recollecting were Minato and Aigis.
Come to think of it, had Aigis even forgotten at all? She mostly kept to herself in the
dormitories, but she eyed everyone with such a tentative expression that maybe she did
remember.
Akechi needed to speak to her.
“You’re looking awfully lonely,” Tsuyoshi said, appearing seemingly out of nowhere and
walking alongside Akechi. Akechi quickened his pace.
“I’m not in the mood for this,” he said.
“Aw, why not?”
“Just leave me–”
Tsuyoshi grabbed Akechi’s wrist so tightly that hot pain raced up Akechi’s arm. Akechi
attempted to twist Tsuyoshi’s arm back to break it, but Tsuyoshi didn’t budge. When Akechi
moved to knee Tsuyoshi in the groin, Tsuyoshi slammed Akechi against the wall.
Stars flooded Akechi’s vision as he tried to find his breath.
“Who the hell–” Akechi gasped. “--are you? What are you?”
“I bet you feel really proud of yourself,” Tsuyoshi hissed. Akechi felt spittle land on his
cheek. “You saved the world. Hell, you even saved a couple of lives along the way. Don’t you
just feel clever?”

Akechi clawed Tsuyoshi in the face. Tsuyoshi didn’t even move.
“Well, newsflash,” Tsuyoshi said. “This is nothing. Nothing. Compared to the hell you’ll be
facing. I hope you’re ready for it.”
Tsuyoshi let go of Akechi, but Akechi grabbed onto his jacket. “What are you?” Akechi
asked again.
A small smirk played on Tsuyoshi’s lips. “Let’s just say that your buddy Takaya looked mild
in comparison.”
Tsuyoshi walked away and faded into the crowd. Akechi stared at his bruised wrist.
Why couldn’t it ever be over?
Fool Arcana: Rank 6

“Akechi-kun!” Aigis exclaimed when Akechi returned to the dorms. She frowned. “What
happened to your wrist?”
“I was mugged,” Akechi said.
“Let me help you with it,” Aigis said.
Akechi sat down at the dining room table and let Aigis rummage through the kitchen drawers
for first aid supplies. She returned with a few ice packs and an elastic bandage.
“First, you must reduce the swelling with ice,” she said. She handed Akechi the ice pack, and
Akechi pressed it against his injury.
“This isn’t the first time I’ve hurt myself, you know,” Akechi said.
“Yes, well, real world first aid is harder than with…” Aigis trailed off. She looked away.
“Personas?” Akechi asked, barely keeping the hope out of his voice.
Aigis’ eyes lit up; Akechi had never seen her expression so joyful. “You remember?” she
asked.
“It would be hard not to,” Akechi said. He pretended that he wasn’t also relieved to have
someone who remembered the truth.
Aigis started spending more time with Akechi after that. Akechi didn’t stop her.

“Hi, Goro-kun!” Ryoji told Akechi cheerfully when he came by the dorms with Minato.
“How have you been?”

“Peachy,” Akechi said.
“What happened to your wrist?” Ryoji asked, his eyes landing on Akechi’s bandaged hand.
“Ignore it.” Akechi smiled pleasantly. “Have you been doing well?”
“Yeah.” Ryoji rubbed the back of his neck and laughed sheepishly. “Sorry for the false alarm
about me moving again. My parents let me come back to Japan. Nice, huh?”
Minato wore an unreadable expression. Surely Minato remembered? Not only was he a wild
card, but he and Ryoji had literally stopped Nyx from killing them all.
“I especially liked the part where you came just in time for the world to end,” Akechi said.
Ryoji’s eyes widened. Akechi’s heart dropped. Had he miscalculated?
But a wide smile spread across Ryoji’s face. “Yeah,” he said. “I really liked that part too.”

Minato and Ryoji were always tired.
Akechi began spending more time with Aigis, Minato, and Ryoji. It assured him he hadn’t
simply imagined the past ten months. However, it was growing more and more painfully
obvious that all was not well.
Immediately after school, Minato would take a nap on the sofa. Sometimes he went straight
to his bedroom and slept for the entire rest of the day. Once, when the four of them tried to go
out for dinner, Ryoji fell asleep and faceplanted into his beef bowl.
“Sorry,” Ryoji had said, yawning and brushing bits of rice out of his hair. “I didn’t get a lot of
sleep last night.”
“Well, I know for a fact Minato did, and he’s falling asleep on top of Aigis even as we
speak,” Akechi snapped. “What the hell is going on?”
“It’s nothing,” Minato murmured.
“Don’t give me that bullshit,” Akechi said. “Why are both of you hibernating all of a
sudden?”
“Because we’re mammals, and it’s winter,” Ryoji said eagerly. “You’re behind the times,
Goro.”
“Ha ha.”
“Your energy levels are unusually low,” Aigis said. “Does it have anything to do with you
sealing Nyx away?”
Ryoji’s expression grew somber. “Maybe.”

“We’re fine,” Minato said, pushing himself from Aigis’ shoulder. “We’re just recuperating.”
“Promise me you will be alright,” Aigis told Minato.
Minato nodded. “I promise.”

The Velvet Room door was gone. Akechi knew this because when he actively went searching
for it, he couldn’t find it anywhere.
“Thanks a lot,” Akechi muttered to the back alley of Paulownia Mall. He had just dragged
Minato half-way across the city for Elizabeth to give her verdict, and Elizabeth wasn’t even
available anymore.
“My contract was fulfilled,” Minato said helpfully. “I’m the Universe, or something.”
“I don’t care what you are,” Akechi snapped. “He never told me that my contract was
fulfilled.”
“Well, the world isn’t ending anymore,” Minato said with a shrug.
Akechi wanted to tear his hair out.

They took Minato and Ryoji to a doctor, just to be safe. The doctors couldn’t find anything
wrong with them.
“They’re perfectly healthy physically,” they said. “Just make sure they’re exercising and
eating good foods. Maybe consider a psychologist. It could be a symptom of depression.”
“I don’t have depression,” Minato said as they walked back to the dorms. A statement Goro
was too tired to contest.
“I’m perfectly healthy physically,” Ryoji said with awe in his voice. “Does that mean I’m not
a shadow anymore?”
“I don’t know,” Akechi asked. “Do you feel hungry?”
“All the time.”
“Then, I’m going to say that you’re human. But maybe you’re some sort of cross between.”
“Wow,” Ryoji said. “Weird.”

On the day of graduation, Minato was sleeping in. If Minato was sleeping in, it was fairly
safe to assume that Ryoji was also sleeping in.

“It would be a shame if they were late to their own reunion,” Akechi remarked. “Assuming
the others manage to remember.”
“We will remind them, if we must,” Aigis said. “I will wake up Minato. Can you wake up
Ryoji?”
Akechi would argue that Aigis had the easier job. Minato was in the very same building as
them. On that note, Minato was a far deeper sleeper than Ryoji was. Ryoji would wake up at
the sound of the doorbell. Minato would struggle to wake up for Armageddon.
“Good luck,” Akechi said as he left the dorms.
Akechi arrived at Ryoji’s apartment and rang the doorbell. He only had to wait a few minutes
for Ryoji to open the door for him.
“Goro-kun!” Ryoji said. “What can I do for you today?”
“Do you go to school anymore?” Akechi asked.
Ryoji frowned. “What do you mean? It’s still early in the morning, isn’t it?”
“If you call nine a.m. early in the morning,” Akechi said. “The only reason I’m missing
school is because I have places to be. You just slept in.”
“Well, maybe,” Ryoji said. “It’s hard, you know. This seal thing. It’s a really good thing I was
there.”
“What do you mean?” Akechi asked sharply.
“Minato and I are sharing the burden of sealing away Nyx,” Ryoji said. “That’s why we’re so
tired all the time, although it should wear off eventually. But if Minato had done it by
himself, it would have drained his life force entirely.”
Akechi shouldn’t have been surprised. Minato acted like he was doomed to die in the days
preceding their battle with Nyx. Still, the realization was… unsettling. The thought of Minato
dying just after they thought they won made Akechi feel sick.
“But you both aren’t going to die, are you?” Akechi asked.
Ryoji shook his head. “I think we’ll be fine.” He gave Akechi an encouraging smile. “So, um,
you said you had somewhere to be?”
“Yes,” Akechi said shortly. “You weren’t there, but right before we fought Nyx, we promised
each other to meet on top of the school roof on graduation day. Can you guess what day it
is?”
Ryoji’s eyes widened. “Oh, crap. Minato mentioned that, and I completely forgot. I was
having a really great dream, you see–”
“Save it,” Akechi snapped. “Let’s go so we’re less late than we already are.”

“You’re so practical,” Ryoji pouted.
“I hate being late,” Akechi said. “Sue me.”

They were late. They were so late, in fact, that by the time they had gotten to the high school,
students were already gossiping.
“Ryoji-kun!” one of the girls exclaimed, rushing up to him. “I didn’t see you at graduation!”
“I accidentally slept in,” Ryoji said. He raised his hand with an embarrassed smile. “Nothing
to be worried about.”
“You missed it, then,” the girl said. “Kirijo-senpai totally jumped off the stage in the middle
of her speech. She and a bunch of other students ran off.”
“Wow, she did that, huh?” Ryoji asked.
“Maybe she got anxious,” another student said. “I know I would be scared to speak in front
of so many people.”
“Yeah, but this is Kirijo-senpai we’re talking about!” The first girl shook her head. “She
never gets flustered. Don’t you remember her speech at the beginning of the year?”
“Yeah, but her father died–”
Akechi dragged Ryoji away before he lost his temper.
“You’re going to have to help me here,” Akechi said as they started climbing up the staircase
in the middle of the lobby. “It’s been months since I’ve even stepped foot in this building.
How do we get to the roof?”
“Don’t worry,” Ryoji said. “I’m on it.”
Ryoji found the flight of stairs leading to the roof rather easily. The others were all gathered
around one of the tables. Ken and Koromaru were somehow there too. Maybe Aigis had told
them preemptively.
Minato was lying on one of the benches, presumably still sleeping. His head rested in Aigis’
lap.
“Is he okay?” Ryoji asked, jogging up to the others.
“Weren’t you the one who said he should be fine?” Akechi snapped.
“He is merely asleep,” Aigis said. “There is no need to worry.”
“I wasn’t worried,” Ryoji lied. “I was just checking.”
“Right,” Akihiko said.

Junpei’s eyes lit up. “Ryoji!” He tackled Ryoji in a hug. Ryoji stumbled backwards.
“What’s brought this on?” he asked, laughing.
“What else?” Junpei asked. “Sure, I might have seen you for the past month, but I couldn’t
appreciate it then. Now, I can actually celebrate your not-being-death-ness.”
“Eloquently said,” Mitsuru said, a teasing smile on her face.
“We can’t all be student council presidents,” Junpei sighed.
“Should we… wake him up eventually?” Ken asked, frowning at Minato. “Why is he
sleeping so much anyway?”
Ryoji explained the same thing he had told Akechi. Aigis’ expression turned to a cold glare.
“Why did you not mention this earlier?” she asked. “Goro-kun and I took you both to the
doctors out of fear for your health.”
“You remembered?” Akihiko asked Akechi.
Akechi nodded. He was mostly surprised that he didn’t think to ask the same question Aigis
was asking. Was he really so distracted by their reunion?
“We were a little nervous,” Ryoji admitted, “that we were both going to die. We didn’t want
to burden you with the truth.”
“You would have rathered you both die without any explanation?” Akechi asked. Judging
from Aigis’ face, she was thinking much the same thing.
Ryoji’s grimaced. “Yeah, I guess I deserve that,” he said. “I don't know what we were
thinking.”
Finally, Minato sat up. He opened his eyes, and his face brightened when he saw the rest of
the team gathered around him.
“Hi everyone.”
“Oh, you’re awake!” Fuuka said.
“Good to see you’re not dead,” Shinjiro added dryly. Koromaru barked in agreement.
Minato frowned. “Of course I’m not…” His eyes landed on Ryoji’s guilty expression. “You
told them?”
“Well, if you were going to die, now would probably be the time,” Ryoji said. “Besides, I feel
way less tired today. That’s a good sign, right?”
Minato didn’t look so sure. “Right.”
“Well enough of this sad talk,” Junpei said. “Let’s all go out to celebrate! It’ll be on me.”

Minato jumped to his feet with more energy than Akechi had seen him exercise for weeks. A
small part of Akechi wondered if Minato had really been sleeping partly to avoid the pain of
having friends who didn’t remember.
Well, Akechi thought as the others started talking about their celebration plans, maybe he
understood why.

“I won the bet,” Junpei told him as the group walked home from dinner later that evening.
“What are you talking about?” Akechi asked.
“I won the bet,” Junpei said again. “Don’t tell me that you remembered everything except our
bet.”
A small smirk grew on Akechi’s face. “I’m sure I have no idea what you’re talking about.”
“Come on, man!” Junpei groaned. “The bet! The deal we made? You promised that you
wouldn’t mention being kicked out for three weeks after we defeated Nyx. And if nobody
mentioned it, you owe me five dinners.”
“Why would I agree to such a ridiculous deal?”
“What, do you need to sign bets on paper to make them official, is that your problem now?”
Junpei looked extremely offended. “You owe me five dinners. You owe me.”
“Don’t get yourself so worked up,” Akechi said. “I remember the bet.”
Junpei’s puffed up energy deflated right before Akechi’s eyes. “So all that about not
remembering the bet…”
“A joke. You’ve heard of those, haven't you?”
“Ha ha.” Junpei sighed and stuck his hands into his pockets. “You’re the worst.”
“On that note,” Akechi said. “I don’t ever recall losing this bet.”
“Are you kidding?” Junpei asked. “You mean to tell me that Minato and Aigis told you to
pack your bags over the course of this month?”
“Of course they didn’t.”
“Then, what’s the big deal here? I’ve won fair and square.”
“I’d hardly call it fair and square when over half of the group had no memory of what
happened.”
“Nope, nope, the bet did not say that everyone had to remember,” Junpei said. “Three people
remembered–”

“Those three were far more concerned that you all would continue on forgetting than what to
do with me,” Akechi snapped.
Junpei’s expression fell. “Well, I guess that’s fair,” he said. “But! They clearly trust you if
they let you hang around. So I still think I win.”
Akechi sighed and pinched the bridge of his nose. “I see that you are incapable of reason.”
“Yes!” Junpei pumped his fists into the air. “Five super epic dinners, here I come!”
Akechi wondered if he would be able to get away with taking Junpei to a restaurant he hated.
Temperance Arcana: Rank 7

“I found this in my father’s study,” Mitsuru said. “I thought you might like it.”
Confusion was the primary emotion going on in Akechi’s head as Mitsuru placed a small,
leather-bound notebook in his hands. Akechi gave her a quizzical expression.
“I’m afraid I don’t understand,” he said.
“Open it.”
Akechi raised his eyebrows as he flipped open the journal. Most of the pages were blank.
Clearly, the journal had been a new purchase. On the first ten or so pages, however, there was
a list of reminders: speak to this person, review this information, check in with Ikutsuki, etc.
Some of them were crossed through.
A few stood out starkly among the rest.
Call Akechi
And a few pages later, on the final page:
Ask about Rematch with Akechi
Attend Mitsuru’s party
“I wasn’t sure what the rematch meant,” Mitsuru admitted. “You aren’t Junpei. You don’t
typically challenge people to rematches.”
“No,” Akechi said slowly. “I don’t.”
Akechi had only played pool with Takeharu once. Had it really been so memorable that
Takeharu wanted to ask about it? Surely, Akechi was missing something. Akechi hadn’t tried
to make an impression. He hadn’t played any of his political games. So why did Takeharu
care about playing a measly game?

Maybe he wanted to test Akechi’s abilities. Maybe he was the one playing games. Perhaps he
wanted to gain Akechi’s trust. But for what purpose? Takeharu sacrificed his life for all of
them.
If Takeharu were still alive, Akechi would have asked him. He would have demanded to
know why he even remembered that inconsequential game.
But Takeharu wasn’t alive. Mitsuru, the only person who might have been able to guess at the
truth, had no idea what it had even meant, much less what Takeharu had meant by it.
“Do you… know what it meant?” Mitsuru asked.
Akechi flipped through the journal, hoping to find some sort of note that would answer all his
questions. But Takeharu hadn’t predicted his death. He hadn’t seen it coming. There was no
note, no envelope sitting in Akechi’s desk, waiting for the day it would be opened.
Just blank pages.
“I played a game of pool with him,” Akechi said dispassionately. “He won and suggested that
we play again some other time. I didn’t think anything of it.”
“When was this?” Mitsuru asked.
“When I almost drowned in the ocean and you sent him to check on me.” A bout of irritation
itched at Akechi. He grit his teeth. “You were worried.”
“I was,” Mitsuru said. “I hadn’t expected him to come personally.”
“He said he always attended to your needs personally,” Akechi said. That particular detail
stuck with him because it had been so absurd. But after seeing Takeharu die when he could
have stayed in the safety of the dorm, Akechi wondered if such a claim had really been so

“Yes,” Fuuka admitted. Her cheeks turned red. “I think I will stick with building things for
now.”
“I could help with burning the place down,” Elizabeth offered. She wrinkled her nose. “This
place could use some redecorating. Except for the television. It’s perfectly sized for you.”
Whatever the hell that meant.
“We’re not burning down the lounge,” Akechi said, which he thought was the more pressing
issue.
“But fire is so beautiful,” Elizabeth said.
“No,” Minato said firmly.
“Fine,” Elizabeth sighed. “But I think I have an idea that you might like, Akechi-kun.”

“How the hell did you find this place?” Akechi asked, his voice shaking. Elizabeth had taken
him alone, which was good, because Akechi found he didn’t care what Elizabeth thought of
his dignity.
They stood in front of the dilapidated building that Strega once used as their headquarters.
Although Akechi didn’t have a clear memory of what the building actually looked like, he’d
think of no other reason why Elizabeth would bring him here.

“It took to some searching,” Elizabeth said. “But your friend Akihiko had a guess that turned
out to be rather fortuitous.”
“You’ve spoken with Akihiko before?” Akechi asked.
“On occasion,” Akihiko said, walking toward them alongside Shinji. He gave Elizabeth a
glare. “I can’t believe you were going to do this without us.”
“You didn’t come with me when I took Goro here,” Elizabeth said disdainfully.
“Yeah, because I had to get Shinji.” Akihiko rolled his eyes. “Man, it’s been a while since
I’ve seen this place.”
“You know it?” Akechi asked.
“Oh yeah,” Shinjiro said. “This was the orphanage we grew up in.”
Akechi tried not to feel too dumbstruck. He wasn’t successful.
“Surprising, huh?” Akihiko asked. “That car you had on your desk reminded me of it,
though. It looked just like the car Shinji threw away once when he was mad about our
situation. I, um, fished it out of the trash and kept it.”
“Still can’t believe you did that,” Shinjiro muttered.
“It was your favorite toy,” Akihiko snapped. “I thought I lost it in the fire. Not that I had been
worried about it at the time, with my sister…” Akihiko took a deep breath. “Anyway, there
were scorch marks on the car, and it got me thinking. When your friend Elizabeth asked if I
wanted to help track down Strega’s old base to burn all their stuff, I figured I’d give her my
hunch.”
“It turned out to be a pretty good one in the end. Guess Takaya was a part of this orphanage at
some point too. Or maybe it was just a coincidence,” Shinjiro said. He raised his eyebrows at
Akechi. “Can’t believe this place is still standing.”
“The structural damage could have been worse, so I think the city was trying to repair it
before they realized it cost too much money,” Akihiko said. “And by then they had a different
location for the orphanage set up, so they abandoned this place until they could find another
use for it.”
“Kept tabs, didn’t you?” Shinjiro said rhetorically. He glanced at Akechi. “Building history
aside, why did you keep that car to begin with?”
Akechi frowned. To be honest, he had put it down and forgot it was there. It should have been
a reminder of that terrible night, but he couldn’t even see it when he picked it up in that dark
closet.
And, as terrifying as things had been, that closet had been a symbol of hope. Hope that he
could actually get out. The car was a reminder of that.

But that was so sentimental that Akechi would die before saying any of that.
“I’m nostalgic,” he said.
“As sweet as this conversation is, I suggest we get on with the arson,” Elizabeth said. “Shall
we begin?”
Akechi stared up at the building. A part of him wanted to turn around and run. He hated the
thought. What had turned him into such a coward?
Takaya had wanted him to face his fear. Fine. Akechi would face Takaya’s remaining mark
on the world, and then he would destroy it.
“Wait up for us!”
The rest of the group jogged toward them. Junpei, Minato, and Yukari took the lead.
“Strega messed with our lives too!” Yukari protested. “Minato told us what was going on. We
want in.”
“We’re a team,” Mitsuru agreed. “We do this together.”
Some of the tension in Akechi’s gut loosened. He kicked down the door to the building with
his head held high. As they burned various cult posters, clothing, and even dishes, Akechi
glared at the flames with a set expression on his face.
Takaya would die. Both physically and from public memory.
Goro just wasn’t sure if Takaya would ever leave his memory.

“Goro, could I speak with you for a moment?” Elizabeth asked as the rest of the group started
heading home from their burning spree.
Akechi stopped walking with the rest of the group and turned toward Elizabeth with an
irritated expression. As fun as destroying all of Strega’s belongings had been, Akechi would
like to leave the scene of one of his worst traumas.
“What is it?”
“It is about that powerful being that wishes you harm,” Elizabeth said. “I think it's time I
explained to you what you’re up against.”
“Did your master give you the okay for that?”
“No,” Elizabeth said. She smirked. “But I’ve decided that your safety is more important.
Please bear with me as I explain.”

“Fine,” Akechi said. Despite Elizabeth’s smirk, it was obvious she was being deadly serious.
Akechi wasn’t one to spurn a warning.
“The man you call Tsuyoshi. He is the embodiment of chaos,” Elizabeth said. “He is
extremely powerful and extremely dangerous. He can manipulate his appearance to his whim,
even alter reality. It is his goal to see humanity destroy itself.”
“How do you know this?” Akechi asked.
“He caused some serious issues maybe ten years ago,” Elizabeth said. “No, I’m not referring
to the Kirijo group incident.”
“I don’t know what you want me to do with this information,” Akechi said. “I’ve been trying
to avoid him.” Mostly. “He comes to me.”
“This being thrives on destruction and chaos,” Elizabeth said. “So continue to choose love.
Eventually, he will realize you are a waste of his time.”
“You want me to defeat Tsuyoshi with the power of love,” Akechi said dryly. “You have got
to be kidding me.”
“If he’s been coming to you, it’s because he wants to manipulate you,” Elizabeth said. Akechi
had never seen her this serious in his entire life. “Please. Do not allow yourself to be
tempted.”
“I’m not going to start working for him.” Akechi rolled his eyes. “But fine. I’ll be careful.”
“That’s all I ask,” Elizabeth said.
“Where did the Velvet Room go, by the way?” Akechi asked. “Minato’s contract might be
fulfilled, but mine isn’t.”
“At this moment, there is no need for it.” Elizabeth smirked. “I’m sure that you will have the
opportunity to fulfill your contract at a later date.”
Trust Elizabeth to be cryptic even when giving Akechi comfort.

“Happy birthday, Goro!”
Akechi flinched as he entered the dormitories after his daily run. Everybody, including
Emiko, stood gathered around the dining room table. One of Shinjiro’s famous cakes sat in its
center, and Akechi tried not to feel dizzy.
Akechi nearly forgot that it was his birthday. He had been hoping that everyone else would
forget too. Last year was dizzying enough with Takaya, Shinjiro, Ken, and Emiko giving him
birthday wishes. Now the entire team plus Ryoji and Emiko were staring at him with wide
grins on their faces.

Koromaru trotted up to Akechi and nuzzled his leg. It brought Akechi slightly back to reality.
“This is a surprise,” he said, walking up to the group.
“Well, nobody did anything for you last year,” Akihiko said. “So we had to overcompensate a
bit.”
“I did the icing,” Fuuka said.
“It’s not poisonous, is it?” Akechi asked doubtfully as Yukari began dividing the cake into
slices.
“I checked,” Shinjiro said. “It actually tastes pretty good.”
Fuuka glowed at the praise.
“I’m glad we actually got to celebrate it on time this year,” Emiko said. “I can’t believe you
didn’t tell me it was your birthday!”
“Last year?” Akechi asked. “Or this year?”
“Both!” Emiko crossed her arms. “Except I already knew this year, so I was a little worried I
hurt your feelings by not bringing it up. The surprise thing was Iori-senpai’s idea.”
“My feelings were not hurt,” Akechi assured her. “And last year, I didn’t know you as well.
My apologies.”
“It’s fine,” Emiko said. She took a slice of cake from Yukari and handed it to Akechi. “We
get to celebrate it this year, at least.”
“Heck yeah!” Junpei cheered. “You’re twelve now, right?”
“Yes,” Akechi said, grimacing at how young that number was. He wasn’t even a teenager yet.
“Wow, that’s almost old,” Ryoji said. “Great work, Goro-kun.”
“It’s not remotely almost old,” Akechi said.
“You might be older than me,” Ryoji said with a teasing tone. “Or I’m way older than all of
you? Wait a minute. When is my birthday?”
Minato paled at the question. None of them had ever considered Ryoji’s age before.
Emiko giggled. “Your friend is funny,” she whispered.
Hilarious.
“It’s kind of hard to believe you were only ten when you, um, moved in with us,” Yukari said,
glancing at Emiko nervously. “I can’t believe that it was allowed.”
“Just a reminder of how misled we were,” Mitsuru said quietly.

Emiko looked around with wide eyes, as if she suddenly realized where exactly she was.
“You never told me you lived in the high school dorms.”
“We weren’t sure what you would think,” Ken said. “Don’t tell your dad or sister please.”
“I think it’s cool!” Emiko nodded. “Don’t worry. Your secret is safe with me.”
The cake was delicious, but Akechi didn’t expect anything else from Shinjiro’s cooking. It
was a wonder that Shinji was ever embarrassed of his skills.
“It tastes great,” Goro told Shinji.
“Yeah?” Shinjiro raised his eyebrows. “And here I had a different delicious treat just for
you.”
Akechi frowned. “That doesn’t sound cheesy at all.”
“Fair point.” Shinjiro pulled a chocolate bar out of his pocket and handed it to him. Akechi
raised his own eyebrows questioningly. “Do you remember last year?”
“When Takaya taunted me about being a day older and you overheard?” Akechi asked.
“Yes.”
“And then you rejected my perfectly good gift.”
“I was in a bad place.”
“You’re always in a bad place.”
Akechi didn’t deny it as he took the chocolate bar. “Well, I’m in a slightly better place now,
and I’m not going to be rude enough to leave this on the floor.”
“Good,” Shinjiro said. “Someone will step on it.”
“Thank you,” Akechi said.
Shinjiro nodded as Junpei ran up to Akechi and pulled him aside.
“We weren’t meant to give gifts, but I got something small for you,” Junpei said. “A token of
my gratitude, I guess.”
Junpei handed Akechi a small photo. Akechi frowned at it.
It was the photo that they had taken on the night Ikutsuki betrayed them. Koromaru was a
fuzzy blur, Junpei and the others looked startled, and Akechi wore a glare that could kill.
“It’s quite the photograph,” Akechi said.
“It’s not much of a gift.” Junpei chuckled nervously and rubbed the back of his neck. “The
others have copies too. It took me a while to remember to have the picture printed, though.”

“No,” Akechi said. “I appreciate it.”
“You do?” Junpei beamed. “That’s great. And look, Goro, I just want you to know that no
matter what happens, if you need a friend to vent to or if you need help, I’ll be there. I’m
always just one call away, you know. You’ve really been there for me when I needed it, so,
yeah.”

“Hey, last time was not my fault–”

Chapter Summary

Guys this is so crazy
