Chapter Notes

tw: references to murder, ptsd, references to child neglect

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The safe rooms in Maruki’s palace were stifling. The couches and walls were the same
blinding white as the rest of the place, and framed ink blots made Akechi feel that he was
about to be analyzed at any minute.
Even now, he could feel Maruki’s eyes on his back. Maruki likely wasn’t literally watching
him, at first, but who knew how far his influence stretched? Could he be spying on Joker
through Akechi? Was Akechi’s mind even his own anymore?
Joker had better decide that their rest period was over soon so that Akechi could focus on
killing shadows. It didn’t look likely, though. All of them were exhausted. Even with the
benefit of nine other teammates, Maruki’s shadows were wearing them thin.
“I have an idea,” Joker said. “While we rest, why don’t we tell scary stories?”
Yoshizawa perked up at the sound of Joker’s voice. Her crush could not be more obvious.
Akechi wished Joker could hurry up and tell her that he didn’t feel the same way, unless
Yoshizawa happened to be the only girl that Joker decided to say yes to. Apparently, Joker
was confessed to on a rather regular basis, but he had yet to acquire a romantic partner.
“Scary stories?” Yoshizawa asked. “I don’t know many of those. Sorry.”
“That’s alright,” Joker said. “I have a really good one. Do you want to hear, guys?”
“I’m trapped in this room with you, so it doesn’t really matter what we want,” Akechi said
bitterly.

Sakura and Okumura shot him nasty glares. Akechi ignored them.
“Yeah, but I wouldn’t want to torture you with the sound of my voice.”
“I don’t give a shit,” Akechi said. “Tell your scary stories for all I care. Just don’t expect me
to participate.”
Secretly, Akechi was relieved to have something to think about that wasn’t his steady loss of
control over his own life. Or was it even his own anymore? Maruki was the one who brought
him back from the dead.
“I think scary stories are a lovely idea,” Okumura said pointedly.
“Just… not too scary?” Niijima asked.
“Great.” Joker clapped his hands together and sat up from the sofa he had been leaning
against. “Hm. Do you think there’s any way to dim the lights?”
Immediately the lights dimmed. Half the group yelped, and Akechi jumped to his feet.
“Who’s there?” he snapped.
Nobody responded.
“Even the safe room subconsciously responds to our desires,” Joker said. “I guess Maruki
doesn’t care about something as inconsequential as the lights.”
Akechi frowned. It made sense that Maruki’s palace would respond to people’s needs, seeing
as that was his entire self-righteous shtick. “I wonder if we can use that to our advantage in
the actual palace. Dim the lights to help us sneak around.”
“Maruki might not like that, though,” Sakamoto said. “We’re trying to stop him, after all. We
can’t use the safe room lights to our advantage, so it probably doesn’t matter as much.”
“All great things to consider after our ghost story session,” Joker said.
“Aren’t you meant to be the leader?” Akechi snapped.
“Yes, and as leader, I say that we should actually rest when we need to rest.” Joker nodded.
“Alright, now that the mood is set, let me begin.”
Akechi rolled his eyes and collapsed backwards onto his own sofa. “Tell away.”
Yoshizawa leaned forward toward Joker, ready to drink in any word. Akechi scoffed at the
sight.
“There once was a boy who lived in a small town.” Joker’s voice became hushed as he began
telling his tale. “His parents were away for business, and his house felt large and lonely in
their absence.”

“Oh, that’s sad,” Yoshizawa said.
“It is, isn’t it?” Joker agreed.
“Oh, damn, I’ve heard this one before,” Sakamoto whispered.
Joker ignored him. “Of course, he didn’t realize there was anything wrong with it. His
parents were always away, and he thought that it was perfectly normal to be left alone for
such a length of time. But, this time was different. This time, there was a murder.”
Akechi half expected thunder to rumble outside. It didn’t of course, because that would be
absurd.
Yoshizawa sucked in a breath anyway.
“An announcer who had been on the news for the past couple of days had been found
hanging from a telephone pole. Dead. The schools even had to stop kids from leaving,
because they couldn’t figure out how to make the children avoid the scene of the crime. The
entire town was alight with gossip.”
“Oh no, gossip. I’m so scared,” Akechi said sarcastically.
Takamaki shushed him.
“When the boy went home, he called his mother. Although he was perfectly capable of taking
care of himself, he thought a murder might be a reason for his parents to come home and
make sure that he didn’t die as well. For all he knew, the murderer was waiting for the perfect
moment to kill an unsuspecting child alone in the house.”
“Did they come back?” Okumura asked.
Akira shook his head. “His mother said that the announcer who died was a whore and
probably didn’t finish her education. She impressed upon the boy to take his schooling
seriously and not to be like her. The boy took this advice very seriously. He decided to spend
the rest of his afternoons doing homework and studying for an upcoming test.”
Akechi bristled. People had said similar things about his mother when she had died, as if they
weren’t the same ones who left her in the dirt.
Fortunately, the others bore similar expressions. Yoshizawa looked as though someone had
killed her kittens. Both Takamaki and Sakamoto looked ready to punch something.
“One night, while he was studying, he fell asleep,” Joker continued. “That was when he heard
it. The sound of static filling the living room. He opened his eyes and saw that his television
was on. This was very strange. He thought their TV was broken. It was pouring rain outside,
and a flash of lightning illuminated the clock on their back wall. It was midnight.”
Joker grinned as though he had a secret that everybody wanted to know. “Now, on top of the
murder, a rumor had been spreading in the town. It was said that if you looked at your
television at midnight on a rainy day, you would see your soulmate. The boy had thought that

was a lot of crap, except here it was. He could see a girl clearly on the television. A girl he
recognized. She worked at the local Junes. Her parents owned a liquor store that was
struggling to stay in business thanks to that very same Junes, and every so often the boy
would see her looking sad as she worked.
“But something wasn’t right. The girl looked like she was in pain. A large shadow seemed to
be attacking her, but the boy couldn’t make out the details. It looked like she was screaming,
but when the boy stood up, the image on the television vanished.”
Niijima shuddered.
“The next morning, the boy woke up especially early. He thought that he had been just
dreaming about the strange girl on the television, but the earlier murders were fresh on his
mind. He decided that if he wanted to follow his mothers advice, he should go to the middle
school and study in their library. If he left early enough, he would be able to have time to
study and get to the elementary school on time.”
“Talk about dedicated,” Sakura muttered.
Joker leaned forward. “Fog coated the entire town. The boy thought he saw unfamiliar shapes
in the fog, just like the shapes he saw on the television. He could even see one dangling from
the sky. He told himself that it was just his imagination. That he was just freaked out by his
nightmare. But as he got closer, he realized that the dangling shadow wasn’t in his
imagination at all. The fog thinned slightly, and the boy saw the girl that had appeared on the
television.
“Her body was dangling off another telephone pole, just like the announcer. Her eyes were
glassy and her skin was pale. Her face looked fixed on that same horrified expression that the
boy had seen on the television. She was dead.”
“What happened after that?” Kitagawa asked.
Joker shrugged, and the tense atmosphere of the room fled immediately. “He called the
police. It turned out that the girl was the one who reported the first murder, so the police kept
his identity a secret. He went to school and mentioned it to no one, not even his parents. The
end.”
The lights turned back on.
“There’s something oddly familiar about that story,” Akechi said, frowning.
“Yeah, well, I lived in Inaba,” Akira said. “There was a serial murder case when I was in
middle school. I guess you can say I was inspired.”
Ah, yes. That was right. The bodies were found dangling from high places. It was the case
that brought Shirogane Naoto, the first detective prince, into the spotlight, but Akechi
couldn’t remember most of the details.
“Don’t tell me it actually happened?!” Yoshizawa gasped, bringing her hand to her mouth.

“No, but I’m pretty good at telling it, huh?” There was something strange about Joker’s
expression. If Akechi didn’t know better, he would say that he was lying. “Ryuji totally
thought it was real too.”
“You tell it in crazy detail man!” Sakamoto protested. “Sue me!”
“Sakamoto would believe anything was real if you tell it convincingly enough,” Akechi said.
“Niijima Sae would likely believe you too, seeing as she bought your story about the
metaverse, even though you were drugged to high heaven.”
“You’d better be glad she did,” Joker said sharply. “Or I wouldn’t be here right now.”
“And I wouldn’t be here either,” Akechi said nastily. He refused to admit that he was relieved
that Joker was alive. It was too mortifying to even think about.
“Then I’m especially glad she did.”
Sakura jumped to her feet and raised her pointer finger. “Maybe we should keep going,” she
said. “I feel pretty well-rested now.”
“Best idea you’ve had all day,” Akechi said. “Joker?”
“Yeah,” Joker said, his mouth still pursed into a thin line. “Let’s go.”

Part 2: My True Self

“Next stop: Yasoinaba.”
Goro stared out the train window as the countryside sped past him. The rice fields and open
sky were a far cry from the busy streets of Tokyo or Iwatodai. It had been years since Goro
had even seen the countryside, and now here it was, surrounding him from all sides.
Goro’s phone buzzed with brand new texts. Goro sighed as he flipped his phone open to read
them.
Emiko: i cant believe u left in such a hurry (╥﹏╥)
Emiko: Right before ur birthday 2!! (＃＞＜)
Goro grimaced. The circumstances behind his departure had been hurried and not well
thought out.
About week prior, in Iwatodai, Goro had just left Akihiko and Shinjiro’s apartment and was
returning to the middle school dorms. A man (Chaos? Personification of Evil?) that Goro had
not seen in over a year accosted him.

“Goro, Goro, Goro,” Tsuyoshi said, wearing his signature smirk. He didn’t look a day older
since Goro last saw him. “I hear you’re going by that nowadays. Have you finally accepted
the name Mommy gave you?”
Goro nearly punched him in the face before reminding himself of Elizabeth’s words.
Tsuyoshi wanted Goro to be angry. He had to fight against that.
Goro grit his teeth. Elizabeth should have known better than to ask that of him.
“Only my friends call me Goro,” he snapped. “What do you want?”
“Oof, that’s cold.” Tsuyoshi sighed and raised his hands in surrender. “I just wanted to see
how you were doing. Keeping out of trouble?”
“I think I should be asking you that,” Goro said. Stay calm. Don’t show any vulnerability.
“But I’m doing fine. Thank you for asking.”
“I love that for you,” Tsuyoshi said. “Anyhow, I have some news I thought you might be
interested in.”
“I’m not.”
“There’s a serial murder case in Inaba,” Tsuyoshi said, easily following Goro’s quickened
pace. “Two people have died already, and I hear another girl was kidnapped. But you already
knew all about that, didn’t you?”
Goro stopped in his tracks. Was that happening already? What year was it? 2011?
“It’s none of my business what’s happening in Inaba,” Goro said. “Leave me alone.”
“Fine, I’m not the boss of you.” Tsuyoshi smiled in a way that was shockingly reminiscent of
Akira. It didn’t help that he still wore Akira’s face. “But who knows what might happen. My
nephew might find himself in a sticky situation.”
Goro stormed off and tried not to feel sick.
Fool Arcana: Rank 7
For the next few days, Goro agonized over what he had been told. He knew that it must be a
set up. Tsuyoshi wanted him to go to Inaba for whatever reason. And in the past, Akira had
obviously never been killed during the serial murders.
But there was always that underlying fear. That fear that Goro’s mere presence was enough to
cause things to change. Goro had never figured out whether the near end of the world had
happened in his timeline. Who was he to assume that things would turn out exactly the way
he wanted them to?
Besides, the threat in Tsuyoshi’s words were obvious. Tsuyoshi wanted him to go to Inaba.
Goro didn’t doubt that he would hurt Akira if Goro didn’t comply.

It was a trap. Goro was going to walk right into it.
He called Mitsuru. “Mitsuru-san?”
“Goro,” Mitsuru said, obviously pleasantly surprised. “What can I do for you?”
“I want to move to Inaba.”
A buzzing silence filled the line. “I’m sorry, come again?”
“Preferably as soon as possible.”
After insisting to Mitsuru that he was merely anxious about his friend living in a town with
murders (no, he did not intend to do anything dangerous), Mitsuru agreed to arrange for his
move to Inaba. After Goro said all his goodbyes, he packed his bags and got on the train
departing for Inaba.
Nobody had been pleased at his sudden departure, but they understood his reasons. They
made Goro promise that if anything dangerous came up, he would call them.
Goro made such a promise under extreme duress. He wasn’t completely helpless; he didn’t
need to call the cavalry every time something went wrong.
Besides, the others were busy with other metaverse anomalies. Mitsuru’s Shadow Ops had
kicked off rather well. Although there weren’t many issues, occasionally there would be
reports of shadows or supernatural acitivity, and they would investigate. Mitsuru wanted Ken
and Goro to “focus on their studies”, so they were rarely allowed to come along. Goro tried
not to begrudge her overprotectiveness.
Now, on the train, Goro typed a quick reply to Emiko’s texts.
Goro: I will have cake and call you about it.
Emiko: u’d better!!
Emiko: I’ll try to visit when we get a break („• ᴗ •„)
Goro put his phone in his pocket as the train began to slow to a stop. The buildings of Inaba
began to come into view. Although the town wasn’t tiny by any means, it was certainly small
compared to the city. The train station alone was half the size of Port Island station.
Goro grabbed his bag and stood by the train doors. They slid open, and he stepped outside.
Nobody was waiting to greet him, but Goro was content with that.
“Excuse me?” Goro asked a nearby pedestrian. “Do you think you could point me in the
direction of the Amagi Inn?”
“The Amagi Inn? Oh, of course.” The pedestrian gave a simple set of directions. The inn
wasn’t far from the station; it would likely only take about fifteen minutes to walk. “I heard
that the announcer who died stayed there, though. You might want to be careful.”

Goro’s smile felt strained. He hated superstitions. “I’ll take my chances.”
Goro bowed and extracted himself from the conversation.
Inaba was quiet. Birds chirped overhead. The occasional car would drive past him,
interrupting rustling banners and fliers with a dull roar. Goro could even hear distant chatter
from the shopping district as he walked to the inn.
The Amagi Inn was an impressive establishment. He’d done his research before arriving. A
historical site, it was one of the only places keeping the industry in the town standing.
Apparently, tourists came for its hot springs alone.
Goro wasn’t interested in submerging himself. It had taken him months to even be able to
stand in a bathroom with a bathtub without his heartbeat quickening.
Goro checked into the inn, and the receptionist handed Goro his keys. “You’re on the third
floor. Room 35. You can check the sign for the hot springs times.”
“Thank you.”
Goro’s room was larger than his dormitory back in Iwatodai. A large futon sat in the back
corner, and a balcony overlooked a garden where some guests were milling around.
Money was obviously not an object for Mitsuru, but Goro still shuddered to think of how
much this room alone was costing her. He would try to figure out a new living situation soon.
He hated owing Mitsuru like this, even if she insisted she didn’t want anything in return.
Still, Goro might as well try to make the hotel room a home. He placed his suitcase down and
pulled out a set of picture frames. He placed the picture of SEES with Takeharu, the picture
of the entire group on Goro’s last birthday, and the picture of Ken, Goro, and Emiko on the
dresser to his left. He put his clothes in the drawers and carefully placed Shinjiro’s will and
letter in the topmost drawer. Alongside it he placed Takeharu’s old journal, some slightly
crumpled paper cranes, Minato’s book, and Ken’s action figure.
Shinjiro was going to deliver Taiyaki to Inaba the following day. Many of the others were
still juggling college on their plate. Those who weren’t attending college or school had jobs.
Goro was not about to ask them to drop everything and travel to the countryside.
“Alright,” Goro muttered. “Welcome to your new life.”
Goro wasn’t going to stick his nose into anywhere it didn’t belong. In the original timeline,
the law enforcement in the area managed to pin the killer eventually. Goro was simply there
to keep any innocents out of the crossfire, if possible. And hell, if he could figure out who the
killer was before the useless police department, then maybe he would give them a bit of
advice.
For now, however, Goro was going to sleep.

Emiko called him first thing in the morning. “Happy Birthday, Goro-kun!”
“Good morning to you too, Emiko,” Akechi sighed.
“Have you eaten your cake yet?”
“Emiko, it’s…” Goro blinked at the clock sitting on the wall across from him. “Five thirty in
the morning.”
“Yeah, and? You can eat cake for breakfast.”
“I just woke up. Give me five minutes to get dressed, at least.”
“Oh yeah! This is your first day of school, isn’t it? Try not to replace me with all of your
super cool new friends.”
“I think you’re greatly overestimating how popular I’m going to be.” Goro pulled his new

“Well, if you do, then I’ll just make sure that Ken never speaks to you again.”
“You’re weaponizing Ken?”
“You’d deserve it for abandoning us.”
“I’m not going to abandon you two,” Goro said. “It’s not likely that I’ll be making any

“Don’t talk about yourself that way!” Emiko scolded. “You’re very nice. I bet you’ll make

“Weren’t you just warning me against that moments ago?” Goro asked.
“Ugh, you are impossible. Hold on, I’ll get Ken to call you.”
Emiko hung up. A few minutes later, Goro answered a call from Ken.
“How’s the small-town life going for you?” Ken asked, a hint of bitterness in his tone.
“I’m sorry for leaving so suddenly,” Goro said. “But I haven’t actually been here for more

“Yeah, I guess that’s true,” Ken said. He sighed. “I know I’m being unfair. I just… you

“I didn’t exactly plan to transfer schools halfway through the year,” Goro snapped. He

“Yeah.” After a brief awkward pause, Ken said, “Look, Emiko wanted me to tell you that you

“Trust me, I would be hard pressed to forget you,” Goro said. “I couldn’t manage it when

“That’s true,” Ken said. He let out a dramatic sigh. “Man, I’m really going to miss Taiyaki.”
“Hilarious.”
“I can’t believe Shinjiro is taking him away from me.” Ken sniffed. “He’s so much nicer than

“It’s too early for that.”
“I have to eat breakfast.”
“Well, I won’t keep you.” A cheerier note had returned to Ken’s voice. “Happy Birthday,

“Thank you.”

Yasogami Middle School was only a thirty-minute walk away. After eating breakfast served

make a good impression with the faculty, at least.
He met his homeroom teacher, Aikawa, in the faculty room, who immediately led him to his
classroom. His class was rather small compared to the full rooms in Iwatodai. Multiple desks

“Class, please welcome Akechi Goro,” Aikawa said. “He transferred here because his

Goro bowed to his new classmates. “It’s a pleasure to meet you.”
“Perhaps you would like to sit in that seat over there,” Aikawa said. She pointed to a lone

It was odd to have a desk to himself. Somehow, Goro hadn’t expected that.
Goro could hear a few of the students sitting behind him whispering to each other.
“What happened to his face?” one girl whispered. “It looks like he got in a gang fight.”
“Maybe the real reason he left the city is because he’s in trouble with the police–”

“Alright, everyone, quiet down,” Aikawa-sensei said. She began the English lesson without

Goro tried not to feel too distracted by the comments. The students at his old Elementary
School had an equally poor impression of his personality, but they knew he was one of the
top students. They thought Goro had picked a fight with some rival student when he returned
to school after Strega kidnapped him, even though such rumors were absolutely baseless. By

It was just a scar. People really should know better than to make a big deal out of it.
The only reason Goro hadn’t put concealer over it was his determination not to let Strega

“Akechi-kun,” Aikawa said. “Could you tell me the conjugation of this English verb?”
Goro stared at the verb Aikawa was pointing at. “Past tense,” he said without missing a beat.
“Very good. Please remember to take notes.”
Goro couldn’t take notes. In an impressive display of incompetence, he had managed to
forget all of his notebooks and leave them in Iwatodai. They had probably found a nice
garbage bin somewhere. He would have to buy new ones later that day.
There was no Emiko to give him an impressed glance. No one to share a notebook with. No
Akira coming out of nowhere to share a sassy quip.
Of course not. Akira was a grade below him.

After classes ended, Goro went to the library to borrow some textbooks before he could buy

“Excuse me,” Goro said, before he made eye contact with the person he ran into.
Goro’s stomach clenched. The curly head of black hair was undeniable.
Akira’s head snapped straight up, his face rounder and so much younger than Akechi

“It’s alright,” Goro said. “No harm done.”
Akira’s face was still bright red. “Sorry. I didn’t sleep well last night. I guess that’s why I

“It’s no matter,” Goro said. He tried to keep his voice under control. There was no reason for

It’s a pleasure to meet you.”

Wasn’t Akira still meant to be in elementary school? He was a year below Goro. Not to

Akira’s eyes were distracted as he brushed past Goro and sat down at one of the tables. Goro

Goro wasn’t sure what he had expected. A sassy quip maybe. Flirting. Hell, even a broody

Goro shouldn’t have expected otherwise. He hadn’t even realized he had expected otherwise

There hadn’t even been a social link. It was just blank nothingness.

Goro forced himself to forget about Akira. He went to the station to greet Shinjiro. Shinjiro

He might not have been quite that weak, but Goro didn’t feel very reassured. The skin around

“I don’t want you to drop the fish in the middle of a coughing fit,” Goro said instead.

"Thanks, but I’m good.”

After SEES destroyed the Dark Hour, Goro became much stingier with his money. He

Ah, so this was a cop who couldn’t take his job seriously. Better yet. Maybe Akechi had

After Goro bought everything he needed, he cut through the shopping district to get back to
the inn. It was the first time he had actually been in the shopping district, and it had a variety
of family-owned businesses. Goro even spotted a coffee house he might like to try at some
point.
Its potential pleasantness was undercut by the closed-down buildings and the abandoned air
of the street. The rain made the atmosphere downright eerie. People were shopping, but the
Junes was far more populated.
It wasn’t hard to put two and two together.
Goro scowled at the reminder of the destructive effects of capitalism when a bright blue light
caught his peripheral vision. Goro stopped in his tracks and stared at the strangely shaped
blue door standing to his right. Nobody else was paying it any attention.
It was a Velvet Room door.
Why the hell was there a Velvet Room door in the middle of nowhere? Inaba was hardly what
Goro would call a center of human evil. It was not the place for world-ending calamity.
Feeling an overwhelming sense of dread, Goro approached the door and opened it. As per
usual, only a bright white light came through the door frame. Goro would actually have to
enter to see what was inside. Goro exhaled reluctantly.

Maybe it wasn’t a world-ending calamity. Maybe Theodore and Elizabeth just wanted to say
hello. Maybe Igor came to remind Goro that he had not forgotten him, as Goro had begun to
suspect.
Besides, if Goro fought shadows, Goro would acquire money. If Goro acquired money, he
wouldn’t have to ask Mitsuru for cash.
A small comfort.
Goro stepped inside of the Velvet Room. Maybe Igor would feel like giving out some
answers for once.
“Welcome back,” Igor said almost as soon as Goro entered. “We have been expecting you.”
Goro blinked. “What the hell happened to this place?”
The Velvet Room was no longer remotely reminiscent of an elevator with a massive clock
hanging on the back wall. Instead, Goro sat in a blue limousine. Bottles of wine sat in the
compartment to his left, and rolling fog filled the view outside the windows.
“This room changes to reflect the hearts of its guests,” Igor said. “But I’m sure you already
knew that.”
“There’s a new guest, I take it?”
Goro glanced at the two new Velvet Room attendants sitting beside Igor. Well, one was
definitely a Velvet Room attendant. Her golden hair and eyes, as well as her all blue outfit,
were a dead giveaway. Theodore sat beside her and waved cheerfully.
“It’s a pleasure to see you again, Goro-kun.”
“You too,” Goro said. “Don’t tell me that there are shadows in Inaba.”
Theodore frowned solemnly. “I will hold my piece, then.”
Fantastic. Just what Goro wanted to hear.
“Who is this?” the maybe-attendant asked, her black hair hidden underneath a blue hat. She
crossed her arms and glared at Goro with blue eyes that didn’t look golden in the slightest.
“Isn’t one guest bad enough?”
“Marie,” the new attendant snapped. She regained her composure quickly. “I apologize for
her. I am Margaret.”
Theodore’s older sister, then.
“Akechi Goro.”
“Yes,” Margaret said. “The others have told me much about you. Lavenza was extremely
taken with the aquarium.”

Goro had nearly forgotten about that. “It was nothing.”
“You know this kid?” Marie asked, still looking extremely irked by Goro’s presence.
“He is my guest,” Theodore said. “His contract has not yet been fulfilled.”
“Speaking of my contract,” Goro said. “I didn’t realize it was something that could be
fulfilled. What are the terms of that?”
“I believe I made them quite clear to you when you first entered this place,” Igor said. “That
you choose your fate of your own free will.”
“So the contract is fulfilled when I have chosen my fate. Is that it?” Goro asked.
“That is correct.”
“These murders, then,” Goro said. “Are they connected to the metaverse?”
“All will be revealed in time.”
Goro tried to make eye contact with Elizabeth to see if she would give him a straight answer
with her expression. Only the responsible faces of Margaret and Theodore stared back at him.
Damnit.

It was still pouring when Goro exited the Velvet Room. The rain soaked through his shoes
and socks even as he tried to avoid puddles in the sidewalk.
The attendant of the local gas station stood underneath the canopy with a passive expression
on their face. Goro tried not to feel jealous of how well they were avoiding the rain. They
would eventually have to leave their post, and unless the rain died down before that point,
they would have their own turn of getting soaking wet.
“Hey, stranger!” the attendant waved at Goro with an obnoxiously cheerful expression on
their face. “I haven’t seen you around. Are you new?”
“I recently moved here, yes,” Goro said. He wondered how many times he’d have to answer
that question. In such a small town, it made sense that everyone was abuzz over Goro’s
sudden appearance. He hoped the rumors that would inevitably sprout up about him wouldn’t
be too untoward.
“Have you heard about the midnight channel?”
The name rang a bell, but Goro couldn’t place why. “It sounds familiar,” he said.
“There’s a rumor spreading around recently that if you look at your television at midnight
during the rain, you’ll see your soulmate. People even say it works!”

A sudden memory came to Goro, unbidden. The story Akira had told him, years ago (or was
it years from now?), about the boy who saw the girl on his broken television. It had been
raining in that story, hadn’t it? Goro had forgotten that detail.
Had Akira’s story been inspired by the rumor? For all Goro knew, Akira’s ghost story was yet
another rumor that had spread around the classroom. Goro would keep an ear out for it.
“Do they now?”
“Why don’t you try it out for yourself?” the attendant asked. “It’s probably going to rain
through the night. You can tell me how it goes.”
“Have you tried it?”
“Would you believe me if I told you it worked?”
“Probably not,” Goro conceded. He didn’t know why, but something about the attendant
felt… off. He wanted to think it was his imagination, but the attendant’s long, curly bangs
were covering Goro’s view of their eyes.
Well, evil people didn’t need to have yellow eyes. And the Velvet Room attendants weren’t
evil at all.
Goro still felt a strange chill crawl up his spine as he started walking away. But when he
looked over his shoulder, the attendant was looking in the opposite direction.
Maybe it really was his imagination.
Regardless, Goro wanted to see this Midnight Channel for himself.

That night, Goro sat in front of his television and waited for the clock to strike midnight.
When it did, well…
A teenage boy did appear on the screen.
Goro knew he was gay, but if his soulmate was going to be so overt about his sexual exploits,
Goro was going to have to pass. The boy was in a bath house, no less. The idea of being in a
room with so much steam made his skin crawl.
It wasn’t all that surprising that the Midnight Channel turned out to be more than a rumor.
However, it was unlikely that the person shown on screen was really the viewer’s soulmate.
Metaverse anomalies never existed just to encourage love and lifelong bonds.
Despite Igor’s infuriating vagueness, Goro could connect the dots. The murders were almost
certainly connected to this Midnight Channel in some way. The question was how. Goro

Could the person on screen have been Tatsumi Kanji? Goro didn’t know much about
Tatsumi, but it was certainly a possibility. Perhaps the kidnappings were a precursor to the

But the kidnapped girl had been rescued. Was someone already doing damage control?
No. This was far too much conjecture with too little evidence. Goro had to investigate before
jumping to conclusions. For all he knew, the kidnappings were completely separate from the
murders and the Midnight Channel. He’d ask around at school tomorrow.

Goro logically understood that it wasn’t Akira’s fault that he didn’t remember him. That logic

His irrational irritation did not stop Akira from being the most convenient person to ask
questions the following morning.
When he arrived at the school about an hour early, he was surprised to find that Akira was

Goro remembered Akira always being surrounded by his endless gaggle of companions. He

Come to think of it, Akira had never talked to Goro about his life before Tokyo. Maybe his

“Good morning, Kurusu-kun,” Goro said, forcing on a smile. “I’m surprised to see you here.”

“Have you heard of the Midnight Channel?”

“Do you know who the person shown on the television last night was?”
“I try not to watch it,” Akira said. “But, yeah. It’s Tatsumi Kanji. He’s a first year in the high

That confirmed Goro’s suspicions, at least. It did bring a few more questions less relevant to

“You try not to watch it?” Goro asked. “Why?”

“You think?” Goro asked promptingly.
Akira scowled. “I think that’s what happened to the two people who were murdered.”
Very astute. But that was why the Phantom Thieves gravitated toward Akira as a leader. He

“You can laugh now,” Akira said. His scowl faded into deep resignation. “I know that

Akira was right about her being rescued, of course, but it was looking more likely that the

Good. Goro could focus on making sure Akira stayed out of trouble. He’d try to track down

Unless, of course, he staked out the Velvet Room, which was not completely plausible when

“Thank you for your help, Kurusu-kun.”
“I didn’t do much.” Kurusu stared down at his closed textbook with an embarrassed

“Of course.”

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

An absurd amount of relief flooded Goro’s stomach. He did have a social link with Akira. He

Or maybe things would remain awkward for the rest of their lives.

For the rest of the week, Goro made no headway in either the case or his relationship with

It shouldn’t matter. Goro was smarter than this. Goro knew better than to be so concerned

wanted to join a biker gang, and he looked as though he would die before entering a

Irritation seized Goro when he spotted Adachi standing by the corner of the gas station.

“I’m always prepared.”

Goro hung up and put his phone on the table as he searched for his wallet. Upon finding it, he

Goro chose a bad time for a craving; it was already quite dark outside. Inaba nights were
starkly different from nights in the city. Whereas the city never truly fell asleep–there were
always noises and lights–Inaba was so silent that Goro could hear his own breathing. He

could see the stars clearly. It was uncanny.
Unfortunately for Goro, upon his arrival, the coffee house was already closed. Typical.
Deciding he still needed caffeine, he grabbed a soda can from a vending machine and began
chugging the liquid sugar. It was so disgusting that Goro had half a mind to spit it out, but he
hated wasting money. He finished the drink and threw it into the trash can with extra vigor.
This day kept going from bad to worse.
The street leading to the Amagi inn was emptier than the shopping district. It clearly wasn’t
considered a hub for socialization. An old car parked on the side of the road was the only
remotely unusual thing in sight.

Therefore, it was very obvious when another pair of footsteps suddenly appeared behind him.
His chest tightening, Goro began to turn toward the sound. He’d barely moved his head when
a hand grabbed Goro firmly by the shoulder and yanked him backwards. Goro’s back hit
another body violently. A painful prick entered the side of his neck. Goro opened his mouth
to shout, but a hand was slapped over his mouth. Only a muffled cry escaped instead.
Hell no. Not again. He refused to let this happen again.
His movements felt slow and heavy as he attempted to elbow the person behind him. His
attacker gripped his wrist tightly, and Goro couldn’t manage to twist it out of their grasp.
He was being dragged somewhere, but where? Goro couldn’t let himself be moved. He
refused to comply.
Goro’s vision was already blurring, but he stomped on his attacker’s foot as hard as he could.
Although he wasn’t at his full strength, Goro heard a sharp cry. He bit down on the gloved
hand covering his mouth–

Akechi wasn’t at school.
Akira thought something was strange as soon as Akechi didn’t come in before the rest of the
students. As students began to fill the halls and head to their classrooms, Akira kept his eyes
peeled for Akechi’s sudden appearance. Maybe he had an emergency. Maybe he was sick.
Twenty minutes before classes started, Akira was forced to leave to get to his own school.
Akechi still hadn’t arrived. For some reason, Akira felt a sick sense of dread churn in his

his mom always said anyway.
Akira just had to focus on his lessons. Akechi would probably be back tomorrow. Maybe he

“Good morning, Goro.”

“I wouldn’t do that if I were you.”

like someone was slamming a gavel repeatedly.
Thump, thump, thump.

“Who are you?” Goro asked. His voice was slurred and distant. What the hell had his

Goro forced himself to sit up again. He refused to lie down and allow himself to be pushed

Akechi’s unblemished face stared back at him, looking not a day younger than eighteen years

His look-alike wore a black suit with a white pinstripe shirt and orange tinted glasses that

Goro didn’t faint, but the nausea he had been fighting came back with a vengeance.

Goro vomited all over his shadow’s shiny black shoes.

His shadow’s eyes glinted. “We are obsessed with power.”
“I’m sorry?”
“I know you’ve noticed my little outfit,” his shadow said, gesturing to his suit and glasses.
“Do you like it?”
“If you’re so convinced that you are an accurate representation of me, then you know the

“I love it,” Goro’s shadow said. “It’s expensive. It represents everything I couldn’t have.

“What the hell are you talking about?” Goro asked.
He didn’t like this. He hated this. Shadows were supposed to reveal the dirty truth, but they
weren’t supposed to be inaccurate depictions. Goro hated that suit. He would never dream of
wearing that suit, of looking anything like Shido.
“Don’t you get it?” Impatience bled into his shadow’s voice. “This suit is power.”
“I don’t care what it is!” Goro shouted, feeling his chest tighten. “I hate that thing—”
“You deny it?” Goro’s shadow laughed. “After that little panic attack you had over not having
any personas? Over being powerless? You’re going to look me in the eyes and say you don’t
value it.”
“I’m not Shido,” Goro said. He couldn’t believe this even had to be said. “I don’t want to
take over Japan. I don’t want to lord over others–”
“Don’t make me laugh,” Goro’s shadow said. “Is that what you tell yourself when you sleep
at night?” His voice went into a mocking pitch. “I’m nothing like my father. I’m different.
I’m going to break the cycle of manipulation and death–”
“Shut up!” Goro punched his shadow in the face. His shadow barely blinked, and Goro’s
knuckles burst in pain. Goro hissed in pain and nursed his fist.

“You’re only proving my point,” his shadow took a step forward, and Goro instinctively took
a step back. “Akechi Goro is nothing like Shido Masayoshi. He only punishes the people who
deserve it.”
“Stop talking.”
“He only hurts those who are in his way.”
“I swear to god–”
“People are only collateral damage when it comes to his grand schemes–”
“Could you shut your mouth for five fucking seconds!”
Goro’s heavy breathing filled the room. He felt a migraine coming on, but maybe it would
distract him from the words coming out of his shadow’s mouth.
He wasn’t like Shido. He was nothing like Shido. He refused to listen to what this monster
had to say. He couldn’t.
His shadow smirked and grabbed Goro by his hair. Goro choked on his gasp of pain as his
shadow yanked him upwards.
“He only shouts at brats who don’t know their goddamn place.”

Yosuke hated high school. More specifically, he hated the homework that came with it.
It was a big relief to have Kanji’s bathhouse dungeon out of their minds. Those enemies had
been difficult, and it had taken them way longer than they expected to rescue Kanji in time.
Fortunately, crisis had been averted. They saved Kanji, and Yosuke had more time to hang
out with his partner. So, naturally, Yosuke spent the entire day with Yu.
Unfortunately, Yosuke now had a ton of homework all due tomorrow.
As Yosuke toiled away over conjugations and math equations, rain started drumming against
his window. Yosuke bit back the urge to groan. Hadn’t they seen enough rain this past week?
Tomorrow’s forecast was rainy sure, but did that really have to extend to the night?
Please let it be already past midnight, Yosuke prayed to whatever might be listening. I do
not want to deal with the Midnight Channel and homework at the same time—
No such luck. With buzzing static, Yosuke’s television burst to life. Yosuke froze and looked
up at the screen.
It was too early for anyone to appear, right? Kanji had only just been rescued!

The Midnight Channel clearly thought otherwise. It wasn’t even a vague silhouette on the
staticky screen. Instead, a middle schooler wearing a red and white feather Hawke shirt
appeared on the screen. A red costume cape one might find at Junes was tied around his
shoulders, but the kid’s truly distinctive feature was the lumpy red scar across his cheek. The
injury looked like it was probably at least a year old.
Apart from those concerning implications, the kid looked so… normal compared to other
appearances on the Midnight Channel. Then again, the kid stood inside a massive hallway
with a red carpet and huge columns. Maybe some sort of government building?
“Good evening, everyone,” the kid said. “I am Akechi Goro, reporting to you live. I’m on the
hunt for a refuge. That’s right: even heroes need a break, and I’m going to find the safest
place in the entire world to make my hideout. Once I find it, no one will be able to hurt me,
and I know exactly where to start looking. Stay tuned!”
The television turned off. Yosuke stared at the screen blankly.
Did the killer put a kid in the television? Like a proper kid? Seriously?
Homework could wait. Yosuke pulled out his phone and quickly called Yu, who answered
almost immediately.
“Hey, man!” Yosuke said, unable to keep some of the panic out of his voice. “Did you see the
Midnight Channel?”
“Yeah…” Yu yawned. “Woke me up. Didn’t recognize the kid, though.”
“Me neither,” Yosuke said. “Maybe it’s because we’re both relatively new here. Let me call
Yukiko and Chie. They probably know who he is.”
Yu made a noise in the affirmative, and Yosuke quickly dialed Chie’s number.
“Hey, Chie,” Yosuke said.
“Yosuke!” Chie sounded about as panicked as Yosuke felt. “Did you see the midnight
channel? There was some middle schooler on there!”
“Yeah, I saw it, Chie.” Yosuke grimaced at her volume. “I actually wanted to know if you
recognized him from anywhere.”
“What, that Akechi kid?” Chie hummed. “Nope. Never heard of him. I’m not even sure I
know of any Akechis in general, actually. I’ll go ask Yukiko. Give me a minute.”
Chie hung up. A few minutes later, she called again.
“Yukiko knows!” Chie cheered. “He’s actually been staying at her family’s inn. She said
she’d ask her parents more about him later.”
“Awesome.” Yosuke let out a breath of relief. Teddie would have been a royal pain in the ass
if they had no information on this kid. His nose was becoming less than reliable as of late.

Yosuke got a text from Yu saying that they’d meet up at Junes after school. Yosuke hoped
that they’d have some proper clues by that time.

Akechi-kun was on the Midnight Channel.
Akira had fallen asleep doing his homework again. He woke up to the sound of Akechi-kun’s
voice, and a pit had fallen in his stomach.
Was this going to be like last time? Would Akria see Akechi hanging from a telephone pole?
Akira might not have known Akechi for that long, but he didn’t want him to die.
Tatsumi and Amagi-senpai had been rescued in time. Maybe Akechi would be rescued too.
As the television turned off again, Akira tried not to feel sick. He could already imagine the
sort of torture his kidnappers must be putting Akechi through to get him to act like this for
them.
If only there was some way for Akira to save him himself.

A shiny black limousine at least the length of two ordinary cars sat parked outside of the
police station. Everyone stared at it as they walked to school. Yosuke caught sight of a
familiar looking woman with distinctive long red hair entering the station, but he couldn’t

When he arrived in his homeroom, Yosuke slid into his desk next to Yu’s. Yukiko sat in the

Yukiko frowned at the students gossiping about the limousine.
“I already told Yu I’d talk about it after school,” she said. “Then Kanji-kun can hear it too.”
Yosuke glanced at Yu, who nodded. Yosuke huffed. “Fine.”
School (as always) stretched on agonizingly, but finally, finally Yosuke was set free. As

When everyone was there, Yukiko was finally willing to provide an explanation.
“My parents weren’t willing to tell me the details,” Yukiko said. “But I figured a bit out for

Yu frowned. “Really rich?” he asked. “Could that have something to do with the limo parked

“Yeah, but if Akechi-kun’s rich, shouldn’t we recognize him from the news or something?”

“Oh, I know!” Chie said. “Maybe he’s been kidnapped for ransom before! I’m sure I’ve seen

“Kidnapped for ransom, are you kidding me?” Kanji asked. “If he’d been kidnapped before,

“It’s true,” Yukiko said. “I’m afraid our security isn’t as up to date as it should be.”
“It was just an idea,” Chie said, crossing her arms and sulking.
“You don’t think that his parents are abusive?” Yu asked quietly. He stared at a stain on the
cheap metal table. “Maybe that’s why he doesn’t feel safe.”
“You’re not saying that he got that scar from his parents?” Chie asked, her eyes widening.
“Anything’s possible,” Yu said. “It’s an explanation, at least.”
“But… he’s not living with his parents right now,” Yukiko said.
“That doesn’t mean you feel safe immediately,” Yu said defensively. He scowled. “It can take
weeks to realize that you’re in a different situation. Besides, his parents are clearly close at

The idea made Yosuke feel sick, but it wasn’t out of the question.
“Maybe we should ask around,” Yosuke said. “Surely there’s someone who knows him,

“Other than his parents?” Yukiko asked.
“They might still be at the police station,” Kanji said. “As much as I would like to go guns

“You’re right,” Yu said. “I’ll talk to the parents later. For now, focus on getting information
from other people.”
“I’ll come with you,” Yosuke said.

Yu frowned. “I can handle it myself.”

“Abusers rarely show their true colors in public.”

As Goro’s head cleared, he found it slightly easier to see through the fog. This ability was not
as much as a comfort as Goro had hoped it would be.
Goro was trapped inside Shido’s office. The desk, the sofas, the bookshelves, even the
window overlooking the city was exactly the same as it was in Tokyo. Goro’s shadow sat at
Shido’s desk, staring at Goro with an amused expression.
Goro felt sick.
“You have to accept me, you know,” Goro’s shadow said tauntingly. “I’m you.”
“If I accept you, will you go away?”
“That’s right.”
Goro grit his teeth. The idea of accepting that this monster had ever been him was sickening.
“Fine,” he said. “I accept you.”
Goro’s shadow sighed. “I didn’t realize you were that pathetic of a liar. We’re so good at
manipulating others into doing our bidding–”
“Can you stop?” Goro snapped. He stood up and found that it was easier to stay standing
without feeling sick. “You keep comparing me to Shido, but I was nothing like him–”

“I’ve already drawn up the comparisons for you,” Goro’s shadow said. “Do I really need to

“I only wanted to put an end to his bullshit–”
“You’re the one full of bullshit.” Goro’s shadow laughed. “If you wanted to put an end to
him, you could have killed him. You wouldn’t have worked with him. You wouldn’t have
killed hundreds of people for the sake of stopping his evil. Face it, you were only after
revenge.”
“Fine!” Goro shouted. “You’re right! I was a murderer! I was after revenge. That still doesn’t
make me like him! Shido only cared about himself!”
“Revenge is selfish!” Goro’s shadow slammed his hand against the desk. Goro flinched.
“Revenge doesn’t have room for others, doesn’t have room for friends! You haven’t had
room for friends since you sold your soul away to that man. What’s one more life if you kill
the only person who cares about you–”
“It wasn’t like that–”
“Wasn’t it?” The smile on Goro’s shadow was chilling. “This is where your justice ends,
Akechi Goro. Do you want to know the best part?”
Goro did not want to know the best part. As a matter of fact, if Goro couldn’t fight this
monster, he might as well invest some effort in trying to escape this hell.
“No,” he said, turning around.
“It’s all reset!” His shadow’s voice was so filled with glee that Goro walked faster, as if he
could manage to separate himself from the thing behind him. “I don’t have to suffer any of
the consequences! I can get away with all of it! Not like that dying idiot–”
“Don’t you dare talk about Shinjiro that way,” Goro said, spinning toward his shadow and
glaring through the fog. It was hard to make out his shadow’s expression, but it was safe to
assume it was smiling. “I don’t care what it does to me; I will tear you apart limb from limb if
you say another word about him.”
“That’s awfully ruthless of you,” his shadow said. How did he manage to turn everything
Goro said to his advantage? “Don’t you realize what you’re doing to him?”
Goro shoved open the door before his shadow could finish. Then, he ran.

It took an hour of staking out for the limousine to finally move. It rolled in front of the Amagi

that all seemed to boil down to irritation.

“Aren’t you a little young to be Akechi-kun’s parents?”

“Taken?” Yosuke asked. When Yukiko and Kanji had gone missing, the police hadn’t liked to

Goro stumbled as he continued to run down the labyrinthian halls of the palace. Or dungeon.
Goro still had no clue where he was. It didn’t matter. He had no personas or weapons, but if
he could get the hell out of this place, maybe things could get back to normal. The rules of
this world could be completely different than the ones in the metaverse.
Goro just had to get out.

Shadows patrolled the halls, and Goro stuck to the corners of the walls as he waited for an
opportunity to dash past them. His level of agility wasn’t what it once was, especially with
the fog making it hard to think. Or maybe the drugs were still working their way through his
system. How much time had passed since he first entered this place?
Time was always strange in the metaverse. It would be impossible to tell. Escaping was all
that mattered.
Thinking that a shadow had moved away from his path, Goro sprinted ahead. He heard the
shadow behind him make a startled sound. Slime squelched against the wood floors as the
shadow started to chase him down.
Damnit.
Goro continued to run. Why did shadows want to attack him in his own palace?
A more dangerous shadow burst out from the initial mass it once was. It used its new arms to
grab Goro by the forearm and pick him up off of the ground. Goro kicked at the shadow
furiously. He tried to claw the hand that was holding him.
It was no use. Goro was nothing without his personas. He had no way of fighting.
The shadow didn’t kill him. It began to drag him back to the room Goro had fled from in the

“Halt!”
A younger voice, but a voice that was a replica of Goro’s current voice, echoed down the

“Who’s there?” Goro snarled, picking himself up.
A child his exact height and stature walked up to him. He mirrored Goro’s thirteen-year-old
self exactly. The only difference was in their clothing. This shadow wore a shirt that Goro
hadn’t seen in years. It was white with red sleeves, and it had a picture of Feather Hawk on

It was a shirt Goro hadn’t worn since before his mother died.
Additionally, the child wore a red costume cape that Goro thought he might recognize from
his early childhood. One that certainly shouldn’t have fit his thirteen-year-old self.
“I’m you,” this other shadow of Goro said. His yellow eyes were wide as he stared at Goro.
“Are you here to protect me?”
Goro tried not to feel too confused. He had two shadows, apparently. What did that even
mean? Admittedly, he had two personas. Maybe that was the cause. One shadow for each
mask. If that was the case, the shadow who was roleplaying as Shido had to be Loki.

The child in front of him was Robin Hood.
“Protect you?” Goro asked.
The shadow Goro’s shoulders loosened. He smiled in a way that Goro had only ever smiled
on rare occasions.
“I’m so tired,” the shadow said. “I’m so tired of fighting. But I guess you can’t protect me.
We’re the same person, after all.”
Goro took a step backwards. He felt as though he had been punched in the gut. What was this
shadow talking about? Was he saying that Goro wasn’t strong enough to protect himself?
Goro knew that wasn’t true.
At least the Loki shadow had been extremely explicit in what he represented. Goro’s previous

This shadow was still looking at Goro with hopeful eyes. He almost looked like he was about
to cry.
“What are you talking about?” Goro asked. He took another step away from the shadow. He

“I’m so scared all of the time,” the shadow said. His voice cracked. “Nowhere feels safe
anymore. Akira doesn’t even feel safe–”
“Akira was never safe,” Goro interrupted. The stairs leading back up to the replica of Shido’s

“Akira doesn’t even recognize me.” The shadow’s voice began to shake now. “I thought

Goro couldn’t watch this. He felt nauseous enough without this child acting so pathetically in

“I need to go.”
“Wait!” Goro’s younger shadow cried as Goro ran back up the stairs. “Don’t leave me!”
Goro didn’t listen.

Akechi’s dungeon was ludicrously fancy. The polished wood floors squeaked beneath their
shoes as they ran around trying to find the stairs. Red carpet adorned the center of the stairs.
Gilded picture frames hung on the walls, although the portraits inside were impossible to
make out.
When they reached the third floor, Akechi’s shadow was waiting for them. Yosuke frowned.
The shadow didn’t look anything like the person on TV. The person standing before them was
not only their age; he also looked like some sort of sleazy politician ready to steal all of their
money for gambling.
“It’s so kind of you to join me,” the shadow said. His voice echoed throughout the large
room, and Yosuke got into a fighting stance. This was usually the part where the victim’s
shadow launched a powerful enemy against them.
“Who are you?” Yukiko asked.
“I’m Akechi Goro, of course.” The grin the shadow was wearing looked downright evil. “Or,
who he once was, at least.”
“Who he once was?” Kanji asked. “What the hell are you talking about?!”
“Since when do people have two shadows?” Chie asked.
“I’m on a quest for revenge against my no-good father,” the shadow said, ignoring Chie’s
question. “Perhaps you would like to help me?”

“No-good father?” Yu echoed. It looked like they weren’t as far off the mark as they had
realized. “What did he do to you?”
“What didn’t he do to me?” Akechi’s shadow laughed. The sound was so chilling that Yosuke
felt like it came straight out of a cartoon. “No matter. I’ve matched his evil. Soon, he will
realize what he has created.”
“Um, revenge is wrong?” Yosuke said. He was a little afraid to piss this guy off. Sure, the
other shadows had also seemed dangerous, but none of them were overtly bad guys.
“If you are not with me, then I’ll do what I’ve done to all the others who are against me.” He
grinned. “Prepare to die!”
“Holy shit!” Kanji shouted as the politician shadow summoned a massive mini-boss shadow
in front of them. “Was I like this?!”
“Um… not really!” Chie said.
“Guys, focus,” Yu said.
Yosuke nodded, adjusting his grip on his kunai. They needed to beat this thing. They’d worry
about Akechi’s true nature later.

The door of the office was locked. No amount of furious kicking was able to free Goro from
its clutches.
“Do you think this will be like last time?” Goro’s young shadow asked. He had finally
stopped crying, but Goro had hoped he wouldn’t start up any more uncomfortable
conversations.
He should have known better.
“What the hell are you talking about?” Goro asked.
“You know…” The shadow took a deep breath and stared up at Goro imploringly. “With
Takaya?”
“Takaya’s dead.”
“I know that!” The shadow finally stopped looking totally pathetic when he showed a bit of
frustration on his face. “But the world is full of Takayas. Do you think we’re going to be hurt
again?”
Goro was not scared. Fear was a weakness. He was angry. Angry at his circumstances, angry
at his inability to escape. He was not scared.
He kicked at the door more furiously.

“If you’re me, and that other thing is me, shouldn’t you know its intentions?”
“No,” the young shadow whispered. “He scares me the most. Every night I dream of
becoming like him again.”
Goro froze. “You think I’m scared of myself?”
“I know I’m scared of myself,” the shadow countered. “Don’t you remember what Takaya
said to us? He said we were just like him. What if he was right?”
“He wasn’t.”
“Do you believe that?”
“Of course, I do. Takaya was a manipulative asshole. Everything out of his mouth might as
well have been a lie.”
“Evil people can tell the truth,” his shadow said. “I was evil, and I told the truth to Akira.”
“What truth was that?”
“I said that maybe things would have been different if I’d known him sooner,” his shadow
said. “They would have been, right? But things don’t feel very different. I know him sooner,
but he’s nothing like the Akira we used to know.”
“Are you seriously implying that I think my only hope of redemption is in becoming friends
with Akira earlier in my life?” Goro snapped. “Does my time with SEES mean nothing to
you?”
“I’m scared of SEES too,” his shadow said. “Everyone in my life leaves. They will one day
too. That’s why I left first.”
“That’s not true.” Goro took a deep breath before he punched the wall and ruined his hand.
“It’s been nearly two years. If they wanted to leave, they would have done it by now.”
“Mother left after nine years.” His shadow’s voice cracked. “Everybody leaves.”
“It was different,” Goro protested, his voice feeling weaker. “She loved me; she just… with
everything going on… it was too much. She probably—” Goro looked away. “She probably
thought she was doing me a favor.”
“You’re only proving my point,” his shadow said with a tremulous whisper. “When has love
ever saved people from dying?”

Using her persona, Chie hit the shadow with a critical physical strike. The shadow fell

“You can’t defeat me,” the shadow hissed. It stumbled back to its feet, clutching his side. “I
am… immortal.”
“Think again!” Yu shouted. “Izanagi!”
Izanagi appeared and brought down its sword. It sliced Akechi’s shadow in half. Yosuke
sagged in relief as it started to dissolve back into its original form.

Goro was regaining consciousness. He sat up to see his shadow collapsed on its knees. It
gasped for breath and looked up at Goro.
“I guess I really am like him,” his shadow whispered. He almost sounded sad. “Defeated
again by a bunch of pathetic idealists.”
“Please don’t reject him again,” the boy in headphones said, breathing nearly as heavily as
Goro’s shadow.
Goro grit his teeth. “Get up.”
“What?”
“I gave the Phantom Thieves three fights before I finally ran out of steam,” Goro said.
“You’re really going to be dissuaded by one measly defeat?”
Goro’s shadow grinned, and he stood up. “Do you admit it, then?”
Goro took a deep breath. The thought of admitting the truth sickened him. He wouldn’t have
even entertained the idea two years ago.
“Yes,” he said. “I… I had lost sight of my original goal. I wanted to give Shido total revenge,
so instead of just killing him, I let him use me to hurt others too. I told myself that it was
worth it for the sake of justice, or that the people I killed were just as bad as him, but it
wasn’t true. It was revenge. I was just saying that to convince myself that I wasn’t becoming
like the very person I hated.”

Goro’s voice cracked, but he didn’t break eye contact with his shadow. “And if I was
becoming the person I hated, then, my revenge was pointless. Which made the deaths
pointless. Which they were.”
His shadow smiled. A real smile. Not the ones full of teeth.
“You finally accept me.”
“I accept that you are a part of me, yes,” Goro said. There was a pleading note to his voice
when he continued to speak. “But I’m not that person anymore. I’ve given up any plans of
revenge. I just want to put that part of my life behind me.”
“Good.”
His shadow disappeared into the familiar form of Loki. Loki shattered like glass, and Goro
felt the familiar feeling of a persona resting inside of his soul.
Exhaustion crashed over Goro, and he sat down on one of the sofas, trying to keep his head
on straight.
“Mission accomplished!” the girl with roller-skates cheered.
“I have so many questions,” the headphones boy said.
“Wasn’t there a different kid on the television, though?” Tatsumi asked.
So Goro had appeared on the Midnight Channel. That was just… fantastic.
The last thing Goro wanted to do was confront another part of himself. Goro wanted to go
home. He wanted to sleep. And he didn’t want to grant these children the clarification they
probably deserved.
“There’s another one,” Goro said, putting his head in his hands.
“I was wondering… how is that even possible?” Amagi asked.
“It’s a long story.”
At that moment, Goro’s younger shadow cracked open the door. “Is he gone?”
“That Shido look-alike is gone, yes,” Goro said.
His shadow’s shoulders sagged in relief. He entered the room properly. “Are you all here to
rescue me?”
“Rescue you?” the gray-haired leader asked.
“I thought this place would be safe,” his shadow said. “But it turned out to be just as
dangerous as the others. I’m scared.”
“Of course you’re scared,” Amagi said. “I was scared too, when I was kidnapped.”

“Are you seriously afraid of accepting that you’re afraid?” the boy with headphones asked.
“Fear is a weakness,” Goro said instinctively. “It hinders you from getting anything done.”
“And yet, I’m scared every minute I breathe,” his shadow said. “I just want to feel safe
again.”
“Please, don’t reject it,” Tatsumi said. “I don’t think we can take another big fight.”
“Fine,” Goro snapped. He was somewhat afraid that this obviously inexperienced group
would accidentally kill Goro if they weren’t careful.
Ha. Afraid.
“Sit down,” Goro told his shadow. “You look like you’re about to pass out.”
Goro’s shadow obediently sat down. Goro sat down across from him and tried to think of the
least embarrassing way to go about accepting that he was a coward.
“I’m not afraid all of the time,” Goro said slowly.
“Sometimes, I feel safe,” his shadow agreed. “I felt safe with Akira.”
“No, I didn’t.” Goro frowned, now feeling confused. “He was my enemy.”
“He was my friend.” his shadow smiled. He reached into his pocket and pulled out Akira’s
glasses, much to Goro’s horror. “Before he knew I was a traitor, I felt perfectly safe with
him.”
Goro wanted to continue arguing, but he wanted to avoid another confrontation. He took a
deep breath and collected himself.
“Fine,” Goro said. “Any other times I’m not scared?”
“Sometimes with members of SEES,” his shadow said. “I used to feel safe with Shinjiro,
after he saved me. I never felt safe around Takeharu or Chidori. That scares me too.”
Goro’s chest clenched.
“Used to?” he asked.
“He’s dying,” Goro’s shadow whispered, continuing to fidget with the glasses. “Sometimes I
wonder if it’s my fault. Everyone around me seems to die. Maybe I did something to cause
it–”
“Shinjiro was dying before I came along,” Goro snapped.
“I know that,” his shadow said. “It doesn’t make me feel better.”
It didn’t.

“Please, don’t reject me.” His shadow was crying again. Goro looked away, overwhelmed
with embarrassment. “Akira’s not the same. People always want me to be stronger, to be
powerful, to not be afraid. But I am afraid. What’s wrong with that?”
“What are you afraid of?”
“Isn’t it obvious?” Goro’s shadow exhaled shudderingly. “I’m afraid of death. I’m afraid of
being taken advantage of again. I’m afraid of losing the people close to me.”
“You’re afraid of everything,” Goro said. He failed to keep the disgust out of his tone.
“That’s not true,” the gray-haired leader said. Goro’s eyes snapped in his direction. “You’re
afraid of losing the things that matter.”
“You’re afraid of admitting that you can be vulnerable,” Tatsumi said. “Trust me. I get it.
None of us are going to judge you, man.”
“Nightmares keep me awake every night,” his shadow continued. “Maybe, if I hadn’t taken
Takaya’s gun, Chidori wouldn’t have died. Maybe, if I had seen through Ikutsuki’s lies
sooner, Takeharu-san–”
“Enough,” Goro said. His voice shook. At this rate, these strangers would know his trauma
better than he did. “That’s enough.”
“I’m afraid of waking up and finding out that all of this is gone,” Goro’s shadow whispered.
“That I’m back in that foster home–”
“You’re right!” Goro shouted, because that was a part of his life he wanted to bury away and
never remember. He jumped to his feet. “You’re right. I am scared. I’m scared that time will
reverse again. I’m scared that Shido will find some way to take advantage of me. I’m scared
that everyone will leave. Are you happy? Is that what you wanted to hear?”
His shadow stared up at him with wide eyes.
“What else do you want me to say?” Goro asked. “That I do blame myself for the death that
follows me? That I’m cursed? That I’m so afraid of losing the power that I have, because if I
do, I’ll lose all the worth I have to anyone else?!”
“That’s not true!” Amagi gasped, as if she knew anything.
His shadow stood up. “You’re not rejecting me, then? You admit that I’m you?”
“Yes,” Goro said through gritted teeth. “You’re me. Happy?”
The shadow beamed. “Thank you.”
He disappeared with a burst of light and was replaced by Robin Hood. Loki appeared from
within Goro and fused with Robin to create Hereward.

For a terrible moment, Goro wondered if he would have to face a third version of himself.
Then, Hereward spoke.
“And now you understand,” the persona said. “Your fear and your hate lead you to a struggle
for power. Now, you must fight a different battle.”
“Um, can all personas talk?” Tatsumi whispered. Amagi shushed him.
“What battle is that?” Goro asked. Apart from when his personas were awakened, he never
had an opportunity to have a conversation with his personas. In a way, however, Goro
supposed that Hereward was being awakened all over again.
“You already march toward it,” Hereward said. “You must fight for more than your own
strength, but I will assist you along the way.”
Hereward disappeared, and Goro felt all three of his personas rest within him.
The palace did not begin to crumble beneath them, but this place wasn’t strictly a palace
anyway. Not in the way Goro understood it. The teens weren’t in a hurry to leave, and
judging from their behavior, they had rescued people from their shadows before.
Now assured that he was mostly out of danger, Goro collapsed backwards onto the couch.
Hunger and exhaustion gnawed at him, and he blinked wearily up at the ceiling.
“Are you alright?” Amagi asked, running up to him. Goro forced himself to sit up before he
embarrassed himself further.
“I’m fine,” Goro said.
“Yeah, this is just a hunch, but I don’t really think fine is the right word for it,” the
headphones boy said.
Goro frowned. “Who even are you people?”
“We’re the investigation team!” roller skate girl said. “I’m Chie. The annoying one is
Yosuke”
“I take offense to that,” head-phones boy, otherwise known as Yosuke, said. “Our tactical
leader here is Yu.” He gestured to the one with gray hair.
“And you’re Amagi-san,” Goro said, pointing to her in turn. “And you’re Tatsumi-san.”
“Yukiko’s fine,” Amagi said.
“Yeah, it feels kind of weird to do surnames after we risked our lives for you and all that,”
Tatsumi said. “Just call me Kanji.”
“And I’m Teddie!” the bear mascot said cheerfully.
Goro’s frown deepened, but he was too tired to argue.

“Do you have any idea on how to get out of this hell hole?” he asked, trying to stand to his
feet. He stumbled forward, and Yosuke caught him.
“Don’t worry, I got you,” Yosuke said.
“I don’t need getting,” Goro snarled. “I’m–” A fresh wave of nausea punched him in the gut.
He blinked away the urge to pass out. “I’m fine.”
“Clearly,” Yu said.
“Didn’t you just accept that it was okay to be afraid?” Teddie asked.
“No, I accepted that I was afraid,” Goro snapped. “There’s a difference. Now, can someone
please tell me where I am?”
“You’re in the TV world,” Yu explained.
“The what?” Goro asked.
“You enter when someone pushes you inside a TV screen,” Kanji explained. “Kinda like a
portal.”
The TV… was a portal… into the TV world.
“Okay, sure,” Goro muttered. “I suppose we leave through the television too?”
“Pretty much,” Yukiko said.
“Just when I thought my life couldn’t get any stranger,” Goro muttered.
“Um, speaking of that… I don’t mean to be insensitive,” Yosuke said, “but what was with
that creepy older shadow? He said a lot of stuff that didn’t make a lot of sense. So did that
younger shadow, now that I think about it.”
Goro grit his teeth. “I’ll explain as we leave.”
Goro didn’t remember much of his explanation, but he only focused on what occurred in his
previous life. He was too tired to try to explain the Dark Hour and SEES on top of that.
His explanation must have been expansive; nobody had any questions by the time he was
done. Well, almost nobody had questions.
“You’re a time traveler?” Yosuke asked. “You expect us to just believe that?”
“Yes, actually,” Goro said. SEES had never questioned the logistics of time traveling. But,
come to think of it, the dark hour was much more time based than this TV metaverse.
And Elizabeth had vouched for him.
Goro missed Elizabeth.

“It is a little hard to believe,” Yukiko admitted. “But stranger things have happened. I mean,
we fight other versions of ourselves.”
“Speaking of that,” Kanji said. “Did we know that if we killed our shadows, we would die?
Because that seemed to be a main theme of Akechi’s story here.”
The entire team went deadly silent. Goro realized how close to death he had been.
“Well, now we know,” Yu said.
“In any case, I can’t make you believe that my story is true,” Goro said. “I could tell you that
Shirogane Naoto will play a key part in this case, but I have no idea how long it will take for
that to happen.”
“Wait, if you’re from the future, does that mean you know who the killer is?” Chie asked.
Goro frowned. “No,” he admitted. “I can’t remember. I’m sorry.”
“You can’t remember?” Yosuke asked.
“I remember this case had a lot of suspects,” Goro snapped. “It makes it hard to recall which
one actually did it. Besides, I haven’t thought about this case in years. Are you going to tell
me that you remember the plot of a television show you saw five years ago?”
Goro had watched the television clips of Shirogane from that era. But Shirogane never
focused on the actual culprit, and Goro didn’t care. He only cared about exuding the detective
prince persona. The actual murderer was already behind bars, so why should Goro give a shit
about who he was?
“That’s a fair point,” Chie said. “I guess we’ll just have to solve the case the old-fashioned
way.”
“Well, it was worth a shot,” Yosuke said. “If something suddenly comes to you, don’t be
afraid to tell us.”
They were in an open area now. Goro peered through the fog. It was hard to see much of
anything, but maybe that was his exhaustion talking.
“How the hell do you see?”
“Oh, we have these glasses,” Yosuke said. “You can take mine.”
“No, no, wait!” Chie said. “Teddie, do you still have the funny ones? The ones that work?”
“Of course, milady,” Teddie said.
“Ew, don’t call me that,” Chie said as she snatched something from Teddie’s hand. Glasses,
presumably. Yu snorted. Chie handed the glasses to Yosuke. “Here.”

Yosuke, who Goro was unfortunately using as a crutch, put the glasses on Goro’s face.
Instantly, the fog disappeared. Some of the pounding in Goro’s head went away as well, and
Goro could see everyone clearly.
The rest of the team stared at him. Yukiko tilted her head.
“Hm, they’re not as funny when the person wearing them looks sick,” she said.
“Yeah, I’m not feeling it,” Kanji said.
Goro took off the glasses and peered down at them. They were those ridiculous joke classes
with the nose and the mustache. Goro sighed and tossed them back toward Teddie. He’d
rather have a headache than look like a fool.
Maybe that was a character flaw. Goro was too tired to think about it.
“Are we almost out?” he asked.
“Yep,” Teddie said. “Just go right through here.”
Teddie gestured to a stack of square televisions. Goro had no clue how they had any hope of
fitting through them.
Somehow, they did. Bright light pierced Goro’s vision, making his headache worse. The fog
was gone, and the obnoxiously cheerful Junes jingle rang overhead.
Goro blinked at the isles of the electronics section. No shoppers were in sight, fortunately.
“Are we… in Junes?” Goro asked.
“Yep,” Yosuke said.
“So, anyone could see us falling out of the television?”
“Well, it's our only access point with Teddie,” Yukiko said reluctantly. “We just look both
ways before entering.”
Goro inhaled deeply. At least falling in and out of televisions wasn’t considered criminal
behavior. The Phantom Thieves had entered Kaneshiro’s palace in the middle of Shibuya for
some inconceivable reason. They didn’t even duck into an alley.
“Listen,” Yosuke said. “Your, um, guardian? Is here in Inaba. But if you don’t want to go to
them, I’m more than happy to give you a place to stay. My parents won’t ask too many
questions. Probably.”
Goro frowned. “My guardian?”
“Kirijo-san,” Yu said.
“She drove in here with a massive limo,” Chie added.

Goro was going to die of embarrassment. Why couldn't Mitsuru take the train? “Thank you
for offering, but I think I can manage.”
Goro stood up. He had barely been aware that he was sitting on the ground to begin with. His
nausea was still ever-present, and he reluctantly leaned against Yosuke again for support.
“To the Amagi Inn, then!” Yosuke said. “Yukiko and I can probably handle it from here,
guys.”
“Yes,” Yukiko agreed. “Chie, didn’t you say you were behind on homework?”
“And my mom will get worried if I’m gone for too long,” Kanji said. “Seeing as I was
recently taken myself and all.”
“And you have to look after Nanako,” Yosuke told Yu. “Dojima-san might be a little
distracted by Akechi-kun’s reappearance.”
Yu nodded. Goro had no idea who the hell Dojima was, but if he was going to be distracted
by Goro, he was either a reporter or a cop.
“Maybe we should drop him off at the police station,” Yukiko said as they started walking out
of Junes. “I know they had questions for me when I came back.”
“I want to sleep, not be interrogated,” Goro snapped. “I’m going back to my room.”
“The man has spoken,” Yosuke said.
They received a few odd looks as they walked back to the inn. When they finally arrived,
Goro could see Mitsuru’s limousine parked in front of the building. It was so painfully
conspicuous that Goro wondered why nobody had talked her out of it.
The receptionist’s eyes widened when they entered the lobby.
“Akechi Goro?” she asked, standing up.
“That is my name,” Goro said.
The receptionist’s face split into a large grin. “Your family is upstairs,” she said.
Family? Surely the entirety of SEES didn’t come to make sure he was alright. That would be
absurd.
“Which room is it?” Yosuke asked.
“Thirty-five.”
“That’s on the third floor,” Yukiko said. “The elevators are this way.”
As they waited on the elevator, Yosuke gave him another serious look. “Hey,” he said. “If you
need any help, don’t be afraid to ask us, alright?”

“I don’t know you,” Goro said.
“Hey, we saved you, didn’t we?”
Goro rested his head against the back of the hotel wall. “Maybe,” he said reluctantly.
“Then, we’ve got your back.” Yosuke grinned. “Not everyone knows about the TV world, or
the metaverse, as you like to call it. Us persona users have to look out for each other.”

“Thou art I… and I am Thou
Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Magician Arcana…”

Marvelous. Goro would worry about that later.
They boarded the elevator and reached the third floor without any further conversation.
Yosuke lead him to his room, and Goro removed his keys from his pocket and fumbled with
the lock. It only took him a few seconds to unlock, and he swung the door open.
Immediately, Goro could hear people jumping to their feet, probably prepared for a fight.
Mitsuru was the only one Goro could see in the room.
“Goro?” she asked. She frowned. “Hanamura-kun?”
“We found him by Junes.” Yosuke laughed nervously. “And helped him home.”
Akihiko ran into view, taking Goro off Yosuke hands. Deeper inside his room, he could see
Shinjiro approaching. His face was obviously distraught.
“Does he need a hospital?” Mitsuru asked.
“I need sleep,” Goro said. “I don’t need to see a doctor.”
“I don’t think he was injured,” Yukiko said. “He might not have eaten a lot, though, so it
might be a good idea to feed him.”

“I can feed myself,” Goro muttered. Akihiko helped him lie down on his futon. Goro sagged
in relief. Had it always been this soft?
“Thank you,” Mitsuru said, her voice was already fading into the corners of Akechi’s hearing.
“We can handle things from here.”
“Damn,” Shinjiro said. His voice floated above Goro as Goro slipped further into sleep.
“What are we going to do with you?”
