“Yosuke?” Yukiko asked as Yosuke was about to leave the inn. “Could I talk to you for a
moment?”
Yosuke frowned. It wasn’t every day that Yukiko wanted to talk to him privately, especially
about something that seemed to be important. Normally, she’d confide in Chie.
“What’s going on?”
“Oh, well, it’s nothing too important,” Yukiko said. Her shoulders slumped. “Actually, that’s
not true at all. I don’t know why I said that.”
Okay. Something was seriously wrong if Yukiko was tempted to lie about it.
“Are you sure you don’t want to talk to someone else about this?” Yosuke asked. He wasn’t
sure if he was able to handle this situation with tact. He had a bad habit of saying the worst
things at the worst possible times. “I mean, this is clearly really important to you. I’m sure
Chie would be willing to listen.”
“You can’t tell anyone about this,” Yukiko said. “I–I don’t want Chie to think poorly of me.”
Ah. So Yukiko wanted to speak to Yosuke because he wasn’t high up on her people she cared
about list. Yosuke would pretend that didn’t slightly hurt his feelings. He was sure that he’d
probably do the same thing.
“Sure,” Yosuke said. “You have my word. I won’t tell anyone.”

Yukiko let out an audible breath of relief. “Thank you.” She twisted her hands together. “I
keep having this horrible thought. About… Yu-kun.”
Yosuke’s stomach tightened. “About Yu?”
“Well, actually, that’s part of the reason I wanted to talk to you,” Yukiko said. “You two seem
to be so close, so I thought you might be able to put my worries to rest.”
“I hope so.” Yosuke crossed his arms. “What is this about?”
“Remember when his shadow came?” Yukiko asked. She kept her eyes trained on a black
butterfly sitting on a nearby vase. “I know you’re going to hate me for saying this, but do you
remember what he said about doing anything to be needed?”
“Yeah. And?”
Yukiko looked away. “Yu came to Inaba right before the murders started happening.”
“You can’t seriously be suggesting that Yu is the killer.”
“No, of course not!” Yukiko looked like she was about to cry. “I mean, I really don’t want it
to be true. But you have to admit there are odd coincidences, and according to you and Chie,
he was the only one who could enter the TV at first. I’m just… worried”
“Yukiko, if he was the one responsible for the murders, don’t you think his shadow would
have something more to say than that he wanted to be needed by others?” Yosuke snapped.
“Well, like I said, it did say that he would do anything to be needed,” Yukiko said. “The
shadow said that he would be willing to cause problems just so that he could be the solution.”
“Your shadow wanted to have a harem of “princes” and live in a castle,” Yosuke said. “Is that
what you really want?”
Yukiko looked like she had been slapped in the face. Yosuke regretted what he said
immediately. He might be pissed, but Yukiko had spoken to him in confidence. His reaction
was probably exactly what she had been afraid of.
“Okay.” Yosuke took a deep breath. “Yukiko-san, are you trying to tell me that Yu was the
one who kidnapped you? Because then, we can have a very different conversation.”
“I still don’t remember who took me,” Yukiko said, staring at the ground somewhat bitterly.
“Do you really think that Yu isn’t the culprit?”
“I know he isn’t,” Yosuke said. “He’s done nothing but help us so far.”
“Well, in that case, I’ll trust you.” Yukiko looked as though a large burden had been lifted
from her shoulders. “Thank you, Yosuke-kun. I feel much better now.”
Yosuke almost responded scathingly, but before he could say anything, Yukiko burst into
tears.

“I’m sorry,” Yukiko said, hiccupping. She covered her face with her hands. “I shouldn’t be
crying like this… I just…”
“No, no, it’s fine.” Yosuke had no idea what to do. “Should I get someone?”
Yukiko shook her head and sat down on a nearby sofa. Yosuke sat down next to her. “I
thought I was done crying…” Yukiko whispered, sniffing. “It was just… so scary. You’re safe
at home, and then suddenly you’re not, and you don’t even remember what happened.”
“Yukiko-san…” Yosuke swallowed. “I’m sorry. I can’t imagine what that must be like.”
Yukiko inhaled shudderingly. “I keep suspecting everyone. I can’t help it. I see someone and
wonder, ‘is that the person who tried to kill me?’ And then Yu’s shadow said all those things
and I guess I just…”
Yukiko trailed off, but Yosuke could guess what she was about to say.
“Panicked?”
Yukiko nodded. She laughed self-deprecatingly. “Sorry. You must think I’m silly.”
“Yukiko. I know we’re not that close, but… I think you’re really brave,” Yosuke said. “It was
scary enough facing my own shadow, and I went to the TV world willingly. And you still
laugh and fight in spite of it all. So… yeah.”
Yukiko cracked a smile. “Thanks, Yosuke-kun.”
“It’s nothing.” Yosuke grinned. “And when we catch the killer, you can slap them across the
face.”
Yukiko let out a startled giggle. “Chie might get there first.”
“Tell her not to,” Yosuke said. “Say, ‘sorry, Chie, but actually I have dibs on slapping this
killer.’ And I have second dibs. Chie will have to go third. Actually maybe Kanji should have
second dibs since he was also kidnapped. Chie gets fourth dibs?”
Yukiko started laughing in earnest.

Goro woke up to the sound of his alarm. Clearly, nobody had turned it off while he was away.
“Oh, shit, I forgot about that thing,” Akihiko muttered groggily.
“What day is it?” Goro asked. He felt much better now that he had rested, although he was
still incredibly hungry. He probably should have eaten before he fell asleep.
“It’s Saturday, June 11,” Mitsuru said.

Goro got out of bed and grabbed one of the snacks he had stored in his dresser. He hadn’t felt
like he had been in the metaverse for more than maybe a day, even if it had been five in the
real world, so he should be able to eat small bits of food without issue.
Shinjiro was still sound asleep on the sofa. Nobody woke him up.
“What are you doing?” Akihiko asked.
“What does it look like I’m doing?” Goro pulled his uniform from his dresser. “I’ve missed
nearly a week of school.”
“The teachers will understand if you need time to recover,” Mitsuru said.
“I don’t need time,” Goro said irritably. “I need things to start getting back to normal.”
“You were just rescued.” Mitsuru’s expression was becoming sterner.
“Yes, and I’m fine.” Goro gestured to himself emphatically. “This isn’t like last time,
Mitsuru. Nobody tortured me; I didn’t nearly die in my attempt to escape. If I recall, I went to
school the day after I came back that time too.”
Nobody had a good argument for that.
“Fine,” Mitsuru said. She handed Goro his phone, which he had foolishly left behind in his
room the night he had been taken. “Please, answer your phone calls.”
Goro spent the rest of that morning calling back every member of SEES plus Emiko. Emiko
was so relieved to have him call that she burst into tears over the line, and Goro was left in
the position of comforting her.
“Don’t ever get kidnapped again,” she said. “I could barely focus on school, I was so
worried.”
“Emiko-kun, please don’t take offense, but you struggle to focus during class when I’m
sitting right next to you.”
“That is not the point!” Goro could hear the sound of Ken’s laughter in the background.
Minato and Ryoji were much calmer in their relief, although Ryoji promised to visit as soon
as possible.
“I have like, two-hundred paper cranes to give you,” Ryoji said.
“Folding paper cranes doesn’t actually solve all of life’s problems, you know,” Goro said.
“Agree to disagree.”
Junpei’s call was a little less conventional.

“I’m really glad that you’re back man,” Junpei said. “Akihiko won’t give me a straight
answer. Is it true that Mitsuru drove to your place in a limo?”

The next afternoon, Goro and Kanji sat alone in the Junes food court. They agreed to change
their meeting location for actual meetings, but they needed somewhere to sit while they

Goro arrived far earlier than the agreed time. This was partly an accident; Goro was less

Regardless, Goro didn’t want to go back to the inn. Thanks to Akihiko’s determination to

It was at times like these that Goro wished smart phones were popular. The distraction of a

Goro quickened his pace.
He heard footsteps come in his direction. On instinct, Goro spun around toward the sound.
He would not allow himself to be taken by surprise this time–

“You saw Kujikawa-san when you were… buying tofu, didn’t you?”
Goro frowned. “Yes, she sold the tofu to us, in fact,” he said. “Why?”

This was a trap. Dojima was trying to catch Goro in a lie, or his questions wouldn’t be so

“We mentioned the recent kidnappings,” Goro said. “It was especially relevant to Tatsumi

“I don’t know…” Dojima still didn’t look convinced. Goro put his hands into his pockets

“It’s a good thing I’m not lying,” Goro lied. “And even if I was, is lying about our interaction

“Maybe not, but are you sure there wasn’t anything you left out of your testimony the other

“What makes you think there was?”

“Call it a hunch.”
“Well, even if your hunch was correct,” Goro said. “Which it isn’t, I’ll have you know that I

“I’m sorry to hear that,” Dojima said, the frustration on his face softening around the edges.

It was almost ironic. An officer of the law telling Goro to stay out of danger. After years of
working with Shido’s underlings, it was almost enough to give Goro whiplash.
Hell, the insistence that Goro stay out of things was more than even Takeharu could do.
Although, if Dojima had the necessary context the TV world provided, he’d likely be more

“I’ll bear that in mind,” Goro said. “Goodnight, Dojima-san.”
“Yeah,” Dojima said. He glanced at the sky and removed the cigarette from his mouth. “Can I

Goro almost told him to go to hell before he spotted the sun dipping below the horizon. His

“I don’t want to keep you away from your family,” Goro said.
Dojima shook his head. “It won’t take that long,” he said. “I’ll still be back in time for

Goro hoped Dojima enjoyed tofu.
“Very well,” Goro said quietly. “I would… appreciate it.”
Dojima looked bizarrely relieved. “It’s no problem.”
Chariot Arcana: Rank 3

Kujikawa’s silhouette appeared in the Midnight Channel again. After meeting at Yosuke’s

Perhaps, but was there really a point in trying if it was doomed to fail?

The second one was winning over. His self-preservation was the only thing stopping him

The idea was getting more and more tempting by the minute. What could Adachi do? Throw

“What does Dojima-san need cilantro for?” Yukiko asked.

“You never know. He might be allergic.” Adachi gave the group an easy-going smile. “So,

“We’re going to visit Kujikawa-chan,” Yosuke said.
“Oh, I see.” A smile split Adachi’s face. “Hey! What a coincidence! I was just on my way

“Then why don’t you come with us?” she asked. Noticing everyone else’s disbelieving stares,

Yes, except he was absolutely useless.

Jester Arcana: Rank 4

It turned out that Yosuke’s definition of staking out really equated to walking back and forth

“Are you really going to accuse everyone who happens to be in the general area without

“I mean, we could try looking for her,” Chie offered half-heartedly.
“If she’s only stepped out, she probably has to come back, right?” Kanji asked. “We might as

They waited. Kujikawa didn’t come back.
“Damnit,” Yosuke said. He buried his head in his hands. “I can’t believe we let ourselves get
distracted by that creep.”
“If it’s any comfort to you, the killer wouldn’t have been foolish enough to kidnap anyone

“That doesn’t really make me feel better,” Yosuke said. “But thanks for trying.”
“Well, you know the drill,” Yu said. “It’s going to rain tonight. We’ll watch the Midnight
Channel. Maybe it will give us enough clues that we won’t need to interview everyone in
town to find her.”
“What?” Goro asked.
“Teddie’s nose,” Kanji said. “Is the worst.”
“Teddie needs us to have information on the victim to be able to sniff them out,” Yu
elaborated. “We’re not sure how it works.”
“We probably did interview everyone in town to find you,” Yosuke said. “Only five people
even knew your name.”
“I guess I’m lucky that you found me at all,” Goro said dryly.

Yosuke fidgeted with the chord to his headphones. “Not really.”
Goro took a deep breath. At least the fog wasn’t poisonous. “I feel so useless out here.”
Yosuke sighed. “Yeah, I know what you mean.”
In the end, Yu and the others only managed to get to the fourth floor. They would have gotten
farther with Goro, but Goro was still relieved. Still relieved that he didn’t have to fight in that
place for hours.
He was such a coward.
Magician Arcana: Rank 2

Teddie stepped in front of the group, looking as alarmed as Goro felt. “What’s happening?!”

Thou hast established a new bond…

One that furthers thy voyage for redemption

Thou shalt be blessed when creating
Personas of the Sun Arcana…”

Chapter Notes

Goro’s admittedly brief forays into the TV world dungeons taught him one thing. He was
getting out of shape. In the midst of the kidnappings and new environment, Goro forgot to
establish a new running routine.
Fortunately, Inaba had many opportunities for running routes. Goro started to run in the
central shopping district, to the floodplain, and back to the Amagi Inn every afternoon. It felt
good to have something to do again.
When Goro texted Emiko saying that running counted as a hobby, she responded with
derision. Goro still thought it counted.
On the Tuesday afternoon after Yosuke’s birthday party, Goro ran past the Velvet Room door
before Marie’s voice stopped him in his tracks.
“What are you doing here?” she asked, standing next to the Velvet Room door with her arms
crossed.
“I’m on a run,” Goro asked, startled by both her question and her presence. “Are you allowed
to be outside?”
“It’s not like anyone can see me when I’m standing this close to the room,” Marie said. She
glared at the door. “And I can’t stand being around those weirdos more than I have to be.”
“Theodore isn’t a weirdo,” Goro said, suddenly aware of his necklace.
Marie snorted. “Are you kidding?”

“He’s a little pompous,” Goro admitted. “But his heart is in the right place.”
“Ugh, fine,” Marie said. “Theodore’s whatever. But Margaret is judgmental, and the nose is a
weirdo. You can’t deny that.”
“I can’t,” Goro agreed reluctantly. He hated Igor’s smug-ass smirk and complete lack of
answers.
Marie glanced away with an impatient expression. “Good.”
Goro took a deep breath and tried to calm down his irritation. “Have you actually bothered to
get to know the attendants?”
“Why are you grilling me about this?” Marie rolled her eyes. “I didn’t realize you were
dating Theo; I’m sorry for insulting his honor.”
“I’m not dating him,” Goro sputtered. “But you’re trapped in that room with them most of the
time anyway. Wouldn’t it be prudent to at least try and get along?”
“Um, no.”
“Fine,” Goro snapped. “Stew in your bitterness, then, if that’s what makes you happy.”
Goro resumed his run. Marie’s attitude wasn’t any of his business. If she wanted to be
miserable, that was her decision.
Goro stopped running shortly after he began. Yu stood in front of two vending machines,
repeatedly putting yen into the slot. A soda can emerged from the bottom of the vending
machine, and a defeated noise like game over music played from the machine.
“What are you doing?” Goro asked, fascinated.
Yu put the soda in a bag and inserted more yen. “Gathering supplies.”
This time, a victory chime emerged from the vending machine. An extra can came out of it.
“What is it doing?”
“It’s a lottery machine,” Yu explained. “If you’re lucky, it’ll give you a free drink.”
“I see.” Goro frowned. “So you stand here and collect soda for our forays into the
metaverse.”
“Yep.” A repetitive beeping rang out as Yu tried to insert more yen. “Damnit, it’s out of
stock.”
“Do you need help carrying it back home?”
Yu shook his head and picked up the bag full of soda cans. The bottom of the bag sagged
downwards. It looked in danger of ripping.

“I’ve got this,” Yu said. He gave Goro a small smile. “Thanks for asking.”
“Right…”
Yu walked away. Goro watched him go, somewhat bewildered. He knew Minato wouldn’t
have wasted his time in front of a vending machine just to get a few sodas. They only could
rejuvenate the smallest amounts of energy and health, even in the metaverse.
But, come to think of it, it was the same kind of stupid shit he’d catch Akira doing from time
to time. Once, Akira and Ryuji left Shujin heaving a box full of what looked like jam bread,
likely bought from the school store.
Akira ate that same jam bread months later in Sae’s palace. The metaverse must have the
ability to preserve food, or else Akira would have gotten sick upon taking a single bite.
Maybe Goro shouldn’t judge. He hadn’t forgotten scarfing down five protein bars to heal
himself from a gunshot wound.
This wasn’t worth thinking about anymore. Goro shook himself free of the thought and
resumed running. Who gave a damn about Yu’s spending habits anyway?
Star Arcana: Rank 2

The rain started coming down for multiple days in a row. Goro took to checking the Midnight
Channel every night, but nobody new ever appeared on the screen.
Unfortunately, staying up for the Midnight channel did not help his already troubled sleep.
“Aren’t you tired of this, Goro?” a voice that sounded like Takaya whispered one night.
“Playing the good guy?”
Goro leapt awake and punched the phantom. He stared at open air. Goro wildly looked
around his room, trying to find the intruder. The door to the hall creaked shut.
Goro ran to the door and opened it. He looked up and down the hall, but nobody was there.
He only spotted some kind of bug flying around the corner. The air in his lungs felt like fire
as he tried to take deep breaths. His heart beat out of sync.
Was it just a dream? Had he only imagined an intruder?
Goro shut the door and stared at the locking mechanism. It was unlocked. Had he forgotten to
lock the door last night?
Goro always locked the door.
Goro crouched to the ground and tried to steady his breathing. Whoever was there, they were
gone now. They didn’t hurt him. They only satisfied themself with taunts.

It was all the more terrifying. What motive could they have had to trespass on his room? How
did they know where his room was?
Goro laughed shakily. His lungs still burned. First, he was afraid of entering Kujikawa’s
dungeon. Now, he was afraid of being alone in his own room.
His shadow was right. He really was a coward.
Goro wasn’t sure how long he sat there. The trembling in his limbs refused to subside, but
light slowly started creeping from the windows.
“You’re better than this,” Goro muttered. “Get up, already.”
Goro didn’t move. An irrational part of his brain told him that Takaya and Jin were waiting in
the hall. If Goro moved, they would find him. Takaya would dunk his head under water, or
Jin would throw knives–
Goro brushed his fingers over the scar on his cheek. The unevenly raised lump was only a
few inches long.
Goro couldn’t sit there forever. Why did the mere thought of moving send electric terror
down his spine?
“Takaya is dead,” Goro muttered. “Jin is dead.”
And even if they weren’t dead, they would certainly be dying from the suppressants. They
wouldn’t be able to hurt him. Goro was fine.
Goro’s phone began ringing from the opposite side of the room. The chimes pierced his ear
drums jarringly. He should pick it up.
He still couldn’t move.
The ringing stopped. After a few seconds, it started back up again.
Somehow, Goro stood up and walked mechanically to his dresser. He picked up the phone.
“Akechi speaking.”
“Akechi-kun?” Akira’s voice trembled. “Can you pick me up?”
“Pick you up?” Goro asked. His mind started to clear as concern took over. “What are you
talking about?”
“I’m by the apartments,” he said. “I don’t want to walk home alone.”
Goro yanked open his drawers and seized a fresh shirt. “I’ll be there in a few minutes.”
“Can you… actually, never mind. Sorry for bothering you.”
“You’re not bother–”

Akira hung up. Goro pocketed his phone, got dressed, and hastened out of the inn.
That morning, a thick yellow fog hung over Inaba, making the town look like the TV world.
Despite his limited visibility, Goro ran in the direction of the apartments. Sirens wailed in the
distance.
What the hell was going on?
It took him ten minutes to find the apartments. It would have taken him longer if it weren’t
for the gossiping crowds and police presence. Goro searched frantically to find Akira amidst
all the pandemonium, but Akira spotted him first.
“Akechi-kun?”
Goro turned his head toward Akira’s quiet voice. He sat on the curb, a few yards away from
the main source of attention. Goro jogged to him.
“Are you alright?” he asked, gasping for breath. “What’s going on?”
“There’s been another death,” Akira said. His voice was raw, and he hugged himself tightly.
Goro felt lightheaded. “What?”
“I don’t even know why I came here,” Akira said. “I thought I saw… and then I saw the
body… have you ever seen a body?”
“Yes,” Goro whispered. “Who was the victim?”
“I don’t know,” Akira said. “I didn’t recognize him.”
It wasn’t Kujikawa, then. But there was nobody on the Midnight channel last night. Goro
checked.
“Who did you think you saw?” Goro asked. He needed answers. It was the only way he
would stay composed. “When you came here?”
“I thought I saw my uncle.” A hiccupping laugh burst from Akira. “Which is ridiculous,
because he’s living in the States.”
“Your uncle?” Goro asked, his ears ringing.
“I don’t want to talk about it,” Akira said. “I don’t know what I was thinking. And then I saw
the body, but I couldn’t go through that with the police again, so I left and let someone else
be the first witness.” Akira frowned. “That’s not bad, right? Konishi-san got killed, and I–”
Akira covered his face with his hands.
Goro didn’t know what to do. He tentatively rested a hand on Akira’s shoulder. Akira didn’t
flinch away from the touch.

“Coming through, police!” Adachi pushed through the still gathering crowds. He spotted
Goro and ran up to him. “Akechi-kun? What are you doing here?”
“I happened to be in the area,” Goro said coldly.
“Yeah, I just got the news. I might have slept in this morning, heh,” Adachi said with an
awkward chuckle. He frowned. “Is your friend okay?”
Akira sniffed and looked up. “I-I’m fine, sir.”
“Oh, I recognize you!” Adachi said. “Kurusu-kun, right? You were the one who–”
“Yes, sir,” Akira interrupted loudly. “You’re Adachi-san? I remember you told me you threw
up the first time you saw a body.”
“That’s right.” Adachi scratched the back of his neck. “Good thing I haven’t eaten breakfast.”
“Adachi, what’s taking you so long?!” Dojima’s voice echoed from down the street.
“Aw, shit. Be right there, Dojima-san!” Adachi fumbled with his wallet and handed Akira a
clump of yen. “Buy yourself a coffee, alright? It might make you feel better. Or, um, hot
chocolate or whatever you kids drink.”
Akira nodded. “Thank you, sir.”
“It’s no problem.” Adachi smiled. He jogged backwards. “Try your best to stay away from
crime scenes from now on, got that? It’s not safe!”
Adachi gave them a parting wave before breaking into a sprint toward Dojima. Goro stood
up. “I think a cup of coffee sounds great,” he said.
Akira nodded and shoved the yen in his pocket. He followed Goro further away from the
crime scene.
Seemingly out of nowhere in the fog, Yosuke ran toward them.
“Akechi-kun?” Yosuke asked, skidding to a halt. “Did you hear the news?”
“There’s been a murder?” Goro asked. “Yes, I have. I take it you came to find out more?”
Yosuke nodded. “The others are all meeting at Junes. Don’t be surprised if one of them gives
you a call.”
“I’ll come as soon as possible, but I’m a little held up at the moment,” Goro said. “Feel free
to start the meeting without me.”
Yosuke’s eyes landed on Akira, and his eyebrows shot up in surprise.
“Oh, hi!” Yosuke said. “Are you a friend of Akechi-kun?”

“Um, yes,” Akira said. He shot Akechi a worried look. “I didn’t mean to interrupt
something.”
“You’re not interrupting anything,” Goro said. “Don’t worry about it.”
“Yeah, it’ll take about an hour for everyone to gather anyway,” Yosuke said. “Yu wants to
make sure Nanako-chan will be safe before he leaves.”
“Oh, good.” Akira looked around nervously. “Can we go?”
Goro took Akira to the cafe in the shopping district. They sat inside and drank their coffees
silently. Well, Akechi drank his coffee. Akira held onto his like a lifeline and stared at the
murky blackness with a nauseated expression.
“You’ve met Adachi-san before?” Goro asked, wanting to confirm his suspicions. Had Akira
seen another body too? If that was the case, Joker’s ghost story might not be as fictional as
Goro had previously thought.
“I don’t want to talk about it.” Akira put his coffee down and stood up. “I need to make a
call.”
Akira walked to the other side of the restaurant and turned his back to Goro, making it near
impossible for Goro to deduce the nature of the phone call. Akira hunched in on himself as he
spoke, but he arched his back a few moments later. He hung up and returned to the table.
“Who was that?”
“Just wanted to tell my parents about the situation,” Akira said. “They’re out of town.”
“They are?” Goro frowned. Somehow, he had it in his head that Akira had perfect parents.
Then again, just because they were busy didn’t necessarily mean that they weren’t loving.
“They have work,” Akira said. “But they’ll be back soon. It keeps us well-provided for, so
it’s fine.”
Akira seemed to be trying to convince himself more than Goro. An uneasy feeling settled
inside Goro’s gut.
“I’m happy,” Akira clarified. “They love me.”
Goro might have argued, but Akira just saw a dead body. Goro might be used to seeing
corpses, but he remembered how sick he felt the first time he saw one.
They drank their coffee in further silence. A few people entered the cafe, whispering to the
owners about the new murder. Akira stood up abruptly.
“Thank you,” he said. “I think I feel better now.”
Goro stood up with him. “I can accompany you back to your house.”

Akira took a deep breath, and his shoulders slumped. “No,” he said. “I’m fine.”
“Are you sure–”
“I’m fine.”
Akira left the cafe before Goro could say another word. Goro stood there, somewhat
dumbstruck. Of course, the Akira he knew always had an aversion to accepting help, but he
had been a bit more… flippant about it.
Goro almost went after him, but a phone call from Chie stopped him. Goro tried not to sound
too tense when he answered.
“Yes?”
“So, um, how do I phrase this?” Chie asked, sounding perturbed. “You know what, forget it. I
don’t think we’re going inside the TV today.”
“No?” Goro asked.
“Yeah, uh–Hey! Get your own phone!” Chie laughed nervously. “Sorry about that. Look,
we’re all going to be meeting up at Yosuke’s place. We can catch you up there.”
“What happened?”
“Um… Teddie came to the real world.”
“He can do that?”
“Yeah, apparently he got bored waiting for us,” Chie said. “I can’t really blame him, but he
sure is acting like a curious toddler right now.”
“How the hell are you going to inconspicuously have Teddie walk through the town?” Goro
demanded.
“Yosuke says he’ll say it’s a promotion for Junes,” Chie said. “It’ll work. I think. Teddie,
what are you doing–”
Chie shrieked. Goro jumped.
“Chie-san?”
“Put that head back on right now!” Chie shouted. “Sorry, I got to go. I’ll fill you in later!”
Chie hung up before Goro could ask about what the hell had happened. Goro stared at his
phone in annoyance. Why couldn’t anyone give him a straight answer anymore?

The sun caused the fog to disappear during the time Akira and Goro had been in the coffee
shop. Goro stood in the shade by Yosuke’s house as he waited for the others to show up.

The group approached Yosuke’s house in the most conspicuous procession ever. They were
going to have to start splitting up if they ever wanted to go one place together. Friend groups
were one thing. A fool would have to miss a massive group of previous victims following a
murder case.
Speaking of conspicuous, Teddie stuck out like a sore thumb amongst the others. At least
Morgana was an ordinary cat in the real world. And even then, most people didn’t take their
cats to school. Teddie waddled down the driveway, hunching forward like an old man.
“Yosuke,” he groaned. “I think I’m overheating.”
“I’ll give you a change of clothes in a minute,” Yosuke snapped. “Let’s hope that I have
something that will fit you.”
“Why couldn’t we have gone shopping at Junes?”
“Because Akechi-kun’s waiting for us,” Yosuke said. “Besides, you refused to have anything
except the most expensive clothing in the entire place! If you were reasonable, maybe you
wouldn’t be so miserable right now.”
“Akechi-kun!” Teddie complained, pointing at Yosuke. “Yosuke’s bullying me!”
“He’s not bullying you,” Kanji said. “He’s just being practical.”
Teddie made a weeping sound of despair. “You too, Kanji?”
“What the hell are any of you talking about?” Goro asked. “What clothing can Teddie
possibly wear?”
The entire group looked at Chie.
“What?!” Chie asked defensively. “How was I meant to say that Teddie had a naked body
underneath his bear costume? Who would be able to take that seriously?”
“Teddie what?”
“I can show you–”
“No, don’t!” Yosuke shouted. “We are literally right at my house. Let me unlock the door.”
Teddie sighed sadly. “Sensei wouldn’t mistreat me like this.”
“I’m standing right here,” Yu said. “You shouldn’t take your clothes off in public.”
“He’s right,” Yukiko said sympathetically.
Yosuke opened the door and let the group inside. The air inside was cooler than the summer

“Wow!” Teddie said. “This is so much nicer than the dungeons!”

“It’s a house,” Yu said.
“You’re so wise, Sensei!” Teddie said. “Can I take off my suit now? Akechi-kun has yet to
see my beautiful face.”
“In a minute!” Yosuke snapped. “Follow me.”
Teddie followed Yosuke to Yosuke’s bedroom. Everybody else sat down in the living area.
“Did you find out more about the murder?” Goro asked Yu, choosing to ignore the Teddieshaped elephant in the room.
Yu looked disconcerted, but he nodded. “The victim was our homeroom teacher, Morookasenpai.”
“And the cause of death is clear,” Kanji said. “It’s blunt force trauma. I think. Nothing like
the past deaths. Teddie said he didn’t smell him in the TV world at all.”
“And he didn’t show up on the midnight channel,” Yukiko added.
Goro frowned. “Probably not the same killer, then.”
“Not the same killer?” Chie asked. “What do you mean?”
It wasn’t obvious?
“This murder is an outlier from the others,” Goro said. “The motive and the cause of death
are completely different. I thought we agreed the victims are all seen on television before
being killed?”
“But he was hanging from an apartment balcony,” Yukiko said. “And you weren’t shown on
the news.”
“We agreed that the killer might not have wanted me to investigate him,” Goro said. He
drummed his fingers against his knee. “Was Morooka doing anything that might aggravate
the killer?”
“Other than criticizing all of our chastity?” Chie asked. “Not that I know of. Maybe the killer
just thought he was annoying.”
“And why make the murder method far more traceable to him?”
“The killer could have decided that throwing people into televisions wasn’t working,” Yukiko
said. “I mean, we’ve saved the last four victims.”
It was a fair point, but if that was stopping him, why hadn’t the killer given up after Goro
came out alive? Hell, even Kanji’s survival would’ve been indicative that the TV wasn’t an
effective murder method anymore.
“I still think it’s likelier that this is a copycat killer,” Goro said.

“It doesn’t make much sense if this is the same person as before,” Yu said, leaning forward
and running his hand through his hair. “You might be right.”
“But why the hell would someone do that?” Kanji said. “I mean, King Moron was the worst,
but I wouldn’t want to kill him!”
“Attention?” Goro did worse things just to be acknowledged.
“You mean that we might have two killers on the loose?” Yosuke asked as he came down the
stairs.
A light-skinned human-looking child followed Yosuke, wearing an oversized blue t-shirt and

the resemblance.
“Looking good, Teddie,” Kanji said.
“Really?” Teddie asked. He looked down at himself. “Yosuke didn’t have a very wide
selection.”
At least Teddie didn’t look as unsettling as Morgana’s human form. Teddie’s body seemed to
match his emotional age.
“You look fine,” Chie said. “Did you hear Goro’s theory, Yosuke-kun?”
“I think I got the gist.” Yosuke grimaced and sat down next to Yu. “You really think that we

“But if this second person isn’t putting people in televisions, shouldn’t forensics have a better

“Also, if I killed someone for attention, I wouldn’t hide. I’d tell someone,” Kanji said.
“He’s right,” Goro said. “Our copycat killer might turn themself in. Assuming my theory’s

“I hope so,” Yosuke said. “There’s not much we can do to stop the killer in the real world.”

Goro bristled. “I said they might turn themself in.”
“I have something that will make you feel better!” Teddie held a pair of glasses above his

“Glasses?” Chie asked.
“For Rise-chan,” Teddie said. “She’s going to be joining the team as support, isn’t she?”

“Well, only if she wants to,” Yukiko said. “We shouldn’t force anyone into this, especially
when it’s so dangerous.”
“Oh, I didn’t think about that.” Teddie put the glasses back into his pocket with a forlorn

“It can’t hurt to check to see if she’s okay, though,” Yosuke said. “Don’t worry. We can ask if

“Really?” Teddie asked hopefully.
“Yep.”
Teddie insisted that they all march back to the central shopping district and speak to

As they approached Maruyuku Tofu, a young man exited the store. With a jolt, Goro realized

“Shirogane-san?” Goro asked.

Well, they didn’t name him the detective prince for nothing. Unlike Goro, Shirogane’s

“That’s right!” Teddie said. “It only works in the TV world.”

“We would appreciate it,” Yu said. “But it’s up to you.”

Akechi’s body hung upside down from a telephone pole near the diet building. He was still
wearing his school uniform, but his striped tie dangled over his face, covering the bullet
wound in his forehead. Despite how very clearly dead Akechi was, the corpse’s expression
was oddly serene.
Goro stared at it quietly. It was odd. He didn’t feel dead. He thought he could feel the wind
hitting his face. But his corpse was right there, dangling ten feet above him.
“We really didn’t expect to find a body,” Akira said. He stood next to Goro, looking older
than Goro remembered but still wearing his Shujin uniform. He stuffed his hands inside his
pockets. “Or, well, I know I didn’t. A part of me didn’t really believe that you were dead.”
“Maybe this isn’t real,” Goro said.
“No.” Akira’s smile was strained. “It is.”
“You never told me about a dead body,” Goro said, his voice accusatory.
“That’s because I didn’t know.” Akira pulled his phone out of his pocket and began typing.
“Maruki kind of fucked everything up on that end.”
“Naturally.”
“Here.”
Akira tossed his phone at Goro. Goro caught it and looked down at the screen. A news article
dated in December 2016 stared back at him. A picture of Goro in one of his interviews sat

beneath the bold headline.
Shocking Truth about “Detective Prince” Akechi Goro Comes to Light at His Recent Suicide
“Suicide?” Goro asked.
“After we changed his heart, one of Shido’s goons made it look like you were working with
the Phantom Thieves and participating in causing the mental shutdowns,” Akira said. “He
moved your body from where he actually found it and put it in your apartment.”

saying anything bad about me, are you?!”
“Oh, it’s nothing!” Tatsumi handed the box of cupcakes back to Goro. “You can go ahead and
put them in the pantry. And when you’re done, could you help me set the table?”
Goro nodded and bowed, relieved to be given a task. “Of course, Tatsumi-san.”

Final exams were one of the things that Goro had not missed while repeating his elementary
school years. The stifling quiet and scratching of pencils against paper that filled the room for
hours on end was nothing to be fond of. The only mercy was that Goro was so familiar with
most of the material that it wasn’t very difficult.
The afternoon after the exams, Akira met him outside the school as usual. Goro let out a
small breath of exhaustion.
“How was it?” Akira asked.
“Fine,” Goro said. “Exhausting, but that’s nothing new.”
Akira pursed his lips as they walked past a group of students comparing their answers. The
most confident looking student stated their answer. A collection of miserable groans chorused
behind Goro and Akira.
“Isn’t this your first time doing final exams?” Akira asked.
Goro could kick himself. “I had midterms in May, so I had a taste of what it would be like
then.”

“Oh.” Akira nodded. “That makes sense. My uncle says that he would almost fall asleep
during finals a lot of the time.”
“I can’t imagine you’ll be doing that next year,” Goro said.
“No,” Akira said. He looked away. “Are they hard?”
Goro really couldn’t be a good judge of what made a hard exam for middle schoolers. He
tried to remember his first final exam experience, but he had been taking studying about as
seriously as Akira was now. Between prioritizing his studies and staying alive, he’d had little
time for anything else. Exams hadn’t been too difficult.
It was why he had no friends before he met Akira.
But Akira was going to another school’s library just to extend his studies. Goro doubted that
he would have any more difficulty than Goro did.
“It’s challenging, but I’m sure you will be fine,” Goro said. “Just focus on the present for
now.”
“You sound like an adult,” Akira muttered.
“Sorry.”
“Well, it is kind of cool,” Akira conceded.
Akira’s house was only a few yards away. Goro slowed down and looked around for
Tsuyoshi’s car. The obnoxious silver shine was nowhere in sight.
“What’s wrong?” Akira asked.
“I thought I heard something,” Goro lied. “Don’t worry about it.”
“You don’t think the killer would come for anyone in broad daylight, do you?” Akira asked.
“You said you were taken at night.”
“I was,” Goro said. “I guess I’m just a little skittish, that’s all.”
“It’s not skittish,” Akira said. “I’d probably be scared too.” He glanced at his house. “If you
want, I could walk with you to your place.”
“That’s not necessary,” Goro said. He was still absurdly concerned that Tsuyoshi somehow
didn’t already know where he lived. He didn’t need Akira telling him. “I can handle myself.”
Akira’s expression closed off. “Right.”

The textile shop was quiet without Teddie gasping and praising every bolt of cloth. Tatsumi
was kneeling on a mat. She smiled when Goro entered.
“Hello, Akechi-kun,” she said. “How was your first day of exams?”
“They were fine, Tatsumi-san.” Goro bowed. “I thought I would help out at the store as
thanks for your kindness.”
“Oh, we’ve already discussed this,” Tatsumi said. “You are under no such obligations.”
“I understand.” Goro’s smile felt more strained. “I want to help. It will take my mind off of
exams.” He needed to start chipping away at the huge amount of debt that was stacked up
against him.
“Well, in that case, I won’t say no to a little bit of help. Perhaps you would like to organize
the back? Kanji isn’t exactly an organized individual, and I’m afraid to admit that too much
labor at once is bad for my back.”
Air entered Goro’s lungs more freely. “I would be glad to.”
Goro stepped into the back room and began organizing the boxes of cloth and thread. There
were a few pieces of clothing as well that he put in their respective boxes and shelves. It
wasn’t what he would call particularly easy work. A few shelves were too high for him to
reach on his own, and he had to grab a stepstool to reach them. By the time he was half-way
through organizing the clutter, a layer of sweat had formed on his brow.
The door slid open behind him. Goro froze when Tatsumi stepped inside the room. Her
humming was too difficult to read. Had he screwed something up?

“Is something the matter, Tatsumi-san?” Goro asked. He put down the box he was holding
and turned to face her. She smiled, which was probably a good sign.
“I was wondering what was taking you so long when you didn’t come out after thirty
minutes,” Tatsumi said. “I suppose I was silly to think you would give up like Kanji.”
“You gave me a job,” Goro said. “I want to perform it adequately.”
“Well, you’ve done more than adequate,” Tatsumi said. “I think I can handle the store on my
own for the rest of the day.”
Goro must have screwed up. Why else would she be kicking him out? “If there’s something I
did wrong, I can fix it.”
“You didn’t do anything wrong.” Tatsumi’s voice was sharper as she shook her head. “Young
boys like you shouldn’t spend all of their time cooped up in storage rooms. You should be
spending time with friends, or, better yet, getting your rest. You have a full day of exams
ahead of you tomorrow.”
“Doing work won’t affect that.”
“Rest is extremely important,” Tatsumi said. She picked up the box in front of Goro and
placed it on a nearby shelf. “I’m not completely helpless, you know.”
“I didn’t mean to imply that you were.”
The wrinkles around Tatsumi’s eyes crinkled at that statement. “I know you didn’t.”

On the second to last day of exams, Goro finally found the emotional energy to go to the
Velvet Room. Rain was drenching everything in sight, but Goro thought that Marie deserved
to get a little wet. And Theodore would probably be thrilled to see water coming down from
the sky.
“Welcome,” Margaret said upon Goro’s arrival. “What brings you here?”
“I thought I would borrow the three of you,” Goro said. “Unless I’m not worth your time.
Marie wants fresh air, and it’s been a long time since I’ve spoken with Theodore.”
“I doubt I’d be welcome,” Margaret said politely. Goro wasn’t in the mood to force her.
Marie was clearly doubtful at best over the excursion. Theo was thrilled.
“It’s been so long since I’ve gone out to see the outside world with you, Goro-kun,” he said
as they stepped outside the Velvet Room. As Goro predicted, Theodore looked up at the sky
with a mixture of shock and awe. “Where is all this coming from? Could it be that there is a
giant shower?”

“Of course not,” Marie snapped, holding her hands over her head. “It’s rain. It comes from
the clouds, or something. Why did you decide to take us outside on such a terrible day?”
“Because I felt like it,” Goro said. “I don’t mind getting a little wet, so you can have my
umbrella.”
Marie took the umbrella and glowered.
“How do the clouds make the rain?” Theodore asked.
“The water goes into the air in the heat,” Goro explained concisely. “The water makes clouds.
The water falls from the clouds to make rain.”
“Amazing,” Theodore whispered.
“It’s just water,” Marie said. She looked up at the water droplets gathering on top of Goro’s
umbrella. “Why is your umbrella see-through?”
“Because that’s how the company designed it,” Goro said. He was already soaking wet.
“Maybe we should decide on an indoor location to spend time with each other.”
“You didn’t come up with a decision yourself?” Theodore asked.
“I thought I’d let Marie decide,” Goro said. “She’s seen less of the outside world than you
have, and part of the reason for this excursion is because I’m hoping she’ll learn to get along

Marie scoffed. “Good luck.”
“I suppose that’s fair,” Theodore said. His frown indicated he did not trust Marie to make a
good decision.
“Why are you asking me?” Marie demanded. “I’m not an expert on this place.”
“You could point to a store in the shopping district for all I care,” Goro said.

Marie pointed to Aiya. Goro had yet to try their famous beef bowls, although Yu and Yosuke

“Rainy Day Special Mega Beef Bowl challenge?” Marie asked.

“That’s right,” the owner said. “If you manage to finish the entire thing, we have a reward for

“I as well.”

About fifteen minutes later, the owner brought out two absolutely massive beef bowls. The

Goro received his beef bowl, which was probably a third of the size of the rainy day beef

“Yes, yes, because you win, you don’t have to pay for the bowl! Congratulations!”
“Really?” Theodore asked. “How delightful!”
“Oh,” Marie said. “That’s it?”
“Thank you so much,” Goro said, mortified by both Marie’s comment and the shocked

After Goro paid for his own bowl, he dragged Marie and Thedore out of the restaurant. He

“Walking to the train station wouldn’t be relaxing. It’d just be a lot of walking,” Kanji said.
“Come on, I’ll show you what I’ve been working on.”
Goro followed Kanji into his bedroom. It was tidier than Goro expected; there wasn’t even
any junk on the dresser.
“Ugh, Ma did warn me that she was going to clean my room this morning,” Kanji said. “Let
me see if I can find my stuff.”
Goro leaned against the wall as Kanji began looting his drawers. He pulled out a half sewntogether rabbit from one of the drawers and began searching underneath his bed.
“What are you looking for?” Goro asked.
“I’m trying to find the buttons,” Kanji said. “I know I have some stashed around here
somewhere. It’s for the eyes. I mean, obviously, you can’t have a stuffed rabbit without
adding eyes to them, right?”
“You’re making a stuffed rabbit?”
“For this kid,” Kanji explained. He sat up and scratched the back of his neck while glaring at
the floor. “He was pretty worked up after losing his, and I thought I’d do something nice for
him, you know? Then again, maybe it is kinda strange.”
“It’s not strange,” Goro said. “It’s kindness.”
“Heh, that’s definitely a word for it.” Kanji stood up and combed his hair away from his face.
“But seriously, where’d the heck did those buttons go?”
At that moment, the sound of the front door opening and closing answered Kanji’s request.
“I’m home!” Tatsumi said from wherever she had been.
“Ma!” Kanji opened the door to his room and stuck his head out into the hall. “Where’d you
put the buttons?”
“What buttons?”
“The buttons in my room! Why’d the hell you move everything around?!”
Goro was glad he was leaning against the wall. His legs were feeling weak. What the hell was
Kanji thinking? He might be Tatsumi’s child, but that sort of behavior was never tolerated.
“Don’t speak to your mother that way!” Tatsumi said sharply. Goro stayed perfectly still and
waited for her to barge into the room. She didn’t. “I put it in the box in your closet, with your
other sewing supplies.”
Kanji leaned away from the hall, looking surprised. “I thought I looked there.”
“Well, that’s where I put it,” Tatsumi said irritably.

Why wouldn’t Goro’s chest stop hurting? Kanji was looking in his closet now, pulling out a
small box and rummaging through its contents. He pulled out a bag of buttons slowly, turning
them over in his hands. Goro’s ears were ringing as Kanji looked toward the still open door.
“You’re right!” Kanji said. “Sorry!”
“Look more carefully next time,” Tatsumi said, still obviously annoyed.
“Right.” Kanji stood up and walked up to Goro. He was smiling as though only something
mildly embarrassing had just happened. As though he wasn’t trying to trigger every nerve in
Goro’s body. “Well, crisis averted–”
Goro punched him in the face.
Kanji stumbled backwards into his desk. He grabbed the desk with one hand for purchase as
he raised his other hand to his cheek.
“The hell was that for?!”
“What is wrong with you?” Goro asked. It hurt to even find the air to speak. “You can’t speak
to her like that! She’s your guardian. You can’t– don’t you realize what she can do if you act
that way?!”
“What are you talking about?”
“Are you a moron?!” Goro’s shouting made his head hurt, but he couldn’t stop. “She does
everything for you, and she has the power to hurt–”
“What on earth is going on here?”
Tatsumi stood in the doorway of the room, staring at Goro and Kanji with an expression that
was either one of alarm or anger. Probably anger. Certainly anger. Kanji had yelled at her.
Goro had yelled at Kanji. Goro had attacked her child.
Definitely anger.
Goro could hear his heart beating. His blood pulsed to the rhythm of his panic and frustration.
Tatsumi was blocking the door, but she was small. Goro could still make a break for it. But
where would he go?
“Um, I’m not really sure,” Kanji said, even though it should have been obvious. What was
more clear than Goro attacking him? Than Goro lecturing him on a topic that was ultimately
none of Goro’s business? “Akechi, maybe you need a drink–”
“What on earth happened to your face?” Tatsumi asked. She stepped deeper into the room.
“And Akechi-kun, your hand–”
Goro couldn’t attack. Attacking would only make it worse. Shouting would only make it
worse. Doing anything would only make it worse.

Goro slipped past Tatsumi and ran.

Goro never ran. It wasn’t a dignified response to fear. A tactical retreat in the face of a
powerful shadow was one thing, and even those were only rarely tolerated. Shido had
demands for Goro to fulfill. Goro couldn’t waste unnecessary time gathering strength when
he was on a deadline.
When Goro screwed up one of Shido’s requests, he’d stand silently as Shido chewed him out.
Sometimes, he didn’t even receive his lecture in person. That was always preferable. Sitting
down on his bed while Shido shouted at him over the phone was a lot less terrible than being
forced to stay expressionless while Shido looked ready to beat him senseless.
He never did, of course. Shido had too much “class” for that. Instead, he used every verbal
weapon in his arsenal to make it clear that he did not tolerate failure of any kind. An
appropriate warning of what could happen to Goro if he didn’t step up his game was enough
to prevent Goro from failing for a long stretch of time afterwards.
“I am the reason you’re not wasting away in the sewers right now,” he used to say. “And this
is how you thank me? Do you think I’m keeping you around for your pretty fucking face?”
Goro sometimes wondered how Shido reacted when the Phantom Thieves sent their calling
card before taking Shido’s heart. Had he tried to call Goro in a fit of rage? Did he make plans
to see Goro dead before the end of the year? Apparently, that was already on his agenda
anyway.
In any case, Goro did not run away.
When Takaya shot him, he didn’t run away. When they faced the literal end of the world,
Goro didn’t run away.
He ran away when Takaya and Jin kidnapped him. He ran away from his younger shadow.
From his own fear. But those were the exceptions. Not the rule.
So what was he doing? Why was he fleeing from Kanji and his mother? Even if he thought
he was in danger, he should be able to face it without hesitation. He shouldn’t be sprinting
past passersby returning home after a long day. He shouldn’t trip over a jutting corner of the
sidewalk just to outpace his own rampaging thoughts.
Goro stumbled forward as he slowed to a walk. The world spun around him. He didn’t even
know where he was. He gasped for breath and ran his hands through his hair. He had to calm
down. He needed to pull himself together.
Goro’s phone was ringing. The shrill sound pierced his eardrums over and over again. Ring
ring. A breath of silence. Ring ring. Another breath. Ring ring, ring ring–
Goro yanked his phone from his pocket and answered the call.

“Akechi speaking,” Goro said. He leaned forward and rested his hand against his leg. He
couldn’t tell if he was about to pass out or vomit.
“Oh thank god,” Kanji said. Goro contemplated the benefits of face planting into the
concrete. “Dude, where are you?”
“That–” Goro inhaled sharply. “—is a very good question.”
“What’s that supposed to mean?” Kanji asked. “I know it took you fifteen minutes to answer
my calls, but surely you haven’t managed to get all the way out of town–”
“Just give me a minute to find my bearings.” Goro stood to his full height. A hill with
pavilions stood to his right. “There’s a pavilion.”
“By a hill?”
“Yes.” Goro’s heart was slowly beginning to slot itself back into place. “Nobody else is
around.”
“Okay, give us a minute and we’ll find you–”
“That’s really not necessary. I can find my way back to your home myself.”
“Um, two minutes ago you didn’t even know where you were,” Kanji said.
“I can ask someone about your address. Please, don’t worry about me.” Goro stared at his
freshly bruised fist. “I’m sorry about your face.”
“We can talk about that later,” Kanji said. “Maybe I should come for you–”
“For fuck’s sake, Kanji, I’m fine!” Goro’s voice cracked. He sat down at a nearby picnic
table. “I’ll be back within thirty minutes.”
“Thirty minutes?” Kanji said. “It’ll be dark in thirty minutes.”
“Nothing will happen.” Goro massaged his temple. His headache had yet to go away. “What
is your problem? Didn’t you want to relax?”
“What sort of question is that?” Kanji demanded. For some inexplicable reason, his cadence
reminded Goro suddenly of Shinjiro. “You’re my friend. It’s kind of hard to relax when
you’re on your own and it’s going to be night–”
“We’re not friends!” Goro’s hold on his phone tightened. “We’ve known each other for what?
A month and a half? Just because you know my history doesn’t mean–”
A lump lodged itself in Goro’s throat. If he said anything more, he thought he might burst
into tears. What was going on with him today?
“I’m sorry,” Goro said shortly. He hung up and slapped the phone down against the seat
beside him. It skidded forward and fell to the ground. Goro didn’t bother to pick it up.

“Get a grip,” Goro whispered to himself. He tensed his forearms in an attempt to keep his
hands still. His hands only shook more sporadically. “Pull your pathetic self together. They
can’t see you like this.”
It was over. There was no going back from this. Goro would have to leave the Tatsumi
residence only a week after he had moved in. In his history of homes, this probably had the
record for the shortest lived.
The sun was setting. Mitsuru would be furious if she knew that Goro was out there alone.
There weren’t any pedestrians around to witness a potential murder. Goro should leave.
And go where? There wasn’t any point in going back to the Tatsumis. They were probably
already packing Goro’s bags for him. Goro was too tired to taste direct rejection.
Maybe Akira would let him sleep over. But if Tsuyoshi happened to be there, Goro would be
in a worse position than he was before. He might as well be walking into a trap that had red
flashing lights.
A stick snapped loudly behind him. Goro jumped to his feet and spun around. The sky was
growing darker, but no silhouette was amongst the trees and bushes.
“Oh look, there he is,” Adachi’s voice said. Goro frowned and turned back toward the noise.
Adachi and Tatsumi walked up the hill toward the pavilion. “Looks like your son was right
after all, ma’am.”
“No need to sound so surprised,” Tatsumi said sharply. “Kanji is a perfectly intelligent boy.”
“Oh, um, my apologies!” Adachi bowed hurriedly. “I didn’t mean to imply.”
“Tatsumi-san?” Goro asked. “What are you doing here?”
“Finding you, of course.” Tatsumi sat down to Goro’s right. “You managed to run a long way
before Kanji-kun got a hold of you. Fortunately, Adachi-san was willing to escort me. It’s not
safe to be walking alone at dark”
“It’s hard to say no when they’re demanding your protection–” Adachi muttered.
“What was that?” Tatsumi said sweetly.
“Oh, nothing, ma’am! Just glad to help.” Adachi chuckled. “Good to see that you’re alright,
Akechi-kun.”
“I’m sorry to take you from your post,” Goro said, too emotionally drained to be angry with
Adachi’s comment.
“Don’t be. I was just doing my job, after all.” Adachi bowed again. “But I should really get
going.”
“Thank you very much for your help, young man,” Tatsumi said. “Be careful out there.”

“I always am.”
If Adachi knew how to be careful, Goro knew how to control his rampaging emotions. So far,
he wasn’t having much luck.
Tatsumi was still sitting as Adachi walked away. Goro did not see any point in sitting down
next to her.
“You didn’t need to find me,” Goro said.
“Oh yes,” Tatsumi said. “Kanji was quite insistent that you did not want to be bothered.
Unfortunately, I was not convinced.”
“I can take care of myself.”
“I’m sure you can,” Tatsumi said. “But it’s my policy that when children run away from me, I
address the issue before it spirals.”
“What is there to address?” Goro spat. He smoothed his expression. “Tatsumi-san, I
understand the situation perfectly. I hit Kanji-kun without even being provoked. I can have
my bags packed before morning tomorrow.”
“Bags packed? What are you talking about?”
“You’re kicking me out, of course,” Goro said. “I understand. I’m sorry for imposing myself
upon your family.”
“I’m not doing anything of the sort.” Tatsumi patted the bench beside her. “Now stop
spouting nonsense and sit down before you pass out before my eyes.”
Goro sat down mechanically and stared at the street in front of him. A single car drove past.
Maybe the driver was having as terrible a day as he was.
“You don’t have to feel obligated to give me another chance, Tatsumi-san,” Goro said. “I
know that I’m too volatile for you to handle. There’s no point in keeping me around when
I’m only going to hurt someone else.”
“Do you think this is the first time someone has lost their temper in my house?” Tatsumi
asked. She gave Goro a severe look. “Do you think Kanji has never punched something or
someone before?”
This wasn’t a part of the script. Goro, normally good at improvising on stage, found himself
floundering.
“I’m sure he has,” Goro said. “But he’s your son, and I attacked him. Surely there are
repercussions.”
“Yes, I expect you to give him a thorough apology when we get back,” Tatsumi said. “You
seem very well-practiced in that regard, so I doubt it will be an issue.”

“Tatsumi-san, I don’t know who you’re trying to impress. There’s nobody here if you’re
worried about your reputation.”
“I’m too old to care about what other people think of me. I’m only here to understand your
side of the story.”
Goro scoffed. “There’s only one story,” he said. “Kanji isn’t a liar. I’m sure he can tell you
what happened.”
“Yes, he said that you punched him, lectured him on respecting his parents, and then left,”
Tatsumi said. “I heard that much for myself. I was hoping for a more thorough explanation.”
“I don’t know why I did it,” Goro said.
“No?” Tatsumi raised her eyebrows. “I didn’t realize you hated Kanji-kun that much.”
“Of course I don’t hate him,” Goro said. “You don’t have to hate someone to be angry at
them, do you?” Goro had been angry at Akira on a near constant basis, and he was sure Akira
was angry right back at him.
“What did Kanji do to make you angry?” Tatsumi asked.
“Were you an attorney in your past life?” Goro asked. “Why can’t you just accept that I had
no good reason for punching your son?”
“Because I doubt that’s true, and I’m not sure I understand why you’re insisting on punishing
yourself,” Tatsumi said. “I’ll ask again. Why were you angry at Kanji?”
“Clearly, it doesn’t bother you as much as I thought it did, but he was being disrespectful.
Most adults don’t tolerate that sort of disrespect.” Goro was unable to hide the suspicion from
his face. “Children are meant to respect their elders.”
“Kanji has never been very good at that,” Tatsumi said. “But it’s not because he doesn’t
respect me. He just speaks his mind. I don’t think it’s necessary to do anything except remind
him about his tone every now and then.”
“Then, I guess this was just a massive misunderstanding on my end,” Goro said. He stood up.
He couldn’t do this anymore. “My apologies. Are you kicking me out or not?”
“I’m not.”
Goro picked up his phone still lying on the dirt. “Okay,” he said. Relief and frustration
churned inside him as he smoothed his hair back. “Fantastic.” He bowed. “Thank you for
your generosity, Tatsumi-san. I will try not to squander it a second time.”
“You haven’t squandered it at all, Akechi-kun.” Tatsumi stood up. “On the whole, you’ve
been a joy to have in my home.”
Right. Goro was a real ball of sunshine.

Kanji’s cheek was already beginning to swell. Goro stood in front of him and contemplated
the benefits of yelling or running away again.
He did neither. Goro still had a place to sleep; he wasn’t going to press his luck any further.
Tatsumi looked at him expectantly. Goro swallowed the lump of emotions blocking his vocal
cords.
“I’m sorry, Kanji-san.” He bowed. “I shouldn’t have hit you, and I shouldn’t have said the
things I said. Please forgive me.”
Kanji looked surprised. Was he not used to being apologized to? Come to think of it, he had
been equally uncomfortable when Yosuke had apologized over whatever the hell had
happened on their camping trip.
“Oh, um, sure.”
It was a wholly incomplete exchange. Goro had no idea what he could possibly say to make it
better.
“Well, that will have to be good enough for now,” Tatsumi sighed. “Kanji, did you start the
rice?”
“Oh yeah, I did,” Kanji said. “I think it’s done. You guys took longer than I expected to get
back. I set the table too.”
The idea of sitting and eating across from Kanji was suffocating. How could he possibly go
back to everything being normal? Nothing about this was normal at all.
“You can take my plate away,” Goro said. “I’m not hungry.”

“Seriously?”
“I just… don’t feel well,” Goro said. “My cold must be getting to me.”
Tatsumi sighed. “Well, I’ll make you a portion if you change your mind,” she said.
Goro bowed and fled to his room. He sat down on his futon and stared at his scratched phone.
Fuuka had texted him at some point, likely when the phone was lying on the ground. She
wanted to meet Goro to deliver the tracker.
Akechi Goro: I’ll meet you by the station.
The smell of meat and spices carried from the kitchen into his room. Goro’s stomach
growled, but Goro sat down at his desk and tried to study instead. He didn’t need Tatsumi’s
kindness.
He didn’t deserve it.

Fuuka arrived at Inaba early the next morning. Goro skipped breakfast and stopped by the
station to greet her.
“Goro-kun!” Fuuka said cheerfully. “You got taller!”
“Teenage boys have a bad habit of doing that,” Goro said dryly. “Your hair got longer.”
Fuuka looked over her shoulder, even though the small braid was likely too short for her to
see. “Well, hair has a bad habit of doing that too. Do you like it?”
“It looks good,” Goro said. The hairstyle genuinely was quite good looking on Fuuka, but
Goro’s smile felt strained. The events of the day before had drained the hell out of him, and
he was afraid that this tracker was an exercise in futility. “Do you have what I asked for?”
“Oh, yeah, I do.”
Fuuka handed a small wooden box to Akechi. Akechi undid the clasps. Extremely small
black disks and a thumb drive rested on a cushion.
“The thumb drive will download the program that receives the signals from the trackers onto
your computer,” Fuuka explained, pointing to the box. “You should be able to see where your
suspect is in real time.”
“We need to have a suspect first,” Goro said. He put the box in his pocket. A few raindrops
started come down, and the last thing they needed was for the expensive technology to get
wet. “Thank you. I really appreciate this.”
Fuuka nodded. “Please be careful.”

“Why does everyone keep reminding me of that?” Goro asked. “Do I look like a reckless
person to you?”
“Maybe a little.” Fuuka winced. “You do have a habit for getting into danger without telling
anyone.”
Goro sighed. “I deserve that,” he said. Especially considering he wasn’t being wholly honest
over why he had trackers to begin with. “Well, tell everyone that I’m being perfectly safe.”
“I will.” Fuuka pulled something out of her pocket. “And before I forget, Ryoji made a good
luck charm for you.”
Fuuka handed Goro a small keychain with a tiny blue paper crane at the end. Goro quickly
put it in his pocket before the rain got to it.
“Give him my gratitude,” Goro said. “I’m sure the crane will protect me when it counts.”
“You never know,” Fuuka said. She pointed to her necklace, which also had a crane as the
pendant. “He’s given one to everyone.”
Goro shook his head fondly. “He should open up an origami business.”
“He’s already asked Minato to be his co-owner.” Fuuka laughed.
Some of the tension and confusion that had overcome Goro faded. No matter what happened
in Inaba, he still had friends waiting for him in Iwatodai. People he understood and trust. He
had almost lost sight of that.

Goro ate lunch at school. He was still hungry when he was finished. A side effect of no
longer being malnourished and not eating dinner or breakfast.
It was no longer raining when Akira and Goro walked home from school, which meant Goro
could attach the small paper crane keychain to his backpack without worrying. It swayed
back and forth as he walked, almost like a second companion.
But origami aside, now that Goro finally had a plan of action against Tsuyoshi, a part of him
had been hoping that his expensive-ass car would show up conveniently.
“Have you seen your uncle recently?” Goro asked.
“He’s been a bit busy, but I saw him the other day,” Akira said. “Why?”
“Do you know where he works?”
“Somewhere in the city. I don’t know the details.” Akira looked contemplatively at the
sidewalk. “I don’t like asking about work.”

Goro couldn’t exactly blame him, especially since Akira’s parents were busier than even
Dojima seemed to be. “I see.”
“Do you want to ask him about his work?” Akira asked. “Is it a project or something?”
Goro barked out a laugh. “If I had a project about work, I’d ask my guardian,” he said.
“Your guardian?” Akira’s eyes widened. “Wait. Was your guardian that woman who came in
the limo when you were missing?”
Goro hid his face in embarrassment. “Yes.”
“Your guardian is Kirjio Mitsuru?”
“In a sense.”
Akira’s jaw dropped. “My dad would die if he knew I was friends with the ward of the leader
of the Kirijo Group.”
“Well, don’t tell him,” Goro said. “I’d prefer not to have too much attention.”
Akira looked hesitant, but he nodded. “Alright. He probably wouldn’t believe me anyway.”
They arrived at Akira’s house and bid each other farewell. Goro headed back to the Tatsumi
residence, trying to ignore the way his dread returned full force.
Goro could run in the clearer weather. He’d quickly change his clothes and leave before
anyone even knew he was there.
Those plans swiftly deteriorated as soon as Goro approached the house to find Kanji standing
in front of the front door, his arms crossed. The swelling on his face had gotten worse. The
bruise was beginning to turn blue.
“I figured you’d be back here sooner rather than later,” Kanji said.
“Kanji-san,” Goro said. He didn’t know what to say. “I’m surprised to see you here.”
Kanji sighed and glanced up at the overcast sky. “Well, it’s kind of a crummy day for this, but
do you want to get topsicles?”
Goro’s grip on his schoolbag tightened. Kanji wasn’t about to confront him about the night
before? “Topsicles? What does that have to do with anything?”
“I’ll buy if you don’t want to,” Kanji said conversationally. Were they speaking in two

“Don’t be ridiculous,” Goro said. “Why on earth would you want to spend time with me after
what happened?”

“Well, you said you didn’t know me very well.” Kanji shoved his hands into his pockets and

“I attacked you.”
“Yeah, exactly. You attacked me. Are you really going to tell me what to do right now?”
He wasn’t wrong. Goro’s shame outweighed his frustration.
“You’re not paying.”
“Fine by me.”

They sat on a bench by the topsicle stand and ate in silence. Kanji kept shuffling in place and
opening his mouth before closing it again. Goro didn’t have any idea on what he could
possibly say.
“Exam scores came out today,” Kanji said. “Did you see yours?”
Goro bit into his topsicle. The chill in his teeth made his head hurt, but it was a welcome
distraction from his mess of emotions. “I was top in my class,” he said flatly.
“Figures.” Kanji snorted. “Yu-kun was too. Maybe the power to hold multiple personas
comes with the power of being smart.”
“Maybe it does.”
“Although, I guess since you’re from the future, it doesn’t really count,” Kanji said. He had

to do school all over again.”
“I’ll live.”
The sound of the occasional student and adult milling through the shopping district filled the
uncomfortable silence between them. Students gave Kanji a wide berth as they passed.
Goro’s topsicle began to melt. The sticky red substance looked almost like blood on his
fingers. The thought didn’t do wonders for Goro’s appetite. He held the topsicle out to Kanji.
“Do you want it?”
“Oh, sure.” Kanji took the topsicle and bit into it violently. He finished it within a few
minutes and handed the stick back to Goro. “Thanks.”
Goro stared at the topsicle stick in his hands. It was about as stained as his fingers. “Well, if
that’s all you wanted, I should go–”

“Wait.”
Goro didn’t move.
“Look, I’m not very good at this talking thing either, but–” Kanji cut himself off and scowled
at his feet. “You can’t keep skipping meals, man.”
“I only skipped dinner.”
“You didn’t eat breakfast either,” Kanji snapped. “You left your bedroom and just walked
right out of the house without another word.”
“I wasn’t hungry.”
“Yeah, right.” Kanji glowered. “You’ve never had any issues eating Ma’s cooking before.”
“Well, I guess yesterday was an outlier,” Goro said. “Did you want me to eat dinner with you

“I don’t want you to starve yourself, if that’s what you’re asking.”
“I ate lunch.”
“That’s only a third of the number of meals you’re meant to have,” Kanji said. “My exam
scores were better than that.”
“Is this seriously what you wanted to talk to me about?” Goro demanded. “My eating
habits?”
“No, I wanted to talk to you so that you wouldn’t be afraid of me, dammit!”
Kanji snapped topsicle stick in his fit of emotion. Goro had an iron grip on his, but he wasn’t

“You think I’m afraid of you?”
“There’s no need to be nice about it. You said it yourself,” Kanji said. “We’re not friends.
And I know you’ve been avoiding me.”
Goro swallowed. “Kanji. What I said, I didn’t really mean it–”
“No, you did.” Kanji smiled. “It’s okay. I get it. I mean, we haven’t really known each other
for that long, and I’m just some loser punk that beats up biker gangs in my free time.”
“That’s not true,” Goro said.
“Then why the hell have you been avoiding me?” Kanji scowled. “Look, you don’t need to

“I’m not scared of you!” Goro snapped. “I’m many things, but afraid of you is not one of
them.”

Kanji snorted derisively. “Right.”
“You’re right,” Goro said. He couldn’t have Kanji thinking he was just like all the other

“So you were afraid of me–”
“Of your reaction!” Goro jumped to his feet. “Most people don’t forgive after being insulted

“Why would I be angry?” Kanji asked.
“There is a giant bruise on your face because of me!”
“Yeah, because you were trying to protect me from my mom, apparently!” Kanji jumped to

Goro didn’t know what to say. He stared stubbornly at the fraying ends of Kanji’s shoelaces.
“Look, Goro… my ma’s a really good person,” Kanji said. “She goes to the hospital for other
people’s children. She’s not like some other assholes out there.”
