“I don’t know if my parents would be willing to drive me up there,” Akira said. “They’re still
really busy.”
“Well, I’d be willing to pay for the campground, but I’m afraid that I don’t have a means of
transportation either.” Goro injected fake disappointment in his voice. “I suppose the idea
was silly.”
“I can ask my uncle,” Akira offered. “He might be willing to drive us up there. But are you
sure about paying? That’s probably not cheap.”
“I can afford it,” Goro assured him. “And don’t feel obligated to call your uncle if you’re not
comfortable.”
“No, no, I want to,” Akira said. There was a small pause. “Camping sounds fun.”
“I’m glad you think so,” Goro said. It was hard to be genuine over the phone, especially
when the whole purpose of the call had a manipulative nature. “Tell me what your uncle says,
and then I can rent a spot.”
“Right.”
Goro hung up. While he was calling about vacation plans, he’d best try to find someone who
could drive the team to the beach. Someone who wouldn’t drive into Inaba in a limousine.
He called Junpei.
“Hey, Goro-kun!” Junpei said cheerfully. “What’s up?”
“Nothing much,” Goro said flippantly. “I’m just trying to track down a serial killer. How has
your baseball team been?”
“Man, you really have a way of bringing down the mood,” Junpei said. “But I’ve been doing
alright. We won our most recent game, you know. I’m really proud of them.”
“You’re a good teammate,” Goro said.
“Ha. That actually means a lot, coming from you. But something tells me that this isn’t just a
social call.”
“You would be right,” Goro admitted. “My team wants to go to the beach, but none of us
have a driver’s license.”
“Are my ears deceiving me? Are you inviting me to the beach?”
“I doubt it will be as nice as Yakushima.”
“Who cares, man? The beach is the beach.”
“You have to be willing to drive eight children,” Goro said. “Do you even have a vehicle with
that much seating?”

“I drive my team around in my van all the time,” Junpei said. “You guys will be nothing.”
Goro let out a small breath of relief. “Thank you, Junpei. You’re a life saver.”
“My favorite thing to be,” Junpei said. “Actually, while we’re on the topic of saving your life,
prepare yourself for a surprise visit from Ryoji and Minato sometime this month.”
“What, do they intend to kill me?”
“With kindness, maybe,” Junpei said. “I know how you don’t like being caught off guard,
though, so now you know.” He put on an excessively spooky voice. “Prepare yourself~”
“Hilarious,” Goro said.

“You’re visiting Goro-kun?” Ken asked in alarm.
Summer vacation was full of opportunities to visit old friends. Ryoji and Minato had agreed
to meet him at Wild Duck Burger, which Ken refused to admit was still one of his favorite
restaurants in Iwatodai.
“It’s a surprise,” Ryoji said. His face screwed up in concentration as he tried to fold his
napkin. “Don’t tell him.”
“So he didn’t invite you?”
“Does Goro really strike you as the kind of person to invite us places?” Minato asked. He
took a large bite out of his burger. “He’s so closed off that he barely texts to remind us he’s
alive.”
“That’s because you never initiate the texts,” Ryoji said. “I always text first, so my
correspondence with him is very good. And Fuuka said that she delivered my good luck
charm.”
Goro and Ken texted each other almost every other day, but Ken wasn’t sure that’d be
appropriate to tell Minato and Ryoji. It might come off as bragging. Which sucked, because
Ken was ready to complain about how little he heard from Goro. A few texts a day and the
occasional phone call was nothing compared to how much time they used to spend together.
“Do you think he’s actually doing okay there?” Ken asked. “Maybe he’s miserable, and he
doesn’t want to tell us. Or maybe there’s another group like Strega that’s threatening him,
or… I don’t know.”
“You could ask him,” Minato said. “He trusts you.”
“Are you kidding?” Ken asked. Goro was one of his best friends, of course, but that didn’t
mean that Goro was going to tell him all his secrets. As a matter of fact, Goro was one of
those types who kept his secrets closer to his chest around the people he cared about. “If he
thought it would put me in danger, he would die before telling me.”

“That’s actually a fair point,” Ryoji said, crumpling up his half-folded napkin and tossing it
onto his plate.
Ken stared at his half-eaten burger. He wasn’t hungry anymore. “Do you think we could
convince him to come back?”
Minato swallowed the last bite of his burger. “Come back?”
“To Iwatodai,” Ken said. “To the Shadow Operatives. We have our fair share of danger, so
it’s not like he can say he wants an adventure. And he has friends here. And it’s safer.”
“He has friends in Inaba too,” Minato said.
“Does that mean he has to forget all about us?”
“Have you forgotten about Goro because he’s away?” Ryoji asked.
“Well, no,” Ken said.
“Then, I doubt he’s forgotten about you.”
"But he’s busy solving murders in this town miles away, and I’m just doing school and
occasionally helping you guys out on missions.” Ken took a sip of his soda glumly. “And his
long-lost future friend is there, so… oh, forget it.”
“Maybe you should talk to him about this,” Minato said.
“He already said he didn’t intend on replacing me,” Ken said. “But I already feel more distant
from him than ever.”
“Sometimes friends grow apart,” Ryoji said. “But that doesn’t mean the bond you had isn’t
still there.”
No offense, but was Ryoji really the authority on this? He literally lived inside of Minato for
ten years, and now he lived with Minato in real life. When had Ryoji grown apart from
anyone?
“Doesn’t it?” Ken asked. “I mean, we need him here. Shinjiro is… is really sick. And he’s not
here to be with him.”
“People are dying in Inaba,” Minato said quietly. “Goro had to make a choice.”
“Well, maybe he made the wrong decision!” Ken slammed his hands against the table and
swallowed back the urge to scream in frustration.
“Then how about this?” Ryoji offered. “You can come with us on our surprise visit. You’ll be
our surprise guest in our surprise visit. And then you can air out your grievances.”
“This is a lot of surprise,” Minato said, glancing at Ryoji uneasily.

Well… it didn’t necessarily sound like a bad idea. Except for maybe the surprise within a
surprise part.
“What if Goro’s in the middle of something?” Ken asked. “I don’t want him to be
uncomfortable.”
“It’ll be fine,” Ryoji said cheerfully.
“Don’t worry,” Minato whispered later as they walked some of the way back home together.
“Junpei told me he already warned Goro. So now you’re just a surprise guest.”
Some of the anxiety within Ken loosened. He didn’t want Goro to be annoyed with him on
top of being more distant with him. “Great.”

While the team took a brief break from forcing their way through the final levels of Kubo’s
dungeon, Goro stepped inside the Velvet Room to see if he had any chance of fusing better
personas. He could at least give some skill cards to Marie and improve his persona’s abilities.
Unfortunately, Marie didn’t seem to be inside the Velvet Room when he entered. Margaret
and Igor smiled perfectly passively, but Theodore glanced at the ground with his famous
anxious expression.
Goro followed Theodore’s line of vision and spotted a small, folded piece of paper sitting on
the ground. Goro picked it up and unfolded it. The handwriting wasn’t anyone he recognized.
The contents of the paper itself was a short poem about the speaker being metaphorically
killed by someone they cared about. Goro stared at it in blank confusion before looking up at
the others.
“Is this yours?” Goro asked Theodore.
“Oh, no,” Theodore said. “I believe it’s Marie-chan’s. She doesn’t like anyone looking at her
work, so I didn’t want to pick it up in case I accidentally caught a glimpse.”
“If she’s so protective over her work–”
“Give that to me!” Marie appeared from behind him and yanked the piece of paper from
Goro’s grasp. Her face was bright red. “Where did you get that?”
“I found it on the floor,” Goro said. “You should really take better care of your stuff.”
“But I put it away!” Marie looked like she was on the verge of tears, but her face hardened
into anger. “Don’t you ever read my poems again.”
“I won’t,” Goro said. “I didn’t realize it was yours.”
“Oh. Good.” She put the piece of paper into her pocket. Goro hadn’t even realized there were
pockets in her skirt. “And tell Yu-kun to stop picking up pieces of paper he sees lying on the
ground! It’s invasive!”

“I’ll be sure to tell him that,” Goro said. “Do your poems often find themselves sprawled on
the ground?”
“I don’t want to talk about it.”
Marie sat down next to Theodore, crossing her arms with a huff. Theodore looked extremely
flustered by Marie’s irritated attitude. Margaret wore a knowing smile. Goro wondered if she
had anything to do with this. If she was, what the hell was she trying to accomplish?
Goro requested Marie help him with a few skill cards and left swiftly thereafter. Goro
wouldn’t have been able to cut through the tension in that car with a meat cleaver.

When they finally reached the final floor of Kubo’s dungeon, neither the shadow nor Kubo
seemed to notice them.
Kubo’s shadow stared blankly in the void, saying nothing at all. Kubo, on the other hand, was
shouting at his shadow.
“Everybody gets on my nerves!” He slashed his hand through the air. “That’s why I did it!
What do you think of that? Say something dammit!”
The shadow said nothing. It stared blankly ahead at the rest of the group. Kubo continued to
ignore them.
“Nobody even thought of me after the first two people! That’s why I killed the third one! I
killed them!”
“You bastard!” Kanji shouted. “You killed people just for attention?”
Kubo finally turned toward them. “And so what if I did? I hate everyone. They should all just
disappear!”
The shadow still wasn’t saying anything. Chie turned toward Yu with a fully dismayed
expression. “Which one is even the shadow?”
“The one with the yellow eyes, duh,” Yosuke said. “But why isn’t it saying anything?”
“I feel nothing,” the shadow said. Kubo turned back toward the shadow with a confused
expression.
“What are you talking about?” Kubo demanded.
“I have nothing,” the shadow continued. “I am nothing. And you are me.”
“That’s not true!” Kubo shouted. “I’m not nothing!”
“If this keeps up…” Yukiko said. “Please, don’t argue with it!”

Kubo turned back toward them. His expression was a mixture of confusion and rage. “Who
even are you guys? How did you get here?”
“You’re asking this now?” Yosuke asked. “We’ve been here for at least five minutes!”
“We came after you!” Kanji shouted.
“Are you the one who killed those people? Who kidnapped us?” Rise asked.
Kubo began to laugh. “That’s right! I killed those people! I kidnapped whoever got in my
way! I’m the one responsible!”
“Actually, we wanted to hear it from your shadow,” Goro said.
The shadow stared blankly at him. “I–”
“Why should you give a damn what this thing says?” Kubo interrupted. “It’s just some
freakish imposter! It’s got nothing to do with me!”
“Just great,” Chie muttered.
“So, you don’t accept me,” the shadow said.
“What–” Kubo passed out. The shadow turned into a floating baby, which constructed a
pixelated shell of a video game hero around itself.
The battle was hellish. The shadow kept reconstructing its outershell, making it extremely
difficult to actually do any damage.
Something the shadow said stuck with Goro, though.
“I need proof that I exist! That’s why… I have to kill you!”
Not only did it prove that Kubo definitely had murderous intent within him, but it gave Goro
very clear image to his motive. Proof of existence.
Is this what he sounded like to Akira? A child desperate to sound like he was in control? A
rampaging killer who only wanted attention?
Goro couldn’t worry about it now. He wasn’t that person anymore, and he needed to stay
focused on helping the others.
When they finally cut down the shadow’s extreme form, it melted back into its mirror image
of Kubo. The real Kubo woke up and got back to his feet.
“Ugh,” he said. “Who the hell even are you guys?”
“We came to talk to you,” Yu said.
“No,” Goro snapped. “We came to talk to your shadow.”

“What if we just asked both of them?” Yosuke said. “The police think you’re responsible for
all of the murders. So? Did you kill Yamano and Konishi-senpai? And Morooka too?”
“I need… to exist,” the shadow said.
Kubo laughed. “That’s right! I killed them!”
“You piece of shit!” Kanji snarled.
As Kubo continued to boast of his killings, his shadow disappeared into a puff of red and
black smoke. Goro stared at the now empty space in confusion. Had Kubo subconsciously
accepted his shadow? Did that make what Kubo was saying true?
“W-where’d it go?” Rise asked.
“It’s gone,” Kubo said, still laughing. “That monster is gone. Take– take that.”
And then Kubo passed out on the dirt ground.

They dragged him out of the TV world and handed him over to the cops. Even when they had
tried to question him in Junes, Kubo gave them next to no additional information. He only
continued to insist that he was the one who killed all three victims.
Goro noted that he was extremely confused when they pulled him out of the television. He
showed no indication he understood that people could enter and exit televisions, even though
that was theoretically his primary murder method.
As the police took Kubo away, Yosuke went up to Goro.
“Do you think that he killed them?” Yosuke asked. “I mean, there’s plenty of evidence
pointing him to Morooka, but do you think he killed Konishi-senpai?”
“What do you think?” Goro asked.
“I don’t know,” Yosuke admitted. “I really don’t want him to have been the one who killed
them. To think that Konishi-senpai would have died to such a bastard… just for attention. It
makes me so angry.”
Just for attention.
Pitiful.
“If it’s any comfort to you,” Goro said slowly. “I really don’t find it likely. He didn’t seem to
understand the TV world in the slightest, and he clearly wanted to be acknowledged for his
crimes. Why hadn’t he come forward months ago?”
“I don’t know,” Yosuke said quietly. “Is it wrong that I don’t want him to be the killer? Is it
wrong that I want the person who killed Konishi-senpai to be…”

“Noble?” Goro couldn’t keep the bitterness out of his voice. “There’s nothing noble about
killing people. If you’re looking for some tragic hero, you’re going to be sorely
disappointed.”
“I know that.” Yosuke glared at the sky. “It’s not nobility I want. I want something more
gratifying than just some attention seeking asshole. I want her death to mean more than that.
Maybe she confronted the killer, and he decided to get rid of her. Or maybe he targeted her
because she knew something—Oh my god, what am I saying?” Yosuke put his head in his
hands and released a shaky breath.
Goro didn’t say anything. The image of his mother, Akira, Takeharu, and Chidori’s deaths
were in the forefront of his mind. Had any of their deaths really meant anything? His mother
had lost against the demons inside her head, ones spawned out of the horrors of her situation.
Akira hadn’t really died at all, but he might as well have been sacrificing himself for his
teammates. Takeharu was trying to save them all from Ikutsuki. Chidori died protecting
Junpei.
But even when they sacrificed their lives for others, it wasn’t their deaths that had meant
anything at all. It was how they chose to spend the very last moments of their lives that really
mattered. They sacrificed their lives. Not their deaths.
Had Goro used the last moments of his first life well? Was he sacrificing himself for the
whole? Or was he like his mother, unable to fight the urge to run away, unable to win against
his own ugly thoughts?
It was the latter. He had wasted his life up until the very end. He wanted his death to at least
make it look like he had tried to choose good, rather than face the consequences of his
actions.
“Yosuke-kun,” Goro said. “Death is never anything but a tragedy. It doesn’t matter why
someone killed someone. Or how that person died. It’s never noble, or beautiful, or filled
with any meaning. It’s vile, and sickening, and rips out a part of you that is never going to
come back.”
Yosuke’s eyes widened. He looked at Goro with a silent sort of grief.
“This killer you’re trying to find… you’re never going to find him,” Goro said. “He could tell
you that he killed Konishi because he wanted to save the world, and you’re not going to be
satisfied. It’s never going to make it okay. Your anger isn’t going to fade.”
“You’re probably right,” Yosuke said. His voice cracked. “But if that’s true, what am I meant
to do? How am I meant to get past this?”
Goro laughed bitterly. “You’re asking the wrong person for that.”
“But you know, right?” Yosuke looked at Goro pleadingly. “I don’t know everything you’ve
been through, but you’ve experienced loss. And you’re still here. You smile, and you spend
time with us. How do you do it?”

“You make it sound like you spend every second of the day moping,” Goro said. “You’re one
of the most lighthearted people in the entire group.”
“Well, I thought maybe pretending I was okay would make it true,” Yosuke said. “But seeing
Kubo brag about the death. I… I don’t think I can keep this up.”
“Then don’t,” Goro said bluntly. “Someone died, Yosuke. Nobody is asking you to pretend to
be okay.”
“Maybe you’re not,” Yosuke said.
“If anyone here begrudges you for being upset, then they’re not worth your time,” Goro
snapped. “Do you think grief is this easy process you just cruise through in a month and then
never think about again? I still think about my mother, and she’s been dead for years. The
pain never goes away. It’s just a question of dealing with it.”
“That’s comforting.”
“It’s up to you to choose how you handle your loss,” Goro said. “Just try not to make the
same mistakes I have.”
“Right.” Yosuke nodded, and his face hardened to resolve. “We just want to stop the killer
from hurting anybody else. I can’t get distracted by revenge.”
“Hey, Yosuke!” Yu called from a distance. He raised his eyebrows at the two of them. “Are
you okay?”
Yosuke grinned and winked. “Yeah, I’m fine. No need to worry about us.” He turned toward
Goro. “Let’s keep this conversation between us, yeah? I don’t want to worry Yu-kun.”
“I don’t think Yu would mind,” Goro said.
“He’s got enough on his plate,” Yosuke insisted. “Promise me.”
Goro couldn’t argue with that. “Fine. I won’t tell him.”
“Thanks.” Yosuke’s grin looked a little more genuine. “I really appreciate it.”

They decided to celebrate turning Kubo into the police.
“He might not have been the original culprit, but he is a killer,” Yukiko said where they were
gathered in the Junes electronics section. “I think we should be able to celebrate that there’s
one less killer walking free.”
Somehow, the agreement to cook dinner turned into a cooking competition in which Nanako
would be the judge. Goro wasn’t sure if they were wise to be putting Nanako’s tastebuds at
risk in such a way.
“So we have Yu, Yukiko, Chie, and Rise competing,” Kanji said, writing the names down in a
small notebook as they walked to the produce section. “Maybe we should have different
categories of judging, and one of them can be Nanako’s preference.”
“Are you kidding?” Chie asked. “What other category is there besides taste?”
“There’s presentation,” Teddie said. “That’s why I always take an hour each day to style my
hair.”
“Yeah, and you use all of the hair gel in the entire house,” Yosuke said. “I’m not paying for
your hair exploits anymore.”
Teddie looked up at Yu pleadingly. “Sensei, Yosuke-kun’s bullying me.”
“I’m staying out of this,” Yu said. “Don’t worry, Kanji. Nanako’s opinion is all I need to win
this.”

“Relying on nepotism for victory?” Goro asked. “I thought better of you.”
“That’s a good point,” Rise said. “Senpai can’t compete if his little sister is the judge! That’s
not fair at all!” A teasing smile crawled across her face. “I’ll be the judge, and then Senpai
will cook just for me.”
“You’re competing too, genius,” Kanji said. “You can’t judge your own cooking.”
“Oh, right,” Rise said. “Well, what are we meant to do, then?”
“I guess Yu’s out of the race,” Yosuke said. “But also, I don’t know if I trust you three to
cook something more than edible.”
“Akechi-kun’s a pretty good cook,” Chie said. “Why doesn’t he compete?”
“I think you all severely overestimate my cooking skills.”
“I think you’re severely overestimating their cooking skills,” Yosuke said. “Sure, their curry
was fine, but it was a few steps away from being completely tasteless. And that was with Yu
helping them.”
“You are so mean,” Chie snapped. “Fine. I want Akechi-kun on my team if he’s not going to
cook for himself.”
“We’re doing teams now?” Yu asked.
“That’s cheating!” Rise protested.
They finally agreed that Goro, Rise, Yukiko, and Chie would compete. Yu would serve as the
taste tester to make sure that Nanako wouldn’t die a painful death from food poisoning. If Yu
survived, Nanako could taste the food.
Upon Yu calling her, Nanako requested an omelet for dinner. As the others grabbed
ingredients, Goro had a bout of self-doubt and called Shinjiro.
“Shinjiro, I’m having a cooking competition with my teammates, and I need a reminder on
omelet making techniques.”
“I just had so many issues with that sentence,” Shinjiro said. “Would it kill you to call your
teammates friends? You literally made a birthday cake for one of them a month ago.”
“This isn’t about that,” Goro snapped. “Will you or will you not help me with this omelet?”
“I don’t know,” Shinjiro said. “That sounds like cheating to me. And if you don’t know how
to cook your own omelet, then you’re truly lost. Figure it out yourself.”
“One of the contestants is literally trying to bribe our leader into helping her,” Goro said,
glancing at Rise promising Yu a million different kinds of autographs. Yu’s expression was
completely unmoved.

“And is he caving?”
“Well, no.”
“Then, I don’t think that I should either. Have fun.”
Shinjiro hung up. Furious at how unhelpful Shinjiro could be, Goro texted Ken.
Akechi Goro: whats your favorite type of omelet
Amada Ken: Ketchup
Akechi Goro: im not doing that you heathen
Amada Ken: Emiko says soy sauce and rice in case u were wondering
Amada Ken: r u making us breakfast
Akechi Goro: come to inaba and then well talk
Amada Ken: noted
Well, just because Goro knew what to make, it didn’t mean he knew exactly how to make it.
Goro took a deep breath and closed his eyes. Shinjiro was right, though. Omelets were easy.
He didn’t need help to create a simple omelet.

The team crowded around Yu’s kitchen, practically elbowing each other to make space to
prepare their omelets. Why did they decide to have four people cook simultaneously in the
same small kitchen? The only blessing was that Dojima wasn’t there to lecture them on the
mess.
When they were done, the team gathered around the small table in Yu’s living room. Nanako
looked slightly overwhelmed to see so many people in her house at the same time, staring at
the four omelet dishes with wide eyes.
“Well, they all kind of look like omelets,” Yosuke said reluctantly.
“Why is one of them red?” Kanji asked.
“That one’s mine,” Rise said proudly. Goro wasn’t sure she should be proud of having a
bright red omelet. “You should try it first, Senpai.”
Yu gulped. Goro could hear him whisper, “This is for Nanako,” underneath his breath as he
took a bite of the mystery omelet.
Almost immediately, Yu’s face contorted. He lurched forward and seized Kanji’s glass of
water. Kanji cried out in alarm as Yu gulped down the entire drink.
“You just stole my water!” Kanji exclaimed.

Yu wiped his mouth with his sleeve and grimaced. “You can have mine,” he said. “Sorry. And
we can’t give this to Nanako.”
“It’s just so good that you have to keep it all to yourself?” Rise asked hopefully.
“It’s so spicy that I think my mouth is bleeding,” Yu said.
“I bet you wish you hadn’t gloated so much before, huh?” Chie asked. “Here, Yu, you can try
mine as a palate cleanser.”
Yu clearly regretted ever being Nanako’s taste tester. He took a bite of Chie’s omelet with a
look of pure resignation. His face twisted in disgust.
“Oh, this is awful.”
“Really? Can I try?” Teddie leaned across the table and took a bite of his own. His eyes
widened. “He’s right. It really is awful! You should try it too, Yosuke.”
“I think I’ll just trust you guys,” Yosuke said. “It was a good try, Chie.”
“Oh, I’d like to have seen you do better!” Chie snapped. “Why don’t you compete? Is it
because you know you’d do worse?”
“Um, it’s because I can admit that I don’t know how to cook,” Yosuke said. “I don’t really
think that’s the same thing.”
“He has a point, Chie,” Yukiko said.
“Aren’t you meant to be on my side?”
Before anyone could tell her not to, Nanako ate a piece of Chie’s omelet. She put on the
fakest smile Goro had ever seen on her.
“It tastes good,” she said.
“Thank you, Nanako-chan!” Chie said. “I knew someone would see things my way.”
“You don’t have to lie, Nanako-chan,” Kanji said. “Nobody will be angry.”
Nanako just continued to smile as she swallowed Chie’s food. She didn’t come in for another
bite.
“Let’s just get Yukiko’s over with,” Yu said.
“How do you know mine’s going to be bad?” Yukiko demanded. “Maybe Goro’s is going to
be completely inedible.”
“I watched him cook,” Yu said. “He was the most intentional out of all of you.”
“Maybe we should have let Nanako compete,” Goro said. “Didn’t she say she knew how to
make an omelet?”

“Yeah, but then we would have had a clear winner,” Kanji said. “Where’s the fun in that?”
Nanako giggled.
Yukiko’s omelet was completely tasteless. Nanako insisted upon trying it too, and she once
again said that it tasted good. Not even Yukiko believed her, although she was obviously
touched by the gesture.
When it came to Goro’s omelet, Yu’s expression of pure relief when he ate his preliminary
bite was enough indication to know that it wasn’t awful, at least.
“That’s actually pretty good,” Yu said. “You have my blessing to eat this one, Nanako-chan.”
“Yay!” Nanako then proceeded to eat the entire omelet. When she was done, she looked up at
Goro and said, “That was really good!”
“Clearly,” Yosuke said.
“Don’t worry, Big Bro,” Nanako said. “You make them better. Akechi-san gets second
place.”
“What?!” Chie exclaimed, “But he wasn’t even competing!”
“In a shocking twist, Nana-chan choses Sensei to be our winner!” Teddie said in a faux
announcer voice. “But perhaps we should have seen this coming all along!”
“Well congratulations, Senpai,” Rise said. “I guess your prize was being able to eat
something. I’m still starving.”
They ended up ordering a pizza for dinner instead.

Late that night, when Goro was back in the silence of his room with nothing but his thoughts,
he sat up from his futon and grabbed his phone.
He couldn’t stop thinking about what Kubo’s shadow had said. What Yosuke had said.
“I need to prove I exist!”
“…Just for attention. It makes me so angry.”
Goro began to slowly input numbers, his hand shaking with each new button press.
“All this is to make Shido Masayoshi, my father, acknowledge me.”
Goro might have ripped up Tsuyoshi’s piece of paper, but he didn’t need that to know Shido’s
phone number. He’d had it memorized for years; Tsuyoshi’s gift only served to jog his
memory.

Goro pulled his knees to his chest and stared at the completed phone number. His thumb

But what would he even say?
“I hate you and hope you die one day?”
“I know that murder isn’t the answer anymore, so I’m calling you to make you aware of my

What would it even accomplish? Shido barely knew Goro existed. That was a good thing.
Goro didn’t want Shido to notice him, didn’t want to make the same mistakes as last time.
Didn’t want to become the sort of person Yosuke hated. Not again.
So why was he awake, holding his phone, thinking about the man that he never wanted to

Because some teenager reminded him of himself?
Because deep down… had Goro ever changed at all? Or was he the same as he always was,
desperate to be seen, desperate to be known by a person who could never, would never love

Goro took a deep breath.
And deleted the phone number.

“Don’t tell me you’re making food in the middle of the night,” he said.

“Pot, meet kettle.” Shinjiro’s voice softened. “What’s up?”
“I…” Goro rested his forehead against his knees and tried to find his voice. “I was just bored.
That’s all.”
A snort. “Right.”
“Shinjiro?” Goro said abruptly, his voice cracking embarrassingly.
“Yeah?”

Oh.

Goro cared about Shinjiro too much to not be by his side in his final moments. It would be

“Oh, thanks.” Kanji looked surprised, even though he had shown some of his crochet animals

“That’s not what I meant.” Kanji pulled a protein bar from the pantry and ripped off the

“I go on runs,” Goro said.

“Well, that’s something,” Kanji said. “But what do you do when you’re not running, or

“I can’t just have one hobby?” Goro asked.
“You can do what you want,” Kanji said. “But I get this impression that you’re bored

“I’m pretty sure I’ve revolved multiple years of my life around those two things,” Goro said.
“Well, no more,” Kanji said. He bit into his protein bar and pointed it at Goro. “You and me

Conveniently enough, Tsuyoshi agreed to take Goro and Akira to the mountains. Goro
carefully placed one of Fuuka’s trackers inside his pocket before he stepped outside and stood
by the gas station at the shopping district where Akira said Tsuyoshi would pick him up.
Goro didn’t have any difficulties spotting Tsuyoshi’s car amidst the mostly empty streets of
Inaba. It pulled to a halt in front of Goro, and Goro slipped inside the empty back seat.
“Thank you for driving us, Tsuyoshi-san,” Goro said cheerfully.
“It’s no issue,” Tsuyoshi said. “I was just on my way somewhere near the mountains anyway.
Stick your bags in the trunk, and we’ll be on our way.”
Goro heaved his bag behind him and dropped it in the trunk. As he put his seatbelt on, he
pulled the tracker out of his pocket as discreetly as possible and dropped it between the two
seats.
Tsuyoshi already had his eyes on the road as he drove out of Inaba. Goro caught sight of his
face in the rear-view mirror. He seemed none the wiser of Goro’s actions, but that didn’t
really mean anything.
“So, Goro-kun,” Tsuyoshi said. “Have you been camping before?”
“I haven’t, actually,” Goro admitted. “I thought it would be fun to do with a friend.”
“I haven’t either,” Akria said.
“Well, Akira-kun insisted you two didn’t need a chaperone, and somehow, his parents
agreed,” Tsuyoshi said. “Try not to burn the forest down.”

“I can’t make any promises for Akechi-kun,” Akira said, wearing a shit-eating grin. Goro
glowered to hide the urge to smile.
“What would I have to gain from burning down the forest?”
“I don’t know,” Akira said. “You just seem like the type.”
“I think you’d be more likely to accidentally burn down the forest than I would be.”
“You two are not increasing my confidence about this situation,” Tsuyoshi said.
Tsuyoshi shouldn’t be there. Goro and Akira were trying to bond, and Tsuyoshi’s presence
was as impossible to ignore as a gun to Goro’s skull. It was uncanny to have Tsuyoshi behave
as the normal uncle when Goro knew he was anything but.
“We’ll be fine,” Akira said.
Goro and Akira talked about more mundane topics for the rest of the drive. Akira talked more
about his parents and their increased presence in the house. Goro mentioned learning to
crochet. Akira must have noticed how uneasy Goro was, because their conversation didn’t
diverge much at all. It was as though they were both reading from a script.
Tsuyoshi finally pulled up at the camp site. Goro fled the vehicle and grabbed his things.
Akira came out soon behind him.
“Stay safe kids,” Tsuyoshi said, smiling jovially. It was nothing like the sinister grin Goro
was used to seeing on his face. “I’ll be back to pick you up tomorrow.”
“Bye,” Akira said.
“Thank you again for driving us,” Goro said, forcing himself to bow. He didn’t want Akira to
realize that anything was wrong prematurely. With any luck, Akira wouldn’t have to be
mixed up in the metaverse until Mementos came into play.
Tsuyoshi drove away. Goro and Akira began to hike to their camp site.
“Did your parents really agree to let us camp on our own?” Goro asked. “That seems…
bold.”
“I lied,” Akira admitted. “I said I was going to study with the smartest kid in the middle
school.”
Mitsuru knew that Goro could take care of himself, so she allowed Goro to go camping as
long as Akira was going to be with him. The murderer wasn’t likely to be hiding in the
mountains. On a slightly more practical note, there were no TVs to be thrown into while

Goro began to click the sections of the pole together. That much, at least, he could remember

Had being sent to Tokyo really been the best thing that had ever happened to Akira? The

Goro had known they were alike, but Goro wasn’t sure he had realized just how similar they

It had helped mitigate the horror of putting a bullet between his eyes.

“I suppose you do,” Goro said. Junpei would have agreed wholeheartedly. “Do you know

Akira wasn’t wrong. A strange tremor coursed through Goro’s body. His younger shadow’s

I’m so scared I can’t even breathe.

Chapter Summary

The chapter that is literally nothing but summer shenanigans
Welcome to persona 4

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for more notes

After work, Teddie insisted that Goro go back to Yosuke’s house with them.
“Teddie, I’m sure Akechi-kun wants to go home,” Yosuke said as Goro handed him his
apron. “It’s already pretty late.”
Teddie stomped his foot petulantly. “Goro-kun promised to teach me to ride a bike, and the
summer is already half-way gone!” Teddie protested. “Now is the perfect time to trap him
into teaching me.”
“It’s not a very subtle trap if you’re going to proclaim your motives to the entire store,” Goro
said.
“Seriously, Ted,” Yosuke agreed. “Can’t it wait until Saturday?”
Teddie shook his head. “I checked the calendar,” he said. “It’s the summer festival on
Saturday. And I can’t wait any longer. There’s a perfectly good bicycle gathering up dents
and scratches from its lack of use.”
“Actually, those dents and scratches are from me.” Yosuke grimaced. “Don’t try to bike while
holding an umbrella. Or schoolbooks.”
“Maybe you just don’t know how to bike,” Goro said, although Goro wasn’t sure he would be
able to successfully bike one-handed.
“That’s why you can’t teach me, Yosuke,” Teddie said firmly. “Goro-kun is the only man for
the job.”

It was obvious Teddie was not going to be swayed. Goro wasn’t in the mood to argue any
further.
“Fine,” Goro sighed. “I fell asleep early yesterday anyway.”
“Hooray!” Teddie cheered.
“You seriously don’t have to if you don’t want to,” Yosuke said. “Don’t let this guy make all
the calls.”
“I appreciate the sentiment, but I did promise,” Goro said. “Let’s hope this doesn’t end in
disaster.”
Since it was the middle of the summer, the sun still hadn’t completely set by the time they
came to Yosuke’s house. Yosuke glanced at his watch.
“My parents should be back within the hour,” he said. “They’re still seeing to some things at
the store. Fair warning, they might invite you to dinner.”
“I’ll try not to impose,” Goro said. “Now where is this bike that I’ve heard so much about?”
Teddie changed out of his bear costume and dragged the bike out of the garage. Goro
couldn’t blame him for assuming that dents and scratches came from disuse. The bike looked
like Yosuke had pulled it from a dump and then let it sit in the corner of his garage for years.
Half of the yellow paint was chipped off, and cobwebs were gathered in between the spokes.
“Wait, let’s pump up the tires,” Yosuke said. “They’re probably really flat.”
Goro was almost certain Yosuke knew more about riding bikes than Goro did. Goro had
learned to ride at some point in his childhood, but he had no memory of when. He likely
taught himself when nobody else was around to tell him not to.
Goro would try his best to teach without accidentally killing Teddie in the process.
“What do I do first?” Teddie asked, holding the handlebars with both hands.
Goro cleared his throat. “Well, first, you get on the bike.”
Teddie nodded and swung his leg over the seat. The seat wasn’t quite adjusted for his height,
and the very tips of Teddie’s shoes were the only thing supporting his balance by the time he
was properly seated.
“Learning to ride a bike is all about knowing where your center of gravity is,” Goro said. “I
want you to take your feet off the ground and try your hardest to keep the bike standing
straight.”
Teddie nodded and lifted his feet. The bike wobbled violently underneath him, and Teddie
crashed to the ground.

Yosuke yelped. Goro flinched. Teddie jumped to his feet and beamed. “I think that was at
least five seconds!”
They tried again. Teddie kept his balance no better than before.
“Maybe start pedaling,” Goro said. “The bike isn’t really meant to stand on its own.”
Teddie clearly didn’t know what Goro meant, because he only lifted his feet off the ground,
kicked the pedals, and fell over yet again.
“It’s all part of the learning process!” Teddie said, untangling his shirt from a stray spoke.
“R-right,” Yosuke said. “Um, Akechi-kun and I need to have a quick strategy meeting.”
Teddie gave them a thumbs up as he wobbled back and forth on the bike. Yosuke dragged
Goro a few yards away from Teddie.
“Um, Akechi-kun,” Yosuke said. “I know you were the one burdened with the responsibility
of teaching Teddie, but can I give you some advice?”
“Gladly.”
“I think, typically, when you teach someone to ride a bike, you hold onto the back of their
seat at first,” Yosuke said. “That way they can simulate the feeling of balance without
actually having to… balance.”
“Oh.” Goro tried not to look too surprised. Come to think of it, he had seen that sort of thing
on television before. He just hadn’t given it much thought. “Alright, we’ll try that.”
“Then, when Ted’s not expecting it, you need to let go of the bike,” Yosuke said, grinning.
“We’ll see how long it takes for him to crash.”
It was weird to stand behind a bike and hold onto the seat. Teddie wasn’t bothered by it, and
Goro at least managed to prevent Teddie from toppling over.
“Teddie, you need to put your feet on the pedals and start pushing,” Goro said. “I’ll stay
behind you.”
“It’s time for take-off!” Teddie began pushing the pedals, inevitably moving the bike forward.
Goro began to jog behind him. “Look Yosuke! I’m biking!”
“You’re doing a great job.” Yosuke gave Teddie a thumbs up. Out of the corner of his eye,
Goro could see Yosuke mouth, “Let go.”
Goro let go and stopped running. Teddie continued to bike.
“Um, Goro-kun?” Teddie asked. “How do I steer?”
Goro had forgotten about steering. From the looks of his horrified expression, Yosuke did
too.

“Just move the handles!” Goro shouted.
Teddie looked over his shoulder. His mouth formed a small ‘o’ of surprise when he saw Goro
wasn’t right behind him. The bike swayed off course, and Teddie tumbled into the grass.
Yosuke looked about ready to laugh, but he jogged up to Teddie.
“You good?”
Still lying on the ground with the bike on top of him, Teddie took deep gasping breaths and
stared up at them with shining eyes. “I did it,” he said. “I biked.”
“Yeah,” Yosuke said. “And then you crashed. Maybe that can be a family tradition, actually.”
Teddie shook his head. “I’ve done enough biking today,” he decided. He pushed the bike off
him and stood up. “You know what has never done me wrong?”
“What has never done you wrong?” Goro asked.
“Roller-skates.” Teddie ran back into the garage and returned with a pair of roller-skates in
his hands. “Yosuke got them for my re-birthday! I’m a master on these babies.”
“Are you now?” Yosuke asked.
Teddie stuck his tongue out at Yosuke as he took off his shoes. He shoved on his rollerskates, haphazardly tied the laces, and stood back up.
“The roller-skates bow to my control,” Teddie said. “I am the king of roller-skates.”
Everything coming out of Teddie’s mouth was pure absurdity.
“Alright, then, your majesty,” Goro said, raising his eyebrows. “Prove it.”
“I will.” Teddie pushed off and began rolling forward at an impressive speed. He continued to
roll until he collapsed face first into the grass with a small ‘umph’.
Yosuke burst out laughing. Goro failed to hold back a snort.
Teddie immediately leapt to his feet, fortunately able to keep his balance in the grass. “Was
that a laugh I heard?”
“I’m not apologizing,” Yosuke said, swiping a few stray tears from his eyes and clutching his
stomach. “That was the best thing I’ve seen all week.”
“Not from you,” Teddie said. “Goro-kun laughed! I thought you hated jokes!”
“What are you talking about?” Goro said. “I don’t hate jokes. I hate puns. There’s a
difference.”
“Is there?” Teddie asked, crossing his arms.

“Ignore him,” Yosuke told Goro. “He’s being ridiculous.”
“What’s going on out here?” asked a deep, unfamiliar voice. Goro tensed, but Yosuke and
Teddie looked totally relaxed as they turned toward the sound.
Two individuals who must have been Yosuke’s parents walked up the driveway. Yosuke’s
father bore a remarkable resemblance to Yosuke as he raised his eyebrows at the scene before
him. “Why does it look like Teddie-kun had a fight with the bicycle and lost?”
“We tied, actually,” Teddie said. “Goro-kun was teaching me how to ride.”
“Goro-kun?” Yosuke’s mother asked. She caught Goro standing stiffly between Yosuke and
Teddie. “Oh, you must be him. It’s wonderful to make your acquaintance.”
Goro took a deep breath and bowed. “You too, Hanamura-san.”
Yosuke was right. They did invite him over for dinner.
Unlike the somewhat tense meals in the Tatsumi household, where Kanji and Goro struggled
to hold a conversation with Tatsumi-san, Yosuke and Teddie’s constant banter kept the
conversation alive. Yosuke’s parents even made jokes of their own about the hectic busyness
at Junes. Goro didn’t contribute much to the conversation, but even then, Yosuke’s parents
asked him about his studies and interests.
It was almost nice.
Aeon Arcana: Rank 3

On Saturday evening, they met at the summer festival. The boys arrived at the shrine sooner
than the girls, and they stood by the mask stand as they waited, watching the other guests mill
around the area.
“Strange,” Yosuke said. “I remember this place being more crowded last year. Is it because of
the murders?”
“Well, I guess I can’t blame people for being scared,” Kanji said. “I don’t see any reporters
around either. They sure have a knack for stirring things up and then disappearing.”
“I bet your festivals were way more crowded in the big city. Huh, Sensei?” Teddie said.
“Oh.” Yu shrugged. “This is my first time coming to one of these.”
“Wait, seriously?” Kanji asked.
“I didn’t see much point in it before,” Yu admitted. “But it looks like fun. I’m glad we
decided to go.”

“We’re going to have to hit all of the stands,” Yosuke said. “Oh! Don’t you fish on the bank?
I bet you’d be a pro at the goldfish scooping game.”
“If you want to see a goldfish, there’s one in Goro’s room,” Kanji said. “It literally only
swims and eats. If you want a real festival experience, you need to go to the ikayaki stand
pronto.”
“We can’t do both?” Yu asked.
“An intriguing counteroffer,” Yosuke said with a wink. “We’ll consider it. Either way, we
should wait for the girls before doing anything.”
“What’s taking them so long anyway?” Kanji asked.
“It’s the summer festival,” Goro said. “I hope you all can be mature about this, but they’re
probably putting on yukata.”
“Oh, that makes sense,” Kanji said with a shrug.
Teddie gasped. “I get to see three beautiful girls in yukata?” A sly smile crawled on his face.
“Perhaps today can finally be Teddie’s lucky day to score a hot stud.”
“Shame,” Goro said. “Teddie isn’t as mature as the rest of us here.”
“What?!”
“You really should stop pursuing the girls,” Kanji said. “You’re way too young for them.”
“And it’s kind of creepy,” Yu said. “That applies for someone else I know too.”
Yosuke looked away. “Sorry.”
Goro’s prediction turned out to be correct. All the girls, including Nanako, paraded into the
shrine in brightly colored yukata. Nanako held a bag of cotton candy.
“Sorry we took so long,” Yukiko said. “It took us longer than we expected to get dressed.”
“Wow, Nana-chan!” Teddie exclaimed. “You look beautiful!”
Nanako giggled. “Thank you,” she said. She looked down at her feet. “It’s kind of hard to
walk, though.”
“That’s the secret, Nanako-chan,” Rise said. “If you want to look beautiful, you have to be at
least a little bit uncomfortable.”
“But you’re always beautiful, Rise-san!” Nanako said, admiration obvious in her eyes.
Rise beamed. “Aw, that’s so nice of you to say.”
“It’s more accurate to say that dressing fancy is kind of uncomfortable at times, huh?” Chie
said.

Nanako nodded. “Mhm!”
Dojima walked up to the group, smiling wearily despite the prominent circles under his eyes.
“Hey, guys. Thanks for looking out for her.”
“Dad!” Nanako spun toward Dojima with a thrilled expression.
“You’re back sooner than I expected, Dojima-san,” Yu said.
“Yeah, well, I miraculously managed to get away from work earlier than usual,” Dojima said.
“They bought me cotton candy!” Nanako held up the cotton candy. “Do you want some?”
“Um, no thanks.” Dojima smiled. “Why don’t you and I go do the target pract– I mean game
with me?”
Nanako nodded. “Let’s go!”
Dojima took Nanako away from the main group. As they left, Nanako spoke at a mile per
minute about her time with the girls.
“She really is a sweet girl,” Yukiko said.
“Of course she is,” Yu said, sounding almost offended that there would be any doubt.
“Alright guys,” Kanji said. “It’s seriously time for us to hit the ikayaki stand. Then Yosuke
wants to show Yu the joys of trying to force a goldfish into a tiny bag.”
“You really have a way of making it sound like fun,” Yosuke said sarcastically.
“You’ve never been goldfish scooping before, Senpai?” Rise asked.
Yu shrugged. “Guess I just never had the opportunity.”
“I remember winning that game once,” Chie said. “My parents didn’t let me keep the goldfish
though.”
“My goldfish is actually from that game,” Goro said. “My friend caught it.”
Teddie gasped. “We can get a pet goldfish for free?”
“Do I really have to say it again?” Kanji said. “Ikayaki first. Goldfish later. I’m starving.”
“Actually, now that you mention it, so am I,” Rise admitted. “Alright! Food first.”
They hit various food stands and watched Yu win the goldfish scooping within thirty seconds.
It was truly a sight to behold. Yu bestowed the goldfish upon Teddie, who declared that he’d
name the fish “Goldie”.
“It’s like my name, but better,” Teddie said.

“I hope you don't expect me to feed it,” Yosuke said.
“Of course not!” Teddie hugged the goldfish bag to his chest gently. “I’ll take Goldie to the
TV world if I have to!”
As Yosuke insisted that was completely unnecessary, an unfamiliar woman walked up to
them. She held a small notebook in her hand.
“Hello there!” she said with a polite bow toward the group before immediately turning to
Rise. “Are you Kujikawa Rise, by any chance?”
Kanji had been too quick to speak when he said there were no more reporters in Inaba. Goro
should have expected this.
Rise’s smile was obviously strained as she laughed airily. “I get that a lot, but I’m just a
lookalike. Would I really be out in the open like this if I were actually an idol?”
“I guess not.” The reporter frowned, but a knowing gleam shone in her eyes. “That’s a shame.
I was hoping to get an interview with her, but I understand that she might want to be left
alone.”
“It can’t be easy being an idol,” Yosuke agreed.
“Well said!” The reporter reached behind her ear and pulled out a pen previously hiding in
her black hair. “That’s alright. Despite what my boss might say, I don’t need an interview
with an idol. And a group of teens might be better anyway.”
“Maybe you should start with introducing yourself,” Goro said, indulging in being
standoffish toward a reporter. As the Detective Prince, he had to be cheerful and polite even
when reporters tried to dig into every inch of his private life.
“Oh, of course.” The reporter lowered her pen and notebook. “My name is Amano Maya. I
work with Kismet Publishing, and I’m currently working on an article for one of our teen
magazines, the Coolest. I was hoping to get an article with Kujikawa-san on the strength it
took to take a step away from showbiz, but I can settle for a high school perspective on
everything that’s been happening in this town.”
“Oh, I know that magazine!” Chie said, brightening. “They had this really good article about
different ways to train for sports.”
“My partner took the pictures for that article,” Amano said with a small smile. “Would any of
you be willing to answer a few questions?”
“Everything that’s been happening in this town?” Yukiko asked. “Do you mean the
murders?”
“Partially,” Amano admitted, only the tiniest of blushes spreading across her light skin. “I
understand if you wouldn’t want to talk about that. But Inaba seems to be a hotspot for
celebrity activity as well. Not only is this Kujikawa-san’s hometown, but rumor has it that
up-and-coming detective Shirogane Naoto has been spotted here as well.”

“He’s famous?” Kanji asked in alarm.
“Not quite as famous as Risette,” Amano said. “But he’s gaining popularity.” She clicked her
pen thoughtfully. “Maybe I can get an interview with him.”
“I don’t know if he’s really the interviewing type,” Yosuke said.
“This interview,” Yu said. “Would it be anonymous?”
“If you want it to be.”
In the end, Yu, Yosuke, Teddie, and Chie consented to be interviewed. They stepped aside
from the main group as Amano asked them different questions. They were too far away to
hear, but judging by their mild expressions, the interview wasn’t too violating.
When they were done, they walked back up to the main group. Teddie was practically
skipping, looking thrilled with himself.
“Thank you so much for your help,” Amano said with another bow. “Have a good evening.”
“You too, Amano-san,” Goro said.
“Oh, and if you do happen to run into your doppelganger…” Amano scrawled her number on
her notepad and ripped off the page. She handed it to Rise. “Tell her to consider giving me a
call. But no pressure.”
Amano walked away and disappeared from view. Rise frowned at the phone number.
Chie smiled. “She was nice.”
“Am I going to be famous now?” Teddie asked. “Like Rise-chan?”
Yosuke sighed. “I really wouldn’t count on it.” He glanced at Rise. “Do you intend on calling
her?”
“Probably not,” Rise said, folding the paper and stuffing it between her obi. “But if I do go
back into show business, maybe I’ll let her have an interview. As a thank you for more or less
respecting my privacy.”

Goro’s phone rang the following morning.
“Hey, Akechi-kun,” Akira said. “You know the summer festival?”
“I might have heard of it,” Goro said dryly.
“Right.” Akira’s voice was embarrassed. “Well, I haven’t had the opportunity to go yet this
year, and I know it’s open for at least another day. I thought maybe you’d like to come with
me later this afternoon?”

“Oh, I’d be glad to.” Goro was unable to hide some of his surprise from his voice. “What
time would you like to meet up?”
At their agreed time, Goro met Akira in front of the shrine. When they entered the festival,
Akira looked around with a dazed expression.
“It’s been a couple of years since I’ve been to one of these,” Akira admitted. “What do you
like to do?”
Goro refused to admit that he had mostly just followed his friends around in recent years.
Before that, he hadn’t attended a festival since before his mother had died.
Goro could have opinions. Goro knew how to have fun without the help others.
Akira looked at him expectantly. An old fear of failure crept up inside Goro. What if Akira
was unimpressed by his choices? What if he was disappointed? Goro wasn’t sure if he was
afraid that Akira would be disappointed by Goro or by the festival itself. Neither options
were preferable.
“My friend swears by the ikayaki,” Goro said.
“Are they good?”
“They were fine,” Goro said.
Akira snorted. “I guess I can give them a try.”
They ended up sampling multiple different foods. Akira ended up enjoying the okonomiyaki
the best. The irony of okonomiyaki being a type of pancake was not lost on Goro, even if
there was no way Akira could have known about Goro’s unpleasant association with
pancakes.
Even surrounded by sweet smells and the festival’s red glow, Goro could picture himself
smiling at the Phantom Thieves all while he planned to kill Akira. He remembered thinking
that they were all a group of fools. But it turned out they weren’t as ignorant as Goro thought.
“You don’t want some?” Akira asked, holding out his plate toward Goro. “It didn’t insult
your family, did it?”
“Insult my family– what are you talking about?”
“You’re looking at it like it offended you personally,” Akira said. He ate another large bite.
“That’s not a normal response.”
“It didn’t offend me personally,” Goro said. “It’s just food.”
“In that case, are you sure you don’t want some?” Akira asked. “You’ve barely eaten
anything all night.”
“I’m not that hungry.”

“Well, I’m starting to overflow,” Akira said. “Have some.”
Goro rolled his eyes and snatched the plate from Akira. He took a small bite of the
okonomiyaki. It was actually quite good.
“There,” Goro said. “Happy?”
“I want it back now, please,” Akira said. Goro returned the plate, and Akira finished the food
off in less than a minute. Had Akira really made such a fuss just to prove a point? What
point? That Goro could enjoy food he resented?
“For someone who was full, you ate that quickly,” Goro said. “Delicious pancakes, were
they?”
“They did taste really good,” Akira said regretfully. “But I actually am full now. Maybe we
could try the target game we saw earlier?”
Goro had been hoping Akira wouldn’t bring up the target game. Although the guns were
certainly toys, he didn’t have the best association with the weapons. Maybe Goro could
pretend they were evokers instead.
“Sure,” Goro said. And then, because a part of Goro could not shake the memory of Akira
being his bitter rival, he added, “We could make a contest out of it.”
“I don’t have the best aim,” Akira said. “Is it whoever hits the best prize wins?”
“That will do.”
Goro went first. Taking the fake pistol, Goro resisted the urge to show off flagrantly and hit
the top prize. Goro wouldn’t know what to do with a pair of earrings anyway. He shot the set
of nice-looking pens instead.
The vendor congratulated Goro and handed him his prize. Akira gave Goro an impressed
nod.
“Well done,” he said.
Goro forced back his smirk. “It’s your turn.”
Akira took the gun and aimed it at a pair of headphones, one of the most difficult prizes.
Akira frowned in concentration, and Goro bit back the urge to scoff. Akira would be better
served to pick an easier target closer to where Goro aimed–
Akira’s cork hit the box of headphones slightly off-center. The vendor looked astonished as
he handed Akira his prize.
Goro probably looked astonished. He should have known better than to go easy on Akira.
Akira grinned. “This is good,” he said. “I needed new headphones.”

“How did you do that?” Goro asked, pretending his pride wasn’t wounded.
“I have an old toy I practice with when I’m bored,” Akira said. “I’ve been doing it less to
prioritize my studies, so I’ve gotten a little rusty.”
Come to think of it, Akira never had an issue hitting enemies with his model gun in the
metaverse. Goro assumed that Akira simply had the cognition of never being able to miss, or
that his time playing Gun About at the arcade had improved his abilities. It hadn’t occurred to
him that there was more to it than that.
“Well, I’m impressed,” Goro said.
Akira beamed. “Thanks.”

“It’s finally beach day!” Chie said. “Let me tell you, I have been looking forward to this.”
“Well, it's something to help me forget about school starting up again soon,” Kanji said. “I
can’t believe summer vacation is almost over.”
“Now’s seriously not the time to think about that,” Yosuke said. “I can’t have fun if I’m busy
thinking about school.”
“R-right. Sorry.”
They all stood in front of Yosuke’s house, waiting for Junpei to arrive and pick them up.
They gathered fifteen minutes earlier than Junpei agreed to arrive, which probably meant
they were going to stand there for half an hour. Junpei wasn’t exactly known for his
punctuality.
“When do you think your friend is going to get here?” Yukiko asked Goro. “It’s already been
ten minutes.”
“If we’re lucky, he’ll be here within the next five minutes,” Goro said. He’d prefer not to
throw Junpei under the bus before the group had even met him.
“I know that this is for the betterment of the group, but it would have been really cool if we
all could have driven to the beach on our scooters,” Yosuke said. “It’s such a nice day too.”
“It’s probably for the best, who knows what might have happened with all of us on the road
anyway,” Kanji said.
“I’ll have you know that I’m an excellent driver,” Rise said indignantly.
“Didn’t you just get your license?” Yu asked.
Rise looked ready to protest, but at that moment, Junpei’s van drove up in front of them.
Goro checked the time on his phone. Impressive. Junpei was actually a minute early.

Junpei rolled down his window and grinned at them. “Did somebody order a trip to the
beach?”
“Wow, Goro-kun,” Teddie said. “You didn’t tell me that your friend was cool.”
“I’m hurt,” Junpei said, still grinning. “How could you not have told them all about me?”
“It hasn’t really come up in conversation,” Goro said.
“Ah, well, they have plenty of time to get to know me now,” Junpei said. “Pile in, everyone.”
They entered Junpei’s van, which was actually tidier than Goro expected. The gray seats
smelled vaguely of fabric softener. Had he recently gotten the vehicle cleaned?
“It’s a short drive, but I have some snacks in the back seats,” Junpei said. “But you have to
tell me if any of you find the penguin cracker.”
“You know about that?” Goro asked.
“Everybody knows about that,” Rise said. “Once I thought I had found it, but it turned out I
had just bitten the head off of a different animal.”
“I found the real deal,” Kanji said proudly. “I took a picture of it.”
“Aw man, you should totally show me when we get back,” Junpei said. “I made a bet with
Yukari that I could find it before she did. Now we eat nothing but those animal crackers.”
“Sounds like a healthy lifestyle to have,” Goro said dryly.
“Well, I’m increasing my chances by having other people go through the animal crackers for
me,” Junpei admitted.
“We’re more than happy to contribute,” Yu said, his mouth half-full of crackers. “I forgot to
eat breakfast this morning.”
“I thought we talked about this,” Yosuke said, his voice pitching in concern. “Breakfast is the
most important meal of the day.”
“I usually eat breakfast,” Yu said defensively. “I just forgot.”
“Oh yeah, like that one week where you kept forgetting every single day?”
“I kept sleeping in, that’s not my fault.”
“You know what? We’ll talk about this later,” Yosuke huffed. “Give me some of those animal
crackers.”
Yu apologetically handed Yosuke a couple of crackers. Yosuke shoved them into his mouth
and chomped on them aggressively.

The rest of the drive went by uneventfully. Junpei didn’t crash, and nobody else argued over
their eating habits. When they arrived at the beach, Teddie was particularly delighted to find
out that no surprise rain clouds had come to ruin the day.
“It had been clear all morning,” Kanji said. “And the weathermen said it wouldn’t rain.”
“And now it might be clear all afternoon,” Teddie said. “Besides, Yosuke-kun told me the
weathermen weren’t always right.”
“He has a point,” Chie sighed.
“I don’t know,” Yu said reluctantly. “They’ve been pretty spot on recently.”
“Alright, everyone!” Rise clapped her hands. “Let’s change into our suits. That ocean is
calling my name.”
“I’m more of a sandcastle competition guy myself,” Junpei said.
Everyone except Goro gave Junpei a confused look. Goro’s expression was far more
unimpressed as Junpei winked.
“Eh, ignore me. Have fun, you guys. I’ll be here when you’re ready to head on back.”
“Thank you very much Iori-san,” Yukiko said with a bow. Everyone else echoed her.
“Don’t mention it.” Junpei smiled. “Everyone needs to have fun every now and then. I’m
planning on catching some rays myself.”
Goro emerged from the bathroom after changing into his swimsuit. Junpei already stood next
to the door.
“Catch.”
Junpei tossed an object at Goro, who barely caught it before it smacked him in the face. It
was a canister of sunscreen, and Goro looked up at Junpei skeptically.
“I didn’t realize you were concerned about sunburns,” he said.
“Let’s just say it’s a gift from Mitsuru,” Junpei said. “Well, no. I bought it. But she told me to
make sure you sunscreened, so it’s mostly her fault.”

“And?”

another panic attack while underwater.

ocean and be lost forever. Goro wasn’t sure how he’d react to losing one of his only

Chie instantly took that opportunity to kick the water toward Goro. A few drops splashed
across Goro’s face, and Goro flinched from the cold. He spat out the small amount of the saltflavored liquid that got into his mouth.

It was somewhat difficult to have a proper water fight when Goro was only standing a few

a very awkward looking competition in which they attempted to splash water extremely long
distances. Very little water actually hit the intended target.
“This is painful to watch,” Kanji said.
“No, no, I’ve almost got him this time,” Chie said.
“You’ve got this,” Yukiko said encouragingly.

Kanji sighed. “Y’all do your own thing. I’m going to keep him company so that I don't have
to keep watching this.” He started to swim toward the shore. “Don’t try any funny business

“Oh, so that’s why you’ve been making less dirty jokes,” Rise said.
“Good work, Yu-kun!” Chie cheered. She waved at Yu, who was standing on the beach and

“What?” Kanji asked, his voice muffled by the towel. “What is it?”
“How the hell can you not notice that your bathing suit has come off?” Goro hissed. “Cover

“Holy shit!”

“There must be more than meets the eye.” Goro tried to move the mirror, but no matter how
hard he strained, the mirror didn’t budge. “Junpei, help me.”

“Got it.”
Junpei and Goro stood on one side of the mirror and pressed their entire weight against it. It

“Yeah, call this a hunch, but I don’t think we can move this thing,” Junpei said. “I don’t think

“It’s obvious that we can’t take that back with us,” he said. “And apart from a mirror being

“Maybe there’s something we’re missing?” Junpei asked.

“Let’s get the hell out of here.”
“Well, as much of a bummer as this turned out to be, I’m glad that none of us almost died.”
“You really have a way of looking on the bright side.”
“Somebody has to.”

Goro received a text from an unknown number by the time Junpei dropped him off in Inaba
that afternoon. Goro almost had a heart attack before he reminded himself that Takaya was
dead.

U̴͙͠n̶̪̒ k̷͔̇ n̶̥͊ ò̸̬ w̷̦̿ n̸̥̓ ̸̉ͅ: : So nice of you to drop by uninvited.

Goro and Akira agreed to spend their last days of summer enjoying each other’s company.
Since it was pouring rain, Akira suggested they try to complete the rainy day beef bowl
challenge.
“Kurusu-kun, have you seen the size of those beef bowls?” Goro asked. “They’re enough to
kill a grown man.”
“People have won the challenge before,” Akira said defensively. “The owner told me.”
Goro didn’t know how best to tell Akira that those people were other-worldly beings who
probably didn’t have digestive systems. “Well, I guess it can’t hurt to try,” he said reluctantly.
Akira beamed. “I knew you’d come around.”
“But if you’re going to try to beat the challenge, don’t think that you’re going to do it without
competition,” Goro said. “Maybe I’ll beat the challenge first.”
“And here I thought that you thought the whole thing was ridiculous.”
“It is. I’m just giving you more motivation to get it done sooner so we can forget about the
whole thing.”
Neither of them made a dent in their beef bowls.

It was still raining as they walked back home. While they tried to stay dry underneath their

Akira shook his head. “He doesn’t come over when my parents are home more often,” he

“A feud?” Goro asked.

“A couple of days?”

child.”
“Don’t you understand how much it costs to even keep you alive?”
His mother’s voice echoed so sharply in Goro’s memories that Goro came to a complete stop.
It had been in response to Goro's begging for some toy the other kids in school had, back
when he was still too young to fully understand their situation. She apologized later,
explained why things were harder in gentler terms. That was often how things went. His

fair.
Akira turned toward Goro in confusion.
“What is it?”
“It’s nothing,” Goro lied. “I suppose it does take effort to take care of one’s children. I just
wished for your sake they were around more.”
Despite everything, Goro’s mother succeeded in taking care of Goro on a daily basis.
“It’s fine,” Akira said again. “I mean, you live on your own, right? Or you did earlier this

“That’s not really the point.”
Akira glowered and opened his mouth to say more. A loud meow interrupted him.
Goro and Akira looked down to see a half-starved cat standing in between them. The cat’s

The cat stared up at them petulantly. Akira crouched down with a small smile.

“Hello there,” he said sweetly.
The cat hissed.
“Kurusu-kun, that thing is going to give you countless diseases,” Goro said. “We should just

“Are you listening to me at all?”
“I’m agreeing to disagree.”
“The cat could hurt you.”
“Don’t be silly.” Akira was still using a baby-voice for the sake of that stupid cat. “He’s just a

The cat rubbed its head against Akira’s leg, pleading for more pets. Akira indulged it.

Akira wasn’t going to count on it.

Kanji poked his head through the doorway of Goro’s bedroom the following evening, causing

Shit. Goro had forgotten that most places had a summer fireworks festival.

BANG.

BANG BANG

Well, that was just fantastic.
“Well, thanks for the clarification, Adachi-san,” Yu said. “I’ll talk to you later.”

Akira changed his mind. Monster Cat was a valid name for a cat. Especially this cat.
Akira’s parents were in the living room, trying to enjoy a relaxing evening. They weren’t
even working from home. They were just watching television. Akira was not about to ruin
that for them.
Which would be all well and good, but Monster Cat would not stop meowing at him like his
life depended on it.
“Shut up, will you?” Akira hissed at him. “I can’t give you pets all day. You have to stay
hidden under the bed.”
Monster Cat did not want to stay under the bed. Monster Cat had been growing more and
more restless as Akira’s parents found more and more time to stay at home. One night under
the bed was fine. Monster Cat was much less fond of five nights in a row of hiding.
Monster Cat expressed this by meowing loudly and scratching at Akira’s desk chair. Akira
thought he might cry.
“I’m sure they won’t be home tomorrow,” Akira whispered. He pushed Monster Cat
underneath his bed more forcefully. “Just try to hold out a little longer.”
Monster Cat’s meow was so pitiful that it made Akira cringe. It also made the sounds of the
television stop from the other room. Akira froze.
“Akira-kun, what’s all that noise?” Akira’s father demanded.

“It’s, um, just me reciting my English!” Akira said. “I have to recite, um, Wordsworth for
English class!”
“Oh, well, try to do it a little more quietly,” Akira’s mother said. “You know we don’t get a
lot of opportunities to relax.”
“I know. I’m sorry,” Akira said. “I’ll be quieter.”
“Thank you very much, sweetheart.”
The TV noises resumed. Akira continued to try to wrangle Monster Cat back into hiding.
“Would you like a cat burrito?” Akira asked as quietly as possible. He grabbed a blanket off
his bed and attempted to wrap it tightly around Monster Cat. “You like cat burritos, don’t
you?”
Monster Cat usually liked cat burritos. That night, Monster Cat liked freedom more. He
hissed loudly and swatted at Akira’s arm. His claws only lightly scratched him, but the pain
was enough for Akira to yelp anyway.
The TV noises stopped again. Monster Cat took advantage of Akira’s distracted state to

you have a good time when we hang out.”
“Actually, correct me when I’m wrong, but I think it’s important that both of us are happy.
That’s what I’ve heard, at any rate.”
“Well, obviously,” Kanji said. Some of the steam drained out of him. “I really am sorry for
making you uncomfortable. It wasn’t very cool of me.”
“You were well-meaning,” Goro said. “I’m not exactly known for my acts of kindness.”
“Yeah, well, I guess there’s such a thing as trying to be too considerate of others,” Kanji said.
“This friendship thing can be pretty tough, sometimes.”
“That, we can agree on,” Goro said. “If it makes you feel any better, I did somewhat enjoy
some of the hobbies we tried. Maybe if I later decide to do them on my own terms, I’ll find

Kanji nodded. “That’s something, at least. But how about we try this again? You wanna get
some topsicles with me?”
“It’s not exactly summer weather anymore.”
“And who says it has to be summer weather to enjoy topscicles?” Kanji asked defensively.
“The stuff’s delicious.”

Well, Goro couldn’t say he disagreed.

Chapter End Notes

Okay y'all. I really waffled on what to do about Naoto. Their story is SUPER transcoded, but canon gives at least a decent explanation for why they were presenting as a
boy but still identifies as a girl, and normally with things like gender identity, I don't like
to directly oppose canon. Also, personally I kinda think Naoto is cool as a female
character. However, I also know that canon really screwed a lot of fans over with the
again super trans-coded storyline (even if the writers didnt intend to make it trans coded,
thats still how many fans perceived it), and it felt weird to just be like "okay I guess
you're a girl now!" when there is an opportunity for trans visibility in the fic. So this is
kinda what I landed on as a compromise. Naoto is still kinda just experimenting, so I'm
leaving it up to the reader to decide if Naoto ends up identifying as cis or nonbinary.
Sorry if it's not what you wanted.
In any case, we finally made it to October!! I lowkey forgot how quickly the second half
of September goes by. Just like part 1 fr fr.
Thank you for reading, I hope you enjoyed, and please be nice in the comments (I trust
you guys but please don't get into arguments with each other about Naoto's gender
identity. It seems like something people might have strong opinions over. Also no
transphobia either pls.) <333
EDIT: friends, this chapter was posted FIVE MONTHS AGO and i'm still getting
comments about how Naoto's character was about sexism in Japan and isn't trans at all.
That is a Very Valid take, but I cannot live the rest of my life with the occasional
comment about what the writers intended with Naoto's character in this fic. Everyone is
entitled to their own opinion, but I'm tired and would like everyone to read this chapter
and accept that some people strongly felt like Naoto should have been trans and other
people very strongly liked the present narrative about male dominated jobs in Japanese
society. Both of these opinions are valid, which is literally Why I had a massive
paragraph in these notes originally. I wish all my readers a lovely day but please lets end
this conversation for my sake. <3333

October fourth wasn’t a day Goro held in particularly high esteem. It was hard to forget how
badly things could have gone two years ago. It was harder still to forget how badly things had
gone that day.
The year before, Ken had asked Goro to come over to Shinjiro’s apartment with him. Ken
had apologized to Shinjiro for trying to kill him, but Shinjiro had forgiven him almost
immediately. Goro, recognizing the trend, apologized for threatening Ken’s life.
In the end, they all agreed to forgive each other. It was hard to be angry after everything
they’d been through since then. It was especially hard to be angry when they were all still
alive and breathing.
Shinjiro was still alive then. Goro had counted that as a miracle.
Shinjiro was still alive now. None of them expected him to make it this long. Maybe they had
more time than they realized.
The day was still hard. Goro might be unsettled by the anniversary, but October fourth was
also the day Ken’s mother died. The day Shinjiro took a life.
Goro called Ken first.
“Hi,” Goro said. “How are you doing?”
“Fine,” Ken said, in a way that meant he wasn’t fine at all.
“You don’t have to be.”

“Yeah…” Ken hesitated. “It’s just hard, you know? Thinking about how bad things were at
first… and then how bad things could’ve gone two years ago. I really am sorry for all the
trouble I caused.”
“I forgave you for that a long time ago,” Goro said. “You can’t apologize every year. It’s not
healthy.”
“No, I guess not,” Ken said. “I’m just… worried. Or guilty. I don’t know. And I know it’s
been four years, but I—I miss my mom.”
“It’s only natural.” Goro squeezed his eyes shut. “I’m not sure if this is what you want to
hear, but it’s been thirteen years since I last saw my mother, and I still miss her.”
Ken stayed silent for a moment before saying, “I think it’s better that way. I mean… to stop
grieving is to stop caring, right? I don’t… I don’t want to forget how important she was to
me.”
After talking a little longer with Ken, Goro was about to call Shinjiro when he received a text
from Yu.
Narukami Yu: Today is Nanakos birthday
Narukami Yu: i wanted to do smth nice for her
Narukami Yu: can u come by junes after school?
As if Goro would have ever been able to say no to that. How old would Nanako be turning?
Seven? Would she be expecting a gift of some sort?
Well, Yu hadn’t told Goro to bring a gift, and he really didn’t have the time to go shopping
when school was in half an hour. Maybe he could quickly buy something at Junes before
Nanako got there.
Goro finally called Shinjiro with a sarcastic “Hello Shinjiro, I’m bored out of my mind,”
which at least got a shaky laugh out of him.
“It’s the little girl’s birthday?” Shinjiro asked when Goro brought it up. “What’s her name?
Nanaka?”
“Nanako,” Goro said.
“Right. And you’re taking her to Junes? Is there some fantasy land in Inaba I don’t know
about, or are you taking a child to a department store for her birthday?”
“You don’t understand,” Goro said. “She loves Junes. It might as well be a fantasy land to
her.”
“I can’t decide if that’s endearing or concerning,” Shinjiro said. “You said her dad wasn’t
around much, right?”

“According to Yu, she likes the jingle,” Goro said. “I’m not sure her fascination with the
place has anything to do with a lack of family outings. But I could be wrong.”
“I could come over,” Shinjiro mused. “Kick some sense into her dad.”
“That would be assault.”
“Well, you only live once, right?”
Goro bit back a remark on how incredibly unfunny that joke was. Shinjiro seemed to read his
silence anyway.
“Well, it’s a good thing that someone gets to be happy today,” Shinjiro said. “All things
considered.”
“Yeah,” Goro said, not sure what to say.
“Don’t worry about me,” Shinjiro said, even though Goro hadn’t said anything. “You have
your own problems to deal with without adding mine to the list.”
“Last I checked, being worried was a mark of a good friend,” Goro muttered.
“Last I checked, the past is in the past,” Shinjiro said. “Both Ken and that little girl need you
more than I do. Seriously, I’ve got Akihiko if my brooding gets out of hand.”
Goro sighed shakily. “Right.”

“I don’t know what to get her!” Chie complained as the group searched the rows of items in
Junes. “Why couldn’t Yu have given us more notice for this?”
“He forgot,” Yosuke said. “Dojima-san told Yu this morning that he was going to be bringing
cake over when he got home from work, and that’s around when Yu panicked and told us.”
“It’s good that Dojima-san remembered Nanako’s birthday,” Yukiko said.
“I hate that we feel the need to congratulate him for that,” Kanji said. “Anyway, I don’t think
you need to stress too hard about what we’re getting her, Senpai. Little kids are happy with
basically anything.”
“Maybe we should get her a book,” Yukiko said. She walked a few paces away toward the
children’s book section. “I loved reading when I was a kid.”
They followed Yukiko to the various picture books on display.
“I don’t know,” Rise said, crouching and peering at a series of books starring penguins. “I
think Nanako-chan is too smart for most of these. She’s pretty mature for her age.”

“What’s this one?” Teddie asked. Teddie picked up a book with strikingly familiar cover-art
of a pink alligator. “Look! Nana-chan likes pink, right?”
“Oh no, we are not getting her that book for her birthday,” Yosuke said. “Besides, I think Yu
told me she’s reading it for school.”
“Oh, that one made me cry like a baby,” Rise said.
“A children’s book made you cry?” Chie asked.
“Haven’t you read it?” Goro asked, staring intently at an empty spot in the shelves. His entire
body ached. “It’s about an alligator that dies by drowning in a pool of its own tears.”
“Oh, did you have to read it for school too, Goro-kun?” Yukiko asked.
“You just wildly oversimplified it,” Yosuke said. “It’s a narrative on how society treats those
different from them and then benefits when they suffer.”
“I really don’t think that was the point,” Kanji said. “I think the point was that you will be
remembered by what you leave behind when you die.”
“Are we still talking about a children’s book?” Chie asked.
Teddie sniffed. “Th-that’s, that’s so sad!”
“You really haven’t read it, Chie?” Yukiko asked.
“Well, I remember it being a kind of big deal,” Chie said. “But I never read it, no.”
“Didn’t the author and illustrator die?” Kanji said. “That’s how I first heard about it. Yeah,
check the little blurb on the inside cover.”
Yosuke looked over Kanji’s shoulder and read,
“Kamiki Akinari wrote this book to convey his own struggles through a genetic disease he
had since childhood. Although he sadly passed away at the age of nineteen, his mother and
friend had it published in memoriam to his life. Yoshino Chidori illustrated its pages. She

a testament to what she left behind.”
“I didn’t know they wrote that,” Goro said.
“Well, I guess teachers aren’t going to want their young students to think too hard about real
people dying,” Chie said. “Fictional alligators are easier to swallow.”
Yosuke nodded. “Yeah– Goro-kun?”
“What?” Goro snapped.
“I just… are you okay?” Yosuke asked.

“I guess it is pretty heavy stuff,” Kanji said. “Maybe we should just put it back.”
“I’m not a child,” Goro said. To his horror, his vision blurred. He blinked furiously. “I just…
I knew Chidori personally. That’s all.”
“Oh,” Yosuke said. His eyes widened. “Oh.”
“I’m so sorry, Goro-kun,” Yukiko said. She took the book from Kanji and put it back on the

“Of course, you didn’t,” Goro said. “I didn’t tell you.”
“Maybe we should get back to finding a gift for Nanako,” Kanji said. “How much time do we

“Oh, shit,” Yosuke said, glancing at his phone. “Fifteen minutes.”

“Happy Birthday, Nana-chan!” Everyone cheered as Yu brought Nanako up to their table.
They hadn’t purchased a cake, since Dojima ideally had that covered. They did buy three
gifts, partly out of franticness and partly out of their sheer inability to make decisions.
Someone might as well have put stars into Nanako’s eyes. “This is for me?”
“Of course it is,” Yu said, putting a gentle hand on her back. “Dojima-san didn’t lie to me
about it being your birthday today, did he?”
Nanako shook her head. She smiled at the others. “Thank you very much!”
“We haven’t even gotten started yet,” Chie said. “I’ll buy you a treat of your choice, and then
