Chie ended up buying Nanako takoyaki, and Nanako sat down at the table and began opening
her presents. For the first gift, Rise had insisted on buying something she could sign for
Nanako, so they had settled on a notebook.
“It has Risette’s signature!” Nanako said, gasping at the front page.
“That’s right,” Rise said. “Even if I never come back to show business, I thought you might
like that.”
“Wow,” Nanako said.
“You can write your thoughts in it too,” Yukiko said.
“Okay!” Nanako said, nodding. “Thank you!”
Teddie wanted to give Nanako something soft, so he got her an admittedly adorable looking
cat plush.

“It’s really soft,” Nanako said, hugging it close to her.
“It’s not quite like a real cat,” Goro said. “But it’s certainly less work than one.”
“What are you going to name it?” Yu asked, looking like he was fighting back a laugh. Goro
knew he was thinking about the unfortunate naming of Monster Cat.
Nanako beamed and held out the cat toward Yu. “I can name him Yu!”
“That’s a great name,” Yosuke said, looking like he was trying very hard not to laugh. Yu
beamed.
The third and final gift was mochi. Yosuke had recalled how much Nanako had wanted some
when they had gone on their school trip. Just as he predicted, Nanako was thrilled.
“This is my best birthday ever!” Nanako said.
“Wow, that’s high praise, seeing as the day isn’t even over yet,” Kanji said.
“Well, this is my first birthday I got to celebrate with Big Bro and his friends,” Nanako said.
“And at Junes!”
Nanako’s mother was dead. Her father was distant. Her beloved “Big Bro” would be leaving
in the Spring. She had every reason to be miserable.
And yet Nanako was still laughing. Still smiling. So hopeful that things would only continue
to get better.
Goro almost envied her.

When Naoto fully recovered, the group met at Yosuke’s house. Naoto wasn’t looking too
worse for wear, although she was obviously incredibly tired.
The team agreed not to mention their theories to Naoto until after hearing her testimony. The
last thing they needed to do was put ideas into Naoto’s head that altered her account of what

“I hate to ask,” Yosuke said awkwardly. “But do you remember anything from when you

Naoto nodded. “You don’t need to apologize. That was the reason I was kidnapped, after all.”
“Oh, um, right,” Yukiko said.
Naoto hummed. “First, I heard the doorbell ring. But when I opened the front door, I saw no

and covered my mouth with something. As I struggled, I was put into something like a sack
and most likely carried on the culprit's shoulder.”

Naoto glanced at Goro. “So, you filled them in,” she said. “Well, I had the tracker in my

Naoto frowned. “The culprit seems to have used a chemical to incapacitate me, but luckily, I

Naoto shook her head. “Not enough to say who exactly. Judging by their actions and body

Everybody glanced at each other knowingly.
“It's after that that things get murky. I felt a single impact, which I assume is when I was

“Shadows become personas?” Kanji asked. “Well, I guess our shadows did become our

“Your personas are the mask you wear to overcome life’s hardships,” Goro said. “And the

“I never thought about it that way,” Yukiko said.
“So, when we mastered our shadows, we got personas?” Yosuke asked. “That’s not too

“That’s just the power of the collective unconscious for you,” Yu said.
“Naoto-kun’s not wrong,” Goro said. “There probably is something larger at play. There

“That’s a comforting thought,” Yosuke said. “For now, I think we should just focus on

Yosuke had a point.
“And we’ll find out who Teddie is too!” Teddie interjected. “I can’t let my insides be a

“Pun-fluence?” Yu echoed, starting to grin.

Teddie gasped. “Goro-kun! You said another accidental pun!”

“Do we?” asked Yosuke.

“I think you mean punsufferable,” Naoto said.

“You too, sir,” Goro said.

Discovering Konishi’s body early in the morning… seeing her fight on the Midnight

Akira’s eyes were haunted as he stared at Goro. “And what if that way gets another person

The benefit of living in the central shopping district was that Goro had a perfect view of
everything that went on near the Velvet Room entrance. By extension, he had a perfect view
of the absolute ruckus every attendant was making when crowding around the door.
And by every attendant, he meant every attendant. Every attendant he knew of, at any rate.
Lavenza and Margaret stood side by side, looking the most composed out of the entire group.

had given her.
Upon being greeted with such a sight, Goro would have been ridiculous not to investigate
further. He approached the group with a confused frown.

to spending time with them.”
“You got all that from collecting litter?”
“Don’t take the people you care about for granted, Goro-kun,” Margaret said. “You don’t

“I never said I did.”
“You don’t need to say something for it to be in your thoughts.”

Emperor Arcana: Rank 8

Tatsumi-san wasn’t home the next evening since she was visiting some friends. The TV in the

It started raining more violently in November. People began to talk about how strange the
weather and fog was becoming.
When Goro and Kanji checked the midnight channel a few days into the month, they saw an
extremely blurry figure. The only thing Goro could make out about them was that they were
small.
When the group met up to talk about it, they couldn’t figure out who the person was. No
child had made a surprise appearance on the television recently. The most they could do was
agree to check the midnight channel again that night. Hopefully, the image would become
clearer.
They also agreed to keep a closer eye on Dojima’s tracker. If someone else got kidnapped,
this time was imperative to confirming whether or not Dojima was the killer.
For both Nanako and Yu’s sakes, Goro hoped that he wasn’t.

Akihiko arrived home from work to find Shinji already working on dinner.
“Got off work early, huh?” he asked.
“You could say that,” Shinji said. He coughed before continuing to chop a carrot with careful
precision.

“What, did they give you a mandatory sick day again?”
“Well, you know how they are– shit.” Shinji accidentally grazed his finger. The cut didn’t
look too deep, but Akihiko hurried to their first aid supply hiding under the sink.
“You should really be more careful,” Akihiko snapped as he grabbed some gauze.
‘Yeah… I’m the worst…” Shinji sounded dizzy.
Akihiko spun around. Shinji had put his knife down and was clinging onto the counter tightly.
His face was sheet white.
“Shinji?” Akihiko asked. His stomach felt like it had twisted his chest up in knots.
“Nothing to worry about.” Shinjiro scowled, but he blinked like he couldn’t quite see what
was in front of him. “Just a dizzy spell.”
He collapsed without another word.

Their kotatsu was broken. Nanako was especially distressed by this, in spite of Yu assuring
her they could go out and buy another one. When Dojima came home that night, she ran up to
him and told him the news immediately.
“Shouldn’t you already be in bed?” Dojima asked. It was a fair question. It was already half
past ten.
“Dad, the kotatsu’s broken. Can me and big bro buy a new one?”
Dojima looked distracted by a piece of paper in his hand, but he still answered Nanako’s

“Mhm,” Nanako said.
Dojima mustered up a smile. “All right, I’ll leave it to you. Get whichever kind you want.”
He was still staring at the envelope. Nanako asked about it before Yu could get the words out.
“Is that a letter?” she asked.
Dojima turned to Yu and held out the envelope. “It’s for you, but…”
Just like the previous warning letter, there was no return addressee or address. It was just
titled: To Narukami Yu.
Yu’s heart dropped all the way to the bottom of his stomach as he took the envelope. Aware
of Dojima’s burning gaze over his shoulder, he opened the letter and read the single sentence
scrawled on the piece of paper.

if you dont stop this time someone close will be put in and killed
Yu was going to be sick. Did this have something to do with the new person on the midnight
channel? Did whoever was threatening him want to make sure that this victim actually died?
“Hey, what the hell is this?!” Dojima demanded.
Dojima snatched the letter from Yu’s hands. Yu couldn’t tell if he was panicked or angry as

“I knew something was up when there wasn’t any return address,” Dojima muttered. He

involved in this case. What are you up to?”
Yu opened his mouth, but no words came out. He wasn’t sure if it was the shock of the letter,
or Dojima’s anger, or if the stress of the case beginning to boil over. All he knew was that if

Dojima was still waiting expectantly. Nanako looked like she was about to cry.
“I– I don’t know what’s going on,” Yu forced out hoarsely.
It was technically the truth. But it wasn’t the truth that Dojima was looking for, and Yu knew

“So, you’re not going to be honest with me,” Dojima said. “I’ve been treating you like

His words stung, but Dojima was right. Yu hadn’t been honest. And now someone he cared

“D-dad,” Nanako said, obviously scared.
Dojima sighed. “We’ll continue this somewhere else, but I’m not letting you leave until I’m

Nanako glanced at Yu for comfort. Yu stood up and tried to hide the trembling in his hands.
“We’ll be back soon,” he said, trying to inject some courage into his voice. He wasn’t quite

He said he was worried.
His parents had said a lot of things were for his own good. In hindsight, Yu wasn’t really sure
that was true at all.

“Okay,” Nanako said. “I’ll be waiting.”

Still no response.
Chie called.
Still no response.

An exhausted chuckle. “Wouldn’t dream of it. You’d kill me from beyond the grave.”
Goro kept Shinjiro on speaker phone as he frantically packed his bags.

Yu and Dojima sat on opposite sides of a gray table. Adachi stood awkwardly behind Yu.
“Alright, speak up,” Dojima said. “What have you gotten yourself into? What was that

For a brief, ridiculous second, Yu considered telling Dojima it was just a prank. That one of

Yu discarded the possibility immediately. There was no point. If the others’ theory was right,

So, Yu took a deep breath, opened his mouth, and told him everything. He explained the

“Persona… people going inside TVs?” Dojima massaged his eyes, and Yu felt inexplicably

Nanako.

Quiz shows were painfully boring. And Chie hadn’t slept that much the night before, and

Yu should have never told Dojima the truth. Maybe then, he could have been recovering in a

“Dad! Daddy, wake up!”

Nanako’s dungeon was one of the most beautiful places Goro had ever seen. Clouds and

“Heaven, huh?” Yosuke asked. “Deep down, Nanako-chan must really miss her.”
“Who wouldn’t?” Goro asked.
Had he ever considered the possibility that his mother was in heaven? Some religious people
had immediately dismissed her to hell due to the nature of her death, or maybe the nature of
her life. The very few kind ones said that she was in a better place.
Goro had never believed it. He had never even really given thought about it. His mother was
dead, and Goro was not. That was all that had really mattered, in the end.
Nanako clearly saw things very differently. Had that made her sadder or happier, in the end?
Goro had no idea.
“We have to get her back,” Yu said. “I’ll need all of you.”
“Of course!” Teddie said fiercely. “We’re going to rescue Nana-chan, no matter what!”
They split into multiple parties. Yu led half the group through the dungeon while Goro and
the other half waited outside. Then, when Yu’s group had completely expended all their
energy, they traded places. When both groups felt like they were on the verge of collapse,
they returned to the entrance and paid the fox an exorbitant fee for healing. Then they’d
return and start the process all over again.
It was an efficient method of tearing their way through the dungeon, but it was also
infuriating. Whenever Goro’s group was benched, they’d pace around for what felt like
hours. Goro wanted to get his hand on another shadow and rip it to shreds. Instead, he was
reduced to waiting outside like a coward.
“We’re going to get him,” Yukiko told Goro.
“I know that,” Goro snarled. “And when I do, he’s going to regret ever touching Nanako.”
“You’re kind of scary when you talk that way,” Chie admitted.

“Do you disagree?”
“Of course not!” Chie said. She grinned. “It’s kind of cool.”
Goro didn’t think it was cool. He hated that this part of himself had come out. The part that
only wanted to kill and exact vengeance on anyone that hurt him.
But he couldn’t make it go away. He couldn’t maintain his composure in the same way Yu
seemed to be capable of. The only thing he could do was try to make sure that only shadows
got hurt in his fury.
Goro didn’t know what he’d do when he saw Namatame. Judging from Yosuke and Kanji’s
stormy expressions, neither did they.
After Goro came back from his third trip into the dungeon, it was obvious that the waiting
game wasn’t doing Yu any favors too. There was practically a hole in the dirt where Yu had
paced repeatedly in circles.
“We’re changing things,” Yu said. “We’re all going to go in together. I can’t take much more
of this.”
The entire group entered the dungeon and emerged at an open space. A high-pitched
shimmering sound rang above them, and Nanako’s voice began to echo from an unknown
location.
“Why did you disappear..? Why did you leave me…? No, come back…”
“Are these Nanako-chan’s feelings?” Chie asked quietly.
“But I'm not lonely...I have Dad with me. I know he's always late coming home...and he never
plays with me because he's so busy...He can't cook or do laundry either...He tries to be nice,
though he's a little scary sometimes...but I love him...Big bro is with me now, too, and his
friends...So I'm not alone...I'm not lonely…”
Goro couldn’t listen to this. Nanako was supposed to have the childhood he never had. She
was supposed to be the one who smiled even when things got hard.
How could he have been this ignorant?
“A little kid… telling herself she’s not lonely so she doesn’t fall apart,” Kanji said grimly.
“That sort of thinking will kill you in the end,” Yu said. “I should’ve been there for her
more.”
“Don’t be that way,” Yosuke said. “You did everything you could.”
“It’s my fault she was taken,” Chie said wretchedly. “I can’t believe I let Namatame get the
jump on me while I was watching her.”

Goro agreed and was more than willing to say so too, but Yukiko had already grabbed Chie’s
hand comfortingly.
“Don’t blame yourself, Chie,” she said. “Besides, we should greet Nanako with a smile when
we rescue her.
“I don’t think she’ll be convinced,” Goro said. “She’s more perceptive than you think.”
“Well, if not for her, then for me,” Yukiko said. “I can’t… I can’t feel like I’m breaking down
before we’ve even gotten half-way there. We need to keep it together so that we can be at our
strongest when we save her.”
“Save her? That’s a funny joke” said a rough voice from behind them.
The hairs on the back of Goro’s neck went on end, and the entire group spun around toward
the strange voice.
Rise gasped. “Senpai, look!”
Dojima stood in front of them, but obviously not the real one. Even if his eyes weren’t a
bright shade of yellow, Dojima had never looked quite so jaded as he looked now. He wasn’t
even pretending to smile.
He looked like Sakura or Takeharu, if you removed all their soft edges and only left misery
behind.
“Dojima-san,” Yu said.
“It’s not him,” Yosuke said quickly.
“Aren’t I?” Dojima’s shadow sighed. He fumbled with a lighter and lit a new cigarette. “My
idiot of a nephew told me about these shadows himself, you know?” Yu flinched. “I’m just as
much Dojima Ryotaro as you are Hanamura.”
“Have you come with the intention to fight us?” Naoto asked.
“Not anything so complicated as that,” Dojima said. “I just came to tell you that it’s pretty
much a lost cause. You might want to quit now and save yourself the pain of failing later.”
“What are you talking about?” Yu asked. “That’s your daughter up there!”
“Everyone dies,” Dojima’s shadow said. He breathed out a large puff of smoke. “My wife
dies, and I can’t find the killer. Nanako gets taken… Even if you kids manage to capture
Namatame, he’ll walk free if you can’t find any decisive evidence linking him to the
murders.”
“If you’re not here to help, then you might as well fuck off,” Goro said. “That’s what you do
best, right? Run away? Hide from your problems?”

Dojima’s shadow sighed, the sadness beneath his eyes deepening. “Got me in one.” He
turned around and started walking away. “God, I need a drink.”
“Dojima-san, wait!” Yu snapped. “Where are they? Where’s Nanako?!”
Dojima’s shadow didn’t answer.

Ryotaro cataloged his injuries.
His ribs were almost certainly broken, and judging from how painful it was to breathe, it was
possible he had a punctured lung. Fortunately, it wasn’t fatal, or Ryotaro would have been
dead by now. His legs were in enough pain that it was safe to assume at least one of them was
fractured. Probably both of them. Ryotaro wasn’t experiencing any symptoms of a
concussion or major head injury, but he was certainly bruised all over his body.
It hadn’t been a pretty car wreck. Ryotaro running headfirst into the television hadn’t likely
been a help either.
With Nanako’s help, he managed to get himself in a sitting position by resting his back
against one of the pillars circling the area. Ryotaro was at least able to keep a good eye on
Namatame, who was eyeing him and Nanako warily. He obviously hadn’t recovered from
Nanako’s impressive self-defense skills.
“Just stay over there, Namatame, and nobody else has to get hurt,” Ryotaro said as loudly as
he could muster. It hurt like hell.
“Dad,” Nanako said. She clutched onto Ryotaro’s shirt as carefully as possible. “Where are
we?”
“Well…” Ryotaro took a deep breath. “You probably won’t believe me…” Another deep
breath. “But we’re inside the television.”
“Really?” Nanako asked. “How?”
This was why Ryotaro was terrible with children. They kept asking questions that Ryotaro
wasn’t remotely equipped to answer.
“I don’t know.”
“Oh.” Nanako was obviously disappointed, likely even scared, by the lack of information.
Ryotaro would be lying if he said he wasn’t scared too. There were too many unknowns, and
Nanako’s life could still very well be in danger. Being on the force hadn’t prepared him for
this supernatural bullshit.
It had been hard to follow Yu’s explanation of the TV world, but Ryotaro wasn’t sure that it
had been Yu’s fault at all. As soon as Yu had said that he and his friends entered televisions to

save the victims, Ryotaro had checked out. Instead of actually listening to what his nephew
had to say, he focused on how frustrated he was with his stupid, reckless kid.
Now, Ryotaro wished he had paid closer attention. Maybe it would have helped them get out
of this place.
Come to think of it, hadn’t Yu mentioned something about a shadow? An alternate version of
someone’s self that came out when they first entered the television? But if that was the case,
where were any of their shadows? Maybe Namatame had entered it before, if he was the real
culprit, but Ryotaro and Nanako certainly hadn’t. Neither of their shadows were anywhere in
sight.
As if summoned by Ryotaro’s thoughts, Ryotaro’s clone emerged from the fog. He looked
like Ryotaro on one of his bad days, when it was easier to try to forget his struggles behind
multiple glasses of beer.
He’d stopped doing that after he slipped up the night Kujikawa was found. Yu looked like he
had half a mind to kill him the following morning, and it had taken at least a day to get the
smell of alcohol out of the house.
And Ryotaro couldn’t bear to disappoint Nanako like that again.
“Thought I’d stop by and make sure nobody was dying,” Ryotaro’s clone said. He glanced
between Namatame and Ryotaro. “But I guess Nanako can take care of herself more than you
can.”
“Dad?” Nanako asked, her voice shaking. “W-why… what?”
“He’s not real,” Ryotaro said, because he couldn’t think of any other way to explain this
phenomenon to Nanako. He couldn’t understand it himself. “It’s just a trick.”
“Actually, I’m the real deal,” Ryotaro’s shadow said. “More real than the man who puts on a
smile and pretends he’s the perfect father.”
“I’ve never pretended to be that,” Ryotaro said. “I know I’ve fallen short–”
“Fallen short?” Ryotaro’s shadow asked. “That’s a new word for it. And here I thought it was
nothing but good old-fashioned neglect. I think I remember your nephew saying a word or
two about that to you.”
Ryotaro was in too much pain to put up much of a fight against this thing. Nanako
whimpered.
“Please don’t fight,” she whispered.
“We’re not–”
“Why keep lying to her?” Ryotaro’s shadow asked. “We know she sees right through it.” he
glared at Nanako. “You know what? We are fighting, and sometimes grown ups need to fight
to get shit done–”

“Nanako, cover your ears,” Ryotaro said immediately, raising his voice over his shadow.
“Don’t listen to a word that man says.”
Nanako squeezed her eyes shut and slammed her hands over ears. She was trembling.
“That man?” Ryotaro’s shadow said. “That’s harsh.”
“Mind watching what you say to her?” Ryotaro snapped. He took a deep breath to keep his
lungs from collapsing. “If you’ve got a problem with me, fine. It’s got nothing to do with
her.”
“Are you kidding me? It’s got everything to do with her!” Ryotaro’s shadow snapped.
Nanako flinched. “She looks so much like Chisato that it hurts. The best thing to do is run
and pretend I’m on some mission for justice.”
“That’s not–” A fresh wave of pain slammed into Ryotaro, and he stumbled over his breath.
“--that’s not true. I have a job to do.”
“And when you’re home?” Ryotaro's shadow sighed exhaustedly. “Admit it, you’re afraid to
even speak to her.”
“That’s not…” But it was true, wasn’t it? Ryotaro did hide from his own daughter, maybe
sometimes without even realizing it. They barely talked outside of meals. And Ryotaro barely
attended meals.
No wonder Nanako gravitated toward Yu. Someone to play with her, to give her attention, to
make sure she was eating. Things Ryotaro should have been doing instead.
“You’re realizing it, aren’t you?” Ryotaro’s shadow asked. “I’m just a shell of a man, content
to run from everyone in my life until I have nothing left. I complain that my nephew doesn’t
trust me. But really, it’s the other way around.”
“I do trust Yu,” Ryotaro said. “Hell, I trust him more than I trust myself.”
“Is that really saying much?” Ryotaro’s shadow asked. “I can’t even protect Chisato, much
less my daughter. Besides, I didn’t believe a word he had to say in his defense. He’s just a
dumb kid caught up in things he doesn’t understand.”
“What do you want?” Ryotaro asked. He was tired of these games. He was tired of being told
things that deep down, he already knew. Things he had been trying to hide away from.
“Again, just making sure that nobody’s dying,” Ryotaro’s shadow said. “I’ll be going now.”
“Wait a minute, you’re leaving?” Ryotaro wasn’t going to be particularly sorry to see it go,
but if this shadow really was him, there was no reason for him to be leaving. “You’re just
going to leave Nanako to fend for herself?”
“Haven’t you been paying any attention at all?” Ryotaro’s shadow asked coldly. “I’m not
going to let Nanako burden me. She can take care of herself.”

Tears started gathering at the corners of Nanako’s eyes. She could clearly hear everything,
and Dojima had half a mind to kill his shadow, damn his health.
“How could you say that?” Ryotaro’s voice shook. “How the hell could you say that about
her? She’s seven. She’s not even half your size.”
“No, Dojima-san,” Ryotaro’s shadow said. “How could you say that? Isn’t that what you said
to Yu last night when he asked about Nanako’s safety? Imagine what could have been
avoided if you had just stopped to listen to him.”
The words hurt worse than Ryotaro’s injuries. He couldn’t even think of a word to say.
Ryotaro’s shadow left just as Nanako burst into heaving sobs.

After hours upon hours of working through the dungeon, they agreed to take a short break in
the real world to eat lunch. Almost as soon as they re-appeared in the Junes electronics
section, Adachi descended upon them.
“Why are you still here?” Yosuke demanded.
“I managed to get a shift patrolling the Junes,” Adachi said. “I was just so worried, you
know? How are they? Dojima and Nanako-chan, I mean.”
“We don’t know yet,” Goro snapped. “We haven’t gotten to them.”
“But they’re both still alive!” Chie said hopefully. “So that’s a plus.”
“We just came out to eat a quick bite before going back in again,” Kanji said. “You’d better
not be wasting our time.”
“Oh, sorry!” Adachi frowned. “How about this? I know I can’t be much help to you guys, but
I can at least buy you a nice large meal, right? That’ll be of some help.”
“That would be great,” Yu said. He had been more subdued ever since they met the shadow
version of Dojima. “Thanks, Adachi.”
“Anything for a friend.”
They followed Adachi into the food court. Goro pulled out his phone. There was no
abundance of missed calls, and, in this case, no news was good news.
He called Shinjiro’s number. Akihiko answered it for him and put the phone on speaker.
“Hey,” Shinjiro sounded more pained than he had the night before. “What happened to
starting every call with ‘hey Shinji, I’m bored out of my mind’?”
“You’re not funny,” Goro said.

Coughing. “I’m a little funny. But seriously, how’s it going?”
“We’re working as fast as we can,” Goro said. “I think we might be nearly half-way
through.”
“Pretty impressive. I hope–” Shinjiro wheezed. “--don’t wear yourselves out too much.”
“Our health is the least of our worries,” Goro said. “We still don’t know how much time we
have.”
“Your lack of self-care–” Another gasp. “--you’re killing me here.”
Goro wanted to smack him through the phone as they sat down at a table. Instead, he settled
for stony silence.
“Alright, alright. Bad joke.”
“And they say my jokes are bad,” Goro muttered.
“Okay… this I’ve got to hear.”
Goro reluctantly relayed the tale of his terrible joke at the Amagi Inn just a week before. It
was bizarre to think that they could be so lighthearted back then. The atmosphere at the table
was so heavy that Shinjiro was probably the most cheerful person in Goro’s presence. Even
Adachi was more somber than usual.
“Okay, that joke is terrible,” Shinjiro said. He coughed. “No... no punchline at all.”
Goro’s grip on his phone tightened. He was probably scratching the casing. “I’ll try to do
better next time.”
Goro spoke to Shinjiro their entire lunch break. He barely ate anything, even though Adachi
provided them with a fairly substantial meal probably costing him his entire wallet.
As they entered the electronics department, Goro was forced to end their call.
“I have to go,” he said. “We’re going back in.”
“Right. Talk to you later.”
“...Yeah.”
Goro hung up. Kanji gave him a confused look.
“Who were you speaking to that whole time?”
“A friend,” Goro said shortly. He wasn’t going to distract the others with his own problems,
even if Goro felt like his entire world was slowly collapsing underneath him.
Kanji was kind enough not to pry.

Shinjiro was exhausted. He could feel his body giving out on him, trying so hard to rest.
Shinjiro practically had to will his heart to keep beating.
Not yet, he told himself. He’d promised Goro he wouldn’t die without making sure that little
kid wouldn’t join him. He needed to know.
Another breath. Another high-pitched beep on the heart monitor.
Beep.
Breath.
Beep.
Breath.
It hurt. But he wasn’t a quitter.
“He’ll forgive you,” Aki said. “If you can’t hold on. You know that.”
“Shut up,” Shinjiro said.
Akihiko shut up.
Almost everyone was gathered in the hospital room. Even Yukari, who Shinjiro was pretty
sure should be in the middle of shooting for her show, was standing anxiously next to
Mitsuru.
“You guys…” Shinjiro took yet another shuddering breath through his ventilator. “Have
terrible bedside manner.”
There was a brief pause, and the only thing Shinjiro could hear was the heart monitor still
slowly beeping.
“I could tell you about the stupid thing Junpei did with his teammates the other day,” Yukari
offered.
Junpei was hilariously horrified by this. “Don’t. You’re going to kill him through secondhand embarrassment.”
Junpei looked like he swallowed a lemon as soon as he said the words. If Shinjiro had it in
him, he would have laughed.
Yukari continued with her story. Or, really, her version of Junpei’s story.
He could hold on just a little bit longer.

Nanako was crying, and Ryotaro didn’t know what to do. Not in the face of the horrible
realization of how badly he had screwed up. He didn’t deserve to call himself Nanako’s
father.
Well, one thing was for sure, he couldn’t just watch.
Ryotaro gently put his hand through Nanako’s hair. Nanako hiccupped, looking at Ryotaro in
alarm.
Damnit. Just how badly had he failed his girl?
“I’m sorry, Nanako,” Ryotaro said. “I’m so sorry.”
“Who was that man?” Nanako asked, obviously trying to swallow back sobs. “Do you… do
you really see me that way?”
“No, no, of course not,” Ryotaro said immediately. Nanako was never a burden. Ryotaro was
just a coward. “None of this is your fault. It’s mine, alright?”
“B-but… you said… that man said…”
“It’s complicated,” Ryoatro said. How could he phrase this without making it worse? “He
isn’t really me. He’s just… all of my worst feelings.”
Nanako’s expression shuttered. “So you do feel that way about me.”
“No, no, Nanako, I swear to you I don’t.” Ryotaro stumbled over his words. He never had
been good at this.
But he needed to get better.
“I’ve been… I’ve been a terrible dad, haven’t I?” Ryotaro whispered. “I’ve been letting my
emotions control me so much that I haven’t given you any time at all.”
“That’s… that’s not true,” Nanako said unconvincingly. “You took me to the festival, and the
fireworks! You got off work early for that!”
“Two times in the entire year,” Ryotaro said dryly. He continued running his hand through
Nanako’s hair. “Not exactly the best track record.”
“You’re a good dad,” Nanako said. As much as Ryotaro appreciated the attempt, it wasn’t
Nanako’s job to comfort him at all.
“You don’t have to try to make me feel better,” Ryotaro said. “I know that I haven’t been
spending enough time with you. I haven’t even really been taking care of you. What sort of
father does that?”
“You’re busy saving people,” Nanako said quietly. “I understand.”

“No,” Ryotaro said. “I don’t have any excuse. I’m sorry, Nanako. I’m sorry I failed you so
badly.”
“It’s okay.”
“It’s not.” Ryotaro tried to turn toward Nanako, and he hissed at the pain. “Look, honey, from
now on, I’m going to do better, alright? I’m gonna… I’m gonna try to be home more often…
and I’ll learn to do the laundry for you… and I’ll play with you when I can, instead of just
reading the newspaper all night.”
Nanako’s eyes widened. “Really?” Her face fell quickly. “Do you promise?”
If Ryotaro ever saw Chisato again, she would probably beat him up, and he would deserve it.
“I promise. And if I go back on it, you have permission to…” A small smile forced its way
onto Ryotaro’s face. “...kick me in the balls.”
Nanako giggled.
And then she burst into a fresh bout of tears.

“Nanako’s my only reason for living,” Dojima’s voice echoed above them as they hit the next
floor. “If anything happened to her, I’d find a way to join her. And maybe then, I could see
her and Chisato again.”
“Dojima-san…” Yukiko said softly.
“We have to keep moving,” Yu said, quickening his pace.
The fog on these floors were a dark red color, where it was obvious Nanako’s influence was
weaker. They took a few steps further and heard Namatame’s voice over-shadow Dojima’s.
“I discovered a new world,” he said. “I must save people. Yes, only I can.”
“The next time I see him, I don’t know what I’m going to do,” Rise said. Her eyes flashed
dangerously, and she glared at the rest of the group, as if daring them to disagree.
“I agree, but Nanako and Dojima-san should be our priority,” Naoto said.
Naoto could get Nanako and Dojima to safety. Goro would distract Namatame by ripping him
to shreds.
They reached yet another open area. Except this time, instead of Dojima’s shadow greeting
them, a giant cross stood in their way instead.
“Why are you getting in my way?” Namatame’s voice asked. “I’m… I’m going to save this
girl!”
The shadow was stronger than they expected. The group still turned it to dust.

But when they were done, everybody looked like they were on the verge of collapse. Even
Goro felt like he would probably pass out if he even attempted to summon his persona again.
“I hate to say this,” Kanji said. “But I think we should turn in for the night.”
“No,” Yu said. He tried to keep walking forward, but he stumbled. “We can keep going.”
“We really can’t,” Rise said. “I’m sorry, Yu-kun. I promise we’ll start again first thing
tomorrow.”
Technically, there was school tomorrow. Everyone came to an unspoken agreement to pretend
it didn’t exist.
“What if it’s too late?” Yu whispered.
“It won’t be,” Rise promised. “We’re really close to them. I can feel it. But we can’t die
now.”
When they stepped into the Junes electronics department, there wasn’t a single customer in
sight, and intercom chimed above them announcing the store was closing in five minutes.
Goro checked the time. It was nearly ten o’clock. They had literally spent their entire day in
that wretched place.
Goro called Shinjiro again, but he was already asleep for the night. Akihiko and Goro
exchanged a few words as he walked back to Kanji’s house. He hung up in time for Tatsumi
to lecture them on where they had been. Goro could barely hear the words.
Tatsumi still fed them, much to Goro’s alarm. Goro ate automatically, his body feeling the
pangs of his ignoring his lunch. When they were done eating, Goro immediately went to his
room and lay down on his futon. He wanted to speak to Shinjiro, to make sure he was alright,
but that wasn’t really an option at the moment.
Monster Cat curled up next to him. Goro forced himself to close his eyes.
He would be of no help to anyone if he didn’t sleep enough. He had to rest.
The pile of corpses only seemed to get higher and higher in his nightmares. Goro took one
look into Nanako’s unseeing eyes and woke up in a cold sweat.
Monster Cat was now fully curled up against Goro’s side. Goro rolled over and curled up
slightly around the cat himself. Monster Cat’s warmth was comforting in a way that sleep
could never be.
As Goro buried his hands into Monster Cat’s fur, he let himself feel younger than he really
was.

Nanako must have tuckered herself out after all that crying. She looked exhausted as she
rested against Ryotaro, clinging to his shirt for comfort. Ryotaro refused to admit that her

weight was probably damaging his injuries. Nanako needed all the comfort she could get in
this place.
Ryotaro’s shadow returned while Nanako slept, and Ryotaro eyed it warily. The shadow made
no move to antagonize Ryotaro, instead staring at Nanako with an exhausted expression.
“I’m not going to reject you, you know,” Ryotaro told the shadow. “My nephew told me…
something about a fight breaking out if I do.”
“Is that right?” Ryotaro’s shadow said, rolling his cigarettes between his fingers. “You’re
willing to admit that I’m you?”
“I would never say those things in front of Nanako—” The shadow’s eyes flashed, and
Ryotaro hastened to continue, “but there was truth to your words, so, yes, I guess a part of
you is me. So, please… I got the message… just leave us alone.”
Ryotaro’s shadow raised his eyebrows and nodded. “Alright, then. I’ll leave.”
Ryotaro blinked, and the shadow was gone. No fanfare. No magical creature to summon in
battle. Just, nothing.
Well, Ryotaro wasn’t exactly in any condition to battle anyway.
Unfortunately, during that conversation, Namatame had started to regain confidence. He
stood up and took a few steps closer to Ryotaro and his daughter.
Ryotaro’s hold on Nanako’s shoulder tightened.
“Can’t you see how beautiful this place is?” Namatame asked. “It even led you to make
amends with your daughter, to accept yourself.”
“That’s what you saw?” Ryotaro asked. “Don’t you realize this place kills people?”
“You’re wrong,” Namatame said. “I’m saving them. Why can’t you realize that this is a
sanctuary?”
“Go to hell.”
“I’ll make you see.” Namatame got to his feet, and his face became frenzied. “I’ll make you
understand–”
“If you lay a hand on my daughter, I will end you myself. You got that?” Ryotaro barked.
“You stay away from her.”
Namatame clearly wasn’t impressed. But he stayed away. That would have to be good
enough. Ryotaro wasn’t exactly in much of a position to fight.
The thought terrified him.

They tried to go to Junes the next morning.
The patrolling cops caught them in their school uniforms. They forced them to go to school,
threatening to call both their parents and the school.
They went to school.
It was probably the most agonizing single day of school of Goro’s life. The hours went by at
such a ridiculously slow pace that Goro had the displeasure of imagining hundreds of new
and unique ways Nanako and Dojima could be dying. All while learning about prepositional
phrases.
And his teacher had the gall to be unimpressed with him when she noticed he wasn’t paying
attention. He had half a mind to bite her head off. Didn’t she realize what was going on this
very minute?
Of course she didn’t. Barely anyone knew.
But finally, the school day ended. Goro sprinted out of the school-building, not even noticing
Akira waiting for him by the front entrance.
“Goro-kun, wait up!” Akira cried, running after him.
Goro forced himself to slow down. Akira gasped for breath as he walked alongside him.
“What’s going on?” Akira asked. “Did something happen?”
“It’s…” A lump clamped down on Goro’s throat, and he didn’t know why. He was keeping it
together for this long. Why was he going to break down in front of Akira, of all people?
“What is it?”
“I can’t…” Goro swallowed. He could. “Nanako-chan was kidnapped.”
Akira’s face slackened. “You mean that little girl? The one who likes Monster Cat?”
“Yes.”
“Oh my god,” Akira whispered. “Goro… I’m so sorry.”
“It’s not your fault,” Goro said.
“No, but–”
Goro couldn’t stay there anymore. He couldn’t listen to Akira try to comfort him while
Shinjiro was still dying and Nanako was still in danger. There wasn’t time.
And Goro was afraid that if he stayed any longer, he would become a sniveling mess.
“I have to go,” Goro said.

Akira blinked. He was obviously surprised and hurt by the sudden declaration. “Oh, um,
okay.”
Guilt wormed its way inside Goro’s throat, alongside that annoying lump that only seemed to
be growing. “I’m sorry. I just. I have to go.”
“No, I understand,” Akira said. “I just… if you need someone to talk to. I’m here.”
“Thank you,” Goro said.
He ran back to Junes, calling Shinjiro all the while.
“Is this… good news?” Shinjiro asked.
“From a certain point of view,” Goro siad. “School detained me, but Rise says that we’re
almost to them. We should be able to get them out by the end of today, if we play our cards
right.”
“Oh. That’s… that’s really good news.”
“If all goes well, I should be able to get to Iwatodai by tonight,” Goro said.
“And the kid will be okay?”
“I promise.” Goro refused to acknowledge any other option.
“That’s… that’s great.” Shinjiro’s voice shuddered. “You’re a really… really great kid. You
know that?”
“Don’t talk like that,” Goro said. “I’ll see you soon, alright?”
“Alright. Just making sure you know.”
Everyone was already waiting for Goro in the electronics section. Goro swallowed. “I need to
go.”
“Don’t do anything I wouldn’t do.”
Goro inhaled deeply. “Right. I’ll see you later.”
“Yeah… bye.”

When they returned to Nanako’s dungeon, Rise stopped short, looking surprised.
“Guys… I think Dojima-san’s shadow is gone.”
“What does that mean?” Yu asked, his voice immediately tense. “Is Dojima-san–”
“He’s still here,” Rise said. “I think he must have accepted his shadow.”

“You think?” Yosuke asked, looking surprised.
“Does it really matter?” Kanji asked. “Dojima’s alive, and we’ve got one less thing to worry
about.”
“Kanji’s right,” Naoto said. “We can theorize about it later, when we know everyone is safe.”
“Better yet,” Yosuke said. “We’ll ask Dojima himself.”
They hurried up the stairs to the next floor of the dungeon. The red fog faded back into blue
skies, and Nanako’s voice echoed above them.
“I’m scared… Mom… Big Bro… Where are you?”
“I’m coming!” Yu cried, even though he must have known Nanako couldn’t hear him.
More fighting. More running. The feeling of precious time slipping from their fingers
following their every step.
And then they finally reached the tenth floor. The giant gates adorned in gold could only
mean they had reached their destination.
“There she is!” Rise cried. “Nanako-chan is behind these gates!”
Yu pushed the doors open with all of his strength.

Namatame had gone from restless to dangerous. Nanako’s exhausted condition had only
gotten worse.
Ryotaro was suddenly very afraid of what was about to come next.
“They’re coming,” Namatame said unexpectedly. “They’re going to take her away.”
“They…?” Did Namatame mean the kids? How the hell did he know that?
“I can’t let them take her away,” Namatame said. “I must save her.”
Ryotaro grabbed hold of Nanako’s shoulder very tightly. Nanako’s hold on Dojima’s shirt
tightened. “Haven’t you been paying attention to what I’ve been telling you? This place kills
people!”
“You’re not going to stop me from saving her. You can’t stop me,” Namatame said. He ran up
to Ryotaro and grabbed Nanako.
“Dad!” Nanako cried.
His injuries be damned, Ryotaro jumped to his feet and socked Namatame in the nose.
Namatame punched him in the ribs. His already fractured ribs.

Ryotaro’s body crumbled against his will. He couldn’t keep his balance. He could barely stay
conscious.
“Get away from her,” Ryoatro said, stumbling toward Namatame with his teeth set. “Get the
hell away–”

Dojima lay sprawled in front of the staircase in the middle of a circle of stone angels.
Dojima-san!” Yu cried. He sprinted ahead of the group, and they hastened to follow. Yu got
down on his knees. “Please be alive, please–”
“Nanako,” Dojima gasped. “He took…”
“Big bro!” Nanako cried weakly.
Everybody looked up toward the sound of her voice. Namatame was holding Nanako in a
chokehold, his arm pressed against her neck. He walked backwards up the stairs.
“You m-mustn’t go!” Namatame said, looking every bit the coward Goro imagined him to be.
Yu’s expression hardened. His eyes flashed in a way that was almost frightening. “Let go of
Nanako.”
“I’m going to save this girl–”
“You’re choking her!” Goro shouted. “Is that the sort of bullshit you call salvation?”
“It’s definitely Namatame Taro,” Naoto said quietly. “We were right… he did come in here.”
“Let go of Nanako!” Yukiko shouted.
An unnatural grin spread across Namatame’s face. He laughed. “So, you’re the ones I saved.
Don’t worry. I’ll save this girl too.”
“Is he high?” Kanji asked. “Quit talking shit and let go of the girl!”
Namatame’s hold on Nanako tightened, and his face contorted into a scowl. Nanako let out a
strangled gasp.
“D-Don’t come near me,” Namatame said.
“Nanako-chan!” Chie cried.
“Everybody, calm down!” Naoto shouted. “We can’t predict his behavior.”
Naoto was right. This was officially a hostage situation, and the best way to deal with those
was to attempt to gain the trust of the hostage taker. If the culprit thought he was being heard,
he was more likely to calm down. It was like dealing with a particularly stubborn child, only
with extremely high stakes.

“We need to keep him talking,” Naoto said, voicing Goro’s thoughts. “If we can discern his
intentions, perhaps we can somehow deal with him.”
Well, if Goro was good for anything at all, it was talking.
“We don’t want to hurt you Namatame-san,” Goro said sweetly, in a way he probably hadn’t
spoken to anyone in years. “We want to help you.”
“Help me?” Namatame’s frightened expression didn’t change. “But you’re trying to take her
away from me.”
“Perhaps you can help us understand.” Goro hoped Namatame’s shadow would turn into a
monster of some kind. He’d enjoy destroying it. “I’m sorry if I misunderstood, but didn’t you
say something about saving her? We want the same thing.”
“Y-you do?” Namatame frowned.
“Why?” Yu asked in a dangerously even tone. “Why are you saving people like this?”
“I see them on that Midnight Channel,” Namatame said. “They’re.. They’re asking to be
saved.”
“Did I ever ask to be saved?” Rise asked. She sounded like she was on the verge of tears.
“Even if we had, you didn’t save us, damnit!” Kanji snapped. “You did the exact opposite!”
“If I hadn’t put you in the TV, how would you have ended up?” Namatame asked.
“Ended up… does he mean we wouldn’t have faced ourselves?” Yukiko asked.
That was the most ridiculous reasoning Goro had ever heard.
“But you guys nearly died!” Chie exclaimed.
“Exactly…” Namatame said.
“Enough of this,” Yosuke said. “Did you kidnap them? Yes or no.”
“Yes.”
Goro didn’t particularly care to hear the reasoning of a killer who thought he was saving
people through death. The only benefit of this inane conversation was that Namatame’s
attention was being taken off of Nanako.
“Why did you target residents who showed up on the television to save them?” Naoto asked.
“Why do they show up on the midnight channel?”
“They kept signaling me… to save them.”
Kanji growled. “You keep saying save this and save that, but all you were doing was
murdering people!”

Namatame looked surprised by that. “Murder… I was saving them.”
“I’m sure you thought you were,” Goro snapped, briefly forgetting himself. “Death is the
only way to salvation, isn’t it? When will you people learn that death isn’t some god to be
fucking worshiped?!”
“All you’re doing is ending innocent lives!” Yosuke agreed.
Namatame grinned. “If you want to think that, go ahead,” he said. “I know you chased us all
the way here… to kill… Well, too bad, because I’m going to save her.”
“Kill?” Yu whispered.
Nanako made a strangled sound as Namatame pressed down harder on her neck. Yu’s eyes
widened into proper panic.
“Just let go of her!” he shouted. “We’re not here to kill anyone!”
“Shut the hell up!”
And then a strange aura rose up around Namatame. His eyes turned yellow, and his grin was
even more unnatural than before. Was his shadow inhabiting his body? Since when had that
been possible? Was it because he wasn’t hiding from his true self?
“What a wonderful world… an unknown, unreachable place… filled with pleasant fog. I’m a
savior.”
“Is that… a shadow?” Yukiko asked.
“Big– bro–” Nanako wheezed. She coughed. “I can’t… breathe.”
“Nana-chan!” Teddie cried.
“We can’t waste any more time,” Yosuke said. He glanced at Kanji. “Let’s do this.”
Kanji and Yosuke charged Namatame’s shadow, pushing him back. In his alarm, he let go of
Nanako. She collapsed forwards into Yu’s arms, already unconscious.
Goro was moments away from taking his sword and impaling Namatame with it.
“Give.. her back…” Namatame gasped.
“Stay the hell away from us if you know what’s good for you,” Goro said.
“I’m… I’m going to save her!”
Namatame’s cry turned into a furious roar, and a huge wave of power pushed everyone
backwards. Yu clutched tightly onto Nanako as Namatame called more shadows to him,
turning him into an enormous angel creature.
Finally, something Goro could actually hurt.

“I–I’m going to save her,” Namatame’s booming voice came from the angel. “Don’t
interfere.”
“Take Nanako,” Yu told Teddie. He looked toward Yukiko and Chie. “You three need to
protect her and Dojima-san.”
Namatame’s shadow cast maziodyne. Teddie and Yosuke barely dodged out of the way in
time. Goro’s entire body crackled with burning electricity, but he stayed standing.
“Are you kidding?” Chie demanded. “I want to beat this guy up too!”
“Chie,” Yu said desperately. “Please.”
“We’ll take care of them,” Yukiko promised. She grabbed Chie by the hand and ran down the
stairs. Teddie followed close behind.
“Alright,” Kanji said. “Let’s teach this son of a bitch a lesson!”
The first half of the battle was more or less simple. Namatame’s attacks were extremely
powerful, but Goro and Yu’s personas had strong enough abilities to make sure nobody
collapsed mid-battle.
Namatame’s strength was still extremely impressive. Even Goro’s strongest attacks only
slightly weakened him. It was a game of endurance. Who would lose strength faster? Who
would dish out enough damage before someone died?
And then Namatame finally began to slump in exhaustion. Goro gasped for breath.
“Just die… already,” he said, readjusting his grip on his sword. His palm was slick with
sweat.
Namatame bowed his head, but he wasn’t dissolving into dust like a dying shadow would.
Instead, a red pulse light came out of his ridiculous peace-sign halo.
And Goro wasn’t in control of his body anymore.
I’m just trying to save her, Namatame’s voice pleaded in his ear desperately. Don’t you want
to save her too?
Of course Goro wanted to save Nanako. So why was he running to Namatame’s side? Why
was everyone else running alongside him? Yu wanted to save Nanako just as much as the rest
of them, so why were they turning against him?
He’s trying to kill her. You have to stop him.
Kanji was already attacking Yu. It was so tempting to follow his lead, but something still
stopped him.
Yu would never try to kill Nanako. He wasn’t a killer.

You thought he was.
No–
Goro’s mind went completely blank.
When he came to, he lay sprawled on the ground. His entire body hurt all over. Kanji helped
him up.
“What happened?” Goro asked, swaying in place. Kanji handed him a soma.
“I’m sorry,” Yu said, dodging one of Namatame’s physical attacks. “I had to–” He summoned
his persona and charged. “--defend myself.”
Shit.
“It happened to all of us,” Kanji said apologetically.
It was like the charm status effect, but at least when Goro was charmed, some part of him
knew that his actions were not his own. Namatame’s mind control was closer to what Maruki
had done. When Goro could barely control his thoughts.
It was sickening, but Namatame was gearing up for another attack. Goro couldn’t afford to
stand around reminiscing.
Goro summoned Hereward. The well placed megidolaon made Namatame lurch forward
even more than before.
“Care to do the honors?” Goro asked Yu. If anyone deserved it, it was him.
Yu’s expression was colder than ice.
“Persona!”
Yu’s persona sliced through Namatame’s shadow at least ten times. The shadow fell to the
ground and turned to stone before crumbling into nothingness.
Namatame stood in its place; his expression confused and frustrated. Goro wanted to punch
him.
“Dammit why…”
Goro slammed his fist into Namatame’s eye. Namatame stumbled backwards and collapsed.
“Goro-kun!” Naoto said sharply.
“What?” Goro asked coldly. “He deserved it.”
“Should’ve let Yu do it, if you ask me,” Kanji said.

But Yu was already sprinting down the stairs alongside Yosuke. Yukiko still cradled Nanako
in her arms. Goro and the others hastened to follow.
“Did she wake up?” Yu asked desperately. He took Nanako from Yukiko and held her close.
“N-no,” Chie said. Her voice wavered. “And Dojima-san isn’t waking up either.”
“This world must not be good for her,” Teddie said. “We need to get her out of here!”
“But we have to be careful with Dojima-san,” Naoto said. “Any unnecessary movement can
cause more harm than good.”
“Do we have any more goho-m’s?” Goro asked immediately.
“Yes, I think so,” Rise said. She reached into her pocket and pulled one out.
“Wait, before that…” Kanji sighed long-sufferingly and nodded toward Namatame. “I guess
we have to bring that asshole along too.”
“Kanji you try to carry Dojima-san on your shoulders,” Yu directed, taking charge. “Yosuke
and Yukiko, can you guys drag Namatame?”
Naoto showed Kanji the proper position to carry Dojima with as little additional injury to
Doijma as possible. Yukiko and Yosuke had each of Namatame’s arms wrapped around their
shoulders and dragged him down the stairs with very little care.
Yu never let go of Nanako.
Rise used the goho-m, and they arrived back at the entrance of the dungeon. The walk back to
the TV world entrance was agonizing at best. They had to slow down to keep everyone in
sight, and Nanako and Dojima still showed no signs of waking up.
“They’re both still alive,” Yu muttered to himself repeatedly. “They’re both alive.”
But for how long?
When they finally made it back to the Junes electronics department, Adachi was still lurking
in the corner.
“Oh my god, you’re back!” Adachi said. He sprinted up to them. “I was kinda worried you
guys weren’t coming out at all– Wait, is that Dojima-san? And Namatame?!”
“Adachi-san, call an ambulance at once,” Naoto said. “Dojima-san is extremely injured, and
Nanako isn’t waking up.”
Adachi already had his phone pulled out. “R-right.”
Nobody exchanged a word with each other until Dojima and Nanako were taken to the
hospital. Yu got on the ambulance alongside Nanako. The rest of the team would be forced to
walk.

As the ambulances pulled away from Junes, Goro pulled out his phone to call Shinjiro.
Twenty-five missed calls from an hour before and multiple text message notifications glared
up at him in the darkness of the night.
Goro frantically opened his messages.
Amada Ken: why wont u answer ur phone
Amada Ken: when u see this call me right away
Goro called Ken without a moment’s hesitation, praying it wasn’t what he thought it was.
Ken answered almost immediately, his voice impatient. “What took you so long—”
“Ken,” Goro interrupted, his voice thin. “What happened?”
“Goro…” Ken’s voice sounded choked, and he hesitated. “You’re too late. Shinjiro’s gone.”

First came shock.
The sort of nauseating shock that seeped into every pore of Goro’s body, making goosebumps
crawl up his skin and his breathing stutter. Goro stood fixated in place and told Ken he’d call
him back. He hung up and stared at his phone.
Gone. Shinjiro’s gone.
The word rang over in Goro’s head like a taunt. Gone. Gone. Gone.
Denial came as quickly as the shock. Ken said gone. Maybe Shinjiro had just run away from
the hospital. Or he moved out of the country. Or–
“Goro-kun?” Kanji rested a hand on Goro’s shoulder. Goro barely felt it. “Sorry to interrupt,
but… are you okay?”
“I–” The words "I'm fine" stuck on the roof of his mouth.
Gone. Gone. Gone.
Shinjiro’s gone.
“Goro?” Kanji asked. “Are you sick or something? You’re kind of freaking me out here.”
No. Shinjiro’s dead.
“I need… I need to go,” Goro said. He could barely hear his own voice over his ears ringing.
“Go? Go where? Aren’t you gonna go to the hospital with us?”

Kanji didn’t understand. He didn’t understand what was wrong.
Because Kanji didn’t know. Goro hadn’t told him. Goro hadn’t told anyone.
“My friend…” is dead. The terrible words that Goro couldn’t stand to spit out.
The others had stopped further ahead of the road. They were waiting for him. They were
probably wondering what was taking Goro so long.
“You’re friend…? What’s going on?” Kanji asked again. His voice was softer. Goro still
flinched.
Kanji didn’t know anything.
Goro shut his phone with a sharp click. He couldn’t look at Ken’s glaring messages any
longer. Instead, he looked Kanji in the eyes.
Kanji’s face was so worried.
Kanji had more important things to worry about than Goro’s problems.
“I have to go back to Iwatodai,” he said. “I’m terribly sorry for my rudeness.”
Kanji furrowed his eyebrows. “What the hell are you talking about?”
“Do I need to spell everything out for you?” Goro snarled. He stepped away from Kanji
furiously. “My friend is dead!”
Everybody stared at Goro in shock. Goro took a deep breath.
“Go see Nanako,” he said evenly. “I need to go back to Iwatodai. Keep me updated.”
He turned around and walked away. Nobody followed him.

Almost the entire team crowded the hospital hallway outside Nanako and Dojima’s rooms.
They’d been sitting and pacing for nearly two hours, waiting for any news about either of
them.
When they first arrived, Kanji explained Goro’s unexpected absence to Yu.
“A friend of his just died, apparently,” Kanji said quietly. “He’s going back to the city.”
Yu understood, but the reminder of death only injected more anxiety into his lungs. He
couldn’t lose Nanako.
Finally, finally, Adachi came back to the group. Everybody stood up eagerly.
“Huh?” Adachi said, sunding surprised. “You guys are still here?”

Where else would they be?
“Adachi-san,” Yukiko said before Yu could say a thing. “Did they find out anything?”
“Well, good news and bad news,” Adachi said.
“Start with the bad,” Yu said immediately.
“They aren’t sure what’s wrong with Nanako-chan,” Adachi said. “Which makes sense if this
is some weird TV phenomenon. They say they have to run more tests before they can figure
out what’s going on with her. And that goes to the perp too. Who knows when we’ll finally
get to hear his story.”
“And the good news?” Yosuke asked.
“Oh, right.” Adachi brightened. “Dojima-san’s awake. The doctors are fairly confident that
he should get out of it alive and well, although he might suffer some lasting pains and stuff
like that.”
Yu had half a mind to collapse in relief. Nanako was alive, and the doctors were at least
confident about Dojima’s recovery. As long as Nanako could fight through whatever aftereffects she suffered from the TV world, things would be alright.
Nanako was a fighter. She would make it.
Things were going to be alright.
“That’s a big relief,” Chie said. “Thank you so much, Adachi-san.”
“Always glad to be the deliverer of good news,” Adachi said. His grin faded into a serious
expression. “But you guys should be getting home. It’s getting late. The last thing we need is
you guys collapsing too.”
“He’s right,” Yosuke said. “Nanako-chan’s going to be fine. Acting all gloomy won’t change
anything.”
Chie grinned. “Oh, how about this? We should have a party for when Nanako gets out of the
hospital!”
“What– isn’t it a little early for that?”
The others began planning Nanako’s coming home party as they left the hospital. Yu stayed
behind.
Adachi stood next to Dojima’s hospital bed. He frowned in alarm when Yu stepped further
inside.
“Huh?” He said. “You’re still here?”

Yu swallowed back a sharp remark. Adachi could be tactless at the best of times, but his heart
was in the right place.
“Where else would I be?”
“I guess I thought you would go back home,” Adachi said. “If you’re worried about Dojimasan, you don’t have to. I’ll keep guard over him.”
“I want to talk to him,” Yu said flatly.
“O-oh.” Adachi stepped away, raising his hands in surrender. “In that case, I’ll just… give
you a moment of privacy.”
Adachi fled the room, and Yu took his place next to Dojima’s bed.
Yu had never seen Dojima out of his gray shirt and red tie. It was almost frightening to see
him dressed in a white hospital gown and forced to take bedrest. Bruises mottled his skin.
When Dojima opened his eyes, he looked pained to do even just that.
“Yu…?” Dojima asked. “…is Nanako…?”
“The doctors still don’t know,” Yu said, echoing what Adachi had surely already told him.
“Right.” Dojima squeezed his eyes shut. “Dammit.”
“Are you okay?” Yu asked. The last time he had seen Dojima outside of the TV world, he had
already been injured from his car wreck.
“You sure… I’m the one who needs that question?” Dojima asked.
“Nanako’s not allowed to have visitors yet,” Yu said.
“That’s not… what I meant.”
Had it only been two nights ago that Yu had sobbed into Yosuke’s shoulder, trying to stop his
life from unraveling entirely?
The tears weren’t there anymore. Yu felt like an old rag. Wrung out and left to dry.
“I’m fine,” Yu said.
“Yeah, right.” Even in its weakened state, Yu detected hints of regret in his voice. “I’m
sorry… if I had trusted you sooner… maybe we could have avoided all this.”
“It’s my fault,” Yu said immediately. “I didn’t trust you either. There was another note, and I
didn’t tell you about it.”
Dojima shifted his head to the side and grimaced. “No… I didn’t give you much reason to
trust me.”

Yu had so much more he wanted to say. He wanted to be angry. To exclaim that Dojima
should have trusted him sooner. He wanted to beg him to live. To recover as soon as possible.
Yu wanted to stay.
But Dojima was obviously too weak to maintain any meaningful conversation, and
exhaustion was truly starting to settle in Yu. Yu pulled up a chair and sat down. He clasped
his hands together and sat quietly by Dojima’s side.
The chair was uncomfortable, and Dojima fell asleep quickly. The hospital machines were
noisy and far from comforting.
It was still better than the chilling silence that waited for him at his home.

Ryotaro drifted back into consciousness when the door to his room shut behind a new visitor.
He forced himself to open his eyes.
Adachi tiptoed further into the room, holding a blanket.
Ryotaro never understood Adachi’s antics. His blasé carelessness even in the worst situations
made him an undependable partner at best. And his lack of respect for protocol made Ryotaro
reluctant to trust him with anything.
Maybe that’s why Ryotaro took slight comfort in injecting incredulousness in his tone when
he next spoke.
“What’re you doing?”
“Oh, Dojima-san!” Adachi said. He looked like Nanako being caught trying to sneak out of
bed past her bedtime. “Sorry. I didn’t mean to wake you up.”
God, Ryotaro missed Nanako. She was only a few rooms over, but she might as well have
been miles away, for what good it did him.
“Don’t tell me… you’re sleeping over.”
“Well, I don’t really intend to sleep, sir,” Adachi said. “But your nephew fell asleep before I
could tell him to hurry home, and I didn’t really want to move him.”
Ryotaro glanced to his left. Sure enough, Yu was slumped against the plastic chair he was
settled in. His eyes were shut, but his face looked set in a frown.
Poor kid looked exhausted even when he was sleeping.
At least he was finally getting some rest.
Ryotaro felt useless as Adachi tossed the blanket on top of Yu. Yu barely even stirred.

“There,” Adachi said. He frowned and glanced at the ceiling. “Though, I guess I will have to
wake him up for school tomorrow.”
“Let him sleep,” Ryotaro said.
“If you say so.”
Ryotaro exhaled shudderingly. “Adachi?”
“Hm?”
“Thanks…” Well, Dojima had been on a streak of swallowing his pride recently. “Sorry for
treating… you so harshly before.”
Adachi chuckled nervously. “It’s alright, Dojima-san.”
Ryotaro closed his eyes. “Haven’t been fair to you.”
“Well, apology accepted, I guess,” Adachi said. “It feels kind of weird to have you
apologizing to me when you’re confined to the hospital bed like that.”
“You’re not hearing it again.”
“Aw, come on,” Adachi said pleadingly. “Admit it. You might seem all scary and harsh on the
outside, but inside, you’re just a big softy, right?”
Ryotaro was exhausted. He let himself fall back asleep before he had to answer.
