This was the fourth time Goro had taken the train between Inaba and Iwatodai.
This ride was by far the longest.
After abandoning the others, he had only briefly stopped by the Tatsumi residence to take his
already packed suitcase. He explained the situation to Tatsumi in as few words as possible.
And then he left.
It was late enough that it was already dark outside. Goro sat with his back ramrod straight
against his chair, staring at the emptiness of the scenery as it zipped past.
A few seats ahead of him, a child was happily exclaiming to her parents about someone she
had played with that day. Her parents smiled and nodded as they listened to their explanation.
They looked so normal. Everyone on the train looked as though this was any other day to
them.
Goro stayed focused on the window. It was easier to control his anger that way.
He briefly called Ken back after he was done reeling.
“Tell me she’s okay,” Ken said quietly. “Tell me that little girl’s okay.”
“I don’t know,” Goro said. “I left as soon as I heard. She’s in the hospital.”

Judging by the stony silence that followed, that answer wasn’t good enough. It wasn't good
enough for Goro either.
“Mitsuru already had his body moved to a funeral home,” Ken said.
Goro closed his eyes. “Okay.”
“What time will you get here?”
“Probably around midnight.”
“…I’ll tell Mitsuru.”
“Right.”
There wasn’t much either of them felt able to say after that. Goro hung up soon after. He
called the others and had a conversation of the same vein with each of them. By the time he
was done, he was completely exhausted.
It still didn’t feel real. None of it felt real.
The train was nearly at Iwatodai when Goro received a text from Kanji.
Tatsumi Kanji: dojima will pull thru. Still dont know what’s wrong with nanako
Goro stared at that message for a long time. As relieved as he was that Nanako wasn’t going
to lose a father, if he had to choose, he’d rather have good news concerning Nanako. This
unknown quantity served as very little solace to him.
Tatsumi Kanji: also ma wants to know when u get to a friends place
Tatsumi Kanji: she’s worried bout traveling this late at night
Goro forced himself to respond.
Akechi Goro: okay thank you for your concern
The train slowly lurched to a stop. Goro took his suitcase and stepped off. Mitsuru said that
someone would be waiting for him by the steps of the station, so Goro headed outside of the
station and looked around.
Akihiko sat at the bottom step.
Of all the people Goro expected to pick him up, Akihiko was the last on his list.
Goro lifted his suitcase and walked down the steps. He silently stood next to Akihiko.
Akihiko looked up at him and sighed.
“Alright,” he said, slapping his knees and standing up. “Let’s go.”
Goro swallowed. “Akihiko—“

“Don’t,” Akihiko said. “I-I can’t hear any more apologies.”
So Goro didn’t. He followed Akihiko to his apartment. Akihiko fumbled with his keys, but
his hands didn’t shake as he unlocked the door.
The apartment was just as it always had been, apart from some clutter. A cutting board and
knife sat by the kitchen sink. A first aid kit sat on the table.
“You don’t mind sleeping on the couch again, right?” Akihiko asked. “Wait—shit. You
probably haven’t eaten dinner yet, have you?”
“I’m not hungry,” Goro said.
“Yeah.” Akihiko’s expression closed off. “I don’t think… I’m not sure there’s any easy way
to make anything with the food in the fridge either. I’ll buy something tomorrow.”
Akihiko began to head down the hall to his bedroom. Before opening the door, he glanced
back toward Goro. “Help yourself if you get hungry. Call me if you need anything.”
“Okay,” Goro said. “I will.”
Akihiko nodded and entered his room. The door echoed shut behind him.
Goro sat down on the sofa and texted Tatsumi to inform her he was safe. He then went into
his contacts and clicked Shinjiro’s number.
Ring… ring… ring…
Why was he doing this? Why was Goro doing the one thing that was sure to make him hurt
more when the inevitable finally came?
Ring… ring…
Why was any of this happening?
“This is Aragaki Shinjiro. For whatever reason , I can’t come to the phone at this time. Leave
a message at the beep. Or don’t. I don’t care.”
Goro hung up immediately.
He had just wanted to hear Shinjiro’s voice again.
“Hey Shinji,” Goro whispered at his still-open phone. He stared at Shinjiro’s number and shut
his eyes. “I’m bored out of my motherfucking mind.”

Apparently, Shinjiro’s will wasn’t very specific regarding funeral arrangements. Akihiko
allowed Mitsuru to arrange the ceremony.
“It will be in a few days, probably,” Akihiko said when Goro asked the following morning.

“Was he—” Goro swallowed back the bile in his throat. “Was he in pain?”
Akihiko shrugged. “Sometimes it looked like he was fighting for every breath he had. But he
fell asleep right before the end. One minute he was sleeping, and the next… well, you know.”
He was asleep. That was good. He wasn’t suffering in the end.
Another, bitter part of Goro wondered what it would be like to have the luxury of dying while
asleep. To be surrounded by friends and family before passing.
He hated himself for it. Shinjiro was dead, and the only thing he could think of was himself.
His grief. His jealous thoughts.
But it was hard to think of anything else. Part of Goro still refused to acknowledge that
Shinjiro was dead at all. A terrible, hopeful part of him thought Shinjiro would enter through
that door and make another snarky comment. That he’d apologize for not being there when
Goro first arrived.
It never happened.
The apartment was painfully quiet throughout the rest of the morning. Akihiko tried to be a
good host, but neither he nor Goro could think of anything to talk about. Eventually, Akihiko
retreated into his bedroom, and Goro tried to read one of his schoolbooks as a distraction.
Still no news about Nanako.
In the afternoon, presumably after classes, Minato reached out and asked Goro if he wanted
to meet at the park. He and Ryoji apparently needed to clear their heads, and they were
inviting everyone else along too.
Goro knocked on Akihiko’s bedroom door.
“Come—” Akihiko grunted. “—in.”
Akihiko was dripping in sweat and doing push-ups. The small punching bag leaning against
the wall looked to be beaten into a pulp.
“I’m going on a run,” Goro told Akihiko. “Do you want to come along?”
Akihiko didn’t even hesitate as he continued doing push-ups. “No, I’m fine,” he said. “Have
fun.”
Goro bit back a concerned comment about Akihiko overworking himself. He knew it
wouldn't be welcome.
Aigis and Junpei took up Minato’s offer. They met at the front of the entrance. Ironically
enough, Ryoji and Minato were the last ones to arrive.
“No offense, but why are you here, Aigis?” Junpei asked. “I mean. You’re not one for
exercise.”

“I was hoping the beauty of the park would distract me,” Aigis said. She glanced behind her.
It really was a beautiful day. The sky was as blue as it ever had been. Even the trees that had
lost all their leaves had a sort of withered beauty about them.
“Didn’t work, did it?” Junpei asked.
“No.” Aigis frowned. “It makes me… angry.”
Minato and Ryoji finally arrived. With the colder months, Ryoji once again wore his favorite
yellow scarf.
“Hi guys,” Ryoji said in faux cheerfulness. “Thanks for doing this with me. And Goro-kun!
Small town life still doing it for ya?”
“Oh, Goro-kun, pardon my rudeness,” Aigis said. “I barely realized you were here.”
“I’ve missed Iwatodai,” Goro said. This was the same park Shinjiro had found him in after
Ikutsuki betrayed them. Had Shinjiro ever realized how much that moment impacted him?
Had Goro known, until this exact moment, how much hope Shinjiro had given him? “Sorry I
didn’t make it back sooner.”
“We understand,” Minato said. His voice lacked some of the emotion it had gained over the
past two years.
“Let’s just go,” Junpei said. “Sorry. I can’t deal with this emotional shit right now. I just want
to let off some steam.”
So they went.

“Sorry, I couldn’t bring myself to make dinner,” Akihiko said that evening. He pulled packets
of frozen ramen from the freezer. “I bought these a few hours ago.”
“I can prepare them, if you want,” Goro said.
“No.” Akihiko scowled. “I can’t… I can’t lie down and do nothing. I know preparing frozen
food takes no effort at all, but that’s why I can’t… I can’t refuse to do even that.”
The ramen was bland and oddly flavored. It barely tasted like good ramen at all. It was
nothing like the noodles Shinjiro took care to season and boil to the perfect consistency.
Goro wanted to throw his bowl against the wall.

Goro wore a suit for the funeral.
He hadn’t worn a suit since Chidori’s funeral. Still, he didn’t even need to look in the mirror
as he tied his tie. The movements were as instinctual as they were when Goro had to wear

that same striped tie for his everyday attire.
Shinjiro would have attended his funeral in that same red coat he wore every day.
Overwhelmed, Goro punched the mirror. Pieces of glass shattered out of place where his fist
connected with its smooth surface. The shards sliced through Goro’s skin. Blood dripped
from his fist, nearly staining his white shirt.
“Goro?!” Akihiko shouted. He sounded scared. “Are you okay?”
Were any of them okay? “I’m fine,” Goro said. He went to the kitchen where the first aid still
sat on the table.
“You’re bleeding,” Akihiko said. He sounded almost furious as he pulled the gauze out of the
first aid kit. “Goddammit, Goro. You’re hurt. That’s not fine at all. Why are you so allergic to
asking for help?”
“Well, excuse me for thinking that we had bigger things to worry about,” Goro said.
“You really think that Shinji would want you to be a martyr on his behalf?” Akihiko snapped.
He grabbed Goro’s hand and inspected the injury.
“Well, I don’t know, do I?” Goro asked coldly. “He’s too fucking dead to ask.”
Akihiko flinched backwards and stared at Goro with a stunned expression.
“He cared,” Akihiko said. “He cared so damn much about all of us. Too much, if you ask me.
So don’t act like he wouldn’t be worried.”
Goro’s anger only flared higher.
“I never asked for him to care about me,” he said. “Maybe, if he had just left me alone, I
wouldn’t be feeling this way right now!”
Akihiko’s mouth turned to a thin line. For a minute, Goro half-wondered if Akihiko was
going to hit him.
“Well, he was just as much a bastard in life as he is in death, I guess,” Akihiko said. “Stay
still and let me clean your wound.”
Goro resisted the urge to yank his hand away. If he caused too much drama over a single
injury, they were going to be late to the funeral. More shame was the last thing Goro needed.
They were still almost late.
Goro didn’t actually recognize all of the guests. Shinjiro made friends in the last two years of
his life. Coworkers at his restaurant, friends of Akihiko that got to know him in turn, even a
few old classmates who he reconnected with. It wasn’t what anyone would call the largest
social sphere, but it was more than Goro had been expecting.

Had Goro really been so distant that he hadn’t known about these people? Some of them
spoke about Shinjiro as if they had known him their entire lives. One of the former
classmates reminisced with Akihiko about a time Shinjiro stole the teacher’s entire printed
stack of tests in the hopes of avoiding the exam altogether.
It sounded like something Shinjiro would do. It didn’t change that Goro knew nothing about
it.
Emiko and Ken attended the funeral, of course. Emiko hadn’t known Shinjiro extremely well,
but she was still familiar with him through association with Goro and Ken.
“I’m glad you could make it,” Ken said stiffly, but Goro had known Ken long enough to
recognize the traces of resentment in his eyes.
“I’m sorry for your loss,” Emiko said, looking close to tears herself.
“I am too,” Goro said. He looked at Ken while he said it.
Ken’s expression shuttered. He glanced away in a fashion that screamed we will talk about
this later.
As long as they didn’t cause a scene during the ceremony, Goro didn’t care what they talked
about.

They didn’t cause a scene during the ceremony.
They may have caused a scene immediately after, as guests were leaving.
“How’s Nanako?” Ken asked.
“I haven’t gotten any news yet,” Goro said.
“Is she going to die?”
“Die?” Emiko’s voice wavered in anxiety. “Who’s dying?”
Sometimes, Goro wondered if it would behoove them to just tell Emiko the whole truth about
the cognitive world. It would save some inherent distance between her and the other two.
But, knowing Emiko, she would want to help fight the shadows, and she had never showed
any signs of having the potential to summon a persona. She would only put herself in danger.
“My friend’s little sister was kidnapped,” Goro said, sticking with as much of the truth as
possible. “They recovered her, but she is currently comatose.”
Emiko was stricken. “That’s horrible!”
“That’s why Goro stayed in Inaba later than he intended,” Ken said. He sounded physically
pained. “He nobly wanted to make sure she was found first.”

The way Ken said it, one would assume that being noble was a capital offense.
Emiko noticed too.
“Are you two fighting?” She asked.
“Not last I checked,” Goro said, glancing at Ken warily. “I wish I could have gotten to
Iwatodai sooner too.”
“I’m sorry your brand-new friends were too important for you to leave.”
“I’m sorry?” Goro asked, absolutely flabbergasted. “Did you miss the part where a sevenyear-old was in mortal peril?”
“Did you miss the part where our friend died, and you weren’t even there to say goodbye?!”
“I spoke to him on the phone every fucking day.”
“And I was actually there!” Ken looked about ready to punch Goro. “What happened to being
here, huh? You promised.”
“I couldn’t exactly predict the entire world was going to go to hell around the same time he
collapsed, could I?”
“You’re blaming him for this?”
“His timing was god-awful.”
“He waited for you,” Ken said angrily. “And you never showed.”
“Guys—” Emiko said.
“He wanted me to stay.” Goro stepped up to Ken threateningly. “Something you seem to fail
to understand.”
“Maybe if we all took a deep breath—”
“You don’t understand how alone I felt,” Ken said. “I thought you would be there, and you
weren’t. You didn’t even call to see how I was doing.”
“First I fail Shinjiro, and now I’m failing you.” Goro was moments away from punching Ken
in the nose. “Is there anyone else you would like to add to that list while you’re at it?”
“You think it’s just me?” Ken asked. “Everyone wanted you to be there. And now the girl you
worked so hard to save might not recover anyway—“
And then Goro did punch him in the nose.
Ken stumbled backwards before launching himself forward and punching Goro in the gut.
Goro was about to respond in turn, but Emiko shoved herself in between the two.

“Stop, stop!” Emiko shouted. “What are you doing?”
Blood was already dripping from Ken’s nose and onto his suit. Goro leaned over and
breathed heavily. He wasn’t sure if his heart was pumping from rage or adrenaline.
“What is going on?” Mitsuru asked, pulling herself away from another conversation.
Neither Goro nor Ken said anything. Emiko glanced between them helplessly.
“Well?” Mitsuru asked. “Are any of you going to be mature about this?”
“It was my fault,” Ken said suddenly. His voice was hoarse and choked, and Goro looked up
quickly. As angry as he felt, he hadn’t wanted to accidentally kill Ken in the process.
But no. It wasn’t his injury impeding his voice. It was the tears rolling down his face.
“Ken?” Mitsuru asked.
“I… I was out of line,” Ken said. “I provoked him.”
“That’s very honest,” Mitsuru said. She didn’t ask what Ken had said to cause Goro to punch
him in the face. Goro was glad to avoid any needless comfort. “But Goro, I expect better
from you. When has fists ever ended a conflict?”
“When you knock your attacker unconscious,” Goro said. He nursed his fist reluctantly. It
was going to need extra care when he and Akihiko got back to the apartment.
“Not helpful,” Emiko whispered.
“I don’t know what you two were fighting about, but you are both mature enough to handle it
with words,” Mitsuru said. “Work this out.”
Ken nodded. Goro glanced at the ground so that he wouldn't have to look at Mitsuru’s
disappointed expression.
“So?” Emiko asked. “Are you going to make up now?”
“I’m sorry,” Ken said. “I don’t know… you were right to stay. I don’t know what I was
thinking.”
Despite the obvious remorse on Ken’s face, it was clear that a part of Ken still wanted to
blame Goro for everything.
“I shouldn’t have punched you,” Goro said. “Sorry.”
“Let’s just avoid making promises we can’t keep from now on,” Ken said. “It might save us
some trouble.”
“Is that a promise?” Goro asked dryly.
Ken glowered.

Death opened old wounds and created new ones. When it came to a death like Shinjiro’s,
with no clear killer, the ridiculous urge to blame anyone who slighted him was a very real
feeling.
A horrible, nasty part of Goro wanted to blame Ken’s mother for Shinjiro’s death. If she had
never died, Shinjiro would never have started taking those suppressants in the first place. He
would still be there, probably telling them to stop acting like toddlers.
Goro never said the words out loud, as much as that nasty part of him wanted to. Ken would
never forgive him.
Goro did understand why Ken was angry at him, but he didn’t regret staying to save Nanako.
Goro did regret not being there for Shinjiro.

Goro stopped coming to school. That, or he was doing an expert job of avoiding Akira.
It wouldn’t be that much of a surprise if he was avoiding Akira. Goro had left in a hurry on
Monday, not explaining what was bothering him so much. And it was obvious something had
been bothering him.
Maybe he was sick. Or maybe something terrible happened.
Either way, Akira was becoming sick with anxiety. The more days that passed without Goro
miraculously reappearing, the more Akira wondered if he would have to take matters into his
own hands.
Finally, Akira went to Tatsumi Textiles and asked Tatsumi-san himself.
“Goro-kun?” Tatsumi asked. “Oh dear, he didn’t tell you?”
Akira shouldn’t have been disappointed. He knew something was wrong.
“Tell me what?”
“His good friend died the other day, apparently,” Tatsumi said. “He returned to the city for
the funeral. He should be coming back soon, though. Feel free to play with the poor cat in the
meantime.”
Good friend? Dead? How? When?
No wonder Goro had seemed so distracted the other day. Akira would be distracted too if
Goro suddenly died without warning.
Still, why hadn’t Goro told Akira himself?
Come to think of it, maybe Akira should have texted him. Whoops.

Akihiko started to behave… oddly normally after the funeral.
Oddly in the sense that he was returning to his normal life. It was as if Shinjiro hadn’t died at
all.
“The last thing Shinji would want me to do is mope around all day,” Akihiko said when he
saw Goro’s perplexed expression. “I have school to catch up on.”
“He hasn’t been dead for a week,” Goro said.
“I know how to count the days.”
“He hasn’t been dead for a week,” Goro reiterated. “And you’re already getting over it?”
Akihiko’s eyes flashed. “Don't think for a minute this is me getting over it,” he said. Goro
almost flinched. Instead, his expression twitched violently. “Shinji lived his last days to the
fullest. I’m not going to spit on his memory by wasting mine.”
An open envelope sat on the kitchen table. Goro recognized Akihiko’s name written in
Shinjiro’s untidy scrawl on its white surface.
Was that one of the letters Shinjiro had passed out to the group back in January last year?
Back when they still genuinely thought the world might end?
Goro had left his in his room in Inaba. The horror of the death was too raw, too fresh. It
barely occurred to Goro that he might want to read the letter at all. How many months had he
spent considering the letter a part of a grim future? A future that Goro didn’t want to think
about until that time came?
It was that time. Goro still found himself oddly reluctant to even think about opening the
letter.
He couldn’t look at it until he got to Inaba anyway. Goro would worry about it then.

Goro returned to Inaba that Friday. As much as he wanted to stay in Iwatodai, both school
and the Dojimas’ conditions drew him back.
Shinjiro’s letter also burned a hole into Goro’s mind. It was an itch he couldn’t get rid of, and
Goro had a feeling he would never be able to rest until he read its contents.
Neither of the Tatsumi’s were home. A note on the table said that Tatsumi had gone grocery
shopping. Kanji must be spending time with the others, likely hanging out at the hospital and
waiting for good news on Nanako.
Goro went straight to his room. Monster Cat meowed at him, perched on top of his climbing
toy.

Goro would pet him later. For now, Goro needed to at least make sure that the letter was still
safely inside the drawer Goro hid it in. He dropped his suitcase on the floor and yanked open
the dresser drawer. Ken’s action figure still sat on top of Ryoji’s scarf. Goro shoved the scarf
to the side.
Goro’s copy of Shinjiro’s will still sat at the bottom of the drawer. Goro had read it about a
thousand times the past two years, but he hadn’t wanted to take Shinjiro’s cooking knives
back to Inaba. It felt rude to just take something that used to belong to Shinjiro and leave.
Akihiko would deliver them when he was ready.
Shinjiro’s letter, on the other hand, was nowhere to be seen.
Goro wondered if this was what Shinjiro felt every time Goro did something lifethreateningly stupid. Every time Goro was somewhere he wasn’t supposed to be.
The letter wasn’t where it was supposed to be. And, as Goro began ransacking his dresser
drawers, he found that it wasn’t anywhere at all.
Where the fuck was it?
“Looking for something?”
Goro spun around, still clutching a shirt he had just yanked from his drawer. Monster Cat
hissed violently.
Tsuyoshi stood in the back corner of Goro’s room, holding a slightly wrinkled envelope
between two fingers.
“Give that back,” Goro whispered. His rage made his entire body shake. “You fucking
bastard, give that back right now.”
“Or what?” Tsuyoshi asked, smirking. “You’ll kill me? I’d like to see you try.”
Goro’s sword was tucked away in his closet. There was no way Goro would be able to reach
it in time. Not before Tsuyoshi pinned him down, or worse, did something to the letter.
“What do you want?”
“I can’t extend my apologies for what happened?” Tsuyoshi asked. “I heard about poor
Shinjiro. But, then again, it was the little brat’s fault he was dying in the first place.”
Every survival instinct in Goro screamed to stay still. To not move a muscle.
Goro was never good at listening to his survival instincts.
He sprinted forward and grabbed Tsuyoshi’s tie. If he could pull it tightly enough, maybe he
could strangle him–
Tsuyoshi brought his hand around Goro’s neck. Goro finally froze.

“Don’t go so mad at me for quoting what you said yourself,” Tsuyoshi said. “The meaner side
of you had a lot of unsavory things to say about your little friend, huh?”
“You don’t have any right to say anything about him,” Goro snarled. He grabbed for the
letter, but Tsuyoshi yanked his hand away just as Goro’s fingers brushed against the paper.
His hold on Goro’s neck tightened as he tutted. “Uh-uh. Grabbing is rude.” With a single
hand, he ripped open the seal of the envelope and pulled out the letter. He angled it so that
Goro couldn’t see a single word. “Now, let’s see what dear Shinjiro had to say to you.”
If it wasn’t already getting difficult to breathe, Goro would have held his breath. As it was,
Goro’s breaths sounded more like short, angry gasps.
“Goro,” Tsuyoshi read. “You probably hate my guts right about now– very true –but I hope
you don’t burn this letter until after you read its contents… Now, there’s an idea.”
“No,” Goro wheezed. He scratched at Tsuyoshi’s arm, trying to get him to loosen his grip on
his throat. Tsuyoshi didn’t even falter. He pinned Goro against the wall. Stars flooded Goro’s
vision. “Don’t. I’ll burn you. If you even think about burning that letter–”
Monster Cat tried to launch himself onto Tsuyoshi, but Tsuyoshi didn’t even blink at the cat’s
claws in his leg.
“You know, I really liked that stunt you pulled back at my little shack,” Tsuyoshi said
conversationally. “A tracker? Very cute. You know the best part? I wasn’t even expecting
such forwardness. I bet you weren’t expecting this, either.”
Goro didn’t beg. But as Tsuyoshi began crumpling the letter in his fist, he was starting to feel
frantic.
“Please,” Goro gasped. “Don’t do it. I won’t poke around in your business ever again, just
don’t burn it–”
Tsuyoshi shushed him. “There, there, Goro-kun,” he said. His eyes still skimmed the letter
with a vengeance. “Don’t cry. All of this whining is really becoming pathetic.”
“You bastard–” It was getting harder and harder to breathe, and his voice was barely audible.
“I’ll kill you. If you don’t give me that letter, I’ll–”
The letter burst into flames.
Goro screamed.
“Well, I’d hate to be killed,” Tsuyoshi said. He dropped the ashes of the letter on the floor.
“There you go. I’m sure you’ll be able to put that back together.”
“I’m home!” Tatsumi called out from the front of the house.
Tsuyoshi dropped Goro. His entire body hit the ground with a painful thump. Goro coughed
and gasped for breath. He needed oxygen.

He needed Shinjiro.
“Whoops, maybe I did too much damage,” Tsuyoshi said. “Don’t want you dying quite yet.”
Tsuyoshi snapped his fingers. The pain in Goro’s neck went away immediately.
Goro saw red. “Get the fuck out.”
Tsuyoshi raised his hands in surrender. “Fine, fine, I’m going.”
Goro was about to scream at Tsuyoshi to leave, but there was a knock on his door.
“Goro-kun?” Tatsumi asked. “I heard voices. Is everything all right in there?”
Goro turned back toward Tsuyoshi. He was gone. It was just Goro and a small pile of ash.
Goro could still feel the phantom pain of fingers wrapped around his throat. He continued
taking overly deep breaths, trying to relish the feeling of air properly entering his lungs.
He stared at the remains of Shinjiro’s letter and tried not to feel the burning rush of emotion
that came with it.
Shinjiro’s last words to Goro. Gone. And Goro would never know what they said.
Monster Cat meowed, almost sounding concerned. Goro remembered the person standing
behind the door.
“I’m–I’m fine, Tatsumi-san,” Goro said.
He used to be such a better liar than this.
“Can I come in?” Tatsumi asked.
Goro stood up and let Tatsumi into the room. Tatsumi frowned when she saw Goro’s face.
“Do they feed you in the city?”
They used to.
“I wasn’t very hungry,” Goro said.
Tatsumi still looked unsettled. “Why do I smell smoke?”
Not to worry, Goro did not say, it’s only the ashen remains of the last words my dead friend
wanted me to read after he died. It wasn’t like it was my last chance to hear from him or
anything. I’ll clean it up.
Goro opened his mouth to say that he was burning a candle.
Instead, he burst into tears.

Goro tried to stop, but the harder he tried to keep the tears at bay, the more furiously they
poured down his cheeks. It was almost harder to breathe normally than when in Tsuyoshi’s
chokehold.
Goro hadn’t cried like this in years.
Without warning, Tatsumi gently wrapped her arms around Goro. Goro stiffened, but she
didn’t move. She just stood there, gently rubbing his back in a way that felt good. It felt like
comfort.
“Would you like me to stop?” Tatsumi asked quietly.
Goro almost said yes, that he wanted to be left alone, that he didn’t deserve this kind of
comfort, that, that—
But he was crying too violently to say anything at all. He unthinkingly grabbed onto
Tatsumi’s kimono for support and shook his head.
Please don’t go, he thought between tears. Oh god, Shinjiro, why did you go?
Grief and rage and hate and love pushed its way out of Goro. Something was furiously trying
to wash the emotions from his system, trying to make him feel as if there was nothing there at
all.
It wasn’t working. The emotions were tangling together, like Goro’s horribly mishandled
yarn when he tried crocheting. They created a painful knot in his stomach, refusing to
become undone.
Without thinking, Goro collapsed to his knees, causing Tatsumi to sit down with a quiet huff
of surprise. She didn’t retract the hug, and Goro buried his face into her shoulder,
consequences be damned. He couldn’t care anymore, couldn’t hold himself up anymore. Not
anymore. Not anymore.
Shinjiro was dead. He was gone and he would never come back. Goro would never hear his
voice again, never bicker with him again, never even worry about his health again. Shinjiro
was dead, and Goro was trapped in a world that hated him. A world that yanked away every
part of Goro that really mattered and left him to die an empty husk of himself.
Goro handled the emotions the only way he knew how.
He screamed. He screamed until he had no air left to give. He screamed until his tears
became nothing but hiccupping sobs.
Tatsumi didn’t flinch away. She didn’t retreat from Goro’s agony.
She stayed.
That only made the knot inside Goro tighten. Tatsumi shouldn’t stay. Tatsumi shouldn’t want
anything to do with him.

Goro was a vile, evil person. He had killed for a living without an ounce of remorse.
Shinjiro was only a kid who made a terrible mistake.
And now Shinji was dead. Goro was alive.
That felt like the greatest crime of them all.

“She’s regained consciousness, but we can’t let our guard down yet. All we can do is

Goro could not kill the doctor. Goro could not maim the doctor. Goro could not shout at the

“I should be there,” Dojima said. “I feel so useless like this.”

“Oh yeah,” Chie said. “People are starting to say that the fog is carrying diseases and stuff.

“At this point, who knows what’s true?” Yosuke asked grimly.

Distracting oneself from the problem did not make the problem go away.

She wasn’t improving. Not in the way that everyone had hoped she would. She was waking

Adachi already ran after Dojima, but Goro still remembered where Namatame’s room was

When they arrived at Namatame’s hospital room. Dojima was already being held back by two

Dojima was losing his fight, trying and failing to free himself from the officers’ grasps. “Let

Far less responsibly, he and the other two officers dragged Dojima-san away, leaving the door

“Don’t act so surprised,” Goro said. “Anyone would have done the same.”

“He must have known that there was no way Namatame was going to be convicted,” Yosuke

“That’s not right!” Yukiko protested.
“The world’s not right!” Goro wanted to claw his heart out of his chest to make the pain go
away. “Do you think we live in a fantasy land where the heroes always win and the bad guys
always get locked away? If things were right, we wouldn’t have need for heroic fantasies to

Rise looked flummoxed. “But–”

A large thump came from the inside of the room. Nobody spared each other a glance before
Yu shoved the door open. They ran inside.
Namatame was on his knees next to his hospital bed. A massive television stood near the wall
a few feet away from him. A cold gust of air came from the open window.
“What are you doing?” Yu asked. His voice held no inflection, but it was so cold that nobody

“You want to run away?” Yu asked. “You’re such a heartless coward that you’re too afraid to

“No, I didn’t, I–”
Buzzing TV static filled the room. Everybody stared at the massive television as Namatame’s

“I failed to save her. It’s because you got in my way.”
“What?” Yosuke asked. “I thought we already defeated his shadow.”
“No… come to think of it, Namatame never faced his other self,” Naoto said. “And we didn't
witness his Shadow returning to his body as a Persona, either...Perhaps that's why we're

Namatame stared at the television with a terrified expression. “What…”
“I failed. But it wasn't my fault. And the law can't touch me anyway..”

Kanji’s expression mirrored Yosuke’s. “Huh? Stop what? We ain't even done anything

The TV turned off.
You can’t do such a thing.

“You don’t know us at all,” Goro said. He pushed himself to the front of the group and

“One push?” Rise whispered.

Everybody turned toward Yu.
Yosuke’s gaze was unwavering. “What do you want to do… Leader?”

The room was thick with tension as everyone waited for Yu’s response. Yu’s expression was
unreadable, but his grief was obvious. Even as Namatame sniveled and begged, the correct
choice was equally clear.
In preparation, Goro grabbed Namatame by the scruff of his hospital gown. He was so light it
was pathetic. Namatame gasped weakly.
And then Yu said the impossible.
“Wait a second…”
“There’s no time,” Yosuke snapped. “It’s now or never!”
“We’re missing something,” Yu said. “Remember? Not everything fits together–”
“Who gives a fuck about what fits together?” Goro asked. He took a step toward the
television, dragging Namatame along with him. Namatame’s breaths came in frantic gasps as
he tried to struggle against Goro. “Namatame put Nanako in the television, and now Nanako
is dead. That seems straightforward to me.”
“But Namatame’s true feelings,” Yu said. “He thinks he’s saving people.”
“We just heard his true feelings on the TV!” Yosuke shouted. “Bad people think they’re right
all the time!”
“Something about this is bothering me, alright?” Yu said. “Yosuke, we’re missing something,
and I can’t kill a man without knowing for sure–”
“We do know for sure!” Goro shouted.

“I don’t understand you,” Yosuke said. “Nanako’s dead. Don’t you realize that? She’s never
coming back because of this sick bastard–”
“We can’t kill someone—” Rise interrupted.
“We’ve got to do this!” Kanji snapped.
“Everybody calm the hell down!” Yu shouted. Everybody shut up. “Goro, put Namatame
down.”
“Just because you don’t have the strength to do what needs to be done doesn’t mean that I
don’t,” Goro said. He held onto Namatame all the more tightly. “Yosuke’s right. We will
never have an opportunity like this again.”
“And if we kill someone without knowing the facts, I will never forgive myself,” Yu said.
“Put him down.”
“It’s true that we haven’t considered anything from Namatame’s perspective,” Naoto said,
obviously trying to placate Goro. “Although there’s no doubt he caused Nanako great harm,
we don’t know anything about his motives apart from what we heard on the midnight
channel.”
“Do you think motives change anything?” Goro asked. “I killed hundreds of people because
of my daddy issues. Do you think the families of my victims give a shit about what my father
did to me?”
“We’re never going to understand him anyway,” Yosuke said. “Who kills people and thinks
they’re saving them?”
“Failing to understand and failing to listen are two different things,” Naoto said softly.
“Goro-kun, there are things about this case that I haven’t reconciled with either. Your

warning letter… It’s not impossible we’re dealing with another culprit.”
“Namatame’s still a culprit,” Goro hissed.
“But Namatame might lead us to the final culprit!” Yu snapped. “He can’t do anything in his
current state. At least allow us to find some answers from him before ending his life forever.”
Goro wasn’t there for Shinjiro because of this bastard. Nanako was dead because of this
bastard.
But Shinjiro believed in second chances. At least, he believed in Goro’s second chance. In
Chidori’s second chance. Would he really approve of Goro killing someone without finding
out all the facts? Would he approve of Goro killing someone at all, even if he really deserved
it?
Goro didn’t know. He couldn’t ask.

Yet… Goro hadn’t killed anyone in this timeline. Akihiko killed Takaya because Goro
hesitated. Because deep down, Goro was afraid to do what needed to be done.
Because he was tired of ending lives.
“You have a second chance,” Shinjiro had said two years ago. “What are you planning on
doing with it?”
Goro let go of Namatame.
Namatame dropped to his knees, still breathing frantically. He muttered hurried and repeated
apologies, but Goro ignored him.
“Fine, but you’d better remember this,” Yosuke said, voicing Goro’s thoughts. “I'll do
everything I can to stop him from repeating what he's done. Anytime, anywhere...anything.”
“I agree,” Yu said. “This… this can’t happen again.”
“We won’t let it,” Yukiko said. “But if there really is another person responsible, we have to
stop everyone responsible, right?”
“Yeah,” Kanji said reluctantly. “We’d just be lying to ourselves by doing anything rashly.”
“Maybe we should get out of here,” Chie said anxiously. “Shouldn’t the police be getting
back any moment now?”
Adachi chose that spectacular moment to run into the room.
“What are you guys doing in here?” Adachi demanded.
“Shit…” Kanji whispered.
“We were keeping an eye on the suspect,” Naoto said quickly. “We didn’t want him to
escape, since the other officers were busy making sure Dojima-san was alright. If Namatame
were to escape, it would ruin the police’s reputation, and their trust in you, Adachi-san.”
Goro hadn’t given Naoto enough credit. She knew how to manipulate people just as well as
he did.
“O-oh, I see.” Adachi eyed the giant television, and his eyes darted down to Namatame, who
was still kneeling at Goro’s feet. Brief understanding crossed his features. “I’ll tighten
security and have him moved out of this hospital as soon as possible. Maybe get rid of that
television too. Looks kind of dangerous. In the meantime, can you not mention you guys
were in here?”
The doctor helped Namatame back to his bed.
“Is he alright?” Rise asked. “He was kind of… upset earlier.”
“He seems fine,” the doctor said. “But he needs his rest. Outside, everyone.”

“We should see Nanako-chan anyway,” Yosuke said reluctantly.
They’d lost their chance to get rid of Namatame. And, as determined as Yosuke was, they’d
likely never have such a perfect opportunity ever again.
“Is Dojima-san alright?” Yu asked Adachi as they left the room.
“He’s fine,” Adachi said. “Well, as fine as you can be, at least. You should probably see him.”
A nurse ran up to them. She was beaming.
“There you are, all of you!” she gasped for breath. “Please, come with me!”
“What happened?” Yu asked immediately, but the nurse was already walking back to the
hospital room. Everyone was too sick with anticipation to ask again.
“Well, hurry up and follow her!” Adachi said. “I’ll keep watch over Namatame.”
They returned to Nanako’s hospital room. The heart monitor was beeping at regular intervals
again.
The heart monitor was beeping at regular intervals again.
“Is this… is this some sort of mistake?” Yu whispered. He was staring at Nanako as if he had
just seen the sun after a year of darkness. “She was… I was…”
“She’s alive!” Chie laughed in relief.
The doctor nodded. “It's very rare to be resuscitated after one's heart and lungs fail, but it
does happen. But until I know why she collapsed in the first place, I can't say for sure how
well she'll recover from here on...Still, Nanako-chan's a fighter, and she's trying desperately
to stay alive.”
“She’s alive,” Goro said, echoing Chie’s words. “Oh my god.”
Nanako was alive.
Goro tuned out everyone else’s exclamations of relief and gratitude. None of it mattered.
Nanako was alive, and Goro hadn’t failed Shinjiro. He had kept his promise. Shinjiro could
rest easy.
Nanako could continue to live.
A large tear rolled down Goro’s cheek as Kanji gently rested a hand on Goro’s shoulder. “Did
you hear the doctor? We’ve got to scram for the night.”
In the background, Yosuke was asking about Teddie’s location. Maybe Goro should have
been worried, but he was still stuck on the fact that Nanako wasn’t dead.

Goro lagged behind the others as he left the hospital room. Everything about that night was
so surreal. Nanako dying… Nanako reviving herself from the dead. It was a miracle.
But miracles didn’t happen.
Ryoji would probably argue otherwise.
Goro glanced behind him. If Goro was lagging behind, Yu wasn’t even a part of the group.
He stood in front of Nanako’s door, looking reluctant to leave the hospital at all. Adachi
walked up to Yu, and Goro found himself stopping to listen in.
The conversation started out mundane enough. Adachi warned Yu not to enter the suspect’s
room again, even though Goro was certain they would be trying it tomorrow.
“I also came to give you another update on Dojima-san,” Adachi said. “He’s asleep now. It
looks like some of his wounds opened up a bit, but they’ve fixed him up.”
“Does he know about Nanako?” Yu asked.
Adachi beamed. “Oh yeah, I heard! You guys were being so dramatic that I got really
worried–”
“Dramatic?” Goro demanded, forgetting that he was technically eavesdropping. The
terminology was just so absurd he couldn’t let Adachi get away with it. He turned on his heel
and marched up to Adachi. “You think that grieving over a dead girl is dramatic?”
Adachi appeared completely flummoxed by Goro’s sudden arrival. “Akechi-kun, what… no!
I just–”
“Goro,” Yu said. He grabbed Goro’s wrist before Goro did anything rash. “It doesn’t matter.”
Goro yanked his hand from Yu, but he didn’t attack Adachi.
“It does matter!” Goro gave Adachi a steely glare. “Nanako was dead. How would you have
wanted us to respond?”
“You all responded perfectly reasonably, of course!” Adachi looked appropriately panicked.
“Look, I clearly missed something. So many things were happening at once, I didn’t even
realize Nanako was actually dead. Or, well, maybe I was in denial. I wasn’t thinking when I
said you guys were dramatic.”
“I’m not the one who needs an apology,” Goro said.
“No, I understand,” Yu said. “It’s really okay, Adachi-san.”
“No,” Adachi said. “I’m sorry. I really don’t think before I speak sometimes.”
“There are worse flaws to have,” Yu said.

“Heh, right.” Adachi ran his fingers through his hair and sighed. “Well, at least I have
Akechi-kun here to keep me on the straight and narrow.”
“I’m not your moral compass,” Goro said.
“No, that’s probably Dojima-san’s job, isn’t it?” Adachi grinned. “I bet he’ll be back on his
feet and yelling at me in no time.”
Jester Arcana: Rank 9

Teddie was missing.
The last time anyone had seen him was at the hospital. He never showed up back at Yosuke’s
house, and he wasn’t answering any of their phone calls, even though Yosuke had given him
a phone nearly a month before.
The group scoured the town to find him that morning. Goro even asked Igor if he knew
where he was, and he received the sort of vague response he had come to expect from anyone
residing in the Velvet Room. By the time they had searched everywhere they could think of,
they gathered in Yosuke’s room in the hopes of finding Teddie waiting there cluelessly.
No such luck.
“Don’t tell me he went back to his world,” Yosuke said, pinching the bridge of his nose.
“But I checked the TV world,” Rise said. “I couldn’t sense him anywhere.”
“Maybe he’s hiding?” Yukiko asked.
“I’m worried about Teddie too, but we must trust him to come back on his own,” Naoto said.
“We only have a short window of time before Namatame returns. We must act now before it’s

Naoto was right. If they wasted this opportunity, they might as well have killed Namatame
when they had the chance.
“Oh, right,” Yosuke said. “That thing about there being two killers.”
“I keep circling back to the warning letters and Goro’s unusual kidnapping,” Naoto said.

“So you think another person tried to kill Goro-kun?” Kanji said. “Another copycat?”
“That wouldn’t make sense,” Goro said. “Although Kubo wanted to take credit for the other

than pleasant personality. If it’s true that the killer targeted me because of my investigation,
it’s not likely a copycat would find that a sufficient reason to kill me specifically.”
“No… he would have to be already involved, wouldn’t he?” Yosuke said. “Your investigation
wouldn’t affect him otherwise.”
“This is all conjecture, of course,” Naoto said. “It’s possible Goro was targeted for another
reason. But if the investigation angle is correct, and if someone other than Namatame

“Not to mention the guy must have known to throw Goro inside a TV,” Chie said. “I mean,

“So you think some mastermind manipulated Namatame into participating in the murders?”
Yu asked.
“I don’t want to jump to conclusions before speaking to Namatame first,” Naoto said. “But

“Then let’s stop wasting time and speak to that son of a bitch,” Kanji said.
With a fake “suspicious object” and Naoto’s authority with the police, they were able to get

And what a tale he spun.
Apparently, after the news of his affair with Yamano came out, he returned to Inaba. Dejected
by the ruin he had brought upon himself and Yamano, he decided to test out the Midnight
Channel rumor. That was when he saw Yamano appear on the Midnight Channel. He
unthinkingly reached to touch her, and his hand went through the television.
And then Yamano was found dead.
When Namatame saw Konishi on the television, he tried to warn her of what might happen.
She didn’t listen. She died too.
Apparently, by the time he saw Yukiko on the television, he was becoming desperate. He
wanted to save her, but she wasn’t going to listen to his warning. Therefore, he thought if he
put Yukiko inside the television, it would be a way to protect her instead. When Yukiko

It sounded like a ton of horseshit to Goro.
“What, like it was some holy mission?” Goro asked. “You kidnapped people from their
homes!”

Namatame flinched. “I thought it was the only way to help them,” Namatame said regretfully.

Namatame might be severely misguided at best, but even he would have surely remembered

A sick feeling rested in his gut. Like there was something he should remember, some dots he

He was missing something.

“Hmm, yeah, I guess that is kind of odd.” Dojima frowned, furrowing his eyebrows. “I don’t

Goro clasped his hands together so tightly his nails dug into his skin. “Glowing yellow eyes?

“It was kind of dark, but… I think his hair was curly?” Dojima grimaces. “Sorry. Again, my

So Tsuyoshi gave Dojima the ability to enter the TV. That was certainly… convenient timing.
But if Tsuyoshi was responsible for Dojima having the power, was he responsible for Yu and
Namatame having the power too?
“Every little bit helps,” Goro said, hoping he hid his dread effectively. He bowed. “Thank

“Sure.” Dojima sighed and slumped back into his pillows. “I can’t wait to put all of this
behind me. Be back at home with Nanako… maybe Namatame will even get convicted.”

“I’m sorry.”

He was sorry.

“I… “ Goro couldn’t implicate the rest of the group in this. “I could have killed him, after the

“You shouldn’t apologize for not killing a man,” Dojima said wearily. “It wouldn’t have

“It could have saved others.”
“Murder isn’t the answer.”
Goro froze. Dojima didn’t break away from his gaze, and Goro’s skin began to crawl.
Why was he upset? It certainly wasn’t the first time he heard that cliche phrase. He was sure
it wouldn’t be the last. There was no reason to be so unsettled. Even if it was a naive way to

“So I’m just meant to leave it to the law, is that it?” Goro asked sharply. “To your precious
legal system?”
“Are you really going to have this argument with a police detective?”
“It’s because of people like you that I had to–” Goro shut his mouth before he got himself
arrested. “That is to say, sometimes murder is the only solution. What about self-defense?”
Dojima’s expression grew more tired. “Look, I’m not saying the world is a black and white
place where we can abide by hard rules. But a kid like you shouldn’t resort to murder before

anyone.”
Goro’s eyes burned, which only made him more furious.
“You don’t know anything about me,” he snarled. “I’m not some innocent little kid who

“Call it instinct.”
“Well, I didn’t ask for your instincts.” Goro got to his feet and bowed stiffly. “I’m glad you’re
not dead.”
“I’m glad you didn’t kill anyone.”
Goro marched away before his ridiculous teenage hormones made him cry in front of
Dojima. He had no reason to cry. He was angry. He was furious that Dojima would belittle
him like that.

He made it out of Dojima’s bedroom before a sob unexpectedly tore its way from his throat.
A kid like you shouldn’t be killing anyone.
Do you think I keep you around for your pretty fucking face?
Goro started to laugh even as tears rolled off his face.
Chariot Arcana: Rank 8

The next day was filled with asking around for Teddie, as well as trying to find any new
information about the killer.
By the time they met up at Aiya for dinner, they had discovered absolutely no new

“So, to sum it up, no new information: the end?” Chie said in disappointment.
Naoto frowned. “The police had an unusually large number of officers in their initial

Why did Akira feel so sick to his stomach?

Maybe Shinjiro would even come back to life and congratulate Goro on achieving the

Yosuke was going to give Yu five minutes. If he didn’t come out of the TV by that time,

Two minutes.
What was Yosuke doing, waiting in Junes at night? He should be going into the TV world to

Three minutes.
Maybe Yu thought he could get through to Adachi. Hell, maybe a part of Yosuke thought Yu
could get through to him. That was why Yosuke was waiting, right? Because he had faith that
his partner would be able to get out of the bind one way or another. With or without Adachi.
Four minutes.
All of this waiting was making Yosuke anxious. Could specters injure people? Adachi hadn’t
shown much hesitation in shooting Goro, but maybe he wouldn’t try to kill Yu? Adachi was
friends with the Dojimas, after all. He wouldn’t kill Dojima-san’s only nephew.
Right, just like he wouldn’t threaten the lives of people Yu cared about. What if Adachi had
been intending to put Nanako and Dojima in the TV all along? He must have had a laughing
fit when both of them fell in. And then he even pretended to help, buying them lunch and
asking to come along–
Yosuke’s stomach tightened.

Five minutes.
No. There was no time for brooding. Yosuke started to walk up to the massive television in

Ran headfirst into Yu.

“Oh.” Yu got to his feet. “Well, you were right. It didn’t work.”
Damn. Why was Yosuke feeling disappointed right now? He had known there was no way
Adachi was going to listen to reason. The guy was straight up evil.
“Well, I told you so– is that blood?”
Yu’s hand immediately flew up to his ear, which had a small amount of blood dripping from

“It’s not nothing,” Yosuke said. “Did he attack you?”
“I was just fighting a low-level shadow on the way and forgot to heal,” Yu said immediately.
“I’m fine.”
“Yeah right,” Yosuke said. “Come with me. I think we have first aid stuff in the back.”

taken, and dies, and I almost kill Namatame, and now Adachi was the killer this entire time.”

It also made no damn sense.
“Come again?”
“I wanted to kill him too.”

“I tried to reason with my friend,” Yu said. “But I guess he was never real to begin with, so I

“And then he shot you.”
“At least he’s being honest about wanting to get rid of me.”
A pit formed in Yosuke’s stomach. The murder case seemed to be coming to a head, but what
about Yu? He was leaving in March, and it was already December. They only had a few
months left.
“Adachi’s just a worthless criminal who doesn’t know a good thing when he sees it. I don’t
want to get rid of you,” Yosuke said. “And I’m sure the rest of the team feels the same way.

“Dude,” Yosuke said. “She totally already has.”
Yu laughed, and a few tears spilled down his cheeks.
“I’m serious,” Yosuke said. “Why do you think she calls you big bro all the time? She’s
probably got the adoption papers all lined up and ready to go.”
“I’d better tell Dojima-san the news,” Yu said. “I hope he’s prepared.”

Yosuke grinned. “I think we have a few of those balloons in Junes,” he said. “You know, the
‘It’s a boy’ balloons.”
“We probably wouldn't be allowed to bring them into the hospital room,” Yu said reluctantly.

“He will if we tell Teddie about it,” Yu said. “We need to keep this a secret from him at all
costs.”
“I’m sure I can find some way to distract him.” Yosuke started laughing himself. “Can you
imagine Dojima-san’s face, though? If he entered the house after spending months in the

Yu and Yosuke broke into violent laughter, barely able to pause to take a breath. It was a good
thing they were in the safety of the staff room, or customers might complain about them

pass out from laughter.
At some point, both of them started crying, and not just from the laughter.
“Damn,” Yosuke said. He pressed his palm against one of his eyes. “I thought laughter was
supposed to be medicine for the soul.”
“Guess it wasn’t made for bullet wounds.”
Yosuke burst out laughing again. “That’s not funny,” he said between breaths.
“Can’t blame me for trying.”
Funnily enough, between the laughing and the crying and probably everything in between,
Yosuke felt way better. It didn’t fix things by any means, but some of the tension fester inside
had been lightened.
Hopefully Yu felt the same.

stubborn to acknowledge it?
No matter which way Akira looked at it, either his uncle or only friend was lying to him. The
thought made him feel nauseous to the point that he wondered if he was getting sick again.
If only Monster Cat could talk. Maybe then he could tell Akira the answer.
“Is something wrong, kiddo?” Tsuyoshi asked the following morning.
He had been coming by more and more often with the prolonged absence of Akira’s parents.
Akira didn’t mind; it helped a lot with the loneliness that usually came when his parents

But when there was a small chance that his uncle could be a bad guy, Akira had a harder time

Akira didn’t think he needed helping, anyway.

“Are you Kurusu-kun?” person-who-might-be-Goro’s-friend asked.

“I’m Narukami Yu,” Narukami said. “I’m a friend of Goro-kun.”
Thought so. But why would one of Goro’s friends seek him out? Unless… “Did Goro send

Aeon Arcana: Rank 8

One of the benefits of living in a small town was the lack of necessity in public
transportation. Naoto and Rise were able to arrive at the Kurusu residence within half an hour

Naoto and Rise texted Goro to inform him that they were unscathed by their conversation

Please. As if Goro had any choice in the matter.

What was Goro saying? Why did he feel so angry all of a sudden? Tatsumi had done nothing

“I don’t know what you mean.”

“If you want me to be honest with you, then I cannot say such a thing,” Tatsumi said. “You’re

A mistake was thinking he could ever manipulate Shido. Killing all those people hadn’t been

But Goro couldn’t explain that. To explain the people he’s killed would be to explain the time

Goro would never be able to forgive himself. But he couldn’t continue to seek other’s
forgiveness either. Not when they didn’t know there was anything to forgive.

Yu went back upstairs. It was only after Dojima tucked Nanako into bed that he approached
him cautiously. Dojima had long since abandoned his newspaper and was now sitting on the
sofa and reading a book.
What was the worst that could happen, right? Dojima hate him? If this plan didn’t work out,
Yu would be leaving in March anyways.
Although, if Dojima hated him, Yu might not be allowed to visit–
“Alright, spit it out,” Dojima said. He closed his book and raised his eyebrows. “It’s obvious
you’ve got something to say.”
Yu took a deep breath and swallowed the anxiety that continued to build up in his throat. “I
don’t want to leave Inaba,” he blurted out.
Yu expected derision, maybe even frustration, but Dojima’s expression only softened. He
gave Yu a sad smile. “Is that what this is about?” he asked. “I know it’s frustrating, but you
have people waiting for you too.”
Yu’s heart sank. Would Dojima believe him at all?
“That’s the thing,” Yu said. “I’m not sure I do.”
Dojima frowned. “What do you mean?”
Yu pulled out his phone and opened up his text logs between him and his mother. It took
approximately one second for him to scroll to the top. He silently handed his phone to
Dojima.

Feeling an odd sense of dread build up in his stomach, Ryotaro took Yu’s phone and looked at
the messages.
4/12
Narukami Yu: a woman was killed
Narukami Yu: im safe though
4/15
Narukami Yu: a girl at my school was murdered too

Narukami Yu: could you answer my phone calls?
7/10
Narukami Yu: im sure you’re not worried since im not dead yet but my teacher was found

For how few messages there were, their actual contents spoke volumes. Ryotaro found
himself scrolling back and forth between Yu’s messages to seemingly nobody at all. Certainly
nobody who cared about him enough to respond.
But this wasn’t nobody. This was Ryotaro’s sister. How could his sister be so thoroughly
negligent that her son had to remind her to answer her phone? Her son who was living
leagues away from her in a town plagued with serial murders?
And on a more personal, selfish level, how could she not respond to the news of the disaster
that struck Ryotaro’s family? About Nanako?
There had to be something Ryotaro was missing. “Have they called you about any of this?”
Yu never talked much about his parents, but Ryotaro had always assumed that he was
enjoying his time in Inaba too much to really take note of them. Ryotaro had never given
much thought to his parents. But, then again, Ryotaro’s parents were also largely absent from
his life. He and his sister had taken care of each other for the most part.
Yu was paler than usual, and he took the phone from Ryotaro. He shut it and clutched it
tightly. Ryotaro almost told him to sit down so that he didn’t pass out.
“My mom’s called every once in a while about the incidents,” Yu said. “She called about you
almost two weeks into November I think.”
“Are you shitting me?” Ryotaro couldn’t help it. He was so surprised. “Your only family in
the country had gone missing, and she didn’t respond until two weeks later?”
Ryotaro was never a model of good parenting; he knew that now. But he couldn’t conceive of
a situation where he didn’t at least make sure Nanako was doing alright if something terrible

had happened. He couldn’t conceive of a situation where he didn’t check on Yu if something
terrible had happened.
“I don’t want to leave Inaba,” Yu said desperately. “I want to stay with you.”
“Yu,” Ryotaro said. “Those texts… you didn’t seem surprised by the lack of response.”
“Well, no,” Yu said.
“And you haven’t complained once about essentially living alone for two months straight,”
Ryotaro said. “When we came back, the house was in perfect condition, and the fridge was
fully stocked up. I assumed you had done some last-minute cleaning for our arrival, but are
you used to living alone?”
“My parents are busy people,” Yu said. His voice sounded rehearsed. “But I don’t think they
ever really wanted me. I’m sure I can convince them to let me stay here, if you’re alright with
it.”
Please say yes, Yu’s eyes pleaded.
Ryotaro had sometimes imagined a scenario like this. A scenario where his sister would need
to be gone for another year. Two years, even. Yu had become another member of Ryotaro’s
family, and he had forged connections with countless people in Inaba. Even one of the
hospital staff was fond of him. Nobody in Inaba wanted Yu to leave.
Ryotaro had pushed away those thoughts. Despite Yu’s own reluctance to leave, Ryotaro still
thought Yu had a healthy relationship with his parents. That his parents missed him.
Ryotaro had never imagined that Yu had barely spoken with his parents throughout the entire
year.
“Alright,” Ryotaro said. He hated his secret relief. “What’s your plan?”
A wide smile spread over Yu’s face. And Ryotaro realized he would protect that smile with
his life.

Goro had fallen out of the habit of his daily runs. Between the mess involving Nanako and

Still, Goro missed running. It had given him a mental clarity that only non-life threatening
exercise could provide. No pressure to succeed, but also not quite as mindless as sitting on
the sofa watching television.
Therefore, Goro put on his shoes and jacket and stepped into the snow-covered Inaba,

Once, Goro had to infiltrate the palace of a businessperson who considered the rest of the

warm.
In the real world, the sensation was similar but less painful than Goro remembered. His lungs
burned in the cold air, but with enough careful breaths, it was more than manageable. The
real difficulty came with avoiding ice on the sidewalks. The last thing Goro needed was to
smash his face into the concrete.
