"You're sure that Shido wants me dead?"
Goro swallowed. "Yes."
"And you're sure that me disappearing is the best way to avoid it?"
"If he thinks you're still alive, you'll be at risk, even if you leave him," Mitsuru affirmed.
"Wakaba, you can't really be going along with this..." Sakura said slowly.
"You and I both know that Shido's been getting a bit too big for his britches recently,"
Wakaba said seriously. "And if he figurs out how to use a place like this to his advantage, and
he wants me dead, then I'm screwed and you know it."
"And we're going to believe these guys?"
"We're literally standing inside a TV!" Futaba protested. "And these guys aren't freaking out
at all! I think they know what they're talking about."
"I'm on Futaba's side on this one," Wakaba agreed. She gave Sakura a meaningful look. "It's
going to be okay."
Sakura sighed and massaged his eyes. "Fine... if you think this is what's best, then... I trust
you."
"Thank you." Wakaba looked at Mitsuru. "Alright, Kirijo-san. What do you want me to do?"
Goro almost passed out from sheer relief.
"We can continue to make the necessary arrangements once I return to Iwatodai," Mitsuru
said, smiling slightly. "For now, I would pretend we never had this conversation and continue
your life as normal. When it's time to move forward, I'll come to you."
Sakura crossed his arms. "You people aren't going to cut any corners, got that? If anything
happens to Wakaba after we go through this effort, then--"
"We will protect her with our lives," Mitsuru said fiercely. "You have my word."
"So... we're good?" Futaba asked slowly, still looking a little apprehensive.

"We're good. I think," Wakaba said. She turned to Margaret. "Pretty lady, do you think you
could answer more of my questions about this place?"
Margaret opened her mouth, looking slightly surprised, but Goro interjected.
"I think we should return to the lodge," he said. "We've been here too long, and if anyone is
watching us, I don't want them to be alerted of suspcious behavior."
"They might just think we're lost in the snow," Wakaba said with a small pout. She slumped.
"But you're right, I suppose. Next time?"
"We'll see," Margaret said vaguely. "Allow me to show you the exit."
Margaret lead them to the exit, and while the others left, she pulled Goro aside.
“Please bring your friends in here as soon as possible,” Margaret told Goro before he left.
“This is a closed realm, and if you do not find Marie soon, I’m afraid it will be lost to us
forever. And with it, all of our memories of Marie’s existence.”
As tactless Marie could be on her best days, Goro didn’t wish to forget she existed either.
Goro didn’t want anything messing with his mind.
“Where were you?” Yosuke asked when Goro returned to the lodge. He was the only one
sitting in the lobby. “We were getting kind of worried, but Yu said he saw Kirijo-san go out
with you.”
“We went on a walk,” Goro said.
“Uh huh,” Yosuke said doubtfully. “Fine, don’t tell me. Just try not to get shot this time?”
“I think I can manage that for now,” Goro said.
“I don’t like the sound of that for now.”
“It’s the best you’re going to get.” Goro sighed. “Besides, I have something I need to discuss
with the rest of the group, but I think it can wait until morning.”
“Care to share?”
Goro explained that Margaret had found Marie. Still worried that one of Shido’s people
would be listening in due to Wakaba’s presence at the lodge, Goro kept the details of the TV
world as sparse as possible. Yosuke caught onto Goro’s censoring.
“I see… well, let’s see if we can find her tomorrow, when the sun’s out,” Yosuke said. “The
others are probably sleeping anyway.”
“Fine by me,” Goro said. If time was so short that they had less than a day to rescue Marie,
Margaret really should have been much clearer in her instructions.

“Goro-kun, Goro-kun!” Futaba said, running toward him from around the corner. Yosuke’s
eyes widened at her sudden appearance. She waved a Nintendo DS in Goro’s face. “Watch
me play Animal Intersection as you tell me all about the future in gaming.”
“What–”
But Futaba was already grabbing his arm and dragging him to her room.
“Um, do you need help?” Yosuke asked.
“I’m sure I’ll live,” Goro said with a sigh. “But if I don’t, you can find Margaret in that cabin
next to the lodge.”
Goro spent the next hour telling Futaba what little he remembered about modern video games
while Futaba inspected his “insultingly old” phone and probably planted a listening device in
it. Goro pretended not to notice and continued talking about new video game consoles.
Futaba was simultaneously thrilled and unimpressed with his knowledge.
“The graphics are better,” Goro said.
“How better?”
“Extremely realistic.”
“Have they released Castle Hearts III?”
“I’m sorry, what?” Goro asked.
“What about the Ultimate Fantasy VII remake?”
Goro frowned. He vaguely remembered Futaba complaining about the lack of some sort of
game that started with Ultimate Fantasy. But that didn’t exactly narrow it down.
“I don’t think so,” he said. Better not to get her hopes up.
Futaba wailed, flopping headfirst onto the ground. “Oh cruel world!” She cried. “Do you
know no mercy?!” She sat up suddenly. “Wait. There’s still hope. What year are you, um,
predicting right now?”
“2017.” Goro highly doubted any of Shido’s goons cared about video game discussions,
much less believed Goro was actually from 2017.
Futaba returned to her previous position on the floor and began to fake sob.
“Futaba, are you still awake?” Wakaba’s voice asked from the other side of the door. “Leave
poor Akechi-kun alone and go to sleep.”
“Ugh, fine.” Futaba got up and sighed. “I suppose I will have to endure this burden with as
much strength as I can muster. Even if I am thirty before either of those games come out.”

“I’m sure you’ll survive.”
“This does not sound like going to bed to me,” Wakaba said.
“I’m working on it!” Futaba returned his phone, pushed Goro out the door, and slammed it
shut behind him. Goro found himself standing less than a foot away from Wakaba.
“Hi there,” Wakaba said.
Goro took two large steps away from her and bowed. “I apologize for taking her time.”
“Don’t even start,” Wakaba said. “I know she dragged you into that. She’s like me in that
way.” Wakaba chuckled. “She’s like me in a lot of ways, actually.”
Goro swallowed. “She’s a good kid.”
“Didn’t know kids had the legal right to say that,” Wakaba said with a wink. “Or wait…
maybe you’re an adult at heart? Can I guess the age?”
“You can try.”
“Um… let’s see…” Wakaba began muttering under her breath. “Kirijo-san said five years
from now, which means that he’s at least five years from the future, but he acts older than 18,
and I don’t know when or how far back he was taken, so…” She smiled and said with
confidence. “How about 25?”
“I’d say I’ve lived closer to 22 years. My actual mental age is up to debate, seeing as
biologically I’m still only thirteen. I don’t know if time travel impacted how developed my
brain is in comparison to an average thirteen-year-old.”
“Wait, seriously?” Wakaba asked. “I have so many questions, but I guess they have to wait.”
“I’d be more than happy to help on another date,” Goro said.
“Oh yeah?” Wakaba asked. “You’re gonna regret that.”
“What’s another one on the list?”
“Fair point,” Wakaba said. “Well, toodles. Maybe if you’re lucky, Sojiro will make you and
your friends curry tomorrow morning.”

They were not lucky. Sojiro didn’t have enough ingredients for an additional ten teenagers.
Goro couldn’t blame him.
Trusting Mitsuru to take care of the rest, Goro joined the others in the TV world to speak to
Margaret. Margaret summarized everything she explained to Goro. Apparently, Marie had
sealed herself off in the TV world in the hopes of erasing all memory of her existence. They
had a very limited amount of time to rescue her before she succeeded.

“But why would she do this?” Yukiko asked.
“We did suspect that she had something to do with the fog,” Naoto said. “But when we
defeated Ameno-Sagiri, the fog went away. Could it be there really is more at play than we
realize?”
“Well, the TV world hasn’t gone away,” Yosuke said. “That alone seems kind of odd, if
Ameno-Sagiri was the one who created it.”
“I guess we have no choice but to investigate,” Yu said. “Maybe Marie will shed some light
on the subject.”
Not having any of their supplies, they packed their bags and returned to Inaba on the bus. The
ride was only approximately an hour long, so everyone briefly dispersed to remove their
clothes from their suitcases and replace them with weapons and medicine before getting back
on the bus. If the driver noticed that they still had their suitcases for no discernable reason,
they didn’t say anything. Maybe they just didn’t care.
It turned out they had wasted all of their time, however. Because as soon as they entered
Marie’s dungeon, all of their items disappeared from their pockets as though they were never
there to begin with.
“What the hell just happened to our stuff?” Kanji asked, patting down his pockets in
confusion. “I swear I had a ton of candy in here a second ago.”
“It must have had something to do with the poem Marie-chan just recited!” Rise said.
“Marie-chan just said, ‘I don't need anything. I just walk by myself’...No way...This place is
being affected by Marie-chan's denial...?”
“This place… is already the absolute worst,” Yosuke said. He glanced at Yu. “Are we sure we
can manage this?”
“We have our personas,” Yu said, his face hardening with resolve. “And we have to save
Marie.”
To make things even better, as soon as they defeated a random shadow, Goro felt as though
half of his energy had been drained suddenly from him.
“Um, why am I so tired?” Chie asked, yawning.
“Marie’s cognition must be trying to prevent us from getting any further,” Naoto said. “How
fascinating. This place seems more like one of Goro-kun’s palaces than the dungeons we’ve
explored before.”
“I think some of the items we’ve found in the chests in this area can help with the fatigue,”
Rise said.
“You mean these seeds?” Teddie asked, already eating a mouthful. “They’re really tasty.”
“Save some for the rest of us, man!” Yosuke snapped.

Teddie’s face fell. “Sorry,” he said with his mouth full.
“Can we eat the branches?” Yukiko asked. It would be a ridiculous question, but they had
eaten stranger things in the metaverse.
“No, those take you back to the start I think,” Rise said. “Like goho-ms.”
“Well, that gives us an opportunity to regroup, at least,” Yu said. “Let’s keep moving forward
for now, but if anyone needs a break, don’t hesitate to say so.”
When they arrived on the next floor, another one of Marie’s poems echoed around them.
Goro cringed. Not only were the poems… less than masterful, but it was also an extreme
breach in privacy. Marie was so defensive of her poems before that he doubted she wanted
them to hear them now, even if she was trying to erase herself from existence.
Another floor. Another poem. Another floor. Another poem.
On approximately the seventh floor, the group finally ran into Marie. Contrasting distinctly
with her usual black and blue color scheme, a massive white robe covered the red dress she
was wearing. But perhaps the most noticeable detail was her bright teal eye. It looked like a
camera lens.
“I can’t believe it,” Marie said, looking stunned by everyone’s arrival. “Why’d you come?
Why?”
“Why do you think?” Chie asked. “I don’t know why you locked yourself up in here, but we
don’t care! We want to help you!”
Marie was not impressed.
“You thought that I was in danger, didn't you? That I might get killed by the Shadows. ...It'd
be better that way. This is a grave...my grave. I'm going to die here.”
“We’re not going to let that happen,” Yu said.
Marie laughed bitterly. “You don’t even know who I am?”
“It’s true then?” Goro asked. “Do you have something to do with the existence of this
world?”
Marie turned around and bowed her head.
“Marie-chan, we don’t care if you helped create the fog,” Rise said. “We just want to help
you–”
“That’s not my name,” Marie snapped. “Marie… that’s not who I am.”
“Then who are you?” Naoto asked.

“I remember...I remember everything. My real name is ‘Kusumi-no-Okami.’ You guys fought
Kunino-sagiri and Ameno-sagiri, right? I'm the same as them. I'm your enemy, one of the
ones who covered your town with fog.”
Goro remembered Ameno-sagiri clearly enough. But Kunino-sagiri…
“Wait a minute,” Yosuke said. “Are you talking about that freaky shadow that came out of
Namatame?”
“That was a Sagiri?” Naoto asked, alarmed. “There’s more than one?”
“Yes,” Marie said. “It was my role to sneak into the world of man and inform the Sagiri what
‘the wish of the people’ was. That's why I'm the only one of them that looks human...Even
without my memory, my body fulfilled my role. In your words, I'm a spy.”
“Does that mean… the reason Ameno-Sagiri thought humanity wanted to be lost to the fog…
it was because of you?” Yukiko asked.
“But you didn’t remember anything,” Yu said. “You can’t blame yourself for unwittingly
helping someone.”
“You still don’t understand anything,” Marie said. “If I don’t die here, your world will
disappear. So please, just leave me alone.”
Marie disappeared, leaving everyone with the startling revelation.
“So Tsuyoshi was correct after all,” Naoto said. “Marie-chan did have something to do with
the fog.”
“But what the hell was all that about our world disappearing?” Kanji asked.
“And if there are a ton of those Sagiri guys, who’s in charge of them?” Yosuke asked. “I
mean, they’re all working together, but wouldn’t one of them be the leader?”
“Whoever the leader is, it’s safe to assume we haven’t met them,” Goro said. “They’re
probably connected to the presence of this world.”
“I’m sorry, I’m with Kanji-kun,” Chie said. “Can we please loop back to the fact that if we
save Marie-chan, the world might go away?”
“She is one of those monsters,” Naoto said. “She might have a valid reason for sealing herself
away.”
“Seriously?” Rise demanded. “We’re not going to leave Marie to die. She might be wrong!”
“We don’t have all of the answers,” Yu agreed. “Let’s keep going in until we figure out
exactly what’s going on.”

Many more floors and battles later, they finally arrived at the final area. Marie stood in front
of a coffin in a large, cavernous room. She glowered at them when they arrived.
“I thought I told you to leave me alone!” she shouted. “Don’t you understand that I’m the
enemy?”
“We need more answers,” Yu said.
Marie’s shoulders slumped. “Oh. Right. You guys seek the truth, don’t you? But I’m so
tired… I just want to end it all.”
“You might think there’s no other way out, but that doesn’t mean there isn’t,” Goro snapped.
“Just explain what’s going on.”
“The other two Sagiri have been defeated,” Naoto said. “Unless there is another, that should
mean you’re free–”
“Free?” Marie scoffed. “Is that what you think? I’m not like you. I don’t have freedom.”
“What do you mean?” Yu asked.
Marie explained that her role as a Sagiri was not just to spy on humanity. She also served a
purpose in controlling the fog. When all of the fog in Inaba disappeared, she absorbed it, and
now she had a torrent of fog raging within her. In disappearing, she hoped to make the fog
disappear with her.
Nobody liked that plan. Marie was determined to stick to it.
“If you’re not going to leave now, I’m going to make you leave by force,” Marie said.
“Please, try to understand.”
Marie began to launch attacks at them. They stayed on the defensive, using status effects on
Marie to get her to give it up already.
Eventually, she did.
“It doesn't matter what happens to me...You're stupid...Hurting yourselves like that. If my
death keeps you from being happy, what am I dying for!?”
“Has it occurred to you that there’s another way to get rid of the fog inside of you?” Goro
asked. “A way to contain it?”
“B-but… I have to… I can’t keep living like this,” Marie whispered.
“We can help you,” Yu said. “We can beat this thing together.”
Teddie nodded. “Don't worry. It'll be okay. I used to be just a Shadow, too. But even I could
change… so I’m sure you can too!”

“What if there is no other way?!” Marie demanded. “What if the only way to save the world
is for me to die?! You can’t seriously be stupid enough to save me just to ruin everyone else’s
lives!”
“You’re afraid!” Goro shouted back, tired of this constant back and forth. “You’re too afraid
to face the truth, so you’d rather disappear from the world entirely!”
“So what?” Marie asked. “It would be better for everyone if I just disappeared!”
“I am speaking from experience when I say that death is not the solution,” Goro said. “And
neither is running from people who care about you.”
“You don’t–” Marie clutched her head. “Ugh!”
“Marie-chan?” Yosuke asked.
When Marie next spoke, it was obvious the person speaking wasn’t Marie at all. “That's
right...There is no need for the truth. Ignorance is bliss...There will be no pain if you never
try to find out…”
“That voice… that’s not Marie-chan!” Yukiko exclaimed.
Yosuke frowned. “Is that what she meant by her mind being overpowered by the fog?! Hey!
Snap out of it!”
“Just stay away from me!” Marie pleaded.
“No! Goro’s right. There has to be a way to get rid of the fog without getting rid of you,”
Yosuke said.
“It’s impossible,” Marie said. “There's no way. If we waste any more time, the fog will take
me over and be set free...If that happens, I won't be able to take my own life. I'll become a
monster…”
“And if we defeat that?” Yu asked.
“What?” Marie asked.
“Are you saying we should wait for Marie-chan to be controlled by the fog, and then defeat
her!?” Rise asked.
“Um, what would happen to her if we did that?” Kanji asked.
“It might work…” Marie muttered. She nodded. “I'll put my mind to sleep before the fog
overpowers it. Of course, the fog will then take over my body, but my mind will still be safe,
beneath it. ...The rest comes down to luck, I guess. Which will give out first: the fog, or my
life?”
“If you think we’re going to lose to some fog, you don’t know us at all,” Goro said.

"I don't know... isn't that kind of a risky gamble?" Yosuke asked.
"Do you have any better ideas?" Chie demanded.
Yu hesitated before saying, "I say we try it."
Marie nodded. "Alright... if you're so desperate to save me... then fine, I won't stop you."
Marie closed her eyes, inhaled, and released the monster within her. Her form shifted into a
large dark figure surrounded by red robes. A creepy eye took over its entire face. It barely
hesitated before launching a barrage of physical attacks. Yu immediately started barking out
orders in response.
The battle was difficult, but the plan worked almost flawlessly. They defeated Kusumi–
Sangiri and returned Marie to her ordinary self. Naturally, no sooner than they confirmed that
Marie was still alive did the ground beneath them begin to shake, much to their alarm.
"Sorry, I forgot to mention," Marie said, still slumped over and exhausted. "I don't need this
place anymore, so it's going to disappear."
Thanks for the warning.
They made a break for the exit, and Goro was suddenly reminded of the old days of fleeing
crumbling palaces. The Investigation Team screamed in the same way the Phantom Thieves
did as they sprinted faster and faster away from falling boulders. Fortunately, even with Kanji
carrying Marie on his back, they made it out of the world relatively unscathed.
After catching their breath inside the cabin, Naoto stood up and said, “Marie-chan, I know
that today has been especially harrowing, but there is something we have to ask.”
“Oh, okay,” Marie said. “What’s up?”
“We’ve been wondering if there was something that was like your boss?” Yosuke asked.
“We’ve defeated all the Sagiris, probably, but was someone in charge of them all?”
“In charge…” Marie frowned, furrowing her eyebrows. “Well… I guess I did hear a voice
when I let the fog take over my body. Um, what did it say...? ‘Humans don't want to know the
truth. What they truly desire is a peaceful world filled with fog’...Something like that,
anyway.”
“That’s cheerful,” Kanji said sarcastically.
“Did it sound like anyone you knew?” Yu asked.
“Well, it sounded like me,” Marie said, looking perturbed. “I don’t know… maybe I’m
misremembering. It also could have been the same voice I heard when you defeated Amenosagiri and the fog flowed into me. I’m sorry; I’m really not sure.”
“If it’s happened twice, it might be more than just a coincidence,” Goro said.

“I guess we could try to ask around town when we get back,” Yukiko said. “But what are the
chances that the source of the TV world is just sitting around town?”
“We won’t know unless we try,” Yu said. “I don’t know about you, but I really want to put
my days of fighting fog monsters behind me.”
“I’d drink to that,” Kanji said. He cleared his throat. “If I could drink, obviously.”

The following day, after school, they sat down in Yosuke’s house and tried to think of where
they could even possibly begin in their investigation.
“It’s not just the TV world we’re investigating,” Naoto said. “But who was the one granting
the power to enter the TV to begin with?”
“Who even originally had the power to begin with?” Yosuke asked.
“Namatame, Yu, and Adachi,” Goro said.
“Not Kubo?” Rise asked.
“Adachi pushed Kubo in,” Yu said, shaking his head. “He was a red herring.”
“So we just have to find a source of commonality between those three individuals,” Naoto
said, frowning.
“Well, they were all kind of new to Inaba, right?” Yosuke asked. “I mean, Yu and Namatame
obviously arrived around the same time, but even Adachi was pretty new at that point. He
came after I moved here.”
“Seriously?” Chie asked.
“But Goro-kun didn’t get the power, and he was new,” Yukiko said.
“Maybe he was too late to the punch,” Kanji said.
“Perhaps there was a trigger?” Goro suggested. He directed his attention toward Yu. “When
you arrived, did anything strange happen?”
“Um, I don’t think so,” Yu said. “It was almost a year ago now, though, so I could have
forgotten.”
“Do you think you could ask your uncle?” Yosuke asked.
Yu called Dojima and put him on speakerphone.
“Hey Yu,” he said. “What’s going on?”
“Dojima-san, do you remember if anything strange happened the day I arrived here?” Yu
asked.

“The day you first came to town...? Hmm, let's see...We were the first ones to greet you,
right? Did we stop somewhere on the way home...? I don’t know about anything strange
happening.” Dojima’s voice became sharper. “Why are you asking this?”
“It’s nothing to worry about,” Yu said.
“Nothing to worry about my ass,” Dojima said. “Don’t tell me there’s something else you
kids are worrying about.”
“We’re just trying to pinpoint the source of the TV world,” Naoto said. “It’s nothing to be

Dojima’s loud exhale sounded like he strongly disagreed. “Fine. Just… please stay safe,

“Don’t worry, Dojima-san,” Yu said. “We will.”
He hung up.
“Well?” Yosuke asked. “Do you remember going anywhere on your way to the house?”
“I think we stopped for gas,” Yu said. “Oh wait! I can’t believe I forgot, but this gas station
attendant shook my hand. I remember thinking it was really weird.”
“Gas station attendant?” Yosuke asked. “What gas station attendant?”
“You know…” Yu waved his hands in the air vaguely. “I think they were blonde?”
“But I thought only an older couple worked at the gas station,” Chie said.
“Yeah, I’ve never met anyone matching your description, I don’t think,” Yukiko said, looking
equally confused.
“Wait a minute…” Goro said. Yu’s testimony sparked a memory of his own. “I think I know
who you’re talking about.”
“You do?” Yu asked hopefully.
“You do?” Kanji asked with a doubtful tone.
“It was when I first arrived at Inaba myself,” Goro said. The memory was hazy at best. “Did
they tell me about the midnight channel? I remember something about them not feeling
right.”
“How strange,” Naoto said.
Yosuke clapped his hands together. “Well, I guess we’re on the hunt for a gas station
attendant, right? How hard can that be?”

Very hard, as it turned out. Despite asking practically everyone in town, even the people who
vaguely remembered the person they were describing had no idea where the attendant lived.
“Are you sure you didn’t make them up?” Yosuke asked Yu.
“Goro remembers them too!” Yu said defensively. “And so does Nanako!”
“Enough people remember them,” Goro said. “They almost certainly exist. We just have to
figure out where to find them.”
“Easier said than done,” Rise said grimly.

They didn’t find anything until the snow melted at the beginning of March. Every day, Goro
checked the gas station. Every day, nobody was there.
“What is with your obsession with the gas station?” Akira asked in confusion after Goro
insisted upon yet another detour on their way back from school.
“It’s hard to explain,” Goro said.
“My uncle says that you should just give up when I told him about this,” Akira said. “But I
don’t even know what you’re trying to do.”
Tsuyoshi didn’t like what he was doing? Good.
“I’m looking for a part time job,” Goro said. “But the person who suggested it to me is never
around.”
“Maybe they weren’t actually an employee,” Akira said.
“Maybe,” Goro said doubtfully.

"I'm sorry for all the trouble I caused for you," Marie told Goro as he walked by the Velvet
Room one day when he went to check the gas station.
"What are you talking about?" Goro asked, stopping in his tracks to give Marie a quizzical
look.
Marie crossed her arms and looked away awkwardly. "You know... I made you and Yu rescue
me... I still can't believe you would do something so risky. And then, after all that, I can't
even remember who the one really behind the fog is."
Goro frowned. "Marie-chan. That's not your fault. And you didn't make Yu and the others do
anything. We wanted to help you."

"I know that." Marie rolled her eyes. "I just... I feel bad, I guess. Especially after everything
Yu and you have done for me. I mean, you even bought me that journal, and took me out to
beef bowls, and I was just... willing to end all of that. All because I was afraid."
"Marie..." Goro swallowed. He hadn't realized that he meant that much to Marie, but now he
felt sorry that he hadn't spoken with her about this sooner. "I know what it's like to feel like
you're causing more problems than solutions. I know how it feels to think you're better off
gone."
"Is that right?" Marie frowned. "How did you... how did you get through it?"
"I eventually realized that people care about me, I guess." Goro clenched his fists and stared
at the patterns on the Velvet Room door. "It's still hard sometimes, but... I realized that it's
better to face my mistakes, to continue living and work to be better, than to give up on this
earth entirely. I know my situation isn't exactly comparable to yours, but..."
"No, I get it." Marie nodded. "I was really scared when I thought the fog within me was
going to destroy everything. But more importantly, I was afraid of hurting the people I cared
about. I'm still... I'm still a little afraid of that, if I'm being honest."
Goro gave her a small smile despite some of the heaviness in his chest. "Me too."
"Well, it's good to know that there are people out there that feel the same way," Marie said,
returning Goro's smile. "And I know I didn't really say this before, but... thank you. For
saving me. Even when I begged you guys not to."
"Of course." A strange, bitter warmth twisted up in Goro's insides. "That's what friends are
for, right?"
"Friends, huh?"
"You've stopped insulting Theo for a living, so I think we can consider each other that."
"Alright." Marie's smile grew slightly. "I guess that's fair."

The first Sunday of March, it began to pour outside. Goro was more than reluctant to go
check on the gas station when the attendant was not at all likely to be there. He worked on his
homework instead. Hopefully, the rain would begin to let up.
Instead, he received a phone call from Yu.
“So,” Yu said. “I found our gas station attendant.”
Goro jumped to his feet immediately, causing his chair to fall behind him. “You what?”
“I’ll explain everything in the TV world,” Yu said. “Can you tell Kanji while I gather the
others?”

They met Yu in the front entrance of the TV world. Immediately, Rise shuddered.
“Why do I sense a super powerful presence?” she asked. “Don’t tell me that’s the gas station
attendant?”
“That’s what I want to explain,” Yu said.
Apparently the gas station attendant was not a gas station attendant at all. She was Izanami,
who created the TV world and granted Adachi, Yu, and Namatame the power to enter it with
a simple handshake. She put the Sagiris inside of Namatame and Adachi, and to make things
extra convoluted, and even more confusing for Goro, Marie was a part of Izanami that broke
off from the whole.
"Wait, wait, wait," Kanji interrupted. "You're telling me that the weird gas station attendant
that almost nobody has heard of... is a freaking god?"
"Pretty much," Yu said.
"And she made the TV world, and the freaky eyeball monster guys, and shook your hand to
give you TV entering powers," Kanji continued.
"Yep again."
"And Marie is her not-evil twin?"
Naoto put a hand to her chin, looking somewhat confused herself. "No, judging from Yu and
Marie's combined testimonies, I assume Marie was a part of Izanami that originally served as
a spy for her but grew her own conciousness somehow."
"When you asked me the true cause of the fog, I could have never predicted this outcome,"
Goro muttered. "And I knew a seventeen-year-old who was actually Death. And lived in my
friend's body for ten years."
"Uh, do we know this story?" Rise asked.
"As interesting as that is, let's stay on task... like the super freaky gas station attendant of
legend," Chie said forcefully.
"This is so weird," Yosuke muttered.
"It was admittedly alarming when the gas station attendant turned into a creepy woman who
floated in midair," Yu agreed. "Definitely did not see that coming."
“But what does Izanami want?” Yukiko asked. “She orchestrated all of this, but why?”
“I think it was curiosity, at first,” Yu said. “But now that I’ve confronted her, she said that
she’s going to pit her full force against us.”
“Does that mean the return of the fog?” Rise asked.

Yu frowned. “I don’t know."
“Regardless, we cannot let her do as she pleases,” Naoto said. “There’s no guarantee that she
will not attempt something like this again if we leave her be.”
“And that whole… you know… pitting herself against us,” Yosuke said. “Where is she,
Rise?”
"Um, this way," Rise said, beginning to lead the way. "Like I said before, her presence is
really strong."
"Yeah, I can even sniff her out!" Teddie agreed.
They arrived at a dungeon surrounded by a glowing blue fog. A red path looked as though it
was suspended in the middle of the sky.
“It’s almost beautiful,” Yukiko said.
“Yeah, but now’s not really the time to be focused on that, right?” Chie asked. “Once we
defeat Izanami, this will all finally be over.”
“Yeah…” Kanji said. “Finally.”
“I know this sounds weird, but if this is the last time we fight in the TV world together, I
want you guys to know that this has been really fun,” Chie said. “Well, maybe fun isn’t the
right word for it…”
“I know what you mean,” Yosuke said. “It’s like the end of an era.”
“Maybe after this, we can just be ordinary high school students,” Yu said.
Goro laughed.
“Hey!” Kanji snapped. “What’s so funny?”
“Sorry, it’s just… not as easy to escape from this life as you might hope,” Goro said. “But I
wish you luck.”
“Now I really want to defeat that Izanami,” Yukiko said. “She’s not dragging us or anyone
else into any more danger.”
Izanami spoke to them as they progressed through the dungeon. Most of it was useless drivel
or taunts. She mentioned bringing Yu to this place in a dream once, which Yu corroborated.
Goro didn’t particularly care. He was becoming sick of this place.
“Despair, emptiness, and hope,” Izanami said on the next floor. “Those are the three
qualities by which I selected those coming from outside...You showed the most grounding of
the three; I would expect nothing less. In which case...I will personally and directly test your
power.”

Rise’s eyes widened. “The three qualities ...Did she mean Senpai, Namatame, and Adachi...?
Izanami saw those qualities in them...? What kind of power does she have...?”
“But which quality was mine?” Yu asked.
“Isn’t it obvious?” Yosuke asked. “Namatame was despair, Adachi was emptiness, and you
were hope.”
“Are you sure?” Goro asked.
“What else could it be?” Kanji asked.
“I could have been emptiness,” Yu said.
“I’m sure we could debate this for hours,” Naoto said. “Nobody is one personality trait. But it
doesn’t matter. What’s important is how you are now.”
“And now, you’re full of hope,” Yosuke said.
“I guess you’re right,” Yu said.
They continued forward. Izanami continued to describe how she had only hoped for her three
pawns to ascertain the true desire of humanity. How humanity’s true desire was to drown in
falsehood until it lost itself forever.
Goro couldn’t argue that some of humanity did wish for that.
But not all of them.
They continued forward.

After what felt like hours of cutting through shadows, they arrived at a large open area.
Izanami floated in the center, covered in white robes similar to the ones Marie wore. Her eyes
were not yellow, but red. It was the first time Goro had seen any entity with red eyes.
“Congratulations on making it this far,” she said.
“Well thank you very much, Ms. Root of All Evil!” Yosuke snapped.
Naoto put a hand on her waist and glared at Izanami. “You granted certain individuals the
power to enter the TVs. You created the Midnight Channel as well. And lastly, you started a
rumor about the Midnight Channel to raise its public awareness...Is this correct?”
“All save one point,” Izanami said. “This ‘Midnight Channel’ you speak of...It is indeed a
device to draw hearts into this world. But it was always your individual wills that would
determine what appeared on it. Humans ache to expose their suppressed sides, while the
prying eyes around them are curious to see them laid bare. The want to show, and the want to
see...I granted a ‘window’ that catered to both. That is all.”

“So the midnight channel just showed who everyone was thinking about?” Yukiko asked.
“And then once the person entered the TV, it showed them more clearly?”
“That explains why the people on the television would show up on the midnight channel,”
Yosuke said. “We were all thinking about them. And then, once someone was in the TV, the
midnight channel served as a window to that world?”
Rise clenched her fists. “Are you saying...all you did was give that initial spark to Senpai and
the others, then watched things unfold? And the rumors spreading, things going
wrong...We're to blame for all that's happened!?”
“People’s curiosity was at fault?” Yukiko asked.
“You humans are so quick to blame powers higher than themselves for their suffering,”
Izanami said. “You refuse to take responsibility for your own actions. Beings like myself
grow tired of watching mankind attempt to rip itself to shreds. Everything was for your
sake...To create the world mankind so wanted.”
“No,” Kanji said. “You only wanted to destroy us!”
“Humanity is weak,” Izanami said. “They seek their own destruction, and so I sought to grant
that desire. Man struggles to understand one another. You can only truly know a finite
number of people within your lifetime...But humans disregard this fact, and try to know more
people than is possible. Only by comparing yourself to others can you define yourselves.
Thus your ever-present anxiety...Your anxiety causes you to see only what you want to see,
and believe only what you want to believe... As I said...your desire is for a world enshrouded
in fog!”
“Don’t put words into our mouth,” Yu said.
"I must agree that the vast majority of people are exactly as you say," Naoto said.
"But we don't intend to live that way," Chie said.
Goro nodded, tightening his grip on his sword. “We’re not some pawns in your game."
A burst of fog exploded from Izanami. Goro brought his arm up to cover his eyes, trying to
peer through the thick cloud that impeded his vision.
The fog slowly cleared, revealing a giant creature in a straight-jacket-like outfit. Its hair flew
in all directions. The sky was bright red surrounding it.
“Alright,” Yosuke said, gritting his teeth. “Guess it’s time for the grand finale.”
“I couldn’t have said it better myself,” Yu said.
"Knowledge of the truth is not everything," Izanami said in an echoing voice. "Yet drunk
with truth, you exceeded your role, and became too involved... Now you will learn for
yourself who's wrath you have brought down..."

Goro rolled his eyes. Why must these entities always be so dramatic?
"We'll see about that," he said through gritted teeth.
And so they fought.
After fighting for nearly a year, the rest of the team had powers to rival Goro’s, especially Yu.
Between the eight of them with Rise’s support, they should have easily torn down Izanami’s
defenses.
But no matter what they did, no matter what they attempted, Izanami barely faltered,
continuing to hit them with devastating attack after attack. Meanwhile, everyone else began
to grow more and more exhausted. After summoning all of his personas at least twice in an
attempt at experimenting with different attacks and abilities, Goro was about ready to
collapse.
"Can't you see?" Izanami demanded. "It's impossible to defeat me!"
“I think we need to change our strategy, partner!” Yosuke shouted after the tenth round of
failed attempts to damage Izanami.
“But what’s even left for there to try?!” Rise cried.
Yu frowned. “Cover me.”
Everyone gathered around Yu, staving off attacks as Yu reached into his pockets and pulled
out a small orb. It looked very similar, although slightly bigger, to the pendant Theodore had
given Goro long ago. The one that still sat around his neck, waiting for its moment to be
needed.
“What’s that?” Kanji asked.
“Igor gave it to me,” Yu said. He threw it into the air. “It reveals the truth.”
Purple light burst from the orb, and Izanami’s form began to change.
“Well then,” Izanami said. “Allow me to show you my full splendor.”
The straight jacket and skirt faded away to reveal disgusting red arms emerging from
Izanami’s skeletal body. Everybody shuffled back in revulsion.
“I… am a god.” Izanami’s voice boomed. “I will teach you the truth of your miniscule
existences.”
“This is way scarier than I thought it would be,” Chie said, her voice shaking.
“We have to win this,” Yukiko said, adjusting her grip on her fan.
“You cannot defeat me through strength alone,” Izanami said. “Soon, you will see.”

That did not stop them from throwing their strongest abilities at Izanami with all of their
strength. As Izanami said, it did little to no damage.
Was there truly nothign they could do to defeat this foe? Surely, if SEES could stop Nyx,
Goro and his friends could find some way to defeat Izanami. Surely-“The time has come for us to end this..." Izanami said slowly, and a horrible sense of
forboding hit Goro. "Goodbye... Accept the reality of your death.”
Hundreds of hands emerged from the ground near Yu, causing Yosuke to push him out of the
way. Yu screamed as they grabbed Yosuke and pulled him under. But Izanami wouldn't give
up. More hands slowly started to emerge, and Goro's chest stopped as Kanji jumped in to
save Yu. Then Naoto. Then Yukiko. Then Chie. Then Rise. And then there was only Yu and
Goro, and Izanami raised her arms to launch the attack again.
Yu looked at Goro pleadingly. "Don't," he whispered.
Goro didn't want to die. Not after everything. Not after coming so far.
But this was Yu's journey, and Yu was his friend, and Goro couldn't let him die.
It wasn't even a hard choice, in the end.
As the hands slowly started reaching out, Goro sprinted forward and pushed Yu out of the
way.
Yu gave him a look of betrayal, but Goro was too occupied by the hands' bony fingers clawed
their way around his flesh in a death grip. “Let go of me,” he snarled, trying to stop the hands
from dragging him under. “Hereward!”
His head was already being dragged under–

Even with everyone's sacrifices, Izanami's arms dragged Yu under as well. He found himself
in a white fog, and for a minute, he considered giving in and dying entirely. What was the
point if everyone else was gone? Was fighting even worth it?
And that's when his social links appeared in front of them. One by one, giving him
encouragement, of reminding him of everything he had gone through in the past year. Until
finally, Nanako stood in front of him.
"Hey... Big Bro?" she asked with a sad frown. "Are you going to leave me behind? I'll be a
good girl... so don't go... I don't want you to go, Big Bro..."
No... Yu couldn't go. He couldn't leave everyone behind. He couldn't leave Nanako behind.
Yu grit his teeth and stood up in a white void, and he felt a rush of power course through him.
A new persona rose up within Yu. A second awakening.

With a flash of white light, he was back in the terrifying red hellscape where Izanami still
stood. Upon seeing him, Izanami launched another instant-death attack on Yu. Yu braced
himself.
Except this time, it missed.
"Impossible... can the will of so few surpass the will of all mankind?!" Izanami exclaimed.
Izanami continued launching devastating attacks against Yu, but to no avail. Nothing could
touch him.
"Why? ...Why don't you understand?" Iznami demanded. "It's impossible for humans to grasp
the truth with their own hands..."
A thrill of exhiliration filled Yu. Maybe this wasn't so hopeless after all. Maybe he could be
like the wildcards in Goro's stories. Maybe he could destroy the unbeatable enemy.
With a deep breath, Yu gathered all the courage within himself, raised his hand, and
summoned his new persona, Izanagi-no-Okami.
"Myriad Truths!" he shouted.
Izanagi-no-Okami burst forth and swung its blade repeatedly against Izanagi. Her terrifying
form writhed in pain at each slice until finally, Izanagi-no-Okami defeated her entirely.
Everybody else returned almost as soon as Izanami slumped forward in defeat. The red sky
returned to a gray hue.
“What the hell…” Kanji muttered.
“I’m not dead,” Yu could hear Goro whisper. “Thank fucking god.”
Yu wanted to cry in relief. They were alive. They weren't dead. His entire team, his friends,
his boyfriend, hadn't just all died for him.
Izanami hunched over herself, gasping for breath. “This can’t be… how can I be the one who
is defeated? How am I the one who is going to disappear? Instead of the endless struggle,
wouldn't it be easier to wrap oneself in lies and live in blissful ignorance...? Isn't that true
peace for humans...?”
“How many times do we have to say it?” Kanji demanded. “To hell with that shit!”
“Very well. Then try and live your way...Power enough to erase my existence...You have
already exceeded what I thought humanity to be capable of...You have lifted the fog in this
world, as well as the fog in your own...And whether that will lead to happiness or not...rests
upon your shoulders.”
Izanami's monstrous form began to disappear. "Children of man..." it said as it dissolved into
nothingness. "Well done!"

"Alright, we did it!" Kanji cheered.
"Please tell me it's really over this time," Chie gasped, still looking out of breath.
"I think, this time, it might be," Naoto said, looking a little uncertain. "But it seems like more
of a beginning for us."
"Trust me," Goro said. "There's almost certainly more on the horizon for all of you."
"Speaking from experience?" Yosuke asked with a sigh. "Well, now, at least we have no
regrets for tomorrow.
Yu managed a small smile. "Right."

Almost as soon as Izanami vanished, the dungeon disappeared around them. Everyone
gasped in alarm and awe as the TV world morphed into a beautiful paradise filled with lush
grass, mountains, trees, and waterfalls. Lillies floated on the surface of the water. No wonder
Teddie thought something was wrong with his home. Without the fog, the TV world was a
completely different place. A soft breeze hit Goro's face, and he gazed at a large moon on the
lilac sky. It was truly beautiful.
"I... know this place," Teddie said. He beamed. "A long time ago, everywhere in this world
used to look like this."
"So this is the world inside people's hearts..." Yukiko whispered, her voice hushed.
"It really is over," Goro said, looking a little awestruck.
"Let's never fight another terrifying monster again," Yosuke said, his face looking far more
relaxed at the new scenery. "If I see fog again, it'll be too soon."
"Well, you're not going to avoid the fog forever," Chie pointed out.
"But a break would be nice," Yukiko agreed.
"This place is so beautiful..." Rise said, crouching in front of a stream. "Do you think we
could have a picnic here sometime, Teddie-kun?"
"You know what?" Teddie said. "Let's do it!"
Goro didn't know how he felt about going into the metaverse for such a frivilous purpose, but
it seemed that the TV world wasn't going to disappear even with the disappearance of its
master.
"Very well," Goro said. "I can provide some pastries, if you'd like."
"Hell yeah!" Kanji pumped his fists. "Goro's cooking, here we come!"

Goro felt his cheeks get warm. "It's really not that good."
"No need to be modest, Goro-kun," Naoto said. "You and Yu-kun are probably among the
most proficient in the kitchen."
"That's Yu for ya," Yosuke said grinning and turning in Yu's direction. "Yu?"
Yu stood in place, his eyes closed and looking more serene than Goro's ever seen him. He
opened his eyes, looking a little startled. "Huh?"
"Is everything alright?" Chie asked.
"Oh... yeah." Yu smiled. "I'm just relieved."
Teddie nodded fervently. "That makes all of us!"

“Big Bro?” Nanako asked that evening, after Yu collapsed on the sofa and resolved to never
get up.
“Mmhm?” Yu said, his voice muffled by the pillow.
“I checked your calendar in your room,” Nanako said. “You haven’t used it since November.”
To be honest, Yu had forgotten he even had a calendar in the midst of the mess of the past
few months. He should replace it with one for the current year.
“Okay?”
“We missed your birthday.”
Yu looked up blearily, feeling somewhat confused. “What?”
“I told Dad,” Nanako said. She looked like she wanted to cry, and Yu forced himself to sit
up. “Your birthday is November 15, and now it’s March! I promised you I would celebrate!”
“Oh, well, it’s not a big deal–”
“It is!” Nanako stomped her foot on the ground. “Dad is getting a cake, and we’re going to
celebrate with all of your friends tomorrow.”
Yu smiled and face planted back into the sofa cushions. “Is that right?”
“Yep!” Nanako’s voice cracked. “I’m sorry for missing it.”
“It wasn’t your fault, Nana-chan,” Yu said. “Thank you so much for remembering it now. It
makes me really happy.”
“Really?” Nanako asked hopefully.

Was something wrong with him? Yu wasn’t sure he could stop grinning if he tried. “Really.”

End of Part 2

Chapter 89: August 21, 2014–March 18, 2012
Chapter Summary

Warning: this chapter is Short
But the cliffhanger was too good to ignore

Chapter Notes

tw: violence, ptsd, gun,

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Mementos was terrifying.
The massive subway tunnels pulsed with flickering red veins, and Akechi continuously
checked over his shoulder to ensure no trains were about to plow into him. In a place as
unpredictable as this, it wasn’t a far stretch to think that the trains might come his way.
But even if a train did come barreling in at full speed, what was Akechi meant to do? Dodge
out of the way? Where? And even if there was a place he could go, the chances of him
getting there fast enough just by running were slim at best. The most he could do was prepare
himself for the end.
Speaking of speed, Akechi needed to get down to the next level as soon as possible. He had
already spent more time than he wanted taking wrong turn after wrong turn, and if he wasted
any more time, he’d practically be begging the reaper to come after him.
One chance encounter with the beast had been bad enough. Akechi barely escaped with his
life.
By a stroke of good luck, Akechi’s next right turn took him to the escalator leading further
down. Akechi paused to catch his breath as he stood on the escalator. He hadn’t been able to
locate his target on that floor, but she had to be close. Akechi could not let the two hours he
spent in this wretched place go to waste.
Fortunately, the swirling red vortex leading to his target was impossible to miss. It might as
well have been a flashing sign pointing in his target's direction.
Akechi forced back any lingering anxiety over entering a portal without knowing exactly
where it led. He was strong. Powerful. Nothing could get in his way.

He ran through the portal. On the other side stood Isshiki Wakaba’s shadow, staring at him
with a wary expression.
Akechi had never met Isshiki in person before. He only knew what she looked like through
photographs. But he still caught himself feeling surprised at how… mundane she looked. Her
shadow wore sweatpants and a t-shirt, as though Goro caught her in the middle of getting
ready for bed.
“I was wondering when you’d arrive,” Isshiki said. “Who knew the angel of death was a
teenager? Or is Shido just hiring child soldiers these days?”
“I’m not a child,” Akechi said, removing his gun from its holster. He aimed it toward
Isshiki’s head.
“Oh, we’re skipping straight to this part, aren’t we?” Isshiki said. “Well, I’ve always wanted
a guinea pig to experiment with. I hope you can take the heat.”
Akechi pulled the trigger, but Isshiki was already transforming into a massive creature
holding two axes and wearing a dark apron. The bullet bounced uselessly off her.
Gun or no, with Loki’s help, Akechi ripped her to shreds.
But unlike ordinary shadows, Isshiki’s shadow returned to her humanoid form after Akechi
defeated her. She sat on her knees, clutching her side and gasping for breath.
If it weren’t for the yellow in her eyes, Akechi almost thought she was the real thing.
It didn’t really make a difference, did it? Akechi was still going to kill the real Isshiki.
“I guess–” Isshiki’s shadow said, coughing. “I guess this is how it ends, huh? Do you think
you could do something for me, before I kick the bucket?”
Akechi had only waited this long to catch his breath. As powerful as he was, the battle had
not been as easy as he hoped it would be. Now, he grabbed his gun once again.
“Tell Futaba I–”
BANG
The bullet pierced Isshiki’s skull, and she disappeared into a pile of dust. Akechi stomped on
it furiously, determined to ensure she wasn’t going to end up rising again.
Akechi was so furious that his head pounded, but he wasn’t quite sure why. How was she
going to finish that sentence? Love? Hate?
It didn’t matter.
“I don’t owe you anything,” Akechi snarled.

Part 3: My Final Destiny

“Wow,” Wakaba said. She surveyed the now gorgeous view of the TV world with an
awestruck expression. “This place is nice.”
“I still don’t understand why you’re here,” Goro said.
He had woken up earlier that morning to see a handful of texts from Futaba saying that
Wakaba would be coming to Inaba and wished to meet Goro in the TV world after school.
Goro’s requests for more details only produced vague answers and general trolling on
Futaba’s part.
“You said you would answer my questions,” Wakaba said. “And this place seems like the
most private we’re going to get. Do you think I’ll be able to meet my shadow here, since
we’re not in that closed realm place anymore?”
“No,” Goro said. “We defeated the source of the shadows in this world. This place is virtually
harmless.”
“Seriously?” Wakaba’s face fell.
“Why do you want to meet your shadow?” Goro asked.
Wakaba poked Goro’s head with the back of her pen. Its tip retracted with a click. “Scientist,
remember? I wanted to face my shadow with the scientific method.”
“Well, I’m sorry to disappoint.”
“Ah well, there’s still plenty of nuggets of information I can get out of you,” Wakaba said.
She sat down on a nearby boulder and opened up her journal. “So. Cognitive world.
Explain.”
“For all you know, I’m about to lie to you,” Goro said.
“Well, obviously, I would like to confirm some of this information for myself,” Wakaba said.
“But finding someone who’s actually been in the metaverse is the sort of progress I haven’t
seen in years.”
“It’s amazing you know about the cognitive world at all,” Goro said.
Wakaba shrugged. “It’s amazing what you find out in the rumor mill. Chat rooms are filled
with weird occurrences happening all over Japan. Rumors coming to life, time grinding to a
halt, demons roaming the streets. It’s amazing, really.”
“Rumors coming to life?” Goro asked.
“Yep,” Wakaba said, popping the ‘p’ sound. “In a town called Sumaru, or something.
Happened a little over a decade ago. Residents recall that the rumors that were spreading

always turned out to be true. A bar selling weapons, the blimp on top of a museum becoming
real… most of them think that their rumor mill just happened to be bizarrely accurate that
year, but others think that cognitive pscience might have been at play.”
“Wait a minute,” Goro said. He was familiar with most of this story, except for that detail.
“Over a decade ago?”
Hadn’t Elizabeth said that Tsuyoshi had caused trouble in 1999? Over something that had
nothing to do with the Kirijo Incident?
“Yes? Same year the Gekkoukan High School blew up, which was another potentially
supernatural incident that I could ramble about…” Wakaba frowned. “Why’s that detail so
important to you?”
“Where did you find out about the rumors coming to life?” Goro asked.
“I can’t remember exactly,” Wakaba said. “A lot of inspiration for my research comes from
chat rooms on the far reaches of the internet. Why?”
“It’s nothing,” Goro lied, filing away the information for later. “Now, what were your
questions, Isshiki-san?”
“Wow, talk about a personality shift,” Wakaba said. “But fine, don’t tell me.”
Wakaba asked Goro question upon question about the cognitive world and how it functioned.
The difference between the TV world and the world he could enter through the metanav. The
Dark Hour and its peculiarities.
And when Goro thought they were finally done, Wakaba set her notebook down in her lap
and leveled Goro with an unsettling gaze. “So, tell me. How did you kill me?”
Goro couldn’t do anything but stare.
“No immediate denial,” Wakaba noted. “Looks like I guessed correctly. So? What was it?
Poison, stabbing, a classic hit and run?”
“The metaverse,” Goro said, feeling oddly distant from the conversation.
“You killed my shadow, then. Triggered some sort of shutdown in my system.”
“Isshiki-san, there’s not much point in asking me questions if you already know all of the
answers.”
“How old were you?” But Wakaba was already doing the math herself. “You said you had it
under good authority I’d die by August of 2014. You’re thirteen right now, so you’d be at
least fifteen in two years. Maybe sixteen? When’s your birthday?”
“June 2.”
“Sixteen then.” Wakaba whistled. “He really does hire them young, huh?”

“I should go.” Goro stood up and turned toward the exit almost mechanically. He felt as
though all his thoughts were floating away before his mind could grab hold of them.
“No, no, wait.” Wakaba stood up and chased after him. “I’m sorry. It was a touchy subject.
But you can’t blame me for being curious. I mean, it is my death we’re talking about.”
“Yes, well, it’s not going to happen this time around, so I’d prefer to pretend it never
happened at all,” Goro said. “Forgive me for being selfish.”
“I don’t blame you, you know,” Wakaba said. “Shido’s able to manipulate most adults. It’s
not a surprise that he managed to convince–”
“Isshiki-san,” Goro said loudly. He couldn’t listen to any more of Wakaba’s misplaced
sympathy. “Please don’t try to make me out as the victim of your murder.”
“What, did you want to kill me–”
“I triggered your mental shutdown while you were standing by the street,” Goro snarled.
“You fell into the traffic and were hit by a moving vehicle, making it look like suicide. Futaba
witnessed the whole thing. To add insult to injury, Shido’s men forged a note to make it look
like you committed suicide because you couldn’t handle raising Futaba, which sent her into a
spiral of self-loathing. It took her years to realize the truth.”
Wakaba said nothing. She looked stunned.
“That is what I did to your family,” Goro said. “And I didn’t feel a shred of remorse for it.
Save your forgiveness for someone who deserves it.”
He left without another word.

Once confirming that Wakaba made it out of the TV world in one piece, Goro sat down at his
desk and opened his laptop. In the search bar, he typed: Sumaru Rumors
The results weren’t anything he hadn’t seen before. There were a few old articles about an
odd serial killings occurring in the area, a few chat rooms that discussed odd coincidences
regarding ridiculous rumors, but nothing that gave any information about Tsuyoshi or his
potential origins. Goro wasn’t sure what he expected.
Something of note Goro did find was that one of the articles about the serial killings was
published by none other than Kismet Publishing, a fact he previously overlooked due to the
unverifiability of rumors coming to life. The very same publishing company that the reporter,
Amano Maya, worked for. She was old enough to remember what occurred in 1999, right?
It was worth a shot, at least.
Maybe it would distract Goro from his earlier conversation with Wakaba.

Goro had long since accepted the fact that Shido manipulated him. That Shido had used
Goro’s anger for his own ends. But Wakaba was moments away from telling Goro it wasn’t
his fault.
Even if Goro wasn’t at fault for being manipulated, he was at fault for killing Wakaba. He
knew what he was doing. He knew what it would do to Futaba. Nobody was holding a gun to
his head.
He didn’t need one of his victims trying to convince him otherwise. He didn’t want Wakaba’s
sympathy, much less her forgiveness.
Goro couldn’t think about this anymore. He needed to clear his head.
Goro left the house and began to walk down the central shopping district to get some fresh
air. While he walked, he called Rise.
“Hey, Goro-kun!” Rise said. “What’s up?”
“Do you remember that reporter we met during the summer festival last year?” Goro asked.
“I think she gave you her number in case you wanted an interview.”
“Oh yeah, I think I remember who you’re talking about,” Rise said. “Amano-san, right? She
interviewed Teddie.”
“Yes,” Goro said. “Do you still have her number?”
“Oh yeah! I saved it. Now that you’ve reminded me, maybe I should give her a call and tell
her I’m going to be starring in that movie. But why do you want the number, Goro-kun?”
“I have something I want to ask her,” Goro said.
“Oh, well, if you say so.”
Rise gave Goro the number, and Goro committed it to memory before hanging up. He sat
down at a nearby bench, added Amano to his phone contacts, and called her.
“Hello, this is Amano Maya. I can’t come to the phone right now, but feel free to leave a
message at the beep!”
Beep.
“Amano-san, I’m very sorry to bother you,” Goro said. “This is Akechi Goro. We met at the
summer festival in Inaba last year. I wanted to speak to you regarding the strange incidents
that occurred in Sumaru thirteen years ago. If you’re willing, please call me back.”
He hung up and exhaled, leaning backwards and staring at the sky. He’d very much like to
not have to worry about a supernatural anomaly for once in his life. And even if he found a
way to get rid of Tsuyoshi, he’d still have to worry about the Metaverse, this god of control,
and, God forbid, Maruki’s little power trip.

Speaking of Tsuyoshi, Goro caught sight of his figure approaching out of the corner of his
eye. He tensed. What the hell did Tsuyoshi want now? Was he angry that they destroyed
Izanami? Did he have some sort of horrible information to taunt Goro with?
Whatever it was, Goro would much prefer to get out of the afternoon generally unscathed. He
shoved his phone into his pocket, turned around, and began walking as quickly as possible
away from Tsuyoshi. Tsuyoshi’s footsteps behind him quickened, and Goro abandoned all
sense of dignity and broke into a jog. Tsuyoshi’s footsteps remained measured, even as they
got nearer.
Goro was approximately ten yards away from Tatsumi Textiles when Tsuyoshi’s fingers
wrapped tightly around Goro’s right arm and pulled him back suddenly. Goro gasped and
stumbled in his effort to stay balanced.
“Goro, Goro, Goro,” Tsuyoshi said, squeezing Goro’s arm forcefully. He grinned down at
Goro, his smile a little too wide and his teeth a little too sharp. “It’s been too long! How have
you been?”
Goro clenched his fists and forced himself to appear relaxed. Although he was sure he was
doing nothing to fool Tsuyoshi, the less he resisted, the less pressure Tsuyoshi would place
onto Goro. Less pressure meant less pain.
Don’t punch him in the face. Don’t press the emergency button. Not yet. With any luck,
Tsuyoshi would say his piece and leave Goro alone.
“Kurusu-san,” Goro said. “I’ve been fine, all things considered. How about you?”
Tsuyoshi laughed. He didn’t sound amused in the slightest. “I’m so glad you asked. Why
don’t you walk with me?”
Tsuyoshi still had a tight grip on Goro’s arm as he spun Goro around and led him away from
the shopping district. Goro forced himself to walk alongside Tsuyoshi, glancing over his
shoulder at Tatsumi Textiles and wondering if Tatsumi or Kanji had seen anything. Hopefully
this wasn’t about to turn into another kidnapping.
“Where are we going?” Goro asked.
“See, Goro, I’ve been thinking,” Tsuyoshi said. “I’ve been doing a lot of thinking, actually.
Dangerous, I know, but I think you’ll understand after I tell you what I’ve been thinking
about.”
Tsuyoshi waited with a prompting silence. Goro stared at him quizzically.
“This is the part where you ask me what I’ve been thinking about,” Tsuyoshi said, his smile
full of teeth.
Goro sighed. “And what have you been thinking about, Kurusu-san?”
Tsuyoshi brightened. “Well, ever since that pesky fog went away, I’ve been thinking about
how your actions have been so… well, to put it simply, you’ve been very disappointing.”

“Disappointing,” Goro repeated. His mouth felt very dry.
“But you’re good at that, aren’t you?” Tsuyoshi’s voice changed very suddenly, and Goro’s
eyes snapped up to his face. Instead of Tsuyoshi’s glare, Goro stared directly at the scowl of
Shido Masayoshi.
No, no, no. Shido should be in Tokyo, not the small town of Inaba. What the fuck was going
on? Was he hallucinating? Since when could Tsuyoshi shapeshift?
Goro instinctively yanked his hand away. Shido’s grip tightened.
“You’ve always been a disappointment.” Shido said, his eyes gleamed an unnatural gold hue.
“A failure of a son. You had one fucking job, and you blew it.”
Goro had to be dreaming.
“Shido-san, I–” Goro sputtered, panic momentarily fogging his senses.
Wait. What was he saying? Shido could not be here. The person dragging him past this row
of houses could not be Shido. “Who the fuck are you?”
“Well, that is the titular question, isn’t it?” Not Shido said. “I’m sure you know I was never
really Kurusu Tsuyoshi either.”
“What the–” Goro blinked away the wave of dizziness that had overcome him. He needed to
stay focused. He fingered the emergency button in his pocket, prepared for the inevitability of
having to press it. “Where are you taking me?”
Shido’s face shifted into Tsuyoshi’s for a split second before he returned to being just Shido.
“Home, of course,” Not Shido said. “Is your sense of direction really that horrendous?”
Home. What did that mean? In spite of the panic continuing to make Goro’s head pound, he
forced himself to actually take a look at his surroundings.
They were in a neighborhood. Akira’s neighborhood.
Shido shifted into Takaya, who grinned wildly. “You might never have understood your true
calling,” not-Takaya said.
And now Takaya was Adachi. “But that doesn’t mean everyone else out there is just as
pathetic as you.”
Back to Shido. They were now directly in front of Akira’s house. Without letting go of Goro,
Shido removed a gun from the inside of his suit.
He’d recognize that revolver anywhere.
This truly did feel like one of his nightmares. Goro blinked furiously. He didn’t wake up.
Why couldn’t he wake up?

“Is that… how they hell did you get Takaya’s gun?” Goro asked.
“I found it in your rich friend’s storage facility,” Not Shido said. “I bet you wished you hadn’t
rescued it from Tartarus, huh?”
Goro didn’t answer as bile burned his throat. He barely understood what was going on.
“First, I’ll fire a warning shot to grab his attention,” Not Shido said. He fired a bullet into the
grass with a heart-stopping BANG. Goro flinched violently. He tried to step backwards, but
Not Shido held him firmly in place.
Not Shido laughed nastily as he placed the barrel of his gun directly in between Goro’s eyes.
I’m going to die here, Goro realized with a spike of horror. He couldn’t escape. He couldn’t
defend himself. He could only stand helplessly as Tsuyoshi in Shido’s skin murdered him.
Goro’s ears started ringing. This was how he was going to die. With a bullet in his head.
Again. But why now? Why did Tsuyoshi decide he was done with Goro? What had Goro
done?
It didn’t matter. Akira was certainly looking through the window to see what was going on.
He would watch Goro get shot by Shido. Would he go on the same quest of revenge Goro
had? Would he make the same mistakes?
“Is this really necessary?” Goro gasped, deciding in that moment he was not beyond begging
for his life. “You don’t have to do this—”
“Goodbye, Goro,” Not Shido interrupted. “Or, wait. I never cared enough to call you by your
given name, did I?” His smile was downright sadistic. “Goodbye, Akechi-kun.”

Thou art I… and I am thou
The connection that you have nurtured has been transformed

Thy bond shall be the compass of redemption
and guide the way for thy heart

The power of the Fool Arcana has been set free
Granting thee ultimate power

Goro wasn’t ready to go.

Not now, Goro thought desperately, bringing his hand up to his neck. Not yet, asshole.
Four things happened in the same split second.
Goro pressed the emergency button.
With his other hand, he crushed the pendant that hung around his neck for nearly two years.
Tsuyoshi pulled the trigger.
And, unheard by Goro, on the other side of the window, Akira screamed.
