Chapter 90: March 18, 2012
Chapter Summary

This chapter goes kinda bonkers so hopefully its not confusing.
Like it should be a *little* confusing but not TOO confusing

Chapter Notes

tw: blood, ptsd, villain monologues, gun

See the end of the chapter for more notes

The familiar tune of the Velvet Room flooded Goro’s senses. Piano mixed with someone’s
haunting voice. The Aria of the Soul, as Minato once called it.
If Goro was here, and not in the real world, it was a bad sign.
Goro opened his eyes.
The Velvet Room had changed again.
The place that had once been a giant elevator and then the inside of a limousine was now a
room with wide windows that looked out onto the ocean. Theodore stood next to Igor, who
sat behind his ordinary round table on a sofa made of a plastic material. The floors and walls
were the same shade of blue that Goro always saw in the Velvet Room, but the walls were
adorned with framed maps and compasses. The floor swayed underneath Goro
uncomfortably. Seagulls cawed in the distance.
Were they on a boat?
“Welcome back,” Igor said.
“Am I dead?” Goro asked.
“Not at all,” Igor said. “While your body is repairing itself in the real world, I summoned you
here. Your contract is very nearly fulfilled.”
“So, this place is…”
“The reflection of your heart, Goro-kun,” Theodore said. “And your heart alone.”

Goro glanced out the window at the endless expanse of ocean. He caught a glimpse of the
small deck. “My heart is a fishing boat?”
“You have been on quite a journey, my child,” Igor said. “One in which the destination is
uncertain and dangerous waves wish to veer you on course.”
Goro clutched his forehead, trying to repel the oncoming headache. The idea of the Velvet
Room changing to reflect him wasn’t what was bothering him. It was literally everything else
about his situation.
“You have faced many trials since you arrived at this place,” Igor said. “I am afraid to say
that the cards have been stacked against you from the beginning.”
“You finally admit it?” Goro asked.
“A powerful force wished to undo humanity,” Igor said. “And you have been forced to make
many difficult decisions. But in spite of the hardship, you had the strength of will to stay true
to your bonds.”
Igor pulled a card from mid-air and threw it toward Goro. Goro caught it and stared at his
own reflection on its surface. He frowned. Was this a card or a mirror?
“My attendants have given you their aid at their own discretion,” Igor said, which was a kind
way of saying they went behind his back. “Now it is my turn to finally offer my own
assistance outside of my usual duties.”
Now Goro was extremely confused. Since when did Igor meddle in anything? He glanced up
at Igor, who had his hands clasped together. He looked entirely unconcerned by his decision.
“We will see each other soon,” Igor said. “But take comfort in knowing that you are the most
fascinating guest I have ever had the pleasure of hosting.”

Thou art I… and I am thou
The connection that you have nurtured has been transformed

Thy bond shall be the compass of redemption
and guide the way for thy heart

The power of the Judgement Arcana has been set free
Granting thee ultimate power

The Velvet Room began to grow white around Goro, but Goro managed to lock eyes with
Theodore before it went away entirely.
“Thank you,” he said. “For everything.”
“No, Goro-kun,” Theodore said, his voice echoing with the swelling music. “Thank you.”

As Goro woke up in the real world, the first thing he noticed was the silence.
Footsteps echoed close to his head, loud thuds that were slowly becoming further away. A
shrill high-pitched sound was muffled in the distance. Goro couldn’t see anything, and he felt
oddly distant from his own body. For a wonderful moment, Goro barely felt anything at all.
And then cold air slammed back into his lungs. With a gasp, Goro inhaled a wet sticky
substance from the grass. The metallic taste shocked Goro’s senses, and the entire world
reeked of blood. Immediately, Goro’s eyes flew open, and he coughed violently, his lungs
trying to expel his own blood.
Goro pulled himself up to his knees. An absurd puddle of red stained the grass beneath him.
He had almost forgotten how much blood could come out of a bullet wound straight through
the forehead.
Almost.
“What the hell?”
Goro’s eyes snapped up at the sound of Shido’s voice. Not Shido, or Tsuyoshi, or whoever
the hell he was, stared at Goro with utter revulsion. He was multiple meters away. He must
have already checked that Goro was dead, and having been satisfied, started to leave the
scene.
“I knew you were a demon, but this is absolutely ridiculous,” Not Shido said, fumbling for
his gun.
Goro jumped to his feet and ran. Sirens began to echo in the distance as he burst through the
front door of Akira’s house, which was blessedly unlocked.
“Goro-kun?” Akira stood by his window. He was as white as a sheet. “But… I saw–”
“No time.” Goro gasped, spinning around and locking the door shut.
He already regretted coming inside. The house did grant him more cover from any gunfire,
but it did nothing to protect Akira from Tsuyoshi’s ire. What would Tsuyoshi do to Akira now
that Goro had foiled his plan?

“But–” Goro grabbed Akira by the arm and sprinted away from the window. Akira screamed
as a bullet shattered the glass and lodged itself in the wall.
“What’s going on?!” Akira’s voice grew increasingly higher in pitch. The front door crashed
open as Goro managed to drag Akira into the living room.
“Do you really think you can outrun me?!” Not-Shido shouted. His voice was so exhilarated
that Goro was afraid to glance behind his shoulder.
Goro slammed Akira to the ground just in time for another bullet to fly above their heads.
Akira hyperventilated beneath him.
“Keep moving.” Goro grit his teeth and scrambled upwards. He took two steps forward
before his heart stopped.
Not Shido was already standing in front of the back door. His gun was pointed toward Goro.
How the hell did he get there so fast?! Did he run there while Goro and Akira were on the
ground?

“Nice try, kiddo,” Not Shido said. “But you’re going to have to do better than that to escape
me.”
Akira jumped in front of Goro, splaying his hands out. “Y-you’ll have to go through me
first.”
“Akira, don’t you dare!” Goro snarled.
Not Shido’s face flickered with agitation. “I’m not after you. Step away from the brat, and
nobody gets hurt.”
“His name is Goro!” Akira shouted. “Not ‘nobody’!”
In any other context, that quip might have been funny. As it was, Goro had never been more
afraid for both of their lives. His mind raced for a solution.
“I don’t want to shoot you,” Not Shido said. His expression hardened. “That doesn’t mean I
won’t.”
They couldn’t run. Tsuyoshi would catch up. And something told Goro that he couldn’t rely
on Tsuyoshi running out of bullets either.
The TV to their right wasn’t nearly as big as the one in Junes. It was still big enough for two
children to dive through.
“Final warning,” Not Shido said, putting his finger on the trigger.
“I’m sorry,” Goro said.

With a burst of adrenaline, Goro wrapped his arms around Akira and shoved him toward the
television. Akira shouted as they both toppled sideways. Their heads connected with the
television screen.
And they kept falling.

Life had definitely been weird for Futaba recently. One day, she was an ordinary girl trying to
encourage social reform by hacking into government files, and the next, she was living in
some sort of video game fantasy world.
Not that Futaba was complaining. The past few weeks had to have been simultaneously the
scariest and coolest weeks of her life.
Especially when Goro and his friends got up to the weirdest crap. Who would have thought
that a gas station attendant was secretly performing a social experiment by giving people TV
powers? It was so absurd it was awesome. She was so stoked that she thought to put a
listening device in Goro’s phone at the ski lodge, even if it didn’t work whenever Goro
entered the TV realm.
Anyhow, overall, Futaba felt like she had been turned into a whacky background character
with a lovable personality. And while there wasn’t anything wrong with that necessarily,
Futaba was looking for more out of her life. That’s why she was always on the lookout for
any problems Goro and co. might come across.
Sure, Goro had repeatedly asked her to stop eavesdropping. But in Futaba’s defense, Goro
was causing her mom to go off the grid for an indefinite amount of time, which was going to
make Futaba’s life a lot harder. Albeit less harder than if her mom had actually died, but hard
nonetheless. Futaba had earned some lighthearted eavesdropping.
It was meant to be lighthearted.
At first, Futaba was confused when some guy started antagonizing Goro. It was hard to make
out all of the words with Goro’s phone in his pocket, but something struck Futaba as not
right. Maybe it was the part where the guy called Goro pathetic. Or was it before then when
he said he was disappointed?
Futaba should’ve done something. She should’ve called Goro. She texted him to ask if he
was okay, but he ignored her entirely.
When Futaba heard the gunshot, all the joints in her body locked up entirely. The second
gunshot came with a loud crashing sound.
Futaba hadn’t even realized she was hyperventilating until she heard a knock on her bedroom
door.
“Futaba?” Sojiro said. Mom was still at Inaba doing research, so Sojiro was making sure
Futaba remembered to eat meals. “Is something the matter?”

Futaba opened her mouth, but only a small squeak came out. Sojiro opened the door anyway.
“Hey,” he said. “What’s up?”
“There was this guy, and Goro-kun…” Futaba glanced at her monitor helplessly. Maybe she
was hearing things? Maybe it was a nasty prank to get Futaba to stop listening in on people’s
private conversations?
“You mean Akechi-kun?” Sojiro asked. “What’s wrong with him?”
“He-he–” Suddenly, the computer started making loud scratching noises again. And then
people started talking to Goro. And Futaba heard Goro’s voice! And more gunshots. Which
was bad. But Goro was still talking! “He’s alive!”
Futaba leapt from her chair and pumped her hands in the air.
“Wait, what?” Sojiro said. “What are you watching?”
And then Futaba burst into tears. It took her a long time to explain in between sobs what had
happened, but the time she had, Sojiro had gone very pale.
“I’m calling the cops,” he said, fumbling with his phone. “Shit, I don’t know their number for
Inaba.”
“I’ll get it,” Futaba said, getting back into her seat. Her computer had gone completely silent,
which probably meant Goro’s phone broke. She refused to consider what that might mean.
She gave Sojiro the number, and Sojiro called the police station. When he was done, he took
Futaba down to the kitchen and began to make her comfort curry. Futaba sat at the kitchen
table quietly, trying not to cry. She pulled her knees to her chest.
“I’m sorry,” she whispered.
“For what?” Sojiro asked gently. He put down the knife he was using to chop vegetables and
turned toward her. “It’s not your fault, whatever happened.”
“I know I shouldn’t be eavesdropping on conversations, but I did it anyway,” Futaba said. “I
think I heard something weirdly personal for Goro-kun. Getting shot is personal, right?”
“Forget Akechi-kun, hearing someone get shot has to be pretty traumatizing for any kid.”
Sojiro sighed. “It’s still not your fault this happened, Futaba. And in this case, at least we
know that someone reported the incident to the police.”
“So my eavesdropping helped?” Futaba asked hopefully.
“Maybe this once,” Sojiro said. “But don’t make a habit of it. You’re right. One day you are
going to hear something that wasn’t meant for your ears. How would you feel if you were
telling Wakaba something private, and I overheard it because I was spying on you?”
“I don’t keep secrets from you.”

“Fine, what if Akechi overheard?”
Futaba made a face. “I guess I wouldn’t like that,” she said reluctantly. She hiccupped as
another sob forced its way to the surface. “Is– is Goro going to be alright?”
“I hope so,” Sojiro said, grimacing.
Maybe Futaba was a coward, but she didn’t think she was ever going to eavesdrop on another
conversation ever again. Especially not if getting shot was a regular occurrence for Goro.
She pulled out her phone and furiously called Tatsumi.

Akira screamed shrilly as they fell deeper into the TV world. The static portal buzzed around
them until they landed in the soft grass with a painful thump.
Goro lay on his back and gasped for breath. He touched his forehead and drew his hand back,
inspecting the blood that came up on his fingers. The only thing he could feel was an odd
lump on his forehead where a hole should be.
Akira was already standing. “What the hell is going on?” he asked, his voice shaking. “Who
was that?”
Goro wanted to shut his eyes and laugh, but he had no idea how safe this sanctuary really
was. Tsuyoshi could come bursting into this world at any minute.
He forced himself to stand up. He picked up his phone from the ground, which must have
fallen from his pocket during the fall.
“Are you okay?” Akira asked, his voice small. Tears filled his eyes. “You look… your
face…”
“I’m fine,” Goro said. “Physically, at least. To answer your other two questions, I have no
clue what the hell is going on, and all I can tell you is that he definitely isn’t your uncle.”
“My uncle?” Akira’s face turned to confusion. “What does my uncle have to do with this?”
Goro ran his fingers through his hair, grimacing at how sticky it was. He began to walk away.
“I’m not having this conversation right now. We have to get out of here.”
“Yes, you are,” Akira said stonily, following him. “I’m so sick of you hiding things from
me.”
“I’m not going to tell you the truth only for you to not believe me,” Goro said.
“You’re not even giving me a chance.”
“I did give you a chance!” Goro’s voice scraped raw against his throat, and he took a deep
breath in an attempt to compose himself. “But you get so goddamn defensive every time I

suggest your uncle might be evil–”
Akira looked as though he had been slapped in the face. “He’s not–”
A thundering shockwave blasted them both off their feet. The sky flashed back and forth
from blue to gray TV static. The landscape became pixelated, looking as though it was falling
apart at the seams.
Goro stumbled to his feet, pulling Akira up alongside him. Tsuyoshi was larger than life, no
longer looking like anyone at all. Golden tentacles covered in green eyes poured out around
him, and a white mask was the only thing covering his face.
“Did you really think entering my domain was a good idea?” The entity’s voice was a mix of
Tsuyoshi and Shido’s voices, but underneath Goro could hear a far shriller voice speaking.
“Oh my god,” Akira whispered. He stumbled backwards. He grabbed Goro’s phone from his
hand and threw it at the entity.
Obviously, it did nothing. Goro accepted that he was never going to see that phone again.
Goro summoned a persona on random and shouted, “Megidolaon!”
The entity didn’t bother to dodge. The blast of almighty damage seemingly did no damage at
all.
He laughed, and the world continued to glitch around him. “You’re going to have to do better
than that.”
Akira grabbed Goro’s hand and began tugging at him. “Goro, we have to run,” he said.
Akira was right. There was no way Goro was going to win this battle alone.
Goro spun around and began sprinting after Akira. The entity’s laughter only grew louder.
“You can run all you’d like,” he said. “It doesn’t change the fact that I hold control of this
world.”
Akira had stopped running, and Goro skidded to a halt beside him. Where there was once an
innocent enough stream, Goro stood on the edge of a precipice. He couldn’t see the bottom.
“Please let this be a bad dream,” Akira muttered, shutting his eyes tightly. “Please, please,
please–”
The world was getting darker around them. The entity was getting closer.
Goro’s pocket felt very warm. He reached inside and pulled out the same card that Igor had
given him. Its reflective surface began to glow a blue hue.
“What’s that?” Akira demanded.

The card was so bright that Goro had to squint. Was it just his imagination, or was it growing
bigger?
The monster shrieked. “Where did you get that?!”
The card yanked itself from Goro’s grasp and floated in front of them. It was now the size of
a small window, and a small force dragged Goro and Akira toward it.
Inconveniently enough, that was also toward the edge of the cliff. Goro dug his heels into the
ground.
The monster continued screeching. Goro cast rakukaja on both himself and Akira just before
they were hit by a devastating blast of magic. Akira shouted in pain. Goro himself felt tears
spring to his eyes.
“Diarama,” Goro whispered, drawing from one of his other personas. Warmth filled his body,
but for how long would they be able to hold?
The card was now the size of a door. It looked more like a massive mirror than a card, and the
once small force was now becoming a vacuum. Goro was unable to do anything as he and
Akira were yanked suddenly off their feet and sucked toward the mirror’s surface.
Instead of hitting the cold surface of a mirror, like Goro expected, Goro’s legs went straight
through it. The silvery blue surface of the card rippled like water. Akira screamed in alarm as
they were pulled deeper into the mirror’s surface.
Goro caught a glimpse of the tentacle monster being yanked off the ground before he was
submerged by inky darkness.

Kanji had received Goro’s distress signal along with everyone else on the team. But when
they arrived at the location texted to them, all that was left was a pile of drying blood in the
grass, a destroyed door and window, and a broken television.
The police were baffled, but they forced the Kanji and the others away from the crime scene.
Apparently, they needed to ‘preserve the evidence.’ Which would make sense if there
actually was evidence to work with.
Kanji caught Dojima muttering as they walked away from the house to watch the crime scene
from a distance. “These kids are going to be the death of me.”
He was worried. They were all worried.
“What the heck happened?” Chie asked.
“You don’t think Goro-kun is dead, do you?” Yukiko asked, her lip trembling.
“You need a body to be dead,” Yosuke said grimly. “Did you see that TV? Don’t you think
Goro might have tried to escape through there?”

“That would also explain the disappearance of Kurusu-kun,” Naoto said. “Neighbors report
that he’s usually home by this hour, but he’s nowhere in sight.”
“Maybe he’s just shopping?” Teddie asked hopefully.
“But why would the TV be broken?” Rise asked. “We never dove through broken
televisions.”
Kanji’s phone chose that moment to start ringing. Kanji chose to ignore it.
“Maybe we should meet in the TV world and try to locate them,” Yu said. “If they went in
here, we’ll have no idea where they ended up.”
Rise nodded. “I hope we can find them before anything else happens.”
Could Kanji’s phone stop ringing?
“Give me a second,” Kanji said. He’d answer, see what this person wanted to say so badly,
and return to making sure Goro wasn’t dead.
“Hello?” Kanji asked irritably.
“Hi, this is Isshiki Futaba, I’m a friend of Goro-kun’s,” a voice of a young girl said. “And
he’d better still be alive!”
“Uh… we’re working on that,” Kanji said. “But how did you know–”
“Some creepy guy wanted him dead because he was a disappointment or something, and then
there was a gunshot, and-and– then he, Goro-kun, I mean, made noise, and then he was with
someone else, and then the phone cut out! Do you need anything with hacking abilities?
Because I can do that. I can help.”
Kanji lowered his phone, still baffled. “Yu-kun, do we need anyone with hacking skills?”
Yu’s brows furrowed together. “No, I think we’re good.” He glanced behind him at the crime
scene. “We should get going.”
Kanji nodded as they started jogging to Junes. “Um, we’re alright for now,” he said. “But
thanks for the offer? How old are you?”
“Ugh, forget it,” Isshiki said. “Just keep me posted, okay?”
“Sure.” Kanji hung up. “Good news, guys! I think you’re right. According to Goro’s friend,
she heard Goro talking before the phone cut out. Or something.”
“You think entering the TV caused the signal to die?” Naoto asked.
Kanji nodded. “Exactly.” Knowing Goro was alive didn’t make him feel that much better,
especially considering that creep Tsuyoshi might be involved. The worry was practically
enough to make him sick to his stomach. “Now let’s hurry up and find him.”

Goro and Akira crashed into wooden flooring, and a wave of dust rose around them. Goro
pressed his palms against the rough surface, coughing and gasping for breath simultaneously.
Akira wheezed as Goro inhaled sharply.
The simultaneously bitter and spicy smell of Leblanc hit Goro like a bullet.
Goro jumped to his feet, suddenly aware of the bar counter next to him. The true Sayuri hung
on the wall, and only a few meters away from Goro were the stairs leading up to Akira’s
room.
“What is this place?” Akira asked.
Why were Goro’s eyes burning?
The bell chimed behind them. Goro spun around as the door swung open.
Kurusu Akira, seventeen years old and bundled up in winter clothes, entered Leblanc.
“Kurusu-kun?” Goro whispered.
Akira didn’t even look at him. He walked through Goro, as incorporeal as a ghost. Goro
didn’t even feel cold as Akira passed.
Goro continued to watch as Akira walked up the stairs and disappeared from view.
The other Akira, still twelve and ignorant, looked absolutely baffled. “Who was that?” he
asked. “What just happened?”
“I–”
“Don’t lie to me,” Akira snapped before Goro could even finish. “You called him Kurusu.
You know who he is. But he’s too young to be my uncle, and my dad doesn’t look like that,
and neither of them are ghosts–”
The lights buzzed as they flickered in and out. Akira froze.
The air began to grow colder.
“We need to get out of here,” Goro said. Tsuyoshi was being dragged through the same portal
as they had. It was only a matter of time before it appeared, and that time was getting closer
by the minute.
“Okay,” Akira said, his voice wavering.
Goro turned to the front door before the lights burned out entirely. Tsuyoshi crashed face-first
into the ground in front of them from seemingly out of nowhere. He was back in his human
form, although Goro couldn’t make out his face in the darkness.

It didn’t matter. Tsuyoshi was blocking their exit, and there was very little hope of them
making it successfully past him.
Goro grabbed Akira’s arm and shoved them both underneath the table nearest to the front
door. Akira was blessedly wise enough to stay completely silent. His face was paler than
ever, but he kept his mouth pressed into a thin line. Goro held his breath.
“Fucking shit,” Tsuyoshi hissed as he got to his feet. “Are you kidding me?”
Akira’s eyes widened.
“Alright Goro, enough with the running.” Tsuyoshi’s eyes glowed a dim yellow in the dark as
he started walking forward. Goro and Akira leaned further away from him as he approached.
“Let’s just discuss this like adults.”
Quiet breaths. Don’t think about hiding from Jin. Akira needed him.
“Oh, I see what’s happening here,” Tsuyoshi said. “You’re hiding, aren’t you? You’re so
afraid that you’ve reduced yourself to hiding behind bar counters.”
Tsuyoshi’s silhouette was approaching the back end of the room. Goro silently moved out
from under the table, pushing Akira to follow him.
“Come out, come out wherever you are!” Tsuyoshi exclaimed as Goro crept to Leblanc’s
door. “I promise I won’t bite.”
Goro opened the door. The bell chimed obnoxiously, and Tsuyoshi’s eyes appeared from
behind the counter.
Goro and Akira ran.
Instead of leading out into Yongen-Jaya, the door lead to a flight of stairs. Goro stumbled
down the spiral staircase, too afraid to look behind him. Akira’s frantic breathing followed.
They ended up in a place that looked remarkably like Junes’ food section. Aisles filled the
room, and there was a produce section ahead of Goro to the right.
The lights began to flicker on and off, and Goro didn’t bother to assess his surroundings. He
dragged Akira behind a large shelf as Tsuyoshi’s footsteps echoed behind them. The lights
burned out, engulfing the Junes in darkness.
“While we play this little game of hide and seek, let me tell you a story,” Tsuyoshi said. His
voice was frighteningly close, but Goro couldn’t spot his eyes. Goro and Akira continued to
creep along the side of the shelf as Goro’s eyes slowly adjusted to the darkness. “You see, it
starts with a friendly little bet.”
Tsuyoshi’s footsteps echoed from the other side of the shelf. Goro froze when he reached the
end. He craned his neck around the corner and spotted Tsuyoshi standing in the center of the
room, his eyes still glowing that dangerous yellow hue. Goro yanked his head back behind
the shelf.

“I thought that humanity would destroy itself,” Tsuyoshi said. “But that Philemon… he
thought it would enlighten itself.” Tsuyoshi laughed. “I mean, what a joke, right?”
Goro glanced at Tsuyoshi again. He couldn’t see his eyes. Hopefully that meant his back was
turned.
“Long story short, Philemon gets these annoying-ass heroes of justice, they defeat me, I fade
into the collective unconsciousness, etcetera, etcetera.”
Goro and Akira ran behind another shelving unit. Their footsteps weren’t as quiet as Goro
had hoped. Tsuyoshi’s footsteps began to head in their direction at a lazy pace.
“After that, I was asleep—or banished, whatever you want to call it—for almost twenty
years. Maybe that seems like a long time to toddlers like you, but it was really closer to a
blink. Do you want to know what snapped me out of it? Any guessers?”
A pile of boxes sat just past the shelves Akira and Goro were creeping behind. If they could
duck behind the boxes before Tsuyoshi could catch sight of them, they might have a moment
to catch their breath.
“No audience interaction at all,” Tsuyoshi sighed. “It was this dumbass named Maruki.
Thought he could become a god. Fused reality with the cognitive world.”
Goro and Akira crouched behind the boxes. A few meters away, Tsuyoshi’s eyes peered
down the aisle they were standing in just moments before.
“Well, reality stayed fucked up for a month or so, which gave me plenty of time to come to
my senses,” Tsuyoshi said. “I found that the world had been through quite a few changes
since I was last online.”
The eyes got closer as Tsuyoshi walked down the aisle. Goro and Akira shuffled around the
boxes to stay out of sight, careful not to make a sound.
“Did you know that Yaldabaoth gave you the metaverse app, Goro?” Tsuyoshi asked. “Do
you want to know why?”
Goro held out a hand to tell Akira to stay put. With any luck, Tsuyoshi would walk away
from the boxes and give them an opening to get to the other side of the room. With any luck,
there was an exit.
“You were so full of bitterness and rage that Yaldabaoth saw you as a distortion.” Tsuyoshi
laughed as his footsteps stopped. He sounded like he was right in front of them. “He wanted
you to be the antagonist in his trickster’s story.”
Goro clenched his fists. Now wasn’t the time to be distracted, but how could he not be? Not
only had he been manipulated by Shido, but he had been manipulated by a deity who wanted
to see Goro be the villain? Was his entire life nothing but being a pawn for someone else’s
game?

“Oh, did Kurusu-kun not mention that?” Tsuyoshi said mockingly. There was no way he saw
Goro’s face– Goro would see his face too– but he must have guessed at Goro’s reaction.
“Didn’t want to hurt your feelings. Or maybe he was afraid of what you’d do if you knew.”
Goro bit his tongue. Don’t react. Don’t say anything. Tsuyoshi wanted a reaction out of him.
Goro couldn’t give him that pleasure. He couldn’t give away their location.
If Goro could see Akira’s facial expression in this darkness, he was sure it’d be baffled.
“Anyway,” Tsuyoshi said. His voice began to grow farther away as he continued walking
away from them. “I thought… wow, so many opportunities for humanity to have been
destroyed while I was gone, and they didn’t take even one? From another perspective,
Philemon had won our little bet.”
Goro crept along the edge of the boxes and glanced around the corner. He couldn’t even see
Tsuyoshi’s silhouette.
“That perspective would be wrong.” Tsuyoshi’s voice hardened. “Philemon is a little cheat,
always handpicking heroes he knows will be able to save the day. Giving them helpers and
personas and the like. His precious wildcards.”
Goro gestured for Akira to follow him.
“Here’s the good news.” Tsuyoshi’s voice brightened. “I’m a cheater too. So I thought, what
if I bring my own wildcard to the fray? Someone who will maybe be a negative influence on
Philemon’s heroes of justice.”
Goro didn’t like where this was going. He and Akira huddled behind a large barrel filled with
who-knows-what.
“Sorry about the time travel thing,” Tsuyoshi said. “I know you hated it. But that was kind of
the point.”
From their new position, Goro could see a bright light emerging from one of the freezer doors
behind a shelf. That must be their exit.
If only Tsuyoshi wasn’t standing directly in front of it.
“You were meant to hate the world,” Tsuyoshi continued. Did he just enjoy listening to the
sound of his own voice? “You were meant to encourage everyone to kill the Appriser. You
were meant to want the end to come so badly that you would do whatever it took to make
sure it happened.”
Goro ducked back behind the barrel and glanced at Akira. He pointed at the large silhouette
of the produce section. Akira nodded.
“Instead, you do what? You make friends! Imagine! A distortion like yourself actually
convincing himself he could heal. That he could start fresh. What a joke.”

As they began to creep toward the produce, Goro tried to ignore the words coming out of
Tsuyoshi’s mouth.
“You can’t be redeemed.” Tsuyoshi’s voice became angrier and angrier. “I thought some time
with that Takaya would convince you to join Strega’s side. But you just ran away like a
coward! Then, of course, I put a request to get your best friend killed, but you came to her
fucking rescue.”
They successfully made it to the produce. Goro looked at Akira and made a throwing motion
with his hand, pointing to the barrel they were just hiding behind. If they could knock over
the barrel, it might fool Tsuyoshi into thinking they’re in a different location, which might
give them an opportunity to run to the door.
“You were actually convincing yourself you were a hero. You actually saved lives with your
presence.”
That was news. Too many people had died that year.
Akira removed a spherical fruit from one of the boxes.
“There was still hope with the fog in Inaba, though. I mean, I sowed mistrust between your
friends by planting that tracker on your leader… I got you all drunk that one time. That was
hilarious.”
Akira took aim.
“I even pretended to be your best friend’s uncle!” Akira froze, his arm half-way poised to
throw. “That’s right, Akira-kun. Goro was right all along! I’m really just a monster in
disguise. How does that make you feel?”
Goro would take the fruit and throw it himself, but he was in a less good position to aim. And
they would need to make a break for it as soon as they made the throw. Would Akira follow
him in his state?
“All in the hopes of getting Goro-kun to do anything to prevent those brats from finding the
real killer. I was so certain Goro would at least kill Namatame, which would have been the
sure path to killing that little girl and ruining the world.”
Goro almost had. Goro had almost done exactly what Tsuyoshi wanted. Would Nanako not
wake up if they had done that?
There was still no time for thinking about what could have been. Goro put a hand on Akira’s
shoulder, hoping to shake him out of it.
Akira yanked himself away.
“But you managed to save the world again. And that brat Marie. And last time with
Yaldabaoth you couldn’t destroy the world when you tried, so there’s no hope there. My plan
failed. And you want to know the most frustrating part?”

Akira took a silent breath and once again took aim toward the barrel. He wound up his arm.
“You’ve managed to convince yourself and everyone around you that you’re the good guy.”
Tsuyoshi laughed nastily. “But we both know the truth. Good guys don’t kill their friends.”
Akira threw the fruit across the room. It hit the barrel and tipped it over with a devastating
crash.
“There you are,” Tsuyoshi said. His footsteps began to approach the barrel. Goro and Akira
made a mad sprint toward the exit door. They skidded around the shelves, and Goro pulled
the door open with both hands.
“Wait a minute…” Tsuyoshi muttered. Either he heard their feet skidding against the
linoleum tile, or he noticed nobody was at the barrel. It didn’t matter. Goro and Akira were
already sprinting down the stairs as Tsuyoshi’s voice faded behind them. “You little fuckers!”
The next floor was filled with yellow fog, looking exactly like the TV world, but the exit was
in plain sight. It was a massive mirror like the one they entered through, and it was glowing
the same blue color as the previous one.
Goro grabbed Akira’s hand and sprinted toward it. As if walking through water, they dove
through the liquid surface. Tsuyoshi screamed behind them.
They landed in a very familiar looking shack. Neither of them wasted any time contemplating
where they were. They jumped to their feet and began to run further away from the mirror.
If Tsuyoshi jumped out after them, Goro wasn’t sure what they would do. They couldn’t play
this game of cat and mouse forever, and Tsuyoshi had far more stamina than either of them.
But the mirror had stopped glowing. Tsuyoshi didn’t come out of it.
“Is he gone?” Akira asked, staring at the mirror with the same level of confusion Goro felt.
Igor had said the strange card was a gift to help him. Did it serve as some sort of prison to
keep Tsuyoshi trapped? Why had Igor waited so long to give Goro the key?
“If he could follow us, he would have by now,” Goro said. He crouched down and gasped for
breath. “Shit.”
His phone was missing from his pocket thanks to Akira’s stunt earlier. Goro did have the
emergency button still, which he pressed. At least somebody would know where to pick him
up.
“You have to explain to me what’s going on,” Akira said. His voice shook. “That was my
uncle. And we were in some weird magic land, and we just walked through a mirror, and
apparently you knew me with time travel? What’s going on?”
So, for the fifth time in this wretched timeline, Goro explained everything.

Silent tears ran down Akira’s face by the time Goro was done. Goro didn’t look him in the
eye.
“I’m sorry,” Akira said.
“Why?” Goro asked. Of all the reactions he expected, an apology was not one of them.
“You tried to warn me,” Akira said. “You told me my uncle was evil, and I didn’t listen at all.
I accused you of lying.”
“Oh, well, I don’t blame you for not believing me.” That wasn’t true. But after everything
that had just occurred, Goro wasn’t particularly inclined to saddle Akira with guilt.
“You should.” Akira stared at his feet. “I’m sorry I’m not him.”
Goro’s mouth felt very dry. He knew exactly what Akira was talking about, but it felt wrong
to say so. “Him?”
“Your rival,” Akira said. “He’s the reason you came here in the first place, right? I must’ve
been a really big disappointment in comparison.”
“You weren’t–”
“I was.” Akira glared at Goro. “Please don’t try to lie to me again. I can’t imagine myself
doing half of the stuff Joker does. I would be disappointed if I was in your shoes.”
“You’re a very good friend, Akira-kun,” Goro said, trying to keep his voice firm. “I don’t
care if you’re not like your former counterpart.”
How could something feel so true and yet so false at the same time? Even Akira looked
disappointed by Goro’s answer.
“If you could choose,” Akira said. “Him or me. Which would you decide?”
“That’s not fair.”
“Which?” Akira’s voice cracked.
Goro missed the old Akira. Some days he missed him so much that his chest hurt, and Goro
wanted nothing more than to wake up in his old reality just to speak to him again.
But to see him again at the cost of losing the Akira he knew now? Would it be worth it?
“I don’t know,” Goro whispered.
Birds chirped loudly outside the shack. Goro could barely hear any passing cars.
“Right,” Akira said, his voice hushed. “Sorry. I shouldn’t have asked.”
“I can’t blame you,” Goro said. He stood up and dusted off his pants. “Let’s get out of this
dump.”

Goro and Akira left the shack, and Goro identified it as the shack he and Junpei investigated
back in August, just with even more scorch marks and even a few holes in the walls. Still, the
chances of it being anything else were slim. How many shacks existed with a giant mirror in
the middle of nowhere?
“But I still don’t understand,” Akira said. “How were we able to go through the mirrors?
Why didn’t Uncl—the monster follow us back out?”
“If I had to guess… the mirror is the entrance to a prison of some kind. For whatever reason,
we can leave, but Tsuyoshi is trapped. The prison must also dampen his abilities, which is
why he returned to human form.”
“I guess… but what’s the mirror doing here in the middle of nowhere?” Akira asked. “And
what’s with the scorch marks?”
“I assume Igor--he’s in charge of personas and wildcards--was preparing the prison closer to
me, but Tsuyoshi caught wind of it and brought it here to destroy it.” Goro frowned. “This is
all speculation, of course. We’d likely have to go back in to find out more.”
“Go back in? Seriously?”
“Let’s not worry about that for now,” Goro said. “I’d like to speak to the others before doing
anything.”
“Alright,” Akira said quietly. “I guess we just have to wait for them to arrive.”
An uncomfortable silence fell over them, and they sat down and waited.

Chapter 91: March 18–21, 2012
Chapter Summary

Wow, that is a LOT of people in one scene.

Chapter Notes

tw: blood, referenced child neglect, ptsd, self-hatred

See the end of the chapter for more notes

“What have they done to it?!” Teddie exclaimed in horror.
The team entered the TV world in the hopes of finding Goro and Akira, but instead they
found that the place now had a terrifying cliffside where Yu was pretty sure there used to be a
stream.
“It’s okay, Teddie-kun,” Yukiko hastened to assure him. “At least the fog hasn’t come back.”
“This place feels… off,” Rise said. “Like something really bad used to be here, but is gone
now. An imprint, I guess.”
“Sure, sure, but what about Goro?” Kanji interrupted, crossing his arms. “Is he here?”
“Akira-kun too,” Yosuke added.
Rise shut her eyes and summoned her persona. Her shoulders slumped a few moments later.
“No sign of them.”
“Damnit,” Kanji muttered.
“What does that mean?” Chie demanded. “Where could they be?”
“I don’t know,” Yu said, his own worry rising.
“Let’s leave and reassess what we know,” Naoto said. “Perhaps someone has found them
while we’ve been gone.”
Almost as soon as they exited the TV world, Yu noticed he had received a text on his phone
with coordinates. He also had a missed call from Kirijo-san.

“Oh, thank god,” Kanji let out a breath. “Goro’s pressed the button again. He’s alive.”
“Alright,” Yu said, texting Kirijo to let her know that they’d get Goro and she should just
focus on getting to Inaba. “Let’s get him.”

It was Dojima’s car that rolled down the gravel lot and stopped almost directly in front of
them. Yu and Dojima both jumped out of the car, jogging toward them.
“Are you okay?” Yu asked immediately. “What happened?”
“Where are you injured?” Dojima asked.
Akira shrunk back from the two of them. “We’re fine,” he said. He glanced at Goro. “I
think.”
“You don’t bleed that much and be fine,” Dojima said.
Goro pointed to his forehead. “Apart from a scar, I seem to have recovered,” he said dryly.
Yu’s face turned almost as gray as his hair. “But that’s…”
“He was shot in the head,” Akira said, almost mechanically. “I saw it. But then he got up
again.”
“That’s not how that works,” Dojima said.
“Well, I sincerely doubt you’ll believe me when I say that I had an immortality pendant
around my neck for the past two years and finally chose to make use of it,” Goro said
sweetly. “Can we please leave?”
To their credit, the only one who looked like he wanted to question it was Dojima, who kept
his mouth shut anyway.
“Alright,” Dojima sighed. “Get in.”
“What happened to your phone?” Yu asked as Akira and Goro climbed into the back seat.
“We couldn’t reach you at all. Not even your weird hacker friend could contact you.”
Akira picked up Nanako’s booster seat and placed it in the trunk behind them. Goro shut the
car door. “Akira threw it at an eldritch monster.”
Dojima sputtered.
“Sorry,” Akira muttered.
“I probably would have done the same in your shoes,” Yu said sympathetically. “What’s this
about an eldritch monster?”

“Are everyone’s seatbelts on?” Dojima asked. He glanced over his shoulder and shot a stern
expression at Goro and Akira. They quickly buckled their seatbelts.
“Remember Tsuyoshi?” Goro asked as Dojima began to drive back up the gravel road.
“Turns out his true form is a tentacle monster. Or something. He wanted to see the end the
world because of some sort of bet with another ultra-powerful being. Or maybe he just hates
humanity, I'm not clear. He was the one who put the tracker in your jacket.”
Akira looked out the window and rested his forehead against the glass.
“Oh. Well, I guess compared to a gas station attendant that’s not really all that surprising. We
knew there was something up with the guy.”
“So they know about the magic stuff?” Akira asked quietly. “And the time travel thing?”
“What’s this about time travel?” Dojima asked.
Oh, for the love of– forget it.
“I’m a murderer who died at the ripe age of eighteen and was sent back to the time when I
was ten years old so that I could fuck things up more,” Goro snapped. “Any questions?”
“That last part was new,” Yu said. Dojima merged back onto the highway.
“It’s my uncle’s fault,” Akira said.
“Why does everything suddenly make sense now?” Dojima muttered, clenching the steering
wheel like it was life support.
“Are you going to arrest me, Dojima-san?” Goro asked nastily. “You don’t have any proof.
Nearly everyone I’ve killed is alive now.”
“Nearly everyone?” Yu asked. “I thought you didn’t start killing people until you were like
fifteen.”
“Fifteen,” Dojima muttered.
“I was very nearly sixteen,” Goro hastened to say.
“He was a hitman masking as a celebrity; try not to think too hard about it,” Yu said.
“And just because I haven’t actively killed anyone in this timeline doesn’t mean I didn’t
accidentally lead anyone to their deaths,” Goro muttered. His mother and Chidori being
prime examples.
“Unless you killed them directly, I really don’t think that can count as your fault,” Yu said.
“Can we not talk about this right now?” Goro snapped. He crossed his arms. “If we give
Dojima anymore of a migraine, he’s going to crash this vehicle.”

“I hate to agree,” Dojima said grimly.
“You’re not going to arrest him, are you?” Akira asked.
Dojima sighed, deflating. “No. I’m not arresting him. Nobody would take the confession
seriously even if I wanted to.”
“That’s what I thought,” Goro muttered.
“On a change of subject,” Dojima said. “Kurusu-kun, I contacted your parents about the
incident. They said they were away on a day trip but that they were on their way back.”
“Okay,” Akira said.
“Kurusu-kun…” Yu said hesitantly. “How often do your parents go on ‘day trips’?”
“Not very often,” Akira fibbed.
“No,” Goro said sarcastically. “It would be more accurate to call them month trips. Those
happen on the regular.”
“He’s lying,” Akira said with a reproachful glare. “They don’t do that.”
“Look, Kurusu-kun, you’re not in trouble,” Dojima said. “But if your parents are neglecting
you, we need to know. It’s a dereliction of care.”
“They care about me,” Akira said. “And besides, my uncle…”
The silence was heavy as cars sped past Dojima, who was driving at the speed limit. “Do you
have any living relatives?” Dojima asked.
“My, um, actual uncle might still be in the states,” Akira said quietly. “I don’t know. But my
parents aren’t neglectful.”
“I can guarantee you that the foster system isn’t going to be any better than they are,” Goro
said.
Dojima sighed. “What do you want me to do?” he asked. “I can’t let you live alone. You’re
not even in middle school.”
“Do you know anyone looking to adopt?” Yu asked quietly.
“I want to stay in Inaba,” Akira pleaded. “And I don’t want to leave my parents.”
“Akira, your parents have left you behind,” Goro snapped. “So much so that you were in the
process of being groomed. You can’t keep living like this.”
“They’re all I have,” Akira said.
“You have me.”

Akira glowered out the window. “Fine. Do whatever you want.”
When they finally arrived back in Inaba, late in the evening, Akira’s parents were already
surveying the wreckage of their home. From the safety of Dojima’s car, Goro watched
Dojima escort Akira to his parents.
The mother wept appropriately over Akira, checking him for injuries and exclaiming how
worried she was. Even Akira’s father looked concerned.
But it was too little, too late. Akira almost died alone due to their negligence. Goro refused to
let that be swept under the rug.
“Are you alright?” asked a voice, causing Goro to jump.
It was Yosuke’s father. Hanamura-san wore a grim expression, probably noticing the blood
all over Goro.
“Oh, Hanamura-san,” Goro said. “Yes… I’m fine. I’m surprised you thought to come here.”
“How could I not? Probably everyone in town heard those gunshots, and then both Yosuke
and Teddie ran off in a panicked rush,” Hanamura said. “When I heard you two disappeared,
I’ve been checking in to see if you and poor Akira-kun show up. It’s a major relief to know
that you both are alright.”
Goro supposed that wasn’t completely unreasonable. “Are you acquainted with Akira-kun?”
“Of course,” Hanamura said. “I haven’t been here long, but he comes by Junes enough for me
to know him. He’s a good kid.”
Goro nodded exhaustedly. “Yeah, he is.”

Mitsuru waited for for him outside the Tatsumi residence. Goro bowed deeply and apologized
for worrying her before explaining everything that happened.
“I’m afraid I lost my phone in our escape,” Goro said. “I’m sorry.”
“Please stop apologizing,” Mitsuru said. “Of course I’ll replace your phone. It’s no issue.”
Goro swallowed. “Right.”
“We can talk more about what happened later,” Mitsuru said, folding her arms in front of her
chest. “Take a shower and get some rest. It’s been a long day.”
Goro entered the house and was immediately attacked—no, hugged—by Tatsumi, who only
embraced him for a fraction of a second before focusing her attention on his blood-soaked
clothes and hair.
“Are you injured?” Tatsumi asked. Goro was too overwhelmed to respond.

“He’s fine, Ma,” Kanji said quickly. “Stop worrying so much, geez.”
But even Kanji looked like he was half-tempted to check Goro for bullet wounds. Goro
brushed away Tatsumi’s worried hand, which was still checking his head for injuries, and
stepped away from the both of them.
“I’m uninjured,” Goro said. “And I don’t know who did this to me, so I think I would like to
shower.”
“I’d say you’d give me gray hairs, but Kanji has already given me a full head,” Tatsumi said.
Goro managed a small laugh. “My apologies.”
“Don’t you dare apologize.” Tatsumi put her hands on her hips sternly. “You take a shower
and put on a nice change of clothes. I’ll have a warm meal waiting for you. You look like you
need it.”
“I’ll help with that,” Kanji said eagerly, following Tatsumi into the kitchen as Goro headed to
the bathroom.
With a breath of relief, Goro finally made it to a shower. He washed the blood from his hair
and skin as quickly as possible. He wasn’t in the right headspace to be in the water for longer
than necessary.
He changed into his pajamas and picked up Monster Cat from his resting place on top of his
climbing toy. Miraculously, Monster Cat didn’t resist. Instead, when Goro sat down on his
futon, he curled up in Goro’s lap and stared at Goro with wide yellow eyes.
Goro stared back as he tried to wrap his mind around everything that had happened.
He had known for years that Tsuyoshi wished him harm. He hadn’t been subtle about it. But
with context… to know that everything Tsuyoshi did was to encourage Goro to ruin
everything for everyone… to be a pawn in Tsuyoshi’s game…
It made Goro sick to his stomach. How many times had Goro nearly fallen for any of his
traps?
If it had taken three years for Tsuyoshi to decide Goro was a lost cause, Goro must have been
doing a pretty good job of nearly destroying the world with his presence.
Goro’s hands shook. He buried them deeper into Monster Cat’s fur.
Tsuyoshi was right. Somewhere along the line, Goro had somehow convinced himself that he
was a hero. A good guy. That he had redeemed himself.
But could people like Goro really be redeemed? Had Goro really changed? Or was he just
continuing his same routine of seeking acknowledgement, and this time that was attainable
by being a good person?
What had Shinjiro’s letter said, if Tsuyoshi thought it was necessary to burn it to a crisp?

Goro buried his face in Monster Cat’s fur, trying his hardest to ignore the way his whole body
shook.

They sat in Jazz Jin. Muhen had greeted them with his usual smile, and the live singer was
performing that day.
“How many times is it now?” Akira asked, placing his elbows on the table and propping his
chin up in his hands.
“What?”
“How many times have you been shot in the head?”
Goro sighed. “It’s only been twice.”
“Shit,” Akira muttered. “I’ve got to up my game.”
“Seriously?”
“We’re rivals,” Akira said. “It’s not fair that you’ve been shot in the head twice while I’ve
only been shot in the head once.”
“I’m beginning to wonder if this rivalry is healthy.”
Akira laughed. “Of course it’s not,” he said. He pulled a gun from the inside of his Shujin
uniform and handed it to Goro. “How about it? Will you shoot me in the head for the sake of
our rivalry?”
Goro glowered and pushed the gun away. “Don’t be–”
But Akira was already dead. His head rested against the table in a pool of its own blood.
Goro jumped out of his seat, startled out of his mind.
“What…”
“I’m not him,” twelve-year-old Akira said, inspecting his own body. “I’ll never be him.”

Goro awoke abruptly to a loud knocking on the door. Goro stared at the ceiling, trying to
gather his surroundings.
“Goro-kun?” Kanji’s voice said from the other side of the door. “Are you awake?”
“Just a moment,” Goro said. After failing to nudge Monster Cat from his chest, Goro pulled
him off and set Monster Cat gently on his futon. Goro opened the door to reveal an extremely
exhausted looking Kanji. “What time is it?”

“Um, one in the morning,” Kanji said. “But she wouldn’t let me sleep unless she could talk to
you.”
Kanji held his phone out to Goro. Goro took it extremely cautiously and held it up to his ear.
“Hello, Futaba,” Goro said.
“You asshole!” Futaba cried, her voice cracking. “How could you lose your phone like
that?!”
“It was quite simple, really,” Goro said, running his fingers through his hair. “Akira-kun took
it and threw it at some sort of eldritch creature masquerading as his uncle. Next?”
Futaba sniffed. “Like Cthulhu?”
“I’m sure I have no idea,” Goro said.
“What did he look like?”
“There were plenty of tentacles and eyes to go around.” Goro sighed. “Is this line of
questioning relevant?”
“It makes me feel better, you jerk,” Futaba snapped. “You really scared me.”
“I apologize.”
“You–you’re so stupid,” Futaba said. “You’re not meant to apologize.”
Goro frowned. “Right. Well, now that you’re thoroughly comforted that I’m alive, could I
please go back to sleep?”
“Alright,” Futaba sighed. “But no more funny business!”
“No promises.”
Goro hung up and handed the phone back to Kanji. “Sorry about her,” he said.
Kanji shrugged. “It’s whatever. It wasn’t getting that much sleep anyways.”
“Right, well…” Goro swallowed. “I’m sorry for worrying you all.”
“It’s not me I’m worried about,” Kanji said. “Are you sure… are you sure he won’t come
after you again?”
“If he could have, he would have,” Goro said. “I’m fine.”
“Was that lie for your benefit or mine? ‘Cause I’m not feeling better.”
Goro bit the inside of his cheek and blinked away the tears that wanted to break free. “Kanji,”
he said shakily. “I’ve had a really long day, so I think I would just like… I think I would just
like to sleep it off.”

Kanji’s expression softened. “Okay,” he said. “But if you need anything, just holler, okay?”
Goro nodded. “I’ll bear that in mind.”

“I don’t think we’re going to be able to host the meeting at my house if there’s this many
people,” Yosuke said, surveying the unusual crowd that had gathered at Junes. Not only had
the entire Investigation Team come to discuss what had occurred the day before, but all of
SEES came as well.
“Is that a robot?” Kanji asked, staring at Aigis with a terrified expression.
“I am Aigis,” Aigis said. “I was created as an Anti-Shadow Suppression Weapon, so it is not
inaccurate to say I am a robot. However, I have developed a will most machines do not
possess.”
“Wow,” Chie said.
“Why are you all here?” Goro asked.
“If you seriously expected us to continue on with our lives when one of our best friends was
shot in the head yesterday, you have another thing coming,” Ken said, rolling his eyes.
“So… is it normal to have a twelve-year-old on the team?” Yu asked.
“I don’t want to talk about it,” Yukari muttered.
“First of all, I’m almost fourteen,” Ken said. “Second of all, don’t worry. I’m your garden
variety thirteen-year-old. No time travel included.”
“I’m sure that makes them feel so much better,” Goro said.
“At least it’s less confusing.” Yosuke laughed nervously. “What does that make Goro-kun?
Limited edition time traveling thirteen-year-old?”
“Wait a minute,” Naoto said, staring at Yukari. “You’re an actor in the newest Featherman
series, aren’t you?”
Yukari laughed nervously. “You noticed, huh?”
“Everyone who knows their stuff notices,” Junpei said. “You’re practically a radar for any
diehard Featherman fans out there.”
“Do you do your own stunts?” Rise asked.
“A little,” Yukari admitted.
“Don’t be modest,” Fuuka said. “Your agility is amazing.”

“Maybe we should return to the task at hand?” Minato suggested quietly. He glanced at
Mitsuru and Akihiko pleadingly. Speaking up still wasn’t particularly his forte.
“Right,” Akihiko said. “Where should we meet up?”
“The TV world should be safe, right?” Yukiko asked.
“I’m not sure,” Goro admitted. “Tsuyoshi did follow us in there, but he didn’t follow us out.”
Admittedly, that strange place didn’t seem like the TV world. But Goro would prefer not to
take any risks.
“Again, my room is way too small for all of us,” Yosuke said.
“Perhaps we should just find a relatively secluded spot outside to speak,” Mitsuru said. She
wore casual clothing that made her look almost unrecognizable compared to her official
public appearances. “There’s likely an abundance of those in a small town like this. Am I
wrong?”
“What about the hill?” Teddie asked. “People don’t usually go up there on school days.”
“Why bother?” Ryoji asked. “We’re such a big group that we might as well just sit at one of
the tables in the food court since we’re already here. I mean, won’t we attract more attention
walking to one place together?”
“He has a point,” Chie said reluctantly.
“Not to mention our foe isn’t a member of the general populace this time around,” Naoto
said. “People are likely to assume we’re just celebrating something.”
They went to the food court and dragged multiple round tables together until they had enough
seats for everyone. Once everyone was situated, Goro explained the previous day’s events
and summed up Tsuyoshi’s speech to everyone.
The rest of the group was appropriately horrified.
“You mean… this guy wanted you to end the world?” Fuuka asked.
“We almost ruined everything,” Yosuke muttered, his face ashen. “Oh my god, we almost
killed Nanako.”
“But we didn’t,” Yu said firmly. “Nanako’s better than ever now.”
“There’s so much about him that we don’t understand, but at least his seemingly random
movements against you make sense now,” Mitsuru said. “I’m sorry you had to go through it
alone.”
“I wasn’t alone,” Goro said.
“You only told us about this guy like four months ago,” Ryoji said. “I think we might have
different definitions of alone.”

“At least you’re not alone anymore, right?” Kanji asked.
“He’s an idiot,” Ken announced abruptly. Goro glanced at him in alarm. Ken grinned
sheepishly. “Not you, Goro, although you have your moments. I meant Tsuyoshi.”
“He’s certainly evil,” Naoto said. “But he seems like a rather calculating individual–”
“Why would he think that Goro-kun would make things worse?” Ken demanded. His grin
grew vindictive. “I wonder what his face looked like when he saved Shinji and me.”
“And his plan to tear us apart with the misplaced tracker was barely effective,” Yukiko said.
She giggled. “Not the most thought-out evil plan.”
“I’m glad you think this is so funny,” Goro said irritably. “Evil genius or not, that doesn’t
change the fact that he’s near unstoppable, and we know next to nothing about him. Speaking
of which, can I borrow somebody’s phone?”
Junpei shot Goro a confused look before he tossed his phone in Goro’s direction. Junpei had
obviously recently upgraded to a smartphone, but it was a far older model than Goro had ever
been used to in his teenage years. The screen was tiny. Still, Goro managed to open it.
“Remind me Amano’s phone number, Rise-chan?” Goro asked.
“Oh, um, right now?” Rise asked, obviously confused.
Goro gave a brief explanation of the odd incidents that had occurred in Sumaru thirteen years
ago and how it might apply to their current situation. Rise still looked somewhat alarmed but
gave him Amano’s phone number.
This time, Amano answered.
“This is Amano Maya, how can I help you?” Amano asked.
“Good afternoon, Amano-san,” Goro said. “My name is Akechi Goro. You might remember
me from a voicemail I sent you yesterday?”
“Oh yeah,” Amano said, her voice immediately more serious. “I tried to call you back, but
you didn’t respond. Since you’re calling with another number, I’m guessing something
happened to your phone?”
“You could say that,” Goro said. “Listen, there’s word that thirteen years ago, rumors were
coming to life in Sumaru in the midst of a serial killing case. Do you happen to know
anything about that?”
“A lot was going on at that time,” Amano said. “I was actually going to call you back to tell
you to stay out of it. It needs to stay in the past.”
There was definitely some truth to the claims, in that case. Goro couldn’t let this opportunity
go.

“Does the name Philemon sound familiar to you?” Goro asked. “Or maybe the spear used to
crucify Christ holds some sort of significance?”
The silence over the line was drawn-out and filled with static. Did they lose connection?
“Where did you hear that name?” Amano asked, her voice haunted.
“I spent my entire afternoon yesterday running from a monster who couldn’t shut up about
how much he hated him,” Goro said. “Something about a bet–”
“Nyarlathotep’s back?!”
“Is that his name?”
Amano hesitated. “Look, you’re still in Inaba, right? Give me half a day and I’ll be right
there. I can explain everything then.”
“Fine,” Goro said. “I’ll be looking forward to it.”
“That makes one of us.”
Amano hung up, and Goro handed the phone back to Junpei.
“What did she say?” Fuuka asked.
“Tsuyoshi’s real name is Nyarlathotep, apparently,” Goro said. “And she’ll be here in around
twelve hours to explain everything.”
“Wow,” Rise said. “Who would’ve thought that a random reporter would be involved in all
this?”

Amano arrived at the crack of dawn the following morning with a man who looked to be
about Dojima’s age. He wore a suit and tie that indicated he had been ripped away from his
workplace rather abruptly. Everyone dragged themselves out of bed and arrived at Junes so
they could meet before school started. Massive yawns filled their table at the food court, even
from the adults.
“The local Junes isn’t exactly a covert meeting place,” the strange man observed.
“We’ve already had this discussion,” Mitsuru said. “Unless you have a conference room on
hand, we’ll have to make do.”
“Um, shouldn’t we do introductions first?” Junpei asked.
“Oh, right,” Amano said. “My name is Amano Maya. It’s a pleasure to meet you.” She
bowed before glancing at Yu. “Since when did you guys have Kirijo Mitsuru on your side?”
“We’re just temporarily teaming up,” Fuuka said.

“It’s nice to meet you,” Yukari said.
“Maybe I should have invited Nanjo,” Amano mused. Mitsuru’s eyes widened. “I was kind of
in a rush. I kinda just grabbed Katsuya and began speeding to Inaba.”
“That would be accurate,” said the man. He cleared his throat. “Suou Katsuya. I’ve worked
with Maya during past… incidents.”
Goro hid his unease toward Suou. Amano was currently their best source of information; he
couldn’t question her decision to bring another person to the party. And if Amano thought it
was necessary to bring Nanjo Kei of the Nanjo group into this too, so be it. Still, Goro kept
his eye on Suou as they seated themselves in the food court.
“Alright, first order of business, information trading,” Yosuke said. “Who wants to go first?”
“I’m very curious to know how you’re involved with Nyarlathotep myself,” Suou said.
“Funny, I was about to say the same thing about you,” said Goro. He smiled. “But I assume
it’s connected to the incidents I reminded Amanao-san of.”
Amano frowned and nodded. “That’s right.”
She proceeded to confirm what Goro already knew about rumors coming to life in Sumaru in
1999. Apparently Nyarlathotep was the cause of this occurrence. Being the representation of
chaos and evil that rose from the collective unconscious, he made a bet with Philemon, who
was the exact opposite. Nyarlathotep bet humanity would destroy itself; Philemon had faith
in humanity to rise above evil. Thus sparked a conflict that would haunt Japanese high
schoolers for decades to come.
“But you defeated him in the end?” Naoto asked hopefully.
“Defeated, but we couldn’t destroy him,” Suou said. “I can’t recall his exact words, but as
long as evil exists in humanity’s hearts, he will find a way to come back.”
“We kind of hoped he was bluffing,” Amano said apologetically.
“It took him nearly twenty years to wake back up,” Goro said. “And that was because
someone was fusing the cognitive world with the real world. If not for that, he might have
stayed dormant for longer.”
“Alright, it’s your turn for an explanation,” Amano said. “Because 1999 was thirteen years
ago, and you don’t strike me as the sort of kid who doesn’t know how to do math.”
At this point, Goro had his explanations down to a science. He skipped the gory details,
summing up that he wanted to kill his father and in the process became his personal hitman.
He briefly explained the cognitive world’s role in Yaldabaoth’s plan and continued to
rephrase what Tsuyoshi –no, Nyarlathotep – told him two days prior.
Amano and Suou were obviously startled, but they weren’t given a chance to stew on the
news in silence.

“Wait, I’ve just realized something,” Ryoji said. “What’s with all these hero groups having
detectives? How come SEES never had a detective?”
“We did have an officer selling us weapons,” Minato said reflectively.
“I’m sorry, what?” Suou said indignantly.
“Don’t be that way, we were getting our weapons from a bar because we manufactured a
rumor about the place,” Amano said. “In hindsight, it was kind of messed up.”
“Back to the task at hand?” Akihiko said, nodding his head pointedly toward the group.
“Unless something’s changed, it sounds like this Nyarlathotep guy is trapped in the mirror
dimension Goro-kun left him in. Don’t we have a shot at taking him out?”
“His senses seemed to be dulled as well,” Goro said. “He should have found us otherwise.”
“And where is this mirror?” Suou asked.
“About two hours away,” Yu said. He smiled wryly. “Convenient, huh?”
“If Igor created the realm, why did he make it so far away?” Minato asked. “Sounds pretty
inconvenient to me.”
“Tsu-Nyarlathotep was spending time at that shack,” Goro said. “I think he took it and
attempted to destroy it.”
“He was seriously strong enough to move that thing?” Junpei asked.
“But not strong enough to break it,” Kanji said. “Guy isn’t as cool as he thinks he is.”
“I wouldn’t take him lightly,” Amano said. “I know you guys have faced a lot over the past
few years, but that’s nothing compared to what he’s capable of. I agree we need to defeat him
though. I’d hate to risk him escaping.”
“I hate to agree with her,” Goro said. “We should stay on guard.”
“But if the place is so far away, it’s not like we can just hop in and out on a day to day basis,”
Yukiko said.
“Maybe we can play it off and say we’re going on a camping trip?” Ken suggested.
“Oh, I was bummed I missed out on that last year,” Rise said.
“You didn’t miss much.” Chie said.
Yosuke, Yu, and Kanji shuddered.
“We’d have to go over the weekend in order to miss as little school as possible,” Mitsuru
said. “Seeing as today’s Tuesday, that means we’d have to wait until the end of the week.”
“I say we miss school,” Ken said.

“So close to the end of the term?” Mitsuru demanded.
“None of us are graduating this year,” Yu said thoughtfully. “It could be worse.”
“How much time do you think we have before Nyarlathotep manages to break out of his
prison?” Fuuka asked.
Amano shrugged. “I don’t know,” she admitted. “That’s something you would have to ask
Igor. I’d ask myself, but it sounds like the Velvet Room isn’t as open as it used to be.”
“The door in the central shopping district disappeared after I fulfilled my contract,” Yu said.
Goro hadn’t seen any Velvet Room doors in Inaba after the fight with Izanami either. But he
hadn’t been looking very closely over the past two days. Maybe something had changed?
“I saw one,” Minato said. “It was near the outskirts of town. I caught sight of it on our way
here.”
“I guess Igor really wants us to take that road trip as soon as possible,” Yosuke said.
“Um, who’s Igor again?” Junpei said.
“Igor presides over the Velvet Room, which aids wildcards on their journeys to save
humanity,” Aigis said. “In other words, he helps Minato-kun and Goro-kun kick our enemies'
asses.”
“Yu-kun as well,” Naoto said.
“Try not to think about it too hard,” Kanji said. “It still kind of hurts my head.”
“You can say that again,” Ken said. Koromaru barked.

It was inevitable that Akira would ask what Goro found out since their extremely
traumatizing bonding experience. Therefore, Goro was prepared for the questions that
propped up on their way back from school the following day.
“You’re not bringing me along?” Akira asked after Goro explained the camping trip plan to
the best of his ability.
Goro frowned. “Would you like me to risk your life?”
“You’re risking your life,” Akira said.
“I have years of experience. And a persona. You have neither of those.”
“But I have the potential to have a persona, right?” Akira asked. “I’m sure if I came along, I
could find some way to summon it.”
It was almost tempting. To fight side by side again. To see Arsene after so many years. But–

“It’s not that simple.”
“I want to help,” Akira insisted. “You can’t leave me here to just wait.”
“And I can’t take you and watch you die because we hoped you would be able to summon a
persona,” Goro snapped. “The answer is no. Deal with it.”
Akira stopped walking. Goro turned around to face him.
“I watched you die,” Akira said coldly. “I watched–” his expression faltered. “I watched
some creature pretending to be my uncle shoot you, and now you want me to sit at home like
nothing happened?”
“Let’s pretend for a minute that you can get away from home for days at a time, even after
your parents are now under suspicion of neglect after what happened,” Goro said. “You come
with us, you summon your persona. Then what? You still have next to no experience.”
“I could help.”
“Or you could die,” Goro snarled. “I am not losing you to your pride.”
Akira’s head jerked backwards. “You think this is pride?”
“That’s what it seems like to me.”
“This-this monster was my family.” Akira’s voice cracked. “I don’t care if he wasn’t my real
uncle. He felt more real than anyone else in my life.”
“He was manipulating you–”
“He cares about–” Akira closed his eyes and inhaled shakily. “He acted like he cared about
me. He took me out to ice cream; he gave me his gloves when I was cold; he helped me when
I was sick and nobody else was there. Not even you.”
Goro’s throat closed in on itself. “I’m truly sorry, but that’s not going to change my mind.”
“I just want to know… I just want to see…” Akira looked away. “Are you sure he’s evil?”
“You heard it yourself,” Goro said.
“But maybe it was a trick,” Akira whispered.
“It wasn’t.”
“I know,” Akira whispered. He ran his hands through his hair. “I know.”
Goro swallowed. “Akira-kun,” he said. “I can’t tell you how you feel. I know that in these
situations, I feel very betrayed and angry. But you risking your life is only giving him what
he wants.”
Akira slumped. “Okay,” he said. “Fine.”

“I’m not trying to shut you out,” Goro said.
“I know you’re not.” Akira shouldered his bag. His expression became more closed off.
“Forget I said anything."

taking a trip down memory lane whoop whoop

“Are you sure going camping so close to the end of the semester is such a good idea?”
Tatsumi asked, looking concerned after Kanji told her the plan.
“It’ll be fine, Ma,” Kanji said. “We’ll probably even study while we’re there.”
“And you’ll be with all of your friends?” Tatsumi asked. “Is it even a real campsite?”
“We have adult chaperones too!” Kanji said defensively. “Kirijo-san will be there. I think
she’s Goro-kun’s guardian or something.”
“Oh, Kirijo-san is a lovely young woman,” Tatsumi said. “If she’s there, I’m sure she’ll keep
you on the straight and narrow. What was her number again, Goro-kun?”
Goro reluctantly gave her Mitsuru’s number. Tatsumi proceeded to spend the next twenty
minutes making sure that Kanji and Goro weren’t about to disappear into the wilderness and
never be heard from again.
Mitsuru was an excellent liar. There was no guarantee they weren’t all going to die to
Nyarlathotep in their attempts to end him.
“It sounds like everything will be okay,” Tatsumi said after she finally hung up. “I hope you
two have fun.”
“Thanks, Ma.” Kanji exhaled in relief.
Goro packed his bags and met the others by Junpei’s van and Mitsuru’s bus. It was almost
absurd for all of them to pile into both of the vehicles like school children going on a
fieldtrip.

“Just so you know, I have a friend meeting us there,” Amano said before they left. “I figured
we want all the manpower we can get for this fight.”
“Who?” Goro asked. They were drowning in people as it was.
“Nanjo Kei,” Amano said. “He was pretty involved with Nyarlathotep even before I got
mixed up in demons and stuff, so it felt only fair that he be invited. My other friends are
kinda in the middle of something far way, and I didn’t want to worry them, so it’ll just be
him.”
“I’m acquainted with Nanjo,” Mitsuru said. “I’m sure he’ll be an excellent ally.”
Goro wasn’t surprised she knew him. The Nanjo Group held a similar level of power and
fame as the Kirijo Group. He relaxed slightly. Mitsuru was usually a decent judge of
character.
“Let’s get going,” Yu said. “The drive is kinda long.”
“He’s right,” Junpei said. “The sooner we leave, the better.”
Without any further conversation, everyone began to climb into one of the two vehicles.
“It’s been a long time since I’ve been camping,” Amano said, sitting in the passenger’s seat

what types of shadows they might see in the dungeon.
“Don’t get too excited,” Suou said from the seat in front of Goro. He effectively had an entire
row of seats to himself.
“It’s been a long time since I’ve fought demons either,” Amano said. “I hope I’m not out of
practice.”
“Your aim seemed as impeccable as always when you practiced yesterday,” Suou said.
“Aim?” Yukari asked. She and Rise sat together in the two seats in front of Suou. “Do you
use a bow too?”
“Oh no,” Amano said casually. “I use one of Katsuya’s guns.”
Goro sputtered. “You what?”
“You’ll have to recall that demons, or shadows as you call them, were appearing in the real
world without hesitation,” Suou said. “At the time we didn’t have access to any fancy
weapons, so I gave Maya one of my guns.”
“It worked out pretty well,” Amano said.
“That’s pretty hardcore,” said Junpei as he drove out of Inaba. Goro had almost forgotten
how many rice fields surrounded the town.

“Meanwhile Kanji-kun usually just brings a folding chair to battle,” Rise said thoughtfully.
“Makes us look pretty unprofessional in comparison, huh?”
“I’m pretty wary of guns myself,” Junpei said. His tone was lightheartedly dubious, but
Akihiko looked out the window with a grim expression. The van felt a few degrees colder
than it had a few minutes ago.
“So, um, does the Investigation Team all use folding chairs to fight?” Ken asked, forcing the
conversation forward.
“Yukiko uses a fan,” Goro said.
“And Senpai and Yosuke-kun use more traditional weapons,” Rise said. “Kanji’s just the one
who stands out the most.”
“I won’t forget Chie’s stint with rollerblades myself,” Goro said. “It’s a miracle she didn’t fall
flat on her face.”
“Aw man,” Ken said. “I want to fight on rollerblades.”
“Can you even use rollerblades?” Akihiko asked dubiously.
“It’s never too late to learn, is it?”
Amano laughed.
“What’s so funny?” Yukari asked.
“Oh, it’s nothing,” she said. “It’s just kind of weird to think how young we used to be.”
“We still are young,” Suou said.
“No offense, but you look the same age as Yu-kun’s uncle,” Rise said.
“And?”
“I’m pretty sure he’s in his forties.”
Suou’s elbow had previously been resting on the windowsill, but he sat up in brief alarm at
Rise’s accusation. He slowly lowered himself back against the window.
“If I manage to reach the average age of death, I still have about another forty years left.”
“Uh oh,” Amano said. “Don’t go having a midlife crisis on us.”
“Assuming we don’t all die today,” Goro said darkly.
“You know, Goro?” Junpei said. “I’ve really grown fond of your cheerful little comments.
They really put a spring in my step.”
“He’s not wrong,” Suou said.

“I can’t die today,” Ken said, shaking his head. “I’ll fail my exams for sure, and Emiko would

Ken snorted.
“I doubt we’ll die,” Amano said. “I mean, we’ve made it this far, right?”
“All the more reason for our luck to run out at some point or another,” Akihiko said.
“I bet the bus is way more cheerful than this,” Rise muttered. “Why didn’t I get on that

“Because it was full,” Goro said.
“And Teddie brought a kazoo,” Rise said, shuddering. “Nevermind. I’m glad to be on the

“Maybe we should play some music,” Junpei suggested. He turned on the radio, and music

By some miracle, both vehicles arrived at the shack without anyone crashing. Teddie stepped
out of the bus looking extremely mournful.
“I’m not sorry,” Kanji said.
“My kazoo…” Teddie sniffed.
“What happened to it?” Ken asked.
“I threw it out the window, that’s what happened,” Kanji said. “We suffered that thing for an

“I don’t know, you could’ve just confiscated it,” Yosuke said. He gave Teddie a sympathetic

“He could’ve stopped when I asked him to,” Kanji said. He crossed his arms and glared at
Teddie mercilessly.
“Sorry,” Teddie said sadly, kicking some fallen leaves nearby.
Kanji glanced at Teddie and sighed. “Fine, I’ll get you a new one. But only if you promise
not to play it in my presence, or I will snap it in two.”
Teddie immediately brightened. “Yay!”

“I kind of liked the kazoo,” Ryoji said as Teddie ran to the bus to grab his tent.
“You only liked it because you had never seen one before,” Yosuke said with an eyeroll.

“It’s good at that,” Yu said. “I’m glad Nanako hasn’t taken interest in music.”
“Just you wait,” Yosuke said with haunted eyes. “Your time will come eventually.”
“Wow,” said a new voice to their right. “This is certainly lively.”
Everyone turned toward the new voice. A man leaned against a motorcycle, holding his white
helmet underneath his armpit. His black jacket had a blue neck-scarf tucked inside, and while
his dress wasn’t particularly formal, his expression and posture held the same air as
Mitsuru’s. Even if Maya hadn’t warned them that a Nanjo was joining the fray, Goro would
have instantly recognized that this stranger was raised in a powerful household.
“Nanjo-san,” Mitsuru said bowing immediately. “It’s a pleasure to see you again, albeit in a
very different setting than we usually meet.”
“Likewise. With the rumors of the Kirijo’s Groups experiments thirteen years ago, I

“But I certainly didn’t expect you to be wrapped up in something like this. Or for there to be

“Didn’t you start out when you were in high school too?” Suou asked.

Goro stepped forward reluctantly. “That would be me.”
Nanjo winced. “Is it legal for someone your age to have a persona?”
Ken groaned obnoxiously in the background, clearly sick of age-related questions.
The group rattled off their names. Nanjo was not as surprised as he could have been at the

As soon as the last person said their name, Chie slumped against a nearby tree. “Introductions

“Shouldn’t we go into the dungeon place first?” Yukiko asked. “There’s still quite a few
hours until sunset. “

“Oh look,” Minato said, raising his arm to point toward the shack. “The Velvet Room.”
Both Yu and Goro spun toward where Minato was pointing. Sure enough, the Velvet Room

it used to be, truly looking like it was taken directly off the side of a boat.
“Persona fusing time?” Yu asked.
“It’s your call, Goro,” Mitsuru said.
Who died and put Goro in charge? He was one of the youngest people in the group. Then
again, from a certain perspective, he was among the oldest.
“Set up camp, maybe eat some snacks, and then we’ll go in before dinner,” Goro said. “But

“Minato and Yu,” Goro said. “If you two wish to sort out your personas, I really could care

They put up tents and assigned people to each one. Being the youngest of the group, Goro,

Goro reached into his pocket, and his hands closed around the slick surface of the card. He

necessary?
Goro pulled out the card and held it up to the mirror. The card glowed, and the surface of the
mirror disappeared into blue light.

“I guess we can go inside now?” Junpei asked.

The sensation of being pulled in was entirely different than the first time Goro entered this

“It does look familiar though,” Yukiko said.

Kanji pointed up at the ceiling. A red scarf noose hung from it.
“I want to throw up,” Yukari said, indeed sounding a bit queasy.
“We can’t seriously be in front of Adachi’s dungeon, though, can we?” Chie asked. “We

“Welcome children,” Nyarlathotep’s voice echoed around them. Junpei yelped. Everyone

“I didn’t miss his habit of theatrics,” Amano muttered, handling her gun with admitted

“He’s not on this level,” Rise said, already having summoned her persona.
“No… he’s on the top floor,” Fuuka said.
“The top floor?” Mitsuru asked. “Which floor is that?”
“I-I can’t tell,” Fuuka said. She blushed. “Sorry.”
“I’d come down there to greet you myself, but I find that my power is… at its best on this

“Bold of you to assume we’ll be the ones dying,” Suou said. His eyes glinted.

“I’ve killed more than one of you once before,” Nyarlathotep said. “I can’t imagine it’ll be

“Well, Goro died…” Ken said hesitantly.
Amano winced. “Let’s not get into it right now. Maybe we should just keep moving.”

“Aw, but why leave when there’s still so much fun to be had?”

“Can’t hurt to try,” Akihiko said.
