Adachi smiled, blood dripping from his mouth. “Hate me that much, huh?” he asked. “Your

“Adachi-san,” Yu asked. He stumbled toward Adachi, his hands raised as if he wanted to help

“It’s not Adachi,” Rise said. “That’s the shadow.”

Adachi’s form disappeared into shadowy dust as he transformed into a blue-cloaked skeleton

He was also laughably easy for the group of twenty-two fighters to kill.
Koromaru barked victoriously.
“Koromaru congratulated us on our easy win,” Aigis said.

“Yeah,” Chie said. “I for one know that my life will be greatly improved if I never have to

After some further searching, they located the stairs. It took longer to climb the spiral

“Let’s just get out of here,” Yosuke said. “I see enough of this place on a daily basis. I don’t

“I’m not listening to you,” Yosuke said. The group began to walk past the fake Yosuke, but

They entered Leblanc. In reality, the entire group would have squeezed between the bar and

Everything else still hit Goro like someone had weaponized nostalgia and used it as a

“Oh, I know that painting!” Yukiko said, pointing to the Sayuri.

Not-Akria wore the same winter clothes that Goro had last seen him in before they infiltrated

Goro insisting Akira let him die. Akira insisting otherwise.
The entire Investigation Team immediately got on their guard. “Is-is that–” Kanji stuttered.
“It’s not Tsuyoshi,” Goro said exhaustedly. It was the first time he spoke since they entered

“It’s kind of a shame that this was only the third floor,” Not-Akira said. “I mean, it would’ve

“Life’s not fair,” Goro said quietly.
“Trust me, I know.” Not-Akira smiled grimly in a way he only had around Goro, back in

“A reflection, is it?” Suou asked. “And who are you reflecting?”
“You shot me once before.” Akira winked. “What’s another time?”
Goro’s hand shook. Akira was blocking their route to the stairs. They would have to attack

But could he?
“I had nightmares for months,” Akira said suddenly. His expression glazed over. “The Engine
Room was a catastrophe, but you know what’s selfish?”
“What?”
“I was glad,” Akira said. “Glad. I thought for sure near the end, you would force me to kill

The entire room was silent. Even Minato and Yu, who looked vaguely puzzled, didn’t say
anything. One of the coffee pots sizzled on a burner.
“Well,” Goro said heavily. “Lucky you.”
“And then I killed you anyway.” Akira looked away. “We could’ve been happy. You could’ve
been happy–”
“You think that was happiness?!” Goro demanded. “Don’t make me sick. You were one of

hubris that he thought for sure you would just go along with your schemes.”
“And I almost did!” Akira glowered at Goro. “Sometimes I wish I had. Sometimes, I wonder
what I was thinking, listening to you when everyone else in the world was living in

“Paradise was my brain filled with white noise and something else manufacturing my entire

am now.”
“You are dead,” Akira whispered. “Truly dead. Do you really look in the mirror and see the
same person that became my friend? I don’t even recognize you.”

Goro’s ears were ringing. He wasn’t sure why. It wasn’t as though Akira wasn’t saying
anything that wasn’t true.
“But he could take you back,” Akira said. He stepped forward. It was as if nobody else was
in the room. It was only Goro and Akira, standing in the ever thickening silence. “He could

“Kurusu–”
Akira grabbed Goro’s hand. Goro couldn’t move away. For a brief moment, he felt tall again.
He could practically feel his old school uniform pressing against his body. His striped tie
around his collar.
“If you just freed him, he would be able to bring you back to me,” Akira said softly. “Don’t
you want that? Don’t you miss me?”
Akechi Goro didn’t believe in the afterlife, but if he did, he was sure that the reality Akira
was offering to him would be Goro’s own personal mixture of heaven and hell.
Goro did miss him. He missed him more than he realized was possible.
But it didn’t change a thing.
Goro yanked his hand away, and reality came crashing back around him.
He was physically thirteen years old. He was in a room filled with his friends. And a world
where Nyarlathotep was free was a world doomed to destruction.
“I can’t do that,” Goro said. “And the real Akira understood that years ago.”
Not-Akira’s expression faltered. A nasty glower formed on his face.
Goro adjusted his grip on his sword and thrust it into Not-Akira’s torso. The shockwave that
came from Not-Akira’s body caused everyone to stumble backwards. Goro yanked out his
sword as Not-Akira burst into white smoke.
The shadow that came from Not-Akira was Arsene. Or, at least, a mockery of Akira’s old
persona. Where the original Arsene was red and black, this shadow was in inverted colors.
Bright blue and white pierced Goro’s eyes. It reminded Goro sickeningly of a sterilized
clinic.
“So much grief, Goro-kun,” shadow Arsene boomed. “Why do you insist upon hurting
yourself always when the cure is within reach?”
“Living a lie isn’t a cure,” Goro snarled. “Why don’t you go back to hell?”
With a wave of his hand, a wave of bless magic fell over the group. Koromaru collapsed
immediately, and everyone else either dodged or gasped at the unusual strength of the attack.
“He’s weak to darkness!” Fuuka cried.

“How do you know that?!” Rise demanded as Minato, Yu, and Goro immediately started
reaching for curse based personas.
“You can’t tell?” Fuuka asked.
“Oh my god, why weren’t you on our team?” Yosuke muttered right before he got hit with a
sleep spell.
“Stay focused!” Minato and Yu barked at the same time.
Goro rolled out of the way of a physical attack as Yu used Myriad Truths on the shadow.
Shadow Arsene jerked backwards at the strength of the attack. Goro summoned Loki and hit
Shadow Arsene with a heavy curse attack.
Shadow Arsene let out a loud hacking sound. “Do you really hate me that much?”
He disappeared into a puff of white smoke.
As everyone caught their breath and helped each other up– Chie was slapping Yosuke
awake–, Goro stared at the empty space Akira used to stand.
His hands couldn’t stop shaking.
He wasn’t real, Goro told himself furiously. Akira is fine.
“Are you okay?” Ken asked cautiously.
Goro turned around. “Never better.”
Goro was never the best liar around the people who knew him, but those two words rang
hollow even to his own ears.
They agreed to stop for the night.

inversely-colored Thanatos, who held barely less power than the reverse Arsene.
Goro was getting kind of sick of fighting these persona look-alikes.
“Goro-kun didn’t want Minato to kill me,” Ryoji said when they were done fighting. He
glanced at Minato pleadingly. “You know that.”
Minato nodded, still looking nauseous.
“We need a break,” Mitsuru decided.
“Good thing this aquarium has an elevator,” Rise said, pointing to the elevator sitting next to
the spiral stairs.

The (absolutely massive) elevator took them all the way back down to the initial floor of the
dungeon. Everyone clambered through the mirror entrance and returned to their tents in a
state of utter exhaustion.
Goro checked the time on his phone. It was still only ten in the morning, and they had started
their venture at eight.
Goro spent the next half-hour taking a hard-earned nap. When he woke up, he found the
others eating a hurried lunch as they prepared to go back in.
“The less school we miss, the better,” Chie said with a mouthful of noodles.
It had indeed been the plan to get through as much of the dungeon as possible, ideally all of
it, that day. Still, Goro couldn’t help but to glance in Minato and Yu’s direction. They seemed
much recovered from their previous states, but there was no point in pushing the group harder
than necessary.
“We can rest longer if we need to,” he said.

“We’ve checked in with everyone else,” Akihiko said without missing a beat. “They’re good
with keeping going.” Akihiko narrowed his eyes at Akechi in suspicion. “Unless you’re not?”
“No, I’m fine,” Goro said. He was mostly telling the truth. “And regardless, Chie has a
point.”
“I’m fine with missing school,” Kanji said.
“Does the mandatory attendance policy mean nothing to you?” Naoto asked with a hint of
despair in their tone.
“I don’t officially go to school,” Teddie said helpfully.
“Yeah, that might change any day now,” Yosuke muttered into his bowl. “So enjoy it while
you can.”
“I don’t know…” Nanjo said. “Sometimes I miss my high school years, demons and altered
realities and all.”
“That was… a sentence,” Amano said, even as a decent portion of the Shadow Operatives
nodded in agreement to Nanjo’s statement.
After everyone finished eating, they re-entered the dungeon. The elevator was fortunately
still there, so they rode it back up to the sixth floor.
“Oh, wait!” Yukari exclaimed as they waited impatiently for the elevator to reach the top.
“There’s a window!”
Everyone turned to where she was pointing. Sure enough, there was a small square window
on the back wall of the elevator. Goro was too far away from it to see the view.
“The ocean, huh?” Junpei asked. He frowned at the window. “Is this an island fortress or
something?”
Goro suddenly remembered the peculiar appearance of his Velvet Room. Were the two
related?
“Or something,” Yu agreed.
They stepped off the elevator and entered the aquarium. The stairs were immediately next to
the elevator doors, so Goro made a quick left and started to climb them.
The next floor revealed the hill overlooking Inaba. It was dark outside, and fireworks
exploded in the distance.
Goro’s chest clenched. Ken flinched.
“You are all terrible friends,” Not-Dojima said. He rested his hand on one of the fences,
glowering at them. “I can’t believe none of you noticed that the eleven-year-old was having a
panic attack right in front of you.”

“Panic attack… what?” Yukiko turned toward Goro with a horrified expression. “You mean
during the fireworks…”
“Ever heard of post-traumatic stress?” Akihiko said. His expression twitched as another
firework went off. Junpei squeezed his eyes shut.
“The fireworks exploding and gunshots sound very familiar,” Aigis said. Yu’s expression
shifted as his fingers brushed against his ear.
“Just hurry up and kill this guy,” Junpei snapped.
Like it was that easy.
In a way, it was.
“Yeah, Goro-kun,” Not-Dojima said. “I know you never liked me anyway–”
Goro already stabbed him cleanly through the heart. He slid his blade out with equal
precision.
Find the target. Attack the target. Destroy its shadow.
Wash, rinse, and repeat.
Dojima’s shadow took a full minute to beat instead of the usual thirty seconds. It hadn’t taken
on a particularly unique form either; it only resembled the Triglav persona.
“The shadows are getting stronger the further up we go,” Mitsuru said when they were done.
Destroying the shadow hadn’t stopped the incessant stream of fireworks, and the group
hurried to the stairs.
“Or the shadows react to the amount of negativity in the room,” Naoto said.
“Or both.” Suou frowned. “They’re obviously trying to get a rise out of us, but it wouldn’t be
outlandish to assume that they get stronger as we get closer to our target.”
“Fantastic,” Yosuke said. He smiled with faux cheer. “Only 13 more to go!”
“Fourteen, actually,” Yu said.
Yosuke slumped. “Better yet.”

“Next is Ken,” Goro said.

Every time he saw Goro kill one of the reflections, Yosuke’s stomach churned.
As he watched two middle schoolers stabbing a reflection even smaller than them, Yosuke

Junpei was getting kind of tired of this place.
Between all of the mind games and the constant stairs, it was really wearing on his patience.
Not to mention the growing anxiety of what would happen once they reached the inevitable
Junpei floor.

Or was it inevitable? Goro never had the highest opinion of him. Maybe Goro never had one

No. It really wasn’t.

Why did the place smell like blood?

It was by far the most peaceful floor in the entire dungeon. Even if it had some of the more

But even if she did believe them, what then? She would thrust herself into danger without a

Mitsuru held her breath as they walked onto the Tartarus rooftop. It made her chest squeeze
to even be near Tartarus, even if it was an imitation.
Everything was fine. The real Tartarus was gone. It wouldn’t come back.
Crosses with broken chains stood behind them. Aigis made a noise that sounded like a

It made sense that this was the place they ended up. This was the floor for the Hanged Man

It had been over two years since his death, and Mitsuru still found herself bursting into tears

Sometimes it felt like the pain would never go away.

“Because he died,” Goro snapped. His voice shook as well, but Mitsuru didn’t miss the relief

After hours of driving, Akira quite frankly might have driven right past his destination if it
weren’t for the strange blue glow coming from the side of the road. Akira yanked his steering
wheel to his right and veered onto a thin gravel road, grimacing as the car bounced up and
down in protest.
The glowing blue light was becoming more pronounced, and Akira slowed the car to a stop.
He didn’t want Goro finding out what he had done. He could get so… so… self-righteous
sometimes.
In his attempt to hide the car in between the trees, Akira accidentally scraped the outer mirror
against a large trunk. Akira grimaced the screeching sound and slammed his foot on the
break. He looked out the window and stared at the cracked mess of the rear view mirror in
despair.
Hopefully his uncle wouldn’t be too angry…
Unless his uncle really was an evil overlord.
Why did this have to be so confusing?
Akira put the car into park and climbed out. He followed the gravel road until he found a
cluster of tents and the charred remains of a campfire. The site was abandoned, but Akira
tried to avoid making too much noise as he approached the shack.
The shack itself was exactly as Akira remembered it. The inside was still as cobwebbed and
dusty as ever, and the mirror stood two feet taller than Akira, glowing in a menacing fashion.
The blue glow that Akira had followed came from a strange butterfly sitting on top of the
mirror. It stayed still for a moment before outside the shack and disappearing from view.
Weird.
Akira cautiously poked the mirror’s surface. The mirror seemed to grow brighter as it rippled.
Akira’s hand slipped inside without any complaint.
Akira yanked his hand back with a small gasp.
This was all so strange. But he had to keep going if he wanted to discover the truth. At the
very least, he wanted to stop Goro from doing anything too reckless.
He just wanted to help.
Goro would see how strong Akira could be.

“I swear, another one of you,” Shido said. “If you say you’re one of mine, I don’t give a
fuck–”
“Nobody here is yours, so ask your question and get on with it!”
“I will not be ordered around by a child!”
Goro’s heart stuttered, but he stayed perfectly still. He could already feel a plastic expression
sliding over his face.
“Try a detective,” Suou said with cold professionalism. It was clearly a bluff, everybody
knew this version of Shido wasn’t real, but it was the sort of thing that the Phantom Thieves
would try on cognitions in palaces. “Shido-san, it has come to my attention that you have
been abusing your power. I came to investigate matters. But if this is how you treat any
child–”
It was amazing how quickly Shido, even as a cognition, could change demeanor.
“This must be a mistake,” Shido said. His voice was both conversational and authoritative,
but Goro knew that it was the calm before the storm. If this were the real world, Shido was
arranging an accident for Suou even as he spoke. “These children began threatening me, and I
admit I became a bit… defensive. I’ll pay you for your troubles, if you’d like.”
If Suou hadn’t been there the entire time, he might have believed Shido. He was alarmingly
good at hiding his true nature and charming the right audience.
Like father, like son.
“I understand,” Suou said. Goro would have gagged if he weren’t so busy trying to breathe.
Ken was saying something to him, but Goro ignored it. “If you could just allow me to
proceed from this path, we can pretend this never happened.”
“Of course,” Shido said. “Give me just a moment. Akechi-kun!”
“Yes sir?” Goro asked almost automatically, his voice sticky and strained.
“Why did you die?”
Goro had almost forgotten about the dying part, surrounded by so many of his friends. But
now he was all too aware of the acoustic echoes of the room, the way the ground refused to
stay steady.
“I died because you killed me.”
“Do you really think I’m a fool? Tell the truth.”

Goro raised his voice. “I died because I let myself be controlled by the likes of you. I died
because I wanted to pretend for a fraction of a second that I could be good. I died because I
thought had no reason to be alive. I died because I wanted you to feel the rage and
dissatisfaction of knowing your perfect puppet failed!”
“You died because you were a coward,” Shido snarled.
“Maybe so!” Goro shouted. His throat hurt, and his voice cracked. “But I will not let you
control me any longer, so just die already!”
The shockwave of Shido’s transformation sent everyone careening backwards. Goro jumped
to his feet and began to run toward Shido’s shadow, but Akihiko grabbed his shoulder.
“Sit this one out,” Akihiko instructed. “We’ve got you.”
“But I–”
“Listen to him,” Ken said. “Please.”
Goro grit his teeth, but Ken and Akihiko were right. He would be a liability in his current
state.
“Fine,” Goro said. “I trust you.”
Why the hell was everyone beaming?

After the last two floors, Yu’s floor was ultimately extremely anti-climactic. Which was a
massive relief, actually. Kanji would have collapsed from emotional exhaustion if another
adult started talking about how messed up Goro’s life was.
Goro hadn’t said much since the creepy sperm-donor floor. He stayed close to Amada and let
Koromaru walk alongside him. Kanji wanted to ask if he was okay, but even if the answer
wasn’t obvious, Goro obviously planned on stabbing anyone who dared bring it up.
After walking down countless hallways in Yu’s house, they gathered in Yu’s living room and
waited for him to speak.
“How?” fake Yu asked, looking directly at the real Yu. “How do you keep going when you
suffer so much?”
Ever the confident leader, Yu stood tall and stared his counterpart directly in the eye. It was
kind of inspiring. “Because the end result is always worth it.”
Fake Yu laughed. “For you, maybe,” he said.
“Last I checked, saving the world is good for everyone,” Kanji said.

“Not for Takaya or Ikutsuki,” fake Yu said, glancing at the older half of the group. “Isn’t that
right, guys?”
“Narukami-kun answered your question,” Yamagishi said. “Could we get to the fighting part
now?”
“You guys are so boring,” fake Yu sighed before becoming inverse Izanami.

Akihiko dreaded this floor.
Goro and Shinji had obviously been close. Goro was one of the few Shadow Operatives who
actually knew Shinji before he officially re-joined the team. So the fact that Shinji had a floor
to himself wasn’t surprising at all.
But Akihiko still dreaded it. He was trying to move forward. Seeing Shinji again, even if it
wasn’t him in the slightest, might take him back to square one. Having an opportunity to see
him again, only for him to say something vile, was even worse.
The maze took the form of the halls of their old dorm. Akihiko almost balked at the painfully
familiar scent of carpet cleaner. As they wandered the maze, Shinji took the extra time to say
a grand total of… nothing.
Absolutely nothing.
It was as if the place knew he should be dead.
Akihiko couldn’t decide if he was grateful or disappointed.
Shit.
The mazes were getting longer with each floor. Whereas it took five minutes to find Ikutsuki,
they had been walking for nearly fifteen minutes without any sign of reaching the center of
the room. Fuuka and Kujikawa assured the group they were getting close, but how close was
close? How much longer would Akihiko have to listen to this dead silence?
“Teddie smells something delicious,” Teddie said.
Akihiko frowned and sniffed. A faint whiff of simmering vegetables hung in the air. It
smelled almost exactly like the meals Shinji would cook nearly every evening.
They opened one of the hallway doors that led into the dormitory kitchen.
Shinjiro stood behind the counter, chopping vegetables. Akihiko couldn’t stop his chest from
squeezing.
“Be careful,” he blurted out before he could stop himself.
Shinji raised an eyebrow. “What?” he asked. “Worried I’m going to cut myself again?”

Most of the girls in the shadow operatives already had tears slipping down their cheeks.
Ken’s expression contorted. Akihiko swallowed down the lump in his throat.
Goro closed his eyes. “Just ask your question.”
“You’re not going to like it.”
“When has that ever stopped me before?” Goro’s voice trembled slightly.
Shinji put down his knife. Akihiko released a breath of relief.
“Did you read my letter?”
Akihiko opened his mouth to say “yes” before he realized that Shinji wasn’t directing the
question toward him. He was staring at Goro with his piercing glare, looking simultaneously
disapproving and disappointed.
And somehow, for such a seemingly innocent question, it was the cruelest thing Shinji could
have asked Goro. Goro’s expression crumbled for a fraction of a second before returning to
painted-on stoicism.
What the hell had Shinji written to Goro?
“No,” Goro said in a hushed tone. “And I know Nyarlathotep is pulling your strings, so don’t
you dare ask me why.”
Oh.
Shit.
“He destroyed your letter?” Akihiko asked.
“We are not talking about this,” Goro said. “You’re not Shinjiro; Shinjiro is dead.”
Shinji glanced at Akihiko. “You’re right,” he said. “I am.”
Without another word, Shinji transformed into his inverse persona, disappearing entirely.

Needless to say, they took another break after that battle.
“Please tell me we’re almost done,” Yukari said as she scrubbed at her tear-stained face with
her palms. Amano boiled water over the campfire. She promised to make hot chocolate for
everyone.
Ken did start crying after that, much to Amano’s alarm.
“Three more floors to go,” Minato said quietly. “I think.”
“And then all that’s left is to fight Nyarlathotep,” Yu said.

“Please don’t phrase that like it’s the easy part,” Suou said, massaging the bridge of his nose.
“You don’t get to talk,” Kanji said, irritated. “You hardly have any context for all the shit
these reflections have said. You don’t know how much this sucks for us.”
Goro privately agreed, but stopped himself from telling Kanji that he was lucky he didn’t
have the faintest clue who Ikutsuki or Takaya really were.
He was too tired to say much of anything anyway.
“Just because I haven’t experienced what you’ve experienced doesn’t mean I can’t have basic
empathy,” Suou said. “It turns out that this entire time, there were kids in need who needed
support, and I wasn’t there to give it. That hurts.”
“None of us were there,” Amano said quietly. “I’m sorry. If we had known, we would have
done something.”
“I should’ve known,” Nanjo said bitterly. “Especially with the Nanjo Group’s connections
with the Kirijo Group.”
“It is over now,” Aigis said. “We appreciate your current assistance.”
They fell into silence. Those who were still crying sniffed and hiccupped quietly as the fire
crackled between them. Goro poked the fire with a stick and watched it pop violently in
response.
“Nanako’s next,” he said, nearly inaudibly.
“What?” Ken asked.
Goro raised his voice. “Nanako’s next.”
The entire Investigation Team’s faces fell. Even Yu looked sick.
“You can try to sit this one out, Senpai, but there’s no guarantee Nanako-chan isn’t going to
try to ask you a question,” Rise said.
Yu stared at the ground between his feet. “I’ll go,” he said, even though it was obvious going
was the last thing he wanted to do.
“Nobody’s forcing you,” Yosuke said.
“I know,” Yu said. “But you’re right. If Nanako’s going to ask anyone something, it’s going
to be me.” He smiled weakly. “Besides… I won’t be seeing Nanako anyway. That will
probably make it better.”
Amano was pouring the cups of hot chocolate. Hit with a sudden burst of frustration, Goro
stood up.
“What’s wrong?” Mitsuru asked.

“I’m going to the Velvet Room,” Goro said, marching toward the Velvet Room door right
outside the shack. “I’ll be back.”
“Oh, okay,” Ken said as Amano handed him a mug. “We’ll save some for you, okay?”
“Sure.”

The piano in the Velvet Room did, oddly enough, serve to calm Goro slightly. It did nothing
to stop Goro from sitting in his cushioned seat as passive aggressively as possible.
“Something troubles you,” Igor said. It was refreshing for him to skip niceties for once.
Goro glanced out the window and glowered at the ocean. Why did his Velvet Room have to
be a fucking boat of all places?
“You could say that,” Goro said.
“My prison held together by the power of bonds has been twisted against its original
purpose,” Igor said. “It seems our enemy’s power is greater than anything else you have
faced.”
Goro rolled his eyes. “Big surprise there. Why’d you wait so long to give me the key? I
could’ve trapped Nyarlathotep months ago.”
“The strength of the prison is only as strong as the bonds you held,” Igor said. “Your bonds
were not at their full strength when I first created it.”
Goro scoffed, even though the explanation actually made sense. “Right.”
“What is it?” Theodore asked. He was frowning. “I understand that this challenge you face is
a difficult one–”
“I don’t give a fuck about the challenge,” Goro snapped. “These reflections are barely
obstacles. I don’t give a damn.”
“And yet you are imbalanced,” Igor said.

“Of course I am,” Goro said. “Every single one of these reflections go out of their way to
make me seem like some sort of victim. That I’m the one who needs protecting.”
“Perhaps your friends protect you because you have forged a bond of loyalty with them,”
Igor said.
Goro bristled. “It has nothing to do with bonds!” he snapped. “I just thought I was past being
this pathetic.”
“Goro-kun,” Theodore said sadly. “You have been hurt by people.”
“Only because I hurt people back!” Goro jumped to his feet. His chair toppled over behind
him. “How is this so hard for everyone to understand?! Takaya took an interest in me because
I was already a killer! Shido took an interest in me because of what I was willing to do for
him!”
There it was. The thoughts that clawed at Goro from the inside. The reality that Goro so
desperately tried to pretend wasn’t there when he stood up to Takaya’s reflection.
The truth.
But neither Theodore or Igor nodded along to what he was saying. They both looked… sad?
“And that’s an excuse for them to hurt you?” Theodore asked.
Goro laughed. “It’s called karma,” he said. “Do you feel bad for a villain when he’s hurt?”
“I could pose the same question to you,” Igor said. “Do you feel sorry for your enemies when
they are hurt?”
“No,” Goro said immediately. “I relish it, I want them to suffer–”
“Stop playing up your evil persona and answer the question honestly,” Theodore said, a little
sharper than usual. He picked up the chair and set it behind Goro. “How did you really feel
when you had Takaya at your mercy? Or Adachi?”
“I swear I liked it,” Goro said, but his resolve wavered.
“Were you happy?”
“No.”
“What were you then?”
“Angry.” Goro slowly sat back into his seat. “I’m always angry.”
“Human anger is a result of other human emotions,” Igor said. “So why were you angry?”
“They hurt me,” Goro said. “They hurt people I cared about. Of course I was angry.”
“Were you scared of them?’

“Takaya, maybe,” Goro admitted. “Not Adachi.”
“Have you considered,” Igor said slowly, clasping his hands together and leaning forward,
“That you might be sad the people you trusted betrayed you?”
“I never trusted Takaya,” Goro snapped.
“The others, then.”
“Even if I was, what’s your point?” Goro asked. “They got what they deserved.”
“And what did they get?”
“Death. Prison. What the hell are you trying to get me to say?”
“I see,” Igor said. “So none of them were tortured or abused for their power?”
Goro let out a shocked laugh. “I’m sorry, did you miss the part where I killed hundreds of
innocents? I have a kill count likely higher than Adachi and Takaya combined.”
“I don’t understand,” Theodore said sadly. “Why are you so insistent on making yourself the
villain in your own story?”
“Because I was the villain in my own story,” Goro said. “And at least then, I had some
semblance of control over my life.”
But that wasn’t remotely true, and they all knew it.
Theodore frowned. “You can have control without hurting people.”
“Not if I’m too busy cowering away from my abusers like a child!” Goro’s breath hitched.
“And don’t you dare tell me I am a child.”
“A great myth amongst humanity is that only the innocent can suffer unjustly,” Igor said.
“Especially children. But adults can be hurt. Evil people can suffer greatly and seek
redemption.”
Goro didn’t say anything.
“You know this,” Igor said gently. “So why are you denying it?”
“Things were so much easier when I didn’t give a damn about anybody,” Goro mumbled. A
part of him hoped Igor wouldn’t hear.
“Easier?” Igor asked. “Or less complicated?”
“Is there really a difference?” Goro sighed. “I’m sick of being afraid. And I’m tired of being
angry. But I’m not sure I know how to be anything else.”
“I’m afraid that healing only comes with time,” Igor said. “But for as long as you are a guest
of this place, you can always find solace here.”

Goro brought his hands to his face and exhaled quietly through his nose. “Okay.”
He stood up and turned toward the door. “Thank you.”
“It’s my pleasure,” Igor said.
“If you ever need anything, we’ll be there,” Theodore said.
Goro felt a ghost of a smile cross over his face. He opened the door and returned to the real
world.
“Welcome back,” Ken said. “You were gone for a while.”
“We were starting to get worried,” Yosuke said.
Real world time and Velvet Room time didn’t line up in the slightest, but Ken had already
finished his entire mug of hot chocolate. Just how long had Goro spoken to Igor and Theo?
“Well, I’m here now,” Goro said. “Shall we get going?”
“Not until you drink something,” Fuuka said. “It doesn’t have to be hot chocolate, but you
should get something in your system.”
“I hate to agree,” Junpei said reluctantly.
Goro sighed and sat back down next to Ken. “Fine.”
“I’ll get you the hot chocolate!” Teddie said eagerly, jumping to his feet. Goro took a mug
from Teddie and began to sip at it quietly.
…It was actually quite good. Even if it was made over a camp fire.
“Three more floors to go,” Yukiko whispered.
“Three more floors to go,” Rise repeated.

This place had a lot of stairs.
Akira wasn’t sure how long he had been climbing, but it had to be for at least a few hours.
And now this most recent floor was a literal maze, and Akira kept running into dead ends.
How the hell did Goro and his friends make any progress?
Speaking of Goro and his friends, where were they? Why hadn’t Akira seen them at all?
Akira sighed and sat down at a nearby bench. He needed a nap. He could continue looking
for Goro later.
“Akira-kun?” Akira jumped at the sound of his uncle’s voice. “Is that you?”

“What?” Akira whipped his head around, confused. “Where are you?”
“I’m trapped,” his uncle said. “You have to help me out.”
“What? No.” Akira shook his head. “You’re a bad guy. I think. Are you?”
“This is all one terrible misunderstanding.” There was a pleading note to Tsuyoshi’s voice.
“Goro wants you all to himself. He wanted to get rid of me.”
“No, I…” Akira’s mouth felt dry. He swallowed. “I saw you… you shot him–”
“You saw me?” His uncle sounded very surprised. “I never shot anybody.”
“No, you did!” Akira clutched his hair, trying to recall the memory.
“Are you sure you saw me exactly shooting Goro-kun?” Tsuyoshi asked. “I don’t even have a
gun.”
Admittedly, he had looked like a completely different person at the time. Goro said that his
uncle could shapeshift or whatever. Time travel was real. Shapeshifting could easily be real
too. Akira shouldn’t let himself be so easily manipulated.
But…
“Well, no… but I know it was you!” Akira said defensively.
“But Goro-kun’s still alive.”
“Well, yes.”
“How would that be possible if I shot him?”
Goro had mentioned something about invincibility. Or something. But that wasn’t the point.
“Even if you didn’t shoot him, you said you pretended to be my uncle,” Akira said.
“I am your uncle.
“No! The evil you hunting us down said that! You monologued about how evil you were, and

“Akira, I never said that.”
Akira covered his face with his hands. “You did, I swear you did.”
“I know this is scary,” Akira’s uncle said soothingly. “I know you’re confused right now.”
“Stop it!” Akira shouted. “I’m not making this up! How else are you in here if you weren’t

“You’re not getting the big picture here,” Akira’s uncle said. “Someone tried to kill Goro,

want to know the truth?”
“Goro wouldn’t lie to me,” Akira said.
“How many months did he lie to you about knowing you all along?”
“That’s different, I wouldn’t have believed him–”
“Well, maybe he doesn’t want you to know this either. Just listen, okay?”
Akira didn’t want to listen, but just like the time the midnight channel revealed a girl getting
murdered, he couldn’t ignore what Tsuyoshi had to say.
“Goro-kun misses the old Akria. The one you saw on the third floor. He created this place
and staged a situation where he was being ‘attacked’ by me. The person chasing you was just
a fake. Then, afterwards, he trapped me in here so I couldn’t escape. He wants to have you all
to himself so that he can mold you to his liking. That’s how you were able to get away so
easily. That’s how he didn’t die when he was shot.”
It wasn’t true. It couldn’t be true.
“Goro wouldn’t do that,” Akira said, his voice cracking.
“Who had opened the door to this place? Because I know it wasn’t me.”
It was Goro. Goro had a key.
And it was obvious how much Goro missed the future version of Akira. He hadn’t exactly
been a good guy in his stories either.
If he was desperate, would he do what his uncle described?
It still seemed inconceivable.
“How do I get to you?” Akira asked. Maybe if he could actually speak to his uncle face to
face, he could get a better read on the situation.
“You have to wait just a little longer,” his uncle said. “A path will open up to you soon
enough.”

Three more floors to go, Yu thought to himself with each new step he climbed. Only three
more. Three more floors to go.
And, honestly, after this floor, the worst would be over. Yu had no idea how the team was
going to manifest in a single floor, and the Teddie floor (which would be Yu’s Marie floor)
couldn’t be any worse than the shadow Teddie that they faced last year.

One more truly awful floor. Two more maybe bad floors.
And then their target.
Three more floors to go.
This maze came in the appearance of Yasogami High’s hallways. That in itself was no

room when it came to face the actual reflection.
The surprise came with the shrill cry that echoed down the hall.
“Big Bro!” Yumi’s voice cried, but the words so clearly belonged to Nanako. “Why couldn’t

Yu didn’t hesitate. He began sprinting down the hall without any directions.

Yukari couldn’t believe the floor belonging to the seven-year-old was the floor that was filled

They didn’t have much time to dwell on it, though, because at the first heart-wrenching cries,

“Yu-kun, wait!” Kujikawa cried.
“Well, he is going in the right direction,” Fuuka said reluctantly as half the group began to

“Big bro!” Nanako continued to cry. She sounded so much sadder, so much more scared than

“I’m coming, Nanako!” Narukami cried. “Please, I’m coming!”
Yukari’s entire job was to bring joy to children, to visit hospitals in costume and smile

Nanako continued to repeat her cries of help, and Yukari ran so quickly that she nearly

She would apologize later.
Fuuka shouted maze directions, which Narukami blessedly followed. He was running faster

“Big bro!” Nanako’s voice was practically screaming now. Everybody’s expressions were

Fuck. Why couldn’t they just reach the end of this maze? Why couldn’t they make her stop
crying?
“Save me–”

She struggled for each and every breath.
She was not the girl Yukari visited. But judging from everyone else’s faces, she had reached

“I failed you.” Narukami shoulders shook more violently. “I failed you.”
“You didn’t fail her,” Shirogane said. “If it weren’t for your actions, she might not have

“So, which is next?” Yu asked after the hellish battle. “Aeon or Judgement?”

Maybe that really wasn’t a good thing at all.
“But you’re nothing like your shadow,” Rise said.

He didn’t sound like he believed Teddie, but Teddie chose to take it as a win. He was even

playing the kazoo without a care in the world.
“I’ll be taking that!” Kanji, Teddie’s new hero, snatched the kazoo from Impos-Teddie’s
hands and threw it to the ground. He stomped on it, and the kazoo broke with a loud crunch.
Teddie lowered his hands from his ears and sighed in relief. A high-pitched sound still rang in
his ears, but at least the actual source of his grief was gone. Finally.
“Hey!” Impos-Teddie said. “I was playing that!”
“And now you’re asking us a question,” Yu said. “Shoot.”
“Oh, a question?” impos-Teddie said. “Am I meant to be asking you one of those?”
“Stop pulling on our leg,” Youske said. “You know that you have to ask us a question to let
us through.”
“Well, yeah,” Impos-Teddie said. “But I got so distracted playing the kazoo that I forgot.”
“You… forgot,” Detective Suou said slowly.
“Yep!” Impos-Teddie laughed, even though it wasn’t funny at all! “I’m such an airhead
sometimes. I used to be hollow on the inside, you know.”
“I’m not an airhead!” Teddie said defensively. “I’m a very smart bear!”
“Prove it!” impos-Teddie said with equal fervor. “What’s two times two?”
Teddie puffed his chest up proudly. That was an easy one. “Four!”
“What’s the derivative of x squared?”
A derivative? What the heck was a derivative? And what was x squared?
Oh… Teddie knew what was going on. It was a trick to make Teddie feel bad about how little
he knew about the world. Well, it wasn’t going to work.

“Everybody knows that letters aren’t in math,” Teddie said boldly. He smiled at the others,
who grimaced.
“Well, actually…” Yosuke began. Teddie wilted, but Yosuke shook his head. “You know
what? Never mind. Please, fake Teddie, just ask us something. It can be anything.”
Maybe Teddie wasn’t so smart after all.
“Oh! Maybe I can do a riddle,” Impos-Teddie said. “Those are kind of like puns, right?”
“Sure,” Ryoji said.
“Okay, okay,” Impos-Teddie said. He jumped off his bike and beamed at the entire group. “I
have a beary good one, so get ready!”
“We’re ready,” Chie said.
“But if it’s anything perverted, I’m ending you,” Yukiko said coldly. Teddie shuddered.
“Okay.” Impos-Teddie cleared his throat. “I may only be given, not taken or bought. What the
sinner desires, but the saint does not. What am I?”
“Forgiveness,” Naoto said quietly.
“Wrong!” Impos-Teddie said cheerfully.
“What do you mean, wrong?” Goro demanded, obviously irritated. Teddie couldn’t think of
anything else that matched that exact description. “What do you want the answer to be?
Death?”
“Wrong again!” Impos-Teddie smiled so wide that Teddie half-expected his face to crack into
little pieces. “Here’s a secret! Everything can be taken or bought! Everything! Your death
was taken from you, wasn’t it?”
Teddie was feeling somewhat confused, but it’s true that Goro was taken from his death. That
was sort of the same thing as death being taken away. Goro seemed to agree, at last, judging
from his wounded expression.
“You can’t take someone’s forgiveness,” Mitsuru said. “That’s not how it works.”
“Are you sure?” Impos-Teddie asked. “I think you’d be surprised.”

“Akira-kun…” Akira’s uncle said as Akira waited for the greenlight to find Tsuyoshi.
Apparently, Goro and his friends hadn’t quite opened the pathway yet. “I’m sorry.”
Akira crossed his arms and huffed. “Why would Goro be trying to get to you if he’s the one
who trapped you here?”

“He wants to destroy me,” his uncle said. “He noticed that you were still thinking about me,
and he doesn’t want you to be distracted.”
That seemed a little far-fetched… “I don’t think Goro would murder anyone. Even you.”
“He has before.”
“How do you know that?”
“Because he told me,” his uncle said. “Villains have a tendency to monologue, you know.
Remember that one movie we watched together?”
Akira almost snorted. It was true that the particular villain his uncle had in mind rambled
about his plans for at least twenty minutes of the run time. Akira and Tusyoshi had nearly
fallen off the couch laughing.
Unfortunately, the memory of being chased by some malicious being while also listening to
an evil monologue took away some of the charm of that memory.
“I don’t know what you heard that illusion say…” Akira’s uncle said. “But I just want you to
know… I’m sorry.”
“You didn’t do it,” Akira said. If you’re telling the truth.
“I know, but I’m sorry for more than just that,” Akira’s uncle continued. “I’m sorry for letting
Goro capture me and leaving you all alone. I imagine social services are looking into your
parents now that Goro was… shot.”
Unbidden, tears rose to Akira’s eyes. Akira sniffed and blinked furiously. “It’s not your
fault,” he said. “My parents were the ones who… who…” were never around.
“But as your uncle, it’s my job to protect you from that,” Akira’s uncle said. “I wouldn’t even
be putting you in danger by asking you to help me if I didn’t think it was the only way I could
help you. If I’m stuck here forever, then I can’t take guardianship of you, and then…”
I’ll probably be tossed around the system, or worse…
Akira suddenly felt sick to his stomach.
“It’s not your fault,” Akira whispered again.
“I’m still sorry.”
Akira swallowed. “I don’t want to be alone.” Even if Goro was there. Especially if Goro was
there.
No… wait. Nyarlathotep was the bad guy. But was Nyarlathotep even his uncle? Was
Nyarlathotep even real? Goro’s story had been farfetched. But his uncle’s side of things also
had inconsistencies.

Akira put his head in his hands and took deep breaths. His uncle had always been kind and
loving to him, but Goro was his only friend.
No matter who he chose, he would have to betray someone. He would have to lose someone.
So who did he trust?

The next floor was the Velvet Room.
It wasn’t the same Velvet Room that Goro was used to. The walls were covered in blue
curtains, and a piano sat next to a blue sofa. The table that Igor likely used for fusions sat in
front of it. Oddly enough, there was a microphone stand as well.
It also was markedly not a maze. A real Velvet Room door sat to the side, but no reflections
came to demand answers of them. The stairs were already available.
“This floor is unlike the others,” Nanjo observed.
“It’s the Velvet Room,” Amano said. She frowned. “Just… without any of the inhabitants.”
“I had almost forgotten what the place looked like,” Suou said.
Minato sat down at the piano and began to haltingly play the Velvet Room melody.
“Since when did you know how to play piano?” Ken asked. “I thought you played the
violin?”
Minato shrugged. “I just started learning.”
“I’ve been teaching him,” Ryoji said, raising his hand.
“This is too peaceful,” Yukari said “It makes my skin crawl.”
“That’s the opposite of what it’s supposed to do,” Yu said.
“Yes, I believe Minato-kun’s melody is meant to make you feel at peace, or whatever
Belladonna says,” the familiar voice of Elizabeth said. The entire group spun around toward
the Velvet Room door. Elizabeth, Margaret, Theodore, and Lavenza stood next to it. “Hello,
Minato-kun.”
“What are you doing here?” Minato asked, immediately placing his hands in his lap.
“A warning, if you will,” Margaret said.
“Your deep bond with the inhabitants of this place has made it impossible for Nyarlathotep to
corrupt it,” Lavenza said. “The power of the Velvet Room seeped into this very room.”
“That’s possible?” Yu said.

“Nyarlathotep has always hated everything our master’s master stands for,” Theodore said.
“A place deeply touched by the Velvet Room is near untouchable for him.”
“But I thought Igor and presumably Philemon created this entire dungeon,” Amano said.
“That’s why it has successfully kept Nyarlathotep trapped and weakened his power,”
Margaret said.
“Unfortunately, the longer he’s here, and the more the rest of you mope about your pasts, the
more powerful he becomes,” Elizabeth said. She gestured toward the stairs. “I hope you are
prepared for the storm you’re about to face.”
“Are we ever?” Suou asked.
“Consider this your final resting place before the battle to come,” Theodore said. He pointed
to an elevator door next to the stairs. “Consider resting before you depart.”
“Oh, I like the sound of that, actually,” Junpei said.
“Is that it?” Goro asked. “A send-off?”
“You know we’re not allowed to interfere more than we already have,” Margaret said.
“Besides,” Elizabeth said. “You have everything you need. You just don’t realize it yet.”
“No need to be cryptic,” Ken said sarcastically.
“I’m sure you’ll figure it out,” Theodore said.

They exited the dungeon to find the sun already beginning to set. Goro wasn’t surprised. If
anything, he was surprised it wasn’t the middle of the night.
“So…” Chie said, rubbing her hands together nervously. “I guess I should get started on
dinner?”
It was a testament to how tired everyone was that nobody immediately started exclaiming in
horror. Instead, Yukiko quietly grabbed Chie’s hand and walked to their tent.
“I’m too tired to cook and so are you,” she said. “Wake us up when it’s time to eat.”
While sleep was probably the best decision, Goro was confident sleep would only result in
unsettling nightmares. Instead, Goro helped Akihiko rummage through their bin of food to
make some sort of dinner. Yosuke and Yu were already half-way through rebuilding the fire.
The smell of wood burning, as harmless as it was, caused a shudder to wrack through Goro’s
body.
Akihiko was similarly on edge, and he glanced over his shoulder, as if to confirm the fire
wasn’t killing anyone.

They eventually decided on making curry. Goro watched the pot of rice carefully, not stirring
it. Akihiko, Yu, and Amano debated on the best ingredients to put in the actual curry mixture.
Goro let the harmless argument wash over him as he watched bubbles rise to the surface of
the rice water and pop just as quickly.
How the hell were they meant to win this? They had faced terrible odds in the past, sure, but
they had never faced the pure embodiment of humanity’s evil. At least their past best enemies
had thought they were serving humanity. Nyarlathotep had no such notion.
Goro glanced up at Suou, who silently sat at the campfire. Amano was now passionately
waxing about the importance of cocoa powder in curry, and Nanjo was napping, so Goro
chose the next best option.
“Suou-san,” Goro said. “You’ve fought Nyarlathotep before. Do you have any insights for
how we can beat him?”
Suou wore a far-away look as he stared into the flames. “It was difficult,” he said. “He used a
lot of attacks that hit all of us at once. I remember nearly dying multiple times.”
“Well, that’s nothing new,” Junpei said.
Amano noticed their new conversation topic and shook her head. “It was different. He hit
hard, and he hit fast. I’d be at my full capacity and he would knock me unconscious
somehow.”
“It should help that there are more of us,” Suou said. “If we were able to defeat him with just
five, I imagine we’ll have some sort of advantage with our numbers.”
“But he’s feeding off of our negative feelings,” Goro said. “The more of us there are, the
more power he gets. And unless I am very much mistaken, I do not have faith in my ability to
enter that fight with a cheerful attitude.”
“There’s no point in worrying about it now,” Mitsuru said, sitting next to Goro with an
exhausted expression. “Whatever comes, comes. We’ll face it like we always have.”
Goro nodded and returned his attention to the rice. Mitsuru was right. They would face
Nyarlathotep like they had faced any other impossible foe.
And if this was finally the time that they lost, maybe Nyarlathotep would have the decency of
letting him stay dead.

Akira wasn’t particularly fond of the floor that trapped his uncle. They stood in a white void
speckled with gold, purple, and black stars. Akira felt like he was suspended in an inverted
version of space. The ground he was standing on was solid enough, but every step he took
caused a ripple effect.
It was nothing like the peaceful space the floor below it had been. The blue room with the
piano. A strange blue butterfly had flown past Akira in that room. It had practically been

glowing.
His uncle stood in the center of the room. His hands were in his pockets, and his shoulders
were slumped. His uncle smiled in relief as Akira stepped forward. His footsteps echoing
strangely in the expanded space.
“Akira-kun, there you are,” he said. “I’ve been waiting for you.”
Akira swallowed and stopped walking. His heart beat so loudly he was sure his uncle could
hear it too.
“You don’t look very trapped,” Akira said. “Why don’t you leave while Goro and the others
are distracted?”
The expression on Tsuyoshi’s face was so pitying. It made Akira’s stomach turn over.
“They’re waiting just outside,” he said. “If I tried to run, they would subdue me in a
heartbeat.”
His uncle didn’t look evil. He looked as he always had been. Kind. Welcoming. Maybe a little
condescending, but he only meant well.
“What do you want me to do?” Akira asked.
“You’re going to have to fight them,” his uncle said. He pulled a dagger seemingly out of
nowhere and held the handle out to Akira. Akira barely believed what he was looking at.
“Goro won’t hurt you. He needs you.”
The truth remained that the image his uncle was painting of Goro was nothing like the Goro
Akira knew. Akira’s Goro took care of Monster Cat in Akira’s stead.
Akira’s uncle had been there when his parents kicked him out of the house.
Goro had spent time with him when he didn’t have to.
So did his uncle.
Goro thought his uncle was dangerous.
His uncle thought Goro was dangerous.
Joker was an icon, a trickster. Joker was fearless in the face of impossible odds, able to
withstand the worst danger, able to save himself and his friends again and again. Joker kept a
smile on his face and always had the right quip at the right time.
Who could blame Goro for wanting him back? Who could blame Goro for resenting Akira
for not being him?
Akira resented himself for not being him.

Unbidden, the words Goro told him earlier that week came to the center of Akira’s mind. “I
have years of experience. And a persona. You have neither of those.”
Maybe Akira didn’t have any experience. And maybe he didn’t have a persona. But he could
show Goro what he was made of.
Akira made his decision.
He grabbed the hilt of the knife.

Chapter 97: March 25–May 30, 2012
Chapter Summary

Final battle time guys

Chapter Notes

tw: violence, injury, ptsd, references to death

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Nobody gave each other any dramatic goodbyes. They had all faced calamity before; they
had all said their goodbyes before. In a world so filled with death, everyone had started living
their daily life like a goodbye, just in case it really was.
In the relative safety of the fake Velvet Room, Goro closed his eyes and took a deep breath.
No matter what happened today, it would be over. Either Goro would be dead and reunited
with Shinjiro and his mother (assuming that was what happened after death), or Goro will
have rid the world of one less evil.
Of course, that still left Shido, Yaldabaoth, and the rest, but Goro chose to relish one victory
at a time. He couldn’t let Shido’s mere existence taint Goro’s everyday life.
Although, that was easier said than done.
“Ready?” Goro asked, directing most of his attention at Yu and Minato.
The three of them had just spent a solid half hour in the Velvet Room, determining which
personas would be best to bring and if they could strengthen them any more than they already
had. Elizabeth, Margaret, and Theodore were more than happy to give their advice based on
their guests' fighting styles. Lavenza contented herself with watching.
Yu and Minato nodded with steely expressions. They would be leading their respective teams
simultaneously. Goro, Nanjo, Amano, and Suou were their own smaller team. Goro would
serve to distract Nyarlathotep. Nanjo, Suou, and Amano would take some of the heat off of
Goro and be a distraction themselves, seeing as they had a past history with him. The other
two teams would stay on the offensive.
It wasn’t the best plan, but it was the best one they had at the moment. Suou, Nanjo, and
Amano weren’t used to being ordered around, nor were Yu and Minato familiar with their

skillsets. While Goro was confident in his ability to take orders, the fact remained that,
theoretically, Nyarlathotep’s attention would be mostly on him. Nyarlathotep was likely to
target the team Goro was nearest to. In a smaller team, Goro could operate on instinct and
still manage to keep the heat off most of their numbers.
Mitsuru still hadn’t liked it when Goro presented it in that light. She forced Goro to wear
their best defensive gear and gave him half their stock of physical and magical ointment.
Goro didn’t complain. He had a feeling he would need it.
“Alright.” Goro exhaled quietly. “Let’s get this over with.”
They began climbing the stairs.

Nyarlathotep in the body of Kurusu Tsuyoshi stood in the center of the void, smiling as the
group approached. He didn’t look remotely worried about their presence.
“Have you come to put an end to my existence, Goro-kun?” Nyarlathotep asked with a
mockingly sad edge to his voice. “After everything we’ve been through together?”
“Especially after everything we’ve been through together,” Goro snarled.
Nyarlathotep’s face fell. “But I’ve only been kind to you, haven’t I?”
“If you call threatening me at every turn kindness.” Goro drew his sword and grit his teeth. “I
have nothing left to say to you.”
“Well, since you were kind enough to open a path for me, all that’s left is to stop you before I
can leave this place,” Nyarlathotep said, still beaming. “Now, I’m not a fighter myself,
but…”
He stepped aside to reveal Akira, holding a dagger.
“My nephew would be more than happy to show you the door.”

Goro’s expression was so shocked, so betrayed. Akira could barely look him in the eyes.
I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’m sorry, rang through his mind like a mantra.
“Akira-kun,” Narukami said. His voice was quiet in its horror. “Get away from him.”
Akira squeezed his eyes shut before opening them again. He adjusted his grip on the dagger.
He had never used a dagger before. Would it be hard to plunge it into flesh?
A wave of terrified anticipation made Akira shiver. The dagger almost slipped from his
sweaty palms, and he tightened his hold, digging his fingernails into the leather hilt.

“Akira–” Goro’s expression was angry again. Goro was often angry. Didn’t it get tiring, to be
angry all the time? “--what the hell are you doing here?”
His uncle was talking again. Akira could barely hear him over the ringing of his ears. “You
could attack me, but Akira will defend me. And I know you won’t hurt your precious Akirakun. Or should I call him Joker?”
Three adults standing nearest to Goro flinched. The woman’s face was so pale that Akira was
slightly worried she was going to pass out.
“You would do this again?” she whispered, her voice shaking. “I can’t believe… except I can
believe it, you sick son of a bitch—”
“I didn’t mean to offend,” his uncle said. “I was just referring to Akira’s past code name, or is
future a better term? Sorry if it’s an awkward coincidence—”
“Just shut up,” the man in the tie said furiously.
Goro’s expression had also gone from angry to furious, but it wasn’t directed at Akira. Goro
wasn’t even looking at Akira. He was looking at his uncle, who was standing inches away
from Akira.
Akira tried to pretend he wasn’t scared. Joker wouldn’t be scared.
“Are we even sure this is the real Kurusu-kun?” Amagi asked tentatively, her eyes darting to
Goro. “Couldn’t he be another reflection?”
“We already saw Kurusu-kun on a different floor,” Shirogane said. “It’s him.”
Goro stared at Akira, his eyes imploring. “Whatever he said to you, I swear to you, it’s not
true.”
Akira opened his mouth to respond when his uncle rested a hand on Akira’s shoulder. Akira
jerked away in surprise, but his uncle’s grip held firm.
Why was Akira wasting time? He had so many opportunities to do something since Goro had
entered this void. So many chances to attack. To catch him off guard. Why had he waited till
now when he would surely see the knife coming?
His uncle was still talking.
“Here’s what’s going to happen,” he said. “Akira and I are going to leave. But I’m going to
need that pretty little key of yours to do it.”
“How do you know it’ll even work with you, dumbass?” Tatsumi asked.
“While this is a cleverly crafted prison, it’s far from impenetrable,” his uncle said. “The key
will work with me the same way it’s worked with Goro-kun.”

“Uh huh, you mean you’re going to corrupt it with your corrupty… power,” said a person
with a baseball cap Akira didn’t recognize.
“What power?” his uncle asked innocently.
Akira could barely breathe. He took a deep breath and tried his hardest to stop his hand from
shaking.
“If you think we’re going to let you walk out of here in one piece, you’re sorely mistaken.”
Goro’s eyes burned as he pointed his sword at his uncle.
He was going to die if Akira didn’t do something right now.
Akira reversed his grip on the dagger as his uncle spoke.
“I don’t want to fight you–”
And he drove the blade into his uncle’s stomach.

The dagger didn’t hurt, but it was a surprise.
Akira, the smartass, knew to yank it out. Blood a gold hue splattered from Nyarlathotep’s
body.
Nyarlathotep had designed the dagger with Goro in mind. It was made sharp enough to put
Goro out of commission, at least temporarily.
Which was why Nyarlathotep felt himself slightly weakened from the sudden attack.
Akira spun around. His eyes ruthlessly found the target of Nyarlathotep’s throat, and he
raised his dagger to meet it.
A shame that Akira was not only inexperienced, but sloppy. He telegraphed his movements
so clearly that Nyarlathotep easily grabbed the worm’s wrist before the blade even got close
to its mark.
Goro’s scream of fear was masked well enough as an angry roar- oh how that fear and anger
invigorated him– as Nyarlathotep twisted the dagger from Akira’s hand and held it in his
own. He yanked Akira against his body and pressed the blade against Akira’s throat.
Akira’s fear tripled.
And to think that the nervous anticipation had been directed at Nyarlathotep all along. How
had Nyarlathotep not seen right through the brat’s schemes? Had this place really dulled his
senses that much?
Fine. The twerp was too smart to be manipulated so easily. Nyarlathotep could work with
this.

He dug the blade a little deeper into Akira’s skin. Akira’s high-pitched whimper sent a thrill
through Nyarlathotep’s flesh.

No, no, no, no, no. This could not be happening. This could not be happening.
It had been bad enough when Goro thought Nyarlathotep had managed to manipulate Akira
into fighting Goro. When Goro thought that Akira was willing to through away everything
they’d been through together. When Goro thought he and Akira had suddenly and invertedly
switched roles.
But now, with Nyarlathotep’s knife digging into Akira’s throat, Goro was faced with a
suddenly much worse possibility. If Akira had fought the group, they might have found a way
to disarm him without killing him. But now, Akira’s life was in Nyarlathotep’s hands. Akira
could die at any moment, and there would be nothing Goro could do to stop it.
Akira’s eyes were blown wide as he glanced between the knife and Goro. He grabbed
Nyarlathotep’s arm and attempted to free himself, but, of course, Nyarlathotep didn’t budge.
“You're sick,” Nanjo hissed as everyone else began to demand Nyarlathotep let Akira go.
“Looks like things didn’t quite go according to plan,” Nyarlathotep said conversationally,
propping his chin on top of Akira’s head. “But I suppose I can just go ahead and kill this
pawn, it’s not like he’s worth anything anymore anyway—”
“Stop it!” Goro shouted, his voice raw in his panic. “Please, I’ll do anything, just don’t—
don’t kill him.”
“Don’t—” Akira began, but he let out a sharp cry of pain when Nyarlathotep moved the knife
a millimeter to the left.
The room became deathly silent.
“That’s more like it,” Nyarlathotep said, his eyes flashing even as he grinned. “Now. Let’s
talk terms.”

Akira shouldn’t have done any of this.
He shouldn’t have tried to chase down Goro. He shouldn’t have wanted to see the truth for
himself. He shouldn’t have lied to the embodiment of evil.
He shouldn’t have stabbed his uncle.
Tsuyoshi… Nyarlathotep… his uncle… did it matter who he really was? He was the same
person who comforted Akira all those times. Who took care of him. Even if Nyarlathotep
wasn’t really his uncle, he had been there for Akira more than his real uncle ever had been.

His neck hurt so much. His vision blurred as tears ran down his cheeks. He wanted to pass
out.
Goro could have defeated his uncle by now if Akira wasn’t being used as a human shield.
Why had Akira tried to go in for a second blow? Why didn’t he just run?
“Here’s what’s going to happen,” his uncle said. “You’re going to give me the key, or Akirakun is going to die. I’ll kill him so thoroughly that not one of your little spells can do
anything about it.”
“You’re a monster,” the weird but cool robot lady said.
“Fuck you,” Goro said, his voice shaking.
“Yes, we’ve established all this before,” his uncle said. “Now, the key.”
Everyone wore defeated expressions. Goro slowly lowered his sword.
No.
Akira couldn’t… he wouldn’t be another pawn in his uncle’s game.
But what could he do?
“What’s the matter?” asked a voice that echoed in Akira’s ears. “Are you simply going to
watch?”

Goro found the key in his pocket just as a determined expression crossed over Akira’s face.
An oddly familiar expression…
“ARSENE!” he shouted, his voice much too young to be the person Goro wanted him to be.
“COME TO ME!”
Arsene appeared behind Akira, creating a small shockwave. Goro stumbled backwards, and
even Nyarlathotep’s eyes widened. His grip on the dagger slackened, and Akira shoved his
arm away as Arsene cast a curse skill on Nyarlathotep. Nyarlathotep dropped the knife as he
raised his arms to defend himself.
Akira collapsed to the floor, coughing.
Goro was halfway across the room before he realized what he was doing.
Someone, maybe even everyone had cast a heal spell by the time Goro got to him. Akira
snatched the dagger and scrambled away from Nyarlathotep before he could grab him again.
Goro grabbed Akira’s wrist and yanked him further away.
“Stay back!” Goro shouted, staggering at the mixture of fear and relief and frustration that
coursed through him.

For once in his life, Akira listened. He turned around and sprinted toward the stairs.
“Oh no you don’t,” Nyarlathotep said. He snapped his fingers, and hordes of shadows sprung
up in front of the exit. Akira skidded to a halt.
“Yu!” Goro snapped. “Focus on the shadows!”
Yu nodded. He and the investigation team sprinted toward the shadows, which already
seemed to have doubled in number. Yu barked out frantic orders as the rest of the group
turned toward Nyarlathotep.
“Let me guess,” Nyarlathotep said. His voice began to reverberate around the room. “The rest
of you are going to deal with me?”
“We’ve done it before,” Amano said, shifting into a battle stance. She raised her gun and
fired at Nyarlathotep’s head multiple times without hesitation.
Nyarlathotep only laughed as he grew larger and larger in size now. Goro took another step
back as the gold and dark blue tentacles sprouted from Nyarlathotep and filled the room.
Nyarlathotep’s body became less defined, morphing into the same golden color as the
tentacles, and the same white mask from before formed over his face. Hundreds of green eyes
coated Nyarlathotep’s body, and all of them stared at Goro or Akira.
“Things were different before,” Nyarlathotep said. His tentacles filled the room like the

Around two weeks after they returned to Inaba, Akira’s parents lost custody of Akira and

Akira did not feel the same.

Ever since that day on the hill, they had given up on openly discussing the Nyarlathotep
disaster. Akira was still deeply scarred by the entire ordeal of having to stab someone he

Maybe, when it was a memory, they could talk about it normally. For now, Goro was content

“You can babysit Monster Cat if you’d like,” Goro said. “He’s good for nightmares.”

“You must be close if you were willing to follow him here,” Maruki said.
“You could say that.”
Maruki frowned. “Akechi-kun, I want to help you.”
“And I don’t want to be here,” Goro said. “I guess neither of us can have our way.”
“Is there anything I can do to make this a better experience for you?” Maruki having the gall
to pretend to be concerned.
Goro felt like he was back at the beginning. Back to being physically ten years old and
refusing to trust anyone, especially not anyone over the age of twenty.
“Why don’t you tell me?” Goro asked. “You’re the therapist. Tell me exactly what’s wrong
that I don’t trust you.”
“Well, I can’t speak for you,” Maruki said reluctantly. “But if I had to guess, you had a
negative experience with a therapist in the past.”
“Instead of letting me be the person I was,” Goro said slowly, his voice shaking. “He tried to
brainwash me into being a better version of me without my consent. Because he thought it
would make me and my loved ones happier.”
Maruki looked stunned. “I’m sorry… that sounds terrible.”
Goro wished he could believe he had gotten through to him. “Let’s hope you’re nothing like
him,” he said.

Aigis knocked on the door to Maruki’s professional office. She had checked the office hours
repeatedly on her online database, and while Maruki-sensei spent a great deal of his time
working at Shujin, he still found time to work at his original practice.
Aigis hadn’t even known about Maruki until Goro brought it up maybe a year ago, admitting
that he had omitted Maruki from his original story to the group. Since Aigis was now a
licensed therapist, Goro thought perhaps she could persuade Maruki to not warp reality to his
liking.
As Aigis predicted he would, Maruki opened the door. His eyes widened upon seeing Aigis.
“Oh, you must be the one who made an appointment with me,” Maruki said. “Um… Asousan?”
Aigis nodded. She did not understand the necessity at first, but Mitsuru said Aigis would
have a much easier time navigating Japanese society with a surname. Aigis was a bit
overwhelmed by the sheer number of choices before Ryoji pointed out that his own surname
literally meant ‘full moon’. With that understanding, Aigis chose ‘Asou’ spelled with the
kanji for ‘peace’ and ‘life’ to represent her own peace with what it means to live.
“Alright, Asou-san,” Maruki said. “Please, come inside.”
Aigis followed Maruki into a small room. Maruki sat at a table near a window, and Aigis sat
on the other side.
“So,” Maruki said. “What would you like to talk to me about?”
“I have been thinking a lot lately,” Aigis said, “about what it means to live.”
“That sounds serious.” Maruki clasped his hands together. “Did you come to any answers?”
Aigis nodded. “It took me a while…” she admitted. “But I concluded that to live is to
continue to fight adversity for what one believes in, for the people they believe in, and to

embrace the ups and downs of life.”
Maruki frowned. “But, if possible, wouldn’t it be better to avoid adversity entirely?”
“Problems won’t go away just because you ignore them, Maruki-sensei,” Aigis said. “It’s far
better to confront issues in order to learn to overcome them.”
“True…” Maruki sighed. “If only there was a way to get rid of all the problems in the world.”
“That would be lovely,” Aigis agreed. “But it’s not the world we live in. And even if I had the
opportunity to forget about the trauma I have faced, I would not choose to.” She didn’t
choose to, back when Ryoji gave them that choice so many years ago.
Maruki raised his eyebrows. “No?”
“While it may have been better if it never happened, all of the things I have experienced have
lead me to where I am today,” Aigis said. “The good and the bad. To forget about the bad
would be to forget about the lessons I’ve learned and the person I’ve become along the way.”
“I suppose you may be right,” Maruki said, but Aigis could tell that she had not fully
convinced him.
“Please, think about it,” Aigis said. “Would you like to forget all of your own hardships?”
Maruki didn’t say anything in reply.
“I understand that there are certain events that we wish would go away,” Aigis said. “But
getting rid of those events would get rid of a part of ourselves. Deep down, I think you must
know that, Maruki-sensei.”
“But is that part of ourselves really worth it?” Maruki asked. “I would much rather lose a
piece of myself for the sake of finally having peace of mind.”
“But I would not,” Aigis said firmly. “And I know of many others who would agree with
me.”
Maruki frowned. “Well, I guess you’ve given me a lot to think about, Asou-san. I’ll bear
what you said in mind.”

That night, Okumura died on public television. It wasn’t remotely the same death as it was
with the mental shutdowns. It was far less graphic. Okumura simply stopped talking midsentence and started to suffer from some sort of reaction.
Goro put his head in his hands. Poison, if he had to guess. The autopsy reports would show
that too, but Shido had people in that field too. They could forge results to make it a mental
shutdown case.
Just a cog in a machine. Goro had only ever been a cog in the machine. Shido had so many
people he could use to make his plans go exactly as he wanted them.
Couldn’t he fix anything?

Haru sat in Leblanc, trying to stop her head from spinning. Everything was just too horrible,
too overwhelming to bear. Even Leblanc’s delicious coffee didn’t taste very good at the
moment, which was deeply unfortunate, because she had been hoping it would make her feel
better.
“I don’t understand,” she told Akira quietly, not looking up from the mug. “We did
everything right.”

“I know,” Akira said. “I’m sorry.”
“It’s not your fault,” Haru said.
The bell rang as someone entered the café. Haru looked up and was relieved to see Kirijo-san
enter.
“Kirijo-san!” Haru said, bowing deeply. “Thank you so very much for coming.”
“Of course, Okumura-san,” Kirijo said. “Goro said you wanted to meet with me?”
“Yes, I just… I know you also lost your father when you were around my age, and I know it’s
not fair to compare experiences, but I have an entire company as well as grief and…” Haru
wilted. “I just don’t know what to do. Goro-kun said you might be able to help.”
“I’m more than happy to help a friend of Goro’s,” Kirijo said. She sat down across from Haru
at the table, and Akira quietly excused himself. “But let’s not get trapped in the business side
of it. How are you doing, first of all?”
“I…” Haru bit her lip, and she felt her eyes well-up with tears. “I don’t know. He was
horrible, but… he was still my father.”
“Of course.”
Okumura took a deep breath and shook her head. “But I’d prefer not to think about that right
now, if you don’t mind.”
“Alright.” Kirijo put on a more serious expression. “What do you know about running a
company?”
“Not much,” Haru said helplessly. “And to make matters worse, I’m still expected to keep my
engagement with my fiancé.”
“Well,” Kirijo said fiercely, her eyes lighting up with a vindictiveness that Haru couldn’t help
but admire. “I can tell you firsthand how to deal with that.”

The group agreed to lay low after Okumura’s death. Over the course of the next month, Goro
waited for someone to ask to join the team.
Nobody did.
The police interviewed the students late into October. Goro smiled sweetly as an asshole
detective asked him to sit.
“Akechi-kun, ah, you’re the other transfer student,” said the polite detective. “It says here
you had some… issues with Kamoshida?”

“That’s right,” Goro said. “I was trying to defend a student from him and he became a bit…
violent with me.”
“I’m terribly sorry to hear that,” said the detective. “It looks like you have an interesting set
of friends. You hang out with the student on probation, Hanamura-kun?”
“He’s a childhood friend.”
“I see.”

“Is something the matter, Niijima-san?”
Sae glanced up from her computer, surprised by Shirogane’s unexpected appearance. But
then again, Shirogane always did appear whenever mental shutdowns or the Phantom
Thieves were involved.
“I was thinking about the Phantom Thieves,” Sae said, tucking her hair behind her ear
thoughtfully. “Don’t you think it’s suspicious that Okumura had a mental shutdown just after
the Phantom Thieves sent them a calling card? And we’ve recently discovered that Principal
Kobayakawa also received a calling card.”
Shirogane’s eyes widened, but Sae spotted a disagreeing frown. “Perhaps that’s what the
official records say… but are you really suggesting the Phantom Thieves are behind the
mental shutdowns?”
Sae bristled. “Isn’t that the most logical conclusion?”
“On the contrary,” Shirogane said, “Too many facts refuse to line up the way they should.
These mental shutdowns have been occurring for years now, but the Phantom Thieves have
only made themselves known earlier this year. Additionally, you and I have both been
investigating these mental shutdowns. Okumura’s death did not look like it shared any of the
symptoms.”
Sae had to begrudgingly agree. She originally thought Okumura had a stroke of some kind
before the autopsy claimed mental shutdown. Still, Sae had no reason to question an official
document. And besides—
“But who else could it be?” Sae demanded.
“If I knew, Niijima-san, we wouldn’t be standing her having this conversation, would we?”

Minato woke up one Sunday to the sound of frantic knocking on his front door. Hit with
instinctive worry, especially with the new animosity toward the Phantom Thieves, he
scrambled out of bed to get it, but by the time he reached the front room, Ryoji was already
opening the door for their unexpected guest.

A small girl burst into the room, quickly bowed, and said, “Sorry to bother you, but Gorokun’s here, right? The new Ultimate Fantasy game finally came out and he promised he
would watch me play—”
“I’m right here, I’m right here,” Goro murmured, stepping out of his bedroom with an
exhausted expression and holding Taiyaki’s fish food in one hand. Ken peaked his head out
into the hall from his own room.
“What’s happening?” he asked. “Did I hear Ultimate Fantasy?”
“Didn’t you know?” the girl demanded. “The new game came out today, and it took all of my
self-control not to start playing it at the stroke of midnight!”
Goro frowned. “Did you own it at the stroke of midnight?” he asked.
Futaba huffed exasperatedly. “No, I had to wait for the stores to open, buy a copy, and now
I’m here, and we’re playing.”
“Do we even have a console in this apartment?” Ryoji asked, because somehow he was
following the conversation far better than Minato was.
“There’s one in my room,” Goro said. “Futaba apparently saved for the past four years to
give me one for my eighteenth birthday.”
“And it wasn’t ulteriorly motivated at all,” Futaba said. “I would never give someone a gift
just so I could crash at their house at six in the morning to play video games with them. And
say hi to their cat. Where is Monster Cat, by the way?”
Ken burst out laughing as Monster Cat, probably summoned by his name, strutted out of the
kitchen and toward Futaba. Futaba immediately bent down and scratched Monster Cat’s head.
Minato blinked, too tired to get the joke. “Um…”
“Anyway!” Futaba said. She grabbed Goro and Ken by the arm and dragged them toward
Goro’s room. “We’ve got a game to play!”
Goro waved goodbye to the two of them just before Futaba slammed the door shut. Ryoji and
Minato stared at each other in the now very blessed silence.
“I’m going back to bed,” Minato said.
Ryoji smiled sympathetically. “I’ll make breakfast.”

Makoto somehow wrangled the group into helping her with preparing for the school festival.
They spent half their time sorting through the names of celebrities that students wanted to
visit the school at a special panel.

“I think Kujikawa might be winning,” Makoto said with a long suffering sigh. “But how am I
going to get a hold of her?”
“Just have Akira call her,” Ann said.
Makoto’s eyes widened. “What?”
“Oh, you weren’t here for this conversation, were you?” Ryuji asked, grinning. “Yeah, Akirakun grew up in the same town as Kujikawa, or something.”
“I don’t actually have her number, unfortunately,” Akira said. “But Goro does.”
“Wait, wait, let me guess,” Ryuji said. “She’s yet another person who was a persona user in
your whacky persona hijinks.”
“Got it in one,” Goro said, marking down another vote for Kujikawa. The field trip to the TV
station must have pushed her to the front of most of the second year’s minds.
“Dude…” Ryuji said. “I was joking.”
“As a general rule,” Ken said. “If Goro’s friends with them, they were a former persona user.
The one exception being Emiko-chan.”
“That has to be an exaggeration,” Makoto said.
“Unfortunately,” Goro said defeatedly, “it’s not.”

The school festival came and went, and finally, Akira called everyone to meet.
“We have to do something,” Akira said. “I know it feels like we’re stuck, but we can’t keep
hiding forever. That’s like saying to Shido that he’s won.”
“Then what should we do?” Makoto asked.
“I say we strike at the source,” Ryuji said. “It’s this Shido guy’s fault, right? Let’s just change
his heart and be done with it.”
“Going straight for the baddie has always worked before,” Teddie said.
“It really has,” Ken said. “Like, genuinely.”
Goro frowned. “I just don’t know if we’re strong enough for that yet.”
“If we keep hiding, we’ll never be strong enough,” Akira said firmly. “I say we put that
bastard in his place, starting tomorrow. Who’s with me?”
Slowly, everybody raised their hands.
