They were no sooner two days into infiltrating the damned palace when Goro heard more
noise than usual coming from the lower levels.
“Wait a minute,” Futaba said, pulling up her holographic display. “I’m getting some strange
readings.” Her eyes widened. “Woah! The security level has gone way up!”
She pulled up an image of shadows multiplying in the grand lobby of Shido’s cruise ship. But
worse yet, Goro could already see men in dark suits pushing their way into the lobby area.
“It’s an ambush,” Goro said immediately.
“Like the one that was meant to happen at my sisters’ palace?” Makoto asked. “But how–”
“No time for that,” Akira said. “Getting out of here is our number one priority.”
“Um, I don’t know about that,” Futaba said, pulling up another screen. “There are tons of
guys blocking our exit.”
Officers had filled up nearly the entirety of the ship’s deck. From the limited view of the
screen, Goro could see them shifting toward the ship’s sides as well. It would only be minutes
before the entire ship was filled with the full power of Shido’s police force.
“Hide,” Ryuji hissed.
They ducked further down a side hall, one that blessedly didn’t turn them into rats. But…

“We can use the rat puzzle as a diversion,” Goro said. “If we turn most of the traps back on,
any real people who try to go through this maze will hopefully also be turned into mice.”
“Alright, but how do we get off the ship?” Haru asked.
“On a ship this size, wouldn’t there be lifeboats?” Yusuke asked.
Goro genuinely couldn’t remember if there were. “That’s assuming Shido’s ego isn’t the size
of Tokyo–”
“We split up,” Akira said authoritatively. Everybody shut up to listen. “In pairs so that
nobody gets ambushed on their own. We have grappling hooks. Use them to stay above the
crowds. I’m going to act as a diversion.”
“No,” Goro said. “That’s reckless and unnecessary.”
“There’s an odd number of us,” Akira said. “And three people is too many to quickly travel
together. One of us has to go, and it might as well be me.”
“We all know how that story ends,” Yusuke said.
“With us defeating the bad guy?” Akira asked with false cheer. He glanced at Goro. “You
wanted me to trust you before. Now you have to trust me.”
That was easy for Akira to say. Akira hadn’t seen himself drugged and beaten and shot.
But there was no arguing with him now.
“Fine,” Goro said. “Oracle, you’re with me.”
“What? Why?” Futaba asked.
“He’s right,” Akira said. “Phoenix’s the strongest, and you have next to no fighting
experience.” He pulled out his grappling hook. “Alright. Let’s go.”
Akira ran down the hall without another word. The men in the black suits began to follow
him.
How had they found them? Then again, perhaps Shido’s own palace was the easiest one to
predict they would be.
There was no time to worry about it now. Goro grabbed Futaba by the arm and sprinted in a
random direction, turning the mice puzzles back on as he went. They ducked down into a
vent and began to crawl. Futaba directed Goro toward a vent that would theoretically lead
them outside the ship. In the meantime, she directed everyone else toward exits.
“How’s Joker?” Goro asked. As they stopped in front of a vent grate. He peered through the
cracks. Sure enough, it seemed to lead outside, but there were cops everywhere.
Futaba could fly out on her persona easily enough. Goro would have to improvise.

“He’s still kicking,” Futaba said, her voice on edge.
“And the others?”
“Everyone’s out except Mona and Skull, and they’re nearly there. Hurry up and kick the grate
open already!’
Goro pulled his gun out and shot at the nails keeping the grate in. Once it looked loose
enough, he shoved at it with his shoulder with all his might. The grate fell out with a loud
pop, and a few officers shouted in pain as it landed on their heads.
Goro’s brief satisfaction was interrupted by tens of guns aimed in their direction.
“Freeze!” shouted one of the officers.
Goro glanced up the side of the ship. There was an outcropping he could launch his grappling
hook at to hopefully get out of the officers’ line of fire.
“What’s Mona and Skull’s status?” Goro asked quietly, not moving a muscle.
“Now come out with your hands behind your head!” the officer shouted.
“They’re out,” Futaba said with hushed victory. “Joker’s still distracting the others.”
“Are you listening?!”
“I want you to escape with your persona,” Goro said.
“What about you?” Futaba demanded.
“What do you think?” Goro asked. “I’m going to save Joker’s stupid ass.”
Futaba’s expression wavered.
“If you do not follow directions, we will open fire!”
“Alright,” Futaba said, her voice somewhat relieved. “Bring him back.”
Goro shot his grappling hook without another word. Thundering bullets pinged off the wall’s
metal side, following Goro’s heels. Goro jumped onto the roof and ducked behind a
smokestack. He glanced at the sky. Futaba’s persona flew above the scores of officers and
disappeared back into the real world.
Okay. Good.
“Joker!” Goro snapped over his transceiver. “What’s your status?”
No response. Shit.
Shouts were coming from the stern. Shouts that sounded distinctly like “We’ve got him!”

Shit, shit, shit, shit.
Goro sprinted toward the edge of the ship roof and glanced down at the crowd below. A
spotlight shone on Akira’s body lying on the ground as one of the officers grabbed him by the
hair and shoved his face into the ground.
Goro grit his teeth and pulled out his grappling hook. It would be dangerous, but maybe he
could grapple to Akira’s body, grab him, and–
“Don’t bother with heroics, Akechi-kun,” said a familiar voice behind him. “It’s futile.”
Goro twisted his body and cocked his gun at the same culprit from before. Same dark
clothing. Same nearly completely covered face.
The only difference was that instead of immediately attacking Goro, the culprit merely had
his gun drawn and pointed toward Goro’s face.
“Who are you?” Goro demanded.
“Someone who makes a point not to be painfully obvious,” said the culprit.
Goro opened his mouth to demand to know what that was supposed to mean, but he heard
footsteps to his right. He spun toward the stranger, who he recognized as Iwata. The culprit
took advantage of his distraction and kicked Goro in the side, causing him to plummet off the
edge of the roof.
Goro landed on the ground with a painful thump, and his vision blurred. Officers grabbed his
arms roughly and snapped handcuffs around them, and the culprit jumped down from above.
“Sorry,” he said, raising the hilt of his dagger. “Captain’s orders.”
Goro tried to summon his persona, but the dagger hilt came down too quickly, slamming into
his skull—

Goro sat in the back of a police car, his vision still swimming. Iwata sat to his right, looking
at Goro passively.
So Iwata wasn’t the culprit after all.
Goro glanced out the window and realized that they weren’t moving. They were simply
parked outside the Diet Building.
“What’s going on?” Goro asked, glancing at his cuffed hands. “Aren’t you arresting me?”
Iwata removed a gun from the inside of his coat and pointed it at Goro, who stiffened.
“Shido-san would like to speak with you,” he said.

Goro felt his chest freeze over. “Representative Shido?” he asked, playing dumb. “Why
would he wish to speak with me?”
“You really want to try that after being caught in his palace?” Iwata asked.
Goro swallowed. “What does he want with me?”
“I’m going to uncuff you,” Iwata said roughly, not answering Goro’s question. “But if you
make any attempt to escape—”
“You’ll shoot me,” Goro said hoarsely. “I got the message, thank you.”

Iwata uncuffed Goro and escorted him into the Diet Building. Fortunately, since all Goro’s
injuries were obtained in the metaverse, he came out without a concussion. Unfortunately,
Goro might prefer a concussion as Iwata opened the door to Shido’s office.
Goro didn’t move at first, staying stubbornly in the hall, but Iwata pushed him inside.
Shido sat behind his desk, a smile on his face when he saw Iwata and Goro.
“Akechi-kun,” Shido said, his eyes glinting from behind his glasses. He gestured to the chair
in front of the desk. “Have a seat.”
Goro set his jaw and kept his feet firmly planted in the ground. “No.”
“No?” Shido stood up the way he always did when he was displeased. “Akechi-kun, you
should know by now. Nobody says no to me.”
“And you don’t get to tell me what to do,” Goro snapped, even as his chest pounded.
Iwata grabbed Goro tightly by the arm and yanked Goro forward. Goro gasped in pain, and
he stumbled, grabbing onto Shido’s desk for support. Iwata grabbed Goro’s shoulders and
shoved him into the seat.
“Like I said,” Shido said with a little smirk. “Nobody says no to me. Iwata, you may go.”
Iwata bowed and left the room without another word.
“What do you want?” Goro bit out. “The last time we spoke, you made it abundantly clear
that you didn’t want anything more to do with me.”
“And your final letter,” Shido said with disgust, “expressed the same sentiment. But that was
before recent… developments.”
“What? That I’m a Phantom thief? Wouldn’t our leader be more worthy of your time?”
“Oh, trust me, we’ve got him in hand,” Shido said, causing a rush of fear to spike through
Goro’s chest. “But your little friend isn’t the one who bent time to his will.”

What? How did Shido know that? How did he know that?
“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Goro said. A half-truth. Goro never bent time to
his own will.
Shido raised an eyebrow. “No? Care to explain this… informative conversation you had with
your meddling friends, then?”
Shido removed his phone from his pocket and played an audio recording. Goro froze as his
own voice came from the speakers.
“I… was the one… originally behind the mental shutdowns.”
So, someone had been spying. Kasukabe, most likely. Damn. Why had they been as naïve as
to believe him when he said they meant them no harm?
“Who gave you that recording?” Goro demanded.
“Despite his complete lack of a spine, Kasukabe has his uses,” Shido said, his triumphant
smirk growing. “And your group had some very enlightening conversations. I hardly believed
it at first, but how could I not when you knew so much? My plans… my internal
operations…”
“Then you know how this ends,” Goro said, grinning even though he was almost certainly
going to die soon. “You lose. You lose everything.”
“Yes, I heard how miserably you failed me,” Shido said, his eyes flashing. “Falling for such a
petty trick by a group of teenagers, allowing yourself to get killed instead of finishing the

“If that’s what you want to call it—”
“But this time, I have the advantage,” Shido said. “Knowledge is power. I let you and your

“Everything?” Goro demanded, jumping to his feet. “Kasukabe’s recordings don’t tell you

Shido’s hand flew toward Goro’s face and hit him across the cheek, causing his head to whip

Goro looked up at Shido with no small amount of alarm, his cheek pulsing in pain. Shido had

Shido wrung his hand out with a disgusted expression, as though it was Goro’s fault Shido

Futaba sprinted the whole way home.
“Sojiro!” she shouted into Leblanc, which was devoid of customers. “If the news says Akira

“Dead?!” Sojiro followed Futaba out of Leblanc, but Futaba was already half-way across
Yongen-Jaya. “What are you talking about?!”
“I’ll explain later!” Futaba shouted back.
She slid into her house and burst into her room.
The good news: Akira and Futaba had prepared for this probability. Shido had done
something like this in the last timeline, so it wasn’t a lot to assume that it would happen
again. Admittedly, the plan was shoddily made and relied on a lot of unknowns. It was a

Alright Sae, Futaba thought as she typed frantically on her computer and called Makoto at the

“You’re no longer on the case, Niijima-san,” he said. “I’m sorry, but there’s nothing I can do

“The suspect already signed a written confession,” said the guard. “There’s no need for

“No.”

“Hanamura-kun is in grave danger,” Shirogane said. “And I need your help to save him.”

Goro kept his expression neutral as he said, “You lost because the Phantom Thieves defeated

“Shido-san,” Goro said sweetly. “No amount of practice is going to make me be able to bend

“If we forget the old reality existed, yes,” Goro said.
Minato’s grip on the frame tightened. “And you’re not tempted at all to leave it as it is?”
Was he? The arrival of the old Akira had brought back an old grief that Goro thought he had
left behind him. Akira was one of the only people who had seen Goro at his worst and still
gave a damn afterwards.
He also wasn’t the same Akira Goro spent the past eight years with.

Shinjiro was alive in this reality. Everyone was alive in this reality.
“No,” Goro said, his words feeling like a betrayal to everything he stood for. “I am. But the
longer I wait, the more opportunity Nyarlathotep has to wake up, and I can’t… we can’t let
that happen.”
Minato closed his eyes. “You’re right,” he said. “Let’s do this.”

Thus began the never-ending questioning of everyone Goro knew.
“How did you meet Shinjiro?” Goro asked Akihiko.
“Well, um… you see…” said the no-longer orphaned Akihiko.
“How do we know Mitsuru?” Goro asked Ken.
“Why do you exist?” Goro demanded of Aigis.
And so on and so forth.
It felt wrong, to force his friends to remember a reality much more painful than the one
Maruki presented to them.
But it was wrong of Maruki to brainwash everyone in the first place. Goro wasn’t forcing
anyone to wake up. He was just strongly encouraging them to do so.

Goro, Akira, Minato, and Sumire of all people decided to make headway into the palace
while they waited for the others to make their impossible choice. Goro was infinitely relieved
upon seeing that Minato was allowed to enter the metaverse with Yaldabaoth out of the way.
Having everyone involved would make clearing Maruki’s palace go much quicker, and with
any luck, Nyarlathotep wouldn’t have the chance to wake up so soon after they defeated him.
“Woah,” Akira said upon seeing Goro’s metaverse outfit. “That’s different.”
“Yeah, he got a new persona while fighting a tentacle monster,” Minato said. “It was very
dramatic.”
“What?” Sumire asked, still missing multiple details of Goro’s story.
“You really had to phrase it like that, didn’t you?” Goro muttered. Minato only smirked in
response.
They made decent headway into the palace, but by the time they rested in the safe room,
Goro was exhausted. He sat down in a chair and put his head in his hands.
“Goro,” Akira said suddenly, sitting up. “After this, why don’t we go to Mementos?”

“Just the two of us?” Goro asked. “Why?”
“Well, I know I’m a little rusty, and this version of me doesn’t have it, but…” Akira ripped
off one of his red gloves and threw it at Goro. Goro caught it with a dumbstruck expression.
“You threw the gauntlet first. We’ve yet to have our rematch.”
“Right now?” Goro asked, staring at the glove in his hand.
“It’s now or it’s literally never,” Akira said, his voice cracking. “You and I both know this.”
Goro didn’t like to think about it.
“Okay,” Goro said. “Let’s go.”

“Can I really do this?” Mitsuru whispered. She sat in her father’s study; it was the only place
she could keep calm. Her hands trembled as she thought about what she would have to go
back to.
Eight years… Mitsuru had lost her father eight years ago. And now that she finally had him
back…
Could she really take him away again?
The door to the study opened, and Mitsuru looked up. Her father entered, looking older than
he did when he died. But in this reality, there was a softness in his features that the stress of
the Dark Hour had stripped away.
“Father,” Mitsuru said, her voice sounding faint to her own ears.
“What’s wrong?” Takeharu asked.
Mitsuru burst into tears. Takeharu sat down beside her and put a comforting hand on her
shoulder. Mitsuru hiccupped as she tried to pull herself together.
“I’m sorry,” she whispered. “I’m so sorry.”
Somehow, her father understood. “None of this is real, is it?” he asked. His voice wavered. “I
died, didn’t I?”
Mitsuru gave a tiny, near imperceptible nod.
Takeharu pulled her into a hug. “I’m so sorry,” Takeharu said, “that I couldn’t be there for
you when you needed it most.”
“I couldn’t save you,” Mitsuru whispered, choking on her tears. She clung to her father as
though he could disappear at any moment. “I can’t… I can’t…”

“It’s not your fault, Mitsuru,” Takeharu said firmly. “It was never, and never will be your
fault.”
Mitsuru’s entire body shuddered, and she buried her face into her father’s shoulder. “I can’t
lose you again.”
“I’m sorry,” was all her father could say.

Akira and Goro faced each other in Mementos, the swirling red subway tunnels serving as
their arena.
Goro remembered the first time they did this. He remembered thinking that Akira was a fool
for trusting him. A fool for following Akechi alone into Mementos. Goro remembered
thinking about how easy it would be to kill Akira there and then.
But Akira had won.
“Don’t go easy on me,” Akira said, raising his dagger in a slightly different grip than the
other Akira. Goro had forgotten about that. He wore a wild grin. “Rival.”
“Are you kidding?” Goro asked. “This time, I won’t lose.”
They fought until they were both out of stamina. They collapsed at practically the same time.
“I think I won,” Akira gasped.
“If you call that winning, we both won,” Goro said sarcastically.
Goro had long since gotten over his fear of trains roaring down the tracks. They lay in
opposite directions, their heads being the only thing sitting next to each other. Goro stared at
the murky roof of the tunnel, watching the red and black hues swirl together into nothingness.
“What’s it like?” Akira asked. “My double’s life?”
Goro did not want to think about the other Akira. He didn’t want to know where he was right
now, or if he even existed at all. It soured the moment.
“Does it look like I know?” Goro asked.
“If the pictures on the wall have anything to say about it, yes,” Akira said.
Goro sighed. “It’s good,” he said. “I think. Your parents lost custody of him five years ago.
He lives with the Hanamuras; they own the Junes.”
“That’s why that picture was there,” Akira murmured. “I was so confused.” He suddenly
laughed. “Does that mean my name is Hanamura Akira? It rhymes, and I hate it.”

“That’s what he said too.”
“What else?”
“We have a cat,” Goro said.
“Yeah? What’s his name?”
“Monster Cat,” Goro said. His face grew hot as Akira began laughing his head off. “It was an
accident! It was just a place holder name, and he wanted to name it Go-Go Goro, which was
out of the question—”
Akira started wheezing.
“Oh my god,” Akira gasped, tears springing to his eyes. “What does Morgana think of him?”
“I believe he’s very jealous of him,” Goro said. “Or so I’ve heard. Once, at his behest, I let
the other Akira babysit Monster Cat at Leblanc. Instead of taking good care of him, he loses
him—”
“He lost the cat?” Akira asked. “How?”
“Because the catnapper was still around and was stealing cats left and right,” Goro said.
“Akira thought there might be foul play from Morgana involved, because he calls me in the
middle of the night saying Monster Cat has been stolen—Why are you laughing?”
“I just can’t believe you can take anything seriously when your cat is named that,” Akira
said, taking deep breaths.
“Anyway, we had to stage an intervention for the catnapper, who was apparently grieving the
loss of her cat Snowball, and we had to get Emiko on the phone just to get her to listen to
reason—”
“Who’s Emiko?” Akira asked.
“A friend,” Goro said simply. “She wants to be a veterinarian, which is why we called her.”
“Neat.”
Goro resumed his story. “And when all was said and done, Morgana lectures Monster Cat on
the importance of self-defense in Yongen Jaya.”
“He would,” Akira said, grinning. “Do you think he realized that the cat couldn’t understand
human speech?”
“You know what’s interesting?” Goro asked. “I think Monster Cat did understand Morgana to
a certain degree. He’s certainly more cautious anytime we go out in public anymore.”
“You should’ve named him Go-Go Goro,” Akira said.

“You would say that.”
“The other me was brilliant for coming up with that,” Akira said. “Actually, I have a
confession to make.”
“And that is?”
“When we played darts, I always wanted to say go go Goro to you before you did the final
throw.”
Goro stared at the ceiling with a deadpan expression. “I wish I could be surprised, but your
counterpart does that to me every time.”
“And you don’t bite his head off?” Akira asked. He put his hand on his chest dramatically.
“Who are you and what have you done to Goro?”
“Ha ha,” Goro said. “Ever heard of eight years?”
“I have, actually,” Akira said with a gravity that nobody ever held before. “I’ve felt all of
them too.”
This was a person who understood, Goro realized, feeling like he took a nasty punch to the
gut. Akira understood what it was like for eight years to pass since 2017. Sure, he hadn’t time
traveled, but he still understood.
It was harder, if not impossible, for the others to understand. They were all experiencing this
year for the first time. It wasn’t their fault either. It was just how it was.
“Me too,” Goro whispered.
“He sounds like a good friend.”
“Who?”
“The other me. Who else would I be talking about?”
“I don’t know,” Goro said. “I guess… I have a lot of friends now.”
Akira’s smile became bittersweet. “Well, I was talking about the other me. It sounds like he
makes you happy.”
“You think so?”
“Goro, I’ve stared at that photo wall every time I’m in that bedroom,” Akira said. “And in
most, if not all those pictures, you’re smiling. And not one of your fake smiles or angry
smiles. A real smile.”
Goro didn’t say anything.
“I’ve never… I’d never seen you wear that smile before,” Akira whispered.

“A lot’s happened,” Goro said heavily.
“I know.” A tear slid down Akira’s face, and his voice shook. “And I don’t know if this was
Akira’s wish, or yours, or something Maruki thought you both wanted, but… you know I
can’t stay here. You know… I never made you happy like that.”
“That’s not true,” Goro said quickly. Akira didn’t say anything, and Goro hastened to
elaborate. “Maybe it wasn’t the same happiness I feel now, but… you were the first person in
my life that gave a shit about me after my mother died. Gave a shit about the person who I
really was. And that made me… that made me happier than you realize. Than even I
realized.”
“But I can’t stay,” Akira said, shutting his eyes. Another tear slipped down his face. “I have a
life outside of here. And the other me has a life here. I can’t steal that from him. I’m not sure
that I want to.”
Goro clung to one of the horizontal bars between the subway tracks. The concrete dug into
his skin. “I’m not sure I want you to either,” he admitted.
Akira looked relieved and heartbroken at the same time. Goro wondered how the hell their
roles ever became reversed.
“Then that’s that,” Akira said, his voice strangled. He brought his arm over his eyes. “Let’s
not… let’s not talk about it anymore.”
“Let’s not,” Goro agreed, blinking away the tears in his own eyes.

“Akihiko,” Shinji said, sitting next to Akihiko at the kitchen table.
Akihiko had been sitting at the table for the past hour, staring at an old photo of Shinji,
Akihiko, and Mitsuru. They all looked so happy together.
“No.” Akihiko said.
“Aki, listen to me,” Shinji said. “Goro’s right.”
“No,” Akihiko said with more force. “You’re not… you can’t be…”
“I’m dead,” Shinji said. “And so is Miki. You have to accept that.”
“You don’t know what you’re asking me to do,” Akihiko said through gritted teeth. His mind
flashed to Shinji lying in the hospital bed, the heart monitor flat-lining. Miki being left
behind in the fire. The recoil of Takaya’s revolver. Akihiko furiously pushed it away. “I can’t
lose you again.”
“And you want to live a lie instead?” Shinji asked. “Let whoever doing this control us
through happiness? Come on. You’re better than that.”

Could Akihiko really live in a world in which he killed two people? Takaya was evil, but
Chidori… Junpei would hate him all over again.
“Am I?”
Shinji slammed his hand on the table, causing the entire thing to shake. “Yes. You are.”

“What about you?” Goro asked. They sat in Goro’s bedroom, where Goro introduced Akira
to Monster Cat. Monster Cat regarded him warily. Did he know someone else was inhabiting
his caretaker’s body?
“What about me?” Akira asked.
“What has life been like?” The without me went unsaid.
“Well, things were pretty hectic at first,” Akira said. “Traversed a politician’s really tragic
mindscape pretty much right after we sorted out Maruki. And there were some strange road
trip shenanigans the following summer vacation. An artificial intelligence joined the team.
You know how it is.”
“And now?”
“Things are okay,” Akira said. “Good, even. Haru’s got her coffee shop up and running.
Zenkichi talked Makoto out of trying to become police commissioner, so she’s going into
social services now. Ann’s a model; Ryuji’s managing a local gym. Yusuke does art. Futaba’s
doing freelance tech work. Sumire’s a pro gymnast.”
“What about you?” Goro asked.
“Oh, I do musical theater,” Akira said.
“Be serious.”
“You don’t think I could cut it?”
“As dramatic as you are, no I don’t think you would manage actually making it to the stage.”
“Ouch.”
“I’m being honest.”
Akira sighed dramatically. “Well, I still pick up a bunch of odd jobs, and I work more and
more at Leblanc for Sojiro, but officially? I’m a teacher.”
“A teacher?” Goro asked, unable to hide the surprise from his voice.

“Yep,” Akira said, scratching Monster Cat behind the ears. “High schoolers, if you can
believe it. It’s my way of making a difference in people’s lives without, you know, stealing
hearts.”
“Do you wear your fake glasses to look smarter?” Goro asked.
“Only on test days,” Akira said with a sly smile.

“I was going to propose,” Junpei whispered into the silence separating him and Chidori, who
sat opposite him at their kitchen table.
A ring sat in one of Junpei dresser drawers, hidden beneath a pile of shirts. The reservation to
their favorite restaurant was for next month.
Junpei had been so excited.
But was that reservation even real? Was the ring? Had Junpei actually done any of those
things?
“I know,” Chidori said.
“You… know?”
“I saw it when it was my turn to do the laundry,” Chidori said. “But I knew you would want it
to be a surprise.”
“Oh.” Junpei swallowed. “What would you have said… when I asked?”
“You really have to ask?” Chidori looked unimpressed, but her face faded to sadness. “You
know I would’ve said yes.”
They dissolved into heavy silence.
“It’s okay,” Chidori suddenly said.
“It’s… okay?” Junpei repeated, looking up with a confused expression.
Chidori smiled slightly. “You’ve already started to reject this reality, so… I saw this on your
dresser.”
Chidori slid a photograph across the table. Junpei picked it up and blinked.
It was Junpei and… his girlfriend. He remembered now…Murasato Ayame. He met her
through one of his teammates. She had dark brown skin and curly hair and a bubbly
personality and was going to law school. She didn’t resemble Chidori in any way. But
Junpei… Junpei loved her. He loved her a lot.

Come to think of it, he had seen her once in this alternate timeline. She was with her ex. It
had been a rough breakup, and Junpei knew that Ayame had wished things had gone
differently, but…
Damn. Maruki really had gone and played matchmaker, huh?
“I’m sorry,” Junpei said. It took a long time for him to be able to start dating again after what
had happened… but after speaking with a counselor about it, he decided Chidori would want
him to find happiness. Still, to be confronted with Chidori now… “I haven’t forgotten about
you, I just—”
“Don’t apologize,” Chidori said. “I am happy. That you found someone, I mean. As much as
I wish things could have turned out differently, I… I hope things work out for you two.”
“Yeah,” Junpei said. “Thanks.”

When the others finally joined the fight, they got through the palace in mere days.
“I still can’t believe you’re the previous timeline’s Akira,” Futaba said, poking Akira’s arm
like he was a science experiment. “But I guess you’re actually from the parallel timeline?
This is so weird.”
“Can you tell us about our futures?” Haru asked.
“Um, unfortunately, I think Goro broke the timeline,” Akira said. “Because I have no idea if
things are going to go the same way they went for us.”
“Wow, thanks a lot Goro-kun,” Ryuji said. “We could have known our futures.”
“I’m so sorry for trying to make your lives better,” Goro said with an eyeroll.
“Perhaps it is best that we do not know,” Yusuke said. “There is beauty in mystery.”
“Yeah, you would say that,” Ryuji said.
“I just can’t believe you don’t know me,” Teddie lamented.
Akira winced. “Yeah, sorry,” he said. “I mean, I sort of know you, I just…”
“It’s alright Teddie,” Yosuke said. “We’ll get our Akira back soon. Uh—I mean, no offense.”
“None taken,” Akira said quickly.
When encountering him half-way through the palace, Maruki initially claimed that he was
only going to come to Leblanc to hear their final decision in February, but Goro told Akira on
no uncertain terms would he let that happen.
“We cannot wait for February,” he said. “We’ve already been in this reality for a week.”

“Wow, you’re really scared of tentacle monster waking up,” Akira said, with a small smirk.
“You don’t understand,” Goro said. “Think Yaldabaoth, but worse.”
“It was pretty bad,” said Ken.
Akira frowned. “Okay,” he said. “I’ll try to find a way to convince Maruki to come to us so
we can give him a calling card, but it won’t be easy.”
“Just do what you can,” Goro said. “I trust you.”

The next day, while Goro waited for Akira to track down Maruki, someone knocked on the
door to the apartment. Minato and Ryoji were out, so Goro opened the door.
Shinjiro stood in front of him, looking healthier than Goro ever saw him. He raised his
eyebrows at Goro, but Goro couldn’t bring himself to react at all.
“Damn, you got tall,” he said.
“Why are you here?” Goro asked, choking on the urge to sob. He clung onto the brass
doorknob, and it rattled beneath his fist. “You know how hard this is, why are you making it
harder?”
“I’m sorry,” Shinjiro said. “But I never got to say goodbye last time, and I heard my letter
met its demise, so I thought I’d come to tie up loose ends.”
“I’m sorry,” Goro said. He couldn’t stop the first tears from coming. “I tried, I swear I tried
—”
“Hey,” Shinjiro said gently. “You saved that girl. You did the right thing.”
“But the letter—”
“Was destroyed by a guy hellbent on making your life miserable,” Shinjiro said. “Aki filled
me in. How the hell is that your fault?”
Goro’s body shook as more tears escaped. At least Goro managed to stop his breath from
hitching embarrassingly.
Shinjiro rested a hand on Goro’s shoulder.
“So, look,” Shinjiro said. “I’m proud of you, got that? You went through hell and came out of
it a better person. And you’ve sure as hell come a long way from that kid who cornered me
with a knife.”
Goro covered his eyes with his hand. “Fuck you,” he whispered, right before Shinjiro pulled
him into a hug. Goro could barely hear himself speak with his face buried into Shinjiro’s
jacket, which smelled like pepper and curry powder. “Thank you.”

“And listen,” Shinjiro said. “I know you’ve been avoiding Takeharu’s calls.”
“I have,” Goro admitted softly.
“Answer him.” Shinjiro hugged him tighter. “You know he wants that final match.”
“Okay,” Goro whispered.
“Also,” Shinjiro said. “Puberty did a number on your voice.”
Goro laughed so hard he snorted.

So, the following day, Goro met Takeharu at Penguin Sniper.
“You’ve grown,” Takeharu said upon seeing him.
“People keep saying that,” Goro muttered. But in this case, he had to agree. It was downright
bizarre being the same height as the man he only ever looked up at.
“Then it must be true.”
And they had their final match. A truly odd burst of nostalgia overcame Goro. Penguin
Sniper would always remind him of spying on Akira, but playing with Takeharu was like
going back in time, when Goro was eleven and always afraid.
“You’ve improved,” Takeharu said as Goro knocked another ball in the pocket.
“Maybe I’ve just gotten taller,” Goro said dryly. “It’s not easy to play when you’re barely
four feet tall.”
Takeharu chuckled. “I wasn’t just talking about your game.”
Goro’s chest squeezed. He didn’t look up until he won the game.
“Akechi-kun,” Takeharu said, looking Goro in the eye. “I’m glad that you’re happy.”
Goro managed a small smile, even as a lump settled in his throat. “And I’m glad… that we
had our rematch. Thank you. For everything.”
Takeharu smiled.

Maruki entered Leblanc with a calm smile, as though he thought he was incapable of losing.
Didn’t he know that Akechi had already beaten him once before?
“Akechi-kun,” he said as he sat down across from them. “I should have known you would be
here.”

“Maruki,” Goro spat.
“You said you made a decision?” Maruki asked Akira. “I must say, I was reluctant to come in
here so much earlier than planned. I hope your decision is favorable.”
Akira didn’t say anything in favor of throwing the calling card at Maruki. Maruki caught it
with a dumbfounded expression.
“I just can’t understand,” Maruki said, half speaking to Akira and half speaking to Akechi.
“I’ve given you what you wanted. So many people you lost are alive and well. I’ve eradicated
all evil in the world while letting people remember certain events that made them stronger. I
even brought back—”
“Yeah, about that,” Akira said, not letting him finish. “Why the hell would you kill the kid
who had the faith to get to know you for the sake of someone who has already kicked your
ass?”
“He wanted to be you,” Maruki said. “He knew he would never live up to the person Akechi
remembered. You mean to tell me you’re not happy, Akechi-kun?”
“He didn’t want to lose who he was entirely,” Goro said. “And I certainly didn’t want to lose
him. Akira has his own life to go back to.”
“But you could be so much happier here,” Maruki pleaded. “All of your friends are happy,
Akechi-kun’s alive, and you both have your memories—”
Akira slammed his hand against the table. “The answer was no once,” Akira said. “It’s no
again. Don’t even pretend to be surprised.”
“Very well,” Maruki said sadly, standing up. “If that’s how it has to be, I suppose I’ll see you
tomorrow.”
“Good,” Goro snarled.
“But know this,” Maruki said. His expression hardened. “All those people whose lives I’ve
made better? Their misery is on your hands.”
He slammed the door shut behind him.

“I guess this is it,” Akira said in the saferoom before facing off against Maruki.
“I guess it is,” Goro said. “I wish… I wish we could have had more time together… before.
Maybe… maybe things could have… we could have…”
Could have what? Grown between them? Let their rivalry shift into something more
intimate? More real?
“I do too.” Akira smiled bitterly. “But I’m glad you’re happy.”

“Me too,” Goro said. A knife twisted inside his chest. “I hope you live a good life.”
“You too,” Akira said. “Try not to get into too much trouble.”
“No promises.” Goro took a deep breath. “I know we may not have known each other for
long, in the grand scheme of things, but I hope you know just how much you changed my
life.”
He held out his hand. Akira grinned even as he cried. He seized it with all his strength.
“And you changed mine.”
Goodbye, Kurusu Akira.

A few weeks later, Akira entered his welcome-back-from-jail party with a tragic expression
on his face. “I can’t believe I missed human Morgana.”
Goro didn’t hesitate before hugging him. He pulled away only a few seconds later.
“What was that for?” Akira asked, confused.
“What were you thinking?” Goro asked, his voice shaking. He lightly punched Akira in the
shoulder. “Just because I miss the other Akira doesn’t mean I want to get rid of you.”
“O-oh,” Akira said, massaging his shoulder. “Well, I mean, obviously I knew that logically.
It’s just… hard sometimes. To know there’s a cooler version of you out there.”
“Neither of you are any cooler than the other,” Goro said. “Don’t you ever pull a stunt like
that again.”
“With any luck, we won’t have to,” Akira said. “You won, right?”
Goro thought back to the sea of grieving teammates after Maruki’s palace collapsed. The
horror in realizing Akira was going to wake up from defeating Maruki in jail, and the other
Akira hadn’t told him.
“If you can call it that.”

Goro, Morgana, Monster Cat, and Akira went out for ice cream the following day. They sat
on a bench in Inokashira park and watched children playing in the snow with their parents.
Maybe ice cream wasn’t the best choice for a winter snack, but Akira said he was craving it,
and Goro wasn’t going to refuse him.
“I’m sorry,” Akira said softly. “For putting you through that. I shouldn’t have tried to make
Maruki see reason.”

“What’s done is done,” Goro said. “And besides. That’s who you are. You want to see the
best in people.”
“And it always comes back to bite me in the ass,” Akira said. “I can’t imagine what it was
like. I just have a two-week hole in my memory.”
“And then you woke up in prison,” Goro said. “It was hard for you too.”
“Hey, I’m glad to have missed two weeks of prison.” Akira shuddered. “In a way, Maruki did
us a favor there.”
“Please don’t give him any credit.”
They fell into a comfortable silence as they ate their ice cream. Morgana lectured Monster
Cat on why ice cream was poisonous for cats. Monster Cat wore a vaguely unimpressed
expression.
“What now?” Akira asked as he bit into his ice cream cone with a satisfying crunch. “I mean,
now that Mementos is gone for real this time?”
Goro honestly kept expecting Nyarlathotep to appear out of nowhere, to pick up where he left
off with taunts and threats of murder.
But Goro hadn’t time traveled. Nobody wearing a face from Goro’s nightmares had come to
haunt him. Maybe they did defeat Maruki early enough. Maybe Nyarlathotep didn't have time
to come back.
But it didn't matter. If Nyarlathotep wanted to come, let him come. They could defeat him
again. Goro would like to focus on the present. The beautiful, unpredictable present.
“You know what?” Goro laughed at the sheer absurdity of it all. “I actually don’t know.”
Akira smiled. “I guess we’ll figure it out together.”

The End
